The towering Great Hero Peak is forged entirely of gold; A single shout deafens for three days.
From this point on, his fangs and claws are revealed; He turns back the "Wild Fox" Chan, Entrusting the phrase that descends from the hall.

Preface to the Original Baizhang Qinggui,
composed by Yang Yi, Hanlin Academician and Marquis of Kaiguo.
The Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang observed that since the Chan school originated at Shaoshi and reached Caoxi, its practitioners had mostly resided in Vinaya monasteries;

although separate quarters were established for them, their methods of preaching the Dharma and maintaining the community did not accord with the proper regulations. Consequently, he was constantly preoccupied with this concern and said:

"If one wishes for the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to be widely disseminated as the source of transformation, so that it may not perish in future generations, how could this [current practice] suffice?"
"Are you following the various Āgama teachings? Or is it that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) are Mahāyāna precepts;
why do you not rely upon them? The Master replied, "That which I follow is neither restricted to the Great nor the Small Vehicle, nor is it distinct from the Great and Small Vehicles.
I shall synthesize the broad and the concise to establish a middle way, fashioning a system of regulations that prioritizes what is appropriate. Thereupon, he initiated...

It is intended that a separate meditation hall be established. Anyone who possesses the eye of the Way and has attained venerable virtue is designated as an *Elders* (*zhǎnglǎo*), which corresponds to what is called an *Ācārya* among those of high attainment and seniority in the Western Regions.

Such a person shall serve as the master of instruction and reside in the *fangzhang* (the abbot’s quarters), which is like the chamber of Vimalakīrti and not a private sleeping chamber. No other halls are to be built; first, [the meditation hall] is planted.
The Dharma Hall signifies that the Buddhas and Patriarchs personally transmitted their entrustment, and that the contemporary master is held in the highest honor.

As for the assembly of students gathered there, regardless of their number or status—whether many or few, high or low—they all enter the Sangha Hall, where they are arranged according to the sequence of their years of seniority (*kṣayamāsa*). Long benches are provided, along with clothing racks and shelves.
Regarding the requisites for lodging: when reclining, one must always lean against the edge of the bed and sleep on the right side in the auspicious posture (*śirṣa-śāyin*).

This is done merely to rest briefly after long periods of seated meditation, so as to maintain the four dignified postures (*īryāpatha*). Except for entering the room to seek instruction, it is left to the diligence or lack thereof of the practitioner whether they move up or down;
they are not restricted by constant rules. As for the assembly of the entire monastery, they gather in the morning and evening for the formal assembly. Long...
When the Master ascends the hall and takes his seat, the administrative officers and the assembly stand in formation like geese, listening intently.

As the host and guests exchange words and exalt the essentials of the school, it demonstrates abiding in accordance with the Dharma. Providing meals and gruel as appropriate, ensuring they are served equally at both times, emphasizes the commitment to frugality and symbolizes the simultaneous practice of the Dharma and food.
By implementing the system of communal labor (*pǔqǐng*), those above and below exert equal effort. Thus, the ten administrative offices (*shíwù liáo*) are established.
In the *Śayanāsana-vastu*, it is stated that one should appoint a leader for each group to manage the affairs of the many residents, ensuring that each person fulfills their respective duties.

Should there be those who assume false names or conceal their true identities to mingle among the pure assembly, causing disturbances and commotion, the *karmadāna* (Vina) must immediately investigate and report them.
To remove one from their assigned quarters and expel them from the monastery is intended to ensure the peace and purity of the assembly.

Alternatively, if the individual has committed an offense, the community is assembled for public deliberation and the imposition of reprimand; they are then struck with a staff and sent out through a side gate, which serves as a demonstration of their disgrace.
Examining this rule in detail, the regulation provides four benefits: first, it prevents the defilement of the pure assembly and engenders reverence.
First, out of faith. Second, not violating the monastic form, because one follows the Buddha’s regulations. Third, not disturbing the government offices, because one reduces litigation and disputes.

Fourth, not leaking [internal matters] to the outside, because one protects the fundamental principles of the school. When the great assembly dwells together, who can distinguish between the holy and the ordinary?

Moreover, when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, there were still groups such as the six monks; how much more so now in this age of semblance—how could they be entirely absent? It is simply that upon seeing a single monk...
There are transgressions, which then lead to universal criticism and derision; yet they fail to realize that by slighting the assembly and destroying the Dharma, the damage is exceedingly great.

Now, if the Chan school is not to suffer even slight interference, it should follow the regulations of the Baizhang monastic system, distinguishing matters according to their requirements and establishing laws to prevent misconduct.
This is not for the sake of the virtuous alone, but rather because it is better to have rules than to have violations, than to have violations without rules.
The teaching: Oh, how great is the benefit of the Great Wisdom Chan Master in protecting the Dharma! From this venerable elder began the independent practice of the Chan school.

He has extensively shown the essential points of the Pure Rules (Qinggui) to later students, so that they do not forget their origins. His various regulations have been collected with exhaustive detail.

Having received the Imperial decree to edit and determine the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp), I have completed the work and presented it as an illustration; I therefore compose this preface.

Preface to the *Qinggui Zhengyi Ji* (Record of the Verification of the Meaning of the Pure Rules): In governing the people, the state relies upon statutes and precedents; in modeling the monastics, the Buddhas and Patriarchs rely upon the precepts and the pure rules (*qinggui*).

Buddhist law is analogous to secular law, yet it is unique in that it consists solely of the Buddha’s own teachings and nothing else. The pure rules correspond to worldly precedents, being derived from the ancestral traditions and adopted accordingly.
This is appropriate. However, the *Qinggui* (Pure Rules) originated with the monk Fayun of the Liang dynasty, who resided at Guangzhai Temple and compiled them by imperial decree.

The reason the Liang period is omitted while the Tang period is emphasized here is that during the Liang, Chan and the teachings were not yet flourishing; it was only upon reaching the Tang that the Dharma became complete and the monastic community thrived.

Baizhang recompiled [the rules], and thus his name is specifically highlighted. The entire work consists of nine chapters; the first, "Praying for Auspiciousness" (*Zhuxi*), describes celebrating and expressing joy.

The meaning of "Sincerity" (Cheng) follows next with "Requiting Kindness," both expressing the heart that enriches the people and benefits the state. Next is "Requiting the Origin," knowing the source from which one drinks.

Next is "Honoring the Ancestors," receiving their grace and commemorating those far departed. Next is "Abiding in Office," clarifying the gravity of issuing commands and regulating conduct. Finally are the "Two Orders" (the administrative and monastic staff).
It enumerates the appropriate duties for each office; next, it details the communal observance of the six harmonies regarding what is to be practiced and what is to be avoided;

next, it addresses seniority according to ordination age, following the Buddha’s regulations for the timely binding and unbinding of the *kaṣāya*; finally, it concerns the ritual implements of the Dharma Hall, which serve as the commands for humans and devas.

Furthermore, it appends the pure rules for the *shuilu* (water-land) rites and incorporates them into the liturgical manuals so that they may circulate widely. How great! The teacher and model for all under heaven is found only here.
Bai Zhang Dazhi was a peerless individual alone. The Record of the Pavilion at the Original Mountain states: "The Way of the Buddha was clarified by Bodhidharma;

the affairs of the Buddha were perfected by Bai Zhang. Although the eras differ and the matters vary, and the principles of tension and relaxation are not uniform, amidst the adjustments of literary refinement and substance, one cannot help but adapt and transform in order to exhaust all benefit. As for the grand framework and major outlines, they have not yet..."
It is a pity that there are those who do not adopt these regulations here. As they have been transmitted for a long time, the authentic and the spurious have become intermingled;

furthermore, as the Buddha-dharma has declined in autumn and the precepts have fallen into disuse, one must lament that these pure regulations will soon be cast aside. To remedy the evils of the times, [these rules must be restored].
"There is nothing more urgent than this" (Yirun). Thereupon, he consulted various editions; this one alone was the most excellent.
Upon examining its outline, it was found to agree with the Tibetan edition and to correspond with the *Zongmen tongyao mulu* (General Catalogue of the Essential Points of the Various Schools).

Its phrasing is concise yet clear, its meaning subtle yet manifest, and its principles and facts are perfectly integrated. Being both pure and complete, it was inquired whether it would benefit those of sharp or dull faculties regardless of time or place.

Although this is so, fearing that beginners may not yet have a thorough understanding, I have again cited the established words of the ancient masters to explain and verify them, so that the essential meaning of the text may become even more manifest.
This work is entitled *The Record of Verified Meanings of the Baizhang Conglin Qinggui* (Baizhang Conglin Qinggui Zhengyi Ji).
The origins of its composition are detailed in the "General Preface" and the "Original Meaning. Once completed, it was entrusted to the printing blocks for circulation by various benevolent persons.
I respectfully preface these few lines at the beginning of the scroll to inform the worthy men of our time.
Written on the day of the *pravāraṇā* following the summer retreat in the third year of the Daoguang era, the cyclical year being *Guiwei*,
by the Bhikṣu Yirun Yuanhong, at the Chamber of the Elder Monks in Huilong Zhenji Temple on Mount Tiao.

The *Baizhang Qinggui* is fully equipped with its regulations and statutes; those who can put them into practice are occasionally found, yet those who master their underlying meaning are exceedingly rare.

Some might say that it merely provides formal ritual procedures and lacks profound discourse on the study of principles (*li*). But do they realize that the various categories for protecting the precepts are themselves the inconceivable nature of the Dharma-principle (*liqiu*)?
Others might say that the text is so rich and the matters so numerous that it is difficult to memorize. But do they realize the significance of the nine gates?

Within this [work], all dharmas are fully contained. Yet, fearing that it might still be too concise, how could I dare to prune away its redundancies? The general outline of this book consists solely of the two types of observance: *zhichi* (observance through restraint) and *zuochi* (observance through action).

Observance through restraint is like the military armory’s arsenal, where soldiers must be fully prepared; observance through action is like the rites and music of the Confucian Temple, where nothing may be omitted.
However, the language is simple while the meaning is profound; it is not something that can be explained to those who are superficial or frivolous. Written at Zhitang, Renhe.
I, Shen, the Retired Scholar, have been shown the *Zhengyi ji* (Record of Verified Meanings) composed by the Bhikṣu Zhenji and the Dharma Master Yuanhong.

Observing its extensive study of the Buddhist scriptures and its compilation into a single work, with the *Shuilu yi gui* (Rite for the Water and Land) appended at the end, I see that regarding all the hidden and essential points, no key ritual procedures (*ke-yi*) were left unexcavated.
The profound implications have been elucidated so that readers may understand them clearly upon opening the volume. Truly, this is a [work of] the Buddha...
This is the grand treatise for the salvation of the world by the Patriarchs; it is the precious raft for the universal deliverance of sentient beings.
Written in the winter of the Guiwei year (1843) by Changbai Songling, Extraordinary Third-Class Commissioner, Acting General of the Zhejiang Vice-Commander, by Imperial Decree.
My friend, the retired scholar Shen Zhitang, requested that I compose a preface for *The Proof of the Meaning of the Pure Rules* (*Qinggui Zhengyi*) authored by Master Yuanhong.
Postscript. I was requested by him to write this preface. Upon reading it, I see that he has deeply realized the principle of "clarifying the mind and seeing one's nature.
It is no wonder that his fame is heard throughout the land and that he has long been esteemed by his contemporaries. This book contains the bequeathed regulations of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

it analyzes and elucidates the matters to be practiced within the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), being most refined and comprehensive. By following its instructions for practice, one can achieve a discipline that is truly majestic, as at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

This single assembly has not dispersed to this day; are they not all distant descendants of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? Nevertheless, the records on the meaning of the Pure Rules (*qinggui*) are but their minor remnants.
It is simply because their minds are intent upon universal benefit that they understand the conventional expressions of the teachings.

As for the profound contemplation of the Three Studies and the subtle truths of the Six Perfections, their principles cannot be fathomed through superficial insight. It is only for the student to integrate principle and practice.
Since both the title and the substance are clearly revealed, Master Yuan’s earnest intention in composing this work may be considered fully realized.
This preface was written by Chen Gui-sheng of Qiantang, former Governor of Jiangsu.
Preface:

How magnificent! How detailed and beautiful are the *Baizhang Qinggui* (The Pure Rules of Baizhang)! They encompass loyalty to the sovereign, filial piety toward parents, service to one’s teacher, reverence for one’s ancestors, the requital of bestowed kindness, and the performance of ritual propriety.
Encompassing Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, its statutes and regulations are fully perfected. Its articles and precepts...
How clear! To sigh that it is truly a sight to be admired. In recent times, the three studies have declined and the monastic communities have fallen into disorder;

thus, ancient regulations have gradually been submerged and former models are half-abandoned. Fortunately, Buddhism still endures and the patriarchal texts remain intact; the source of the *bhikṣu* community is vast.
There was one named Yi-run, my own teacher, who, whenever he encountered the scriptures and records of the past and present, saw each school guarding its own tenet. Upon meeting...

In matters of emphasis and suppression, one cannot avoid mutual contradiction, as seen in works such as the *Fayuan suijin*. While these are not biased or stagnant, they nonetheless suffer from a lack of coherence.
If one wishes for harmony without confusion and distinction without divergence, it seems there remains something yet to be achieved. It was at this point that my Master [acted].

These have been compiled into a complete whole, totaling more than one hundred volumes. They are titled the *Zimeng Mingmai Ji* (Record of the Vital Pulse of the Monkhood), with each section appended with explanatory commentaries and divided into twelve collections.
The first collection narrates the Three Jewels and their origins; the subsequent ten collections concern the Nanshan school.
*Chánmó*, Tiantai, Xuánshǒu, Cí'ēn, Fǎxìng, Chándìng, Mìmù, Fānyì, and Jìngtǔ. Regarding the *Bǎizhàng qīngguī* and other texts, they were gathered at the Hài Hall.
Since the materials collected were so numerous, their publication was pending; however, the *Qīngguī* and the *Shuilù* were first entrusted to the engravers.

Once the transcription was complete, I bathed and recited them, feeling as though I had entered the Dharma assembly. Thus, through the manifestation of the gravity of the *Qīngguī*, I attained [this realization].
The new manifestation of realized meaning is such that the Way exists before one’s eyes; it is grasped by the heart and understood by the spirit.
Its forging of the ancient and the modern, its elucidation of the subtle essence, cannot be altered by a single word. I only wish that everyone would devote themselves to this:

then that which flows clear cannot be muddied by turbidity, and that which is made round by the compass will naturally be square by the carpenter’s square. Adhere to these old statutes and spread them abroad.
This collection of lectures is truly fit to serve as a bridge for later students of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
On the Buddha’s birthday in the fourth month of the second year of the Daoguang era,

by imperial decree, [the author], formerly a Six-Rank Military Officer of Shaanxi who had received the Bodhisattva Upāsaka precepts, was summoned to serve as a filial, incorrupt, and upright official.
The disciple of Renhe, Shen Qiqian of Zhitang, Liao-sheng, respectfully inscribes this preface with a prostration. To consider the matter:
the compass is used to form circles, and the compass is kept clear so that they do not become confused. Thus, the monastic community possesses the *Chonggui* (Pure Rules). One...
This is a written record. The *Chingui* (Pure Rules) was composed by Fayun during the Liang dynasty at the imperial command;
it was further elaborated by Master Baizhang of the Tang dynasty. Since that time, more than a thousand years have passed, and as the eras have become distant, oral traditions have varied.
Only upon obtaining the verified meanings from Great Master Hongsou are the records fully complete. I previously held the entire collection and observed [the following] within its nine chapters.
The way you, my lord, are looked up to and relied upon by all, as well as the dual sustenance you provide to both the waters and the land, serves as a model for the monastic community;
its benefit is truly unsurpassed. Since the year of Gengshen, our city of Hangzhou has twice suffered the ravages of war, and the entirety of the Buddhist scriptures has been lost.

Out of compassion for those who have newly entered the path and find nothing upon which to rely for practice, and with the intent that those who seek to realize the meaning of the Dharma may do so, I have personally edited this work and commissioned its re-carving. Thus, I invite Hui... [to join me].

Master Huiji of Yueh Monastery jointly solicited funds for the carving [of the blocks]. Consequently, prior to the commencement of the engraving, he personally supervised the preparation and publication within the Three Altars (Santan) model of the Tiantai school.
After more than a year, the work was completed and placed in the scripture repository to facilitate its wide circulation.

He vowed that those who engage with this work would not only attain the profound meaning of the pure and serene state, but that their every movement would accord with the established standards, thereby honoring the Patriarch.

The institutional systems of the monastic forests are all rooted herein. Indeed, while the realization of the mind and the seeing of nature are fundamentally not bound by verbal explanations, one must follow established regulations to rectify both conduct and cessation.
It is here that one first unravels the patriarchal texts and subsequently proclaims the Buddha-dharma;

from this source, one accords with the fountainhead of the mind throughout successive generations, for there is nothing that does not originate here. May future students understand that the Dharma-gate has its beginning in this.
This is the general outline.
Written by the junior disciple Cheongdo Pujō of Haechōsa Temple in the middle autumn month of the year of Sin-mi (the tenth year of the Tongzhi era). Preface.
Since the Xianfeng era, I have lived in seclusion by the sea, remaining within my dwelling for ten years without venturing out.

In the early summer of the Xinwei year, the Master Puzhao, the host of Haichao in Hangzhou, presented me with a newly engraved edition of the *Chanyuan Qinggui Zhengyi* (Verification of the Meaning of the Rules of Purity for Chan Monasteries) and requested that I write a few words at the end of the volume. I firmly declined, but being unable to refuse, I moistened my brush and wrote: "I humbly..."
I have heard that the Great Sage manifests himself without fixed form; his every movement and stillness serves as a model for others. Yet those of inferior intelligence possess limited knowledge;
even the slightest actions may result in fault or transgression. This is especially true in this Dharma age of the Semblance Period (*nimitta-kāla*), when the time since the Sage’s passing is remote.

We are like destitute children who have wandered lost to foreign lands, frantic and unable to distinguish their way; we are like laborers who have strayed into perilous paths, unable to discern between black and white.
My work, *The Code of Pure Regulations*, was originally composed in four fascicles by Chan Master Dazhi Huaihai of Baizhang Mountain in Hongdu during the mid-Tang dynasty.
At that time, the monastic communities immediately accepted it as their authoritative standard, a tradition that has continued until the present day for over a thousand years.
Reaching into the early Daoguang era of our own dynasty, at Hui-long Temple in Pingyao, Hangzhou...
The Great Master Yuanhong of Zhensiji Temple was one who attained mastery in both the religious and secular teachings, and who integrated Confucianism and Buddhism into a single whole.

He reflected that while the ancients valued substance, people today value literary refinement; yet, without substance, one cannot preserve the primal simplicity, and without literary refinement, one cannot fully express one’s meaning.

Thereupon, he compiled from the recorded sayings of the virtuous masters of successive generations all those passages that would be beneficial for the restoration of ancient foundations and the initiation of new undertakings.

Regarding those who engage in agriculture, commerce, the observance of precepts, Chan meditation, and the exposition of the teachings—each of these various traditions is analyzed with meticulous detail according to specific circumstances, individuals, times, and places, and is added herein one by one so that those with aspirations for this Way may adopt them as appropriate.
This is intended to spare them from the reproach of being panicked and indecisive at the last moment, like a rat caught between two ends. Thus, sixteen sections have been compiled in total.
The scrolls were entrusted to the carving blocks and stored at the Sūtra Repository of West Lake for circulation.
During the period of the Gengxin year of the Xianfeng era, they suffered successive destruction from warfare, and all the printing blocks were completely obliterated.

Master Pu urgently sought out the old editions; first he emptied his alms-bag, and subsequently he solicited contributions from the virtuous. He had them re-carved into volumes and returned them to storage.

As for the cost of this scripture-house, its exact expenses need not be discussed here. I merely admire his tireless and earnest devotion—a single-minded resolve to benefit all things and all people—and shall therefore cause this record to endure for all eternity. This is the postscript.

Nevertheless, although we disciples of the Buddha need not regard literary elegance as our primary skill nor devote our minds to its study, when employing language to describe facts, one cannot help but expect it to be appropriate and fitting.
For this reason, I have recorded it here according to the original text, so that...
Those who employ it will find its realization already complete; they need no longer manipulate their conscious intellect, yet it is not without some small benefit.

Regarding the *Chingui* (Rules of Purity), apart from the Tripitaka editions, printed copies are rare in the world; consequently, those who transcribe them may inadvertently commit errors through lack of care.

Some have arbitrarily increased or decreased [the text], leading to successive errors through transmission that gradually lost its original authenticity. This concerns the legacy rules of our patriarchs and the structural system of the monastic community;
it is by no means a trivial matter. Having obtained this edition, I find it to be more accurate when compared with the Tripitaka version, yet its general purport does not contradict the original.
Considering that such an excellent text exists, I felt it was urgent to circulate it.

Consequently, disregarding my own meager and humble abilities, I have appended a brief commentary below each section to provide proof and clarification, so that readers may understand the text clearly upon opening the volume and no longer harbor doubts.
I further requested several venerable elders to revise and correct it repeatedly before I ventured to publish it.
If [it should be] granted...

May those who are learned and wise in all quarters deeply embody the intent of the Patriarchs and skillfully accord with the needs of the times; should they then rectify this teaching, it would be most fortunate indeed.
*The Original Meaning of the Baizhang Conglin Qinggui*.
Composed by the Bhikṣu Yirun of Zhenji Monastery in Ancient Hangzhou;
reviewed by Miaoyong, the Abbot of Jiezhu Monastery in Yuecheng, as a commentary on the *Chanyuan Qinggui*.
First, the five fundamental meanings are clarified: 1. The person is used as a metaphor for the Dharma to form the name. 2. [The second point...]
1. The provisional and the ultimate rely upon one another as the essence (*tattva*). 2. Upholding the Vinaya and providing internal protection as the school’s tenet (*siddhānta*).

3. Carrying out affairs according to the Dharma as the function (*vṛtti*). 4. Using both "milk" and "curd" as the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the first [point], the title is derived from the person who is likened to the Dharma:

(First, explaining the person. The two characters "Bai-zhang" refer to a person. "Bai-zhang" is the name of the mountain; it was colloquially called Mount Daxiong. It is located on the Longxing Road in Hongzhou, three hundred *li* from the prefectural seat. Today it belongs to Fengxin County in Nanchang Prefecture. Master Huaihai was from Fuzhou. Long...

He was the son of the Wang family. In his [Mao] year, he shaved his head under the Venerable Huizhao of West Mountain; he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Fachao of Mount Heng; and he attained the Dharma from Chan Master Mazu Da ji of Jiangxi. He was thus a second-generation successor in the orthodox lineage descending from Nanyue.

He resided at the Chanzisi of Great Wisdom and Longevity on this mountain, where he vigorously propagated the Chan school while concurrently upholding the Vinaya regulations. He once observed that the monastic rules compiled by Fayun of Guangzhai Temple during the Liang dynasty, which had been presented to the Emperor by imperial decree, were not entirely harmonious with current practice.

He then re-examined the Vinaya-piṭaka at length, synthesizing its broad principles with concise applications to establish regulations and models that were suited to the needs of the times. Furthermore, reflecting on the principle of setting an example through one's own person, he personally engaged in manual labor every day to serve as a model for the community. When some urged him to desist from such work, he replied:

The Master said, "I have no virtue to weary others. The assembly obstructed him, so he ceased eating. Thus, the saying "if one day you do not work, one day you shall not eat" spread throughout the world. He passed away on the seventeenth day of the first month in the ninth year of the Yuanhe era.

He lived to the age of ninety-five. In the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era, he was buried on this mountain. In the first year of the Changqing era, an imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Dazhi, and his stupa was named Dabao Shenglun. He circulated the *Chanyuan Qinggui* (Pure Rules of the Chan Monastery). In the first year of the Daguan era of the Song dynasty...

The posthumous title "Juezhao" (Awakening Illumination) was conferred, and his stupa was named "Huiju" (Gathering of Wisdom). He re-edited the *Chiqi* (Rules of Purity). In the third year of the Yuantong era of the Yuan dynasty, the posthumous title "Hongzong Miaoxing Chanshi" (Chan Master of Vast Lineage and Wondrous Conduct) was bestowed. By imperial decree, the monk Dexun was ordered to revise the *Chiqi* for promulgation throughout the monastic communities (*conglin*).

In the past, the itinerant ascetic Sima Tou-tuo once composed a commemorative record for Baizhang Mountain, which contained the phrase: "A Dharma King dwells here; he is a teacher and model for all under heaven. This truly refers to our Master. According to maps, there are several places named Baizhang Mountain; this is the Baizhang of Hongzhou.

Furthermore, since the Tang dynasty, there have been several individuals with the personal name Baizhang who were prominent; this refers to the Venerable Ancestor Huaihai being called Baizhang. This concludes the brief explanation of the person. (△ Next, the explanation of the metaphor. Regarding "monastic communities" [conglin], there are two [parts]).

"Zi" (Character) is a metaphor. "Conglin" (Forest) carries the meaning of a dense gathering of grasses and trees; it serves as a metaphor for a monastic compound (*saṃghārāma*), a place where the community of monks resides and where practitioners settle their minds to cultivate the Way. It is capable of nurturing the sprouts of the Path and leading one toward the attainment of the fruits of sainthood, thereby bringing benefit and merit to all sentient beings.

Furthermore, this name and its meaning are fully evident in the Sūtras and Vinaya. A verse from the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokadhātuniraya-parivarta*) in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva’s tree of wondrous Dharma grows from an upright mind; with faith as its seed and compassion as its roots, wisdom constitutes its trunk."

Skillful means are the trunk; the five perfections are the dense foliage; meditative concentration is the leaf; supernormal powers are the flower; and omniscience is the fruit. Furthermore, in the "Parable of the Herbs" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, various plants and forests are used as metaphors for those who receive transformation according to their individual capacities.

Moreover, in the Vinaya, when four or more monks—even up to hundreds or thousands—dwell together in one place and perform rituals and affairs in harmony like water mixing with milk, they are all called a "forest" (*vana*). Regarding the term *bhikṣu* (or *biqiu*) applied to such monks, it is said that in the Western Regions this grass possesses five virtues: first, its nature is soft and supple, which metaphorically represents the virtue of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the Saṃgha;

by subduing body and mind, one does not become coarse or wild. Second, its trailing vines spread out horizontally, which metaphorically represents the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*) in the Saṃgha; in transmitting the Dharma and saving sentient beings, the lineage extends continuously without end. Third...

4. Its fragrance is heard afar. This is a metaphor for the virtue of the monastic precepts (*śīla*). Because the fragrance of the precepts is so aromatic, one is held in high esteem by the multitude. 5. It does not turn its back on the sunlight. This is a metaphor for the virtue of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).

One constantly turns toward the sun of the Buddha and the light of wisdom, thereby liberating oneself from all false views and evil karma. Thus, a *bhikṣu* is called a *bhi-kṣu*. Based on these two metaphors of the tree and the herb, it is evident that those who act as monks rely entirely upon cultivation as their foundation.

As it is said: "If those who dwell in the community possess virtue and integrity, then the monasteries will daily find peace; if they do not, then the monasteries will daily face peril. If the assembly of monks possesses these five virtues, then both their reputation and their reality will be attained. If they do not... [the text ends here].

Truly, all mourning rites have ended. Thus, how easy is it for a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) to dwell in, and how easy is it for a *bhikṣu* to fulfill his vows? This concludes the brief explanation of the analogy. Next, regarding the explanation of the Dharma: the two characters "Qinggui" (Pure Rules) refer to the Dharma. First, explaining them in terms of concrete practice:

it means to apply a model of crystal clarity and purity to daily life in order to protect the Buddha’s teachings. Furthermore, "Qinggui" refers to the regulations, systems, and categories of the Dharma. In the tenth fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karmavācanā*, the Buddha said:

"Suppose there is a matter concerning which I have neither previously permitted nor prohibited. If this matter conforms to what is impure and violates what is pure, then it is impure and should not be performed. If the matter conforms to what is pure and violates what is impure..."

This is precisely purity; it should be practiced accordingly. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "That which was established by the Buddha should not be discarded; that which was not established by the Buddha should not be newly established. All of these constitute the meaning of pure regulations (*qinggui*), and they represent the intent behind Baizhang’s compilation. Furthermore, the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* states:

"When requesting monks as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) to offer prayers, one should enter the monastic quarters (*saṃghārāma*) and inquire of the administrative official (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*). If one says, 'I now wish to invite monks to offer prayers,' the official shall reply, 'If you invite them in proper sequence, you will obtain the assembly of worthy and holy monks from the ten directions,' and so forth.

The commentary notes: "Monastic quarters" refers to the forest monastery (*sīmā*). "Administrative official" refers to the person in charge of affairs. "Inviting in proper sequence" refers to the pure regulations. Furthermore, in the tenth *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* of the *Dharmaguptaka-śīla-sūtra*:

[The messenger] says: "Venerable sir, for your sake I have sent this price for robes; please accept it. That bhikṣu should speak to that messenger thus: "I should not accept this price for robes. If I need a robe, I shall accept one that is timely and pure.

The messenger says to the bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, is there anyone who acts as an attendant? The bhikṣu who needs a robe should say: "There is. Whether they be a monastery servant or a lay follower (upāsaka), these are the attendants of the bhikṣus."

"Always act as the attendant for the bhikṣus," and so forth. The commentary states: "One dares not personally accept the price of robes; instead, one has an attendant receive it on one's behalf. One shall accept them only when the proper time arrives and they are pure, thereby maintaining the monastic regulations (*qinggui*). Furthermore, the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra* says: "There are those who, though they do not violate the *śīla*, do violate the rules of conduct.

The commentary states: "The Sanskrit term *śīla* is translated here as 'precepts' (*jie*). Rules of conduct (*guize*) are precisely the monastic regulations (*qinggui*). Thus, we know that the monastic regulations of the forest hermitages (*conglin*) already existed during the Buddha’s lifetime.

Even in our own land [China], from the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty onward, monks were gathered together in forest hermitages. Practicing according to the Vinaya constitutes the monastic regulations. By the era of Baizhang in the Tang dynasty, these Chinese monastic regulations had been in practice for over six hundred years. As the Dharma remained long, corruptions arose.

The Patriarch encountered this very situation and thus undertook a thorough reorganization to benefit future generations. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Dedication" chapter, states: "The Bodhisattva takes the gift of Dharma as foremost; it gives rise to all pure and wholesome dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) and encompasses the mind that inclines toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).

This is what the Great Patriarch meant. Next, regarding the explanation according to principle, Jizhu Miaoyong stated: "The Pure Rules (*qinggui*) are the wondrous, perfect, and eternal Way inherently possessed by our own minds.

Now, while the mind is fundamentally perfect and luminous, it appears differentiated into the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*)—both the environment and its inhabitants—due to the distinction between delusion and awakening. Nevertheless, the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is identical and complete; this is the 'rule' (*gui*) of our own mind. 'Complete' means that it encompasses the ten realms, both environment and inhabitants, without exception. 'Identical' refers to the resonance [of the mind with reality]."

The causes and effects of delusion and awakening are without differentiation. The "compass" (gui) is that which establishes the phenomena and principles of the myriad dharmas without partiality. That which is without partiality is the "Center" (zhong). That which is without remainder is the "Provisional" (jia). That which is without differentiation is the "Empty" (kong). Empty, Provisional, and Centered—these are the three contemplations of my own mind.

These three contemplations are the function of the compass. The Empty contemplates the True: it severs even the slightest speck of dust. The Provisional contemplates the Conventional: it encompasses all that exists. The Centered contemplates both yet does not abide in either.

In the True, one is the True and all is the True; there is no conventional and no centered that is not True. In the Conventional, one is the Conventional and all is the Conventional; there is no True and no centered that is not Conventional. In the Centered, one is the Centered and all is the Centered; there is no conventional and no True that is not Centered. True...

It is the mundane, it is the conventional, and it is the ultimate; these are the three truths (triratna) of my own mind. These three truths constitute the fundamental substance that is to be regulated. Because this original substance is difficult to restore, the Dharma is established to restrain it:

in Buddhism, this is called the Vinaya Piṭaka; in Confucianism, it is called the codes of law; and at Baizhang, it is called the *Ching-kui* (Pure Rules). Although there are differences between the worldly and the world-transcending, their purpose in ceasing evil and giving rise to good is identical in meaning despite differing in name.

What is called *Ching-kui* is precisely this Dharma. This brief explanation of the Dharma concludes here; for a detailed account, see the following "Chapter on the Assembly" and the "Explanation of the Precepts."

2. Regarding the fact that the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*) are mutually required as the essence [of the teaching]: (The *Tianchi Fajù* states: "The Way is rooted in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Yet ritual, music, laws, and regulations are the provisional means for gathering and transforming beings.

Without the provisional, the teaching would have no way to be established, and the Way would not be practiced. Therefore, Confucius composed the *Chunqiu* and recorded the *Liji*, fully providing the provisional means of laws and regulations. He wished to remain wordless and to unify all through a single thread, thereby manifesting the reality of the awakened limit.

This is precisely our Buddha’s great model (*mahā-vidhi*) for the three realms, which maintains the myriad transformations; all of these arise from the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of self-awakened noble wisdom. Thus, the provisional and the real of opening, closing, maintaining, and violating are mutually required to manifest the essence and function of faith, understanding, practice, and realization.")

This is consistent. At the single assembly on Vulture Peak, the multitude numbered over a million; they were so harmonious and free from discord that it was more than the blending of water and milk. This is what is meant by being "unruly yet not chaotic" and "trusting without words.

Upon beholding the golden countenance, they were moved to transformation; thus, there was no need for repeated exhortations or instructions. Yet, when it came to protecting the good and warding off evil through the establishment of the *vinaya* rules, every detail was meticulously set forth and analyzed without omission.

Furthermore, in his final testament at the *Nirvāṇa*, he said: "O Bhikṣus, after my passing, you must revere the *Prātimokṣa*; it is your teacher. Thus, while the King’s transformation of the great chiliocosm provides a model for future generations, it does not, in sum, transcend the non-duality of principle and phenomenon.

This is for the purpose of instruction; it is clear. Following the remnants of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the teaching first began to spread to the East. At that time, the Buddha-dharma was flourishing, and thus the formalities of ritual and ceremony were naturally not considered urgent. Since the arrival of Bodhidharma, the mind-essence has been transmitted directly.

While there have indeed been many who attained actual realization, among them were not a few who followed empty paths and fell into a void of mere intellectual abstraction. Consequently, they came to regard the deportment of movement and posture as something unnecessary, and the regulations of rank and system as something unworthy of study. They failed to realize that provisional means (*upāya*) ultimately lead back to the ultimate reality (*tattva*); yet how could reality ever be divorced from the provisional?

It was for this reason that the Great Wisdom [of the Patriarchs] produced the *Qinggui* (Rules of Purity) to assist and support the *Vinaya*, to provide order for the monastic assembly, and to ensure that the forest hermitages (*aranyas*) remained solemn and pure, where the "dragons and elephants" (great practitioners) could stride with power. Truly, the principle does not neglect the phenomenon; and the Buddha...
Within the section on phenomena (*vastu-mukha*), not a single dharma is abandoned; therefore, the essence consists of the mutual requirement of the provisional and the real.

Third, that which takes "supporting the Vinaya and providing internal protection" as its primary principle: the Vinaya-piṭaka of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles can be summarized in a single phrase as "maintaining both prohibitions and prescriptions. These monastic regulations (*qinggui*) are likewise so constituted.

The various hall codes, prohibitions against transgressions, and defenses against wrongdoing are subsumed under the category of "maintaining prohibitions" (*śīla-saṃvara*). The various rituals, such as Zen meditation and the recitation of the Buddha’s name, are subsumed under the category of "performing prescriptions" (*vidhi-anuṣṭhāna*). Possessing these two—prohibitions and prescriptions—they support the Vinaya; externally, they manifest through ritual decorum.

Virtue moves people to give rise to right faith; internally, they protect the True Dharma and constantly turn the Wheel of the Dharma. This occurs not by design, yet it happens spontaneously, benefiting both oneself and others. This is what is meant by "upholding the Vinaya as the internal protection" being the primary principle.

If one does not maintain the precepts and does not practice the pure regulations, one is a partisan of Māra, destroying the Buddha-dharma from within. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "The Buddha-dharma cannot be destroyed by non-Buddhists or celestial Māras;

it is like a worm within a lion’s body that eats the lion’s own flesh. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* asks: "How can a thief, wearing my robes, peddle the teachings of the Tathāgata for profit? They commit all manner of karmic deeds while claiming them to be the Buddha-dharma, yet they slander ordained bhikṣus who possess the precepts, calling them followers of the Hīnayāna path. Thus, they lead others into doubt and error.

He measured sentient beings and saw that they were falling into the Avīci Hell; for this reason, as the Buddha approached his parinirvāṇa, he upheld the Vinaya to discourse upon the eternal. The general meaning is that a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts is truly one who maintains the precepts only when he can rebuke and expel those who break them. This present *qinggui* (Pure Rules) [is based on that principle].
Master Yi also followed this principle; therefore, he took "upholding the Vinaya as internal protection" as his central tenet.

Fourth, "taking the performance of affairs according to the Dharma as its function" means that there are two kinds of affairs: first, fixed-time affairs, such as New Year’s Day, Qingming, the Buddha’s birthday, and the anniversaries of the patriarchs’ passing, which are performed at predetermined times;

second, non-fixed-time affairs, such as celebrating birthdays, offering prayers, entering or leaving a monastery, which are not fixed in their timing due to preceding and following activities. Although these affairs are numerous, they are fully encompassed by these two categories. In all cases, one clarifies the principle through the phenomenon. To clarify...

Principle is that by which transformation is bestowed; yet, when matters become obstructed or hindered, one must be skillful in adapting and changing so that the transformation may be universal. Lately, the monastic community has rarely understood this meaning. It is not that they have abandoned it and failed to practice it, but rather that the ritual texts are erroneous.

Furthermore, those who are rigid and pedantic often stubbornly cling to them without understanding, leading to obstructions that make implementation difficult. This constitutes a grave malady for the *qinggui* (monastic regulations), and it is no wonder that the Way of the Dharma is gradually declining. If one wishes to reverse these prevailing abuses, one must first elucidate and propagate this principle.

I, Run, though unworthy and humble, have taken this excellent text as my fundamental authority. I have appended corroborating meanings to elucidate its discourse and clarify its principles, so that everyone may behold the legacy of the Patriarchs in such exquisite detail.

If one can manage affairs according to the Dharma, then it will be seen that demons are transformed into Buddhas, the heterodox are turned into the orthodox, the unruly are eliminated, the great assembly is brought to peace, ritual propriety is unified, virtue and morality are nurtured, the monastic groves are revitalized, and sentient beings are transformed—leaving nothing undone.
Thus, it is truly believed that the life-force of the Sangha Jewel cannot endure for long without the precepts and pure regulations.

Five. Regarding the use of both milk and curd as analogies for the characteristics of the teachings (Master Tiantai Zhiyi used the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s analogy of the five flavors—from milk produced from a cow up to clarified butter—to judge the Tathāgata’s lifetime of teaching into five periods:

first, the *Avataṃsaka*, likened to milk; second, the *Āgama*, likened to curd; third, the *Vaipulya*, likened to fresh butter; fourth, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, likened to matured butter; and fifth, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa*, likened to clarified butter. Therefore, this monastic code (*qinggui*) also borrows the precedent of judging the scriptures to judge that milk and curd are used together.

As for the teachings of the five periods: the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka* were taught simultaneously; their coarseness and subtlety are intermingled and fused, such that every land and every atom is nothing other than the one true Dharma.

The realms (*dhātu*) refer to worldly discourse, the occupations for sustaining life, and so forth—all of which accord with the True Dharma (*saddharma*). Now, these Pure Rules (*qinggui*) follow the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* in their meaning; when practiced by those of superior faculties, principle and phenomena are unimpeded, and all things are perfectly interfused, comparable to the essence of milk.

As for the *Āgamas*, although they primarily expound the four truths of arising and ceasing, the regulations of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) therein already embody the principles of the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*)—the non-arising and non-acting—just as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) comes from cream, and cream comes from curd.

These current Pure Rules are modeled after the *Āgamas*; they likewise take the Lesser Vehicle as their paradigm to ensure that practitioners strictly observe the rules and measurements, establishing a foundation that shall not be destroyed. This is like a human body with its four limbs intact, where beautiful clothing can be displayed; it is like the application of white powder in the art of painting.

Originally there was no deficiency; the colors may be continued, and it is fit to be compared to the flavor of curd. Therefore, milk and curd are both employed as the characteristics of the teaching. In the past, Master Zongyuan said: "In the examples of the Chan school, although there are not two different sets of Vinaya, the internal style of the patch-robed monks is a distinct kind of regulation.

If one makes use of this while on the journey, one will naturally be pure and lofty beyond the ordinary. If, however, one encounters it with a wall-like mind, it truly diminishes the respect of others. For this reason, having traveled through monastic communities and studied under various masters, whatever has been beneficial to my见闻 (what I have seen and heard) is fully prepared to serve as a guide for the essential rules.

With this, I adorn the precious monastery and establish the banner of the Dharma. This is what is meant by 'within the gate of Buddha-works, nothing can be omitted. It is also like the Bodhisattva’s three clusters and the Śrāvaka’s seven [groups of precepts]."

This fascicle: How could it be that the establishment of the Dharma delights in complexity? Rather, the teaching is established according to the capacities of beings. May those of initial capacity and junior students hope to examine and deliberate upon this well; may those of superior virtue and lofty character deign to provide verification and insight.
Record of the Verified Meaning of the Baizhang Conglin Qinggui, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huaihǎi of Mount Baizhang in Hongzhou during the Tang Dynasty;
verified for meaning by the Bhikṣu Yirun of Zhenji Monastery in Ancient Hangzhou.
Preface to the First Chapter on Praying for Prosperity through Scriptural Recitation, reviewed by Miaoyong, Abbot of Jizhu Monastery in Yuecheng.
It is said: That which is most precious to humanity lies in the illumination of the Way; therefore, from antiquity, sagely rulers have revered our Western [Tradition].
The teaching of the Sage does not treat our followers according to worldly etiquette; this is to honor the Way.

We respectfully observe that the present dynasty has shown us the utmost favor, specifically exempting us from taxes and corvée labor so that we may dwell in peace and devote ourselves entirely to the Way.
This imperial grace is vast and profound, beyond words to describe. As those who have become monks, we must—
May I awaken to and clarify my Buddha-nature and reverently observe the precepts, so as not to fail the most profound intentions of this Great Dynasty.

Furthermore, may I offer prayers morning and evening for the nation’s prosperity, so that the Buddha’s compassion may bestow hidden grace and the Heavenly Mind may grant silent favor, enabling our Sovereign to guide the people through the transformation of non-action and lead the world to a realm of benevolence and longevity. Only then—

This may serve as a slight repayment for the myriad favors [received]. Regarding those matters that manifest in daily life, I have carefully and reverently recorded them to preserve their proper standards.
The Opening Ceremony for the Sacred Festival.
On the occasion of the Imperial Birthday, a *Vajra-Amitāyus* Dharma Assembly will be inaugurated for several days (the duration as appropriate).
Monks shall not be granted leave, as this demonstrates their reverence. Three days prior to the inauguration, the Guest Prefect shall prepare paper and go to the Secretary’s Office.

The Guest Prefect performs a single prostration with the forehead touching the ground (*chuli*) and says: "The Imperial Birthday Assembly will be inaugurated on such-and-such a day; we request that you compose the draft for the memorial."

(The Secretary is absent; the Recorder acts as substitute; both are absent; the existing draft is used [as seen below]). Once the Secretary has completed the drafting, he prepares the list and presents it to the Abbot for review.

Having done so, he personally delivers it to the Guest Hall and performs a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chuli*) in response to the prior salutation. The Guest Master uses yellow paper to write the notice, as well as the couplets and the transverse banner.

And the commentaries, etc. One day prior to the commencement of the ritual, the Guest Hall shall request the *karmadāna* (Venerable Leader) to consult together on the number of monks for the recitation and to assign them in successive rotation.

Once this has been finalized and presented to the Abbot for his inspection, he shall immediately invite the Abbot to lead the assembly in chanting sutras to pray for the longevity of the Emperor on the following morning at the hall.
The Hall Master shall be instructed to sweep and clean the hall in preparation for the inauguration of the *Vajra* [Rite].

At the Immeasurable Life Bodhimanda, the site was laid out with solemn adornments and various banners were suspended. An official notice was posted to the left of the mountain gate, and a placard was hung [as follows]:
On the [day] of the [month], in respectful celebration of the Imperial Birthday of Myriad Years, the assembly of the entire monastery shall proceed together to the Great Hall for the morning service.
There, they shall proclaim secret mantras and recite the name of the Medicine Buddha. We humbly pray...

May the Buddha-sun shine with pervasive clarity; may the Sage’s life-span be boundless. (Other matters follow; the ritual protocol is the same as above, with only the name of the specific matter being changed accordingly.
Regarding the recitation plaque: each day, there shall be no more than twenty-four monks and no fewer than ten, rotating in order according to the roster.
On the first day of the observance, various offerings are arrayed within the hall, including a memorial document written on yellow paper for the superior offering. On this day, the Abbot...

He shall preach the Dharma, whether ascending the hall (*shàngtáng*) or holding a small assembly (*xiǎocān*), acting as appropriate according to the circumstances (the ritual protocol is found below in the chapter on the Abbot). ○ (Appendix:

Proof-reading documents, temple name plaques, couplets, and the six classics and one repentance rite from the notification documents; these should be recorded in their respective quantities as appropriate).
I humbly submit that the auspicious destiny has opened wide; the Sage has appeared and all things behold him. His profound grace is universally diffused;
the Sovereign rejoices and ten thousand people depend upon him. His protective canopy is impartial—whom could discern the height and depth of Heaven and Earth?

(The Rector says: "On this auspicious day, the [month] of [year], at [province/prefecture/county] monastery, the Abbot, Dharma-transmitting Subject-Monk, respectfully assembles the monastic community to reverently proceed to the Treasure Hall, chanting the secret scriptures and extolling the sacred names.")

To accumulate these vast causes, we pray for the ten-thousand-year reign and eternal peace of His Majesty the Emperor. We respectfully request the great assembly to join in the recitation of the *Vajra*, *Amitāyus*, and *Ratnaketu-Paranirmita-Vaśavartin* Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and so forth.

Upon the conclusion of the recitation, the Abbot delivers a small discourse (*xiao can*). On the first and fifteenth days of the month, after the morning gruel, the assembly gathers in the refectory to chant the *Four-Part Vinaya Precepts*.

After the meal, they chant the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (the ritual details of which are found below in the section on the Uposatha). The Hall Master first prepares the altar, placing a single Buddha image in the center with incense and candles fully arranged. Both sides...

On the side table, prepare the Vinaya texts, the *yuqing* (fish-shaped gong), and other items. Await the opening of the minor period of silence (*xiaojing*). When the bell is struck three times, the attendant transmits the incense burner, and the assembly gathers.

After unfolding their ritual implements and performing prostrations, the Abbot offers incense. The Rector (*weina*) recites the incense hymn (*xiangzan*). Once the Abbot has finished his prostrations, he ascends the seat;
the two orders of officials also follow in succession, adjusting their robes and taking their seats. The Rector strikes the *qing* (gong) to open the scripture, and they proceed with the recitation.

At the conclusion of the dedication of merit, the assembly descends from their seats. The community unfolds their sitting cloths and performs three prostrations, after which each returns to their own place. If it is during the winter months and one is in the meditation hall (*chàn-táng*), the recitation may be omitted.

The attendant in the quarters (*shì-liáo*) collects the recitation tablets for the precepts. On the eighth day of the month, the three recitations of the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* follow the same procedure.

Furthermore, according to ancient regulations, on the first and fifteenth days of the month, after the second board has struck following the morning gruel, a general tea service is held in the refectory (*zhāi-táng*), at which time the regulations are proclaimed.
Briefly stated: nowadays, the Chan school has provisionally relaxed the precept against eating at improper times, moving the communal tea ceremony to the second board of the evening.

This is explained below in the section on the Abbot regarding the new and full moon (i.e., this recitation of the precepts on the new and full moon is also a provisional concession made by the Chan school; according to the Vinaya regulations, it should properly take place on the final day of the dark and bright fortnights).

Furthermore, according to ancient regulations, every day at the two meal times of rice gruel and vegetarian feast, the assembly of monks descends from the hall and ascends to the main hall. There, the Rector (Vina) recites the *Amitāyus Dhāraṇī* three times, dedicating the merit to extend the imperial longevity. Additionally, each month there are the four fasting days (*caturdaśī*) and the six fasting days (*ṣaḍaśīti*).

Regarding the Ten Days of Fasting: the first, fifth, and ninth months of each year are designated as "months of goodness," during which recitations are performed to offer prayers for the longevity of the Emperor. At the morning service on these days, following the completion of the Heart Sūtra, the Great Ritual for Longevity (Dae-jukyeon) is chanted with a sincere heart.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding the designation of the four fast days as "the Mandate of the Auspicious Destiny" (Jingming), it began in the third year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.

By imperial decree, the four fast days, along with the first, fifth, and ninth months of each year, were established throughout the empire such that monasteries must establish prayer halls (*daochang*) and refrain from killing living beings.
According to the *Tripiṭaka*, Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, travels annually through the four great continents;

he governs Jambudvīpa during the first, fifth, and ninth months, and for this reason, slaughter is prohibited. However, when the regional governors (*fan-zhen*) of the Tang dynasty assumed office, they invariably rewarded their soldiers with feasts that required the large-scale slaughter of animals;
thus, the practice of not taking up office during the first, fifth, and ninth months was established as a prohibition against killing.
Now, those who mistakenly regard this as a taboo are in error. Even the practice of recitation during the four periods of fasting is in accordance with the Buddha’s injunctions;
it causes people to understand the meaning and illuminate the source of their own minds. If there are faults, one should correct them; if there are none, one should increase one's diligence.

It is not merely for the purpose of reciting sutras to expiate transgressions and repay one's debts of gratitude. Alas! Although one may not understand the meaning when reciting to expiate transgressions and repay debts of gratitude, the practice still persists.
Regarding these rites, there are now some that have been abandoned and no longer practiced; this is a profound violation [of tradition].

According to the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) and the *Yunqi chongxing lu* (Record of Venerable Conduct from Yunqi), there was a monk named Shi Sengyun who resided at Baoming Temple and was renowned for his lectures.

On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, as he was about to recite the precepts, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The precepts can be recited by each person individually; why labor over them so many times?"

He heard that he might order one monk to establish the doctrine so as to enlighten those of later generations; the assembly would not dare to oppose him, and consequently, the recitation of the precepts was abolished.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the assembly gathered, they suddenly lost sight of Yun.
They searched for him in all directions and found him within an ancient tomb, his body covered in blood. When asked the reason, he said: "A fierce warrior holding a great..."
[The assailant] drew his sword and rebuked him with a harsh voice, saying: "Monk! Who are you that dares to interrupt the recitation of the precepts and falsely presume to expound the principles?
I shall immediately strike down your body with this blade! His pain was so agonizing it was unbearable; he was then supported back to the monastery, where he repented with all his heart.
For ten years, he practiced with a sincere heart and the utmost reverence, reciting the precepts according to the prescribed ritual.

On the day of his death, a rare fragrance came to welcome him, and he passed away with joy. At that time, everyone praised him for having reformed himself while still in this world. Yunqi Lianchi said:

At present, people still study the sūtras and śāstras while disparaging the vinaya. For two thousand years, there has been no one who continues to observe the fortnightly recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
Undaunted by this, I have not hesitated to restore these neglected practices in the mountains; yet, even now, people still do not believe me.
The retribution is vividly manifest; there is evidence for this in the case of Master Yun. May those who read this reflect upon it.
*Bai-zhang Cong-lin Qing-gui Zheng-yi Ji*, Scroll Number One Hundred.
*Bai-zhang Cong-lin Qing-gui Zheng-yi Ji*, Scroll Number Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huaihǎi of Mount Bǎizhàng in Hongzhou during the Táng Dynasty;
the Bhikṣu Yírùn of Zhēnjì Monastery in Hángzhōu, Qīng dynasty, expounded the meaning;
and verified by Mìoyǒng, the Abbot of Jièzhū Monastery in Yuèchéng.

In the second chapter, "Requiting Gratitude," it is stated: Rituals and sacrifices are performed to repay kindness and recompense virtue. Among all forms of gratitude, however, the debt owed to the state is paramount.
We respectfully observe that our flourishing dynasty honors the Buddha and extends its favor to the monastic community; thus, it embodies...
Those who show compassion for them have reached the ultimate; from sage to sage they have been handed down without any interruption.
How could the disciples of Śākyamuni fail to commemorate him? It is for this reason that the regulations for the National Memorial Day were established. As for the various heavens—
There is the grace of those who protect the Dharma; thus, there is the regulation for offering sacrifices to the deities. There is the grace of the sun and moon in their illuminating presence;
thus, there is the regulation for protecting the sun and protecting the moon. There is the grace of the *dānapati* (donors) in their faithful offerings;
thus, there are the regulations for praying for fine weather, praying for rain, and dispatching locusts. All of these are acts of repaying kindness. Furthermore, there is...
Furthermore, those who seek grace do so through the prayers of the *Veda*. Because the Celestial Honored One manifests a celestial body to protect the Dharma, his vows are vast and profound;
thus, there is a response whenever there is a resonance. Therefore, the Praise of Nanshan says:
"The General Veda provides the most abundant protection. If he sees demonic hordes attempting to delude and disturb bhikṣus, he rushes forth in a state of solemn urgency."
To prune [the weeds] at the appropriate time may be called an excellent expression of the Celestial Honored One’s heart that protects the Dharma.
Now, within the monastic communities, whenever disasters or other calamities occur, there is no prayer made to Veda that does not manifest a miraculous response.
Knowing how to seek grace, they also know how to repay it; therefore, this is appended to the chapter on Repaying Kindness. As for the Kitchen God (Zhaoshen), by means of—
The assembly relies on food and drink for its sustenance; originally, this was one of the five sacrifices (*pañca-yajña*). Therefore, it is placed at the end of this volume.

Regarding the Buddhist services held on the National Memorial Day (*koku-ki*), which coincides with the anniversary of the passing of our former Sage (the day he ascended to heaven, also called *shōga*), the guest hall prepares for it the night before.

Hanging the Plaque. (The plaque reads: On the memorial day of the ascension to heaven of Emperor [Name], at the morning service, the assembly of masters shall proceed together to the Great Hall to recite the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī and chant the Buddha’s name.
We humbly pray that the Sacred Mind may look down upon us and that the Sun of the Buddha may increase in brilliance. (Written on yellow paper: The Holy Seat of Emperor [Name]. Offerings.
In front of the Buddha Hall, incense, flowers, lamps, candles, and fruit offerings are arranged upon the altar. On the morning of the main day, the assembly of monks gathers like clouds;
incense is burned and the ritual incense-burner is passed. The Abbot offers incense, and the Rector recites the Incense Praise (*Xiangzan*). The chanting proceeds as usual.

On this day, an altar is established in the Great Hall to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Guest Master invites the Abbot to offer incense. When the offerings are presented, the Abbot ascends [the altar].
Incense is offered and tea and soup are served. When the recitation is finished, the Rector (Weina) performs the dedication, saying:

"At [Name] Temple in [Name] Prefecture, the Dharma-transmitting presiding monk [Name], on this day, the [day] of the [month], respectfully encounters the anniversary of the imperial memorial service for Emperor [Name].
We have carefully assembled the monastic community to chant sutras and mantras. We now respectfully extend this dedication of the extraordinary merit thus gathered. We pray that..."
The spirit wanders through the eight extremities, riding upon cloud-chariots and wind-horses in carefree ease.

His station is realized as the Central Heaven, where he enjoys the bliss of jade palaces and crystal towers. To all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time... (etc.). (Recite the hymn.

We respectfully commemorate our late Lord, who protected the Dharma with complete devotion. Our loyalty and sincerity incline toward him beyond words; we offer this report from the depths of our hearts.
The Field. With sincere devotion, chant for the benefit of all beings prior to heaven. Namo to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Who Ascends to the Celestial Realm (Recite three times).

The Commentary on the Meaning states: This [ceremony] was established by the late Emperor when he ascended to the Way of Heaven; it is therefore appropriate that it be performed. Regarding the offering to the Devas (*deva-pūjā*):

if one is performing only the offering to the Devas, the *kṣāṇavāsin* (Guest Hall Master) shall, on the day prior, hang the name tablets of the various masters who offer to the Devas in the Dharma Hall. If the ceremony includes a sutra recitation or repentance rite (*sūtra-śamatha*), then the repentance tablets are hung, with the addition of the "Five Watches" (*pañca-prahara*) tablets for the offering to the Devas.

On the evening before, the altar must be strictly purified and the ritual seals (*mudrā*) issued. As for the general procedure for the devotional service of offering to the Devas: on the day prior, the *kṣāṇavāsin* shall direct the *dhūpajyotiṣka* (Incense Lamp Master) to sweep and cleanse the Dharma Hall thoroughly.
Furthermore, hang up banners, streamers, lamps, and colored silks, and arrange various articles for adornment and offering.

In the center of the hall, at the uppermost position, set up a high seat and install the three spirit tablets for the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Next, on both the left and right sides, lay out incense tables surrounded by offering vessels.
Present these offerings to the assembly of attendants in the *Guangming* (Light) Rite, as well as to the deities who preside over the affairs of the Three Realms.

The forty-six spirit tablets are likewise arranged with incense, flowers, lamps, candles, and other offerings. Next, in the center of the vermilion courtyard, the station for the celestial immortals is established;
the ritual objects provided are identical [to those for the ancestors]. All offerings—whether vegetables, noodles, or rice—must be abundant and prepared according to the Dharma.
One must by no means use raw, cold, or inedible items, as this would incur the fault of irreverence. Thus, they are all prepared in unison.

Preparations: On the evening of the day before, after the period of stillness has ended, the drum is struck three times. The Guest Master (zhikè) notifies the Rector (wéinà) and others to assemble together.

Next, the host of the meal (zhāizhǔ) is invited to offer incense. Once the assembly of masters has attained solemn purity, the ritual documents (fúdié) are immediately issued to be delivered in advance to the various heavens.

The ritual procedures are as usual, with the addition of the following concluding verses (*zàn*): "In the Assembly of Radiant Light, the various devas who protect the Dharma, The sun, moon, stars, and constellations that illuminate the human world, May they grant us peace and security; may our offerings be sincere, And may our merit and longevity extend forever.
*Namō Dengyunlu Púsà Mòhēsà* (Recite three times, returning the merit each time). On the following day at the fifth watch, the Master of Repentance purifies his person.
The attendants prepare the lamps, candles, and offerings in the Dharma Hall. The Guest Prefect strikes the drum three times, and the assembly of masters gathers together.
The Guest Prefect invites the patron to offer incense; other matters are recorded in the ritual manuals (*kēyí*) and are not detailed here.

There are two versions of these manuals, the detailed and the abbreviated. The detailed version circulates separately; the abbreviated version is contained in the *Chanmen Rिसु* (Daily Recitation of the Chan School). Only the format for the forty-nine memorial tablets is provided here.
Arranged to the left: Homage to the Central Heavenly Teacher, the Original Master Śākyamuni Buddha (on the central tablet).
Akṣobhya Buddha of the East; Ratnaśrī Buddha of the South; Amitāyus Buddha of the West; and Svararāja Buddha of the North.
The Buddhas of the past: Ratnakusumaguṇasāgaravaiḍūryakāñcanaparvata-prabhāsana Buddha; Ratnavijaya Buddha; Vimalajvalanaratnaprabhāsarāja-lakṣaṇa Buddha;
Suvarṇajvālāprabha Buddha; Suvarṇaśataprabhābhāsitagarbha Buddha; Kāñcanaparvata-tattvacchattra Buddha;
Suvarṇakusumajvālālakṣaṇa Buddha; Maholkā Buddha; Ratnalakṣaṇa Buddha. (These fourteen Buddhas are inscribed together upon a single memorial tablet.)
[Upper Center] Homage to the Golden Light Ocean, the Subtle and Wondrous Dharma Torch, the Sovereign King of Sutras.

[Upper Left] Homage to the Great Bodhisattvas of the Assembly of Radiant Light: Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa, Bodhisattva Suvarṇaprabhāsa, Bodhisattva Suvarṇagarbha, Bodhisattva Nityakaruṇā, and Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
(These six are written together on one tablet. [Upper Right] Lord of the Sahā World, whose commands are peerless.
The Honored One, Great Brahmā Deva-rāja, together with his retinue (Left 1; hereafter, at the end of each position, add the six characters "together with his retinue").

The World-Ruler dwelling on earth, Śakra-devendra, the Sovereign King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Left 2). Dhṛtarāṣṭra Deva-rāja, the Guardian of the World in the East and Lord of the Gandharvas (Left 3).
Virūḍhaka Deva-rāja, the Guardian of the World in the South and Lord of the Kumbhāṇḍas (Left 4). [West]...
The World-Protector of the South, the Great Dragon King Lord, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa (5). The World-Protector of the North, the Great Yakṣa Lord, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa (6).
He who personally subdues hostile Māras and vows to serve as a mighty warrior, the Honored Deity Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada (7).
The Especially Honored Lord who dwells in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the Honored Deity Maheśvara (8). [He] governs the twenty-eight divisions.
The Honored Deity Vaiśravaṇa, General of Ghosts and Spirits (9). The Honored Deity Mahāprajñāskandha, Possessor of Great Wisdom and Great Eloquence, Capable of Bestowing Dhāraṇīs (10).
The Honored Deity Mahāpuṇya, Who Causes All Sought After to Be Accomplished According to One’s Needs (11).

The Honored Deity Vajrapāṇi, General of the Gods, Who Deeply Pities the Fourfold Assembly and Provides External Protection for the Three Continents (12). Who Increases and Brings Forth [Virtue], and Realizes...

The Honored Deity of the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā, who manifests merit and is steadfast (13). The Honored Deity of the Bodhi Tree Goddess, whose shade extends over the site of enlightenment, where cause and effect mutually adorn one another (14).
The Honored Deity of the Mother of Ghosts (Hārītī), from whom all ghost kings are born, who protects both men and women (15).
The Honored Deity Mārīcī, who moves before the sun and moon and rescues those from the calamities of war (16). The Hundred Illuminations.
Benefiting sentient beings; the Honored Deity of the Sun Palace, the Great Sun, who with a thousand rays destroys darkness (17). The Lord of Stars and King of Constellations;

the Honored Deity of the Moon Palace, the Great Yin, whose cool light illuminates the night (18). The Honored Deity of the Sāgara Dragon King, who guards the secret treasury of the Dharma Jewel and presides over all dragons (19).
The Honored Deity of King Yama, who wields authority over the hidden realms and acts as the lord of the hells.
(Left 20) The Five Sacred Peaks reside in the east: the Honored Deity Tianqi Renyuan, Lord of Mount Tai. (Left 21) The two Iron Ring Mountains:
the Honored Deities, Lords of the Eighteen Hells and Kings of the Ten Courts of Darkness. (Left 22) The Deity of Space, the Deity of Earth, and the Deity of Day.
Night-Spirits (Rātridevatās). The assembly of all protective deities and spirits. (Left, No. 23) The four formless realms:

the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, the Sphere of Nothingness, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, and the Sphere of Infinite Space. The various Great Heavenly Kings. (Right, No. 1) The four dhyānas of the Form Realm:
the Five Śuddhāvāsa Heavens, Akaniṣṭha, Sudarśana, Sudṛśa, Atapa, and Abṛha. The various Great Heavenly Kings. (Right, No. 2) The four [dhyānas] of the Form Realm.

Dhyāna (Meditation). The abode of the non-Buddhists; the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (Asaṃjñisattva-deva). (Right three) The four dhyānas of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu). The abodes of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana):

the Heaven of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala), the Heaven of Merit-born (Puṇyaprasava), and the Heaven of No Clouds (Anabhraka); the various great heavenly kings. (Right four) The third dhyāna of the Form Realm: the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna) and the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha).
The Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttābha). The various Great Heavenly Kings. (Right 5) The Second Dhyāna of the Form Realm. The Ābhāsvara, Apramāṇābha, and Parīttābha heavens.

The various Great Heavenly Kings. (Right 6) The First Dhyāna of the Form Realm. The Lord of the Heavens, Mahābrahmā; followed by the Brahmā-purohitas and the Brahmakāyikas. The various Heavenly Kings.
