(Right 7) Between the Desire and Form Realms. Manifesting as Pāpīyas. The Five Emperors, the Great Māras, and the various Māra-devas. (Right 8) The Desire [Realm].

Dwelling at the summit of the realm is the Great Maheśvara Heavenly King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (9). Dwelling next below in the Desire Realm, constantly receiving pleasure through transformation, is the Heavenly King of the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (10).
Occupying the center of the Desire Realm is the Tuṣita Heaven, with its Heavenly King of Contentment (11). Dwellers in the void of the Desire Realm are the Yāma Heavenly Kings (12).
Residing upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, there are eight in each of the four directions, totaling thirty-two great [kings].
(13) The Heavenly Kings (right). (14) Dwell upon the waist of Mount Sumeru; the various devas and sons of devas of the four quarters (right).

(15) Because they originally dwell in the void, they correspond to the auspiciousness and misfortune of the world; the various celestial bodies and constellations (right). Beneath Mount Sumeru, there are three tiers in succession.
The gods of Constant Pride, the Garland-Bearing gods, the Firm-Headed gods, and all the sons of heaven (16). At the Assembly of Radiance, he manifested his traces among the eight classes of beings:
the Kinnara King, the Garuḍa King, the Mahoraga King, and all the spirit kings (17).
At the Assembly of Radiance, he manifested his traces as the master of the vessel-world: the deity of the Nairañjanā River, the Great Deity of Rain, and the Great...
The Deity of Food and Drink; the various deities of Wind and Water; the Fire Deity and other deities. (Right, eighteen. The monasteries of the eighteen *gāmas* in the eastern and western lands;

the monasteries of this temple; the assembly of holy beings who protect the Dharma. (Right, nineteen. The Heavenly Stems and Earthly Branches; the sixty *tàisuì* (annual earth spirits); the deities of the twelve palaces (*dvādaśa-rāśi*);
the various great stellar lords. (Right, twenty. The *tàisuì* of the current year; the administrative offices of one’s natal palace (*mìngpǐng-gōng*); the dark realm of the path of karma.
The Official: All Star Lords (21). The Provincial Governor of such-and-such Province; the Prefectural Governor of such-and-such Prefecture; the County Magistrate of such-and-such County;
the Venerable God of the City Walls (22). The Local Deity of this Mountain; the Local Deity of such-and-such Ward (namely, the local deity of the donor’s residence; 23).

As for the ritual protocols for making offerings to Heaven, they are roughly as set forth in the Daily Recitation manual and are performed according to the regular liturgy. Herein, the memorial is prepared.
The ritual proclaims: We humbly reflect that on the assembly at Vulture Peak, you received the words of the Tathāgata’s entrustment;
within the field of Magadha, you realized the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruling Sovereign. All living beings rely upon you, and you dwell loftily above the three realms.

We are fortunate to have received your descent; we pray that you will graciously grant us clear discernment. Now, within this world-system of four continents, in Jambudvīpa, the Great Qing Empire, [in the] province, prefecture, county, and capital...
Mapping out the land, we shall reside beneath this shrine. We shall serve the Buddha, observe the fast, and make offerings to the heavens. For what purpose do we pray for protection?

(The essential intent is briefly stated in two phrases. This letter is from [Name]. (Whether it be an official acting as the petitioner, a local magnate, or commoners and gentry, each shall provide their name and surname.
On this day, with heads bowed and incense held, we take refuge with a sincere heart in the Lord of the Assembly of Radiance, Śākyamuni Buddha, the Golden Light.
To the assembly of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the Eight Classes of Devas and Dragons, and all provisional and ultimate sages: beneath the golden lotus seats, we respectfully submit our petition.

We humbly ask for what purpose... [here detail the specific wishes sought]. We have specially selected the [day] of this month to reverently present pure offerings of *fu* and *gui* vessels, universally honoring the Primordial Lord of Heaven.
We pray that you will deign to bestow your celestial grace and graciously accept [our offerings].
I humbly submit this petition with utmost sincerity. I pray that the Buddha’s heart will look upon me with compassion and that the celestial virtues may be widely extended.

May grace be bestowed according to original vows, manifesting a response as clear as an echo. When the human mind is unified, the celestial hearing becomes acute; may your majestic spiritual power be fully displayed to support the transformation of the Dharma.
The above memorial is respectfully submitted to the Triple Gem and the various heavens. I pray you will swiftly bestow your grace. I am overcome with awe and trepidation.
Submitted with utmost sincerity. On the [day], [month], and [year]. [Name] respectfully presents this memorial. Regarding the meaning of the text:
there are three translations of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* in the canon. First, the four-fascicle version translated by Dharmakṣema during the Northern Liang dynasty;
this is the currently circulating edition. Second, the version compiled by the Sui monk Baogui in collaboration with Zhìdé of India. There is... [text continues].
In three fascicles, translated by the Tang monk Yijing; in ten fascicles, with its textual meaning complete and exhaustive, titled the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra*.
As for the current ritual for making offerings to the gods, it follows only the Northern translation; yet, the offering to the twenty devas therein is far too brief.
There are forty-nine positions here, all of which follow the three translations; thus, one can clearly see the ancient regulations. They are extremely detailed and subtle.

Now, I shall excerpt a passage of verses from the "Chapter on the Goddess of Great Eloquence" in the eighth fascicle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra* to corroborate these ancient regulations. The Sūtra says: "I now summon and invite all the Śrāvakas of the Buddha."
May you all swiftly come and fulfill my heart’s aspiration. May all the truthful words I seek be free from falsehood.

From the Akaniṣṭha heaven above, as well as the Śuddhāvāsa deities, Mahābrahmā, the Brahmakāyika gods, and the entire assembly of Brahma-kings, down to the lord of the Sahā world throughout the three thousandfold universe, together with all your retinues—now, I...
I summon you all: I pray that you descend with compassion, out of pity, and grant us your collective protection.

The gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), those of the Heaven of Enjoying Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*), and the hosts of the Tuṣita Heaven where Maitreya shall attain Buddhahood; as well as the various hosts of the Yāma Heaven.
And the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the assembly of the Cāturmahārājika Devas, all the hosts of devas, and the spirits of earth, water, fire,
and wind who dwell upon Mount Sumeru; the deities of the seven seas and their three classes of followers, along with all their retinues—
Pūrṇabhadra, Pañcaśikha, the sun, moon, and all the constellations— may all such hosts of devas bring peace and security to the world, for an eon and beyond.
The various devas do not delight in committing sinful deeds. They pay homage to Hārītī and her youngest beloved son.
So too do the hosts of nāgas, devas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
"By the power of the World-Honored One, I have summoned and invited them all. According to this scriptural passage, one must prepare offerings in accordance with these ancient regulations;
only then can one achieve spiritual resonance. Let future worthies take heed of this."
Regarding the protection of the sun and moon:
whenever a solar or lunar eclipse is foreseen, the Guest Hall should hang a notice in advance [stating]: "On such-and-such day at such-and-such time, there will be a solar (or lunar) eclipse.

At that time, the assembly of venerable monks throughout the monastery, upon hearing the bell, shall proceed together to the front of the Great Hall to protect the sun (or the moon). When the appointed hour arrives, they shall perform the rite.
The administrative office prepares offerings facing the direction of the sun (or the moon). When the great assembly gathers like clouds at the sound of the bell, the abbot offers incense.
After the rector has recited the "Incense Cloud Canopy" three times, everyone recites together:
Namo to the Bodhisattva Sunlight Pervading Illumination (or, for Hu-yue, recite "Moonlight"). Continue until the light returns to its full orb. For the upper offering:

first recite the Heart Sūtra, followed by the Mantra for Transforming Food into Nectar, and so forth, until the offerings are complete. The Rector proclaims the memorial text (*shu*). The Memorial Text for Protecting the Sun states:
"Humbly considering that eating on this day may portend a deviation from the five cycles [of the calendar], we revere the majesty of Heaven and fear the sixth [calamity]."
As calamities were about to arise, we have followed the sentiments of the people to provide protection and have reverently relied upon the power of the Buddha to offer prayers for averting them.

Accordingly, I now lead the assembly of monks to sincerely recite, in unison, the sacred name of the Bodhisattva Sunlight Pervasive Illumination from the Eastern Lapis Lazuli World, thereby extending our protection.
We pray that the essence of the sun will swiftly grant its radiance back. We humbly beseech that the five colors—
The Yellow Path opens and shines brightly, illuminating the lands below. As the masses of yin dissipate, the virtue of yang flourishes, manifesting and revolving across the heavens.

(Having completed the *Xuanshu*, recite the Praise of the Sunlight: The circular radiance pervades everywhere; the Sage’s virtue is immeasurable. The myriad phenomena and the Sea-Seal Samādhi manifest as celestial verses; throughout the realms of sand-grains, all are graced by the light of his benevolence.
Universally saving both the dead and the living, may we together rejoice in the Great Wheel-Turning King. *Namo to the Great Sun of the Solar Palace.*
Venerable Celestial Bodhisattva (recite three times; each time, refer to the *Huihu yue shu*).

I humbly submit that the moon, as the essence of the Yin, presides over the night and is relied upon for its illuminating presence; yet Heaven now displays portents of calamity among the common people.
Now that an eclipse has occurred, we are both cautioned and filled with dread; thus, we offer prayers and perform rites of expiation.

For this reason, leading the assembly of monks, we reverently give rise to a sincere heart and recite in unison the sacred name of the Bodhisattva Moonlight-Universal-Illumination of the Eastern Lapis Lazuli World, thereby extending our plea for protection.

We hope that the lunar radiance will swiftly grant its clear light. We humbly pray that all demonic vapors may vanish without a trace, and that the full orb may manifest its great brilliance once more.
Upon the earth, mountains, and rivers, the Jade Hare lives forever; the myriad phenomena are contained within the palace of the Vast Cold. (At the conclusion of the recitation, chant the praise:

Fragrance wafts from the cassia buds; the precious mirror is perfectly round. The silver river is clear and cool, surrounded by the many stars; its light shines forth in vastness. Where it was incomplete, it is now made whole again.
Homage to those who benefit humans and devas. *Namo Yuegong Taiyin Zuntian Pusa* (Recite three times; after each, disperse). The Commentary on the Meaning states:
This is to repay the kindness of the sun and moon for their illumination. As for what is called an eclipse:
when the sun and moon meet, if the sun is obscured by the moon, it is a solar eclipse; when the sun and moon face one another, if the moon stands in opposition to the sun, it is a lunar eclipse.

It is also called "eclipse" (*uparāga*). When black vapors approach and press upon it, it is called "thinning" (*upatapa*); the sun and moon become yellowish-red and lose their luster, appearing as if they were being oppressed by some object.
When their form and color are diminished or deficient, it is called "eclipsing" (*grahaṇa*);

the sun and moon are impaired and invaded, like leaves being eaten by insects. Furthermore, this thinning and eclipsing is one of the seven calamities; both humans and all other beings [suffer from it].

Because we receive the grace of being illuminated by [the sun and moon], we must protect them. As for this protection, it means that the ordinary people of this world should each exhaust their sincere hearts to turn back the signs of Heaven.
Someone may ask: "If one is protecting the sun and moon of one's own realm, why recite the names of Bodhisattvas from the East?
The answer is: "Because name and meaning correspond. By invoking those great names, one rescues one's own sun and moon."
Furthermore, the Buddha-dharma is boundless, and the heavenly minds respond with obedience; it is therefore appropriate to praise it thus.

That the concluding verses still refer to the "Sun Palace" (Sūryamaṇḍala) while the "Moon Palace" (Candramaṇḍala) retains its original designation is because, if one speaks according to principle: the "Sun" is reality (*bhūta*), for it is eternally full.

Through the wisdom of reality (*bhūtajñāna*), it illuminates the principle of *tathatā*, universally extinguishing all the delusions and darkness of sentient beings, and causing them to ascend [to liberation].
The Mountain of Nirvāṇa: if one is momentarily unaware [of it], one is like a dead person; therefore, one must guard it. "Moon" means "deficient.
Because there is waxing and waning, one uses expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) to illuminate worldly affairs and universally eliminate all the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings.
It causes one to roam in the cool, pure ocean; yet if one harbors even a single thought of attachment or stagnation, one will fall into pits and ditches—therefore, one must guard against this.
If one performs the moon-protection rite after midday, it is not necessary to present the superior offerings, for the various devas eat early and do not accept offerings made in the afternoon.
Nevertheless, one may still offer incense, tea, and candles.

The Mid-Autumn Moon Sacrifice is held on the fifteenth day of the eighth month. Before the evening congee, a signboard is hung in the Guest Hall (the board reads): "This evening, all members of the assembly shall gather together."
Upon hearing the sound of the bell, everyone proceeds together to the front of the Great Hall to prostrate before the moon.

At the second board of evening twilight, the Kusi (Storehouse Office) prepares the offering positions before the Great Hall facing the moon; the offerings consist solely of incense, flowers, pure tea, and lamps.

The Guest Master strikes the bell three times, and the assembly gathers. The incense burner is passed around, and the Abbot offers incense. The Rector recites the "Incense Cloud Canopy" (three times, then continues).
[Recite] the Bodhisattva Candrāloka-Candramas three times. Recite the Bhaisajyaguru Dharani twenty-one times. Spread out the ritual implements.
Prostrate twenty-four times before the Honored Celestial Deity Bodhisattva Candrāloka-Candramas. Having completed the prostrations, rise with the implements and chant the hymn of praise.

The clouds part and the sky is clear; alone she reveals her graceful beauty. Pure and flawless, her form is naturally full. One moon traverses the heavens in a single cycle, shining universally upon the boundless reaches.
Her gracious light covers the great chiliocosm. Homage to the Honored Deity of the Moon Palace, the Bodhisattva Mahācandramas.
(Recite three times. Each person returns to their own quarters. Upon hearing the sound of the drum, everyone assembles in the refectory for the universal tea ceremony (*fucha*).

To each person, one moon-cake is added. Regarding the meaning: it is traditionally said that the Buddha was born in this month during the Mid-Autumn Festival; therefore, the whole world offers sacrifices to him. According to Buddhism...

Regarding the ritual for making offerings to the moon (*candramas-pūjā*), it should appropriately take place in the forenoon. This is because the moon is akin to the heavens, and the various devas do not accept offerings made after midday.
This accords with pure regulations; one need only arrange the offering seats, providing flowers, incense, candles, and water, but no food items for the offering.
Lately, however, monastic communities have followed worldly customs in their moon rituals, a corruption that has persisted for a long time. It is truly regrettable.
There are even those who claim to pay homage to the Bodhisattva Moonlight Pervasive Illumination (Candraprabha-vikurvaṇa) or to the Bodhisattva Moon of Liberation (Vimukticandra).
Furthermore, when making superior offerings, there are those who employ the ritual procedures for the Buddha’s meal; this is especially erroneous. The ignorant do not recognize this.

This has been passed down erroneously from one generation to the next. Those of high intelligence throughout the various regions should correct this. Someone may ask: "The sun and moon move in their courses; their virtues are not two different things.
Yet now we sacrifice only to the moon and have not seen a sacrifice to the sun. Why is this? The answer is: This follows the conventional rites of the world.

Because the secular world does not esteem the worship of the moon, its virtues remain largely unappreciated. Furthermore, as for the moon: it relies upon its luminous reflection within the dark recesses of the Yin;

the myriad species depend upon it for their refreshing coolness. When one discusses its merit, it ranks as the second only to the sun. Yet, as for its virtue, there are many aspects that closely resemble the Way of our Buddha.
Its spiritual illumination is self-sustaining; even when eclipsed or obscured, nothing can diminish its radiance. How brilliant it is! Its shadow...
It manifests as all manner of waters; that its reflections never differ regardless of the size [of the vessel]—how impartial it is!
It reflects even the slightest glimmer of light; how perfect it is! It remains pure and self-identical; how tranquil it is! It enters into turbid waters yet remains unstained;
how chaste it is! Its circulation continues without ceasing; how constant it is! Its waxing and waning do not deviate from their proper seasons; how...
As for this faith: its radiance pervades the myriad phenomena, yet it possesses no responding mind—how empty it is!
It reflects the stars and constellations while shining uniquely—how blazing it is! It faces all things before one's eyes—how universal it is!
If one can awaken to the mind by means of the moon, then original enlightenment will illuminate itself, and obscurations will be unable to darken it. Is this not the brightness of the moon? Broad.
Benefiting all without partiality, and regarding both the gracious and the resentful as non-dual—is this not the impartiality of the moon?

In every instance there is the Way, and in every phenomenon the Dharma is fully manifest—is this not the fullness of the moon? Abiding amidst clamor yet ever tranquil—is this not the stillness of the moon?
Dwelling in filth yet uniquely pure—is this not the integrity of the moon? Self-strengthening without ceasing—is this not the constancy of the moon? To be trustworthy...
It nourishes even the swine and the fish—is this not the moon’s reliability? It responds in accordance with all things that come before it—is this not the moon’s emptiness?
Because its affinity for the Buddha-way is such as this, the preaching at Vulture Peak often employs the moon as a metaphor.
Hanshan then said: "My mind is like the autumn moon; nothing can be compared to it. Alas! The virtue of the moon may indeed be called magnificent.

Now, at the junction of the Mid-Autumn Festival, it is called the "Month Birthday. Although this is a popular tradition, the heavens are high and the air is crisp, making the light exceptionally clear;
the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) seems as if it were before one's very eyes. It is fitting, therefore, to offer exclusive worship at this time.
Is this not indeed appropriate? Someone else may ask: "The Buddha ordained that bhikṣus do not prostrate to devas or humans.
Now, the Moon Palace is likewise similar to the various heavens; why then should one prostrate? Answer: The Vinaya regulations are established based on their outward manifestations.

Those [deities] are worldly gods who have not yet attained the fruits of the Path; therefore, prostration is not permitted. Prostration was prohibited because it was feared it might diminish their merit. This is the pure rule (qinggui).

To speak based on the fundamental principle: among all the celestial deities, many are manifestations of holy sages. One may now pay homage to their virtues and revere them for their protection of the Dharma;

thus, prostrating is permissible. However, if they possess neither virtue nor protective power, and have no connection to Buddhism, one should follow the Buddha’s regulations, and it is correct not to prostrate.
If, for the sake of fame or profit, one flatters and curries favor with worldly etiquette, that is improper.
Then both self and others will be harmed; the inauspiciousness is extreme.
The ritual procedures for praying for clear weather are fully contained in the *Vajrajvālā-vṛṣṭistambhana-sūtra*, which was spoken by the Buddha Vipaśyin. However, this...
The Sūtra exists only in the Great Canon and is difficult to practice in the world; for now, we shall follow worldly custom.
If rain persists without clearing, the Guest Hall first informs the Abbot, and subsequently hangs a placard at the center of the main gate (the placard reads): "Prayer for Clear Skies.
Furthermore, a yellow paper tablet is used, upon which is written: *Namo Vajrajvālā-vātavarṣa-nivāraṇa-sūtra*, [from] the Jvālā Assembly.

The names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, seventeen characters in total, constitute a single lotus seat. When established in a certain location, the altar site must be strictly purified according to the Dharma, and offerings must be arranged.
The presiding abbot must maintain a focused mind with redoubled care, and the monastic community must each strive for solemnity and order.
Whether it be officials offering incense or the monastery’s permanent residents making offerings with sincere resolve, all must exhaust their utmost sincerity in hopes of turning back [calamities].
Since the will of Heaven must not be met with a hollow response, when the appointed time arrives, a written record of the intent is first submitted.

The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) informs the Hall Superintendent (*tangsi*), who notifies the assembly through the Guest Hall. A plaque for the prayer for clear weather and recitation of scriptures is hung according to the standard ritual.

During the two periods of the midday and evening meals, the bell is struck to assemble the community for the chanting of sutras. This is performed for three days, five days, or seven days as circumstances require. Ten monks take turns in rotation.
[The number of] personnel may be several dozen. They are divided into several shifts to chant in succession; this is called the "Uninterrupted Wheel.

One must ensure a response from the sacred powers before concluding the rite with the final distribution of incense and repentance (this applies to all prayers). [Daily, at two sessions, after returning to the hall following the offering, when the Chan Hall strikes two boards and the Guest Prefect strikes the great bell three times, the altar immediately burns incense and candles.

The Chan Hall ceases its silence and opens for "small silence. The assembly inside and out dons their robes and carries their ritual implements to enter the altar. The Abbot offers incense, and the assembly sings: *Da...* (Great...)
Compassionate Holy Lord, divine verses of the Middle Way, perfectly fused and unimpeded, wondrous beyond measure.

To bind the realm and purify the altar, may the assembly proclaim them; may the burning afflictions be transformed into cool serenity. *Namo* Cool Land Bodhisattva (recite three times). Then, as appropriate:
*Namo* Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (recite three times). Recite the Great Compassion Mantra twenty-one times, and contemplate Avalokiteśvara.
Chant the sacred name one thousand times (or recite the Bhaisajyaguru Dharani forty-nine times; then chant the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha one thousand times).

Upon completing the circumambulation and recitation, strike the *yin-qing* twice and return to your position. Stand facing upward. Once the Venerable Rector has struck the *qing* to conclude the chanting of the Buddha’s name, [the ritual master] next raises the Petition for Clear Skies, saying:
"The celestial gates have long been locked and remain unopened; day and night, torrential rains lash with black winds. To eliminate calamities for the people and seek auspiciousness..."

On this day, as the year turns and a single red orb suddenly emerges at its appointed time, there is a certain temple in a certain county, a certain prefecture, and a certain province within the Great Qing Empire of Jambudvīpa, the Southern Continent of the Four World Systems.

I, [Name], the abbot of this temple (if there are officials of the local administration acting as patrons, their names and surnames should be listed one by one), today with a sincere heart offer incense and take refuge in Śākyamuni Buddha, the Teacher of the Sahā World. Light...

In this assembly of flames, before the Buddhas, sages, and worthies, the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, and the honored deities who oversee affairs, we respectfully communicate our sentiments from before each lotus seat.

We look up in prayer for your radiant presence to descend and grant us a responsive manifestation. (We, the undersigned), observe with deep concern that excessive rain has become a calamity, such that the production of goods cannot be achieved;
the hundred rivers overflow their banks, and the people have no place of rest. This is surely the result of the collective karma of sentient beings; it is only through [the power of] the High...
His Majesty takes the preservation of life as his virtue. For this reason, with sincere heart, he has respectfully established a ritual site for praying for clear weather.
Daily, the assembly of monks recites divine mantras and the names of the Buddhas, looking up to invoke the various saints to pray for sunny skies and that a swift and manifest response be granted.

We humbly pray that the clouds of delusion be swept away across the four fields so that all dark and baleful influences may vanish; and that the brilliant sun be made to shine from the center of the heavens, so that its radiance may surely illuminate all.
Illumination. May the five elements each follow their proper order, and may all myriad creatures fully realize their lives. This petition is respectfully submitted.

We humbly entreat the Buddhas and devas to perceive this clearly and the dragon deities to carry it out. [Date]. Submitted by the Abbot [Name] and others. (Upon the conclusion of the recitation, the following hymn is chanted:
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, take pity on sentient beings; To seek the bright sun that breaks the thick clouds, So that after long rain, a new clarity may be found.
Radiance fills the earth; all things rejoice in prosperity. Namo to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Assembly of Radiant Flames. (Recite three times.
The assembly simultaneously performs four prostrations with implements held. The Rector strikes the chime and leads the chant; the assembly bows. Namo to our Root Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha.

(Three prostrations) Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha Tathāgata. (Three prostrations) Sunlight Pervasive Illumination, Moonlight Pervasive Illumination, and Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara. (Three prostrations for each)
Homage to the *Vajrajvālā-vāta-varṣa-nivāraṇa-sūtra*. [Offer three prostrations to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Jvālā Assembly.

Once the Three Refuges are completed, return to the hall. Immediately, change to the second group of monks and chant as before. In this manner, they shall take turns so that the "fish-voice" (the continuous, resonant chanting) never ceases.
For all offerings, follow the standard ritual. This liturgical manual should be written in duplicate. On the first day of the observance, perform the dedication at the initial hour.
Burn one copy as an offering to the Triple Gem and the various devas, seeking their swift response.
One copy is to be placed before the Buddha on the altar, recited once at each session with dedication of merit. Once the weather clears, perform a great dedication ceremony and burn it.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: That which gives life to things is the sun; yet the sun’s excessive intensity becomes the cause of withering and scorching. That which moistens things is water;
yet the water’s inundation becomes the beginning of rot and decay. Therefore, unseasonable winds and rains, as well as droughts that persist beyond their proper time, are all disasters.
It is logically fitting to seek [divine favor] with devotion, hoping for harmonious winds and timely rain.
When rain is prayed for after a long period of drought, a placard for the prayer for rain is hung above the mountain gate.

Next, following the text of the *Mahāmegha-praṇidhāna-varṣa-sūtra*, the altar is prepared and established. A clean site is selected, twelve paces square, to serve as the place of practice (*maṇḍala*), and the altar is constructed.
Within that space, facing east, there is a site one foot high and ten paces square. Take clean yellow earth and plaster it around the perimeter of the altar.
In the center of the altar, set up a platform two zhang square to serve as a high seat, covered with a blue canopy.

Inside the canopy, arrange one seat for the presiding monk and one high table. On both sides, arrange low seats and low tables for those reciting the scriptures, according to the number of persons. All...
The seats and mats, as well as the table curtains, shall all be blue. To the east of the high seat, at a distance of three cubits, set up a blue curtain.
There shall be one high table; upon this table, arrange the offering vessels, along with milk-rice and various fruits (the same applies to the south, west, and north).

Offerings are made for the Dragon King, who has one body and three heads, together with his entire retinue, facing west. To the south of the high seat, at a distance of five cubits, offerings are made for the [second] Dragon King.

The five-headed [deities], together with their retinues, face north; seven cubits outside the west side of the high seat, one makes offerings to the Dragon King, who has one body and seven heads, together with his retinues, facing east.
Nine cubits outside the north side of the high seat, one makes offerings to the Dragon King, who has one body and nine heads, together with his retinues, facing south.
At each of the four corners of the altar, one erects seven blue banners. One.
Beneath each banner, place a burning oil lamp. In front of each lamp, at the four corners, set vases filled with various fresh flowers.
Around the perimeter of the altar, at a distance of one step or several steps, construct walls using mats; these shall have gates on all four sides.
On each gate, paint two rows of dragons as guardians, which serves to establish the boundary (*sīmā*). As the Sūtra says: "Use either ashes or water to form the boundary."
As for the *pàn* (boundary-markers), these shall now replace them. The dragon-heads all face the gate and coil like serpents, their tails interlocking with one another.
Outside the gate there is a screen, also made of mats. A monk of high conduct and strict observance of the precepts is selected to preside over the altar.
The two orders [of monks] shall also select monks of pure preceptual conduct to chant the scriptures.

Furthermore, two monks shall be chosen to enter the altar as attendants (*śi-tse*) to perform the duties of offering incense and pouring water. All these monks shall wear dark blue robes and undergo ritual purification through bathing and fasting, exactly as prescribed in the sutras.
Day and night they shall maintain strict purity, reverently making vows and reciting the scriptural texts for one or two seven-day periods.
Within seven days, or at the latest by the twenty-first day, one will naturally invoke the harmony of Heaven, and sweet rain shall respond to the prayer.
The *Zhengyi* states: "This was a general explanation above. The altar uses yellow earth as a substitute for cow dung. [The term] 'cow' refers to the ox."
These are the white oxen of the Snowy Mountains who feed exclusively on the fragrant herbs of the mountains; their dung is fragrant and pure, and thus fit for use.
All other oxen are foul-smelling and impure, and thus unfit for use. In my eastern land, we cannot obtain this, and therefore we use clean yellow earth as a substitute.
Furthermore, regarding the "blue" mentioned in the *Sūtra of Adornment*, blue corresponds to the north, which is black; it takes its quality from the element of water.
Furthermore, one *zhou* is equivalent to one current *chi*; three *zhou* are simply three *chi*.
Next, regarding the description of the Four Directional Dragon Kings’ images: the dragon kings’ images are painted upon a folding screen (*chabi*).
The screen is two feet six inches high and one foot six inches wide. The base of the screen is one foot two inches high. The central panel of the screen is covered with silk fabric. Each...
According to the directions and following the number of heads described in the scriptural characteristics, they are depicted on the painting:
the one in the east has three heads; the one in the south has five heads; the one in the west has seven heads;
and the one in the north has nine heads. Each is surrounded by their respective retinues, with billowing ocean waves below and [the heavens] above.

The vapors and the retinue of the Dragon Kings are so numerous that they cannot all be depicted. Now, for each direction, four members of the retinue are painted standing on the left and right, with their respective numbers following those of the central lord.
Next, regarding the description of the scripture pavilion (*sūtra-kośa*): the pavilion is established at the center of the altar, facing east, to cover the high seat (*bhadrapīṭha*).
It is twenty feet square and nine feet high, with a central elevation resembling a roof. It is constructed from blue cloth and supported by black-lacquered wooden pillars.
Furthermore, cords dyed black are fastened to the four corners and tied down to the ground; this arrangement surrounds the perimeter of the eaves.
All were draped with *srak* (necklaces) and adorned with purity, appearing as solemn as a jeweled realm.

Next, regarding the altar, table, and seat for the presiding monk: the presiding monk shall face east. There shall be one table and one seat, both made of wood, placed slightly to the west within the high seat.
The table is two chi and six cun in height and three chi square; it is covered with blue cloth and set out.
The sutra is placed upon it and covered with a blue cloth; when reciting, the cloth is lifted. The seat is one chi and six cun high and two chi square, and it is spread with a blue cushion.

Next, the arrangement of the tables and seats for the two orders of the assembly is explained. The tables and seats for the two orders are set up on both sides of the main altar, facing each other from north to south.
There may be two or four, according to the number of persons present. The tables are nine inches high and two feet square; they are likewise made of wood.
The curtains and the canopy for the scriptures are all the same as those for the main altar. When sitting, one rests directly on the ground, which is spread with a square green mat measuring two chi.
Next, regarding the incense, flowers, and candles: there is one incense burner to offer burning incense, and two candle stands to light wax candles.
Furthermore, in front of these, set out one incense burner to use powdered incense and incense sticks, lighting them within it to burn the offered incense pellets.

Place two trays at the sides, filled with various exquisite incenses such as agallochum (*agaru*) and sandalwood (*candana*), and instruct the attendants to replenish and burn them from time to time, day and night without ceasing, to manifest sincere reverence.

Set four flower vases, each one chi and five cun in height and one chi and two cun in diameter, capable of holding three *dou* of water, at the four corners of the altar in front of the banners and lamps. Use black [ink]...
It is made of glazed porcelain. The base below is entirely black lacquered. Various kinds of fresh flowers from plants and trees are inserted within;

it is filled with powdered stone (shidai) mixed with water. Fresh water must be poured in daily so that it does not remain overnight, and the flowers must also be replaced daily with fresh and beautiful ones.
May this pure fragrance never cease, and may we pray that the dragons and devas rejoice.
Next is the explanation of the fruit offerings. For each meal, there are five vessels of milk-rice; likewise, for each meal, there are five vessels of assorted fruits.
Each vessel must have a stand, with heights and sizes appropriate to its contents. As for the fruits, one should select fresh, high-quality, and rare varieties in sufficient quantity.
Regarding those designated as "supreme offerings," the banners are described next. Twenty-eight banner-poles are used, set at the four corners of the altar, with seven at each corner.
They are made of new blue cloth, one *zhang* in length. The poles are lacquered black; their tops are adorned with copper hooks, to which the banners are attached.
Below, a black seat is used. A single pole is installed, positioned exactly at the four corners of the altar;
three poles each on the left and right, curved and embracing like a square ruler, perfectly aligned and uniform, identical on all four sides.
Next, the arrangement of the lamps is explained. There are twenty-eight lamps in total, placed at the four corners of the altar, each occupying a position corresponding to one of the seven banners.
They are made of copper, five *cun* and four *fen* in height; the upper basin is one *cun* and six *fen* deep, with a circular diameter of five *cun*.
It is supported by tiered platforms, each with a single pedestal carved with dragon patterns; pure oil burns within, emitting light day and night that illuminates everything.
The preceding ritual for the altar is now complete. Next, one should perform the rites according to the sūtra. The sūtra states:
"I now summon all the dragon kings and others to this assembly. Based on this, as one is about to pray for rain, one must first perform the invocation.

Once the altar has been established, the monastic community shall collectively observe the fast and precepts, bathe, and enter the altar with both internal and external purity. The presiding master, together with two assistants, and...
The abbot, wearing blue robes and draped in a blue vestment, arrives at the Great Hall at the hour of the Rabbit (morning).
Having offered incense and performed three prostrations before the Buddha, the presiding master raises his voice and says:
Jade dew in the azure heavens; golden ripples upon the ocean of awakening. Fragrance of the *puṇḍarīka* flower disperses through the *trichiliocosm*;
samādhi washes away deep-seated ailments. From a little water, much is made; a single drop purifies mountains and rivers. *Namo* to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva of the Cool Land.

(After the three recitations are finished, the ritual master [biaobai] holds up a pure water cup and says: Namo to the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. (Recite three times. Then, recite the verse:)

The Bodhisattva’s ambrosial water from the tip of his willow branch can cause a single drop to pervade the ten directions, completely eliminating all foul odors, impurities, and defilements, and consecrating the ritual site so that it is entirely pure.

There is a secret mantra in the teachings; we shall now reverently recite it. (The assembly recites the Great Compassion Mantra together. The Ritual Master sprinkles the consecrated water and proceeds slowly.

First, he circumambulates inside the main hall to the right, then exits the hall and circumambulates outside one circuit to the right. Gradually descending from the altar, he circumambulates back up to the altar three times. When this is finished, each person returns to their position. Once everyone is standing still, the Ritual Master strikes the chime.)

[Recite the mantra. (Raising [the incense]): Namo to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King of Amṛta. (Three prostrations. After a short pause, the Abbot leaves his seat, proceeds to the center, and offers incense.
Next, the Ritual Master and then the Abbot each offer incense. Having returned to their positions and standing facing upward, they chant the Incense Praise.)
The fields are cracked like tortoise shells; the drought-demon brings calamity. The masses of people pray with devotion, all rushing in haste; the grain crops suffer grievous injury.

We pray for the descent of the precious nectar, so that the entire world may obtain refreshing coolness. (Recite "Fragrant Cloud Canopy" three times. The Ritual Master says: With single-minded devotion, we pay homage from the crown of our heads.

The Three Jewels, eternally abiding throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm (three prostrations. The Dharma Master calms his mind and enters contemplation, visualizing all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of dragon kings and holy beings of the ten directions, who all behold him from afar with their divine eyes, hear him from afar with their divine ears, and fully know his thoughts with their knowledge of others' minds.

Knowing that this Great Qing Nation, in such-and-such a province and such-and-such a prefecture, has suffered from a long drought without rain, they have all descended here, having been invited according to the sutras through the ritual construction of this altar.
Having visualized their arrival, he then says:)

With reverence, we open the Tathāgata’s exposition of the Dharma; we have frequently proclaimed the Sūtra for Requesting Rain. As the wheel and canopy began, the profound meaning of practicing compassion was wonderfully revealed.
A high seat was prepared and yellow earth spread upon it, as a pure altar was devoutly consecrated; bright lamps were lit to illuminate the azure banners.

In accordance with the sutras, we invoke the deities; thereby suffering is extinguished and joy is bestowed. Through the spiritual efficacy of the various dragons, clouds arise and moisture flows down, bringing great delight to all classes of people.
Today, in the Great Qing Empire, in [Province], [Prefecture], for [Year] and [Month], a severe drought has persisted for a long time.

The crops are half withered, on the verge of becoming a famine. Therefore, in accordance with the sutras, we have established this altar to pray for the descent of sweet rain, so as to save the myriad beings.

The people [responded]. However, they feared that there might be errors in the altar rituals or deficiencies in the monastic precepts, such that the practice would fail to accord with the Dharma and thus be difficult to invoke spiritual resonance.

They heard with urgency that the Great Cakra Vidyā-mantra can eliminate these faults. With sincere devotion, the assembly together recited the Great Cakra Vidyārāja-mantra seven times to stabilize the altar rituals.

(The mantra is found in the *Śrī-bali-vidhi*; having recited it seven times, the Dharma Master, the ritual officiant, and the abbot all opened the beginning of the scripture and invoked the opening of the sutra.)
One hundred and eighty-eight dragon kings, all together holding incense burners and burning incense, the ritual master proclaims:
"With single-minded devotion, we invoke [Name] Dragon King, and so forth. (Invoke ten kings at a time; after each invocation, append the concluding phrase:

"We pray that you, by means of the knowledge of others' minds and the power of supernatural travel, in accordance with the Buddha’s command above and out of compassion for sentient beings below, come swiftly to this province."
"Sweet rain.

When the final recitation has concluded, the Dharma Master kneels long on his knees, joins his palms, and, in accordance with the sūtra, directly performs the rite of Great Compassion and recites the mantra for bestowing all happiness.
Having finished, the Dharma Master and the表白師 (the Invocation Master) then ring their bells slowly.
Having recited the mantra three times in a slow and clear manner, and having finished playing the drums and cymbals, the Dharma Master strikes the chime once.
After further reciting the prose sections of the scripture, he again follows the text to invite all the Tathāgatas. All participants hold incense burners together and burn incense.
The officiant then proclaims:

With single-minded devotion, I entreat [Name] Tathāgata. (Recite one invocation for every ten names. Having completed the invocations, continue with the concluding phrase: May all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, [grant their grace].
He exercises unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), commanding that such-and-such a province quickly send down sweet rain.
[The ritual is performed] by fifty-four persons in six rounds of invocation. When the final round of invocation is completed, the Dharma Master remains kneeling for a long time with palms joined;
he strikes the *qing* once and directly recites the scriptural text on the responsive manifestations, as well as the efficacy of the mantra-holding.
Rising to one's feet, the ritual master (biaobai) strikes the bell, and all chant the mantra in unison, reciting it slowly and clearly three times.

After the sounding of the chime and the striking of the drum and cymbals are finished, the Dharma Master stands and makes his announcement, and they together recite the mantra eleven times, each time three repetitions. When this is completed:
The chime is struck. After the drums and cymbals have been sounded, the Dharma Master strikes the sounding-block and recites the scriptural injunctions from the sutra in six sections.
For each section, he recites the mantra three times. Upon completion, the chime is struck and the cymbals are sounded again. The Dharma Master kneels long with palms joined;

after striking the chime once, he recites according to the sutra the ritual for binding the altar. Once this is perfected, he rises and, together with the *biaobai* (officiant), holds up the incense burner.
Verse of Dedication. One prostration for each line. The officiant and the assembly chant in unison:
"The merit of this supreme practice for seeking rain, And all its boundless, victorious blessings, I dedicate.
May every region suffering from drought Swiftly receive abundant, sweet rains. This is for urgent relief as if against a blazing fire; it is performed to quickly eliminate obstacles.
May rain fall. We pray that the Triple Gem, along with the dragons and devas, out of compassion for sentient beings, will cause rain to fall according to the season.
All Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time; all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; the Great Prajñāpāramitā. (Having completed the triple refuge, descend from the altar.)
The masters of incense and lamps at this altar must protect it with all their hearts; no idle or miscellaneous persons shall be allowed to intrude.
After the second watch in the afternoon, the Dharma Master, the Second Chief Ritual Official, and the Abbot—these four individuals—shall enter the altar.

They will strike the fish-shaped gong and chant the *Vṛṣṭi-sūtra* (Rain-Requesting Sutra) aloud. Thus they shall request rain in the morning and chant in the afternoon, continuing daily without interruption until [the goal] is attained.

The heavy rain then ceased. Aside from this altar, ten monks—fewer than four being unacceptable—were to be assigned in rotation within a nearby hall to take turns reciting the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* twenty-one times and the sacred name of Avalokiteśvara one thousand times.

Upon completing the dedication of merit, they were to perform twelve prostrations to Avalokiteśvara. After the Three Refuges were concluded, the second shift would be changed to take over the fish-bowl. As before...
This ritual cycle continues day and night without ceasing to seek swift rain. All matters concerning the supreme offerings and other rites follow the standard protocol.
On the spirit tablet, inscribe:
"Homage to the Dragon King of Infinite Adorned Ocean-Clouds, Majestic Power Wheel-Covering, together with his entire retinue."

(When the upper offerings are completed, recite the hymn: The Dragon Kings and the assembly of holy ones possess immeasurable majesty and virtue. Respectfully obeying the Buddha’s command, they scatter the crystal nectar. With great compassion, they descend upon the ritual arena, providing moistening and refreshing coolness;
their flowing drops fill the ten directions. *Nema*! To the Dragon Kings, the assembly of holy ones, and the Bodhisattvas at the Cloud-Wheel Assembly.

(Recite three times. Attach the draft of the rain-prayer petition. This petition should be written in four copies. On the first day of the rite, perform the transformation at three locations. Alternatively, prepare paper talismans for the three officials and [perform] together with the three...)

The ritual manual states: It is even more marvelous to place each [paper talisman] in the hands of the officials to be transformed. Offer one to the Triple Gem, one to the various devas, and one to the various nāga kings. Retain one path for daily recitation until the rain has ceased. Then, perform a great circumambulation toward the sun and burn the talismans.

The Commentary states: We humbly observe that excessive drought has brought disaster, causing all things to wither; this is a punishment sent down from Heaven due to the many transgressions of the people below.
Only the Buddhas open the gate of compassion, and thus divine mantras possess the power to respond to prayers for averting calamity.

For this reason, we respectfully give rise to a sincere heart and establish a rain-praying ritual site (*dharmapūjā-maṇḍala*). We humbly set forth our circumstances, looking up in hope that you will deign to hear us.

Now, according to the Great Qing Empire, in such-and-such province, such-and-such prefecture, such-and-such county, at such-and-such monastery, the presiding monk is [Name] (if the local officials are the petitioners, their names and titles should be listed one by one).
On this day, with a devoted mind, we offer incense and take refuge in the Great Cloud-Wheel Lord, Śākyamuni.
To the Buddhas of the Ten Directions, the assembly of Buddhas, sages, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, and the honored deities presiding over affairs beneath their lotus seats:
We respectfully submit our petition. It is because in this locality, at this particular time, there has been a prolonged drought for many days with little rain falling.
Springs and sources have dried up, and all things are withered and parched. The common people suffer as if being roasted in a cauldron. The officials...

Office-bearers, our anxiety is like that of one being parched by heat. We have heard that within the Buddhist teachings there is the *Mahāmegha-vṛṣṭi-saṃpādana-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, which is most efficacious in invoking spiritual resonance.
Therefore, on such-and-such a day, we, [Name] and others, shall inaugurate the ceremony and offer prayers according to the Dharma, assembling a great multitude of monks.

I have empowered this scripture and its dhāraṇī; yet, fearing that the ritual principles may not be exhaustive and the rites may not accord with the Dharma, it may be difficult to move the dragons and devas to grant pardon, and thus a sweet rain may not immediately descend.

For this reason, I respectfully prepare this memorial to first petition the Triple Gem and the assembly of holy beings, next to petition the various devas of the three realms, and finally to petition the assembly of dragon kings and spirits. I beg you to deign to look upon me with compassion and take pity on all sentient beings.

May the transgressions of those sharing the same vocation be pardoned, and may the grace of universal equality be bestowed. May clouds and thunder arise from the mountains and rivers so that rain falls in profusion;
may the living beings be rescued from their plight amidst the mire and fire—this indeed is a difficult task!

Next, we pray that the Wind Lord and Rain Master will receive our offerings above and provide protection below, while the Deity of Crops and the Earth Lord will fulfill their duties with heartfelt concern. Thus, may these abundant crops likewise yield a harvest in autumn, and may the seasons be harmonious.

The harvests have been bountiful, and the myriad people delight in their vocations. With utmost sincerity, I prostrate myself and submit this memorial. (First Memorial) Respectfully offered for the Three Jewels to bear witness beneath the Golden Lotus Platform.
(Second Memorial) May the various heavens clearly discern [this] beneath the Jewel Throne. (Third Memorial) May the Dragon Deities and all other deities [bear witness] beneath the Jewel Throne.
On the [day] of the [month] of the [year]. We, the presiding abbot [Name] and others, respectfully submit this ninefold petition.

Attached: Inscription for the Hall. *Mahāmegha-cakra-maṇḍala* (This inscription is to be hung in the center of the corridor below this hall, together with the couplets on both sides; all shall be written in formal script using white powder on black paper).
A great downpour of sweet rain fell; the fields were thereby nourished and sustained.
Vastly spread was the beneficent grace; grasses and trees were clothed in life and growth.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: The ritual procedures for praying for rain are all excerpted from the Buddhist scriptures; it is only in the matters of establishing the altar, arranging the seats, and hoisting banners...

The production of images of the Buddhas and so forth involves vast expenditures. While it is naturally easy to arrange if performed by lay officials, if it is undertaken out of devotion by the monastic community, one may substitute paper and wood for gold and silk; it requires only sincere devotion and meticulous care.
Furthermore, since the sutra contains the passage stating that even when rain falls indiscriminately, this scripture can cause it to cease, it is evident that this sutra also [possesses such power].

It may be used for praying for clear weather; however, one should simply change the two characters "xiángzhù" (descending dew) in the liturgical text to "sùzhǐ" (swiftly ceasing), change "qǐyǔ" (requesting rain) to "qǐqíng" (requesting clear weather), and furthermore, it is appropriate to replace the wording of the memorial (*shūyǔ*). This is my humble opinion and private deliberation.

I respectfully submit this to your lofty wisdom. Furthermore, I have established another altar to recite the Great Compassion Mantra (*Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī*), praying that it may swiftly grant its response.
As it is said: "If whatever one seeks is not fulfilled, it cannot be called the Great Compassion Heart Dhāraṇī."

If, in mountain villages or remote wildernesses, the matter is not one handled by local officials, one need only invite authentic high monks from near and far to seek fulfillment with utmost sincerity according to their respective specializations;
even so, they can cause rain to fall. The *Brief Record of Miraculous Responses at Yunqi Huayan* states:
There was a monk named Daoying, son of the Chen family, a native of Puxian County. At the age of eighteen, his father—

He arranged for him to marry, and they lived together for five years, vowing never to touch one another. Later, following Master Faju from Bing County, he listened to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and subsequently shaved his head.
He entered Youshi and Baiti Monasteries on Mount Taihang to practice *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
During a severe drought, he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to pray for rain; two old men, each attended by two youths, would come at times.

While listening to the lecture, Ying was struck by his extraordinary appearance and questioned him; he then realized he was a sea deity. Consequently, Ying said, "Now act as my patron and please send down a light rain.
The old man commanded his two youths, and the youths immediately emerged from the window opening. In a short while, a great rain poured down in torrents.
People both far and near all relied upon him. This [account] concerns his lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and how he moved Heaven so that timely rain poured down in torrents.

Furthermore, the *Fahua chiyen ji* (Records of Miracles of the Lotus Sūtra) states: During the second year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, Dharma Master Yun Guang was summoned to the inner palace to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, whereupon heavenly rain fell as precious flowers.
During the Tianjian era, when the Emperor suffered from a severe drought, he questioned Master Zhi. The Master said: "Yun..."
He was able to bring forth rain. The Emperor consequently requested him to preach the *Lotus Sūtra*. When he reached the section on "Universal Moistening," it rained heavily;
the high and low lands were all sufficiently saturated. This was an instance of rain being moved by his preaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Furthermore, it is said that during the Sui dynasty, at Nantianzhu Monastery, there was the monk Zhen Guan of the Fan family from Qiantang. From his youth, he possessed extraordinary features; his tongue was purple with a rosette pattern, and his left...
On his right hand was the mark of a *ṛṣi*. He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* every day, fixedly completing one section. In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, there was a severe drought;

at that time, he was invited to lecture on the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, whereupon heavy rain poured down in torrents. This was an instance of bringing rain by lecturing on the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
Furthermore, it is said that during the Song dynasty, there was the monk Zhongli of Mingzhou, a son of the Chen family from Yin. At the age of seven...

He left the household life and was granted the title Mingzhi (Wisdom of Enlightenment). During the Xining era, he resided at Nanhu and succeeded Shenzhi on the dharma seat, daily proclaiming the teachings of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
During the Yuanyou era, he again took charge of Yanqing Temple, where he practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* repentance ritual for seven years.
As the practice was nearing completion, one day while in meditative contemplation, he saw a great boat with the Master seated in its center traveling along. From this point on, his eloquence...

A spring of wisdom gushed forth. The Master recited the *Lotus Sūtra* more than ten thousand times; in his rites for averting disasters and praying for rain, there was no instance where the divine efficacy did not manifest.
This was because he had recited the *Lotus Sūtra* while concurrently practicing repentance, thereby bringing about rain.

It is further said that in the Song dynasty, at Mount Daowei in Kuaiji, the monk Zongli, having received full ordination, went to Gusu and relied upon Shenwu to practice the *Lotus Sūtra* for a full three years. Suddenly—
He beheld Samantabhadra, who passed before him traveling through the air. He then proceeded to the new city’s emerald pond and devotedly practiced the *nien-fo* samādhi.
In the first year of the Zhenghe era, during a drought, he prayed for rain; the Dragon King manifested his golden body, and sweet rain fell in abundance.
This was rain brought about through the recollection of the Buddha. Furthermore, the *Record of Experiences of Vajradhara* states:

During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, in the third year [715 CE], Lü Wenzhan served as the Vice Magistrate of Langzhong County. He had a refined fondness for Buddhist scriptures and devoted his mind especially to the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, reaching more than thirty thousand recitations.
His spiritual responses were extraordinary. As he grew old and his years declined, his three front teeth fell out simultaneously. Suddenly—
His life was as it had been before. While he was in Langzhong, a severe drought occurred. The Provincial Governor, Liu Jun, ordered him to pray for rain;

after he had recited the scripture only once, a torrential downpour ensued. Furthermore, during a period of heavy rains, the Regional Inspector again ordered him to chant the sutra to pray for clear weather, and the skies cleared immediately.
This was an instance of reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to induce rain. Moreover, at the end of the Ming dynasty, in Hangzhou, Master Lianchi...
The Master returned to Hangzhou after his period of study and, wishing to seek a secluded mountain retreat to cultivate the Way, saw that Yunqi Valley was serene and quiet;
he thus halted his travels there and built a thatched hut. At that time, a severe drought occurred, and the villagers requested the Master to pray for rain.

The Master said, "I, an old monk, stay here knowing only how to recite the Buddha’s name; I possess no incantations or arts for praying for rain. The villagers replied, "We only ask that the Great Master recite it."
The Buddha, having granted his request, emerged from the mountains and practiced *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation) at Tianban. Rain soon arrived;
the villagers, moved by his virtue, joyfully provided assistance, and thus a Buddhist monastery (*brahmacarya-sthāna*) was established. This, too, was brought about by means of *nienfo*.

Therefore, one knows that for prayers for rain to be effective, they must rely entirely upon the merit accumulated by a high monk throughout his daily life to achieve spiritual resonance. Furthermore, it requires the patron to offer sincere prayers according to the Dharma.

Only then would it be appropriate. If the host does not observe the fast and precepts, and the monastic community lacks virtue and morality, then even if one performs the ritual as a mere matter of social obligation, it will be difficult to move the favor of Heaven.

This may even descend to such a state of clamor and impurity, with wine, meat, and frivolous play; in such cases, not only will there be no spiritual resonance, but it will be utterly contrary to the Way.
There are further transgressions.

Regarding the ritual for praying for snow, no tradition has been transmitted. I privately believe that one may adapt and apply the methods for praying for rain through expedient means. Master Wuzu Yan once said:
The opening verse of the recitation states: "Of the year, only this month remains; yet the heavens have never seen snow fall.
We announce to the dragon deities of the three realms: let each of you inform one another, so that silver may be spread across the heavens and the earth, appearing both timely and seasonal.
Furthermore, we hope for the compassion of the great assembly to recite divine mantras and provide their assistance. This is appended here.

Regarding the Dispatching of Locusts: Whenever the dispatching of locusts occurs, the urgency is like fire. Although there is no specific sutra for dispatching locusts, there is an ancient ritual for petitioning Heaven.

First, the Guest Hall (Kètáng) notifies the Abbot (Fāngzhàng); next, a plaque is hung [with the inscription] "Dispatching Locusts" (qiànhuáng). This plaque is suspended above the Main Gate (Shānmén). Furthermore, a plaque is hung in front of the Guest Hall [reading]: "The..."
On the [day] of the [month], I, the Dharma-protector [Name], for the purpose of dispelling locusts, recited the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* for several days.

On the [day] at the fifth watch of dawn, I made offerings to the deities and performed prostrations according to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Repentance Ritual* for several days, praying for the clearing away of locusts and a bountiful harvest for the year.
The myriad people delight in their vocations. The illustrious names of the various masters are listed below: Master [Name], Master [Name].
Other ritual protocols are explained in the subsequent section on the Abbot’s duties under the heading of "Recitation. Herein is recorded the format for the memorial petition (*shu*):
Now, according to the Great Qing Dynasty, in the [Province] of [Place], the [District] of [Place], at the [Temple] of [Place], the Abbot is [Name] (or, if the official has recently passed away).

[Insert the name of] the host, or a local resident, or an official (whichever is appropriate, write their name and title in full). On this day, with prostrations and the offering of incense, I take refuge in the Lord of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Assembly, the Benevolent and Compassionate Honored One.

To the various deities stationed within the assembly of Radiant Light—the Brahmās, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, the spirits of the physical realm, and the holy hosts who oversee affairs—beneath all these precious thrones, I respectfully communicate my purpose. I reflect deeply that locusts are swarming like clouds...

O Heaven, we can only worry about the impending calamity of famine. Fearing that the lingering remnants [of the plague] have entered the earth and will spread like creeping vines beyond remedy, it is impossible to take effective measures through human effort alone unless they are driven out by divine power.

Therefore, on the [blank] day of this month, I have reverently summoned a sincere heart to inaugurate a ritual arena for the expulsion of locusts and the protection of the seedlings. Daily, I shall commission monks to chant the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

Sutra: At the fifth watch, offerings are made to the devas, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* repentance ritual is performed. We humbly pray that by this merit, calamitous insects may be eliminated, and wind and rain may be cleansed;
that their species may be swept away without remainder, and they may be cast into the rivers and streams to be transformed according to their own karmic retributions.
The people find peace in their vocations; all things flourish in their natural growth. We, [Name], cannot bear our pressing urgency and look up toward you with the utmost devotion. [Date].

The Abbot, [Name], and the local officials, [Name], prostrate themselves nine times and respectfully submit this memorial. (On the first day of the ritual, burn one copy of this petition to present to the celestial court;

keep another on the altar to be recited daily until the locusts cease, at which point it is returned to the assembly and burned as a dedication. Upon the conclusion of each recitation, chant the hymn of praise.)

Protecting the seedlings and guarding the crops, the presiding deity honors the sacred spirits. Driving away locusts, she brings prosperity to the people’s livelihood. Luxuriant ears of grain fill the field ridges; vegetables and fruits are fresh and abundant.
For this protection and nourishment, my gratitude is profound. Recite "Naima Xiaozazhang Pusa" (Bodhisattva Who Eliminates Calamities and Obstacles) three times.
All other matters, such as the superior offerings and so forth, shall follow the usual ritual procedures. This includes the dedication of merit upon the cessation of locusts;
the "Assembly for Protecting Green Seedlings" from other texts is also subsumed herein.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Locusts are a calamity sent by Heaven. According to ancient regulations, one recites the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and performs the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-pūjā*, making offerings to the various devas, thereby attaining swift and efficacious response.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" in the second fascicle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*: "This sūtra can illuminate the palaces of all the devas; this sūtra can bring joy to sentient beings."
...joyful. ...Furthermore, this sutra can eliminate the famine of high grain prices, and so forth. Moreover, the "Chapter on Goddess Puṇyavatī" states:
"By these causes and conditions, the essence of the earth increases; the Earth Deities and all the devas are filled with joy;

and the sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, and fruits of the sown rice and grains flourish and grow luxuriantly," and so forth. Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Earth Deity Dharaṇī" states: By means of...
For this reason, within Jambudvīpa, medicinal herbs, trees, roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits flourish and grow luxuriantly;
their beautiful colors, fragrances, and flavors are all fully perfected, and so forth. Furthermore, the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" states: "By the power of this sutra..."
The various devas rejoiced, and the hundred grains and all fruits became lush and abundant, and so forth.

According to this, it can be seen that this sutra truly has the power to dispel locusts and ensure total abundance and ripeness. It is only right that it be widely circulated everywhere and recited in every place.
If this is practiced constantly and without interruption, the world will be at peace, calamities will be dispelled, and blessings will increase; nothing surpasses this sutra for these purposes.

Thus, the Tang Dynasty translation refers to it as the "King of Sutras, Most Victorious. It is a pity that, recently, apart from the Water-Land Hall (Shuilu Tang), this is rarely seen or heard of in the world.
If there is no copy of this sutra in remote mountain areas or secluded places, one may take the portion contained within the *Daily Recitation of the Chan School* (Chanmen Risi).
The Ritual Protocol for the *Zhaitian* (Fasting for the Devas) begins with "From the Jade Dew of the Azure Heaven" and concludes with the "Praise to the Vast Compassion of the Buddha.
It may also be performed by chanting the entire scroll; however, one should simply change "Wholeheartedly Entreat" (*yixin fengqing*) to "Wholeheartedly Prostrate" (*yixin dingli*).
The *Record of Miraculous Responses of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* states: "The Song dynasty monk Congli was a native of Xiangyang. He resided at Pingtian Monastery in Taizhou..."
He was secluded, grave, and silent, never manifesting joy or anger on his countenance. In his daily life, he invariably maintained the precepts with profound sincerity.
During the Qianhua era of the Liang dynasty, there was a summer drought; the assembly requested the Master to pray for rain.

He subsequently recited the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, and after three days, rain was moved to fall. When King Qian Wusuku heard of this, he summoned him to the palace and established a *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* repentance hall.
...and so forth. Based on this, since it can bring rain, it must also be able to drive away locusts;
however, this requires a virtuous monk of high caliber who is easily moved by spiritual resonance, as it is not something that ordinary, mediocre people can accomplish.
Alternatively, one may also substitute for him by sincerely reciting the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī. As it is said: "If all that is sought is not fulfilled..."
This is not the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī. Rather, seek it by taking the place of reality;
then every dharma will be capable of responding, and one’s prayers to Vaiśravaṇa will be answered.

Whenever a famine occurs and the monastery’s provisions are about to be exhausted, or for matters such as new construction or repairs, the Rector (Vina) and the two orders of officials shall inform the Abbot;
having done so, they will set a fixed date. Externally, they shall invite a solicitor to announce the matter to potential donors.

Internally, the Guest Hall shall post a notice (the plaque reads): "From the [day] of this month, upon hearing the sound of the bell, the assembly of masters shall don their ceremonial robes and proceed together to the Great Hall (or the Vaiśravaṇa Hall) to recite the *Śubhadevatā-dhāraṇī* and offer prayers to Vaiśravaṇa.

The Guest Hall shall request the Secretary to prepare two draft petitions in advance (the matters addressed and the phrasing must be appropriate). One is for the commencement of the propagation of the teachings, to inform the sagely ears.

1. The Ritual for the Complete Propagation of the Teaching: At each session, after two periods (ban) of the day have passed (or after the opening of the minor retreat), the bell is struck three times.

The assembly gathers; the Guest Master invites the Abbot to offer incense. After the Rector has recited the Incense Praise, they chant "Namu" to the Dharma-protecting Bodhisattva Weituo Zuntian three times.
