descending from the five turbidities, he manifested his birth (at the Mountain Gate). He cast off precious robes and donned tattered garments, fanning the true wind in the final age.

He abandoned the illusory city and ascended to the Treasure Place, raising the sun of wisdom in the midst of heaven (under the eaves of the Great Hall). Without Buddha and without Māra, he proclaims the Dharma in every land.
Proclaiming the True Dharma: neither defiled nor pure, may every mote of dust bathe the golden body (outside the Scripture Recitation Hall).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: Lately, monasteries have merely provided images of the Prince’s birth, yet have not been heard to perform the rite of bathing the Buddha;
this is truly a deficiency in the ritual tradition. The *Buddhabhiseka-sūtra* appears in the "Cai" (才) volume of the Ming-Qing Tripitaka. According to what is taught in the sūtra, first—
Construct a square altar, using pure clay mixed with scented water for its center. Spread out a mat, and upon a bathing platform placed on the seat, set a bathing basin.
Inside the basin, place a small bathing bed, and upon that bed, install an image of Prince Siddhārtha.
Each person shall take a small amount of water with two fingers to bathe the Buddha while reciting verses and mantras. The water used for bathing the Buddha [is then to be distributed] by each...
Washing one's own head is called "Auspicious Water" (*maṅgala-jala*). After bathing, one uses cotton to wipe oneself clean, and then offers [the water] upon the seat, and so forth.
This Buddhist practice encompasses the entire body of the Tathāgata’s teachings throughout his lifetime. Now, I shall record its origins and development in full to instruct beginners.
According to Indian tradition, the land is divided into five great kingdoms: East, South, West, North, and Central. The Buddha was born in Central India (*Madhyadeśa*).
In the kingdom of Kapilavastu, of the imperial lineage, his caste was Kṣatriya and his clan Gautama. In Sanskrit, Gautama translates here as "sugarcane.
His progenitor, a royal seer (rājarṣi), was killed by a hunter’s arrow; his blood entered the earth and produced two stalks of sugarcane.
When they were opened by the sun's heat, one produced a son named King Ikṣvāku, and one produced a daughter, Queen Bhadrā, who bore him sons.

He became a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) and was called the Solar Clan (Sūryavaṃśa) because he was scorched by the sun; his lineage continued for seven hundred generations until reaching King Śuddhodana.
After fulfilling his meritorious practices over many kalpas, the Buddha descended from the Tuṣita Heaven into the womb of Queen Māyā at the palace.
This occurred in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, though some say it was the twenty-sixth year, the Jia-Yin year.
In the fourth month of the year, he was born and named Sarvārthasiddha. Seven days later, his mother ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
he was then nursed by his maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī. When he reached the age of nineteen, he leaped over the city walls and went to the forest of the seer Udraka Rāmaputra.
There, he took up a sword to cut off his hair, cast off his precious robes, and exchanged them for a *kāṣāya* from a hunter to wear as his garment.
Kāśyapa traveled to several places where sages practiced their studies. He then crossed the Ganges River to the north and reached Mount Gayā, where he sat in meditation for six years.
To sustain his vital energy, he practiced asceticism, consuming only one sesame seed and one grain of barley per day. He further reflected:
"If I were to attain the Way with such a weakened body, those non-Buddhists would claim that self-starvation is the cause of Nirvāṇa. Thereupon, he bathed in...
At the Nairañjanā River, he accepted the milk-rice from the cowherd maiden and proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Śakra-devendra spread out auspicious kusha grass for him to sit upon; there, he sat cross-legged and made this vow: "If I do not attain the Way, I shall not rise from this seat.
Māra Pāpīyān sought to harass and persecute him, yet despite a hundred stratagems, he could not disturb him in the slightest. Māra then spoke these words: "You now..."
"You ought to rise quickly and return to the palace; if you do not, I shall seize your feet and cast you beyond the great ocean.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, like a lion king, was without fear or alarm and addressed Pāpīyas:
"In the past, you made offerings to a Pratyekabuddha and observed the eightfold precepts of the fast; by virtue of this merit, you have become a heavenly king. However, I have already—"
Throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), I have fully accomplished difficult and ascetic practices.
There is not even a space as small as the tip of a needle on this great earth that was not a place where I practiced asceticism in the past.
Even if the hosts of Māra were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they could not cause a single hair of mine to tremble. How is it that you now wish to hurl my body beyond the great ocean?
Māra spoke again, saying: "In the past, I gave alms to a Pratyekabuddha and thereby attained the status of a celestial king;
this matter is clear. As for what you have now said, what proof do you have? Thereupon, the Bodhisattva extended his hand and pointed to the earth, saying: "This one shall know me.
At that moment, the Earth Deity emerged from the adamantine foundation of the earth, joined her palms, and said: "Truly..."

"As Your Reverence has instructed, from this place onward, I shall serve as its deity. There is not even a space here the size of a needle’s point that is not a place where the Bodhisattva has practiced his fundamental conduct.
When Māra heard these words, he fell down in confusion, prostrated himself, repented of his transgressions, and departed.
Having thus defeated the army of Māra, on the eighth day of the second month, at the moment the morning star appeared, he attained sudden and great enlightenment.

He attained the Unsurpassed Way and realized the Most Perfect Enlightenment. According to worldly tradition, this was on the eighth day of the twelfth month, because the Zhou calendar begins with the eleventh month (the *zǐ* branch).
At that time, he was thirty years of age; it was at the Aranya site of Bodhi in the kingdom of Magadha.
For the sake of the Great Vehicle, he expounded the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for the Bodhisattvas; those of the Small Vehicle neither saw nor heard it, remaining like the deaf and blind.

Upon being entreated by Brahmā and Śakra, he then proceeded to the Deer Park, where for five people, including Kauṇḍinya, he preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and the causes and effects of humans and devas.
This continued for twelve years, at which time he was forty-two years old; thereafter, he arrived at the Vaipulya assembly.
Above, by means of the Mahāyāna teachings, he turned the Great Wheel of Dharma and expounded the Dharma of the Six Perfections to refine his disciples.

He preached such sūtras as the Vimalakīrti and the Laṅkāvatāra for eight years; this was when the Buddha was fifty years old, during which time he primarily taught the Prajñāpāramitā to refine their attachments.
Another twenty-two years passed; at that time, the Buddha was seventy-two years old, and he preached the Lotus Sūtra, continuing until the eighth [year].

In the year [of the cycle], as all his disciples were capable of bearing great responsibility, he bestowed upon them the prediction of their future Buddhahood; only then would his original intention be fully realized.
This was the *wenshen* year, the fifty-third year of King Mu’s reign. At that time, the Buddha was seventy-nine years old and was about to manifest his *nirvāṇa*.
He first went to the Tuṣita Heaven (*Tuṣita-deva-loka*) to preach the Dharma for his mother. There, he also taught the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī, and five hundred bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and seventy thousand arhats, unable to bear witnessing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, entered extinction simultaneously.
On the fifteenth day of the second month of the following year, the Buddha was outside the city of Kuśinagara.

The time for Parinirvāṇa had arrived; the ten realms all assembled and each presented exquisite offerings, yet the Buddha accepted none of them. Finally, Cunda presented an offering, which the Buddha did accept.
For the sake of the bhikṣus, he expounded upon permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and commanded them to take the precepts as their teacher and to dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness.
He further declared: "The unsurpassed True Dharma has now been entirely entrusted to Mahākāśyapa."
"Kāśyapa, I shall serve as a great refuge for you all, just as the Tathāgata has been.
Furthermore, because Ānanda was being harassed by Māra outside the Śāla grove, I commanded Mañjuśrī, saying:

'Ānanda, my younger brother, who has served me for more than twenty years and attained the eight inconceivable qualities; he hears the Dharma and receives it with retention, like water poured into a vessel.'"
Desiring that they should receive and uphold this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Mañjuśrī received the command and, by means of a mantra, subdued Māra and brought Ānanda back.
The Buddha said, "There is a brahmin named Subhadra, one hundred and twenty years of age, who has not yet abandoned his arrogance.
You should inform him that the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa at midnight. He then returned with him; having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, [Subhadra attained realization].
He attained arhatship. The Buddha addressed the great assembly: "Since I attained the Way and delivered Kauṇḍinya, this is the last, Sūbadhara, whom I have delivered.
My task is now complete. On the night of the fifteenth day of the second month, at midnight, I shall preach the *Śāsanānuśāsanī-sūtra*."
He further extended his sincere exhortation: "You bhikṣus, after my parinirvāṇa, you must revere the Prātimokṣa;
it shall be your great teacher, no different from my remaining in the world," and so forth.

Then, beneath the twin trees, he lay on his right side and entered the successive meditative absorptions (dhyāna) in both forward and reverse order, twenty-seven times in total, remaining silent and still.

[The Buddha] turned [the coffin] around three times and addressed the great assembly. Taking the Great Parinirvāṇa—the true reality of ultimate emptiness—as his fundamental source, he entered parinirvāṇa.
His disciple Anuruddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and informed Lady Māyā;

descending from heaven, the World-Honored One rose from his coffin and preached the Dharma to comfort his mother. He then spoke again to Ānanda: "You should know that for the sake of future generations..."
Because of the sentient beings who are unfilial, [the Buddha] emerged from the golden coffin and inquired after his mother’s health.
When seven days had passed, Kāśyapa emerged from his meditative absorption and, knowing that the Buddha had entered *nirvāṇa*, traveled on foot with five hundred disciples from Vulture Peak Mountain.
With choked sobs, he paid homage. The Buddha manifested his two feet emerging from the coffin; at that time, it had already been fourteen days. Humans and devas each held...
The fragrant wood was brought to the site of the cremation, where he transformed it into fire to self-immolate. It was only after seven days that the process was complete.
The assembly collected his relics, which filled eight golden urns. Eight kings, including Ajātaśatru, vied with one another to seize the relics, but they eventually heeded counsel and desisted.
The eight kingdoms each requested one golden casket to take back to their own countries for veneration.
One hundred years later, King Aśoka again collected all the *śarīra* relics and commanded those possessed of supernatural powers to construct eighty-four thousand stūpas in a single night.
Each stūpa was to enshrine one relic. He further commanded the Arhat Venerable Yaśas to distribute the eighty-four thousand [relics].
Guang followed the light to distribute the śarīra relics to the stupas. The eight classes of beings, both human and celestial, all received their portions.

According to ancient records and oral traditions in my land of Zhendan, there were nineteen such stupas. Among them, the most renowned for its spiritual power today is the single stupa at Ayuwang Temple in Ningbo.

Regarding the Buddha’s Attainment of Enlightenment (in other versions, before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one first recites the incense hymn (*xiangzan*), then offers the formal petition (*baigongwen*); once the petition is finished, the offerings are presented; this sequence is the reverse of the present case). On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, the Buddha attained enlightenment.

The Guest Hall shall post the notice in advance on that day. In the evening, at the second board, the assembly bows to the Buddha. On the actual day, from the offering of prayers for the Emperor (*zhusheng*) up to the ascending of the hall to preach the Dharma, the procedures are the same as those for the Buddha’s Birthday.

On this day, after the midday meal, offerings are prepared before the Buddha. When the assembly gathers, incense is burned and the censers are passed. The Abbot offers incense. The Rector (*weina*) intones the hymn. The Abbot performs three prostrations, does not withdraw his sitting cloth, and remains kneeling while presenting tea, vegetables, and other offerings—all of which are delivered by the attendants. The Guest Master sets out the tables and places the items upon them.

[The Master] raises [the incense burner], performs three prostrations, and stands. Upon reaching the *Nian puguangyang zhou* (Mantra of Universal Offering), he remains kneeling. The *Weina* (Choir Leader) steps forward from the ranks, offers incense, spreads his ritual implements, and performs three prostrations. Kneeling for a long duration with palms joined, he makes the formal announcement (*baizuo*). This procedure applies to all offerings made before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; one need only alter the wording of the announcement.
I reverently hear that the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood after immeasurable kalpas; how could he have required further cultivation?
Out of compassion for sentient beings who remain unaware in their daily lives, he manifested his prior awakening to awaken both himself and others, thereby perfecting the Way of Enlightenment.

Throughout the mundane and supramundane realms, he is honored as the World-Honored One. He expounded the transformative rites of this age and followed the legacy of previous Buddhas, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree at the palace of Māra.
Hidden and without radiance, the Udumbara flower has appeared; the Wheel of Dharma blazes forth and turns eternally.

Thus, at the beginning, it was likened to the first light of the rising sun, while at the end, the plucking of the flower was shown as the authentic transmission. As for this descendant, what does he know? Yet reciting the bequeathed words, he feels a sense of solemn urgency.
On the eighth day of this month, we reverently encounter the anniversary of the Tathāgata’s attainment of enlightenment. We, the assembly gathered here, offer a modest tribute of worship.

May it be our wish that form and emptiness, light and darkness, all proclaim the subtle and wondrous sound of the Dharma; and may all wriggling and moving sentient beings together realize the marks and characteristics of wisdom and virtue.

(Having finished the recitation, perform one prostration, rise from the seat, return to your position, and chant the praise: On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, the Awakened Sovereign manifests his numinous power at the Bodhi-maṇḍa.
When the Inner Way was first established, at midnight he beheld the morning star. He universally rescued those lost in emotion; all that was dark and obscure became radiant light.
(The third section of the *Canyue Zang* concludes here. If one establishes an altar and performs recitations on this day, the ritual procedures are as usual. The appended verses follow below.)
Before Mount Bodhi, he realized the Way upon beholding the morning star;
within the great trichiliocosm, he raised the sun of wisdom to radiate its brilliance.
The commentary on the meaning states: When the World-Honored One first attained enlightenment, he sighed, "How marvelous! All sentient beings possess [the Tathāgata-garbha]..."
The marks of wisdom and virtue are already present; it is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that one cannot realize them.

Alas! It can be seen that this Way can be accomplished by every person. That people fail to accomplish it is simply because they are submerged in the deluded thoughts of the five sensory objects and emotional desires.
Therefore, though their ears hear the Way daily, they are like the deaf regarding bells and drums; though their eyes [see it daily...]
To perceive the Way is like a blind man regarding the sun and moon. Now, as for the greatness of the Way, heaven and earth are insufficient to serve as its measure;
therefore, one who lacks the capacity to encompass heaven and earth is insufficient to enter the Way.

As for the nobility of the Way, carriages and official robes are insufficient to constitute honor; therefore, one who does not regard carriages and robes with the disdain of dust is not [sufficient to enter the Way].
This is sufficient for entering the Way. As for the distance of the Way, even kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are insufficient to serve as its limit.

Therefore, one who lacks the realization that a single thought-moment is ten thousand years is not fit to enter the Way. Thus it is said: "To speak of the Way is easy; to accomplish the Way is difficult. The Way is not difficult;
it is people themselves who make it so. As the ancients said: "If the Way could be presented as an offering, there would be none who would not offer it."
O Lord, if the Way is such that it may be advanced, there is none who does not advance in it; if it is such that one may share it with others, there is none to whom one does not give it.
Your descendants—how profound are these words! They speak of what is called "self-nature and self-deliverance.
Therefore, on this day, we disciples of the Buddha should reflect deeply upon the words that all possess the marks of wisdom and virtue; we should not disparage ourselves or succumb to despondency.

On the fifteenth day of the second month, the anniversary of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, the guest master shall post a notice in advance on the day before (the notice stating): "Tomorrow we respectfully commemorate..."
On the occasion of the Nirvana of our Master Śākyamuni Buddha, the evening assembly master hears the sound of the bell.

The community collectively dons their robes and takes up their ritual implements, proceeding to the Great Hall to pay homage to the Buddha. (The evening two-board [bell] service for paying homage to the Buddha is identical to that of the Buddha’s Birthday. The rites for the Emperor’s longevity on the actual day are identical to those of the New Moon and Full Moon services;

the only difference is that after completing the circumambulation of the Buddha, one performs twelve prostrations before the Śākyamuni Buddha. After the morning recitation, the altar for the *chàn* (repentance) rite is laid out in the Great Hall, and a notice is posted by the Guest Hall. The notice reads: On this day, upon hearing the sound of the drum, the entire assembly...

The Master, according to the order of the ranks, proceeds to the Great Hall to pay homage to Śākyamuni Tathāgata. He performs the *Nirvāṇa Liturgy of Worship and Praise* and recites the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teachings*.

(The Guest Hall and the Rector assign the ranks; ten persons per rank ascend the hall in succession. They ascend the hall after the morning gruel. The ritual protocol is found below in the chapter on the Abbot. At the midday bell, the offerings are presented.

The ritual is the same as that for the Day of Attaining Enlightenment, with only the wording changed as follows: "Reverently considering that the Benevolent One responded to the world, realizing the Truth through silent stillness, and dwelling within the vastness of the thousand realms..."
Venerable One, you embrace the four modes of birth as your children; your form manifests in accordance with things, yet fundamentally it is identical to the body that transcends all marks.

Your teachings arise in response to the capacities of beings; how could they differ from the path beyond words? Since the Wheel of Dharma first turned, your traces of transformation have flourished ever more.

When the "half-syllables" were first expounded, you were like one striking away ignorance without weariness; when the "hundred-coin" [full] teaching was later entrusted to you, you were like one redeeming a life through tireless effort. You have caused all sentient beings to universally...
O you who are vexed by such afflictions! You now dwell securely within the Tathāgata-garbha; the four minds are fulfilled, and the three virtues have returned.
This means that not a single person is allowed to attain parinirvāṇa alone, but all are led to parinirvāṇa through the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, entering into nirvāṇa is beyond the reach of thought or speculation. Now that we are far from the Śāla Grove, we deeply mourn the loss of our former connection.
The Semblance Dharma still endures, and I have humbly followed the bequeathed instructions. Now, on this day of mid-spring, I look back with longing upon the ritual of bowing toward the north.

With water-weeds from the ravines and pond-lilies from the streams, I briefly manifest the rite of offering food. As I offer incense and praise his virtue, I slightly express my sincerity of grief and longing.

I only pray that your vast compassion will look down and graciously grant your clear inspection. (After the recitation, one prostration; return to position; chant the hymn: Great Compassionate Father, Unsurpassed Physician.

"O King, out of compassion for his ailing son, he employed skillful means and manifested his own death. Yet the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is truly eternal; his lifespan is in fact immeasurable. (Chant the *Canyue Zang* three times.

For other days, follow the precedent of the new and full moon. At the end of the evening bell, perform the dedication of merit. Once the sutra recitations and repentance rites are finished, immediately return to the hall. Do not go to the Abbot’s quarters.

Those confined within the realm of transformation ultimately perish, following the impermanence of the world. Dwelling within the illusory, one returns to the Real; this is called "Nirvana" (*jimiè*). (Paste the scripture here.)

In the Hall of Repentance: Great Samādhi is eternal and constant, abiding forever for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; with perfect capacity and universal response, he manifests a thousand billion bodies before the Buddhas.

(The original preface states: "Nature" is the great foundation of humanity. It vibrates through heaven and earth, yet its beginning is unknown; it exhausts ten thousand ages, yet its end is unknown. Both Buddhas and sentient beings equally possess this nature.

To awaken to it is to ascend to wondrous enlightenment; to be deluded by it is to drift through birth and death. From kalpa to kalpa, through the various realms of the six paths, karmic retributions revolve without end. We rely upon the vast and flowing holy teachings as our refuge.

We disciples, though we humbly wear the robes and are enrolled in the lineage of the Dharma, take the practice of these teachings as our discipline (*vinaya*), the proclamation of these words as our doctrine (*dharma*), and the transmission of this mind as our meditation (*dhyāna*). Only by following what we call the Great Foundation can we become one with the Buddha’s entire essence and wondrous functioning; only then may we truly be so called.)
"O Son of the Buddha! You continue the life of wisdom. To offer posthumous mourning on the anniversary of his passing—is this not a worldly rite?
The Commentary on the Meaning states: According to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, on the day of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, offerings were presented like clouds and tears shed like rain.
Alas! How sorrowful it was! Furthermore, reading the *Qingmingzang* (Clear and Bright Treasury), within the "Chi Shi" (Hastening Reality) fascicle, [it concerns] Śākyamuni...

The Text for Paying Homage and Praising the Tathāgata’s Parinirvāṇa: This text depicts the appearance of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa as if it were right before one’s eyes, fully conveying a sense of longing and devotion.
Lately, few people have known of it; it has been neglected and not brought forth, which is a profound forgetting of one's roots.
I reflect upon the Great Master Weisiqi, who initiated the Nirvana Assembly at Ayuwang Temple in Ningbo, gathering the assembly to perform rites of repentance and pay homage to the śarīra;

this has been established as an annual custom. Someone asked: "I have heard that the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas pervades all places and, fundamentally, neither appears in the world nor enters into nirvana.
What need is there for a memorial day? Furthermore, regarding the school of the Chan lineage..."
When the true command is raised alone, even Buddhas and Patriarchs do not exist; how then could there be Nirvana?

Now, within this state of no-arising and no-ceasing, you delusively perceive arising and ceasing, making offerings, prostrations, and repentance above. Is this not clinging to objects and losing the mind, failing to penetrate the principle of nature?
The Master replied: "You know that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, yet you do not know that its manifested traces have passed away.
You know that the essence of the Dharma is all-pervasive, yet you do not know that its manifested traces occupy a specific location. Without manifested traces, how could the Dharma-body be revealed?
Without śarīra, who would know of the manifested traces? Since you say the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, how could there be any separation from the response-body?"

It is said that the essence of the Dharma is all-pervasive; how could it be obstructed by the śarīra alone? You wish to cast aside phenomena to seek the principle and discard existence to discourse on emptiness;
yet if you are still deluded regarding phenomenal characteristics, how much more so regarding the nature of reality? Long ago, when Mahākāśyapa was about to enter Mount Kukkuṭapāda, he said:
One must first pay homage to all the stupas before entering meditative concentration. Now, Kāśyapa, you are the first patriarch of the Chan school;
could it be that you do not comprehend the nature of reality and thus act in this way?

You should know that the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is inconceivable—neither eternal nor annihilated, neither existent nor non-existent. You ought not to give rise to conceptual discrimination through biased views. This is surely because of what you...
They maintain that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, yet they fail to comprehend the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) in benefiting sentient beings;
this is truly due to their lack of profound clarity regarding the principles of the teachings. Alas! Since the Master initiated this assembly...

Subsequent generations have followed this practice, continuing it without decline to this day. This ensures that every person knows the grace of our Buddha and fulfills the sincerity of repaying their origins.
How could the merit of this Master be measured? Nevertheless, performing the rites for the śarīra need not be restricted to this specific assembly.
If one wishes to repent of transgressions and repay one's debt of gratitude, there is no restriction on the time; it may be done at any moment. — Yun
The *Qichong xinglu* states: During the Tang dynasty, there was Zilin, the son of the Fan family. His mother, Lady Wang, did not believe in the Three Jewels.

Zilin fled to the Eastern Capital and took refuge at Guangshou Monastery, where he received the precepts under the Vinaya Master Qingxiu. Suddenly, he longed for his kin and returned home to visit them.
His father had lost his sight, and his mother had already been deceased for three years. Consequently, he went to a mountain shrine, spread out his sitting mat, and vowed to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*.

She beheld the Lord of Mount Tai and inquired about her mother’s place of rebirth. That night, the Lord of Mount Tai summoned her and said, "Your mother is currently in a prison, undergoing various sufferings.
Your neighbor wept with compassion and requested that she be spared. The Lord said, "You may go to Mount Mao to pay homage to the Stūpa of King Aśoka; perhaps then she may be saved.
The neighbor immediately went to the stūpa and prostrated herself in sorrowful weeping. When she had reached forty thousand prostrations, she suddenly heard a voice calling out.
The neighbor’s voice called out from the air; looking up into the sky, he saw his mother, who said to him, "By your power, I have been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

With that, she vanished completely. In the *Lianchi zan* (Praise of the Lotus Pond), it is said: "Maudgalyāyana was moved by the Buddha's teaching to provide for the Saṅgha, while the son Lin was moved by the divine instruction to pay reverence at the stūpa.
That supreme filial piety penetrates to the gods and spirits—how could this not be believed? This constitutes the ritual for rescuing one's parents.

As for those who have obtained benefit by venerating the stūpa—those whose own physical transgressions and defilements were restored to purity through the ritual veneration of the stūpa—they are beyond counting.
Furthermore, the form and characteristics of the śarīra manifest according to individuals and the times, undergoing transformations that are unfathomable;
the numerous instances of seeing and hearing these cannot be fully recounted. Thus, both the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and his compassionate vows are beyond measure.

This is beyond the reach of thought and deliberation. One should simply maintain firm faith without doubt, and with the utmost reverence and full observance of ritual, a wondrous response will surely be granted.

On the thirtieth day of the ninth month, the birthday of Bhaisajyaguru Buddha. For the morning service on the birthday of Bhaisajyaguru Buddha, incense is burned and the censer is passed; the Abbot offers incense, and the *Weina*...
Then, the incense is offered with a hymn of praise. Upon completing the circumambulation of the Buddha, one performs twelve prostrations before the name of Bhaisajyaguru Buddha.
At the time of the morning gruel, the Guest Hall hangs a notice (the notice reads): "Today we respectfully encounter the anniversary of the birth of Bhaisajyaguru Tathāgata.

When the midday gong is struck and the sound of the drum is heard, the assembly of masters shall don their robes and carry their requisites, proceeding together to the Bhaisajyaguru Hall for offerings. (The following applies to all Buddhas...)

This protects the body. By reciting it, one can eliminate all suffering from illness, calamities, obstacles, evil dreams, malevolent spirits, ghosts, and all inauspicious matters.
*Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ*—that is, *Oṃ māṇibhadrāya hūṃ*. This is known as the Six-Syllable Mantra;
it is the subtle, essential heart-essence of Avalokiteśvara. It should be recited and maintained in succession with the Cundī Dhāraṇī for the sake of benefit.

It is even greater. Furthermore, the Buddha-Mother Cundī, seeing that sentient beings dwelling in this defiled age find it difficult to maintain the precepts of fasting and purification, has therefore proclaimed this mantra.
It does not restrict the consumption of pungent foods or alcohol, nor does it discriminate between the pure and the impure; one need only recite it with a sincere heart.
This can cause those of short lifespans to increase their longevity immeasurably, and all sufferings of illness shall be extinguished. Whatever one seeks, [it shall be fulfilled].

Everything follows the mind. If one recites it according to the ritual for one million times, once the karmic retribution is exhausted, one will attain rebirth in the Pure Land, serve all Buddhas, universally hear the wondrous Dharma, and realize Bodhi.
If the syllable *oṃ bhrūṃ* is not added, there is fear that the recitation will not achieve success; therefore, use this mantra together with the aforementioned vidyā-mantra in a single location.
Recite the mantra; accomplishment is certain. Upon completing one hundred and eight recitations, perform the dedication of merit.
When making the supreme offerings, add the transformed food and nectar, offering each three times to all. The verse for dedication says:
Now that I recite the Great Cundī Dhāraṇī, I immediately give rise to the vast vow of Bodhicitta: May my concentration and wisdom quickly become perfectly clear;
May all my merits and virtues be fully accomplished; May my supreme blessings adorn me everywhere; May I together with all sentient beings attain the path of Buddhahood.

(This is the dedication for transcending the world. If seeking worldly dharmas, one should change it to: I, disciple [Name], reverently serve the Buddha and uphold the Cundī Dhāraṇī for the sake of...
"Seek such-and-such a matter; may I attain its fulfillment early," and so forth. (For all who uphold the Cundī Dhāraṇī:

at each of the six periods of the day, or at the very least during the morning and evening periods, if one maintains this practice throughout one's life, one may recite it freely and informally without needing to keep count. However, one should use a Cundī mirror; except for the morning and evening periods when one recites while facing the mirror, one should place the mirror in a pouch and carry it on one's person, reciting as one pleases.)

After a long time, one will certainly obtain a response. Aside from the various Cundī sūtras found within the Tripitaka, there are also works such as the *Xianmi yuantong chengfo xinyao ji* (Collection of the Essential Methods for Attaining Buddhahood through the Perfect Interpenetration of Exoteric and Esoteric Teachings) and the *Zhunti jingye jiyao* (Essential Collection on the Pure Deeds of Cundī) which are currently in circulation.

The birthday of Mañjuśrī is on the fourth day of the fourth lunar month. The ritual for the birthday of the Great Being Mañjuśrī, including the assembly of the congregation and other procedures, is the same as that for the birthday of Bhaisajyaguru.
First, recite: *Namo Mahājñāna Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva* (three times). Then, chant [the following].
From the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the "Entering the Dharma Realm" Chapter, the Section on Contemplating Mañjuśrī:
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was walking along the path and, observing the bhikṣus, addressed Sāgarabuddhi, saying:
"Sāgarabuddhi, you should observe the pure body of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence; none among all gods or humans can [equal it]."
It is inconceivable. You should observe how Mañjuśrī’s perfect halo shines through with clarity, causing immeasurable sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy.
You should observe how Mañjuśrī is adorned by a network of light, which extinguishes the immeasurable suffering and afflictions of sentient beings.
You should observe how Mañjuśrī’s assembly is complete, consisting entirely of bodhisattvas who have come from afar.
Gathered by past roots of goodness, you should observe the path traveled by Mañjuśrī:
for eight paces to the left and right, it is level and magnificently adorned. You should observe the place where Mañjuśrī dwells:
throughout the ten directions, there is always a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) that revolves in accordance with him. You should observe the conduct of Mañjuśrī...
The path is fully adorned with immeasurable merit. On both its left and right sides, great hidden treasuries of various precious jewels emerge spontaneously.

You should observe Mañjuśrī: from the flow of his roots of goodness cultivated by having made offerings to the Buddhas in the past, treasuries of adornments emerge from among all the trees. You should observe Mañjuśrī: throughout all the worlds...
The Lord of the Interval rains clouds of ritual offerings; prostrate with reverence to make this offering. You should observe:

when all the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the ten directions, are about to preach the Dharma, they all emit light from the white tuft between their eyebrows, which comes to illuminate his body and enters through the crown of his head. (Recite this once; then recite the eight-character *dhāraṇī* mantra of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva one hundred times.)
(Recite eight times: Oṃ akāramukha-cakra. (When the mantra is finished, recite the *Bhakṣaṇī-mantra*, the *Amṛta-toya-mantra*, and the *Sarva-pūjā-mantra* as usual. The *Vina* announces:)
I reverently hear that the Great Being was originally the teacher of the seven Buddhas; thus he is called the One of Great Wisdom.

In his manifested traces, he dwells at the excellence of the Five Peaks, where he is titled "Pure Coolness. His realm of tranquil light is his home wherever he goes, and his pure and wondrous form-body appears through causes and conditions.
I reflect upon that which is sustained by the great vows of Mañjuśrī and set in motion by the illusion-like samādhi—without direction, without substance, neither form nor emptiness.
Therefore, I burn incense and prostrate my head, universally relying upon the light of Prajñā, while singing hymns and offering praise.

All have planted the seeds of Bodhi. On this, the fourth day of the first month of the Qinghe period, coinciding with the anniversary of the Great Sage’s birth, the assembly of monks has gathered like clouds to surround him in worship and offering.

We humbly pray that the dimly obscured consciousness of karma may vanish entirely upon beholding his shadow, and that the turbid, vexed mind may find sudden clarity upon gazing upon his radiant light.
(When the Karmadāna has finished his announcement, he recites the eulogy for Mañjuśrī:
His traces abide upon the Five Peaks; his body spans the blue lion. Benevolent clouds cover all universally as the rain of Dharma is bestowed. He wondrously expounds the teachings at Vaiśālī.
The Teacher of the Seven Buddhas, whose universal transformation reaches unto this present age.
*Namo* to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī of Great Wisdom. (Recite three times; the assembly bows three times and each returns to their respective place.)
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Sanskrit name is Mañjuśrī, or alternatively Mañjuśiri; these are variations in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit sound.
This is translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode) and also as "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (Miaojixiang). Because his myriad virtues are perfectly luminous, they all penetrate the very source of nature.

Therefore, he is called "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode). Because one obtains benefit through seeing, hearing, upholding his name, and reciting his mantra, he is called "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (Miaojixiang).
First, recite the "Chapter on Contemplating Mañjuśrī," which appears in the sixty-first fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Next, recite the mantra, which appears in the *Mañjuśrī-mūla-mantra-sūtra*. The Buddha told Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva: "These eight characters possess great majesty..."
Regarding this *Te* Dhāraṇī: in the distant past, it was spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers.

It is for the protection of all kings who practice the ten wholesome paths of action, so that they may attain their wishes, enjoy long lives, possess incomparable merit and virtue, see the cessation of warfare, and have peaceful lands.
It is able to bring great benefit to all sentient beings and sever the three... [triple afflictions].

Those in the evil realms shall have their various wishes and requests fulfilled. If a person hears or recollects this mantra even for a moment, the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes will be immediately extinguished;

how much more so if they constantly recollect it! The merit of such a person cannot be surpassed even by those on the tenth stage who are destined for Buddhahood, let alone by other devas and the like.
If a mantra-holder is pressed by urgent circumstances, they need only be able to restrain their body, speech, and mind.
Regarding karma: the ten non-virtues are forever severed. By merely holding this mantra, one also attains accomplishment.
This excludes those with improper minds who do not resolve for bodhicitta, and so forth. As for the "Five Peaks," they are the Five Terraces (Wutai), known as Mount Qingliang.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas," states: "In the northeast there is a place called Mount Qingliang. From ancient times..."

The assembly of bodhisattvas dwells therein. There currently resides the bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, together with his retinue and ten thousand bodhisattvas, who constantly expound the Dharma within that place.
Furthermore, the *Ratnagarbha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed Vajrapāṇi, Lord of the Secret: "After my parinirvāṇa..."
In the northeast of Jambudvīpa, there is a country named Mahācīna.
Within it is a mountain called Pañcaśīrṣa, where the youth Mañjuśrī dwells and travels about, preaching the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, it was surrounded by and made offerings to by immeasurable devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings;

this mountain is located in Wutai County of Dài State, as fully described in the local gazetteers. Moreover, that Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas is stated in such texts as the *Cittabūmidarśana-sūtra*.
Additionally, the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra* states: "In the past he was the teacher of Śākyamuni; now he is a disciple of the Buddha."
Two Honored Ones do not manifest their teachings simultaneously; therefore, it was I who acted as the Bodhisattva.

In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Maitreya Bodhisattva says to Sudhana: "Mañjuśrī’s great vows are such that they cannot be possessed by any other bodhisattvas, even those numbering immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas. Good son, the youth Mañjuśrī..."
His conduct is vast; his vows are boundless. He gives birth to all the merits of a bodhisattva without ceasing.

Good son, Mañjuśrī is constantly the mother of immeasurable Buddhas and constantly the teacher of immeasurable bodhisattvas, teaching and bringing to maturity all sentient beings, and so forth. All of the above is explained according to the fundamental [nature].
To speak of this according to his manifested traces (*vyañjana*), the *Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Bhadra, "This Mañjuśrī, out of great compassion, was born in this land in the village of Tālaka, into the family of the Brahmin Brahmadeva.
At the time of his birth, the house and dwelling were transformed like a lotus flower, and he emerged from his mother’s right side."
He was born with a body the color of purple-gold. Upon touching the ground, he was able to speak like a celestial youth.
A canopy of the seven treasures followed and covered him from above. Ten kinds of auspicious signs appeared. It continues:
"Because this bodhisattva dwells by the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he manifests either birth or parinirvāṇa within the worlds of the ten directions to benefit sentient beings."
A verse says: The Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, not forsaking his vow of great compassion, manifests transformed bodies as followers of heterodox paths;
sometimes wearing crowns or remaining naked, sometimes among groups of children, he plays about in villages; or he appears as a poor man.

He manifests with a decrepit appearance for the sake of old age and illness, or appears as one suffering from hunger and cold, wandering through various regions to beg for alms, causing people to give even a single act of charity that fulfills all their wishes. Having inspired them to develop faith, he preaches the *pāramitās*.
Leading ten thousand bodhisattvas, he dwells upon Mount Wudang (Five-Peaked Mountain), emitting billions of kinds of light; those who behold him see their sins extinguished. It is further said:

Four hundred and fifty years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī shall go to the Snowy Mountains to proclaim the Dharma and transform five hundred rishis. Having brought them to maturity,
he and the rishis will fly through the void to his birthplace, where he will sit cross-legged beneath a nyagrodha tree and enter the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
He manifested various auspicious signs, just as the five hundred sages each displayed their supernatural transformations and entered nirvana.

His other various divine powers, his preaching of diverse essential teachings, his manifold beneficial deeds, and his various spiritual responses are recorded extensively in the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras;
they cannot be described in full detail here.

The Birthday of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is on the twenty-first day of the second month. The ritual for the birthday of the Great Being Samantabhadra is the same as that for the birthday of Bhaisajyaguru.
First, recite: *Namo Mahācaryā Samantabhadra Bodhisattva Mahāsattva* (recite three times, then chant).
Chapter from the *Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva*. There was a bodhisattva sitting in the full lotus posture named Samantabhadra.
His body was the color of white jade, and he had fifty kinds of light; each light consisted of fifty kinds of colors, which formed a halo around his neck.
From all the pores of his body flowed golden light, at the tips of which were immeasurable transformation buddhas and transformation bodhisattvas who served as his retinue.
They followed him, walking with serene and slow steps, raining down great jeweled flowers as they approached the practitioner.
The elephant opened its mouth, and upon its tusks, celestial maidens from the various ponds played music and sang, their voices exquisite as they praised the Mahāyāna, the Way of Single Reality.
Having seen this, the practitioner rejoiced and paid homage, once again reciting the profound sūtras and prostrating throughout the ten directions.
Then, together with immeasurable Buddhas, they paid homage to the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, as well as to Śākyamuni and the great Bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra, and made this vow:
"If by my past merit I am destined to see Samantabhadra, may the Honored One, Samantabhadra, [grant me this sight]."

"Reveal my physical body. (Recite once; then continue the recitation. "Namo to the Great Practitioner Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" (one hundred and eight times). Next, recite the *Bhāṣita-āhāra-pariṇāmana-mantra* (Transformation of Food), the *Amṛta-mantra* (Nectar), and the *Sarva-saṃpatti-dāna-mantra* (Universal Offering Mantra), as is done for Bhaiṣajyaguru. The Rector makes the following announcement:
Homage to the Great Being. You are the assistant to the Sage within the Flower Treasury World (*Avataṃsaka*) and the bridge across the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The lands as numerous as motes of dust all traverse the path of your great conduct; the hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates are all sustained by your great vows.

You are the eldest son of the *Avataṃsaka*, wherein principle and phenomena are perfectly interfused; you are the guide to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), wherein wisdom and power are vast and great. Now, then...
The twenty-first day of the second lunar month, coinciding with the auspicious occasion of the Great Being’s birthday, the monastic assembly gathered like clouds to arrange offerings.
We humbly pray: through the power of the Mahāyāna that universally enters all gates, may all realms of sentient beings be universally benefited;

may all obscurations and defilements be eliminated without remainder, and may every sublime practice be fully accomplished. (After the *Vina* has finished this announcement, the *Pu-xian Zan* [Praise of Samantabhadra] is recited.)
The Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra bring forth boundless accumulations of merit. Such wisdom is named Samantabhadra; all things therein are perfectly complete.
Adorned with myriad virtues, its benefits pervade both humans and devas.
Namo to the Great Practitioner Samantabhadra Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Recite three times; the assembly bows three times and each returns to their original place).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: Speaking in terms of the Flower Treasury World (*Huāzàng*), Vairocana is in the center, Samantabhadra is on the left, and Mañjuśrī is on the right.
This is because, in the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Samantabhadra is likened to the eldest son and Mañjuśrī to the youngest son. Speaking in terms of wisdom and practice...
It is said: Mañjuśrī represents great wisdom (*prajñā*), while Samantabhadra represents great practice (*caryā*).
Since practice takes wisdom as its precursor, Mañjuśrī resides on the left and Samantabhadra resides on the right.

When making offerings to sacred images today, one follows this fixed order of wisdom and practice, placing Mañjuśrī first and Samantabhadra second. Therefore, among the four great famous mountains within the realm... [the text continues].
First is Mount Wutai, where Mañjuśrī resides; second is Mount Emei, where Samantabhadra resides;
third is Potalaka, where Avalokiteśvara resides; fourth is Mount Jiuhua, where Kṣitigarbha resides.
According to the Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra, in a past kalpa, when Amitābha Buddha was a universal monarch (cakravartin), Avalokiteśvara was his eldest son, named...
Asaṃkhyeya was the second crown prince, named Nima; Mañjuśrī was the third crown prince, named Rājavarga;
and so on until the eighth crown prince, named Mindu, who is none other than the present-day Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Thus, their original essence and manifested traces coincide, and their causes and effects correspond; such are all their virtuous marks and spiritual powers.
Their employment of the Dharma, their preaching, their beneficial conduct, their ritual recitations, and their spiritual responses all pervade the Three Baskets (Tripitaka);

these cannot be fully recorded here by means of brush and ink. For instance, during the Tang dynasty, the two monks Hanshan and Shide manifested numerous supernatural wonders, each having a collection of poems that has been transmitted to the world.
All have regarded them as emanations of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra; this tradition passed down through generations is indeed extraordinary.
This is the record.

The birthday of Avalokiteśvara is the nineteenth day of the second month. Regarding the birthday of Avalokiteśvara: (The ritual procedures for hanging the plaque, making offerings, and so forth are the same as those for Bhaisajyaguru. First, recite:

Namo to the Greatly Compassionate Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (recite three times; then recite): From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the "Universal Gate" Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the verse says:
"The World-Honored One is fully endowed with wondrous marks; I now ask him again: O Son of the Buddha, by what causes and conditions is he named 'Avalokiteśvara'?
You who are honored for being fully endowed with wondrous marks, please answer Ajita in verse: Listen, Ajita, to Avalokiteśvara..."

The movement of his voice is skillfully adapted to all regions. His great vows are as deep as the ocean; throughout inconceivable eons, he has attended upon many thousands of billions of Buddhas and made vast, pure aspirations.

For your sake, I shall briefly explain them: by hearing his name or seeing his body, and by bringing him to mind, one’s thoughts will not pass in vain, for he can extinguish the suffering of all realms of existence.
Even if someone were to harbor malice and push one into a great pit of fire, by recollecting that Avalokiteśvara...

By the power of the sound [of Avalokiteśvara’s name], a pit of fire is transformed into a pond; or if one is adrift upon the vast ocean, amidst the perils of dragons, fish, and various ghosts, by the power of recollecting that Avalokiteśvara, the waves cannot drown them.
Or if one is on the peak of Mount Sumeru and is pushed over by others, by the power of recollecting that Avalokiteśvara, one remains in the sky like the sun.
Or if pursued by evil men and falling toward the Diamond Mountains (Vajraparvata), by the power of recollecting that...

The power of his voice cannot harm even a single hair. Or if one encounters hostile bandits surrounding him, each brandishing a blade to inflict injury, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will all immediately give rise to a heart of loving-kindness.
Or if one suffers the hardship of royal punishment and faces execution at the end of one’s life, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the blade shall instantly break into pieces.
Or if one is imprisoned in shackles and manacles, with hands and feet bound in fetters, by recollecting him...

Through the power of sound, one attains liberation with ease. Regarding curses, various poisons, and those who wish to harm the body—if one calls to mind the power of that Avalokiteśvara, they shall instead return to the person who sent them.
Or if one encounters evil rākṣasas, venomous dragons, various ghosts, and the like—if one calls to mind the power of that Avalokiteśvara, none of them will dare to cause harm at that time.
Even if surrounded by ferocious beasts with terrifying sharp teeth and claws—if one calls to mind that...

The power of his voice: though they rush swiftly toward the boundless directions, the venomous snakes, vipers, and scorpions whose poisonous breath blazes like smoke and fire, shall upon recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara turn back of their own accord as soon as they hear his voice.
Amidst thundering clouds, crashing lightning, falling hail, and torrential rain, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, these shall be dispersed and vanish at that very moment.
When sentient beings are beset by calamity and oppressed by immeasurable suffering, [the power of] Avalokiteśvara’s wondrous...
With the power of wisdom, you are able to rescue the world from suffering; endowed with the power of supernatural faculties, you extensively cultivate the skillful means of knowledge.

In the lands of the ten directions, there is no realm where you do not manifest your body. Within the various evil destinies—the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals—you cause the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death to be gradually and completely extinguished.
You possess the contemplation of reality, the pure contemplation, the contemplation of vast wisdom, and the contemplation of compassion.
The Contemplation of Compassion: I always pray and constantly gaze upon the stainless, pure light. The Sun of Wisdom shatters all darkness; it can subdue the winds and fires of calamity.
Universally illuminating the world, its essence is compassion and its precepts are like the roar of thunder. Its merciful mind is a wondrous great cloud, pouring down the Dharma-rain of sweet nectar.
It extinguishes and removes the flames of affliction. Whether in legal disputes before government officials or amidst the terrors of battle arrays, one should call to mind that Contemplation...
The power of his voice causes all enemies to retreat and disperse. With his wondrous voice, Avalokiteśvara, with his Brahma-voice and ocean-tide voice, he surpasses all sounds of the world.
Therefore, one should always keep him in mind; at every thought, do not give rise to doubt. Avalokiteśvara, the pure and holy one, can act as a refuge for those in suffering and the perils of death.
Possessing all merits, he gazes upon sentient beings with eyes of compassion—a vast ocean of accumulated blessings.

It is immeasurable. Therefore, one should prostrate once (and then recite the sacred name of Avalokiteśvara one hundred and eight times. The remaining ritual procedures are as usual, with only this change in the words).

I humbly submit that as the season of Zhonghe arrives, the moon reflected in water reveals the form of sovereign mastery; as the Jiazhong month accords with the musical pitch-pipes, the *tanhua* flower manifests the auspicious omen of universal penetration.
The thirty-two transformations manifest the power of compassionate vows, so that every child of this Sahā world may call upon the Name;

the light of compassion extends across ten million billion leagues, so that the Teacher of Sukhāvatī may ever assist in the work of transformation. I earnestly consider those of us, such-and-such, who drift...
In the ocean of worldly toil and the land of entangling afflictions, the six sense-faculties flow recklessly, resulting only in the loss of rushing toward the dust;
the three wisdoms are long obscured, and the merit of returning to one's original nature has not yet been seen. Were it not for the Great Compassionate Father, who would rescue this destitute son?

Now that we encounter the Buddha’s birthday, we respectfully offer these fragrant incenses, praying that you will behold our humble sincerity and compassionately accept us. (Having finished the recitation, bow once and return to your seats.)
The eulogy says: Holding a willow branch in hand, with the Tathāgata upon his crown, he sits upright in the lotus throne of jewels.

His compassion for suffering is most profound; a single thought can turn [the tide]. The gates of immeasurable mercy open. (After reciting the Holy Name three times, perform three prostrations. On this day, one may either perform the ritual of repentance or maintain the name.)

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding Avalokiteśvara’s salvation from suffering and deliverance of sentient beings through the response to the holding of his name, both the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* provide detailed accounts.
Furthermore, the records in other texts are too numerous to enumerate in full.

Here, I have briefly recorded several instances among the most manifest responses experienced by monastics, so that one may see how such numinous traces are clearly evident. From *Miscellaneous Records of Mountain Hermitages*.

The Record states: In the past, Master Guding of Mount Jing was naturally a dwarf from birth; his lips were curled back, his teeth exposed, his voice raspy and hoarse, and his skin was cracked and withered.
A physiognomist examined him and said, "With these four base features concentrated in the body of a dwarf, it is clear that you will never speak in your life.
The Master vowed to pray to Avalokiteśvara and maintained his practice daily.

The names of the holy ones were beyond counting; he paid homage to their images nightly, totaling over a thousand times. Thus, for twenty years, his humble appearance was transformed into one of auspicious fortune:
his lips became full and relaxed while his teeth remained concealed; his voice grew resonant and smooth, and his skin shone with luster.

Later, when he encountered the same physiognomist from before, the man congratulated him, saying, "Master, your present marks of excellence indicate that you shall occupy the Dharma seat and greatly propagate the school's tradition. That very year, he entered the world [as a teacher].
Lóngjiào resided at Mount Jìng for twelve years; he reached the age of seventy-nine. This recitation and prostration to Guānyīn transformed his lowly status and premature death into noble longevity.
Furthermore, Juézhào Huī of Shòucháng Temple in Wēnzhōu spent the summer retreat at Fúcí.
He hung a sacred image in his quarters and performed devoted prostrations every night. One day, he suddenly saw water from a pure pitcher [flowing]...

The image surged forth from the wall, and his entire body was filled with joy. From that point on, his cultivation deepened further and his wisdom became increasingly clear. This illustrates how recitation and prostration induce wisdom.

Furthermore, Yuan, the former attendant of the Illumination Hall at Tiandong Temple, had long suffered from many illnesses. In the *bingchen* year of the Hongwu era, [he experienced a miraculous response].
His illness grew increasingly grave. He exhorted the temple manager to encourage him to recite the sacred name of Avalokiteśvara; he recited it ten thousand times daily.

On the seventeenth day of the tenth month of the following year, at the hour of the horse (noon), he reflected that his condition was such that death was not far off, and thought it best to change his recitation to that of Amitābha Buddha.
Just as he was beginning this thought, he suddenly saw a woman holding a pure pitcher appear before him.
Zhao was startled and at a loss. After steadying his mind, he observed closely and realized it was a manifestation by a Bodhisattva.
Zhao wept and, confessing his transgressions, sought mercy; in a short while, the apparition vanished. Five days later, he was completely freed from the suffering of his illness.

This illustrates how prostration and recitation can eliminate disease. The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states: "At the beginning of the Yixi era, Huiqian of Jiaxiang Temple in Shan-yin knew [the truth] of himself..."

As his life drew to a close, he focused his thoughts on the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) and sincerely prayed to Avalokiteśvara. He beheld the holy countenance [of the Bodhisattva] in advance;
though his illness was grave and protracted, his countenance remained as it had been in his ordinary days. His attendants all smelled a wondrous fragrance. Shortly thereafter, he passed away.

Among the monastics and laypeople who saw or heard of this, there were none who did not marvel and praise him. This was the result of his devotion to recitation and the resulting rebirth in the Pure Land. To summarize: Avalokiteśvara...
O Great Being, your contemplation upon sentient beings is profoundly deep; your faith is long-practiced and steadfast, and your sincerity is most earnest.

Chapter Four: Honoring the Patriarchs.
The commentary states: Each person sacrifices to their own ancestors, honoring the beginning of their physical life. This physical life begins with craving;
yet, while the body eventually transforms and craving eventually exhausts itself, the spirit of the nature alone remains unclouded.
It does not persist by relying on birth, nor does it perish along with death. Therefore, Buddhism necessarily teaches people to clarify this.
Later scholars, however, remained stuck to names and words and failed to grasp its essential intent.
Since the teachings flowed eastward to this land, those who truly received its transmission have been few.

When our ancestor Bodhidharma arrived and demonstrated the Way of Direct Pointing, people finally attained a vast clarity and beheld the wondrous nature of their own self-nature (*svabhāva*). From that time on...

From that time until now, the tradition has been handed down without interruption. Those who later transmit the ancestral Way and succeed to the ancestral position are like fuel for fire or vessels for water;

"Wait until sixty-seven years after my parinirvāṇa; you shall then go to China (Zhendan) and establish the great medicine of the Dharma, directly reaching those of superior faculties.

Is it morality? Is right livelihood morality? Having observed in this way, one has nothing to grasp in the body, nothing to cling to in cultivation, and nothing to dwell upon in phenomena.
The past has already ceased; the future has not yet arrived; the present is empty and still.
There is no agent of action, and no recipient of retribution. This world does not shift; that world does not change. Among these, what dharma is there?
It is called the holy life (*brahmacarya*). From where does the holy life come? To whom does it belong? What is its essence?
By whom is it performed? Is it existent or non-existent? Is it form (*rūpa*) or non-form? Is it sensation (*vedanā*) or non-sensation?
Is it perception? Is it non-perception? Is it volitional formations? Is it non-formations? Is it consciousness? Is it non-consciousness?

Thus, because the dharmas of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) cannot be apprehended; because the dharmas of the three periods of time are all empty and quiescent; because the mind has no grasping or attachment;
because the heart has no obstruction; because that which is practiced is non-dual; and because of mastery in skillful means, one receives the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).

Therefore, because one contemplates the signless Dharma, because one knows that the Buddha-dharmas are equal, and because one is endowed with all Buddha-dharmas—this is called the pure Brahma-conduct.

From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata," the verse says:

"Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed is immeasurable—hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Throughout this time, I have constantly preached the Dharma and transformed countless billions."

I cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha-way. Since that time, throughout immeasurable kalpas, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, I have manifested nirvana through skillful means, yet in reality I have not entered extinction; I constantly abide here preaching the Dharma.

I always dwell here, and by means of various supernormal powers, I cause deluded sentient beings not to see me even though they are near. When the multitude perceives my passing into extinction, they offer extensive worship.

Śāriputra, they all harbored longing and devotion, giving rise to hearts of yearning and reverence. Once the sentient beings had gained faith and submission, their natures became upright and their minds supple;
with single-minded desire to see the Buddha, they did not spare even their own bodies or lives. At that time, I and the assembly of monks together emerged from Vulture Peak Mountain.
I then said to the sentient beings: "I am always here and do not perish; it is only through the power of skillful means that I manifest extinction."
I do not pass into extinction. In other lands where there are sentient beings who revere, believe in, and delight in me, I further preach the unsurpassed Dharma among them.

You have not heard this, and thus you merely say that I have entered parinirvāṇa. Seeing all sentient beings submerged in suffering and affliction, I therefore do not manifest my body to them, so as to cause them to give rise to longing and yearning; because their hearts are filled with such devotion, I then appear before them.
I preach the Dharma with such supernormal powers that for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have always remained on Vulture Peak Mountain and at other various dwelling places.
When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa and it being consumed by a great conflagration, my land remains peaceful and secure, constantly filled with gods and humans.
Its gardens, groves, and various halls and pavilions are adorned with all kinds of jewels; the jeweled trees abound with flowers and fruits for the enjoyment of sentient beings.

They sport and enjoy themselves; the devas beat celestial drums and constantly perform various musical entertainments. They rain down *māndārava* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes see it as being consumed by fire, filled entirely with grief, terror, and manifold sufferings.
These sentient beings of sinful karma, due to the causes and conditions of their evil deeds, shall not hear the Three [Jewels] for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Those who possess the name of "Jewel," who cultivate merit, and who are gentle and upright—all of them shall see my body here preaching the Dharma.
At times, for this assembly, I speak of the Buddha’s immeasurable lifespan; to those who have seen the Buddha only after a long time, I speak of how difficult it is to encounter a Buddha.
Such is the power of my wisdom; the light of my insight shines immeasurably, and my life-span lasts for incalculable kalpas, having been cultivated through long-term practice.
What has been attained—O wise ones among you, do not harbor doubts regarding this; you should sever it so that it is forever exhausted. The Buddha’s words are true and not false.
Just as a physician with skillful means, for the sake of treating a mad son, says he is dead though he is actually alive, and no one can say that he speaks falsely;
so too am I the Father of the World, rescuing those afflicted by suffering. For the sake of ordinary beings who are deluded, though [the Dharma] is real, I...

I always know which sentient beings are practicing the Path and which are not; according to what is appropriate for their deliverance, I preach various dharmas.
I constantly maintain this intention: by what means can I cause sentient beings to enter unsurpassed wisdom and swiftly achieve accomplishment?
