As is the nirvāṇa of the limit of the nature of self (*ātmatā*), so too is the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata. As is the limit of the nature of all phenomena...
Nirvāṇa. The nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is also like this. As is the nirvāṇa that is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), so too is the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because nirvāṇa is without birth and without emergence. If a phenomenon is without birth and without emergence, then it has no cessation.
Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not speak of the ultimate nirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas for the sake of bodhisattvas, nor does he...
He manifests these matters for their sake. Why is this? It is because he desires to cause them to see all Tathāgatas constantly present before them;
within a single thought-moment, they see all Buddhas of the past and future, their physical forms perfectly pure and clear, as if they were in the present.
Furthermore, they do not give rise to thoughts of duality or non-duality. Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are forever free from the notion of "one."
Because they have severed all conceptual attachments, O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world in order to inspire joy in sentient beings;
they manifest parinirvāṇa in order to inspire longing and devotion in sentient beings. Yet, in reality, there is no appearance in the world for a Tathāgata, nor is there any parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata eternally abides in the pure Dharma-realm, conforming to sentient beings...
He gives rise to the thought [of awakening] and manifests nirvāṇa. O Son of the Buddha, it is like the rising sun that shines universally upon the world;
its reflection appears in all vessels of pure water, pervading every place without coming or going. Yet, if even one vessel is broken, the reflection no longer appears.
O Son of the Buddha, what do you think? Is the non-appearance of that reflection the fault of the sun? He replied:
"No, it is not so. It is merely because the vessel is broken; the sun is not at fault. Son of the Buddha, the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise:
it manifests universally throughout the dharma-realm without before or after, and within the vessels of the pure minds of all sentient beings, there is nowhere the Buddha does not appear."
The vessel of the mind is always pure; thus one constantly beholds the Buddha-body. If the mind is turbid or the vessel is broken, then one cannot see him.
Son of the Buddha, if there are sentient beings who should be delivered through nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata manifests nirvāṇa for them;
yet in reality, the Tathāgata is neither born nor does he perish, and there is no such thing as his extinction. Son of the Buddha, it is like the element of fire, which, toward all...
“In the world, fire performs its function; at times, in a certain place, that fire may be extinguished. What do you think? Is the fire in the entire world extinguished?
He replied, “No, World-Honored One. “Son of the Buddha, it is the same with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
While he performs buddha-works throughout all worlds, in a certain world, his work may be completed.”
When [the Buddha] has finished [teaching], he manifests entry into *nirvāṇa*. How could this mean that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas in all worlds have completely passed into extinction?
Son of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, you should know it thus: the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, Son of the Buddha, it is like a magician who is well-versed in magical arts; by the power of his magical arts, within a trichiliocosm...
Throughout the world—in all lands, cities, towns, and villages—he manifests an illusory body, sustained by the power of illusion, remaining for an eon.
Yet, in other places, having completed his illusory work, he conceals his body and does not appear. Son of the Buddha, what do you think?
Does that great master of illusions, simply because he has concealed his body and disappeared in one place, vanish and cease to exist in all places?
"No," he replied. "O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise. He possesses perfect knowledge of immeasurable wisdom, skillful means, and various illusory arts.
Throughout the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), he universally manifests his body, maintaining it so that it remains forever until the end of the future.
Or, in a single location, according to the minds of sentient beings, he manifests once his tasks are completed."
Nirvāṇa. How could one say that because the Tathāgata manifests entry into nirvāṇa in a single location, he has therefore attained final extinction everywhere?
Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in this way.
Furthermore, son of the Buddha, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, manifests the time of nirvāṇa, he enters the Immovable Samādhi (Acalasamādhi). Having entered this...
Having entered samādhi, from each and every body he emitted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great rays of light.
From each ray of light emerged incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lotus flowers; within each lotus flower were unspeakably many exquisite jewel-flower medicines;
within each flower-medicine was a lion throne; and upon each lion throne sat a Tathāgata.
He sits in the full lotus posture. The number of that Buddha’s bodies is exactly equal to the number of all sentient beings;
they are all adorned with supreme and wondrous merits, having arisen from the power of his original vows. If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured...

Having seen the Buddha’s body, they all receive transformation. Yet that Buddha-body abides eternally until the end of the future, skillfully transforming and delivering all sentient beings without ever missing the proper time. O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata’s body has no fixed location;
it is neither real nor unreal. It is simply through the power of the original vows of all Buddhas that, whenever sentient beings are ready to be delivered, [the Buddha] immediately appears.
Manifests. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand it in this way: the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, [attains] Great Parinirvāṇa.

O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata dwells within the immeasurable, unobstructed, ultimate *dharmadhātu*, the realm of empty space, *tathatā*, *dharmatā*, that which is neither born nor extinguished, and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
yet for the sake of all sentient beings, he manifests according to the time through his original vows.
Because they are upheld, there is no rest; they do not abandon any sentient beings, any lands, or any dharmas.
(Recite once. Connect with the transformation of food into nectar, etc., as in the *Dazuji*; only change the white words [the prose] as follows):

I respectfully hear that this Dharma Master followed in the footsteps of Tiantai and was titled Xianshou; he served as the patriarch of the Huayan school and established its unique system of teaching and contemplation.
He burned one of his fingers at Qizhou, vowing to awaken to the Buddha Vehicle, and lectured on the Mahayana during the Tang Dynasty.
Those on heterodox paths have turned their hearts; from this point, the ten gates are suddenly opened and the five teachings eternally preserved.
Serving as a guide for a thousand autumns and a model for ten thousand generations, we now encounter the anniversary of your parinirvāṇa and offer this humble incense. We humbly pray:

The lamp of wisdom shines forever; the patriarchal seal shines anew. May you protect and inspire future generations, so that the lineage may flourish for all time. (After the recitation, one prostration, return to position, and chant the praise:
How great is Xianshou! His model endures for ten thousand ages. At the age of childhood, he burned his finger to establish a great vow, vowing to seek the very source of the Dharma.
His eloquence suspended the subtle and the profound; his writings and commentaries have been transmitted without interruption. Namo to the Patriarch Xianshou, the National Preeminent Dharma Master.
(Recite three times; the assembly bows three times; each returns to their original place.)
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Master’s name was Fazang, his courtesy name Xianshou.

He was posthumously granted the title Guoyi (National One) and served as the third patriarch of the Huayan school in the Eastern Land. His secular surname was Kang, and he was a native of the kingdom of Kangju.
He was born on the second day of the eleventh month in the seventeenth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, contemporaneous with Zhiyi of Tiantai. Their lifespans overlapped.
Two hundred years have passed since he departed. He was dedicated exclusively to propagating the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Within that sūtra, there is a chapter titled "Bhadrapāla" (Worthy Head), and among the ten Bodhisattvas, there is one Bodhisattva who is also named Bhadrapāla. Therefore, he was given the name "Xianshou" (Worthy Head) based on these two characters.
This is precisely how the name of this school was established. The doctrines and contemplations it establishes are largely identical to those of Tiantai, with only minor differences.
It takes the "Nirvāṇa Chapter" from the *Prādurbhāva-parivarta* as its fundamental teaching; what it venerates coincides exactly with the matters of taboo.
Tiantai also employs the "Life Span Chapter" of the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* for this same purpose. Lately, various... [text continues]

Avoidance. For the practice of recitation, one should apply the mind diligently to the *Sūtra of the Many Hearts*, the *Nien-fo Ch'ing-wang Chou* (Recitation of the Name of Amitābha), or the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

This is appropriate when performed before the spirit-tablet of an ordinary person. However, as for the various ancestral masters and eminent monks who have long since transcended the three realms, how could they rely on such [recitations] for their deliverance like ordinary beings?
Therefore, the various patriarchs of today each follow their own school and perform the recitation accordingly.

Recite. Just as the Patriarch Daruma recited the one hundred and eight phrases of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* before his predecessors to take the seal of the mind from the Chan school—there being nothing like these one hundred and eight phrases—so too did the Patriarch Baizhang recite the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* before his predecessors to ensure it accorded with the monastic regulations (*qinggui*).
Furthermore, the Vinaya Patriarch Daoxuan recited the verses of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, and the distant patriarchs of the Lotus Society recited [the same].
The Chapter on Mahāsthāmaprāpta: It is hoped that the various lineages will not fall into confusion or disorder.

Once the descendants clearly understand their respective ancestral traditions, the spirits of the patriarchs will likewise increase in their joy and affection. This interpretation seeks to establish a meaningful connection rather than remaining vague;
by following the names and examining the reality, it truly accords with the needs of the occasion. Although newly formulated by later generations, it is certainly not in contradiction with the truth.
Regarding the former sages and the patriarchs of the various schools, since their mantra recitations were distinct, so too was it for the successive generations of their descendants;
thus, as they continued in an unbroken stream, each had its own specific destination.

The anniversary of the Venerable Daoxuan, the Patriarch of the Vinaya, is on the third day of the tenth month. [The Master of Nanshan, the Patriarch of the Vinaya, Daoxuan’s Anniversary Ritual (the same as for the Patriarch Da; first recite as follows):]
Namo to the Patriarch of Nanshan, the Vinaya Master Daoxuan (Recite three times).
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha, in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind," states in verse: "A person of clarity with strong patience and wisdom can uphold such a Dharma.
Before attaining the path of Buddhahood, they shall securely obtain five kinds of benefits. First, the Buddhas of the ten directions will always regard them with compassion."
1. Protection; 2. At the time of death, a joyful mind of right view; 3. In every place of rebirth, becoming a friend to all bodhisattvas; 4.
A mass of merit, with the perfection of ethical discipline fully accomplished; 5. In this and future lives, the fulfillment of natural morality, merit, and wisdom.
These are the children of the Buddhas; let the wise contemplate this well. Those who calculate based on a self and cling to signs cannot believe in this.
This Dharma is not a place for planting seeds even for those who have extinguished their lifespan and attained realization.
Those who wish to nurture the sprouts of Bodhi and illuminate the world with light should observe with stillness the true nature of all phenomena:

that they are neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated, neither identical nor different, and neither coming nor going. Thus, within this single mind, one should apply skillful means with diligence.
Adornment is what a bodhisattva ought to do; one should study it in its proper sequence. Regarding those in training and those beyond training, do not give rise to discriminatory thoughts.
This is called the primary path, and it is also called the Mahāyāna. All evil conceptual proliferations are extinguished from this place;
all the *sarvajñā* (omniscience) of the Buddhas emerges from this place. Therefore, O sons of the Buddha, you should generate the great [resolve].
O valiant one! Regarding the pure precepts of all Buddhas, you should protect and uphold them like a bright pearl. All Bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in this;
those of the future shall train in it; and those of the present are training in it now. This is the sphere of action of the Buddhas, praised by the Holy Lords.

I have explained this in accordance with their teaching. May the immeasurable mass of merit resulting from this be dedicated to sentient beings, so that we may together proceed toward [enlightenment].

All-knowing One! May those who wish to hear this Dharma swiftly attain the Way of the Buddha. (Recite once. Follow with "Transforming Food into Nectar," etc., identical to the memorial service for Master Da.

Substitute as follows: We respectfully hear that the Vinaya abides in the world as the foundation of the Holy Path. Upāli compiled it in Western India, while the Great Master manifested his response-body in the Eastern Land.
He inherited the lineage from Zhishou and initiated the teachings at Zhongnan. All of China together revere the light of the precepts; throughout Zhendan...
All acclaim him as the Master of the Vinaya. Moved by his virtue, he was attended by devas and humans; the Buddha’s tooth relic was bestowed upon him to manifest his excellence.

Relying on the Buddha’s regulations, he constructed the *kṣetradhara* (precept altar), which future generations have long relied upon. Following the celestial instructions, he compiled the biographical records, providing essential support for the Dharma-ending age.

Now, coinciding with the anniversary of his return to heaven, we specially present these pure offerings. We humbly pray that the wind of the Vinaya may forever flourish and the seal of the Patriarchs may shine once more.

The fragrance of the precepts perfumes the nine provinces; the rain of the Dharma moistens the seven assemblies. (Having finished the announcement, one prostrates once, rises, assumes the formal posture, and returns to one’s place.

The eulogy is intoned, and the assembly chants: Pārāśarya has reappeared; the Vinaya studies flourish anew. The Master of Nanshan utters a thunderous voice; the three aggregates and two observances are renewed.
The ocean of precepts is clear and serene; the True Dharma shall forever flourish and shine. Homage to the Lord of Nanshan, Vinaya Master Daoxian Chengzhao.
(Recite three times; the assembly bows three times; each returns to their place.)
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Master’s name was Daoxuan, his courtesy name was Shixiang, and he is the first patriarch of the Vinaya school in China.

During the reign of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty, an imperial edict was issued for all monasteries throughout the land to depict his likeness and fashion statues in his honor. Emperor Yizong posthumously conferred upon him the title "Holy Teacher Chengzhao.
This is recorded in full in the fourteenth fascicle of the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song). Today, [this image] is offered and venerated through recitation.
The final verses of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* are divided into three sections. The first sixteen lines concern the meaning of praising and encouraging the benefits of upholding the precepts.
The next twenty-four lines concern the meaning of observing the essence of the precepts as the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

The final sixteen lines concern the meaning of exhorting the protection of pure precepts, along with the dedication [of merit] for one's own benefit and the benefit of others. May this be offered to those above.
This refers to engraving [the meaning] in one's heart through this recitation. One may also recite the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth [sections].

Regarding the two precepts on not making vows or oaths, see the section on "Maintaining the Office" (*Jūji-hō*) under the entry for "Announcing Incense" (*Kōkō-jō*). You must recite them thoroughly and reflect upon them, thereby exhorting yourself.

The anniversary of the passing of the Venerable Patriarch Huiyuan is on the sixth day of the eighth month. The Anniversary of the Passing of the Great Patriarch Huiyuan, Lord of the Pure Land (the ritual is identical to that for the Patriarch Da; first state:).
Namo to the First Patriarch of the Nianmen School, the Venerable Master Huiyuan (recite three times, then join in recitation):
The Śūraṃgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Causes for Cultivation and Realization of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Amitābha.
Twelve Tathāgatas followed in succession throughout one kalpa; the last of these Buddhas was named Sūryavairocanaprabhāsa."
That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. It is like this: suppose there is one person who is single-mindedly mindful and another who is single-mindedly forgetful;
these two people may meet and yet not meet, or see and yet not see. Yet, because the two are mindful of each other, their mutual mindfulness is profound.
In this way, it continues until birth after birth; they are like a form and its shadow, never diverging or differing from one another.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish and pity sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child has run away and fled, though the mother remembers him, what can she do? But if the child remembers his mother...

Just as when a mother remembers her child, the mother and child will not be separated throughout their successive lives; so too, if sentient beings remember the Buddha and recite his name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and the future.
They will not be far from the Buddha, and without relying on expedient means, their own minds will naturally open.
Just as a person who has been perfumed with incense has a fragrance upon their body, this is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light.

In my original stage of practice, I entered the patience of non-arising through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha; now, within this world-realm, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of dhyāna]. I have made no selection among them, but by gathering all six sense faculties and maintaining a continuous flow of pure mindfulness, I have attained samādhi;

this is the foremost method. (Recite the *Wǎngshēng zhòu* three times, recite the Buddha’s name one hundred times, then recite the *Biànsì zhòu* fourteen times, and the *Gānlù* and *Pǔgòng* mantras three times each. The Venerable Rector joins his palms and says:)

I respectfully report that the Patriarch of Pure Practice was indeed Master Huiyuan in person. Having manifested his traces at Yanmen, he opened the Dharma at Mount Lu and led one hundred and twenty-three people with a single mind toward rebirth in the West.
On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month, they joined their words together to take a collective vow.

Announcement from Donglin Monastery: The world universally admires his lofty character; the Western Teaching has spread its fragrance, and for ten thousand generations all shall partake of its benevolent grace.
Now, on this auspicious day when the lotus blooms, we, the assembly, reverently offer this incense of the heart. We humbly pray that you will not forget your original vows.

Following Amitābha to provide guidance, universally ferrying the compassionate vessel to deliver sentient beings to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. (After the recitation, one prostration; return to position; chant the praise:
The First Great Vow: Contemplate Amitābha; by the Forty-Eight Vows, he delivers the Sahā world. From the nine grades, golden waves surge forth.
Interlaced with jeweled nets, they ferry sentient beings across the river of craving. Homage to the Patriarch Master Jingye (Recite three times;
the assembly prostrates three times; each returns to their place).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The biography of the Master appears in the sixth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) and need not be elaborated upon here.
As for the recitation of the "Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Mindfulness of Amitābha by Mahāsthāmaprāpta" as an offering, this section provides the most direct and straightforward instruction.

Master Youxi’s commentary states: Regarding the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), one who practices mindfulness of the Buddha takes the Buddha as the object of the mind and binds the mind to the Buddha.
Mind and mind continue in succession without interruption. At that time, no internal thoughts arise and external objects do not intrude.
Turning back to the source is returning to oneself; reversing the flow restores the unity of the mind. When one truly does not undergo any sensations, one attains right reception (*samyak-samādhi*);

therefore, it is called the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi (*nien-fo san-mei*). First, the analogy is established: "One person is single-mindedly intent on remembering" is a metaphor for the Buddha constantly mindful of sentient beings, considering how to deliver them from the suffering of the triple world.
"One person is single-mindedly intent on forgetting" is a metaphor for sentient beings who are solely preoccupied with greed.
The five sensory objects cause one to willingly undergo the sufferings of the six realms.

These two types of people—whether they meet or do not meet, whether they see or do not see—are metaphors for how the Buddha constantly meets and sees sentient beings, while sentient beings constantly fail to meet and see the Buddha;
this illustrates the fault of sentient beings not recollecting the Buddha. The two people remembering each other is a metaphor for the Buddha constantly recollecting sentient beings.
Sentient beings also at times recollect the Buddha; this is what is called the two kinds of profound mindfulness.
If one can recollect in this way, then in birth after birth one will constantly see the Buddha, and in land after land one will behold the Tathāgata. Therefore it is said:

"In this manner, from birth to birth, they are like a form and its shadow, never becoming separated. Next is the application of the analogy, which cites a close metaphor to illustrate the point, as follows:
"Coming to pity and cherish sentient beings, as a mother remembers her child" corresponds to one person being exclusively mindful.
"If the child has fled and gone away, though she remembers him, what can she do? corresponds to one person being exclusively forgetful; this corresponds to the fault of not recollecting the Buddha.
Next, the correspondence regarding the attainment of recollecting the Buddha: "If the child remembers his mother," this teaches the method for the child to remember his mother.
One should be like a mother remembering [her child] when one is called a person who recollects the Buddha. One must apply earnest effort and not for a single moment think of the five worldly desires;

this is called "binding the mindfulness. Only then can one be named as being "like a mother remembering [her child]," even though the mother and child have been separated through successive lifetimes.

They are not contradictory or far removed from one another. Furthermore, "recalling the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti*) refers to constant and thorough contemplation; "mindfulness of the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti*) refers to the mind being focused on a single object.
Regarding the phrase "one will certainly see the Buddha in the present or the future": "in the present" refers to instances such as Master Huiyuan’s three visions of the holy form;
"in the future" refers to instances such as the Buddha welcoming one at the time of death, or seeing the Buddha when the flower blooms.

"To be not far from the Buddha" means that those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha do not merely see the Buddha; they are also not far from the Buddha and shall certainly attain Buddhahood before long.
"Without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind" means that as soon as a thought arises, it takes the realm of the Buddha as its object.
Here, phenomena and principle are perfectly integrated, and subject and object are transcended. This refers to what is called: "At my original stage, by means of mindfulness..."
The Buddha-mind enters the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). If it were not so, how could one immediately accord with non-arising without relying on skillful means?

Thus, faith is not deceptive. As for the person who is stained by incense, this is a metaphor for sentient beings who are originally not Buddhas, yet through the mindfulness of the Buddha, they suddenly possess the fragrance of Buddhahood.
Regarding the name "Adorned with Fragrant Light," it is because the Buddha is manifested through mindfulness, and mindfulness is the cause.
"Buddha-fragrance" means that the fragrance of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas adorns the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of sentient beings.
The three phrases beginning with "I, in my original ground" conclude the correspondence between the causes and effects of one's own practice.

Now, the three phrases beginning with "In this world" refer to benefiting others after attaining the fruit. Having already used this to save oneself, one then uses this to teach others; likewise, by...
This power gathers in all living beings; I make no selection. Regarding the "gathering of all six sense faculties," mindfulness belongs to the mental faculty (*manas*).
While this primarily concerns the locus of cultivation, it also incidentally encompasses all the other faculties, such that each faculty recollects the Buddha.
If the mental faculty is purified, all the faculties are gathered; therefore, there is no selection. Throughout daily life, one recollects only Amitābha, and only the Pure Land.
To seek this with uninterrupted continuity is precisely what it means for pure mindfulness to succeed one another. Such a dharma-gate truly surpasses all other gates;
therefore, it is called "entering samādhi," and this is the foremost.

Regarding the Memorial Services for the Founding Patriarchs: Whenever the memorial day for the founding patriarch of this temple or those of successive patriarchs arrives, the Guest Master (zhikè), having informed the Abbot one day in advance, shall immediately post a notice board.
(The board shall read: "Tomorrow is the solemn occasion of the memorial day for [Name] Patriarch; all members of the assembly, please attend."
That evening, when the morning service has concluded, upon hearing the sound of the bell, everyone proceeds together before the image to prostrate. At the midday signal, the offerings are presented.
○ In the Shadow Hall, the attendant hangs the portrait of a specific patriarch and reports it for offering. Regarding fruits and vegetables, there must be one or two seasonal items;
this is what is meant by "offering what is appropriate to the season. Incense, candles, and tea offerings are set out. When the evening service is finished, the bell is struck.
Three prostrations. The assembly gathers before the image. The abbot offers incense and tea. Having completed the bows, the rector calls for the spreading of sitting cloths (*zhangu*).

They perform three prostrations to the patriarchs, then withdraw the cloths and say, "I pay my deepest respects. When the ceremony is concluded, they return to the hall; there may be a liturgical service involving chanting and recitation.

The *vinaya* master (weina) and the guest prefect (zhike) shall pre-announce the invitation to the various masters. Once the signboard has been hung, they notify the hall master (*dianzhu*) to prepare and arrange the ritual altar (*jingtan*).

On the following morning, after the morning service is completed, the ceremonial protocol is the same as before; however, only the founding patriarch (*kaishan zu*) and the Dharma-successor master (*sishi fa*) ascend the hall during the forenoon session, while the others merely present offerings.
When the midday gong sounds and the offerings are presented, the assembly gathers. The abbot (*zhuchi*) bows in greeting (*wenxun*) and offers incense (*nianxiang*).

After the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) has finished reciting the incense hymn (*gandha-stotra*), he leads the assembly in chanting "Namo to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Lotus Pond Assembly" three times.

As the assembly takes up the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, they wait until the *sthavira* (Abbot) has completed two of his three prostrations. At this point, the *śrāmaṇera* (Head Seat) and the *xi-tang* (West Hall) take their positions first, standing at the sides of the Abbot.
Next, six officers from each of the two orders take their places on either side; the rest of the original ranks follow, moving forward by half a step to stand near them.

The Chief Seat (Shouzuo), the West Hall (Xitang), and the Abbot—these three persons kneel in the "eight-character" formation. Two Attendant Monks (Zhike) stand by the image, attending to the proceedings in order.
They receive and transmit the offerings: first tea, then the chopsticks. Starting from the head of the Eastern Assembly, they are passed one by one in sequence until they reach the Chief Seat.
The Chief Seat receives them with both hands and presents them to the Abbot. Once the Abbot has raised the sacrificial vessel, he passes it on.
In the West Hall, each item is passed down in successive order until it reaches the head of the Western Class, who hands it to the Guest Prefect (Zhikè) to arrange.
The vegetables, soup, snacks, and rice are all served according to the meal protocol of the Abbot’s quarters. Once everything is set out, those on both sides stand up and return to their positions.

They wait until the Abbot has completed eight prostrations; only then is the *Amitābha Sūtra* finished. After the recitation of the dharanis and the hundred recitations of the Buddha’s name are concluded, the Abbot takes up [the incense].

[Incense is offered. After the Dharma has been preached, the Rector (Vina) recites the memorial text. The hymns of praise [are composed according to the tradition of the specific lineage; they are not provided here in full]. While the Abbot is offering tea, the assembly bows.

Once the bowing and the hymns are finished, the Rector calls for them to "unfold their mats" (zhanju). The assembly performs three prostrations to the Patriarchs. When the prostrations are finished, he calls for them to "prostrate to the Preceptor" (dingli heshang).

When that is finished, he calls for them to "rise from their mats. Each returns to his own place. This procedure applies only to the Founder (Kaishan), the Restorer (Zhongxing), and the Dharma Heir (Sifa).

The ritual for receiving the precepts (i.e., from the tonsure master). For the other patriarchs, no altar is set up and no sutras are chanted; there is no individual kneeling to present offerings, but only the offering of tea upon the altar.
However, this portrait hall must be entered only by those who have rendered service to the temple or who hold the Dharma as its abbot;
only then may they take their place and receive the prostrations of the assembly. They are not treated as equals. As for the memorial tablets for their death anniversaries:
A notice shall be posted in each of the guest hall, the storehouse, and the quarters of the *vinaya-dhara* and the attendant; this is so that no errors may occur.

Zengyi said: "This is to report the virtue of those who founded the monastery and the merit of those who have succeeded in maintaining it. As one who drinks water knows its source, it is fitting according to ritual to offer sacrifices to them;
they should not be forgotten or neglected."

Regarding the anniversary of the Dharma-successor’s passing: whenever the anniversary of one’s own Dharma-teacher’s passing occurs, [the procedures for] making offerings and so forth have already been recorded in the previous discourse. However, for this ritual service, the abbot must personally provide his own funds to the treasury office to arrange the memorial rites and offerings, as well as the chanting of sutras.

He shall instruct the secretary to prepare a document of dedication (*huixiang shu*); if it is not possible to prepare one separately, then write according to this model of the dedication document (first recording one's native place and the dates of birth and death). Respectfully contemplating the Master...

The Master was by nature compassionate and kind; his appearance transcended the notions of self and other. He succeeded to the regulations of the monastic groves, his conduct matching that of Baizhang;

he established strategic principles within the Zen hall, his virtue surpassing ten thousand peaks. He transmitted the heart-lamp of Linji for nearly ten or more generations, pointing directly so that one might part the clouds and behold the moon;
he enjoyed a worldly lifespan of nearly ten or more years, finally departing from the dust and toil of the mundane world.

Thus, he returned to simplicity and restored his true nature. Now, as this day coincides with the anniversary of his passing, I, his disciple [Name], am deeply ashamed that I have merely inherited the grace of the robe and bowl, failing to live up to the metaphor of the green dye surpassing the blue.
For this reason, I have invited the assembly to recite [Name] Sutra for one day, offering my sincere and earnest supplications to the Compassionate Honored One.
I hereby inaugurate this Dharma assembly for humans and devas. By means of these merits, I respectfully offer this requital.

I prostrate and pray that before the peak of Vulture Mountain, you may transcend and dwell in the station of Wondrous Enlightenment; and within the Land of Tranquil Light, may your body of eternal bliss abide in the signless state.
[Date]. Written by the disciple [Name], etc. (The remainder follows the standard format for recitation).

The Commentary on the Meaning states: This is to repay the kindness of the transmission of the Dharma. One’s parents give birth to one’s physical body (*rūpakāya*), whereas one’s former teacher gives birth to one’s life of wisdom (*prajñājīva*).
The physical body is illusory and unsubstantial, while the life of wisdom provides inexhaustible benefit.

Thus, while the kindness of one’s parents is already difficult to repay, the kindness of one’s former teacher is even more difficult to repay. How could this meager offering of water-moss and pond-weed ever suffice?
"Are you not being negligent? Consider, for instance, how Ba Ling composed three 'turning words' as a memorial service for Yunmen; such was the depth of the former masters' dedication.
Yet today, in this age of the Dharma's decline, not only do they neglect memorial rites, they have grown indifferent to them altogether.
Worse still, there are those who scheme for fame and status, betraying their hearts and forgetting their origins to seek succession under others—this is truly lamentable."
How lamentable! The *Secret Essentials of the Chan School* states: Under the seat of Master Wuzu Fayan, there was a student named Kaishengjue.
Having initially studied under Changlefu Tiejiao for a long time without gaining anything, he heard of Master Yan’s Dharma path and went directly to his seat.
One day, in the meditation hall, [the Master] asked him: "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still but his servants. Furthermore—"
"Who is this Way? Jue said, "Bearded Zhang San; dark Li Si. Master Yan approved of these words. At that time, Venerable Yuanwu was the Head Seat (Zuoyuan).
The Master brought up these words to him, and Yuanwu said, "Excellent, indeed, but I fear it is not yet real.
You must not let this pass; you must search further beneath these words. The next day, when [the Master] entered the room for private instruction, Yuanwu posed the same question as before.
Jue said, "Yesterday I told the Master. Yanshi asked, "What did you say? Jue said, "Hú Zhāngsān, Hēi Lìsì. Yanshi said, "Not so, not so. Jue asked, "Why did the Master say it was so yesterday?
Yanshi said, "Yesterday it was; today it is not. At these words, Jue attained great enlightenment. Jue.
Later, he appeared in the world and resided at Kaisheng. Seeing that the Dharma assembly at Changlu was flourishing, he succeeded to the lineage of Tiejiao.

He did not investigate the person from whom he had originally attained realization; when it came time to offer incense, he suddenly felt as if his chest were being pounded. Consequently, an abscess developed at the painful spot, forming an opening.
He used a cake of milky incense to plug it, but it did not heal after a long time, and he eventually passed away. Alas, this was a transgression!
This was the bitter retribution for having neglected the heavy debt of gratitude. May future students take care not to follow this same disastrous precedent.
Furthermore, the *Yunqi Chongxing Lu* (Record of the Venerable Conduct of Yunqi) states: Huai-zhi of the Song dynasty was a native of Jin-hua.

Having studied the exegesis of the sutras since childhood, he was inspired by a Zen practitioner and abandoned his lectures to travel to visit various masters. In his later years, he arrived at Dongshan and received the Dharma from Chan Master Zhenjing Wen.

After a long time, the Master took his leave. Zhenjing instructed him, saying, "Your Zen is indeed of an extraordinary caliber; it is only a pity that your karmic conditions are not yet sufficient. Zhizhi bowed and received these instructions.
Upon arriving in Yuanzhou, the local people requested that he take up residence at Yangqi, but he declined and departed to travel along the Xiang River.
Subsequently, Tanmu invited him to head Shangfeng and Beichan, but he accepted neither. He then established a hermitage on Mount Heng for twenty years.

In his later years, there was a verse that said: "Ten thousand affairs brought to rest, entrusted to the simple and the foolish; My traces allow wild deer to join me at times. Unbuckling my hempen robe, I make a pillow of my fists;
Through many lifetimes, my dreams remain within the Green Ivy Hermitage. In his later years, he joined the community at Long’an.
At Long’an, he stayed in the Hall of Ultimate Joy (Chuizhi-le-tang) and remained there until the end of his life. Master Lianchi praised him, saying: "Renown and success are what people [seek]..."
I wish to comply with his final instructions and resolutely refuse all requests; can this not be called difficult?
Nowadays, people crave fame and profit and cast aside ritual and righteousness, going to such places in droves without even being invited—how could they possibly remember the Master’s command?

The Memorial Service for the Two Masters Who Ordained and Taught the Scriptures (as per the preceding ritual; the incumbent must also personally provide funds from his own resources to the administrative office to arrange the offerings and the chanting of scriptures and mantras; the only difference lies in the dedication prayer).

I reflect deeply that I, [Name], throughout hundreds of kalpas of existence, have lived in vain and died in vain. Fortunately, I have received the tonsure and the dharma-robes [if receiving the scriptures, change "tonsure and robes" to "compassion"].

[By] receiving the teachings, one gains entry into the Buddha’s gate (when bestowing scriptures, change this to "the Dharma-gate"). Reflecting deeply upon this most profound kindness, I truly harbor sighs that it is difficult to repay.

Tracing back to those former days when my solitary spirit returned to stillness, I sank into the deep waves of the ocean of sorrow. On this anniversary of the memorial, my five internal organs are filled with grief and trepidation;
I lament the boundless vastness of Heaven. Therefore, I have invited the assembly to recite the scriptures for one day, to offer a small measure of my sincere devotion.

Sincerely, I prostrate myself and pray: May the Sun of the Buddha shed its radiance to incinerate the karmic obstacles of all sentient beings; may the Wind of Compassion blow everywhere to sweep away the transgressions of beginningless time.
May they be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss with a mere snap of the fingers, and sit upon lotus pedestals at the mere thought of it.
May their Bodhi never regress and their Prajñā remain ever-luminous. Written on this day, month, and year, by the unfilial disciple [Name].
The Commentary on the Meaning states: "Tonsure and the conferring of scriptures" refer to the first two of the five types of *ācāryas*.

Although one may not have received the formal Dharma-transmission, because they have undergone tonsure and dyeing of the robes, or have been granted the scriptures and so forth, citing these examples demonstrates that one does not forget one's origins.
However, disciples of antiquity possessed ever-firmer faith even after their teacher had passed away; as for the disciples of today...
This is because while one's teacher is still alive, it is easy to maintain one's own way; how much more so when merely remembering the anniversary of their passing!

This is truly because, at the very beginning of leaving the household life, one did not actually intend to rely upon a true master to resolve the matters of birth and death; rather, it was merely a temporary coincidence.

Therefore, such a person’s mind finds it easy to yield when confronted with profit, and easy to be deluded by evil friends when they encounter them. When their teacher reprimands them for their faults...
When one is correct, it is easy; yet there are those who go so far as to abandon the correct and enter the deviant, with some even returning to lay life from the monastic order.
How lamentable is the decline of the Buddha-Dharma! According to the Vinaya, the Buddha established that a disciple must not depart from their teacher too early;
only if the teacher is truly ignorant or fails to observe the precepts is departure permitted. The *Yunqi Chongxing Lu* (Records of Revered Conduct at Yunqi) states: During the Tang dynasty, Qing...
Jiang, from his youth, realized that all things are like illusions and bubbles. He took the Dharma Master Tanyi as his preceptor (upādhyāya) and recited the sutras and Dharma;

everything he encountered was immediately understood. Those who recognized his potential remarked, "This is a 'thousand-li colt' of the monastic community. Once, he slightly offended his teacher, whereupon he abandoned him to travel abroad.
Having traversed many dharma assemblies, he reproached himself, saying, "I have wandered half the world, yet I have not found anyone like my original teacher."

It was too late. He then returned to the Master’s quarters. When the monks had assembled, he carried a bundle of thorny branches and proclaimed aloud, "Qingjiang has come again to seek refuge with the Master;

I only pray that you will accept me. At that time, one master reviled him. Qingjiang shed tears of rain and apologized, saying, "My former thoughts were ignorant, but my later mind has attained awakening.
I hope the Master, in his great compassion, will grant me joy. Thus he entreated him most earnestly.

The Vinaya Master took pity on him and thus resumed their relationship as teacher and disciple as before. When the first master passed away, he went to visit National Teacher Zhong and received the essential transmission of the Mind.
Master Lianchi praised him, saying: "He abandoned sages and worthies to recognize his error; he did not retreat even when faced with insults and abuse."
One may truly say he was both enlightened and sincere. How could it have been otherwise that he ultimately transmitted the seal of the mind?

As for those of shallow faith, a slight resentment causes them to depart forever without returning; a mild reproach leaves them harboring grudges they never forget. To have encountered an enlightened master in vain—what benefit is there in the end?
It is like meeting a sovereign emperor and failing to obtain even a single official post. What a pity!

(Appendix: Memorial Services for Parents) The memorial services for one's parents differ slightly in ritual from those for others; they concern only one’s own kin and are not shared with the general assembly. On the day prior to the service, the Abbot shall instruct the Attendant to deliver the ritual offerings to the storehouse and arrange the memorial banquet.

If a recitation service is to be held, the Attendant shall immediately inform the Rector and the Guest Office. The Guest Office shall then post a notice, which reads: "Tomorrow, the Abbot shall perform a memorial service for his father’s [or mother’s] anniversary of death (or birth, as appropriate)."
[Revision] To recite [Name of Sūtra] for one day, please invite the following number of sūtra masters, listed below: Master [Name], Master [Name].

When the evening service is held in the hall, the abbot shall instruct the attendant to set up offering seats to the left of the Abbot’s Quarters (fangzhang). Having prepared incense, flowers, lamps, and tea, these are offered before the tablet. Once the evening service concludes and the assembly returns to the hall, the abbot goes alone outside the mountain gate.

Facing the direction of the lay family’s residence, he focuses his mind and silently invokes them, saying: "I, the Buddhist son [Name], tomorrow encounter the anniversary of my late father or compassionate mother. Therefore, I have now established this seat within the temple to make offerings. I only pray that..."

My father and my mother, through inconceivable natural affinity, became aware of this in due time; they immediately knew that their son was here making this request and came accordingly. When the third of the three requests was made with utmost sincerity, one should visualize the appearance and voices of one’s parents as if they had actually come in response to the invitation.

Having visualized that the parents have arrived, one should silently say: "My father and my mother have come together to the temple. Having finished this visualization, one should immediately enter the temple, perform four prostrations before the prepared seat, offer incense, and present [the offerings].

Offer tea. Visualize that your parents are seated with solemn dignity; feel joy and happiness, bow four times, and withdraw. That night, the abbot personally uses a *pútuán* (grass mat) and sits at the lower edge of the place where the tablets are set. He silently recites the sacred name of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva ten thousand times.

The following morning, after the morning service is concluded, the abbot alone proceeds to the place where the tablets are set, offers incense, and presents tea. At the signal of the midday bell, he requests several masters to recite the sutras while they perform the offering before the tablets; the ritual is the same as before, though not performed individually for each one.

Kneeling, they present their offerings and likewise do not perform prostrations. If they do perform bows, they wait until the preaching of the Dharma is concluded. Once the verses of praise (*stotra*) have been recited and the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*) completed, the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) says: "Prostrate to the Upādhyāya; each shall return to his own place. When the evening recitation is finished, the dedication of merit is performed as usual.
Then, one addresses the Buddha with a memorial (*śū*) for the deceased, saying: We humbly submit that the Tamer of the Śākya Heaven is the Guide across the ocean of enlightenment;

the sacred texts of the Three Piṭakas are contained within the jade caskets; and the six-fold harmonious community consists of the superior men of the golden land. We dare to pour forth our private devotion and venture to trouble Your Perfect and Radiant discernment. (Continue by entering the details of the lay residence, hometown, lineage, and so forth.)
Residing beneath this shrine, I, the bhikṣu [Name], recite the sūtras and make offerings to the Buddha on behalf of my deceased father (or mother).

Today, with a sincere heart, I offer incense and take refuge in the Lords of Transformation of the two lands, Amitābha and Śākyamuni, within the Land of Ultimate Bliss. I specifically dedicate these merits for the posthumous spirit of my late father, Lord [Name] (if for a mother, change to "my late mother, Lady [Name] of the [Family] clan"; if dedicating to both parents, use the names of both).
To this day, I single-mindedly offer incense and take refuge in the Lords of Transformation of the two lands, Amitābha and Śākyamuni, within the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

To the Buddhas and Holy Sages beneath the golden lotus seats, we respectfully communicate our intent. We humbly petition on behalf of our late father (Name), who enjoyed a lifespan of [number] years. His original destiny was such that he was born on the [day], [month], and [time] of the [year], and his great limit ended when he passed away on the [day], [month], [year], and [time]. (If offering for a mother, or for both parents, adjust accordingly. We reflect deeply upon our stern lord [or, if for a mother, "our compassionate parent," or if for both, "our compassionate parents"]. We pray that you will grant us your compassionate protection. May he be reborn in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, where he shall dwell eternally in peace and joy. May he transcend the three realms and forever sever the cycle of birth and death. We pray that this merit may extend to all sentient beings, that they may all attain liberation. We prostrate ourselves with utmost sincerity. May it be so. [The text] has been revised to read: "The virtue of my parents was as weighty as Mount Tai rising ever higher; their grace in nourishing and raising me was as deep as the vast ocean, difficult to measure.
Unhappily, they passed away early, and I have yet to repay even a speck of dust of their sacrifice. Days and months pass in succession, and time swiftly flees.

Now, on this day, the [blank]th of this month, as the anniversary of their passing approaches its [blank]th cycle, I rely upon the power of the Great Awakened One to offer this supreme requital for their toilsome labor."

By virtue of this merit, we invite several monks to recite several sections of the [Name] Sūtra, thereby aiding [the deceased’s] journey through the clouds and ensuring their early departure from the dark realms.

We humbly pray that those already among gods and humans may further increase their five blessings and roam at ease as they please; and that those not yet freed from the various realms of existence may ascend to the nine grades of rebirth and attain mastery according to their hearts’ desire.
This memorial respectfully requests the Three Jewels to bear witness to this recitation of the sūtra. Recite the sūtra.

Memorial for the Dedication of Merit for the Ancestors. On the [day], [month], and [year]. Written by the Bhikṣu [Name]. (The memorial is completed. The Abbot then instructs an attendant to take leave of the masters who have been reciting the sutras.)
The Commentary on the Meaning states: This is to repay the kindness of one’s parents in raising and nurturing one, as well as the kindness of permitting one to leave the household life.
According to the *Mahāyāna-mūla-jātaka-citta-bhūmi-parīkṣā-sūtra*, the Buddha taught four debts of gratitude (*catvāra upakāriṇaḥ*), among which the debt to one’s parents is foremost.
The *Liang Emperor’s Repentance Ritual* says: "Next, one must further reflect upon the kindness of one’s parents in raising and nurturing one. [The text continues: "With a mind of..."
"Carrying them in her arms and nursing them, her love and deep affection were such that she would rather endanger her own life than fail to establish her child in safety," and so forth.

The Buddha said, "Among all the kindnesses in the world, none surpass those of one's parents. Now, one who abandons the household life has not yet attained the Way; they must only diligently study their practice.
By performing good deeds and accumulating merit without ceasing, one will surely be able to repay the debt of gratitude for their laborious kindness. He further said:
If among them there are parents who have passed away while young, they are difficult to encounter again; one can only contemplate them in silent longing.
Since one has not yet attained supernatural powers or the divine eye, one does not know where the parents' consciousness has been reborn after relinquishing its retribution.

One should only strive to establish the power of merit to pursue and repay their kindness. By practicing goodness without ceasing, success will surely be achieved when the merit is perfected. As the Sūtra says:
To perform meritorious deeds for the deceased is like sending provisions to one traveling far away. If they have been reborn among humans or devas, their merit will increase;

if they dwell in the three miserable realms or within the eight difficult conditions, they shall forever be freed from all suffering. If they possess true faith and receive the teachings of the True Dharma, they will immediately attain transcendent awakening;
thus, their parents of seven generations and their kinsmen throughout kalpas will have all their anxieties and fears eliminated, and they shall together attain liberation.
This is what constitutes a wise person—one who possesses ultimate compassion and filial piety, and who offers the highest form of gratitude.

Based on this, performing rites for the posthumous salvation of the deceased is in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings. The *Record of Yunqi’s Venerable Deeds* states: Fayan of the Liang dynasty was a native of Yangxian.
He entered the monastic order at the age of seven as a disciple of Baoliang of Zhuangyan Temple. Talented, brilliant, and outstanding, he began lecturing at Miaoyin Temple.
Scholars flocked to study the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Vimalakīrti* sūtras. Xing was sincere and filial; he was exhausted by his efforts to provide physical care for his mother.
During the period of mourning for her, his emaciation exceeded the prescribed rites. After several days of not eating, Dharma Master Min said to him:

"The Sages established the rites so that the worthy might conform to them from above, while the unworthy might reach them from below. Furthermore, even in Confucianism, it is held that 'grieving does not destroy one's nature. How much more so in Buddhism?"
There is a profound saying: "If one wishes to repay the kindness of life, on a proximate level, one should constantly attend to the countenance and demeanor [of one's parents];
on a remote level, one should inspire them toward Bodhi to guide their consciousness. You ought to quickly contemplate these far-reaching principles so that there may be a successful crossing over.

How can you indulge your emotions as if they were trivial and mundane? Yun then cut short his mourning and modestly offered some thin gruel. Lianchi praised him, saying: "When Zengzi’s mother died..."
For seven days, not even water or broth entered his mouth. This was the conduct of Master Yun during the mourning period;

even if it were Zengzi himself, what could have been added to this? As the saying goes: "To claim that the followers of Śākyamuni abandon their parents—is this not contrary to reason? Furthermore, it is said that during the Later Zhou dynasty, there was Dao-pi.
He was a member of the noble gentry of Chang’an and a scion of the Tang imperial clan. He entered the monastic life at the age of seven.

At nineteen, he encountered the imperial procession’s visit to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang), during which Chang’an was laid waste by fire. He then carried his mother into Mount Hua and settled in a mountain cave. At that time, grain prices soared;

Daopi abstained from grains himself, seeking only alms to provide for his mother. When his mother asked whether she had eaten, he feared that her concern for him would distress her, and thus [he remained silent].
He replied, "I have already observed the fast. His mother said, "Your father perished in battle at Mount Huo;

his bones lie exposed to the frost and dew. Are you able to collect them and bring them back for burial? He then went to Mount Huo, gathered the white bones, and recited sutras day and night, chanting:
"By the power of the sincerity of those who came before, one may recognize their bones by dripping blood upon them. Among this mass of bones, may that which belongs to me move."
It was his father’s remains. He focused his mind upon them with single-minded devotion, never turning his eyes away for even a moment. After several days, a skull leaped forth from the heap of bones;

Chapter Five: The Abbot.
The commentary states: "Abbot" (zhuchi) is a title for one who presides over and maintains the Buddha-dharma.

When a monastic community establishes an abbot, it relies on that person to uphold the Dharma, ensuring that it remains forever present and does not perish. Now, the Dharma is the Way of the Great Sage.
Precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom are the foundation for upholding the Dharma. The various affairs of the monastic garden are the means by which [the Dharma] is upheld...
This is the business of the Dharma. When the foundation is established, the business is orderly; when the business is orderly, the foundation becomes even more firm.
Therefore, the person who serves as abbot is of the greatest importance. Examining the history of the abbotship at Vulture Peak, Mahākāśyapa presided over it;
at the Bamboo Grove, Śāriputra presided over it. Since Buddhism entered China...
Four hundred years later, Bodhidharma arrived; another eight transmissions brought us to Baizhang. At that time, the Dharma was transmitted solely through the realization of the Way.
Although he resided together with the community, the regulations were simple and concise, and the ceremonial protocols were not yet fully established.

Previously, there was no title for the abbot of the Chan school. As the Chan school gradually flourished, from the kings and ministers above to the scholars and commoners below, all turned toward its influence to inquire about the Way.

Since the unification of the lineage and the essential principles of the school could not, by the force of circumstances, be entrusted to anyone other than a single individual, it followed that if this one person did not assume a formal title commensurate with their station, the Way would remain obscure.
If one does not honor the person as the embodiment [of the Dharma], then the Teaching cannot be established.

Thus, it began that a single individual who was peerless and outstanding was appointed as the presiding master of the Chan school and addressed as "Changlao" (Elder), for he was honored both for his seniority and his virtue.
He further constructed a spacious hall to house the assembly and established two ranks to divide the labor; thus, the regulations were splendidly ordered.
Nevertheless, although the status of the abbot was honorable, regarding manual labor, he still shared equally in the toil with the community.
Even one as virtuous as Baizhang maintained the discipline that "if one does not work for a day, one shall not eat for a day."
Thus, the significance of the abbot’s office can be understood. Consequently, in that era, those selected by the assembly or appointed by official decree often declined their invitations;
even when nominated, there were those who did not go. This was because they truly regarded the responsibility as weighty and harbored no personal ambition for its rewards.
As for the present day, however, the focus has shifted to the abundance of granaries and storehouses, and the security provided by carriages and servants.
The abbots all hold this as their private property. It is no wonder, then, that they sell it at exorbitant prices and seize it by force, regarding it as a rare treasure.

Alas! If the abbot is not the right person, a single temple will fall into ruin and waste, leaving harm to future generations for several hundred or even a thousand years, such that it can never be restored. How could this be a minor matter? When selecting a successor hereafter—

Therefore, may you examine this with care. Those who occupy these positions ought to be prudent. If, in truth, the right person is found to reside in such a position, then they will clarify the Way and establish the laws, assigning tasks and presiding over affairs so that everything is successfully accomplished.
