[If] the *upādhyāya* does not respond by displaying the implements, the assembly follows suit with one prostration using their implements. When the ceremony is concluded, they return to the hall.

The attendants (*shizhe*) all exit the ranks and prostrate to the *upādhyāya*, though sometimes the prostration is waived. Regarding matters such as the offering of incense and food, see the "Ritual for Feeding Monks" below.

On the Emperor’s Birthday, the New Year, the Buddha’s Birthday, the Day of Enlightenment, the Opening of Winter Retreat, and the Closing of Summer Retreat, the Abbot ascends to the hall even if there is no formal meal.

The Prior serves as the host for the request. The ritual procedures are the same as above, with the sole exception that there are no offerings of incense, introductory donations, alms for the meal, or general donations.
For all formal ceremonies such as ascending the hall, the assembly removes their hats during the winter months (the ritual for a patron requesting the Abbot to ascend the seat is identical to this).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: Whenever one ascends the seat to preach the Dharma, one must listen with a sincere mind and take careful notes.

One must not harbor thoughts that the teaching is difficult to comprehend and thereby give rise to a sense of discouragement. Nor should one harbor thoughts that it is something already familiarly heard and thereby give rise to a sense of complacency.

One must listen and contemplate with an open mind; only then will the karmic potential be awakened. One must not follow those who merely mimic the words, grasping only at verbal cleverness—what is called "a snake drinking [its own] venom."
Water becomes poison; when cows drink water, it becomes milk. Likewise, through earnest study one achieves Bodhi, while through frivolous study one incurs birth and death.
Thus, even if the master of the Dharma is not a worthy person, one must not give rise to thoughts of contempt toward them, for that would only obstruct one’s own mind.
This is what is meant by "rely on the Dharma, not on the person. Therefore, when hearing the Dharma, quiet your ears and eyes and listen with focused attention.
Gather the faculties and their objects together. Should any doubts arise, consult me without weariness. Hold the Way in your heart, sweep away habitual tendencies, and unify the single mind.
Through diligent cultivation, the power of contemplation will deepen; through refining and polishing, the gate of practice will become increasingly pure.

In this manner, after a long time, concentration and wisdom will arise, and one may perceive the nature of one's own mind. As for the exposition of the Dharma, it is necessary to provide the essential framework.

When students request further instruction, questions and answers are thereby formed. Since the matter of birth and death is of paramount importance, these inquiries must resolve doubts directly and decisively;
one must not lead the blind by the blind, for that would mislead both others and oneself. If you consider yourself unworthy of such a task, there is no harm in declining.
Regarding those capable of turning [the mind] away from affliction: it would be appropriate to request a single wise and enlightened head seat (śrāmaṇera) to act as a substitute.

Furthermore, when a Zen practitioner (chánkè) puts forth a question, one must be most sincere and reveal the truth. Should one peddle talent or display cleverness, one will inevitably incur an evil retribution.
The *Secret Essentials of the Zen School* (*Chánzōng mìyào*) states: According to the Zen records, Master Ming of Xingjiao asked this under the seat of National Teacher Shao of Tiantai.
He said: "Kāśyapa holds Śākyamuni’s robe of one *zhang* and six *chi* at Mount Kukkuṭapāda, awaiting Maitreya’s descent into birth.
When he takes that robe of one *zhang* and six *chi* and puts it on his body of one thousand *chi*, it fits perfectly according to measure.

Now, if Śākyamuni’s body is one *zhang* and six *chi* while Maitreya’s body is one thousand *chi*, is it that the body understands itself to be short, or does the robe understand itself [to be long]?"
"Is it long? Ming asked. The Master said, "You understand it, after all. Ming then shook his sleeves and went out.
The Master said, "Little fellow, if I had answered you that you were wrong, there would have been cause and effect.
If you were not wrong, I would have seen it through. Seven days later, Ming spat up blood. Master Fuguang urged him, saying, "You must go quickly to repent. Ming then went to do so.
The Abbot wept bitterly and said, "I pray that the Master will show compassion and allow me to repent. The Master said, "It is like a person who falls to the ground and rises from the ground;
I have never taught you how to rise from a fall. The next day, [Xuefeng] spoke again, saying, "If you will allow me to repent, I shall serve you for the rest of my life.
The Master then uttered these words: "The Way of all Buddhas is equal, yet it appears as high or low. (Recorded by Shixian)
Kāśyapa, it is like a seal being pressed into clay. Based on this, one can see that posing such questions is no easy matter.
To indulge in cleverness for even a moment is to have the axe in one's own mouth; should one not be cautious?
Evening *chán* (Small *Chán*; including the Five *Chán*s):

The Daily Routine of the Abbot. With the propagation of the Dharma as his primary duty, apart from the occasional ascent to the hall (*shàngtáng*), the Abbot must by no means neglect the preaching on the first day of the lunar month (*shuò*) or the anniversary of a saint’s passing (*shèng*).

When ascending the seat for the Five *Chán*s, once the two orders of officials have reached the area below the seat, they proceed directly to their respective ranks to stand; only then does the Abbot ascend the seat.
No incense is offered. Furthermore, as for what is called "investigation" (chan): whenever the assembly is gathered for instruction, it all benefits this investigation.

When the ancients guided their disciples, they caused them to consult and inquire morning and evening, never failing to stimulate and exalt this Way at any time. Therefore, one must investigate every evening.

This is called the "Late Session" (wǎn cān). Alternatively, after the morning recitation, the assembly ascends to the Abbot’s quarters; the ritual is the same as for the "Formal Assembly" (shàng táng), and this is called the "Small Session" (xiǎo cān).
Furthermore, whenever the retreat is entered or concluded, during winter nights or year-end nights, or when presiding over memorial services for the deceased, the Small Session is always held.
There is no fixed location; depending on the number of people present, it may be held in the Abbot’s quarters, the Dharma Hall, or in front of the refectory. In advance, [a notice] is hung...

Small Session Plaque (*xiǎocān pái*). On the four seasonal festivals and the eight nodes of the year, one may invite the Head of the Assembly (*bānshǒu*) to hold the whisk (*bǐngfú*) in the Great Hall after the recitation is completed.
One must also hang the "Whisk-Holding" plaque in advance; on the side of the plaque, attach a strip of red paper and write: "Inviting Master [Name]."

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Formerly, when Chan Master Fenyang Zhao resided at the Taizi Yuan in Fenzhou, he had abolished the evening dharma assembly because the climate of the Bingzhou and Fenzhou regions was bitterly cold.
A strange bhikṣu arrived, shaking his mendicant’s staff, and said to the Master, "There are six great beings (mahāsattvas) within this assembly;
why do you not preach the Dharma? Having spoken, he ascended into the air and departed. The Master recorded this in secret.
A verse says: "The Hu monk with the golden staff’s radiance Came to Fenyang for the sake of the Dharma. Six men became great vessels; They entreated him to propagate it.
At that time, Chuyuan and Shouzhi were known as the preeminent leaders. Chuyuan was none other than Ciming.
Later, while he was residing at Shishuang, Yangqi Huai served as the *jian-si* (superintendent). He entreated Ciming to preach the Dharma during the night. Ciming said:
At dusk, he ascended the seat. [The Master] asked, "From where did you obtain this rule? Xu replied, "Is it not the evening assembly at Fenzhou that constitutes the rule? Mizu nodded in approval.

On the first and fifteenth days of each month (with the addition of the tea discourse), there is a holiday. On these dates, one gathers before the Zen hall to have their heads shaved and change into clean robes. After the midday meal, a "small stillness" period is held for bathing.

Once the evening service is concluded, one pays respects at the patriarchal altar and visits the abbot’s quarters, where either an evening discourse may be given. Upon returning to the hall, one listens for the drum.

The abbot calls for the general tea service; the assembly listens as the monastic regulations (*śikṣāpada*) are proclaimed. Upon returning to the hall, the abbot separately invites the two orders of officers to tea.

This serves two purposes: first, to examine the understanding of the practitioners; second, to deliberate upon the administrative affairs of the monastery (according to the Vinaya, the *poṣadha* ceremony is held on these two days).

On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, during the morning service, the incense burner is passed around to offer prayers for the Sages. The *vinaya* master calls for the assembly to gather.

They pay respects to the Patriarchs and proceed to the Abbot’s quarters for a small discourse (*xiaocan*), which is similar to that held on New Year’s Day; however, they pray specifically for the Four Holy Ones. Once the hymns of praise to the Buddha have been chanted in the Main Hall, they proceed to the time for communal recitation of the Buddha’s name.

Several members of the Great Assembly strike the ritual instruments together, after which they exit the hall and proceed to the [Fourth... (Note: The final phrase "到四" appears to be an incomplete reference, likely indicating movement toward a fourth location or a fourth section of the ritual sequence.)
Before the Holy Ones, perform incantations, praises, and prayers. At the time of the morning gruel, the Guest Hall shall hang the Plaque for the Upper Offering (*shanggong pai*). (The plaque reads:

"All members of the Sangha, upon hearing the sound of the drum, proceed together to the Great Hall and before the Four Holy Ones, as well as to the Shadow Hall, to present the upper offering" (the remainder is found in the preceding *Zhuxili Zhang* [Chapter on Prayers for the Emperor’s Longevity] within the *Sijing Zhai*, and is detailed in the subsequent *Dazhong Zhang* [Chapter on the Assembly] under the section on the *Posadha*).
On the third, eighth, thirteenth, eighteenth, twenty-third, and twenty-eighth days of each month, the abbot hangs the "Entering the Room" (入室) plaque.
Those who enter the room do so for the master to examine and discern the student, urging them toward what they have not yet attained and correcting their deviations.
[The Master] said: "It is like smelting gold in a crucible; lead and mercury do not remain. It is like a master carver working jade; common stones are utterly discarded.

This may be practiced regardless of whether it is dawn or dusk, and without selecting a particular location. When a student enters the room to seek instruction, they must sincerely don their robes and carry their ritual implements.
Having first informed the *vinaya-dhara* (the attendant), the *yuèzhòng* (the director of the assembly) leads them outside the room to stand. The attendant then strikes the door."

Three prostrations. Inform the Abbot in general. If the Abbot grants permission, lead the students into the room, spread out the full set of ritual implements, perform three prostrations, and kneel long with palms joined to request instruction.
One must disclose one’s entire lifelong practice of study with complete sincerity and without any concealment.
One must not arrogantly display one's own views or recklessly concoct heterodox theories and nonsensical talk. And so forth.

Maintain a natural mind of compassion. Regard even the pricking of a needle as painful. Be supported and encouraged to advance. Once the instruction has been fully given, stand up and bow in thanks, then withdraw.

Exchange greetings with the attendant and return to the hall. Do not be negligent or self-indulgent, allowing the years and months to pass in vain, thereby betraying the lifelong resolve you made to study and practice.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding the matter of entering the room [for instruction], the student must seek instruction with sincerity, and the teacher must provide guidance with a compassionate heart;
only then will they not fail each other. If the student’s practice of inquiry is insincere, and the teacher’s insight into the Way is unclear, [they both fail].
Even if one were to imitate the original in drawing a cat, it would merely be a matter of conforming to conventional stories.

Lately, throughout the various quarters, with the exception of one or two true cultivation centers for Chan, even the practice of entering the room has rarely been carried out; this is all the more lamentable.

According to the ancient regulations for the *xunliao* (inspecting the quarters), every third and twenty-eighth day of the month, the *Renwang jing* and other scriptures are recited. Four times a year, the *xunliao* is conducted through the quarters.
A *xunliao* plaque is hung before the Sangha Hall to notify the assembly. In the center of each quarter, the seat of the Abbot is prepared, and incense is provided for burning.

And for tea and soup: wait for the abbot to arrive, strike the small wooden board, and assemble the residents of the quarters. Stand in a line outside the door and perform a greeting. Follow the abbot into the quarters.
The master of the quarters burns incense and pays respectful homage to the abbot; together with the assembly, they perform one bow, offer a greeting, and sit.
The abbot shall inquire after those who are aged or infirm and inspect the quarters for any deficiencies. After conversing, the abbot shall rise, and the assembly should likewise do so.
One spreads out the sitting mat (*kaṭhina*) and bows in thanks for the visit. If the visitor declines formal greetings, one merely exchanges polite inquiries and sees them off.

On the first and fifteenth days of the month, when inspecting the quarters, one does not hang up the name plaque. Nowadays, however, the practice of inspecting the quarters on these two dates and the recitation services on the third and eighth days of each month are no longer performed;

instead, prayers are offered at the shrines of the Four Saints and other locations whenever the new moon occurs to serve as a substitute for the recitations. As for the matter of inspecting the quarters, the abbot performs this every morning.

During the evening recitation of the *Nianfo* (Buddha-remembrance), one should pay homage to the sacred images in each hall of the monastery, inquire after the elderly and the sick as the occasion arises, and inspect the affairs of the monastery.
Regarding this, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "For five reasons, the World-Honored One would conduct inspections of the monks once every five days."
1. To prevent disciples from becoming attached to conditioned activities; 2. To prevent them from becoming attached to worldly discourse; 3. To prevent them from becoming attached to sleep; 4.
For the sake of the monk who is tending to the sick; 5. To cause young bhikṣus to observe the Buddha’s majestic deportment and give rise to joy.
Now, as the abbot follows the ritual protocols bequeathed by the Buddha, he likewise conducts a tour of the quarters (*xunliao*).
The ritual for beginning and ending a *pushe* (general discourse) is similar to that of a *xiaocan* (small inspection). A *xiaocan* is spoken solely by the abbot, and its language must be direct.
*Jie* (Excerpts). Similar to the *Shangtang* (Ascending the Hall), the *Pushe* (General Discourses) comprise many different types.

As for those delivered by the Abbot (*zhuchi*), they may be given when the incense is announced (*gaoxiang*), or during the incense-announcement prior to the summer retreat, or during the mid-summer retreat;

or they may be specifically for a certain matter, or requested as an instruction (*kaishi*), or to resolve doubts, or spoken for the sake of practitioners, or to exhort students, or to stimulate and elevate [the understanding of] the ancients.
Because the discourse was thus extensive and its meaning complete, it is titled "Universal Exposition" (Fusetsu). Alternatively, individuals may be commanded to speak each in turn;
their words are then examined and analyzed (the records are made using paper, written in formal script, and the dharma words are actually posted beneath the corridors of the meditation hall).

Announcement of Incense (Gǎoxiāng): In the monasteries of old, the summer retreat was established according to the Vinaya; every year before the summer retreat began, there was an "announcement of incense. Until this announcement had been made, it was not permitted to enter the quarters. This announcement took place in the Abbot’s quarters (fāngzhàng) or the Dharma Hall (fátáng). Nowadays, in the Chan school, on the day of posting the seating charts for the winter retreat, a signboard is hung in the Guest Hall (kètáng) after the early morning congee.

The sign reads: "Announcement of Incense. After the second board-strike for the light meal, the great bell is struck three times. The administrative office (kùsī) proceeds to the altar of Weituo Bodhisattva to set out offerings, with incense and candles burning brightly. They wait for the Chan Hall to conclude its period of silence and open the "small silence" (xiǎojìng), at which point they assemble.

The assembly of the monastery, having donned their robes and taken up their ritual implements, proceeds together to the left and right of the Vajrapāṇi Hall. Once they have assembled in order, the Abbot offers incense. The Rector leads the recitation:

"Namo to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gandhavyūha. (Three times. As usual, after the offerings are completed, everyone prostrates three times with implements fully spread. They then stand facing one another. The Abbot addresses the assembly in a loud voice: "To harbor evil thoughts in a dark room..."
The divine eye is like lightning. The retribution for good and evil follows like a shadow follows a form. There may be differences in timing—sooner or later—but in the end, none shall escape the net.

I respectfully inform the great assembly: each of you must contemplate this with earnest attention. Be reverent and cautious; be on guard and be careful. (Having finished the announcement, he proceeds before the altar of Wei Tian Wang.

He offers incense in three installments, performs three prostrations, kneels long, joins his palms, and announces aloud: "I, the Abbot [Name], if the monastic community is not well-governed and the Wheel of Dharma does not turn..."

Those who oppress the assembly for their own benefit or who encroach upon and damage the permanent property of the Sangha—may they, within this present life, have their emoluments cut short and their lifespans diminished;

may they be afflicted by malignant diseases or encounter calamities. To manifest this retribution to the great assembly, may they fall into the three miserable realms among the various evil destinies at the time of death.

May the divine witness be present to serve as a warning to those who come after. (From here on, each of the following vows must be thoroughly mastered in advance so that one may announce them during the incense offering. Having announced them, perform one prostration and withdraw to stand.)

The Head of the Assembly (standing at his original position), together with the four class leaders, proceed to the altar before Vajrapāṇi. Standing in the center, they offer incense and perform prostrations in unison. Then, kneeling long and joining their palms, they announce in a single voice:

"May I, the head of the assembly, [Name], if my three karmas are not diligent, my four modes of deportment are not solemn, or if I indulge in tyranny and violence, thereby betraying the Sangha’s permanent property—may I, in this present life...

[Having finished the announcement, they perform one prostration and withdraw to stand at their original positions. The following sections are all the same. Next, the Rector (Vina) offers incense in three portions, performs three prostrations, kneels long, joins his palms, and announces in a loud voice: "I, the Rector..."

(Insert Name). If you harbor private biases, plot to oppress others through influence, betray the community, or fail to fulfill your duties as an administrator, may I suffer [the consequences] in this very life, and so forth.

(Next, the General Supervisor, the Head of the Monastery, the Deputy Steward, the Custodian of Robes and Alms-bowls, and all others who have handled wealth, clothing, food, or drink, shall gather together before the Hall of Wei Tian. The one standing in the center shall offer incense in three installments.)

[The candidate] performs three prostrations, kneels long, joins the palms, and announces in a loud voice: "I, the monastery supervisor [Name], am narrow-minded toward the assembly and my heart of affection for the assembly is thin."
"May those who encroach upon the public for private gain and obscure the laws of cause and effect cause me, in this very life, to [suffer such retribution], and so forth.
(Next, the *zhòngzhī* [head of the assembly], *zhíguò* [guest prefect], *sēngzhí* [monastic steward], and all others who manage the community and attend to affairs shall proceed together as above.

"I, [Name], head of the assembly, if I harbor hatred for the poor and love for the wealthy, value the laity while slighting the monastics, waste the monastery’s permanent assets, or act only to gratify my own whims—may I, in this very life, [suffer such retribution], and so forth. (Next, the meditation hall practitioners, [Name] and others; if there are many, ten persons shall form one group and proceed together as above.)

[Upper] I, [Name], of the pure assembly. If I am indolent and seek only ease, fail to attend to my own duties, waste the offerings of the faithful, or bring disgrace upon the permanent property of the Sangha, may I suffer such-and-such [consequences].
(Next, list the administrators and others, ten persons per group, all proceeding together as above: I, [Name], of the administrative staff.
If one does not exhaust their fundamental attachments, they will mislead the multitude and waste the property of the Sangha while seeking only their own peace; let me speak at length [on this].

(After all members of the assembly have completed the incense offering, they stand facing each other on the left and right with palms joined. The *yuèzhòng* strikes the small fish-bell. They recite the second precept from the "Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Chapter" of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, without yet reciting the vow.
The Buddha spoke the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the "Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Chapter": "O Sons of the Buddha, you should always give rise to all vows. Be filial and obedient to your parents."

Preceptor and fellow practitioners, I pray that I may encounter a good teacher and virtuous spiritual friends who will constantly instruct me in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya—the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten adamantine stages, and the ten bhūmis—so that I may attain understanding and practice according to the Dharma.

May I firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts, never departing from them in thought after thought, even at the cost of my body and life. If all bodhisattvas do not make this vow, [they cannot be called true bodhisattvas].
One commits a minor offense. If, O Disciple of the Buddha, having made the ten great vows, one upholds the prohibitions of the Buddha and makes this vow:

"I would rather cast this body into a blazing, fierce fire, or into a great pit or a mountain of knives, than ever violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods of time by engaging in impure conduct with any woman. Furthermore, one makes this vow: "I would rather [use] hot iron..."
A net of iron mesh, a thousand layers thick, shall encircle my body. Never, with this body of broken precepts, shall I accept any clothing from faithful donors (*dānapati*).

Furthermore, I make this vow: "I would rather swallow glowing iron balls and great torrents of fierce fire for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than, with this mouth of broken precepts, eat the food of faithful donors."
Setting aside food and drink of a hundred flavors, he further made this vow:

"I would rather let this body lie upon a floor of glowing iron within a cage of fierce flames than ever accept a hundred kinds of couches and seats from a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts.
He further made this vow: "I would rather let this body endure the piercing of three hundred spears for one or two kalpas."
He shall never, with this body of broken precepts, accept the medicines of a hundred flavors from a donor of faithful heart. He further makes this vow:

"I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of boiling iron for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than, with this body of broken precepts, accept from a donor of faithful heart a thousand kinds of dwellings, houses, gardens, groves, fields, or lands. He further makes...

This is my vow: I would rather have this body smashed with an iron hammer from head to foot until it is reduced to fine dust, than ever accept the respectful prostrations of faithful donors with this body of broken precepts. Furthermore, he made this vow:

"Rather than this, I would prefer to have my two eyes gouged out with hundreds of thousands of red-hot iron knives and spears; I shall never, with a mind of broken precepts, look upon the beautiful forms of others.
Furthermore, I make this vow: rather than this, I would prefer to have my sense of hearing pierced by hundreds of thousands of iron awls for one or two kalpas;
I shall never, with a mind of broken precepts, listen to pleasant sounds. Furthermore, I make this vow: rather than this..."
With a hundred thousand sharp-edged knives, he cut off his nose; yet, he never again, with a mind of broken precepts, greedily sniffed various fragrances.
He further made this vow: "I would rather have my tongue severed by a hundred thousand sharp-edged knives than, with a mind of broken precepts, eat the hundred-flavored pure foods of humans.
He further made this vow: "I would rather have my [body] hacked and split by a sharp axe..."

Throughout one's life, one must never, with a mind of broken precepts, greedily cling to pleasant tactile sensations. Furthermore, one should make this vow: "May all sentient beings attain Buddhahood.
If a Bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense. (Having finished reciting, chant the Verse of Dedication in unison:

I pray to the Honored One, Wei T'ien Zun; Your majestic spirit clearly metes out reward and punishment. May blessings descend abundantly upon the virtuous and good; May all the wicked and evil meet their due retribution.

Transgressions! I pray to the Honorable Lord Wei: His majestic spirit metes out rewards and punishments with clarity; those who are public-spirited and loyal receive abundant blessings, while those who are private and crooked meet with total misfortune.
I pray to the Honorable Lord Wei: His majestic spirit protects the monastic groves. Should anyone destroy the rules and regulations, calamity shall strike their person immediately.
I pray to the Honorable Lord Wei: He strictly examines the sincerity of both the true and the false. Those present here who offer incense, I vow to record and distinguish them all.

Illumination. I pray to the Venerable Lord Wei (Weizun): strictly examine the oaths and covenants of the assembly. One word shall correspond to one word; every sentence shall be answered with clarity.

In the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha, there are precepts for making vows. Because of these, one is encouraged to uphold the precepts; because of these, one is healed if they have broken them.
If one says that the mind remains upright, why is it necessary to establish a vow? Those who merely adorn themselves with such words desire to find peace of mind through them.
For one's own benefit, one makes a vow before the deity: "Why must I dwell in the monastic groves? The mace of the Veda-deva is fearsome; one must be cautious and not deceive oneself.
When a person who betrays their heart comes here with brazen audacity, they strike at the manifest power of the divine spirit, inviting threefold calamities upon themselves.
If the monastic groves are on the verge of decline, the wicked and the depraved will gradually enter; I pray for the sacred power of the deities to swiftly grant their eradication.

[After the recitation is finished, the *Vaiśravaṇa-stotra* is chanted. The assembly performs three prostrations, rises, and each returns to their respective quarters. When the evening service is concluded, the administrative officers conduct a tour of the quarters. Furthermore, after the new abbot has entered the monastery and the officials have requested him to establish the schedule, he offers incense for the sake of the assembly.

Subsequently, after the formal opening of the hall (*kārttika*) and the offering of incense, the abbot instructs his attendant to have the *pūsè* (General Discourse) plaque hung in the Guest Hall. The ritual procedures for this are similar to those of the *xiǎocān* (Small Private Instruction). After the abbot has provided instruction to the assembly and descended from the seat, he may appoint the head of the assembly, or even the leader of the retreat (*cāntóu*), to conclude the proceedings.
One should successively and individually stimulate and exhort this Way; that is, to examine and test the practitioner. The *Zhengyi* states:
"Regarding 'announcing the incense and making a vow,' a vow is a mind of firm resolve. At the outset of practice, the mind is weak and requires guarding and maintenance;
therefore, one makes vows and pledges to guard oneself. If the intention of the vow is not aroused, the Way..."
By what means is this accomplished? The *Ekottarika Āgama*, Sūtra 38, states: "A bhikṣu who does not make a vow shall never attain the Way of the Buddha.
The merit of such a vow is beyond measure; it leads to the state of ambrosial extinction (*amṛta-nirodha*).
Therefore, in protecting and maintaining a monastic grove, one must perform the 'incense proclamation' (*gaoxiang*) to manifest one's purity. Thus, [the practice of] purity...
Whether one is pure or impure, only oneself knows; others cannot know it. Though others may not know, the spirit truly knows.
If there should be a foolish monk who deceives the spirit with falsehoods, claiming that the spirit is merely made of clay or wood, he might perhaps succeed in his deception.
Yet, if he hopes for such luck to escape the retribution for his evil deeds—even if the retribution does not manifest for a time—he will ultimately suffer calamity. There is no power to avoid it.
"Those who flee—should they not stand in awe? Someone may say: 'Vows (praṇidhāna)' are words of excessive expectation, and 'oaths' (samaya) resemble the language of curses;
these seem unsuitable for one engaged in spiritual practice. I reply: An "oath" is the courageous and resolute intent within a "vow. As for "curses," [they are different].
The "poisonous harm" refers to a malicious intent among enemies. How can you consider courageous and fierce resolve to be poisonous harm?
Take, for instance, the Four Great Vows; are they not vows? If a Bodhisattva’s practice were devoid of these four vows, there would be no foundation for attaining Buddhahood.
Would you then regard them as malevolent incantations and harbor doubts about them? In short, the ritual of the "Announcement of Incense" is of vital importance to the monastic community.
It is no small matter. When the incense offering (*gaoxiang*) is practiced, everyone knows to feel awe; even those who might resort to prevarication become few.
When the incense offering is abolished, the distinction between the phoenix and the owl is lost; even those who might stand out as exceptional and remain steadfast become few.

Thus, when the monastic community (*conglin*) is about to flourish, the incense offering is practiced; when the monastic community is about to decline, the incense offering is abolished. This is the mechanism of flourishing and decay.
Thereupon, they divined the matter. Yū’ān Zhígǔ said: "Master Cíháng Pǔ presided over Tiāntóng for twenty years.
He never ate apart from the assembly, nor did he ever neglect his duties even when ill. His personal frugality was extreme, yet his treatment of the community was most generous.

A young disciple, having completed his term as steward, returned to pay respects to the Master and said: 'I have exerted all my strength in managing the affairs, increasing the surplus by one-and-a-half times; I dare not [be remiss]...'"
He took it himself and placed it in the permanent endowment (*sthavira*) of the monastery. Puk was enraged and said, "Everything you have acquired was taken through craftiness;
these are unrighteous goods. How can the permanent endowment accept such unrighteous property? He refused to accept it and expelled the man as well. Alas!
It is already rare to hear of a junior monk’s private wealth being placed in the permanent endowment, yet he was still angry that it was not accepted and even expelled him.
The person who maintains this and offers the incense—how supreme is their purity! The ancient Way was thus; they are worthy to serve as a model for teachers and disciples.
Let those who offer the incense know this.

Regarding all recitations: whether arranged by the monastery’s permanent endowment or initiated by a donor, they must both be planned in advance. Here, we follow the protocol for donors.

When a high-ranking official arrives, the Guest Prefect (zhikè) shall join the assembly to welcome them (the ritual is described below). If it is not a high-ranking official, the Guest Hall shall receive them (in the same manner as when providing meals for the Sangha).

On the day prior, the altar shall be prepared with strict purity (up to the concluding dispersal, as seen in the "Chapter on Ritual Blessings"). A plaque shall be hung, inscribed as follows: "In the [Month], [Day]..."

On the [day], the Dharma-protector [Name] of the [position] office, for the purpose of [specific matter], shall recite the [Title of Sūtra] and prostrate in the [Title of Repentance] for a total of [number] days.
The various masters shall take turns by rotation, with [number] names assigned each day, as listed below:
[Name] Head Seat Master (Śrāmaṇera) [Name] West Hall Master (Xītáng Shī), etc. △ Alternatively, they may be rotated daily, or replaced every three days.

From the head of the assembly down to the pure monks, everyone shall be assigned duties equally, both internally and externally. When the time for purification arrives, the Scripture Master first proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to prostrate before the Upādhyāya and request his instructions.
Having done so, he enters the altar hall. The Guest Prefect requests the patron to offer incense.

Once the purification is complete, the Guest Prefect calls out, "I request the patron to pay respects and thank the assembly with three prostrations. Then each person returns to their place. If the patron is a high-ranking official, these formalities may be waived as a matter of expediency.

The ritual: On the following day, the sutra is opened. The guest prefect (zhikè) is instructed to invite the presiding master to offer incense. On the main day, the proclamation of the memorial (shūsū) and the offering of food are performed.

Upon completion, the report is made to the abbot’s quarters. In all cases, sutra and repentance masters are not permitted to accept social engagements outside the monastery. As for the offerings to the sutra masters and the communal offerings, these shall follow the ancient precedents of each respective house.

Originally, following the *Niansong tiaole* (Regulations for Chanting), the nine sections of the *Shuilu yigui* (Rite for Water and Land) were appended; these have now been moved to a separate volume at the end. (Appendix:

In ancient monasteries, practitioners lived in lofty seclusion beyond the mundane world; apart from offering prayers for the state (*zhuxi*), they did not engage in social courtesies. This was precisely because [the monastery] was occupied with matters of great importance.
This is unclear. With no leisure even to trim one's nails, how could one possibly engage in social obligations? This would further dissipate one’s contemplation of the Way.

Moreover, if one has not yet crossed over oneself, how can one deliver others? Thus, a sutra states: "The single matter of yoga is the work of Bodhisattvas who have ascended the stages (bhūmi) for the benefit of sentient beings;

it is not appropriate for ordinary beginners. Nevertheless, I fear that monastic communities may become lax and impoverished, lacking what is necessary, and that the practitioners (nàzǐ) will grow indolent in their cultivation.
As the Dharma-gate declines, one has no choice but to perform recitations briefly. Should one enter the altar, one must conceive of it as a *bodhimaṇḍa*.
Facing the scriptures and images, one should regard them as if facing the Buddha. Recite their texts, contemplate their meanings, practice their rites, and realize their essence.
One must ensure that body and speech are in accord, and speech and mind are in accord—without dullness, without distraction, without indolence, and without greed.
Benefit. Know cause and effect; know shame and remorse. Be ever vigilant and diligent. If one is thus, then without intending to deliver others, one delivers them;
without intending to benefit others, one benefits them. This is what is meant by: "Others give wealth to me; I give the Dharma to others.

Such equal giving is no different [from ordinary charity], yet it may still be considered a provisional means. It is like blowing a bellows—if one does not produce sound (or perhaps does not recognize the characters), one must observe.

They chant the sutras while pounding grain with mortars and pestles (without performing visualization and entirely lacking sincere intent); they perform prostrations and repentance while facing the honored image, yet their eyes gaze in other directions.

To recite sutras and repentance liturgies with the mouth while the mind harbors other thoughts—such conduct will inevitably cause the decline of the monastic community in the present and lead one to suffer in future lives.
It turns the Dharma-treasure, which is for the benefit of oneself and others, into a criminal record of self-deception and the deception of others.
How can one not be cautious? All regulations are respectfully set forth below. First, as for those who recite the sutras:

Upon seeing one's name on the plaque, one should immediately bathe. The following morning, when reciting sutras and performing repentance rites, one must ensure that the eyes, mouth, and mind are fully engaged.
One must not interject idle or miscellaneous speech during the recitation and repentance, nor should one speak while remaining in the midst of the service.
If one engages in idle chatter or laughter during the recitation of sutras or repentance rites, a fine of one *qian* and eight *fen* of silver shall be imposed.

If one engages in playful conversation after the recitation has concluded, a fine of eight *fen* of silver shall be imposed. During the chanting, one must not turn the head or look about to observe people or objects;

one must recite with single-minded devotion, ensuring every syllable is distinct. For those who fail to chant audibly, a heavy fine shall be imposed upon completion of the rite for the transgression of insufficient recitation.
If the purification is not thorough, a fine of three *fen* of silver shall be imposed. If one reaches the end only after reciting more than one page, a fine of six *fen* of silver shall be imposed;

the sutra and repentance rites must be supplemented through further recitation. The presiding ritual master (*zhǔfǎrén*) must not allow the mind to wander or harbor delusive thoughts, but should follow the text word-for-word and perform the visualization with utmost sincerity.
The officiant (*biǎobáirén*) must not be hasty or overly concise, but should likewise follow the text step-by-step.
The texts should be recited in proper sequence. The sounding of bells, drums, and other instruments should likewise be dignified and refined; they must not be discordant or fragmented.
During sutra recitations, repentance rites, or *bali* offerings, one must not begin to remove the Buddha images or ritual implements before the religious service has concluded.
Regarding the offering of food: one must follow the text word for word, maintaining sincerity while forming mudrās, reciting mantras, and performing visualizations.

These three karmas must be in accord; one must not slur the words, click the tongue, or rush through the proceedings to finish quickly. The same applies to the ritual petitions. Both those inside and outside the hall, as well as those attending to the incense and lamps, must be sincere and pure.
One must handle the fire and candles with great care, and within the halls for the terrestrial and aquatic deities, one should be especially redoubled in solemnity and caution.
Incense, candles, offerings of fruit, and the like, should not be used if they have fallen to the ground, nor if they have already been offered.
Vegetables, rice, and other foods must be cooked until flavorful; they must not be placed with their bases facing upward, nor may dry items or raw living things be used as offerings.
Those who commit quarrels shall be fined eight fen of silver; those who lose their dignified decorum due to such disputes shall also be fined silver.

One *qián* and eight *fēn*. Those who do not comply shall leave the monastery. The silver thus penalized shall be recorded separately in a ledger and reserved for the repair of sutras, repentance rituals, and Buddha statues.
The storehouse must be carefully managed and maintained, along with all necessary supplies.

One must not act with negligence or superficiality. Regarding the above regulations, you must faithfully accept, believe in, and uphold them. Otherwise, you will bring calamity and misfortune upon yourselves.

The existing Pure Rules shall now punish you; furthermore, in the future, there will certainly be karmic retribution. How can one not be cautious? Dated [Year, Month, Day]. Recorded again by the Abbot (Name).

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Whenever there is recitation, it is for the purpose of turning the Wheel of Dharma. Lately, however, the monastic community has largely become negligent and lax in this regard;

the resulting transgressions are not small. The *Yunqi Fahui* says: Formerly, at Lizhi Temple in Wuzhen, there were two monks, teacher and disciple, both of whom were known for their prudence and integrity.
Those who recorded their sutra recitations and repentance ceremonies increased day by day, and because of this, the temple became prosperous. And...
He was stingy; he neither used [his wealth] himself nor gave it in charity. Later, he fell ill, and his kinsmen brought him home to treat him.
Soon thereafter, he passed away. His lifelong accumulations were entirely taken over by his kin. Ten years later, he appeared in a dream to those close to him and said:
"My recitations and repentance rites are incomplete, and the examinations in the underworld are extremely urgent; my suffering is beyond description. As for the people of this world..."
The tradition says: "Lightning flashes; he recognizes the characters and reads them back. This testimony is not false. I have recorded it to warn those who respond to karmic conditions.

It is further said: "The water and land [rites] are linked head-to-tail; the sutra recitations and repentances continue in succession without interruption. This refers to the sequence for requesting the sutras.

They are as frantic in their pursuit of monastic officials as those seeking official posts; they are as bustling in requesting masters of the scriptures as those reporting joyful news. While the daily performance of sutra recitations and repentance rites flourishes, the true Way and its virtue decline day by day.
When the monastic communities have reached this state, they are truly in a state of profound decay—a sight that merits nothing but deep lamentation.

On the occasions of the Qingming Festival, the Zhongyuan Festival, the first day of the tenth lunar month, and New Year’s Eve, the *hu* (grain-offering ritual) is performed to sacrifice to the ancestors. On the afternoon of that day, a notice shall be hung in the Guest Hall.

(The notice reads: "This evening, on this auspicious occasion of [insert festival name], the *hu* will be offered in the Dharma Hall" (or modified according to the needs of the donor). The Abbot shall occupy the central seat.

In the guest hall, the storehouse, the attendants' quarters, the *yuèzhòng* (recreational leader), and the rotating assignments— whether there be offerings or stipends— the roles of the central seat (*zhōngzuò*), the ritual master (*biǎobái*), the attendant seat (*shìzuò*),

the scribe (*xiěshū*), the guest master (*zhīkè*), the kitchen staff (*chúfáng*), the altar monitor (*zhítán*), the incense and lamp keeper (*xiāngdēng*), the tea server (*chátóu*), the guest usher (*zhàokè*), and those who prepare offerings shall all follow the established precedents of their respective houses.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding the practice of establishing the *hu* (a measure of capacity), errors have become numerous by the present day. Briefly stated, there are ten such errors.

According to the ritual manuals (*vidhi*) of the Secret Section (*Guhyatantra*), when one intends to perform the *bali* offering, one must first establish a boundary (*sīmābandha*) to create a purified ground (*śuddhabhūmi*).
As for the method of establishing the boundary: one uses wooden stakes to fix the four corners and encloses them with cords, ensuring that neither humans nor animals may enter the boundary.
Thereafter, the food-offering altar (śrāddha-maṇḍala) and the spirit altar—commonly called the Cold Forest Platform (śītavana-vedī) or the Orphaned Spirits Platform—are established.

Furthermore, two offering seats for the guests are set up within the boundary. From the food-offering altar to the orphaned spirits altar, three lengths of white cloth are used to create three "Jeweled Streets" (ratna-vīthī).
At the beginning of the *xiu* hour, the Dharma Master, together with the officiant (*pratideśaka*), [proceeds].
First, recite the Great Compassion Mantra and sprinkle purified water in the four directions.
Visualize that within this realm, through the power of the divine mantra and the power of visualization, it is transformed into a pure land to serve as the foundation for the altar.

After reciting the mantra three times, the Dharma Master stands fixed in the center before the food-offering altar, with the ritual officiant (biaobai) assisting on either side. The Dharma Master then follows his visualization within the realm.

The pure ground is vast and boundless. As the drums and cymbals resound, using the *qixing* (seven-star) wooden board, chant the melody for "Amitābha Buddha’s Body is Golden" and sing the verses for the Pure Ground in unison: "In every direction and corner, may there be no earth of rubble, gravel, or sand dunes;
may the ground of lapis lazuli jewels be as level as the palm of a hand, soft and sublime—may it be peaceful."
Abiding there, it is adorned like the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*): the ground is composed of wondrous jewels, strewn with various flowers;

gardens, groves, ponds, and pools are present in full abundance. Through the fulfillment of the vows of the Great Dharma-sound, it manifests from the supramundane realm, fashioned from various kinds of the seven treasures.
With immeasurable light illuminating every place, may all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwell therein in peace.
Upon finishing the chanting, beat the drums and clash the cymbals vigorously. The Dharma Master himself recites this verse: "First, I bind the seal of the Great Wheel Vidyārāja;
The consecrated site is thereby rendered entirely pure. Now, according to the teachings, I recite the secret mantra, Causing all that I perform to be accomplished.
Having spoken thus, he silently recites the mantra of the Great Wheel Vidyārāja twenty-one times. [Mantra:]
Regarding the detailed ritual procedures for the offering of food (*bali*): once the recitation of mantras is completed, one immediately raises clouds of incense and so forth.
Now, in this [tradition], the Secret Mantra section has fallen silent and the rite of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) is not performed; this is the first error.

Furthermore, according to this sutra, the Buddha stated that the *droṇa* used in the kingdom of Magadha is the measure for this food and this water, which are equal in extent to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and are inexhaustible when consumed. Now, based on my...
In this country, one *hu* (斛) is equivalent to five *dou* (斗). When offering food, one should use five *dou* of cooked rice to form a mountain of rice;
five *dou* of seasoned vegetables boiled in a bucket to form a mountain of vegetables; and five *dou* of clean cold water in a jar.

Thus, one fulfills the Buddha’s regulations by creating a sea of milk. Once the offering to the solitary spirits has been completed, at dawn on the following day, divide this vegetable-rice into three portions:
first, offer it to the aquatic species, such as those in a pond for releasing life or in great rivers and seas;
second, offer it to the furred creatures, such as those in a sanctuary for releasing life or in mountain wilds; third, offer it to others, namely beggars or the destitute.
For those who suffer: if there is no place for releasing living beings, one should instead give them to the poor and suffering in distant lands.

Recently, I observed that their rice did not fill a single cup and their vegetables did not suffice for a single chopstick. When questioned about such meager food, they would say, "Seven grains pervade the ten directions," yet there was no water at all.
Little do they realize that the principle of "seven grains pervading the ten directions" applies to the two meal times of the monastic community.
At the commencement of the ritual meal, the method for manifesting [the food] is performed as usual; however, its capacity cannot be great.

As for the offering of food (*śīda*), it is established specifically for this purpose; therefore, the ritual procedures must be fully prepared. In accordance with the Buddha’s injunction, the *Magadha-śu* (Magadhan measure) method is employed.

Therefore, it is said that one establishes the *hu* measure and performs the *zhāi* fast. Furthermore, through the power of divine mantras (*dhāraṇī*), a single meal can be transformed into immeasurable food, sufficient to satisfy all classes of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, so that they all attain full satisfaction.
Moreover, one fears that these various classes might hold the noble in high esteem while looking down upon the lowly.
Using strength to oppress the weak, obstructing the orphaned and young so they cannot obtain food, and causing inequality—these transgress the Buddha’s compassionate salvation;

therefore, I pray to the Triple Gem and all the deities to oversee this altar and issue their commands, so that my offerings may be entirely without hindrance, making no distinction between high and low, nor choosing between enemies and kin, but being equal, universal, and pervasive. Lately, however, much has not been as it should be.

Regarding the ritual, one should simply use the *haku-shu* (measuring-hand gesture) and not provide *haku-han* (measured rice). This is precisely because, as long as the food has not been fully distributed, the rite remains a hollow formality;

this is the second error. Furthermore, the matter of offering food (*shikishoku*) relies entirely upon possessing precepts (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and observational wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as hand gestures (*mudrā*) and mantras (*mantra*).
As for the rhythmic chanting, it serves merely to assist the path. In the present case, [the officiant] does not select...
Their precepts and meditative concentration are lax; their visualizations are not matured; their hand-seals (mudrās) are erroneous; and their mantras are blurred.

They take nothing but the melodic chanting as their primary duty. It is not only common monks who act in this way; even those of high standing in the monastic communities practice such things without scrutiny.
They go so far as to treat alcohol as an offering of respect and use peaches and pomegranates as ritual offerings, remaining unaware of their transgressions. This is the third error.
Furthermore, regarding the ritual for the orphaned spirits (*gu-si*): its original purpose was to be named "the distribution of food" (*shi-shi*).

Thus, the emphasis lay on having abundant rice, abundant vegetables, and abundant water, so as to universally relieve hunger and thirst. As for items such as paper clothing for posthumous support, these too are merely acts of giving (*shi*) on the Way.

Nowadays, it is the opposite of this. Offering only vegetables, rice, and water—provisions that do not accord with the Buddha’s regulations—the host family consumes them themselves instead, resulting in great waste.
There is no sincere intent for spiritual resonance, and thus the suffering ghosts are not relieved from their hunger and thirst; this is the case throughout the world.
To fail to realize this inversion is the fourth error. Furthermore, when establishing an altar to worship the solitary spirits (*gu*), one summons all ghosts to come.

The emphasis lies upon the three types of giving (*dāna*): providing them with food and drink is the gift of material sustenance (*āmiṣa-dāna*); providing them with the breaking of prisons and the destruction of offenses is the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*);
and providing them with the Three Refuges and the names of the Seven Tathāgatas is the gift of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*). However, this...
The three types of giving all yield benefit when performed before the altar; thus, the冥錠 (míngdìng) offerings should likewise be placed before the altar.
They may only be incinerated after the recitation of the Uṣṇīṣavijaya Dhāraṇī is complete. This ensures that all beings are fully satisfied in terms of Dharma, food, and wealth.

Only by first quenching their hunger and thirst and then leading them toward the good realms can the rite be truly beneficial. It appears that in recent times, the *Yamaka-mukha* (Flaming Mouth) ritual has failed to summon the hungry ghosts.
End. First, proceed along the way to burn the paper offerings for the netherworld. This ensures that the host of ghosts cannot obtain all three [of their desires] simultaneously.
Those who cherish netherworld wealth will lose the opportunity to hear the Dharma and receive food; those who cherish the food of the Dharma will lose their netherworld wealth.
Furthermore, if the offerings are not burned before the altar, there will be no supervision by the deities. It is to be expected that among the host of ghosts, the strong will deceive the weak. In...
It is unavoidable that [the offerings] are distributed unequally. Furthermore, some scatter paper money and food directly at the base of pomegranate or peach trees;
because the hungry ghosts fear this, they do not dare to come and receive it. Or, when the fire has not yet died down, one sweeps away the ashes; thus the offerings become fragmented and unusable.

Yet the whole world does not recognize these as errors—this is the fifth misconception. Furthermore, the ritual altar for the *śrāddha* (offering of food) is entirely derived from the Esoteric Section (*guhyamantra*). Now...
To speak briefly: use two large square tables. The front table serves as the altar for making offerings to the Buddha.
On the first row are an incense burner, candle stands, and flower vases. On the second row are flowers, incense, lamps, unguents, fruit, music, and images of the six goddesses (*ṣaḍ-devī*).
These six goddesses may be made of carved wood or of bronze and tin, finely decorated with colors. There are six [of them].
Each occupies its own position and is colored white. She has one face and four hands; she is youthful and graceful. Her two legs are positioned with the left dancing and the right kneeling.
Each of her two hands holds its respective offering, facing toward the Buddha. The Flower Mother (Puṣpamātṛ) holds a flower; her garment is pale red, signifying generosity.

The Mother of Incense holds incense; her robe is yellow, symbolizing ethical discipline (*śīla*). The Mother of Lamp holds a lamp; her robe is red, symbolizing patience (*kṣānti*). The Mother of Ointment holds water;
her robe is white, symbolizing diligence (*vīrya*). The Mother of Fruit holds fruit; her robe is reddish-yellow, symbolizing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
The Mother of Music holds a musical instrument; her robe is greenish-blue, symbolizing wisdom (*prajñā*). Beneath their images, they all tread upon lotus flowers; beneath the flowers, they all...

A single syllable *HŪṂ* is written upon the surface of the standing pedestal. When the assembly chants the *HŪṂ* and the eulogy of its emergence, the Dharma Master need not perform hand gestures or mudrās;
he should simply settle his mind, close his eyes, and visualize the forms and colors of the six goddesses, each emerging from a *HŪṂ*.
Once they have emerged, their faces and hands radiate light, and each holds [their respective attributes].
With incense, flowers, and other offerings, one makes offerings to the Triple Gem; this is called "offering through visualization.
Third is the Buddha Pavilion for the Ritual Procession, situated in the center, shaped exactly like a precious stupa. Inside, Vairocana Buddha is enshrined.
Behind the Buddha Pavilion, a copper pole is erected, with a small hook at its top from which a single banner is suspended, upon which is inscribed the Central Tathāgata Vairocana.
Furthermore, offerings are made to the four Buddhas of the four directions, each facing the central Buddha.
Behind each lotus seat and amidst flames, a copper pole is also erected, topped with a small hook upon which a single banner is suspended.
These banners bear the inscriptions of Akṣobhya Tathāgata of the East, Ratnasambhava Tathāgata of the South, Amitāyus Tathāgata of the West, and Amoghasiddhi of the North.

From the beginning up to the invocation of Kṣitigarbha, all is for the purpose of seeking the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;

one takes the Three Jewels as witnesses, merely requesting their deliverance and the extraction from suffering. All the verses should be recited with a clear and rapid voice. Now, however, it is the opposite:
first, various recitations are performed before the seats arranged below the altar, and only subsequently does one proceed to the upper altar, even to the point of invoking each deity individually.
Please do not lament for the solitary ones. Various calls and chants delay the auspicious moment until the breaking of the prison.
From the invocation of the hungry ghosts up to the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī, one should properly direct the mind toward visualization and recite slowly; yet instead, it is as frantic as the wind.

As for the matter of the ritual, to first withdraw the altar implements before the rites are complete is, on the one hand, to treat the Buddhas and Sages with disrespect, and on the other, to deceive the spirits and deities;

that the entire world fails to perceive this is the seventh error. Furthermore, regarding the bestowal of food and the establishment of the boundary (*sīmābandha*) upon the upper altar, it should take place at the end of *xi* (the hour of the Dog) and the beginning of *shu* (the hour of the Boar).
This is because the two hours of *shu* and *hai* constitute the period of pure yin, during which spirits and deities [are most active].
At the time when [the spirits] are fearful, if one bestows upon them the food of the Dharma (*dharmāhāra*), they will receive great benefit.

At the very beginning of the first *jiaozi* (the first hour of the night), the Yang energy begins to turn and the Yin energy begins to wane; thus, the ghosts become fearful. Even if one bestows the food of the Dharma, they do not come to receive it.
Lately, there have been those who do not yet ascend the altar at the end of the *xu* hour, finishing only at the fifth watch, or even ascending the altar twice during a single night.

Third: This is merely a wasteful expenditure of wealth and property, an empty deception of ghosts and spirits. It satisfies only one's own mental vows, yet shows no regard for the dark spirits. This is the eighth error.
Furthermore, when performing the ritual of bestowing food (śrāddha), one universally establishes karmic connections with spirits; one ought first to grant them fearlessness (*abhaya*).
Therefore, one first establishes boundaries to prevent humans and animals from entering the precincts, so as to allow them to remain in their proper places.
For humans represent the Yang, while ghosts represent the Yin; since Yin always fears Yang, people must not run about before the altar where food offerings are presented.
If one cannot help but participate, one should proceed from behind the altar. Lately, some have used the name "Excellence of the *Lanpen* Assembly" or the title "Blessing and Protection for Peace.
They hang lanterns and colored decorations in profusion and display paper deities extensively.
Men and women gather in a boisterous manner, as if watching a fine play or witnessing extraordinary acrobatics; furthermore, the clamor of large gongs and music adds to the noise.
In noisy and bustling places, one uses only the human *yang* qi to press upon them.

Not only will ghosts and spirits dwelling afar not dare to respond to the summons, but even the ancestors of one's own household will be startled and flee to other regions. If this occurs, the offerings of wealth and food are established in vain;
instead of forming a karmic bond with the spirits, one merely incurs their resentment. The world at large remains unaware of this; such is the ninth error. Furthermore:
Examining the Tibetan canon, regarding the original origins of the *śrāddha* (feast of offerings), there is only the *Buddhabhāṣita-yamāntaka-preta-tāraka-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, translated by Amoghavajra.
There is also a version translated by Śikṣānanda titled the *Buddhabhāṣita-mukhadāha-preta-tāraka-dhāraṇī-mantra-sūtra*.
These are both retranslations of the same original text; they differ only in the *pariṇāmanā-vidyā* (mantra for transforming food).
This was all that was said. Amoghavajra further translated the *Yogacaryābhūmi-saṃgraha-uddhṛta-yamāntaka-kalpa-ānanda-paritrāṇa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
Subsequently, an ācārya again based himself upon this sūtra and abridged it as the *Yogacaryābhūmi-saṃgraha*.
The Ritual Manual for the *Yankou* (Feeding the Hungry Ghosts) is currently found within the Northern Canon (*Beizang*).

It is concise and direct, consisting solely of the single method for the universal invocation of the six realms within the *dharmadhātu*, as well as the mudrās and mantras for invoking the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Alas, people of this age, fond of embellishing what they hear and say, have added various separate invocations, laments for the solitary, and other such matters that circulate in the world; these are what are commonly known as [the "elaborated" versions].
This refers to the *Hai-shang yan-ko* (Sea-side Yankou). It caused the original scroll from the Tripitaka to remain neglected and unused.
When Dharma Master Siji saw that the practices on the sea violated the Buddha’s regulations, he excised the redundant and superfluous portions.
Unbeknownst to him, later generations added further elaborations; this is the currently circulating edition. Furthermore, according to the Yunqi edition, I have collated and corrected it.
In the original texts and so forth, there is no mention of establishing boundaries for the five directions.

Since these are called "boundaries for the five directions," they ought to be established according to what was previously explained regarding boundary-setting; thus, the four Dharma masters in the four directions should likewise [perform their respective rites].
Each [of these texts] maintains its own mantra: the *Śūraṅgama* in the northeast, the *Mahākaruṇā* in the southeast, the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā* in the northwest, and the *Prasannatārā* in the southwest.
Now, they merely sit empty-handed in the four directions, failing to recite the mantras while falsely claiming to practice contemplation; this is the tenth error.
There are these ten errors; they are not only useless, but I fear they may even cause harm. As the common saying goes:

"The *yankou* (feeding the hungry ghosts) for shortening one's lifespan is precisely this. Should those who preside over the offering of food not be cautious? Therefore, for those who wish to study the practice of offering food:
Externally, one should reverse these ten errors to achieve the ten truths. Internally, one should give rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta.
First, one must practice the wisdom of contemplation and the various mudrās and mantras until they are thoroughly mastered; they must not be erroneous.
If there is even the slightest error, the mudrā will not be formed, the worthy sages will not be pleased, and whatever one prays for will not be accomplished. Thus one performs the rite.

To solemnize the assembly: whenever there is public business in the monastic community, the Guest Hall strikes the *xùbǎn* (sequence board) three times. The two orders of officers arrive together at the Guest Hall and deliberate according to the regulations to reach a consensus.
They present their proposal to the Abbot; if the Abbot approves, it is carried out. If not approved, they deliberate further. This applies even in cases of dispute.

Regarding those who engage in quarrels: the Head of the Assembly shall initiate the process. The Guest Master shall immediately report the offense, and so forth; each case shall be judged according to the facts, and punishment shall be meted out based on the gravity of the matter.

If one has violated a fundamental precept (mūla-śīla), or if the incident caused by the offense is particularly grave, one shall inform the Abbot for public deliberation, or report it to the relevant authorities, or expel the individual directly.
When expulsion is carried out, the formal notice of expulsion shall be posted at the head of the mountain gate (the main entrance). Post the notice of expulsion.
At the appointed time, the great drum is struck three times, and those to be expelled are driven out with staffs. Those being expelled are permitted to exit only through a side or small gate;
if any members of the faction attempt to privately protect them, they shall likewise be expelled from the monastery.

If there is fist-fighting or verbal quarreling, regardless of whether one has reason or not, all involved shall be expelled from the monastery. If one person raises their voice and makes a physical gesture while the other remains silent, [the same penalty applies].
However, regarding one who does not remain silent: if their argument is deficient, they are at fault; if they leave the hall with a loud voice while their argument is correct, they are at fault.

One who can remain silent shall not be punished. If one remains silent while their argument is deficient, they shall be punished alongside those who raised their voices by providing a meal for the assembly.

Those who are obstinate shall be expelled from the hall, unless they seek repentance. When the assembly is about to receive offerings, such a person shall kneel long on the floor of the refectory while the *sengzhi* (monastic steward) supervises the eating of the monks.
[The procedure] concluded. He addressed the assembly, saying: "Now, so-and-so has committed such-and-such an offense. Standing before the Sangha, he seeks the assembly’s repentance.
The great assembly replied in unison: "Amitābha Buddha. The Abbot instructed the offender, saying:

"So-and-so, since you reside within this monastic grove, you ought to strictly observe the pure regulations and extensively cultivate wholesome dharmas. Why have you, on the contrary, committed such shameless acts?"

...and so forth. Now that you have sought the communal confession, you ought to repent with sincerity and renew yourself. If you commit this offense again, internally there shall be monastic regulations to expel and punish you;

externally there shall be national laws to interrogate and penalize you; and after death, there shall be the retributive suffering of the three miserable realms for you—is it not something to be feared?
Are you able to repent with true sincerity? He replied: "I have received the compassionate discourse of the Venerable Master. I, [Name],..."
[The offender] should sincerely repent. Having finished speaking, they prostrate three times to the Abbot once more. [The Abbot] says, "The assembly of monks is within.

After the prostrations are completed, the midday meal is concluded and they return to the hall. Furthermore, for minor offenses, one may be penalized by kneeling for several incense sticks (*xiānxiāng*) or by providing rotten food to the assembly.
For other violations, such as disturbing the silence or striking the bell or wooden board incorrectly, the penalty is to kneel for one full incense stick (*xiānxiāng*) in the main hall.

Donning the formal robes and carrying the ritual implements, one kneels in the refectory, or before the Abbot’s quarters, the four administrative offices, or the main hall, to seek repentance and then cease.

○ Regarding the kneeling for incense: if an offense was committed within the hall, one kneels in that hall; if an offense was committed outside the hall, one must kneel in a place where everyone can see, such as the Buddha Hall or the refectory.
When kneeling, one must join the palms and straighten the waist. Should anyone dare to be negligent, [punishment shall be added].
Punishment with the staff is fully detailed in the regulations for each respective hall below. ○ Furthermore, offenses committed outside the hall are punished by the Guest Prefect (Zhike);

offenses committed inside the hall are punished by the Rector (Weina). If one leaves the assembly without permission, avoids work out of laziness, or seeks personal comfort while failing to obey the supervision and exhortations of the Head of the Assembly (Zhizhong), they shall be punished by the Hall Manager (Zhishuai).
If one fails to follow the rules in the mountains or fields, it is the responsibility of the Guest Prefect.
First, the matter is presented to the Abbot for instruction.
