If there are those who do violate them—excluding cases of criminal offenses or grave crimes which, by precedent, belong to the secular authorities—if monks offend one another among themselves..."

They should be regulated by pure discipline. Whether it be engaging in strife and violating the bounds of propriety, defiling conduct through negligence, embezzling communal property, or privately misappropriating money and goods, they should follow the family precepts;
one must not broadcast their external disgrace, as they all claim the title of Śākyaputrīya.

Adhering to secular custom, they are treated like kin, yet they must observe the ancestral rules. Punishment should correspond to the nature of the offense: for grave matters, the assembly shall gather to administer flogging and banishment.

For minor offenses, the punishment shall be the forfeiture of provisions and the suspension of communal meals, with a public notice issued. If the matter involves money or goods, the offender shall be held accountable and the items shall be recovered;
all shall be impartial and just, so that the offender may feel remorse and reform. As the ancient "Verses on Discipline" state: "Theft of property and acts of strife..."
Those defiled by alcohol and lust corrupt the ranks of the Sangha; they must be swiftly sent away from the pure assembly. To tolerate and retain them is to ruin the community. It is further said:

"For those who have committed a grave offense, their robes and alms bowl shall be burned. One should assemble the multitude and, using a mountain cane to symbolize shame, expel them through a side gate.
Formerly, when Chan Master Da Hui resided at Yuwang Monastery, he posted a notice for the Hall Administration: "Monks quarreling over ignorance is certainly not good."
Regarding monks—whether they are in the right or in the wrong—they are all expelled from the monastery. Sometimes it is debated that one is in the right, yet they are still banished;

this may seem inappropriate at first glance. What is not understood, however, is that a monk ought to practice patience. If one insists on being in the right and engages in contention, this is precisely ignorance;
therefore, such individuals are banished together with others. This is why the monastic regulations are so strictly upheld. Yuan’an’s *Zhígu* states: "In the past, at the time of the Dharma..."
Under Master Yun’s seat, Ming-shui Sun served as attendant. Once, when Master Lin was checking into the monastery, Sun requested tea for the newly arrived guest on Lin’s behalf.
Lin had gone out, so Sun entrusted the matter to a monk at the neighboring mat; however, after some time, he forgot about it.

When they gathered before the abbot’s quarters, Lin was not present. Yuan-tong went to invite him, but upon his arrival, [Master Yun] ordered him to leave his seat and stand before the assembly, reprimanding him.
[Yuan] said, "The monastic protocols of the mountain gate are established to manifest supreme dignity; therefore, you have been negligent. Why is this?

Lin replied, "I was indeed listening to the drum, but was suddenly pressed from within, so I lagged behind. It was not that I dared to be disrespectful. Yuantong, with a stern expression, rebuked him, saying, "My drum is no castor bean;
would you urinate as soon as it strikes you? Xun stepped forward and requested, "Xun has committed a transgression. I ought to receive [punishment]."

[The abbot] imposed a punishment. A monk from the neighboring mat stepped forward from the assembly and said, "This is not the fault of the attendant alone; the newcomer was unaware as well. I accepted the responsibility and failed to remember;
I shall take the penalty and leave the monastery. Thus, the three men took the blame upon themselves. Yuancong highly esteemed their righteousness and pardoned them all. Alas!
To discipline the assembly in such a manner, and to grant forgiveness in such a manner—this noble spirit is worthy of emulation and truly lives up to the tradition.
"He is a model for teachers. Someone said: "There are wicked monks. If one admonishes them openly, they do not comply; if one silently ostracizes them, they do not understand.
When they violate the world's social norms and transgress the national laws and codes—cases that cannot be handled by the monastic discipline—what should be done?
He replied: "This depends on weighing the circumstances of each case; one must not adhere to a single fixed method. To cling to the protection of the Dharma [in a rigid way] may, on the contrary,..."

There are those who would destroy the Dharma. Between sparing a single individual at the cost of bringing disgrace upon the Triple Gem, and sparing the Triple Gem while confining the calamity to a single person—which is preferable?
If there is no slight interference, one should follow the monastic regulations and allocate matters according to the circumstances.
However, if there is interference, or if the individuals are obstinate, malicious, and deceitful beyond the possibility of conversion or guidance, they may only be sent to the authorities.
One must deal with them according to the royal law; there can be no exemption. Someone asked: "The Buddha’s mind is centered on compassion and benevolence.

Now, the monastic regulations (qinggui) are extremely strict and detailed. Is this not contrary to the Buddha’s intent? He replied: "You do not understand that the strictness of the monastic regulations is not the strictness of severity;
it is the strictness of rectitude. When the Sangha is governed by the strictness of rectitude, the assembly of monks will become upright."
When one maintains the Dharma with strict integrity, the gates of the Dharma are established; when one restrains the mind with strict integrity, the ground of the mind becomes upright.
Therefore, to reprimand or banish someone is an act of compassion. To employ strictness as compassion is the Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*).
As for those who manifest eccentricities to seek fame or display violence to intimidate others, they are worlds apart from the strict integrity of pure regulations.
This must be distinguished. This dialogue is taken from the *Yunqi Fahui*. Regarding the instruction for *tongxing* (novices):

[Ancient Regulations] "The *tongxing* refers to those such as the *zhisui*, *zhaoke*, and the like who are laypeople; therefore they are called *tongxing*. Nowadays, in the monasteries, those who are ordained monks should not be called *tongxing*; this must be distinguished.

Thus, the *tongxing* are the same category as the *zhisui* and *zhaoke* of the monasteries; they are also called *suizhong* (those following the assembly). In ancient times, regarding those outside...

When those who come to resolve their minds for renunciation or seek to study under a teacher, one fears that their resolve may be feigned and that it will be difficult to distinguish the genuine from the false;
therefore, one first grants them the Three Refuges, designating them as "novices" (*tongxing*) or "pure attendants" (*jingren*).

This marks that they have entered the pure conduct of the Triple Gem and are free from the turbid defilements of the five desires. Lately, however, this role has been restricted to manual labor and physical service.
Those of this ilk falsely claim to be "men of the Way. It is an error for those who follow the discourse on non-action to [neglect] the Three Refuges. Zen Master Foyin’s instruction says:
From the time you leave your parents until the end of your days, your primary refuge must be the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Be diligent and focused in your morning prostrations and recitations;
remain silent in the hall during the stillness of night. Be earnest when performing communal labor; cherish and protect the monastery’s property and utensils. One—
A single grain of rice weighs a thousand pounds. Respond with care to every word from the mouth; do not be reckless in dealing with affairs. Speak in a low voice and act with measured deliberation.
When entering or leaving, restrain and collect your body and mind; let your gait and deportment be orderly and dignified.

When encountering a monk in the corridor, offer a greeting and stand aside with hands joined, waiting for him to pass. Since you have renounced worldly ties, follow the regulations of the monastic community. Master.
During times of long instruction, you must not raise your voices to plead or protest. By day, when there is no other business, study calligraphy and commit the sacred scriptures and texts to memory.
Be diligent and careful in performing your tasks for one another; do not deceive the monastery’s permanent assets. Your robes and cassocks should be plain and dark;
do not flaunt sharp, novel, or flamboyant styles. Carefully restrain body and mind so that they are not defiled by worldly sentiments. Deeply...
Contemplate the cycle of rebirth within the six realms; use this as a warning to inspire a sense of dread.

When leaving the household life, one must uphold the Buddha’s words. Do not fail to believe that one will suffer in the three miserable paths. Serve your teachers and elders with a humble mind. Bring merit to aid yourself by revering the Triple Gem.

Junior novices should maintain humility and harmony toward their seniors. Do not even look upon alcohol, meat, or gambling. Do not engage in idle gossip or frivolous debate. Constantly yearn for the holy teachings. How could one...
How can you let your time pass in vain? After death, what reliance will you have? Not only will you fail the Fourfold Debt of Gratitude, but you will also bring shame upon your ancestors.

Having left your kin and severed your attachments to join a teacher, your original intent was to transcend the mundane world and deliver others. With resolute determination, you vowed to practice the Way;
through introspection, you realized that the cycle of rebirth knows no rest. Having attained this human body after ten thousand kalpas, you must feel shame and know its origin. Depart!
Eliminate laziness and torpor; discipline body and mind with spaciousness. Be authentic in practicing the minor precepts from the outset, so that as you grow, you may become a steadfast monk.
Through Zen practice, repay the Buddha’s kindness; vow to seek sudden enlightenment. Having fortunately attained ordination in this life, do not let such an encounter pass unheeded.
Let every thought-moment never retreat from the roots of goodness, and let every heart grow into the tree of awakening. If...
If one can practice in this manner, one will certainly realize the path to Bodhi. (These instructions should be posted in one's own quarters so that they may be seen at all times to alert the mind.)

The Commentary on the Meaning states: A *tonghang* (novice) is one who studies the Way and serves as an attendant to the Sangha; thus they are also called a "Way-person" (*daoren*) or a "pure person" (*jingren*).
For this reason, it is essential to exercise strict discipline and rigorous authority over the *tonghang*, so that they do not commit evil.
The *Shan'an zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of Mountain Hermitages) says: Qian Lai resided at Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing. A pure person there stole a dog belonging to a lay neighbor, boiled it, and—
He ate it and thereby acquired the reputation for "cooking dogs" at Lài. Furthermore, Jing Shi resided at Chengtian Monastery in Gusu;

while traveling by boat to a donor's house, he stopped at a lecture site in Shuoluo. There, a monastery attendant stole a sheep belonging to a local resident and cooked it for food. Jing Shi thus acquired the reputation for "eating sheep. Alas!
Stealing dogs and stealing sheep are acts committed by subordinates for their own private gain; why then should the abbot be held responsible?
This ill repute likely stems from ordinary lapses in instruction and a failure to maintain careful observation.
As the abbot, you should be prudent at all times;
this is for the sake of the practitioners' general edification.
Regarding the "practitioner" (xingzhe): there is a general sense and a specific sense. In the general sense, it does not refer solely to those who are formally designated as practitioners;

rather, all who cultivate the path are called practitioners. Therefore, there are Buddhist activities that speak of this universally. In the specific sense, this title is restricted to the Abbot (fangzhang).

These are individuals who serve labor and exert physical effort. Generally, those previously instructed as *tongxing* (novices) belong to the small assembly of householders, whereas these practitioners belong to the small assembly of those who have left the home life (*pravrajita*).

Those who seek merit by generating the resolve [for enlightenment] should fill these positions; although there was formerly the name "Universal Exposition" (*pushe*), there were no formal texts for such an exposition.
For the most part, it is simply the abbot establishing teachings according to the capacity of the occasion. As for the implements held by these practitioners:
These matters are appended here as the early morning duties (four *bǎn* prior). Lighting the lamps at the Dharma seat; opening the water supply; providing face-washing water;
the Abbot’s prostration before the Buddha; carrying the lanterns; sweeping inside and out at dawn; wiping the tables; fetching water;

and preparing the bedding, curtains, tables, and floors for the guest rooms both inside and out—all must be kept clean. Furthermore, this includes the tasks of serving tea, bringing forth the midday meal, and washing the bowls.
Attend to your duties. Be present whenever summoned; those who cause matters to go awry shall be punished. You must be diligent and frugal in your conduct, avoiding neither hardship nor toil.
Carry out these practices with meticulous care.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: All Buddhas of the three periods and all great Bodhisattvas have emerged from the gate of practice.
Among those who possess the Way, there has never been one who was not once hidden among those engaged in manual labor and physical toil. Yuyan (Yuanwu) cited an ancient account, saying:
When Xuedou served as the guest prefect under Dayang, he conversed with guests at night, discussing the merits and demerits of the ancients and the present. When it came to Zhao...
Regarding the story of Zhaozhou: as the dialogue went back and forth without end, an attendant standing by stood there watching. A guest who had been hiding and laughing withdrew.
Xuedou called out to the attendant and rebuked him, saying, "How dare you laugh like that in the presence of a guest?

The attendant replied, "I knew that guest was capable of scrutinizing the past and present, yet he lacked the eye to determine the past and present; therefore, I dared to laugh. Xuedou asked, "What do you understand of Zhaozhou’s meaning? The attendant said, "..."
The other replied with a verse: "A single rabbit lies across the ancient road; As soon as the gray falcon sees it, he seizes it. The hounds that follow lack any spiritual nature;
They vainly search for it at the old spot by the withered post. Xuedou was greatly astonished and subsequently formed a close friendship with him.
Some say this practitioner was Zong from Chengtian Temple; others say he was Han Dabo. Alas! The ancients...
Although such correct knowledge and vision exist, they remain hidden from the ranks of practitioners; yet they can be seen among those who truly practice.
One should not look down upon them merely because of their manual labor or physical exertion.

Furthermore, as practitioners themselves, one should aspire to transcendence, using practice to assist the Path. One must not settle for mere manual labor and physical toil, nor lack far-reaching resolve.
This is the great aspiration.

When a special messenger arrives to deliver the Dharma robe, the guest hall shall first receive them with the etiquette due to guests, providing tea and refreshments; they shall then immediately instruct the attendant (zhaoke).

The messenger informs the abbot. Either the abbot goes in person to the guest hall that very day to receive him, or, if it is late, he is escorted to his guest room with the instruction to meet in the morning.
First, a tray is used to present the Dharma robes and the gifts of faith, which are placed upon the Dharma seat.
Thereafter, the guest master (zhikè) accompanies the visitor to see the abbot. Once the formal greeting has been performed, the special envoy delivers this address: "I, [Name], from..."

(Below: "The Dharma robes of Venerable Monk [Name] are presented as a token of faith. I hereby respectfully offer them... (and so forth). Immediately, the Abbot invites him for tea and refreshments and escorts him back to his guest room.

The following morning, after the morning service is concluded, he delivers a *xiao-can* (small informal discourse) on receiving the robes; this may take the form of either ascending the seat (*shengzuo*) or entering the hall (*shangtang*).

(If other gifts were sent, it is not necessary to deliver a formal discourse. Alternatively, if the Master from whom he received the Dharma has already passed away, an altar for the spirit is set up in the right-hand room of the Dharma Hall.
The junior monks descend from their seats to perform the sacrifice, using the ritual text and chanting the sutras, according to the etiquette for receiving a final letter, as explained below.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: "This is the observance of the ritual for honoring one's teacher. It is not only the case with the dharma robes;
even when receiving the teacher’s admonitions and reprimands, one must receive them with sincerity and reverence to fully fulfill the duties of a disciple. — Yunqi Zhuhong.
The Record states: During the Jin dynasty, Fayu served Dao’an as his teacher. Later, he resided at Changsha Temple in Jiangling, where he lectured on various sutras;
those who received his instruction numbered more than four hundred. At that time, there was a monk who drank wine, and although the Master Fuyu punished him, he did not dismiss him.
Hearing of this from afar, Dao’an placed a single cane of the Jing clan inside a bamboo tube, sealed it, and sent it to Fuyu. Fuyu opened the seal.
Upon seeing the staff, he immediately said, "This is because of the monks who drink alcohol; I have failed to lead them with diligence, and have thus distantly incurred this cause for sorrow.
He then struck the bell to assemble the congregation, placed the bamboo tube before them, burned incense in reverence, and prostrated himself on the ground.

He commanded the *karmadāna* to strike the staff three times, while shedding tears and reproaching himself. Within the jurisdiction, both monastics and laypeople were moved to sigh in lamentation, and consequently, they redoubled their efforts in their practice.
Those who [act thus] are very numerous. In his *Praise of the Lotus Pond*, [Zhang] said: "Alas!

If people of today were to open the seal of 'peaceful old age,' there would be few who would not shatter their bamboo tubes and break their staffs to utter insults. That a holy master and a worthy disciple exist a thousand years hence—of these two gentlemen, I still consider them many."

Regarding the practice of *yanguan* (closing the gate): the model for this first originated from the *Nirvāṇa-samādhi-sūtra* (Complete Enlightenment Sutra), where the Buddha established a fixed period for practitioners of meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*).
Originally, the period was set at one hundred and twenty days; however, when *yanguan* was introduced to the Eastern Land (China), it was mostly conducted for three [months].

This constitutes the formal commencement of the period. It is the practice for one who, having attained realization through traveling on pilgrimage (*yǎngdào*), to cultivate the Way. When the time arrives, the assembly is gathered in the Great Hall and the Wei Hall. The offerings for the "Original Barrier" (*běnguān*) are presented;

the Rector (*wéinà*) recites the incense hymn (*xiāngzàn*), and the Master of the Barrier (*guānzhǔ*) offers incense and performs prostrations. Once the offerings before the Buddha in the hall are completed, the Rector proclaims the memorial (*shūsū*). The Master of the Barrier remains prostrate behind the Rector. The memorial reads as follows:

I humbly submit that to investigate the truth and sever delusion, one must dwell in solitary seclusion within deep forests; to cultivate contemplation and clarify the mind, one must maintain one’s resolve while concealing one’s form in a quiet place.
Diligent effort without retreat is the primary gateway to the Path of Goodness, whereas negligence and indulgence lead to exhaustion and are the very root of transgression.

(Insert place of origin, age, and the matter sought here. I reflect earnestly that, having transcended worldly defilements, one ought to distance oneself from places of clamor and distraction. Already...

Having the honor of being among the ranks of the Sangha, I shall dwell in this realm of purity and leisure. This "closing of the gate" (yan guan) practice is specifically dedicated to a particular purpose;

with a period of three years as its term, it shall serve as an auxiliary for the cultivation of recitation and ritual. It begins on the [day] of this month and concludes on the [day], [month], and [year].
Residing at [Name of Temple], I shall conduct myself according to the Dharma while remaining in seclusion. I humbly pray that my thoughts may follow from stillness.

Attained! The root of the One Truth is manifest; wisdom naturally arises from concentration. The sprouts of the myriad practices flourish; not a speck of dust can stain them. Closing the door is itself the deep mountains.
When the ten wisdoms accord with the truth, one ascends to the stage of enlightenment upon leaving conceptual thought.

This preface respectfully requests the Three Jewels to bear witness. This is the "Preface for Auspiciousness upon Closing the Door. Dated [Year, Month, Day], written by [Name] (after making offerings at the meditation hall, the Master of the Retreat...).

Donning the formal robes and carrying the ritual implements, the attendant proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to request that the abbot seal the retreat gate. The abbot emerges; the gatekeeper prostrates three times with his implements unfolded. He invites the abbot to the exterior of the gate room, where they stand facing each other.

One monk fans him and another holds the staff, standing in attendance to the left and right. The gatekeeper stands behind the abbot. The Rector chants the praises. When the praises are finished, the lead chime and the responding chime strike three times in unison. The abbot delivers a Dharma discourse. Upon its conclusion, the abbot escorts the gatekeeper back inside as he enters the gate.

Once the gate has been sealed and locked, the abbot immediately affixes a Dharma inscription to the outside of the gate wall. After the Vajrapāṇi Praise is completed, everyone returns to their respective places.
"Opening the Barrier!

Opening the Barrier! The time has come. (The assembly gathers again at the door of the barrier room; first, the Dharma is preached to open the barrier, after which the offerings are presented. The Rector then proclaims the *Yuanguan Su* [the Memorial for Closing the Barrier], saying:)

I humbly submit that the secret treasury of the *an-gu* (summer retreat) fully manifests the patterns for manifesting the Way; the *nāga* entering meditative absorption universally displays dignified deportment and movement.

Being eternally constant and unchanging, how could this hinder its application to specific conditions? When stillness reaches its ultimate limit, penetration follows; how could it obstruct the activity that pervades the entire Dharma-realm?

[Insert here: place of origin, year of birth, and the matter sought. I earnestly reflect that I, [Name], am like a blind turtle in quality, and my wisdom is but a mere torch compared to the sun. I look toward...

The ultimate Way of the One Vehicle is like a destitute child who has wandered far from the ox-cart; for three years the empty barrier has been closed, as if one were lost at a rabbit-trap while missing the path of the elephant.

To have wasted the granary of faith in vain and cast away one’s time in emptiness—while my person has merely found security within this small chamber, entirely owing to the Buddha’s power of protection—I now look forward to the completion of the opening of the barrier, specifically relying on the merit of repentance to offer my gratitude. Thus, I begin...

The Selection (Yue): I humbly pray that by the merit of this Perfect Barrier (*yuan-guan*), the imperial domain may be firm and secure, the Emperor’s Way may flourish far and wide, and the people and all things may enjoy abundance and peace.

May wind and rain be timely and harmonious; may those in the six realms of existence equally ascend to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); and may the three realms forever find rest from the three calamities.
May deceased relatives realize the fruits of enlightenment and attain rebirth in the Pure Land; may donors receive grace and obtain blessings. Furthermore, I pray that the Abbot [Name]...

A) The wind of the Way spreads afar; the tally of the Dharma increases. The monastic groves flourish, and the ocean-like assembly is peaceful and harmonious. Virtue and practice are cultivated equally, and merit and wisdom are fully perfected.

To the right, this memorial respectfully requests the Three Jewels to bear witness. This is the Memorial for the Completion of the Retreat and the Expression of Gratitude to the Lay Benefactor (Anwen).

[Date] (So-and-so) presents this memorial. (The dedication of merit follows the usual ritual. The retreat master performs the rites of gratitude. Once the assembly of masters has concluded, each returns to the retreat master’s quarters to pay homage to the Abbot, and then proceeds to express thanks to the various administrative offices.)
The Commentary on the Meaning states: An ancient saying goes, "Zhaozhou was eighty years old and still traveled as a mendicant; it was only because his heart had not yet become tranquil.
Based on this half-verse, one can truly know that closing the gate in seclusion is the practice of nurturing the Way after attaining realization.
Records such as the *Yunqi Chongxing Lu* all record that after Master Gaofeng Miao attained sudden enlightenment, he remained at Longxu for nine years.

He bound together bundles of wood to form a hut, wearing but a single robe throughout both winter and summer. Later, he went to Mount Tianmu, where he constructed a small chamber like a boat within a stone cave on the western cliff and inscribed it with the name "The Barrier of Death.

Above, water cascaded down; below, the ground was marshy; and it was buffeted by wind and rain. He eliminated attendants and discarded all luxuries, eating only once every two days, yet remaining as composed as ever.
The cave could not be ascended without a ladder; thus, he removed the ladder to sever all external ties, even from his own younger brother.
My son Hãn was unable to behold him. Alas! If the Way of the sages were thus confined within closed doors, how could it ever have been perfected?

Compared to the present practice of seclusion behind closed doors, where everything is manifest in its myriad forms, the difference is as vast as that between heaven and the abyss. How can one not lament the decline of the Way?
Welcoming the Venerable Elder (The Six Rites): Welcoming and Inspecting the Quarters, Part One.
Whenever a venerable elder from another monastery arrives, the gatekeeper immediately notifies the Guest Hall. The Guest Hall reports this to the Abbot and informs the Meditation Hall.

The Rector (Vina) announces: "A monk from [Name] Monastery has arrived; please all don your robes and carry your requisites to welcome him. Outside, the bell is struck, and the assembly exits the hall to go to the mountain [monastery].

[The assembly] waits for the guests to arrive. The *vinaya-dhara* (Weina) says: "Great Assembly, prostrate to Venerable Master [Name]. When the prostrations are finished, the Abbot accompanies the honored elder to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*).

The Abbot offers incense, and after the bows are completed, the *vinaya-dhara* calls out to the assembly: "Spread your sitting cloths; prostrate to Venerable Master [Name]. When the prostrations are finished, he further says: "Prostrate to the Abbot of the Abbot’s Quarters.
When the prostrations are finished, the attendant on duty serves tea and fruit, and the robes and bowls are provided according to the honored guest's needs.

Once the guest quarters have been prepared with curtains, bedding, and mattresses, as well as the Dharma seat for preaching, the attendant in charge of the guest hall (zhiké) next goes to the guest hall to deliver the guest list (dān).

Upon arrival, the attendant joins his palms toward the abbot and says, "The guest list is ready; I request that Master So-and-so be present. The abbot follows him to the hall. Once the formal greetings are concluded, everyone sits down comfortably.

In the evening, the plaque for the recitation service is hung, which reads: "Upon hearing the sound of the bell, look for the guest list of Master So-and-so; each person shall bring their ritual implements."
Ascend the hall. After the evening service is concluded, the bell is struck. Proceed to the seat of the venerable elder (zunsu) and wait for the abbot (zhuchi). Before the seat, offer incense.

Upon completion of the prostrations, the rector (weina) calls the assembly to unfold their sitting cloths (zhangu) and says, "Behold the single robe of the Venerable Master. When the prostrations are finished, stand still as before.

If the abbot, by means of a skillful expedient, requests the venerable elder to provide instruction, do so; if not, return immediately to the hall. The attendants (shizhe) shall arrange [the seating].

When the bowing and prostrations are completed, tea and refreshments are served next. Whenever the host and guests converse on matters concerning the Dharma, the attendant shall listen with a clear and reverent mind;
whatever may be recorded, he shall immediately transcribe it.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: From the initial invitation to the final escorting back, all acts constitute the reverent treatment of teachers and friends, emphasizing the etiquette of honoring virtue and conduct.
Those designated as "Venerable Elders" (zunsu) are so called because their virtue and conduct are worthy of honor; even if their specific virtues and conduct cannot be fully known.
Since he was a venerable guest, there was the principle of host and guest and the propriety of ritual respect;
furthermore, it was intended to allow the student to habituate himself to the way of honoring elders and to abandon arrogance. Yuan'an (Yuanwu Keqin) cited an ancient account, saying:

"Chan Master Xueyan Yuanmian and Shengmo were study companions. Once, [Shengmo] knelt to receive [Xueyan's] reprimands. When someone asked him about this in astonishment, the Master said: 'Nowadays, in various quarters...'"
Or when teachers, disciples, and dharma-kin engage in disputes that invite public reproach—like parasites within a lion’s body devouring the lion’s own flesh—this is truly lamentable.
I write this to stir and encourage them. Alas! When the ancients served their friends with such lofty integrity, their spirit remains unsurpassed through the ages;
how then could one be disrespectful toward venerable elders elsewhere? This applies especially to those from whom one has personally received instruction.
Overnight guests: Is this not more significant?

After ascending the seat for the second time and inspecting the quarters, he orders the guest master to go before the overnight guests and perform one prostration. With palms joined, he says: "Venerable Abbot, the two orders of the assembly, tomorrow morning..."
"Please, Master So-and-so, out of your compassion, ascend the seat. If the venerable elder consents, he then performs one prostration and reports back to the Abbot.

Whether it be the Abbot personally inviting him or regardless of whether the occasion is a formal ascent of the high seat or a small-scale discourse (*xiao-can*), on the morning of the following day during the morning service, the red robes are delivered to the venerable elder's quarters.
The announcement for the ascending of the seat (*shèng-zuò-pái*) is made. Once the morning service is concluded, the bell is struck and the assembly lines up facing the Abbot’s quarters.

The Abbot ascends the seat; he does not offer incense nor recite verses of praise. The Rector calls out: "Spread your ritual implements; prostrate to the Abbot. They follow with one prostration with implements spread. When the prostrations are finished, the Abbot says:

"Today, this Venerable [Name], whose virtue and conduct transcend the ordinary and whose Dharma-eye is perfectly clear, has arrived at this place. This is due to the great fortune of our long-standing karmic ties as a community; we reverently request that you open the hall. The Rector says: "Prostrate to the Abbot," and they perform one prostration.
When finished, the *jing* is struck to lead the way. The abbot and the assembly proceed in order to the quarters of the venerable elder (*zhensu*).

The abbot offers incense; if the venerable elder is of equal standing to the abbot, then the chief administrator (*jianyuan*) offers the incense, or else the head of the assembly (*ban-shou*) acts as proxy.

Once the offering is complete, the rector (*weina*) calls out, "Spread your sitting cloths and prostrate to Venerable So-and-so" (at this time, the abbot returns first). After the prostrations are finished, he calls out, "The last one shall go first," and they proceed to the Dharma seat.

When a venerable elder ascends the seat, he offers incense, recites verses of praise, and proceeds to preach the Dharma to provide guidance; the ritual is identical to that of the *shangtang* (ascending the hall).
However, when preaching from the high seat, the bells and drums are struck and the mallet is sounded to announce the session (all other details remain as above).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: This is the etiquette of the superior honoring the inferior and mutually stimulating one another. As the *Zhigu song* (Verses on Picking up the Past) says:
"In the past, when Master Yue arrived at Xuedou, he was in the prime of his youth and his eloquence was extraordinary.
Xuedou would always seat him at tea assemblies, providing a special couch to honor him. Consequently, his reputation soared. When it came time for Yue to enter the world [as an abbot], there was..."
The Venerable Lan came from Xuedou; Yue tested him and was greatly amazed, praising him before the assembly. He followed him for many years before departing.

That the seniors did not hesitate to recommend him despite their differing lineages allows us to imagine what the juniors might have been like. Yufan’s eulogy says: "Yue is a fang-toothed, clawed new lion;
before the cliffs of Xuedou, he can perform the backward somersault. To see the worthy and yet fail to show them respect—how could one do such a thing?"
It is not in accordance with propriety. Geese-winged mats are spread to present fragrant essences; I play the *se* while you stroke the *qin*.

With the breeze of benevolence and the reputation for the Way, you transform the barbarians. Master Lan’s orchid fragrance reaches Yunfeng Peak; at Xuedou’s tea gathering today, the jade tablet is returned.
The third-ranking abbot (luotáng dìsānguǒ) is a Great Venerable Elder (dà zūnsù). After the morning gruel has been served, he should be formally invited once again by the Abbot (zhùzhí) in person.

If the Venerable Elder consents, the attendant on duty (zhíyuè shìzhě) shall immediately notify the Guest Hall (kètáng) to post a notice board. (The board reads: "We respectfully invite Master [Name] to preside over the hall for the opening of the session."

[The Master] indicates [the teaching]. △ Immediately, he informs the Rector (Karmadāna). The Rector addresses the assembly, saying: "We now invite Venerable So-and-so to enter the hall and provide instruction. All you fellow practitioners, each maintain your dignified demeanor and wait in attendance.

Before the Buddha statue, incense and candles are prepared. The Guest Master (Karmadāna) informs the Abbot, saying: "All preparations within the hall are complete; we request Venerable So-and-so to enter the hall. The Abbot accompanies the Honored Elder to the entrance of the Meditation Hall (Zen-dō).
The Guest Master strikes the signal board twice. The Head of the Assembly and the Rector strike [the gong].
The striking [of the board] ends the reception; the others stand still. The venerable elder either performs the ritual of entering the hall or simply pays obeisance to the Buddha.
Once this is done, the abbot yields his seat to the guest; the venerable elder likewise yields his seat to the abbot as they take their places.

The guests and host sit with mutual humility. The Rector says: "Great Assembly, prostrate yourselves before the two Venerable Elders. When the prostrations are finished, they again stand still on both sides. The Abbot says: "All of you have come here specifically for this occasion."

I have been solely occupied with my own personal affairs. Alas, I, [Name], am of shallow wisdom and meager strength; I have been unable to extract the nails and pull out the wedges for you all, thereby failing to fulfill your original aspirations. Now that Master [Name] has arrived here, it is truly a blessing of past karmic conditions.

This monk has labored on the Way for many years and possesses the eye of the True Dharma. You should regard him as one rarely encountered and reverently request his instruction. We only hope that this monk will, out of compassion, provide guidance to each and every one of you.

"Ten thousand hopes! Ten thousand hopes! Once the Venerable Elder has finished his exhortation, the Rector says: "All fellow practitioners, pay your respects to express gratitude to Master So-and-so. When the prostrations are completed, he says again:

"All fellow practitioners, escort Master So-and-so back. If the request is declined, he stops there. The Abbot accompanies him back to the Abbot’s quarters, where the Attendant serves tea. When the tea service is finished, he is escorted back to his quarters.

If the Venerable Elder does not consent to descend to the hall, the various Head Monks and others each don their formal robes and carry their ritual implements, proceeding to the Venerable Elder’s quarters.
At the guest quarters, he requested instruction.
Zhengyi said: "In ancient times, when an abbot attended to a student, he did so solely by means of this one matter to refine them.
Therefore, when host and guest meet, as soon as they enter the gate, they immediately earnestly inquire about this one matter and act as a representative to uphold it."
In its former prosperity, it was now an unfortunate state for the Dharma gate that the discourse between host and guest was largely mundane.
To reveal the way of realizing the Path was a rare occurrence, which caused students to wander thousands of li in vain, expending their efforts in fruitless inquiry.
How distant are the ancient regulations; when will they be restored? Alas!
The Fourth Section on Inviting for a Meal:

Whenever a meal is invited for a venerable elder, the attendant first prepares an incense table, chairs, and tables, as well as the sequence of tea and fruit offerings, within the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*).
The abbot first instructs the head of the assembly to wait and accompany him for the meal. When the time arrives, he orders one member of the assembly to attend.

One person [approaches] the seat of the Venerable Elder. Before the seat, they perform one prostration, join their palms, and say: "The Abbot invites Master So-and-so to partake of the midday meal. The Venerable Elder arrives, and the host and guest exchange formal greetings.

He is escorted to his seat in the central position (*zhengwei*). He takes up the incense and offers tea. When the rites are concluded, the Venerable Elder proceeds before the seat of the Abbot, takes up the incense, returns the prostrations, and takes his place in the seating order.
Subsequently, the heads of the various ranks (*ban-shou*) all face the seat of the Venerable Elder to perform their salutations; next, they face the Abbot.
When the ritual of offering incense is completed, each person returns to their assigned seat according to protocol. The attendants all exit the ranks to perform a prostration;
if they are exempted from this, they simply bow once. Next, tea is served, followed by fruit. Two attendants per table serve the dishes one by one, each maintaining full decorum and dignity.

Attend with focused care. Ensure that shoes, slippers, bowls, or chopsticks do not make any noise. When the meal is finished, according to the ritual protocol for host and guest, wash the hands, chew a willow branch (*yángzhī*), and rinse the mouth.
Then escort the guest back to his quarters. The attendant shall immediately serve tea and continue to attend as usual.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: Formerly, Gao’an said, "In the great task of teaching and transforming others, nothing takes precedence over morality, virtue, ritual, and righteousness.
If the abbot honors morality and virtue, then students will prize respectfulness; if he practices ritual and righteousness, then students will feel shame at greed and competition.
If the abbot displays a lack of decorum and arrogance, then students will fall into the vice of insolence and violence; if the abbot displays agitation of countenance..."

If such disputes were allowed, scholars would suffer the calamity of conflict and strife. The former sages, perceiving this before it happened, selected men of wisdom and sagacity to preside over the monastic communities (conglins).
Thus, all could look up to them with reverence, and people were transformed through their influence even without being explicitly instructed.
Consequently, the dignified demeanor with which these honored guests receive visitors—both their gestures and commands—are worthy of serving as models for future generations. Its...

How generous and sincere were these preparations! Lately, however, everything has become uniformly negligent and superficial; host and guest have grown mutually disrespectful, and rites, righteousness, and moral virtue are gradually being extinguished, almost entirely. How tragic!
Section Five: Visiting the Hall and Inspecting the Quarters.
Whenever a venerable elder visits the hall and inspects the quarters, the Guest Hall first hangs a notice board (the board reads): "The Venerable Master [Name] will visit after the second board."

The inspection of the hall and the quarters. △ Next, the Chief of the Assembly (Weina) informs the Head of the Class. The Weina addresses the assembly, saying: "Today, such-and-such Master is visiting the hall;
all fellow practitioners should maintain full decorum. A single chair is prepared in the meditation hall. The Guest Master leads the venerable elder to the exterior of the hall.

Strike the signal board twice. Announce: "So-and-so Abbot enters the hall. While awaiting the arrival of the venerable elder for his entry into the hall, once the ten-direction prostrations have been performed, the attendant (yuezhong) shall set out a chair in the center.
The lead assembly member invites the venerable elder to take his seat. The rector says: "Venerable assembly, prostrate to So-and-so Abbot. If he declines, then stop.
When the prostrations are finished, the venerable elder exits the hall. The guest master strikes the leading chime and proceeds to each of the quarters to offer greetings.

The Guest Master announces: "A certain monk from [Name of Temple] is visiting the quarters; please pay your respects to [Name of Monk]. Once the rounds are completed, he invites him back to the Abbot’s quarters for tea and conversation.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: This is the Venerable Elder’s response to the etiquette of receiving guests and inspecting their quarters.

Within this response, there may be instances where the guest hall is further instructed to notify the storehouse to prepare a vegetarian feast for the assembly; or there may be cases where only fermented bean curd is provided for the assembly;
or there may be occasions where the inspection of the various quarters itself serves as the response, with no food provided for the assembly. These are ancient customs.
But nowadays it is not so. If one were to receive a single guest without providing for the assembly, the multitude would surely rise up in clamor. Alas!

When the Sixth Patriarch was about to return to his mountain, the guest prefect (zhikè) hung up a notice in advance. (The notice read: "Venerable Assembly, upon hearing the sound of the bell, please escort [the guest] off."
At [Name] Temple. When the Abbot returns to the mountain: △ When the time arrives, the Guest Hall attendant first goes to the Abbot’s quarters. He bows once toward the Venerable Elder and says:

"Master of the Assembly, the Mountain Gate awaits to escort the Abbot [Name] back to the mountain. Thereupon, the Venerable Elder departs. The Abbot escorts the Venerable Elder as far as the Buddha Hall.

Once the Venerable Elder has finished bowing to the Buddha, the bells and drums are struck. The Rector calls to the assembly, saying: "Spread your sitting cloths; prostrate yourselves before the Abbot [Name]. As it is said:
[The Abbot] declines. [The procession] stops immediately. They proceed together to the mountain gate (*sānamukha*) and stand in formation with palms joined, escorting him as he departs.

After he has gone for a short while and can no longer be seen, the assembly returns to the temple. The *vinaya-dhara* says: "Venerable Assembly, go to the Abbot’s quarters (*upādhyāya-kuṭī*) and pay homage to the Master. The Abbot declines, saying: "Please all return to the hall to sit for the incense period.
The *vinaya-dhara* leads the assembly back to their own hall.
The Commentary on the Meaning says: The etiquette of senior masters (*zunsu*) in coming and going honors moral virtue (*daode*), not fame or rank.
A true senior master, even if lacking fame or rank, should likewise honor the Dharma in this way to encourage those in training. Yuan’an’s *Zhigu* (Gleanings from the Past) states:
Formerly, Chan Master Luohan Nan succeeded to the Dharma of Yunju; he was not known by others at first. Later, he went to the East...

Lin Zhaojue struck the bell to assemble the community and went out to welcome him at the edge of Qingxi Stream; the assembly was greatly astonished, and the reputation of Master Nan thus became renowned.
Furthermore, when Foyin resided again at Yunju, Chan Master Linyuan Sou came from Longshan and remained incognito among the monks.
When Foyin learned of this, he ascended the seat and invited Yuan to serve as the head of the assembly (Zuoyuan) and pay his respects.
The land was fertile and rich; all observed and were moved by this, and their cultivation of the Way flourished daily.

Furthermore, during the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, Zen Master Zhuan’an Gui was commissioned by imperial decree to open Mount Yandang Nengren Temple. At that time, Zen Master Zhenxie Le resided at Jiangxin.
When he heard that Master Zhu had arrived, fearing that his karmic conditions were not yet ripe, he crossed the river to welcome Master Zhu back to the Abbot’s quarters.
There, he performed nine prostrations in full detail to inspire the people of Wenzhou; consequently, they all turned toward him with great harmony and reverence. Alas! Such were these three abbots.
This may be called a profound honoring of morality and virtue, fully observing the rites of hospitality due to a venerable elder. Those who read this later should emulate it.
The Dharma Protector has arrived.
Whenever a high-ranking official arrives at the temple, the gatekeeper informs the Guest Hall (Ketak), which then notifies the Abbot (Fangzhang).

The Abbot, together with the Head Monks (Banshou) and the Administrative Head (Janyuan) and others, waits at the Mountain Gate (Shanmen) to receive him. Several attendants don their ceremonial robes (Daiyi) and stand in formation before the Buddha hall.

They wait for the official to offer incense, at which time they chant the incense hymn (Xiangzan). When the Abbot strikes the chime (Qing), the ceremony concludes. The official is then invited to the Abbot’s quarters for tea. The Abbot presides over the reception.

Accompany and attend to them. When they depart, the current head of the class (ban-shou), the director of the monastery (jian-yuan), and others shall wait until they have been escorted out through the mountain gate.
For all other patrons and protectors who arrive, one must ensure that the etiquette is thorough and respectful;

one must not treat them with negligence or disdain, causing the external protectors to lose heart. (If a discerning layperson from afar arrives, they should be treated according to the rules for patrons. After the escort has concluded, the current head of the class and the meditation monks (chan-seng) shall visit the guest quarters to discuss the essentials of the Way; these opportunities must not be missed. In all cases, they shall meet according to the rites of host and guest.)

The Commentary on the Meaning states: In cities adjacent to monasteries, such occurrences are frequent; one must simply ensure that one’s deportment is perfectly composed so as to inspire reverence in others.
As for the application of expedient means according to the occasion, however, this depends upon the individual.
The *Shan’an Zalù* (Miscellaneous Records from Mountain Hermitages) says: During the Yuan Dynasty’s Yanyou era, at Xiatianzhu on Fengshan in Hangzhou, there was the Dharma Master Yi from Goryeo...

The Prince of Shen, the Imperial Son-in-law, received an imperial decree to pay homage to Avalokiteśvara at Putuo Mountain. Passing through Hangzhou, he provided the funds to establish a vegetarian feast at Mingqing Temple.

He invited the abbots of all the mountain monasteries; when the time arrived, the Prince of Shen took his seat at the head of the hall, while the various officials took their places in order below him, and the abbots of the various mountains were lined up along both corridors. Fengshan approached the throne and asked the Prince: "For what purpose is today's vegetarian assembly?"

“What is it? the King asked. Fengshan replied, “Great King, since you have said you are hosting a vegetarian feast for the various mountains, the Master of the Mountain (the host) ought to have no fixed seat, yet Your Majesty has taken the seat of honor while the various mountains are lined up along both corridors, some even sitting on the floor.

How is this different from the *luo-zhai* (a common, informal meal)? In terms of ritual propriety, I fear this is not appropriate. Upon hearing this, the King was filled with shame and remorse, and immediately offered his apologies. Then—

At that time, the junior monk descended from his seat, stepped forward to bow to the masters of the various mountains, and established the protocol of host and guest; thereafter, the assembled officials withdrew to their positions along the two corridors.
When the meal was finished, the King took Fengshan’s hand and said, "Had it not been for my teacher, this ceremony would likely have failed.
This is what is called 'providing skillful means according to the occasion' to open the hearts of others—Fengshan is such a person. Nowadays, people of this age favor flattery."
This is a grave matter; this dharma must not be employed lightly. Nevertheless, the noble precedents of the ancients must also be known.

Regarding the sixfold etiquette for visiting venerable seniors at various mountain monasteries: it is when they come to us that we perform these rites. In the case of visiting various mountain monasteries, it is we who go to them.

Although there are differences between "self" and "other," their rites are inherently the same. This can be understood from the aforementioned protocols for welcoming and attending upon venerable elders (*zunsu*).
As for points where they differ, these depend on the specific circumstances of one's residence or absence, as well as the particular teachings being discussed; these are not recorded here.
Regarding the celebration of the abbot’s birthday: one day in advance, the storehouse prepares incense and candles and sends them to each hall.

The guest master goes to the abbot’s quarters to inquire whether there will be recitations the following day. If there are to be recitations, he shall immediately hang the notification board (as detailed below). If not...

Cease recitation immediately. At the morning service on the following day, each person shall take up their ritual implements. Throughout the entire monastery, incense and candles shall blaze brightly; incense is burned and the censers are passed.
The Abbot offers incense, and the Rector (Vina) raises the precious censer and intones the praise for the burning of famous incense. There is no invocation for the longevity of the Emperor.

One then recites the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and circumambulates the Buddha as usual. Returning to one’s place, one spreads the ritual implements and performs three prostrations to Śākyamuni Buddha and ten prostrations to Bhaiṣajyaguru Buddha.

Two prostrations. Three prostrations each to the Sunlight, Moonlight, and Ocean Assembly. Rising and arranging one's robes, the recitation is completed. The bell is struck three times. The Rector says:
"The assembly shall proceed together to the Abbot’s quarters to celebrate the Venerable Master’s birthday. Upon arrival, they take their positions in order on the left and right.
The Rector invites the Abbot to ascend the seat. The Rector calls out: "The assembly respectfully wishes the Venerable Master a long life on his birthday. [They bow] with their heads to the ground.

Perform three prostrations. After the prostrations, one may either preach the Dharma or not preach it. It was settled last night: if preaching occurs, it shall follow the standard procedure for a *xiaocan* (informal discourse).

If not preaching, then upon completion of the prostrations, rise from your seat, return to the hall, and [attend] the morning bell. At the midday bell, the assembly uses noodles; the offering follows the format used on the first and fifteenth days of the month.
In the refectory, fermented soybean curd (*fu*) is served. Matters such as celebratory ceremonies are generally not permitted (if... [the text continues]).
Recitation. The ritual protocol is as seen above; however, the commentary notes a distinction:
I humbly observe that as the precious candle first brightens, its shimmering golden light causes the Mount of Longevity to sway;

as the jade casket first opens, the vast waters of the Dharma surge forth as spiritual tides. Relying upon the eternal abiding of the Buddha-Dharma, I rejoice in the fortune of my birth and encounter. (Place of origin, name, year of birth, and circumstances). Truly...
[Recite] "So-and-so. Having received the radiance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, I have been unworthy of the robes and bowl within this precious monastery.

While I am subject to the fragmented existence of an ordinary being, virtuous conditions truly arose from the compassionate embrace of my mother. Now, on this occasion of my mother’s birthday, I harbor a grief that knows no limit.

For this reason, I respectfully assemble my fellow practitioners and together proceed to the precious hall to prostrate before the [specific] repentance altar and recite the [specific] sutra. I humbly...
May the foundation of the Holy One be eternally firm and the monastic assembly flourish, so that teachers, elders, and parents may receive grace from both the past and the present;

and may ancestors, forebears, and kinsmen obtain blessings far and near. Furthermore, I pray that [so-and-so] may cultivate their spiritual practice with steadfastness, universally employ wisdom and compassion, maintain a healthy physical body, and enjoy pure leisure in the latter years of life. May they adorn every birth with myriad virtues and realize each stage of awakening.
Possessing the six supernormal powers with mastery, I further pray that by this merit, all sentient beings may equally transcend [the mundane world].
May they all rely upon the foundation of a single virtue to achieve inexhaustible blessings. The above memorial respectfully requests the Three Jewels to bear witness.

(Number of days) of celebratory text for a birthday. On the [day] of the [month] year, Bhikṣu [Name] presents this memorial. (At the time of dedication, the Abbot shall instruct an attendant to offer congratulations on behalf of the various masters; other rituals are as usual.)
The Commentary on the Meaning states: This follows worldly etiquette to honor the virtue of the Abbot who maintains the community and propagates the Dharma.

In ancient times, Emperor Wen of the Tang dynasty, though a sovereign of ten thousand chariots, did not celebrate his own birthday with music; how much less so for a monk? Therefore it is said: "One should practice this when among the assembly."
When at rest, one should remain still; while walking, it is also permissible to recite mantras. When at rest, ceasing all clamor is the primary rule.

When the donor arrives for the meal offering to the Sangha, the Guest Hall attendant shall receive them and immediately report this to the Abbot. Next, he shall instruct the Attendant for Incense and Rituals to carry the incense and ceremonial offerings.
Pointing this out, he places [the offerings] upon the incense table of the Abbot’s quarters. He then entrusts the robe and bowl to the attendant.

Next, he leads the patron to the Abbot’s quarters, where they pay respects to the incumbent. The incumbent receives them with courtesy, offering several words of praise. When the tea ceremony concludes, the guest master delivers the formal notice;
however, if the visit is merely for that day’s arrival and departure, no notice is sent. If the visitor is a high-ranking official, the bell must be struck to assemble the assembly at the gate.

Welcoming. (As previously stated for the reception of the Dharma protectors. The Abbot orders the Chief Administrator to prepare meals and offerings for the assembly in accordance with the patron’s resources.
One must not deplete the monastery's permanent assets nor impose undue hardship upon the assembly; the arrangements should be moderate. Hang up the "Upper Offering" plaque. (The plaque reads:

"Venerable Assembly, upon hearing the drum, proceed together to the Great Hall and the Hall of Wei to present the upper offering. Strike the midday wooden clapper to signal the commencement of the offering.

At that time, hang the monk’s signboard for the meal (the board reads): "The Dharma Protector [Name] of [Place], for the sake of [specific matter], has established this vegetarian feast to provide offerings for the assembly" (if it is a meal for the *shàngtáng*, hang the board on the day prior;

if it is a grand "as-you-wish" (*rúyì*) feast, it should be hung outside the mountain gate three days in advance). △ When the time for the meal arrives, the guest prefect leads the patron to perform the bow for the meal, then leads them to the kitchen and storehouse to thank those who have relieved him of his labor.
Once the thanks are completed, the abbot invites the patron to the meal, and the head of the administrative office (*jiānyuàn*) accompanies him.
(Whether it be one or two head monks, or even the general supervisor) regarding all funds for the vegetarian feast, they may be distributed equally according to the donor’s intention.

As for public offerings (*gongchin*), sequential offerings (*xuchin*), and guest-gifts (*kesong*), these follow the donor’s heart; the Guest Hall is not permitted to solicit or haggle. For donations of five *liang* or less, there are no public offerings.
If only fermented bean curd and rice are served, there are no offerings at all, nor are any presented to the altar. From six to ten *liang*, [public offerings are provided].

Externally, one *qian* of silver shall be contributed from each of the two households as a public offering (*pūjā*). This shall follow the established customs of the various families. The wording of the memorial (*śāstra*) shall also be adapted to the circumstances.
The *Zhengyi* states: According to the *Jiegu*, during the Song dynasty, the lay practitioner (*upāsaka*) Hong Qingshan served as the Regional Commander (*Jiedushi*) of Jiangdong.
While staying at Chizhou Yuya, Master Zong invited him [Hongren] for a night conversation.

Hongren asked, "In which sutra is it seen that feeding a hundred ordinary people is not as good as feeding one virtuous person, and feeding a thousand virtuous persons is not as good as feeding one who is without dwelling, without action, and without realization? Master Zong replied: "The *Sutra of Forty-two Sections* says:

'To feed a hundred ordinary people is not as good as to feed one virtuous person; to feed a thousand virtuous persons is not as good as to feed one who dwells nowhere, acts nowhere, and realizes nothing. Then...
This is right mindfulness and solitary liberation. To be able to provide food for such a person brings merit equal to that of all Buddhas.
Many predecessors have known this principle. Hong asked, "Who were they? Zong replied, "To speak of recent examples:

when Qin Shaoyou was exiled to Tengzhou, he composed his own funeral elegy, which contained the line, 'Who will provide food for the yellow-robed and black-robed [monks]? When Dongpo heard of Qin's..."
Upon receiving the news of his death, [the donor] sent five taels of silver by letter, instructing Fan Yuanzhang to provide a vegetarian feast for the monks on behalf of Qin.

When东坡 (Sūn Dōngpō) was returning from the north and reached Bīlíng, he passed away due to illness. A student of the Imperial Academy collected funds in Tōkō to provide a vegetarian feast for the monks at Huìlín Monastery.
This was recorded at the beginning of the epitaph for Sūn Dōngpō composed by the Imperial Censor Hóng. Hóng asked: "Is there documentary evidence for this offering of alms? Zōng replied: "Yes."
He said, "Have you not seen the 'Luming' (Feeding the Deer) in the Xiao Ya of the Mao Shi? It describes feasting the ministers and honored guests;
one provides food and drink, and further presents silk and woven goods in baskets and boxes to convey one's profound sincerity.

This is because food and drink alone are insufficient to fully express reverence, so gifts are added to manifest earnest devotion. Hong said, "Now that I have heard the Master’s words, I understand the purpose of providing meals for the monks."
Regarding this meaning, I have every year provided meals for the monastics at Zen temples. Someone once asked:
"Why is it said that money intended for feeding the monastics may not be used for other purposes? I replied: "It is because the cause and effect do not coincide.

Formerly, on Mount Yungai in Hunan, Master Zhi was sitting in his chamber at night when he suddenly smelled the scent of burning and heard the sound of shackles and locks. Looking toward it, he saw someone carrying fire.
As for the one in the cangue: the end of his cangue leaned against the door threshold. Zhi asked him in alarm, "Who are you? He replied, "I am so-and-so, who formerly resided on this mountain.

It was improper for me to use money intended as an offering for the Sangha to construct a sangha hall; thus, I violated the intention of the faithful donors and caused cause and effect to become discordant.
Therefore, I undergo this suffering. I hope that you will appraise the value of the sangha hall and provide funds to fulfill the offerings for the Sangha."
"Only then can you be spared. Zhi used his own resources to repay the debt exactly as he had been told.

One night, he dreamed that the man thanked him, saying, "Relying on the Master’s power, I have escaped hell and been reborn among gods and humans. After three more lifetimes, I shall again become a monk."

Even now, the burn marks upon the threshold of the gate still remain. If those who provided goods for the Sangha to construct a monastic hall—goods intended for the communal use of the monks—still receive such retribution for their misappropriation, what then can be said of those who today steal the permanent property of the Sangha to make it their own? As for the retribution they shall receive, how could it possibly be anything less than severe?
However, this has been discussed in terms of the physical objects received as offerings; as for the initial resolve of those who provide faithful offerings, [the consequences are even more profound].

It is also appropriate to be impartial. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in the past there was a donor who provided food for the Saṃgha, yet he made offerings only to the elders and not to the juniors.
At that time, the various Arhats, out of compassion, employed their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) so that all of them manifested the appearance of being old.
They venerated and made offerings to him with joy. When the recitation of the *pranidhāna* was finished and they were about to receive the food, [the monks] all returned to their original forms.
After receiving the food, that young bhikṣu preached the Dharma according to their capacities, causing their minds to attain equanimity.
Furthermore, in the Western Regions, the elder Jyotiṣka once established a great *mahā-maṇi-bhakta* (Great Wish-Fulfilling Feast) for seven days in order to seek the venerable Piṇḍola-bharadvāja.
One should offer fresh flowers and place them beneath the seat of the Noble Sangha. Furthermore, a single vase of fresh flowers on the table serves as a test.
If the Noble Sangha has accepted the offering, the flowers will not wither even after the seven-day period has concluded;
otherwise, the flowers will wither. By the end of the seven days, the flowers will all have withered, O Elder.
His wishes were not fulfilled; filled with both anxiety and regret, he lifted [the image] once more, seeking to have his desires granted as they were.
Yet, it was still not accomplished. His heart was filled with great shame and remorse, and having no further strategy to employ, he made a great vow:
"I must seek your descent. If this is not achieved, I shall take death as my limit. On the seventh day, he wept bitterly in supplication, hoping for a spiritual response. At that time—
There was a beggar who pointed to a mendicant sitting nearby and said to the elder, "Is this not the Venerable Piṇḍola?

The elder rejoiced and prostrated himself in worship. Piṇḍola said, "I wished to attend the first assembly, but you, acting as my gatekeeper, because I was slightly cold and had not covered my body with a robe, forcibly obstructed and refused me, striking my head."
[The Buddha said: "Right. My flesh was crushed and became a sore. At your second assembly, I came once more to attend, but the gatekeeper again barred me because my robes were torn and I was naked.
Now, out of compassion for your sincerity, I have borrowed a robe from a kinsman to clothe my body;

The *Zhengyi* states: The *Sanzang fashu* says that the Sanskrit term *arhat* translates into Chinese as "One Beyond Learning" (*wuxue*).

This means that their cycle of birth and death has been exhausted, and there is no further dharma to be learned. It is also called "Non-arising" (*wusheng*), meaning that they have completely severed the afflictions of views and thought.
They no longer undergo rebirth within the three realms. They are also called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat), meaning they are worthy of receiving offerings from devas and humans.
They are also called "Slayers of Thieves," meaning they are able to slay the thieves of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because they possess the three types of higher knowledge (*trividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and immeasurable merit, they are termed "Great. These Arhats, by virtue of receiving the Buddha’s command, through their supernormal powers...
By his power, he has extended his own lifespan and remains in the world to protect the True Dharma, and even now has not yet entered parinirvāṇa.

Whenever he encounters a time when a great, unrestricted assembly for giving is being convened in the world, he together with his retinue conceals his noble appearance and mingles with the common folk, secretly receiving offerings so that the donors may obtain supreme karmic rewards. (From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*)
They said: "We are now truly śrāvakas; by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, we cause all to hear.
We are now truly arhats; among all the worlds—gods, humans, māras, and brahmās—we are universally worthy of receiving offerings.
Based on this, the merit and karmic fruit of making offerings to an arhat are both inconceivable. Thus it was in the past.
Chan Master Wuxiang’s Verse on Offering to the Arhats: The True Men who receive offerings keep their eyes fixed on the heights;
They travel back and forth across seas and mountains without wearying. One knows that wherever they appear as auspicious omens, They cause celestial flowers to fall upon their woolen robes.
The road to Shiliang Fangguang is not far; from within the Hall of Nāgapuṣpa, I beckon with an open hand. Who is the master among the five thousand venerable ones?

Releasing Living Beings (to release them as they arrive; one must not restrict the timing, for fear of harming their lives. One should set up a table facing outward and place willow twigs, pure water, and a ruler there. The Dharma Master and the patrons prostrate.

The assembly gazes upon the various species with eyes of compassion, mindful of their delusion and sinking in suffering, and gives rise to deep pity. (Having recited this three times and the assembly having reached the state of the Threefold Harmony, the Dharma Master struck his ruler once and said:
"O Sons of the Buddha, I shall now further explain for you the characteristics of arising and the characteristics of cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination, so that..."
"You have thoroughly understood the phenomena of arising and ceasing, and having realized non-arising and non-ceasing, you are equal to all Buddhas and have realized Great Nirvana.
(Having spoken thus, he then raised [his hand]): "That is to say: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form;

name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; birth conditions..."
Old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair [cease]. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease. With the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.

With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases. With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases. With the cessation of existence, birth [ceases].
Cessation. With the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction cease. (Recited three times. The Dharma Master strikes the sounding block once and says:
"O Sons of the Buddha, I have now, according to the Mahāyāna sūtras, conferred upon you the Three Refuges, the Ten Epithets, and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. This is now complete.

[Expiation. May [the transgressions] be removed. May you be reborn in a favorable realm and draw near to the Buddha to hear the Dharma. You should now cultivate a sincere mind and follow me in repentance. (Having finished the announcement, he then recites:
All evil karma created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion, Produced by body, speech, and mind— I repent of all these roots of sin.

Some will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; others will be reborn among humans. Upholding the precepts and practicing cultivation, they shall no longer commit evil.
