The Commentary on the Meaning states: Since ancient times, there have been many instances where sages and worthies, at the time of their death, were beset by malignant diseases from which they could not escape;
these were all brought about by the karmic retribution of past conditions. Nevertheless, this did not prevent them from being sages and worthies.

Whenever a junior disciple (*xiǎoshī*) undergoes illness, they should maintain careful filiality; do not harbor thoughts of negligence because of a malignant disease. Yú'ān (Yuanwu Keqin) cited an ancient account, saying:
"Sīxīn (Shishuang Chuyuan) was the son of Nánɡōng (Nanyuan Huiyong). He dreamed that a deity told him, 'Master, you shall be afflicted by a malignant disease.
He subsequently suffered from leprosy. He set aside his monastic duties and returned to a small hermitage to nurse his illness. This was recorded by Sīxīn’s junior disciple, Kècí (Kezhi).
His name was Yangqi. He returned to the hermitage to attend to his master’s illness, begging for food in the villages with diligent and tireless filial piety. Lingjiu said to Cui:
"I had intended for my successor to Huanglong to be one whose path and conduct were both esteemed; I did not expect that in the latter half of his life, he would encounter such adverse conditions."
"Without this, how could I have reached this day? Now, whether I hold fast or let go, I possess total freedom. With a single sigh, he passed away.
His cremation filled the fields with fragrance, and his *śarīra* relics were innumerable. Yuan’an composed a verse: "The Great Sage manifested his past transgressions;
Even under the twin trees, he suffered back pain. My Master’s karma may be punished, But a divine being foretold it in a dream. [Small]

The Master heard that the affairs were concluded and the formal inquiries had ended; he made a special point of returning to observe the [disciples'] settled state. At the thatched gate, fallen leaves accumulated and the green moss lay still;

on the grassy steps, no one was present as a solitary blue magpie darted about. Closing the door and carrying his alms bowl, he went to the village houses; beneath the eaves, a sick monk lay exposed, his lone figure cast in shadow.
Returning to the hut, the fire was extinguished and the sick monk was hungry; a resentful rat leaped and scurried, its restless spirit clearly manifest. Long has he been ill.
It is difficult for others to understand. As for my own innate nature, I have maintained it; fortunately, Master Qin has some relief.
As the lingering rays of the setting sun fade, he lets out a sigh upon his departure; the sunlight strikes the pine-window, making it cold. Furthermore, regarding the sick person:

if they are unable to maintain right mindfulness, the caregiver must provide detailed instruction through the Dharma-door of rebirth by means of the ten recitations. This must absolutely not be omitted.

When the time for the transition to the afterlife and the approach of death arrives, all those attending the patient should chant the Buddha’s name with one voice to assist in the rebirth in the Pure Land.

After the practitioner has passed away, only when a single stick of incense has been consumed should the funeral arrangements be handled. If there are items to be distributed or assigned, they must be divided equally to avoid [disputes].
Do not engage in contention. If the robes and bowl are meager, one should strive for frugality. Leave instructions to the junior disciples that they must not wear hempen garments or wail in mourning;
instead, they should request the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) to preside over the funeral. (If there is no presiding mourner, others should handle the arrangements through the Guest Hall and the Storehouse.

All Buddhist rites should be performed as appropriate, following the precedent for deceased monks, so as not to waste the monastery’s resources nor exhaust the community. If the Abbot has rendered distinguished service to the monastery, [special honors may be accorded].

(The same applies to the administrators. The monastic community should commemorate his legacy; whether the robes and bowls are somewhat abundant or not, they should all offer generous offerings and express their condolences.
The *Zhengyi* states: "One's lifelong merits are verified at the moment of death.
It is not necessary that there be physical suffering, nor is it necessary that there be no suffering; one need only observe whether the person is composed or not. The *Chanzong biyao* says:
When Chan Master Dongshan Liangjie was about to pass away, he asked the assembly, "After leaving this shell-and-leak body, where shall you go to meet me?
The assembly had no reply. He then ordered his hair to be shaved, his body washed, the bell to be struck, and took his leave of the assembly.
He sat upright and passed away. At that time, the great assembly wailed and lamented, not ceasing for the duration of a full day.

The Master suddenly opened his eyes and said to the assembly, "For those who have left the household life, the mind does not cling to things; this is true cultivation. To toil through life and begrudge death—what benefit is there in grief and sorrow?
He then instructed the administrators to prepare a "foolish feast" (a funeral meal) for seven days. When the food and utensils were finally ready, the Master likewise followed [the ritual].
When the communal meal was finished, he said: "In the monastic life, there is nothing to do. Generally, at the moment of departure, one must not cause commotion.
Return to your quarters, sit upright, and pass away in stillness. Furthermore, when Chan Master Cuiyan Zhenji was about to enter extinction, his illness manifested with great severity.
He lay upon straw mats on the floor, turning over and over without ceasing for even a moment. Attendant Zhe wept as he said:
"Throughout your life you reviled the Buddhas and scolded the patriarchs; why then have you come to this? The Master gazed at him intently and said, "Do you also hold such views?
He then rose and sat in the full lotus posture, called for his attendant to burn incense, and as the smoke rose, he entered nirvana.
These two ancient worthies both suffered from illness at the time of their deaths, yet they were able to exercise such mastery and freedom. Is this not...?
Regarding the evidence of such merit, the scriptures further state that when a person is about to die, hearing the sound of bells and chimes increases their right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

It is essential that these sounds be struck before the breath has ceased. Nowadays, people wait until long after the deceased’s breath has stopped, only beginning to recite mantras and strike the chime at the moment of placing them in the coffin; by then, it is already too late. Nevertheless, this is the practice of later generations.
Regarding this matter: if the deceased, while alive, cultivated pure karma, then upon reaching this moment, to further receive the assistance of others is like adding flowers to brocade.
If the deceased, while alive, did not cultivate pure karma, then at this time they must rely entirely on the power of others;
even if one continues to recite the name until their breath has ceased and they have been placed in the coffin.

Thereafter, although one may still receive benefit, how much of that benefit will there be? Thus, while it is true that aids to the Way (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are certainly not to be neglected, how can the actual realization of the Way (*pratipatti*) be delayed?
However, at the moment of death, one should assemble like-minded companions to practice *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation) in shifts to assist them in attaining rebirth through right mindfulness;
this should continue until the breath ceases and a single stick of incense has burned out—it must not be omitted.

Regarding the entry into the coffin (the character "棺" [guān]; all other editions have altered this to "龕" [kān], which is a major error; see the detailed verification of the meaning for a refutation):
whenever a person’s illness becomes critical, a coffin must be prepared in advance. The materials used for the coffin are thinner than those used for ordinary coffins, so as to facilitate cremation.

Once the breath has long since ceased, the body is then carried in by the "fish-drawers" while reciting the Buddha's name and placed into the coffin. A presiding abbot from another monastery should be invited in advance to arrive at the time of the ceremony and deliver a discourse.

The coffin is sealed. Alternatively, the head of the assembly may preach the Dharma; this must be done while kneeling (all junior dharma-heirs must likewise kneel with palms joined). Once the coffin is sealed, [the ceremony concludes].

(Other individuals—namely, the current abbot of the temple who delivers the dharma discourse, or the head of the assembly as appropriate—should seal the coffin. The *vinaya-dhara* (*weina*) announces:

"The merit of the recitations performed above is dedicated to the newly deceased Great Abbot of the Hall" (other individuals may substitute "certain office-holder" or "Venerable So-and-so"). (At the moment of entering the coffin, one solemnly invokes:
"To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time; to all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.")
The guest hall shall immediately hang a notice inviting the assembly of masters. Four persons shall form one shift, taking turns in succession.

Upon arriving before the altar, they shall recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* and chant the Buddha’s name, continuing day and night until the coffin is raised. For the morning and evening services, the entire assembly must attend together to recite.
The *Rector* performs the dedication, saying: "The various evil karmas committed by the deceased all stem from the beginningless..."

Greed, anger, and delusion arise from body, speech, and mind; I repent all roots of transgression. May the spirit of the deceased remain undisturbed, and through right mindfulness, proceed directly to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
There, may they personally attend upon Amitābha and the assembly of sages, practicing the ten stages (bhūmi) to realize eternal bliss.
[Recite] "All Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time... and so forth. If the deceased monk has left behind any assets, add the following recitation:

The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and other texts state: △ According to ancient regulations, when a monk passes away, he is placed in the coffin wearing his washed, clean old robes, with his usual seven-piece outer robe (*saptaka-cīvara*) draped over them.
His head remains uncovered and his feet bare; a rosary is hung upon his hand, and his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) is folded and placed before his feet.
Once he has been placed inside, the coffin is immediately sealed shut with lime and lacquer. Even if relatives arrive, they may not open it again. No mourning hall (*xiaotang*) is set up, nor...
The funeral procession is arranged extensively, yet one does not wear hempen sashes or white mourning garments; there is no public announcement of the death by going out in the four directions;
there is no gathering together of patrons and their kin; nor is a formal ritual arena established with worldly protocols. Rather, one simply continues the regular recitations.
As for items such as robes and alms bowls, they are all offered to the community (if even the abbot acts in this manner, others may be understood by analogy).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: Lately, the practice of sitting in a burial niche has become a widespread custom, yet it is not realized that this violates the Buddha’s regulations.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in its latter section, when the World-Honored One was at the city of Kuśinagara beneath the twin śāla trees, he lay down and entered parinirvāṇa;
he was placed in a coffin and then passed away. Alas! The Buddha is the Most Honorable One of the three realms, yet even he lay down and entered [parinirvāṇa].
Regarding coffins: monks who study the Buddha should likewise use coffins; this is clear. Therefore, the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* states:
"When dead, one lies down and does not sit. From these four words alone, it can be seen that during the time of the Sixth Patriarch, deceased monks were also placed in coffins lying down.

The practice of "sitting and departing" (seated death) arises entirely from a desire for fame. If, in fact, one’s power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*) is profound in daily life, [one need not seek such a spectacle].
They were able to depart while seated or manifest transformations while standing, sitting in their coffins without hindrance.

If, throughout one's life, one was occupied with external affairs and did not practice seated meditation (*paryaṅka*), yet at the end of life one is forcibly made to sit in a coffin, how much effort would that require? Moreover, since the consciousness has not yet fully departed, one cannot avoid great suffering.
Yuyan quotes from ancient records, saying: "In the early years of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, the Monk Puhua of Zhenzhou was about to demonstrate [his passing]..."
He died. He had previously begged from people for a single straight robe; some gave him a padded jacket, others a cloth cloak, but he accepted none of them.
Linji had a coffin sent to him, which he accepted with a smile. He then took leave of the assembly, saying, "Tomorrow, Puhua will die at the East Gate.
The people of the district followed one another out to witness it. The Master said, "It is improper to bury him today."
The diviner Qingwu said, "Tomorrow he will depart through the southern gate; people shall follow him. He further said, "Tomorrow he will depart through the western gate, which will be auspicious.

As people began to emerge less frequently, and having emerged would soon return, the people's resolve gradually slackened. On the fourth day, he personally carried his own coffin out through the northern gate;
shaking a rattle, he entered the coffin and passed away. This is also one piece of evidence for the use of coffins.

Once the coffin has been brought in and placed within the main hall, the curtains and screens are hung between the pillars, and various ritual vessels are set out according to the rites performed for the living.
A portrait is hung upon the central Dharma seat to establish the spirit’s position. On each seventh day, memorial altars are arranged; at other times, only the incense burner is maintained.
Vase, plain flowers, incense, and candles; offer tea, soup, congee, and rice at the two appointed times.

If elders from the mountains or officials come to present offerings, the junior disciples shall stand to the left of the remains and respond to their bows. They shall guard the funeral shrouds at night.

The coffin shall remain for twenty-one days before cremation and interment in a stupa. The stupa should be three feet high; one must not waste resources on stone masonry, as elaborate funerary rites provide no benefit.
Matters such as decorated pavilions, musical performances, and the like should not be employed at all; rather, the monks should simply lead the way while reciting the Buddha’s name.
As for all the regulations and protocols of the abbot, they shall remain as they were before, welcoming all visitors and never deviating from established custom.

Ornamental furnishings and the like must not be moved to other locations. In all cases of inheriting the Dharma, ordaining a disciple, or conferring the tonsure, one should observe a period of mourning in spirit alone.
As the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* states: "After my passing, do not act according to worldly sentiments by weeping and shedding tears."
When receiving condolences from visitors, wearing mourning garments is neither for my disciples nor is it the True Dharma; this is the ancestral instruction and should be observed accordingly.
If a member of the two orders falls gravely ill, they shall enter the Upper Guest Hall. Upon their death, the coffin shall remain there for four days.

As for any monk in the general assembly who falls gravely ill in his private quarters, he shall enter the Inspection Hall. After death, he shall remain in the Inspection Hall for one day, at which point the body shall be cremated.
Transformation. One does not perform other activities, nor does one arrange for a place of offerings.
The commentary on the meaning states: Master Yunqi Lianchi said, "Regarding 'mourning in spirit' (*xinsang*), it merely means simplifying the wailing and leaping;

it does not mean that one does not manifest grief and suffering. According to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, although there is no system of mourning garments, when the Buddha was about to enter *nirvāṇa*...
At that time, the assembly beat their breasts and cried out so loudly that blood appeared. Now, when we, his disciples, face his funeral, how can we not grieve?

It is only that we must not join the worldly in their clamorous wailing and disorder. Furthermore, I have observed that recently, whenever an abbot has passed away, [the monks behave in such a manner].

His disciples prepared his memorial tablet and sought a renowned calligrapher to inscribe his stupa. They invariably recorded that during his lifetime his parents had received extraordinary dreams, and so forth;
and that after his death, when cremated, certain parts remained indestructible at such-and-such a location, with countless śarīras appearing, and so forth.
Are there not these several points? Would he not thus become a venerable master? [The Master] replied: "In our school, what is esteemed is solely precept, concentration, and wisdom."
This is true cultivation. To possess the actual virtues of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya is what matters; all else is merely secondary.

As for instances where, upon cremation, certain faculties remain unimpaired and *śarīra* relics flow forth—this is surely proof of the pure cultivation practiced throughout one's life, and how could such a thing be easily attained?
Only when the coffin is closed can the judgment be finalized; only then are gold and brass distinguished from one another. Even if one were to desire it recklessly...
How can one deceive a person of such beauty? It is merely a basis for a momentary laugh.

I record all of this here to inform those in the world who lament their teachers yet fail to attain the Way. *Yuan’an Zhígǔ* says: Zen Master Yǎn of Yúnmén’s preaching of the Dharma was like clouds and rain;
he absolutely disliked having it recorded. Whenever he saw someone attempting to do so, he would invariably scold and drive them away, saying: "You mouth..."
"No need. You are merely repeating my words; at some other time, you will surely sell me off.
These mechanical words from within the room—Xianglin used paper as his clothing and recorded whatever he heard. Alas! He did not even take pleasure in recording the Dharma."
How much more so regarding the false embellishment of other words?

For the cremation, when the coffin is raised for the funeral pyre, the Guest Hall prepares by hanging a notice on the afternoon prior. (The notice reads: "Tomorrow, after the morning congee, please notify..."

The drum sounds. The Master of the Assembly is requested to don his robes and take up his ritual implements to escort the newly deceased Head Abbot to the cremation pyre (if it is anyone else, they are generally referred to as a "deceased monk," and the Master of the Assembly need not take up the implements). On the morning of the following day, after the second board has sounded for the early congee, the great drum is struck three times.

The assembly gathers before the coffin and recites one scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra*. This continues until the offering of incense and the preaching of the Dharma are completed, at which point the chant begins:
Having finished the praise, the Rector (Vina) says: "We now wish to lift the sacred coffin for the grand ceremony of cremation.

We respectfully rely upon the great assembly to recite the Great Name of Amitābha, thereby expressing our humble devotion and providing spiritual support for the path to enlightenment. The assembly recites the Buddha’s name as they escort the coffin to the altar of transformation.

Having made this announcement, he immediately recites the passage beginning with "The Western World of Ultimate Bliss," and the leader of the assembly steps forward to lead the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
They set out. The assembly followed in step, each harboring feelings of sorrow. If the distance was great, the *jianyuan* (superintendent) would follow the coffin;
otherwise, one *zhiké* (attendant) would block the way by the roadside for the crowd, escorting them only as far as one or two *li* before returning. Thereafter, alms (*kṣaṇa*) were distributed.

Only about ten members from the two ranks of officials followed the coffin, escorting it to the front of the altar of transformation (*huatán*). The offerings and the preaching of the Dharma were conducted as usual. This is recorded by Mingde.
The fire has been lit. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Administrator) announces: "The newly passed away Great Abbot" (for others, say: "Venerable [Name]").

Having entered into peaceful extinction in accordance with conditions, we shall now perform the cremation according to the Dharma. To transform this body that spent a hundred years propagating the Way, we shall cause it to enter the realm of *nirvāṇa*.
We rely upon the great assembly to chant the Buddha’s name, thereby assisting the enlightened spirit. Having finished the announcement, he recites a Buddhist verse.
Recite the Buddha’s name for a set duration. When the recitation is finished and the assembly has chanted the praises, the *weina* performs the dedication of merit, saying:

"The above recitations are offered in support of the Abbot (or, for others, 'for the Venerable [Name]'). May they attain rebirth in the Pure Land; we only pray that the mirror of wisdom may radiate its brilliance."
The true wind scatters its radiance; within the Bodhi Garden, the flowers of awakening bloom. Within the ocean of *dharmatā*, the dust of the mind is washed away.
As the three libations of tea are poured and a single incense burner is lit, we bid farewell to your journey through the clouds. *Vandana* to your honored spirit.
(After the recitation, the assembly all rise together to exchange greetings and then depart.)

The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Buddha’s regulation regarding the cremation of deceased monks was intended to cause them to transcend the provisional state of the *pariccheda* (segmented existence) and realize the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*. Laypeople do not perceive this;

thus, while it might be considered a mere error or an unfeeling act for them to speak of cremation, it is truly foolish for there to be monks who, out of fear of cremation, leave instructions in their wills not to be cremated. This is ignorance.
This is indeed a grave error. Furthermore, it is a misconception to claim that he was the abbot of a single generation; thus, the account that his body was not cremated is also erroneous.
If he were truly like the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi, who had realized the indestructible and immutable body (*akṣaya-kāya*), there would be no harm in preserving it for offerings.
However, if he had not attained such indestructibility, cremation would have been appropriate. In the past, Chan Master Chushi passed away in the third year of the Hongwu era.
At that time, cremation was prohibited. The Master wished to follow the Buddha’s regulations, and Emperor Taizu specially issued an exemption for this case.
Alas! How sagacious and enlightened the Holy Ruler was; how could a foolish monk not feel ashamed beyond measure? Someone once asked Master Lianchi:
"Is it permissible to perform 'living cremation' at the point of death? The Master replied: "The method of living cremation is [a practice] of the Mahāyāna..."

[The prohibition] is relaxed. In the Hinayana, [killing] is forbidden. In the Mahayana, because the power of compassionate vows is already profound and the power of forbearance is fully developed, it may be relaxed.
The Hinayanist knows only self-benefit; their compassionate vows are slight, and furthermore, their power of forbearance is not yet sufficient.
If, when facing danger, they lose their right mindfulness, how could the harm be overestimated? Moreover, some might do so out of greed for fame after death, or...
Because a momentary impulse is not right mindfulness, it will inevitably bring about bitter fruits; how can one fail to restrain it?
Furthermore, there are those possessed by demons; their daily inclinations are improper, their deluded knowledge is heterodox, and they draw near to demonic influences.
Māra took possession of him; first he incited the thought of burning his own body, and subsequently brought about the act of self-immolation.
Under the influence of Māra’s power, he sat upright amidst the flames as if feeling no pain at all. Suddenly, Māra departed, and the agonizing, bitter suffering became beyond description.
For hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, he became a ghost of untimely death—a truly pitiable and lamentable fate. Thus one should know:
To cremate [the body] after death, or to cremate it before death, is in neither case the orthodox regulation. Monastics of the Final Dharma must strictly uphold the correct practice.
Furthermore, when preaching the Dharma for deceased monks, one fears that their realization of the Way may not be clear and that their souls may be obstructed or attached;
thus, one truly desires to awaken them. Regarding all Buddhist rites following the passing of an abbot:

The virtuous and renowned masters are invited together to preach the Dharma. As for the other members of the monastic community, they attend to matters such as sealing the coffin and raising it from the bier.

The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) and the *śrāmaṇera-prathama* (Head Seat) consult with the Abbot; either the Abbot himself preaches, or he commands a member of the assembly to do so on his behalf.

Only when the Abbot presides over the ritual does he personally offer the funeral oration (*huo-shuo*), though in modern times he may also command a member of the assembly to do so, which violates ancient regulations. As for...
The practice of "striking the sounding block while preaching the Dharma" originated when ancient worthies spoke spontaneously in response to specific circumstances;
it was not performed with deliberate intent. The *Shan'an zalu* states: "When Wuzhun resided at Jingshan, he struck the sounding block for the funeral rites of the Venerable Guan."

It is said: "One who contemplates the great ocean finds it difficult to regard it as mere water; when the waves and billows are exhausted, they are but a single bubble. Now, the ocean ceases and the bubble perishes.
Turning one's head and treading upon that which is one's own... and so forth. From this point on, the practice of giving names and expounding the Dharma began.
Later, eminent and virtuous masters followed this example; thus, even today in the monastic communities (saṃghārāma), it has become a fixed convention to chant the names [of the deceased].
By merely stringing together words and patching them together, they are utterly devoid of the eye of the school (zōgen). Yet, what fruit is there in what is called "opening up" for the deceased?

Furthermore, it is not only when preaching the Dharma for deceased monks that they chant names; even when bestowing the verse of the transmission of the Dharma (hōge), they mostly rely on the name as their basis.
As for this matter, since it is neither the true nature of the Ground nor its original color, it merely tends toward cleverness and wit;
even if one were to explain it to perfection, it would still belong only to frivolous speech (prapañca). What benefit is there in it?
**The Second Day of the Enshrinement and Cremation** On the day prior to the enshrinement, the Guest Hall (Kètáng) shall post a notice (pái) stating:

"Tomorrow, after the small meal (xiǎoshí), upon hearing the sound of the drum, please assemble the assembly of masters before the stupa of the Abbot (zhùchí). [For others, the notice shall read: 'Please assemble before the Universal Common Stupa (pútóngtǎ). We shall escort the sacred remains (línggǔ) into the stupa."

Stūpa. △ On the following day, after the second board of the morning meal, the drum is struck three times. The *vinaya-dhara* leads the assembly to enter the stūpa. If the distance is great, no signboard is hung;
instead, only ten to twenty officials from the two orders are invited. They station themselves in formation before the stūpa, perform prostrations, and complete the chanting of praises.
The *vinaya-dhara* then makes the following announcement: (For the recently deceased Head Abbot, say: "The newly passed away Head Abbot, Great Monk. (For others, the wording is modified.)
Venerable [Name] (having cremated the remains according to the Dharma, shall now enshrine the relics within the stupa).

Having torn asunder the net of a hundred years of worldly toil, he enters the gate of Nirvana on the Single Path. We rely upon the pure assembly to reverently and solemnly recite mantras to assist the awakened spirit.
Having made this announcement, recite one scroll of the Amitābha Sūtra and the Mantra for Rebirth three times, awaiting the Elder of another monastery (or one of renowned virtue) to speak.

The Dharma service is concluded. (In other cases, the head of the temple community recites. The assembly recites the Buddha’s name. The guest prefect opens the stupa; having lowered the remains into the stupa using a rope, he secures the stupa with its lock.

The ritual master collects the recitations and chants the hymn of praise to Amitābha for the dedication of merit. The ritual master says: "The recitations above have assisted in the rebirth [in the Pure Land].
We pray only that those who dwell at street corners where the grass grows tall, or among the flowers by the water-mill, may find rest within the Land of Peaceful Light."
The crown-protruding mark (*uṣṇīṣa*) is eternally perfect; you are forever liberated from the tainted, defiled body of this Sahā world.

As tea is poured for the third libation and incense burned in a single burner, we respectfully escort Your Revered Spirit upon its journey through the clouds. *Vandana* (Homage). (When the recitation is finished, the assembly all perform a greeting toward the upper direction and each returns.)

The Commentary on the Meaning states: According to ancient precedents, only the founding patriarchs and the patriarchs who restored the lineage, provided they have rendered great service to the permanent property of the monastery, are entitled to have separate stupas constructed for them. Ordinary abbots, however, are interred in the general common stupa (pútóngtǎ).
Among these, there are stupas for successive generations of abbots; as for the positions of these stupas within the courtyard, they may be three, five, or seven.
Regarding the nine different types [of stūpas]: if one constructs only three stūpas, the central position shall be for the presiding stūpa;
to its left, the general memorial stūpa for the bhikṣus of this temple and the ten directions; and to its right, the general memorial stūpa for the śrāmaṇeras of this temple and the ten directions.
As for the nuns' stūpas, they shall remain at the nunnery and are not permitted to be attached to the monks' temple. Alternatively, five stūpas may be used.
As for those [stūpas] situated in the middle: in the center-left are the bhikṣus of the home monastery; in the center-right are the bhikṣus of the ten directions.
On the left side are the śrāmaṇeras of the home monastery, accompanied by upāsakas; on the right side are the śrāmaṇeras of the ten directions, likewise accompanied by upāsakas.

Moved by the karmic affinity of the water-jar and cloth, he manifested the bond of celestial kinship with the Tathāgata’s beloved younger brother. Upon awakening to the overturning of the *cīvara*-pole, he received the Mind-Seal from [Mahākāśyapa].

The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Sanskrit name Ānanda translates here as "Joyous Celebration" (Qingxi). He was so named because he was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment;
the king’s heart rejoiced, and the entire nation celebrated with delight. He was the second son of King Śuklodana, the Buddha’s paternal uncle, and thus the younger brother of Devadatta.
His face was like the full moon, and his eyes were like blue lotuses. He left the household life at the age of eight.
He served the Buddha as one of the thirty attendants and was foremost among those of great learning.

Within the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he received a prediction from the Buddha that in a future age he would attain Buddhahood, becoming known as the Tathāgata Śāgaradharabuddhidharaṇīsvabhāvavikurvaṇarāja (The King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Mountain-like Ocean Wisdom).
Furthermore, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Ānanda and I simultaneously gave rise to the bodhicitta in the presence of the Buddha Gaganagañja. Ānanda...
He always delighted in much hearing and was ever diligent; for this reason, I have already attained *bodhi*.
Ānanda has protected and upheld my Dharma, and shall likewise protect the Dharma-treasury of all future Buddhas until the time of their *parinirvāṇa*.
The Buddha praised Ānanda, saying that he possesses eight inconceivable merits and various other supreme excellencies. He then commanded Mañjuśrī to subdue Māra and take charge [of the assembly].

Ānanda attended the assembly and received the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when Mahākāśyapa convened the collection of the Dharma-piṭaka, he had Ānanda ascend the lion throne to proclaim the various sūtras. When Kāśyapa was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda for its preservation and maintenance.
Ānanda traveled abroad to propagate the teachings for twenty years; once, he arrived at the palace of a king.

Outside the city walls, in a bamboo grove, he heard a bhikṣu reciting a verse: "If one lives for a hundred years, but does not see the drying up of the floodwaters, it is not as good as living for a single day and being able to behold that [truth]. Ānanda said with a sorrowful expression, "This is not a Buddha-verse.
It should say: 'If one lives for a hundred years, but does not understand the law of arising and ceasing, it is not as good as living for a single day...'"
One day, he attained understanding and explained it to his teacher. The teacher said, "Ānanda is old and decrepit;
his words are not to be trusted. Later, when Ānanda heard that the bhikṣu was still reciting the previous verse, he reflected upon it himself.
"Now this bhikṣu does not accept my teaching; he is of no benefit to the world. It is fitting that he enter parinirvāṇa.
He then proceeded to the royal palace and took his leave of King Bimbisāra before departing. The king followed him as far as the Ganges River.

Ānanda boarded a boat and was in the middle of the river's current when the king prostrated himself and said, "O Lamp of the Three Realms, I pray that you do not enter parinirvāṇa. At that time, there were five [snow lions] on the Snowy Mountains...
One hundred rishis, seeing that Ānanda was about to enter parinirvāṇa, flew through the air to him and requested ordination.
Ānanda immediately used his supernormal powers to transform the Ganges into a field of gold and preached the Dharma for the rishi Madhyāntika and the other seers, whereby they all became arhats.
At that time, Madhyāntika wished to enter parinirvāṇa first, and Ānanda entrusted him with the following charge:
The Buddha prophesied that you would establish the Buddha-dharma in the kingdom of Kaśmīra and thus would not enter parinirvāṇa;
the others all entered extinction at the same time. Ānanda leaped into the air and performed eighteen transformations, then entered the *vāyu-vega* (wind-sprint) samādhi.
He divided his body into four parts: one part he gave to Śakra-devānām-indra; one part to the Dragon King Sāgara;
one part to Vaiśālīputra; and one part to King Ajātaśatru. At each of these four locations, a jeweled stūpa was erected.

By relying on the words of this scripture, one may ward off malevolent spirits and demons, just as worldly people write and affix talismans to protect the *Ziwei* and *Huangdao* celestial paths.

For this reason, the monastery established two positions—Keeper of the Repository and Librarian—to exclusively oversee these matters. This included the placement of cases and volumes, as well as the repair of damaged or incomplete texts.

If that person requests leave or departs for other business, they must first be required to take them back. As for those who lose them, they shall be penalized with a copyist’s fine and compelled to reimburse the loss before leaving the monastery.

The place where the printing blocks are stored must have a balance between light and shade; if exposed to wind and sun, they will easily crack, and if kept in excessive darkness, they will easily decay.
In all matters concerning the preparation of paper, ink, and brushes, as well as the binding with thread, it is best to ensure that everything is clean and sturdy.
To disregard [the preservation of the scriptures] and fail to economize effort is a fault equivalent to treating the Dharma lightly.

The *Zhengyi* (Exegesis on the Meaning) states: "To edit and arrange the scriptures is to manifest reverence for the Jewel of the Dharma; this matter is of vital importance to the life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*)."

Therefore, this office is also a heavy responsibility for a single temple; it is especially vital that the abbot does not begrudge expenditures, for then restoration and maintenance will be easy, and even the administrative officers will consequently act with greater diligence.

As for the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), the carving of woodblocks for the printing and circulation of the scriptures is the foremost great undertaking for the flourishing of the Buddha-dharma. I, a fool, [regard this as such].

I believe that having numerous painted pillars and carved beams is of little benefit; it is not as good as having a continuous flow of yellow scrolls and red-bound volumes that will never be exhausted.

To truly benefit future generations is no small matter. This is evident today in the fact that both monastics and laypeople are able to obtain written copies of the scriptures for reading and recitation—this is due to the carving and printing of the Great Canon at Lêng-yen Monastery in Chia-hsing.
This is a remnant of the grace of the Imperial Edict. Had it not been for this single instance of publication, the number of manuscript copies would surely have been few.
Since Sanskrit texts are difficult to procure and inconvenient to carry, would this not be a great deficiency for both monastics and laypeople?

Therefore, for all abbots of monasteries who are determined to propagate the Dharma: if you are indeed refined and precise in both doctrine and practice, you may naturally benefit others according to their capacities.

However, if the affairs of the abbotship are so numerous that you have no leisure for this, then you should, to the best of your ability, carve and print several essential scriptures currently in circulation and distribute them to those monks and nuns who lack the means. Regarding the construction of monasteries (i.e., *saṃghārāma*; this name has been used since antiquity, hence they are called "monastic dwellings"), the *Sangui zhengfan* (The Correct Model of the Three Refuges) states:

In the Sanskrit language, *saṃgha* translates here as "harmonious assembly," referring specifically to the five groups of renunciants. In the Sanskrit language, *ārāma* translates here as "garden of the assembly."
This is precisely where the monastic community resides; it is currently called a *saṃghārāma* (monastery), which is a term that combines both Chinese and Sanskrit.

This is so. It may be acceptable for lay donors (*dānapati*) to resolve to undertake such work; however, for those who have left the household life, it is absolutely inappropriate to devote oneself to it with such zeal.
One should know that one's own personal practice is what is essential. This is the aspiration of the superior class of monastics.

One must not misappropriate or conceal the offerings of the faithful, nor seek profit through fame, taking the founding of monasteries as a means to enhance one’s reputation.
Consequently, this leads to the plotting of schemes and the formation of cliques, whereby one employs clever stratagems and forceful seizure. This causes...

When the hearts of people are such as this, the Buddha’s intention can be understood. Even those monks who maintain their proper station and practice asceticism through diligent solicitation may not be well-versed in the Vinaya studies;

Thus they undergo suffering in vain and instead incur evil retribution; as it is said, "Heaven has not yet been established, but Hell is already formed. Is this not perverse?
Furthermore, regarding the abbot: although he does not solicit funds externally, if other monks falsely claim to be soliciting privately, one should post a notice outside the temple stating:

Chapter Six: The Two Orders.
The commentary states: The establishment of the two orders [of monks and nuns] is for the purpose of managing affairs on behalf of the community;

through this, they uphold the fundamental principles and proclaim the Way, thereby adorning the legacy of the Patriarchs. Even those who manage the treasury and oversee various administrative duties all serve to assist and support the monastic community.
The relationship [between these roles] is of great importance. Therefore, regarding both mundane and supramundane dharmas, there is nothing with which one does not become proficient;

to accomplish oneself and to transform others, possessing the full embodiment of all functions, is the most esteemed ideal. Next, some may preserve a single quality or exercise a single capacity, yet if they exhaustively fulfill their duties without shame, the monastic community likewise relies upon them with joy.
Although the sequence of ranks is divided, in antiquity, it was common for those in different positions to interchange and assume each other’s responsibilities.
There was no distinction between self and other, nor any suspicion of superiority or inferiority. Now, however, they are clearly divided and do not consult one another.

Furthermore, the distinction between internal and external, as well as the ordering of ranks and status, is likewise a matter of the times' prevailing trends; though these matters are not as they were in antiquity.

In principle, there is as yet no contradiction. Yet, when it comes to monopolizing administrative power, forming cliques, acting with unilateral authority while the multitude clamors, and reaching a state of precarious instability where one cannot tolerate another—is this not indeed erroneous?

This depends on those in charge to carefully select their subordinates, to repeatedly issue ancestral instructions to warn them, to incorporate them into formal regulations, and to skillfully harmonize them; in this way, the community may perhaps flourish.
No material was discarded, and no person’s labor was wasted. Some were busily engaged in monastic affairs, while others sat in meditation and practiced with diligence.
It seems that the traditions of the founding patriarchs have not distanced themselves from our own day.

He was entrusted with the records and accounts, totaling seven items. He adorned the Dharma-vessels and maintained clear conduct in his comings and goings.
Regarding the flow of silver and coins, he recorded them in ledgers accordingly, calculating the accounts twice every month. As for fruits and foodstuffs, he cherished and preserved them.
Serve guests with meticulous purity and refinement. When the Abbot goes out on official business, both internal and external affairs must be attended to with particular care.
When a guest arrives at the Abbot’s quarters (Fangzhang), whatever matters they have come to discuss shall be clarified by the Guest Master (Zhiké) and settled by the Chief Administrator (Janyuan).

Regarding whether to offer tea or a meal, one must treat them with hospitality according to the situation and their needs. Any offerings of incense or gifts must not be opened privately; they should be shared with the fellow monks.
Furthermore, practitioners and others must maintain a dignified and upright demeanor; they must not engage in idle chatter or play.
As for items in the guest quarters—whether being used or stored—each must be handled appropriately so as not to cause loss. [Date], the Abbot instructs.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: The robe and alms bowl are entrusted to those who serve as the abbot’s closest confidants; they accompany him in all his movements and are charged with the heavy responsibility for his property.
Indeed, whether the abbot’s reputation flourishes or declines, and whether his resources increase or diminish, everything depends entirely upon these attendants;

thus, one must not fail to exercise caution. *Zhigu* says: Master Shichuang Gong was solitary and austere in his spiritual practice yet excelled in administrative capability; he long relied upon [Master] Hong at Tiantong.
As for Zhì, he held various administrative duties, both minor and major, and there was no task he did not undergo. When he returned to visit his mother, she said, "You serve as a leader of men;

if you do not clearly understand the law of cause and effect, you will surely bring trouble upon me in the underworld. Gōng replied, "Regarding the permanent property of the Sangha, I have not deceived even by a hair's breadth;
there is nothing to worry about. Alas! One who fulfills administrative duties while being able to remain honest to the last degree—this is [the mark of a true practitioner].
There is no sense of shame [in this].

Regarding medicine: externally there is the *dianzuo* (steward), and internally there is the medicine itself. One must provide the abbot with tea and refreshments at the proper times, attend to him on his left and right, assist with his robes and bowl, and show compassion to the practitioners (*xingzhe*).
This office requires that abundance and frugality be kept in proper balance; one must be especially strict in observing the precepts.
Eating and drinking apart from the assembly. Regarding the reception of guests: for external guests, there is the Guest Master (Chikaku); for internal guests, there is the Receptionist (Shōkaku).

This office originally resided in the Meditation Hall (Zendo), with two persons rotating by day to serve in the Abbot’s Quarters (Hōjō). One serves as the Duty Holder (Tōchi) and does not leave the chamber. Whenever guests arrive, he personally receives them. Thus it was.

Inform the Abbot. Whether it be for the preparation of meals or the authorization regarding robes and alms bowls (*cīvara-pātra*), report this to the kitchen and the storehouse so as not to cause any delay.
If there are items of trust, clearly hand over the robes and alms bowl. When the rice gruel and meals are served in the two halls, one shall act as the supervisor on duty.
At morning and evening services, burn incense and light lamps while attending the Abbot’s seat, never remaining far from him. It is essential that one’s deportment be refined and elegant.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: According to the *Saṃgharakṣita Sūtra* and as recorded in the *Lianghuang Chanwen* and other texts, one novice monk stole seven fruits, another stole two portions of cake, and yet another stole a small amount of stone-honey syrup; all were reborn to suffer the retributions of the three miserable realms.

This was because these items were the property of the Saṃgha (the monastic community), whether they were consumed privately or given away privately, in either case constituting a violation of the precept against stealing.
Furthermore, the *Zen School’s Secret Essentials* (*Chanzong biyao*) states: Zen Master Sengzhao was a preeminent disciple of Mount Nanyue.

Possessing unimpeded eloquence and supreme in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he once used a pinch of salt from the communal store to prepare for a vegetarian feast. After the meal, he entered meditative absorption and suddenly saw the sign [of the debt] arise.
Three years later, it had increased to several dozen *hu*. He hurriedly sold his robes to purchase salt to repay the community; only then did the sign vanish.
Alas! How awe-inspiring!

Regarding the meaning of the attendant (*shishi*) who serves in attendance, there is both a general sense and a specific one. In the general sense, everyone from the moment the incense is burned until the conclusion with the Holy Sangha (*shōsō*) is called an attendant.
In the specific sense, this office refers exclusively to the one who attends the Abbot (*jūji*), for whom diligence and prudence are the essential requirements. Every day, first...
In the abbot’s quarters and within the Dharma Hall, one shall prepare incense and change the water before the Buddha, wipe down the tables, and sweep the floor until everything is perfectly clean.

Thereafter, one shall attend to the abbot by providing him with water for washing and tea, collecting and replacing his robes and sandals, inquiring after his well-being morning and evening, and attending him while he enters or exits.
One shall serve labor and perform duties, anticipating his needs and welcoming guests; when they arrive, one shall offer tea and attend to the distribution of food in the refectory.
When there is business requiring two officers to attend the guest hall for deliberation, they shall present their credentials to the guest hall and be assigned alongside the other officers.
The one who receives these credentials is the abbot; he shall communicate with those above and below him, just as a filial son serves his parents.
This office must not be held by one too young; it should be filled by an elder.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Since ancient times, all eminent practitioners, when first attending at their teachers' sides, have been able to endure the most unbearable hardships before they could attain the wondrous Dharma of non-attainment. This is the principle of valuing the Dharma over the body;
it has been so from antiquity, as detailed in the Vinaya Piṭaka and the *Śrāmaṇera-yao-lüe* (Essentials for Śrāmaṇeras), where the text says: "Wen Yunqi’s Record of Reverent Practice."

It is said that during the Tang dynasty, there was a man named Tong, who served as a high-ranking official in the Six Palaces. Having visited Niaokuo (Bird’s Nest) to seek ordination, he was initially refused entry;
yet, being persistent in his request, Niaokuo eventually shaved his head and allowed him to attend upon him. For sixteen years, he served with tireless diligence, yet received no formal instruction.
When he wished to take his leave, Niaokuo asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "I wish to travel to various regions to study the Buddha-dharma."
He departed. Baizhang said, "The Buddha-dharma is also present here in small measure. He then picked up a tuft of cloth-hair and blew upon it;
Dantong suddenly attained great enlightenment. Consequently, he was called the "Cloth-Hair Attendant" (Bumo Shizi). Master Lianchi said:

"People see that the attendant attained enlightenment beneath the cloth-hair, yet they do not know the strength of his sixteen years of enduring toil. Without such many years of diligent labor, [this would not have been possible]."
How could there be such matters today? Those who have encountered an enlightened master should fortunately not allow a restless mind to take advantage of the opportunity.

Regarding the duties of the Attendant to the Holy Monk (Sengsheng Shizhe) within the Hall: he prepares the bedding; when the Abbot descends from the hall, he clears the seat, serves tea, and wipes the bamboo rakes and incense boards.
He attends to the incense burner before the Abbot during the seven-day retreat, as well as the tasks of dismissing the session and serving tea and fruit. II.
At that time, the meal hall is passed and the evening service concludes. (Above are the eight attendants of the *shiliao*;
their names are posted on the *candeng* [bedding list] in the meditation hall. This concludes the third *liao*.)
The Commentary on the Meaning states: "The Holy Monk (Śāstṛ-saṃgha) refers to the image of the divine monk enshrined within the meditation hall (zhandáng).
The meditation hall was anciently called the 'Monks' Hall' (sēngtáng) because many monks reside together in one hall.
The one enshrined and offered to within this Monks' Hall is the Great Holy Monk Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya. It is the specific duty of the attendant of this Holy Monk to remain exclusively within the hall."
Within [the Sangha Hall], one serves the incense and lamps of the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ). When the Abbot enters the hall, this attendant also manages matters such as the tea service for the Abbot;

thus, he is named the Holy Monk Attendant (Śāstṛ Upasthāyaka). Lately, as many Buddhas have been enshrined within the meditation hall (Candana), the image of the Holy Monk has remained entirely without offerings.
Furthermore, the name "Sangha Hall" has been changed to "Meditation Hall," and the two characters "Holy Monk" [have likewise fallen into disuse].

The meaning of this is that there is no fixed place for attachment. Altogether, there are eight administrative officers in the Attendant’s Quarters who constantly remain in close proximity to the Abbot.
Furthermore, as it is customary in recent times to appoint those of youthful age to these positions, they must strictly observe the established regulations:
they must not speak of others' shortcomings in the presence of the Abbot; they must not engage in frivolous laughter among their fellow officers; and they must not be indolent.

Seeking personal ease—these three matters one must especially guard against and refrain from. *Zhigu yun* states: When Biéfēng Yìn was abbot at Xuědòu, a junior disciple complained about the faults of the head officers.
Biéfēng rebuked him with a stern voice, saying: "You are my junior disciple; it is appropriate that you exercise forbearance toward those above and below you.
Instead, you expose the shortcomings of others. Staying by my side, you will surely ruin my affairs. He struck him with his staff and expelled him. Those who heard this...
He marveled at this. Furthermore, when Hongzhi was serving as Attendant to Chan Master Chun, he was debating with a monk in the quarters when he could not help but burst into loud laughter.
Chun happened to pass by and heard it; that night, he questioned Hongzhi about it. Hongzhi said, "I was merely speaking with the monk in a rough manner, and I could not restrain myself from laughing.
Chun reprimanded him sternly. Moreover, there was the attendant Zhe of Zhenru, who practiced seated meditation.
He was exhausted from meditation. He used a round log as a pillow while sleeping; when he fell into a deep sleep, the pillow would roll away.

Upon waking, he would rise again and sit upright as before, making this his constant practice. Some remarked that his mental exertion was excessive. Zhe said, "My affinity for Prajñā has always been thin.
If I do not carve myself and rouse my will, I fear I shall be dragged away by deluded habits. Moreover, [all things] are like dreams and illusions."
Truly. How can one establish a long-term plan? Alas! Regarding these three matters, one should be cautious, taking them as a prior warning. ○ The above concludes the section on the Western Order.
As for the practitioners (*xingzhe*) and lay attendants (*jingren*), these two categories of officials are appended to the preceding chapter on the Abbot (*zhuchi*).

The Dongxu Duguan (Director of the Eastern Wing) is also called the Dusì (Chief Administrator). This office did not exist in ancient times; it was established later because the affairs of the monastic community became numerous and complex.
Thus, this official was appointed to assist the Abbot from above and to support the Jiyuan (Superintendent) from below. Although his authority is not equal to that of the Jiyuan—
One manages affairs with diligent effort, yet the primary requirement is to maintain overall control; for this reason, it is also called the position of General Manager (*tongli*).
Regarding its rank, one stands at the far eastern end of the main hall, kneeling to the left, shoulder-to-shoulder with the *weina*. When walking, one follows behind the *jianyuan*.
In the refectory, one’s seat is above that of the *jianyuan*. Only after ten years of service managing the affairs of the monastery may one be appointed to this post.
The *Chi* (Director) holds a position of reward and ease; he stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) outside the hall (the supporting evidence for this is found below).

The *Jianyuan* (Director of Affairs) is the head of the Eastern Order; acting as the right-hand man to the Abbot, he oversees all secular affairs, such as cultivating fields, managing grain and rents, handling the receipt and disbursement of money and rice, maintaining ledgers and accounts, and attending to the communal meals and the needs of donors.
All these are positions of office. However, in all matters, one must consult with others; only after reporting to the Abbot and obtaining his approval should one act.
Do not act arbitrarily or according to your own whims. When instructing the laborers and workers, do not indulge in tyranny or violence.

If you are appointed to manage the estate or the storehouse, you must be impartial and never harbor private factions. In short, one must possess five qualities to be qualified for such an office. First:

First is compassion, showing kindness and regard for the assembly. Second is integrity, being utterly free from partiality or private interest. Third is prudence, maintaining no negligence toward matters great or small.
Fourth is diligence, never seeking ease or comfort. Fifth is proficiency, ensuring that no task is left unresolved.
A rector such as this is what the community constantly relies upon. Conversely, the harm caused by one who acts otherwise is evident. As for his position, he stands at the Great Hall.
At the end of the western row, he kneels behind the abbot. ○ The Vice Abbot (Fusi) is the deputy of the Chief Administrator (Jianguan);
his administrative duties are identical to those of the Chief Administrator. In all matters, he cooperates with the Chief Administrator in harmony.

As for all miscellaneous and trivial affairs that the Chief Administrator is unable to oversee, they rely on the Vice Abbot for management. Regarding the inflow and outflow of funds and grain, [he acts] accordingly...

The above records the collection and management of expenditures. The storekeeper is required each day to prepare a detailed account of the income and outgoings, totaling however much there may be, and to sign and seal a "flying slip" (feidan) to present to the Abbot;
this is called the "daily slip" (risdan). Every ten days these are compiled together, which is called the "ten-day slip" (xunsdan). At the end of each month, a final settlement is made.

This is maintained throughout the year. Alternatively, on the fourteenth and thirtieth days of each month, one goes to the Guest Hall to convene with the two orders (the administrative and monastic staff) to settle accounts item by item, overseeing both assets and liabilities;
this is called the "Daily Yellow General Ledger. One copy is kept in the Abbot’s quarters and one in the storehouse.

○ The *zhishi* (administrator) is also known as the *zhiliang* (grain manager). His primary duty is to manage the grain supplies, conduct affairs with government offices, and concurrently oversee the boundaries of fields, mountains, and estates.
Regarding matters such as fixed quotas, the annual payments of money and rice must be settled early so that no one is compelled to perform corvée labor at the temple; this is the foremost priority.
Once the grain receipts and vouchers have been completed, they must be handed over to the abbot for safekeeping and may not be kept by oneself.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: Since these four attachments involve matters of great importance, their causes and effects are likewise grave and must not be treated with negligence.
The *Secret Essentials of the Chan School* says: "In the past, Master Shidi of Tiantai was tending cattle at Guoqing Temple.
When the temple monks were reciting the precepts, Shidi drove his oxen to the front of the Sangha Hall, clapped his hands, and laughed loudly, saying: 'How leisurely!'"
You gathered together at the head [of the assembly]. The Head Seat scolded them, saying, "You madmen! How can you create such a clamor and disturbance during the recitation of the precepts?
Shide replied, "I am not herding oxen. These groups of oxen are mostly the administrative monks of this monastery.

He called out the names of each deceased monk one by one; the oxen responded to each voice as they passed by. The entire assembly was struck with astonishment, and everyone thought of reforming their ways.
[This was] a transgression. Alas! How can one not take this as a warning? *Zhigu yun* (Gathering from the Past) says: Formerly, Master Baoshou served as a storekeeper at Wuzu Monastery.
While the abbot, Master Jie, was ill and taking medicine, he required fresh ginger. An attendant went to the storehouse to fetch it, but Baoshou rebuked him.
When Master Jie learned of this, he ordered money to be returned to buy [the ginger]. Only then did Baoshou give it. Later, when Dongshan was short of personnel, the district...
Shoushu entrusted his precepts to Jushi, who was known to him. The precepts stated: "The man who sells raw ginger can leave.
Shou later appeared in the world and resided at Dongshan, whereupon the phrase "Baoshou’s raw ginger is as pungent as ten thousand years" circulated throughout the world. Thus it is said.
The Ku-si (Treasury Office) manages the funds, goods, tea, fruits, and other items of the storehouse; it also oversees all communal provisions such as soy sauce and pickled vegetables.
It requires four individuals who are honest and conscientious, and they shall jointly hold the keys to the storehouses.

The Commentary states: The *Seng’an zá lù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Monastic Hermitage) says: When Huǐyuán was serving as the head of the storehouse (*kūsī*) at Zìtuó, he was diligent and thorough in his execution of duties.

Regarding the regulations of the storehouse, he did not violate them even by a hair’s breadth. Yet, fearing he might still have committed some transgression, he further inscribed upon the wall of his quarters:
"A drop of water and a grain of rice all belong to the assembly of monks; to strive to please people's sentiments is, in principle, impossible to sustain. When...
May those who wear fur and horns live long through the coming years. Those who understand cause and effect should take note of this.
The *kūtō* (storehouse official) is exclusively responsible for disbursing funds and inspecting all items for food and consumption;
he is one who must shoulder both the burden of duty and the toil of labor. A person of careful integrity may be appointed to this office.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: This citation of the text is too brief. Now, following another version, I supplement it as follows:

"Oils, salts, and other such items shall not be served indiscriminately. When the assembly eats vegetables, there are differences between fresh and pickled varieties; these shall follow the established customs of each household."

These are established as the standard. All administrative duties regarding the distribution of oil shall proceed according to the regular rules. In the Meditation Hall, straw sandals are issued once every five days;

the straw sandals for the monastic residents (fandan) are issued once every three days. On the first and fifteenth days of the month, oil, candles, tea leaves, incense, and straw sandals for all locations are issued in accordance with reports.
For all offerings to the Buddhas above, the vegetables and fruits must be of five colors; however—

In the portrait hall (*yǐngtáng*) and at the ancestral pagoda (*zútá*), one prepares the soup, side dishes, and vegetable offerings; there are vegetarian meals, and one distributes the preserved foods to the subordinate temples.

When there is business within the storehouse, one assists in its management and oversees the gates as well as all utensils. One who is capable of acting with impartiality and selflessness may serve in this office.
When rice is brought in, count it and store it in the granary. Sieve it thoroughly to remove sand and husks. Inspect it frequently to ensure it does not become moldy or spoiled;

this is the rule. Make diligence and cleanliness your primary concern. When pounding the rice, ensure the grain is refined to an appropriate degree, neither too coarse nor too fine, and do not allow it to be mixed with chaff or broken grains that would make it difficult to eat.
Furthermore, regarding the five types of grain provisions and all utensils, you must ensure they are properly harvested, dried, and stored according to the rules.
May there be no wanton waste. For guests, provide guest rice and guest noodles;

issue these at fair market rates according to established custom. Regarding the "Explanation of Meaning": In ancient times, among the various officers of both the inner and outer halls, there was originally no distinction of high or low status.

The Sixth Patriarch attained the Dharma while serving as a rice-head; do not look down upon this office because it is a menial position. Furthermore, those who hold this office should likewise not disparage themselves.
Measure [the requirements] accordingly. The charcoal master (*tantou*) and the hearth master (*lutou*) shall prepare firewood and charcoal to ward off the cold.

Whether by soliciting donations from the patrons (*huazhu*) or drawing from the temple’s assets, they must ensure there is sufficient supply, yet avoid any waste. Furthermore, they shall oversee the maintenance of the hearths and exercise great care regarding fire and candles.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding those who jointly supervise the *weilu* (hearth circle), since it is easy for time to be wasted during a communal hearth gathering, each person should cultivate the Way.
One must not peruse secular books, nor engage in calligraphy or painting. One must not engage in idle chatter, laughter, or contentious debate.
One must not warm shoes or socks over the fire, nor cast dirt or grease into the flames. One must not poke at the fire so as to cause sparks to fly.

Ashes must not be left to accumulate for long or piled up in disorder; they must be shoveled away according to the established order. Any who violate this shall be reported to the Guest Hall for punishment.

The Office of Seals (Yinfáng) is responsible for managing the woodblocks for scriptures, recorded sayings, and other texts. These must be constantly inspected and maintained so that they do not become damaged, rotted, or disordered.
No one is permitted to privately carve or seal them. The location where the blocks are stored must have a balance between light and shade, yet remain close to wind and sunlight.

Otherwise, it will easily tear; if the Yin is too constricted, it will easily rot. In all matters concerning the preparation of seals—such as the paper, ink, the surface of the document, the nails, and the thread—cleanliness and durability are paramount.
One must not privately solicit silver or money. The fixed prices for various items shall not be increased or decreased according to private whims.
A ledger of continuous flow must be used to record these clearly, either by the quarter or as appropriate.
At the end of each year, the administrator shall hand over the accounts to the abbot for settlement. This is the duty of those who circulate the Dharma-treasure;
each should resolve to do so and exert their utmost effort in its preparation. Cause and effect are never deceptive; be cautious and strive diligently.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Keeper of the Seal Office is responsible for managing the carving of seals; he must possess keen vision and be able to distinguish between correct and erroneous calligraphy.
Lately, however, there have been many monks who are fond of the delusory and who forcibly cite the bequeathed words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to stubbornly cling to heterodox views.
Believing themselves to be correct, they compiled these as *yulu* (recorded sayings) and immediately circulated them by soliciting donations from lay patrons for printing.

If one fails to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and instead blindly accords with personal sentiments, once such works have been published and disseminated, the harm done to people will be profound. As the *Shan'an zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Mountain Hermitage) states:
"Qianjiang Zhao, Zhizhi Yuan, and Xiuan-an Yi—these three were all ordinary monks of common station, utterly devoid of the Correct [Dharma]."

I have seen him recklessly compose his own records of sayings. Furthermore, there was the Abbot Huī, who would divide the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* into sections and compose spurious verses for them, which he then carved into printing blocks for circulation. At that time, Shùzhōng Yùn was at Tónggǔ;
when Huī came to visit him, Yùn asked Huī, "What is the central tenet of this sutra? Huī remained utterly confused and ignorant. This is nothing less than deceiving the world and stealing a name.
How so? When illustrious elders of renowned virtue and gentlemen who protect the Dharma encounter such a catalog as this, they ought to reject it and put a stop to it.
By all means, do not act out of worldly sentiment or offer biased praise by writing prefaces or colophons for it.

You must consider that slandering the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* results in rebirth in the Avīci Hell; take this to heart. As for heterodox works such as the five sections and six volumes, etc., [the same applies].
I have long observed your strict prohibitions and have not dared to allow such works to be circulated or submitted.

However, there are some recently produced texts that gloss over the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs by interspersing them with the delusory and erroneous terminology of heterodox teachings, such as those concerning the refinement of elixirs or the projection of the spirit.
Furthermore, there are those who attach absurd commentaries to texts such as the Heart Sūtra and the Diamond Sūtra and circulate them by printing;
these are all difficult to anticipate. One must especially reject and destroy such works to uphold the True Dharma and eliminate future calamities.

When carrying out purchases from outside the storehouse, as well as when transporting firewood, rice, bamboo, timber, and other goods, one must ensure that the handover and receipt are clearly documented.
In the event of loss or theft, compensation shall be paid according to the quantity of items lost. When there is work at the storehouse, one shall assist during idle hours.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: According to another version, it is supplemented as follows: "If there are many people carrying goods, appoint one person to lead the group and manage the inventory.

When departing, they proceed in single file like a string of beads; when returning, they may walk at a relaxed pace. If the leader loses track of the inventory or items are missing, he shall be fined to compensate for the value.
As for travel expenses, any excessive or indiscriminate spending shall result in a tenfold restitution upon discovery."
Appendix: Regulations for the Management of Permanent Endowments (Including Eighteen Articles) Cherish the property of the permanent endowment as you would protect the jewel in your eye.
To promote prosperity, there is nothing better than eliminating abuses. Be entirely public-spirited and free from private interest. The offerings of the faithful are like rich fat;
if they are defiled by personal use, they become an ocean of karma. As for the cause and effect regarding the monastery, clear discernment is the key.

The Foundation of Merit. The inscription reads: "All things belong to the Saṃgha; even the slightest [offense] is difficult to avoid. Guard them within your own person; you must be reverent and cautious.
Pure as a clear pool, upright as a straight trunk—without crookedness or partiality, what cause for worry or distress? Should there be even a single lapse,"
The dragons and devas will examine you. As the Abbot, you are that upon whom the great assembly relies; you must cultivate a great and sincere heart to support the monastic community.
You must reform abuses and promote what is beneficial; you must not pass your days in negligence, seeking only empty fame.
If one acts contrary to reason and refuses to follow the exhortations of the assembly, they shall be punished and expelled from the monastery.

The assembly must maintain its integrity, with individuals appointed to every necessary post. What matters does the *karmadāna* (superintendent) oversee? He must manage all affairs, providing constant vigilance and making regular rounds throughout every location.

Do not allow communal affairs to be neglected. If the community has business to attend to, everyone must report it to the Chief Administrator (Jianyuan). Failure to report shall be punished; those who cause affairs to go astray shall be expelled from the monastery.

If the Chief Administrator acts autocratically and does not consult with the two orders of officials, he shall be lightly punished; if he causes affairs to go astray, he shall be punished and expelled.
The Assistant Treasurer (Fusi) shall record all income and expenditure of the monastery’s property clearly; failure to maintain such records shall be punished.

Punish those who cause confusion through negligence. Regarding all fields, mountains, and other assets, once the revenue and silver have been received, they shall be inspected by the two orders together and sealed.
When they are to be used, the seal must be opened before the assembly; those who open it privately shall be punished.

As for the treasury office (*kūsī*), regarding various types of utensils and their respective duties, they must be clearly handed over to the relevant department. When that department retires from its duties, [the items] shall be... together with them.

The Chief Administrator and others shall, as previously instructed, verify and hand over each item individually. Those who violate this shall be penalized. If items are lost or damaged, their names shall be recorded and they shall be made to compensate;

if they forget [the loss], they shall compensate on behalf of the offender. The silver used for compensation must be used to purchase the original items without substitution. Those who violate this shall be penalized.
The Head of the Treasury shall manage all objects and oversee all internal and external transactions. He shall not withhold what ought to be given.
Punishment shall be imposed on those who give privately what should not be given; such a person shall be subject to double the penalty.

Regarding the distribution of incense, candles, oil, rice, fruits, vegetables, and so forth, punishment shall be imposed on those who deviate from established regulations by increasing or decreasing amounts out of private interest. Regarding the buying and selling of goods or the collection of rents, punishment and compensation shall be imposed on those who secretly seek profit.
Upon leaving the monastery, once the rice, wheat, and other provisions have arrived, they shall be clearly inspected and accounted for, and the accounts shall be recorded immediately for reference.

Usage. This concerns the life-force of the entire community; it is not permitted to transfer accounts to shops or to sell goods. Should anyone violate this, they shall be collectively expelled by the assembly.

Regarding all property: if public funds are used for private gain, or if items are diverted, borrowed, or exchanged based on personal favoritism without clear disclosure, the offender shall be penalized with compensation. Furthermore, regarding food and drink: one must not act against the assembly or indulge in excess.
Those who waste oil, candles, and other such items shall be punished. Food and drink must be inspected at the proper times;

those who provide spoiled or rotten items that cause illness to the community shall be punished. Damaged goods must be compensated for. Property belonging to deceased monks may not be misappropriated.

When purchasing items for the sick, they must certainly be provided; whether the amount is large or small, it must follow public regulations. Those who violate this shall be punished. [This applies to] all locations.
Items for practical use, such as incense and candles, shall be prepared in advance; those who fail to provide them when required shall be penalized.

All fines paid in silver or coin shall be dedicated to public use. Those who exempt themselves from the duties of the *pōwù* (monastic service) shall have their exemptions revoked, and those who misappropriate funds for personal use shall be penalized and required to reimburse the loss.
The supervisor shall oversee the management of craftsmen and tools; all items entering or leaving the premises shall be accounted for accordingly.

Record this clearly. Those who fail to record shall be penalized; those who lose records shall be penalized and required to reimburse the loss. Those who seek personal ease by failing to supervise the craftsmen, or those whose work accounts are erroneous or unclear, shall be penalized.
On the fourteenth and thirtieth of every month, the two orders [of monks] shall assemble to calculate the accounts.
The secretary shall report the accounts; if the calculation is lost or omitted, he shall be penalized. Annually, the grain tax ledgers and vouchers shall be submitted to the authorities.
The abbot shall take charge [of the records]. Those who store items privately shall be punished.

The attendants of the storehouse must, when handing over their duties, clearly enumerate each item before the assembly. The new attendants must verify these; those who fail to do so shall be punished. ○ Date:

The Commentary on the Meaning states: According to the Vinaya section, there are four kinds of monastic property (*saṃghika-vastu*). First is "permanent property" (*sthāvara*).
"Permanent" refers to the dwellings, furniture, trees, fields, gardens, people, livestock, rice, wheat, and other such items belonging to the community of monks (*saṃgha*).
