Because their substance is restricted to that specific location and does not extend to other boundaries, they may only be used and are not permitted to be divided or sold; therefore, it is specifically termed "permanent. Second...

First, the permanent property of the ten directions refers to items such as food and drink prepared for the Sangha within a monastery, the substance of which belongs to all ten directions and is not restricted to its original location.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "To eat without striking the bell constitutes the offense of stealing," because this clarifies that all monks of the ten directions have a share.
Third, the permanent property present before one; this is of two kinds.
First, the presence of the object; second, the presence of the Saṃgha. This is because the object is bestowed solely upon the present Saṃgha of this particular location.
Fourth, the presence of the permanent endowment of the ten directions; that is to say, the property of a deceased monk is identical in substance to that of the ten directions.
[This applies] to the present Sangha of the ten directions, because [the property] is to be divided among them. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If one steals the property of the deceased Sangha, from whom does one incur the fundamental offense? It answers: "If the *karmavācanā* has already been performed, one incurs it from the assembly that performed the *karman*.
If the *karmavācanā* has not yet been performed, one incurs it universally from all assemblies of those who preach the True Dharma. Now...
Detailed Classification of the Property of Deceased Monks: Monks arriving from the ten directions who are present before the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) may receive [the property];
those who arrive after the *karmavācanā* may not. Lǎn'ān said: "These four kinds of permanent property (*sāṃghika-vastu*) must not be violated by even a single thread or a grain of dust;

the retribution for such an offense is not light. From the sages of the past to those of the future, their exhortations have been most earnest. Whether I am traveling abroad or residing at home, I [adhere to this]."

I have never failed to keep this earnestly in mind, yet fearing that I have not reached the goal, I composed a verse to admonish myself: "The property of the Sangha of the ten directions is as heavy as a mountain;
How could it be easily repaid across ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes? Though the Golden Mouth has spoken of it together with others, I have never believed it;
In years to come, how can I avoid the gates of the Iron City? Difficult to obtain is a human body—ponder this well! When the horns of rebirth appear...
"Over many years, one can only laugh at those who covet another's grain; in a single moment, they lose half a year’s worth of provisions. *Zhigu* says:
Chan Master Hong was a successor of Master Xiang of Mount Xiufeng. While he resided at Mount Qixia, a nobleman sought to bury his relative.
When the coffin arrived, Hong lay firmly across the grave pit, preventing the funeral rites from being completed. The Prefectural Governor, Imperial Censor Chou...
He sent someone to advise him, saying, "The permanent property of a thousand years belongs to the Sangha of a single day; Elder, why do you struggle so bitterly over it?
Daohong replied, "One cannot destroy the permanent property of a thousand years for the sake of the Sangha of a single day. Ultimately, the matter was dropped.

The position of *Sengzhi* (Monastic Registrar) originally has no fixed rank; it derives its meaning from the principle of the monastic community taking turns on duty, as well as from the sense of being the most upright among the monks.
One who fills this office should not be sycophantic, nor should they be evasive, nor protective of their own interests, nor partial toward any faction.

They shall act as the deputy for the Abbot in overseeing matters beyond his immediate reach. Whether entering or exiting at morning or evening, the entire assembly—both internal and external—must maintain solemnity and reverence. Therefore...

This is also called "Investigation" (jiǔchá). Starting from the Head of the Class (bānshǒu) down to the Head of the Assembly (cāntóu), the duty rotates every five days, with the new and old officers handing over responsibility.
After the evening recitation of the Buddha’s name in the Great Hall is completed, the former *sēngzhí* (monastic administrator) first requests the bamboo rattle (*zhúbì*).

Once the recitation before the Buddha image is finished, the former *sēngzhí* performs the ritual prostrations facing the ten directions (*shífāng lǐ*). Upon completion of the prostrations, he takes the bamboo rattle down and hands it to the new *sēngzhí*.
One prostration; exchange greetings. One person inquires after the health [of the abbot]. The new *shengzhi* (duty monk) receives the bamboo rattle and performs the ritual of the Ten Directions.

Upon completion of the prostrations, each returns to their original place. Every morning at the third board, he urges the lighting of the path lamps from the Abbot’s Quarters (*fangzhang*) through to the various quarters, urging the assembly to ascend to the hall.
He strictly inspects all locations and watches until dawn for the opening of the mountain gate. He oversees the assembly as they pass through the hall and ascend to the hall for services.

The Gatekeeper: The morning gruel and midday meal are served in two sessions, while simultaneously prohibiting negligence. When the assembly returns from the outdoor work (chupo), they must arrange their respective belongings according to the Dharma.
In the evening, the lesson master urges the assembly to enter the Hall together. A short time after sunset, he checks that the mountain gates are locked.

He waits for the incense to be lit within the Hall and then urges the lighting of the path lamps and the glass lanterns in various locations. At the second board, if there is business, the Guest Hall shall deliberate.

Regarding matters: if there are no matters, then one has finished. After the period of stillness, conduct patrols in their respective areas. After the fourth incense stick has been lit for the Great Stillness (*dàjìng*), prohibit the lighting of lamps.
When the sixth incense stick is completed, inspect the road lamps and carefully examine the fires and candles in the kitchen and tea room.

Whenever a seven-day Zen retreat (*chánqī*) occurs, all affairs outside the hall must be managed. This is the protocol for the *zhí-mǔ* (senior administrator) regarding the abbot and various other officials. If there are...

When there is a transgression, it is reported; when there is a fault, there is punishment. Not following private sentiments is the principle of public integrity within the monastic community (saṃghārāma).

One must maintain a mind like water and uphold the law like a mountain; only then can the deportment of the monks be maintained in proper sequence, their comings and goings follow the regulations, their duties not be neglected, and they attend the incense-sitting sessions together.
They shall assemble without error for the meal hall and the hall of worship, and the striking of the bells and drums shall be divided [according to the rules].
[The Head Monks] shall ensure that propriety is maintained both internally and externally. Should the Abbot fail to comply, they shall kneel before the Patriarchs’ Hall while burning incense.

Should the assembly fail to comply, they shall report the matter to the Abbot, who shall impose punishment according to the regulations. Once these officials have been properly appointed, they may remain in office indefinitely and need not be replaced.
Their appointment occurs during the morning gruel or midday meal in the refectory; the Guest Master first places a bamboo staff upon the Abbot’s table in the hall.

First, the new *sengzhi* (monastic administrator) extends his ritual implements toward the superior and performs three prostrations with the head to the ground. The Guest Master approaches the seat and offers one greeting;
he then raises a bamboo staff once, lowers it against the new *sengzhi*, and hands the staff over to him. They then face each other and exchange greetings.

When the new *sengzhi* (monastic administrator) approaches to inquire after the guest master (*zhikeshi*), the latter shall immediately prepare the *sengzhi*'s lantern outside the hall door and personally hand it over to him.
All other ceremonial protocols shall still follow those set forth in the "Regulations for Appointing Officers."

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding what is called the "Monastic Registrar" (Sengzhi), since the community of a monastic grove must necessarily be orderly and disciplined, one who is upright and incorruptible among the assembly is selected to serve as the inspector. Within this role, the affairs are extremely numerous and琐碎 (trifling);

fearing that the energy of a single person would be insufficient for such tasks and making it difficult to remain in the position for long, the two orders of officials are required to take turns in the succession of duty. This is so.

This is called the "Monk on Duty" (Sengzhi). As for matters concerning the great affairs of the monastic community that must not be delayed or neglected, regardless of whether one is an internal or external executive officer, all may manage them as the occasion arises.
If there are matters that ought to be spoken of, each may also maintain their own perspective and speak directly without concealment;
it is not necessary to wait for one's turn as the Monk on Duty. Even if the Abbot himself commits an offense, he too may be addressed.

During the time of the morning gruel and midday meal in the refectory, one kneels before the assembly and makes this declaration: "A ruler has a minister who remonstrates; a father has a son who remonstrates.
If there are minor matters that do not obstruct the community and do not harm the permanent assets of the monastery, even the *Sengzhi* (the monastery steward) should handle them with skillful means.
For it is the case that everyone cannot avoid minor transgressions. As the *Zen School’s Secret Essentials* states: "Only the Buddha..."
There is but one person who is without fault; who among others could be so?
When a disciple perceives a fault in their teacher—whether real or imagined—their mind is naturally corrupted, and they can no longer obtain the benefits of the Dharma. One should reflect thus:
"Because my merit from previous lives was incomplete, I did not encounter a Buddha. Now that I have encountered this teacher of mixed conduct, I..."
One should reflect upon its faults, for they themselves obstruct one's *prajñā*. The faults of the teacher do not adhere to me; I merely receive the Dharma of *prajñā* from the teacher.
It is like a dog-skin bag containing excellent goods: one should not discard the treasure because of the bag.
It is like a person of poor character holding a torch to illuminate the path: one cannot reject the light because the person is base.
Yet they have abandoned their own clarity and cast themselves into a ditch. This is what is meant by "rely on the Dharma, not on the person.
If one cannot rely [on another], it is difficult to dwell together; when this single period of life is fulfilled, I shall simply depart for elsewhere. Why use so many words?
The Zhizhong (Director of the Guest Hall) is the head of those who attend to guests. Outwardly, he responds to the needs of donors; inwardly, he harmonizes the community.

Since he seeks to blend with his surroundings and share in the common dust, he must also shoulder both labor and resentment. He should constantly observe the worthiness or unworthiness, diligence or laziness of the assembly, promoting the upright and removing the crooked, without partiality born of love or hatred.
He must attend carefully to all matters, great and small, concerning the guest hall and the outdoor quarters. Regarding the task of escorting... [text continues]
Regarding the new appointee (*xinzhí*): one must necessarily explain what is appropriate for their former position, thereby alerting their mind and ensuring they act in accordance with their duties.

The *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning) states: "The supplementary text from the *Tā* says: 'One should know the various correct principles, guest etiquette, and all matters concerning the placards, such as the distribution of offerings during the meal and the allocation of administrative duties.
Whenever sending off a new appointee, one prepares tea and a list of items, and offers greetings, saying:"
It is said: When going out to the slopes (outdoor work), one must supervise the laborers and avoid dangerous rapids, while also attending to any unfinished tasks on the slopes.

The Guest Prefect (Zhike) is responsible for receiving guests. Whenever a guest arrives—whether monastic or lay—and is someone with whom he has not previously met, regardless of their status, he must treat them with humility and courtesy, inquiring after their name, residence, and purpose for visiting. He must not [behave otherwise].

One must not be negligent. If one encounters a suspicious person, one should maintain outward courtesy while remaining inwardly on guard; one must not indiscriminately trust them, lest the matter be compromised.
If a distant monk seeks lodging, or a stranger arrives as a guest, one should carefully examine their background and scrutinize their appearance and demeanor.
If they are unfit to be kept, one should politely decline them with kind words. However, if a distinguished guest—whether ordained or lay—should arrive, [one should treat them with due respect].
Upon arrival, they shall be received. The guest prefect (zhàokè) shall then be instructed to announce them to the Abbot (zhùzhí). Thereafter, they shall be led up for an audience.

Those of secondary rank shall be entertained in the Guest Hall (kètáng), where they should engage only in informal discussion on Buddhist principles; it is improper to discuss worldly affairs or pass judgment on people.
For further details, refer to what is stated in the regulations of the Guest Hall.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The position of Guest Master (zhike) requires one who is clear-sighted regarding worldly affairs and proficient in literary composition;

only then can they respond to others without hindrance. Since those who come and go range from the refined to the vulgar, having a capable Guest Master not only ensures that the Buddha-Dharma is honored, but also prevents the monastic community from being subject to reproach. This office must not be treated with negligence.
(Attached: Duties of the *Zhaoke*) The *Zhaoke* is responsible for the management of guest quarters, ensuring they are clean and orderly. When guests arrive, he attends to their tea and meals.
Upon receiving incense, letters of introduction, or gifts, he delivers them to the Abbot and hands them over to the attendant on duty (*dangzhi shizhe*).

If guests are to stay overnight, he shall attend to their bedding and other necessities, and oversee matters such as luggage and lighting in the guest rooms. He holds the keys and locks; should anything be lost, he shall be penalized.
Compensation. In all matters of attending guests, it is forbidden to privately solicit gifts from them or similar matters. Those who violate this shall be investigated and severely punished.
In all matters concerning the receptionist’s attendance at tea and meals for guests, one must serve with diligent courtesy and must not fail in dignified deportment.

Whenever summoned, one must arrive immediately before [the guest] and stand respectfully with palms joined. When there is no business, one should remain quietly in one's own quarters and must not move far away. Tea and refreshments...

Guests' meals and other matters are conducted according to the instructions of the *chikaku* (guest master). ○ At the third board, the tea master prepares the night patrol lamps, boils the hot water, and prepares the facial wash.

He waits for the hall master to strike first for the offering of water. After the morning gruel, he strikes for silence and burns the "opening-silence" tea and four sticks of incense, followed by boiling the hot water.
After the midday meal, he burns the second board tea; he strikes for silence and burns the "opening-silence" tea and four sticks of incense.

Incense for the feet; boiling water for burning incense; boiling water for burning incense after the evening recitation; waiting for the two-board tea, the small-silence tea, and the four-branch-incense tea.
If conducting a seven-day meditation retreat (*dhyāna-saptāha*), add six-branch or eight-branch incense and boiling water.

For ritual affairs (*buddha-kārya*), manage the washing of the face as required. It is not permitted to take hot water again at dawn to wash the face, except in cases of old age, illness, or for those of high rank.
Guests: Hand towels should be washed clean. It is not permitted to request water for washing clothes at improper times.
The Hall Attendant (Daiwan Tou): Before the gong is struck to signal the start of the meal, he must arrange the bowls and chopsticks in unison.

He shall burn incense upon his designated desk and serve the vegetables and rice with care, ensuring that the bowls do not clatter against one another through clumsy handling. Only after the meal has concluded may he clear away the bowls.

The person on duty shall eat at the first session (*dītáng*). They shall wait until those for the second session have arrived before entering the hall. After eating, they must pay close attention to clearing away the bowls and chopsticks;

those who lose, forget, or damage them must compensate for them. When serving *pǔchá* (general tea), they shall go to the meditation hall (*cāntáng*) to receive the tea pitcher and tea bell, returning them immediately after the tea service is finished.

When serving a meal, they shall spread the *púdùn* (rush mats); they shall collect them immediately after the prostrations are completed. Once the meal is finished, they shall post the notice that the meal is over.
For the *dān* (attendant), the floor is swept once every three days. They follow the assembly up half the slope. On their assigned day, they oversee the quarters.

Whenever the seven-day meditation retreat (*cānqī*) holds the "break from sitting" meal (*chifàngcān*), they light the pillar lamp and strike the small wooden board (*xiǎobǎn*) three times. Once the break from sitting is concluded and the bowls have been cleared away, they immediately extinguish the lamp.
Those serving as *zhírì* (on-duty) are exempted from the evening recitation; the rest follow the assembly.
The gatekeeper shall attend to the gate day and night, opening and closing it at the proper times without error.
He must pay close attention to those entering and exiting to prevent petty persons from sneaking in or stealing items.

If the mountain gate is knocked at night, he must first notify his fellow residents before opening it together with them. If venerable elders, officials, or scholars arrive, he must report their arrival immediately.
Guests—monastics and laypeople from distant regions who come with a spirit of sympathetic joy—must not be refused. Those on duty shall oversee the quarters and guard the gate without moving a step.

Regarding this, the *Jueyi* (Exegesis) states: "In antiquity there was a verse concerning the gatekeeper which said: 'Whoever acts as a gatekeeper, upon seeing a guest, shall immediately rise to welcome them.'"
Do not discriminate between the poor and the wealthy; treat everyone with courtesy and respect. Diligently sweep and clean the entrance and courtyard. Do not raise your voices or laugh too loudly.
One should show reverence to one's neighbors and look after the children. The gates of the monastery are wide open; visitors need have no cause for hesitation.
If you intentionally obstruct people, it will lead to trouble despite having no private motive. Rise early at the break of dawn; once it is late...

Then the gates shall be closed. Be careful to guard against fire and candles; it is a fixed rule not to light lamps. Having already assumed these duties, one must not leave the precincts of the mountain gate.

At evening, a strict inspection must be conducted; do not allow strangers to remain. For all matters concerning sutra recitations and memorial services, public offerings shall be distributed according to the regulations.
If anyone again solicits private donations, they shall be investigated and, upon discovery, strictly expelled. This applies to all young women as well.
Women, do not engage in idle conversation with them. The ground of the Triple Gem is pure; one must strictly avoid suspicion and reproach.

As for those who beg and are not monks, do not allow them to enter the gate. Fearing they may cause disturbances within the forest of the Sangha, and fearing they may appear unseemly—whether entering or exiting during the bustle of the day, one must always keep a watchful eye;
if entering or exiting during the stillness of night, one must inspect even more carefully. Do not...
It is said that those who cling to the Lesser Vehicle are deeply bound by the gateways [of sectarianism]. Only those with clear vision and refined minds may preside over the mountain gate.
Attached: Regulations for the Guest Hall (Twenty-seven Articles).

To carry one’s bag and shoulder one’s bowl is fundamentally for the purpose of seeking the Way. Parting the weeds and gazing at the wind [of the Dharma] has never been for any other reason. Since you have deigned to visit us, [we shall proceed accordingly].

One should refrain from clamor and arrange all affairs accordingly; in every matter, one should follow the assembly. Whether in motion or stillness, one should be solemn beyond the common crowd; whether at leisure or in haste, one should stand preeminent among the multitude.
Possessing a dharma that can be strictly observed and a decorum that can serve as a model—such a vessel of the Dharma may truly be called a member of the eminent stream.
All regulations are hereby respectfully presented for your joint consideration. When guests arrive, the tea, soup, snacks, bedding, and seating must each be prepared with meticulous care.
If you do not know the guest, you must inquire after their name and place of residence; you must never be negligent or disrespectful.
Those who violate this shall be penalized. The Guest Master on duty, regardless of whether they have other duties or not, must wait quietly in the Guest Hall.
Those who fail to observe the proper times shall be penalized. Ascend the hall early and late in the evening. If there is no *sengzhi* (monastic steward), the guest prefect shall take charge.

This includes overseeing the road lamps and the rush-mat seats in the Great Hall, as well as supervising the standing positions and ranks of the various masters. If anyone fails to arrive, their presence shall be investigated for official business; those who err shall be penalized.
Upon hearing the sound of the wooden clapper, the masters shall proceed to the hall for meals. If there is no... [text truncated]

Upon arrival, the guest prefect shall immediately take charge by striking the board and receiving the rolling board, as well as supervising the assembly in the refectory; those who err shall be penalized.

This applies when the head of a division presides over the incense-burning ceremony, during the eight seasonal festivals and offerings, or when members of the two orders depart from the monastery on official business.
It must be understood that once the Guest Master (zhiké) has personally made the request, he shall then instruct the Attendant Guest Master (zhàoké) to make the request.
When officials arrive or depart, as soon as the notice arrives, the Attendant Guest Master is dispatched to inform the Abbot (zhùzhí). The Guest Master first acts as an attendant to serve tea;
he follows the Abbot until the guest is escorted out. Those who err shall be punished. At the second board, the Guest Hall deliberates on affairs, and the Deputy Steward (fùsì) proposes purchases.
The sale of goods and expenses; the annual observance of the *pō* ceremony; the *yuèzhòng* (joyful assembly) reporting on matters within the hall; the attendant reporting to the abbot;
the upper and lower *tōngshì* (attendants); and the *zhīkè* (guest master) managing seasonal greetings and human relations—all such matters, great and small, shall be carried out accordingly.
Once the deliberation is concluded, they shall collectively inform the Abbot. For matters concerning the various masters within and without the monastery, one should report them to the Guest Hall.

The Duty Guest Master (Zhiri Zhike) shall adjudicate with justice; those who fail to attend to such matters shall be penalized. If a dispute arises that leads to verbal contention, one must report it to the Guest Hall. The Duty Guest Master shall uphold the public interest and speak plainly.
Should the parties remain unsatisfied, he shall request the assembly of Guest Masters to deliberate on a public punishment. If they still refuse to comply, they shall be publicly expelled.
The Monastery: Should anyone yield to private interests and adjudicate matters with partiality, they shall be punished together with the offender.

As for outsiders or miscellaneous persons who cause disturbances within the temple, the Guest Master (zhike) shall intervene to advise them; if he fails to act and looks on while the day passes, or if he is cowardly and does not step forward, he shall be punished.
If the Guest Master has no business, he shall be punished for failing to attend the communal meals, the hall services, or the work periods, except in cases of illness.

Regarding illness: if various masters enter or leave without reporting their departure or notifying the guest hall of their temporary absence, and if they wander abroad at leisure or act with negligence, those in charge who know of this and fail to report it shall be punished equally.

As for all matters pertaining to the guest hall, whether there be those who usurp authority and act arbitrarily, or those who harbor mutual jealousy among their colleagues, or those who show partiality out of private favoritism—[all such shall be dealt with].
The assembly of fellow practitioners shall be informed and a penalty shall be deliberated upon. Although the guest master (*zhike*) is not on duty that day, he must not wander about outside;

violators shall be penalized. Upon the arrival of Zen guests (*chankè*), they shall not be treated according to the standard protocol. Venerable elders from various quarters shall be accommodated in the Guest Room for Superior Guests (*Anshang Kefang*).

Those who have returned as former administrators and have long served the monastery with merit shall also be accommodated in the Guest Room for Superior Guests and shall serve as guests for five days.
Next, the quarters for the Venerable Ones are established. For newly arrived Zen practitioners and those who have resided for a long time, they are treated as guests for three days.

For those who first enter the assembly or are junior students, they are treated as guests for one day, after which they immediately follow the communal activities. As for those from various regions who congregate here, if they arrive in the morning, they are given one meal;

if they arrive in the evening, they are given one night’s lodging, after which they are requested to practice separately and are not settled in guest rooms. Those who cause confusion or error shall be penalized.

[The guest] comes from another monastery. When the Elder arrives, he is invited to wash his face, change his robes, and drink tea; then, the Abbot is informed, after which the guest is led for an audience.

This continues until the end of the midday meal, when the guest performs the *xunchan* (inspection of the quarters) following the Abbot’s quarters. A single attendant is assigned to the guest’s quarters, while the remainder are assigned to guest rooms.

If the guest inspects the hall or the various monastic offices (*liáo*), the entire assembly bows in unison. A seat is set up to the right of the Dharma Hall; however, if the guest is inspecting the two orders (*liǔxù*), it is arranged separately.
Regarding the inspection of single beds (*dān*): the person concerned does not enter the hall or tour the quarters, nor do the assembly members pay them obeisance;

only the two orders (*liǔxù*) inspect their beds, and they in turn look back upon the two orders. When a donor provides a vegetarian feast and distributes alms (*shànqìn*), the Vice Abbot (*fùsì*) shall coordinate with the Guest Master (*zhīkè*).
Public deliberation shall follow the established regulations. For the offering of light meals during the retreat, the Guest Hall (kètáng) for receiving guests is excluded;

otherwise, the same rules apply to both the internal and external monastics. Regarding the distribution of *dakṣiṇā* (alms), single or double distributions shall be conducted according to the prescribed rules.

When visiting monks, dharma relatives, or fellow practitioners arrive, they shall all stay temporarily in the Guest Quarters (*kělíáo*) before being assigned to their respective halls as appropriate. Those who enter the hall indiscriminately shall be penalized. In all matters...

Those seeking to reside [in the monastery] must first examine the regulations for communal living. Those wishing to enter the meditation hall must first review the regulations for the Chan Hall and consult with the senior administrators to assess their resolve.
Only those who are truly sincere seekers of the Way may be permitted to occupy a private room.

However, those with heterodox knowledge or views, or those who are coarse, wild, or stubborn, shall not be allowed to enter the hall as they would hinder the community; those who attempt to smuggle such individuals in shall be punished.
All items, including bedding and curtains in guest rooms, must be inspected and maintained according to the regulations.

One must not privately lend any external bedding or allow outsiders to occupy the quarters. Should anyone attempt to exchange old items for new ones, they shall be required to compensate at a rate of two-to-one.

Those who are unable to compensate for losses shall be held accountable and their quarters shall be moved. Whenever there are Buddhist ceremonies, the guest prefect (zhaoke) shall be ordered to post the necessary notices in advance;
those who cause errors shall be penalized. Whenever letters or gifts arrive, one must inquire where they are to be sent and immediately record this in the register;
alternatively, they may be received and delivered on the spot with full handover. Furthermore, the reply letter must be returned to the messenger; those who cause errors shall be penalized.

If members of the guest hall (kètáng) engage in disputes or cause a commotion, they shall immediately be removed from their quarters and expelled, regardless of whether they are in the right or wrong.

Should any person rely on force or prejudice to obstruct the administration of the community, refusing to harmonize with or consult their fellow residents, and thereby hindering the affairs of the monastery (chángzhù), they shall be punished with a double fine and expelled from the quarters.
Whenever anyone vacates their quarters, their belongings must be minutely inspected to prevent the accidental taking of communal property.

If one fails to report the arrival of a resident as required, they shall be penalized. Whenever a candidate seeks ordination, their background must be inquired into, and it must be verified that they are fully equipped with the Sūtras, Vinaya, robes, alms bowl, incense offerings, seating silver, and other requisites.
Once these are all prepared, the candidate is led before the administrative secretary to be registered in the official ledger.

If permission is granted improperly or erroneously, the official shall be penalized. (Regarding the incense offerings and other items, refer to the section on the Ordination Period in the seventh fascicle. Once everything is in accordance with the Dharma, the candidate is led to see the Abbot and immediately sent to enter the Hall, where they first perform prostrations.)

After the Buddha has performed the prostrations to the ten directions, the candidate for ordination is invited to enter the hall. Having performed three prostrations to the Buddha, they are next called to perform three prostrations to the various masters. Once these are completed, the Master of Ceremonies calls for the candidate to perform three prostrations of gratitude to the Preceptor who introduced them [to the assembly].

In response, the candidate says, "I prostrate once to the Buddha," and immediately exits the hall. Regarding the distribution of monetary offerings and gifts, as well as official protocol and etiquette, these matters must be deliberated upon by both orders of the community.
Those who act according to their own private views shall be penalized; those who cause errors or omissions shall receive severe punishment. (The regulations for the *Sengzhi*).

Examples may be seen in the previously mentioned section on "Duties of the Administrative Office" (marked by ○). [Date] Recorded again by Resident Abbot So-and-so. The Commentary on the Meaning states:
When donors come and go, and silver or coins are received or disbursed, these matters mostly pass through the hands of the Guest Hall.

Thus, the workings of good and evil causes and effects are manifest and unfailing. The *Xinghu* (Record of Conduct and Protection) says: Formerly, at the White Pagoda Temple in Yangzhou, Daochang was in charge of the monks’ affairs.

While he was freely using the monastery’s property, suddenly several officials from the underworld entered the temple in broad daylight. They dragged Sengchang to the ground and were about to cut off his head.
Startled, Chang cried out for his life. The officials said in a harsh voice, "If you return all the assets and wealth of this entire room to the Sangha, we shall release you and let you live.
Chang bowed his head and said, "I dare not disobey your command. He immediately struck the bell to assemble the community. When they had all gathered...
He gave away his clothing and belongings to create an image of the Buddha and provide offerings during a vegetarian feast. Three days later, the official from the underworld returned;
seeing Daochang with only one alms bowl and one robe, he departed without speaking. From that time on, Daochang exerted himself in diligent practice and ultimately achieved both wisdom and conduct.
Thus, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* says: "It would be better to eat the flesh of one's own body than to steal the property of the Triple Gem. Dongshan Liangjie said: "The permanent property..."
One must rely on the power of the precepts for support; do not employ them recklessly to indulge greed and ambition.

Guarding the property within the gate of the Triple Gem, cherish it as you would the two pupils of your parents' eyes. Though one may be clever and cunning in secret, there are naturally gods and ghosts who will punish one in the underworld.
If one takes even a hair’s breadth without private intent, one will avoid being reborn as a horse or a donkey in a future life. (Above)
The Fifth Quartering concludes.

Regarding the Kitchen Steward (*karmadāna*), ancient tradition says that the Head Seat (*śrāmaṇera*) regulates his character, while the Kitchen Steward regulates his life. He oversees the food and drink for the assembly; do not treat this matter with indifference.

All offerings must be prepared with utmost refinement and purity. Protect and cherish the monastery’s permanent assets (*sāṃghika-vastu*); do not waste them through reckless extravagance. Attend to the gruel and rice in the kitchen accordingly.

One must not join a different assembly. When carrying the buckets of congee or rice to the hall, one should first look toward the *zhaitang* (refectory), burn incense, and perform prostrations before proceeding to enter the hall.

The remaining details are as described in the regulations for the kitchen and quarters (*kitchen-liao-gui*). (The following sections are all the same. **On Placing Dishes:** Regarding the preparation of offerings and side dishes, they must be cooked until done and seasoned properly. One must not taste them beforehand.
One must not use raw vegetables or similar items to line the bottom of the vessels, thereby showing irreverence toward the Buddhas and deities; such an act constitutes a transgression.

The fault is no small matter. One must not privately prepare food for a partial group. If it is food for the great assembly or for guests, one should first taste it to ensure the flavors are properly balanced;
one must not be careless and ruin the taste, nor should one use it to curry private favor.

Both the giver and the receiver shall be punished; however, this does not apply to those who are ill or have made a formal vow. This rule includes the striking of the *hu-pan* (calling board) and the rolling of the *gun-pan* (rolling board);
if there is no *diànzuò* (steward), both duties belong to the person in charge.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: According to the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*, the Buddha said: "As for what you see as the second jar, it was [a monk] who served as the kitchen supervisor for the Saṅgha.
He consumed the soft, delicious, and fine offerings for himself first, while distributing the coarse, astringent, and inferior portions among the members of the Saṅgha.
Because of these causes and conditions, he has entered the hells and become a great flesh jar, suffering from being burned by fire, which continues unabated until this day."
As for the third jar you see: during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a monastery attendant (*śrāmaṇera*).

While preparing food and drink, he would eat the finest portions himself or give them to his wife and children, while taking the coarse, bitter, and inferior portions to distribute among the Sangha. Because of these causes and conditions, [he has now become a jar].
In the hells, one becomes a great vessel of flesh, suffering as it is scorched by fire without ceasing even to this day.

When the fragrance of the rice reaches the monastery and the signal gong is struck, the porridge and rice must first be offered; next, they are served to the Zhai-tang (Dining Hall), Ke-tang (Guest Hall), Shan-liao (Monks’ Quarters), Yuan-fang (Garden Lodgings), Ta-yuan (Stupa Courtyard), Lao-tang (Hall for the Elderly), and Bing-tang (Infirmary).
Those who provide private portions outside of these are subject to punishment. During the summer months, the amount of porridge and rice should be measured according to the number of people.

Regarding the arrival and departure of the assembly, one must monitor the addition or subtraction of water and rice; if there is a surplus, it should be prepared for consumption early so that it does not become sour or spoiled.
○ Second, the Rice Cooker (i.e., the Head of Guest Meals) prepares light meals daily, with the assistance of the Rice Cooker or the Guest Hall.

Alternatively, while serving in the *shìliáo* (attendant quarters), once the number of guests has been reported, one enters the storehouse to fetch rice. The *xiǎoshí guōbā* (scum from the morning meal) is returned to the storehouse to await the distribution according to the *xíngdān* (distribution list).
As for the *guōbā* from the guest meals, it is distributed on a rotating basis among three locations according to the list: first, the Guest Hall (*kètáng*); second, the Meditation Hall (*chándàng*);

and third, the Abbot’s Quarters (*fāngzhǎng*). Regarding the vegetables for the three daily meals, the vegetable steward (*cài-tóu*) must consult with the Chief Cook (*diǎnzuo*) to ensure they are prepared cleanly and cut [to the proper size].
Regarding communal meals: everyone should assist one another so that there is no waste. The *Zhengyi* (Exegesis) states:
The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* says, "As for the first jar you see, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, it was an ordained person who served as the kitchen supervisor for the Saṅgha.
He would set aside food intended for the morning meal until the following day; and what was intended for the following day's meal..."
On the third day, due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and was made into a large vessel of flesh, suffering the torments of being burned by fire that has not ceased until now.

As for the "Fire Head" (the officer in charge of the fire), every morning after three strikes of the board, he burns the rice porridge cauldron; the striking of the meditation hall boards and the incense marks the end of his duty.

[The Head Cook] remains quiet. Once the rice for the morning meal has finished cooking, he continues to sit and supervise it; no one is permitted to take the fire. After the wooden clapper is struck, there is no restriction.

When the junior monks eat their rice, they do so over a large fire; the evening congee is prepared in the same manner. The Junior Fire-Attendant waits for the incense to be sent from the Meditation Hall.
Cook vegetables in the wok. Serve small portions of vegetables to the diners. Cook over a low fire. When there are vegetarian fried tofu dishes or steamed mantou, everyone helps together.
Whenever the fire is extinguished, sweep the area in front of the stove immediately. Be careful with fires and candles.
Do not allow wood to accumulate beneath the stove; clean it up every evening. Inside the chimney, sweep once every first day of the month.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* says: "That which you see as a tree of flesh was, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, a renunciant who served as firewood for the Saṃgha.

Because he used the Saṃgha’s firewood to warm his own quarters or gave it to his acquaintances, by this causal condition he entered hell and became a great tree of flesh, suffering from being burned by fire, which continues unabated until now. Furthermore, regarding meditation...
The *Zongmiyao* states: In the Western Regions, there was the Venerable Dharmamitra, whose wisdom was profound and far-reaching and who was fully endowed with merit.

He was exceptionally skilled in penetrating the characteristics of samādhi and meditative concentration. In the kingdom of South India, there were two bhikṣus whose minds were gentle and who had long delighted in the wholesome Dharma;
hearing that the Venerable One was foremost in seated meditation, they immediately went together to visit him.
At that place, in his dwelling, there were three levels of caves.
At that time, the two men went into the lower cave and saw a bhikṣu wearing tattered robes, with an ugly appearance, sitting upright before a hearth, kindling a fire for the Saṃgha.
Then the two bhikṣus asked, "Venerable Dharmamitra, where are you? He replied, "I am currently in the Supreme Cave;
you should go there at once to see me. Thereupon, the two men proceeded to the upper cave and saw the aforementioned bhikṣu already seated within it. Then one bhikṣu said to his companion: "This..."
"Old bhikṣu, why do you appear to be like those we saw earlier? At that time, a companion bhikṣu who was wise and quick-witted said to him:
"This venerable one is still able to spread his fame; how could he not come here and sit?
He then stepped forward to pay his respects and asked: "Venerable sir, your majestic reputation is rare in this world. For what reason have you come here yourself?"
He bowed and lit a fire for the Sangha. Dharmamitra said, "You should now listen: I have contemplated birth and death;
if my head and hands could be burned for such a long duration, I would indeed burn them all away for the sake of the Sangha."
How much less so for other parts of my body, or even being burned by fire—what difficulty could there be in that?
I recall that in five hundred past lives, I constantly took birth as a dog; emaciated, impoverished, and exhausted, I never once had enough to eat.

However, in the distant past, I encountered a man who was drunk and vomited upon the ground; I ate it and was satisfied. Furthermore, in the past, there were a husband and wife who were making gruel...
When he grew up and went outside, I saw that there was no one there. He put his head into the vessel and ate his fill of the porridge, but his head could not come out.
When the husband and wife returned home, they became angry at the food; they devoured the porridge and immediately severed my head.
For five hundred lifetimes, I received this canine body. Although I was once satiated, I lost my life. Reflecting on this, I realize that birth and death are long-lasting and pervasive.
"In the five realms of existence, one undergoes immeasurable suffering; therefore, I now do not shrink from toil, personally lighting a fire for the sake of the assembly of monks.
When the two bhikṣus heard these words, they deeply contemplated the immeasurable faults and afflictions of birth and death, and immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

The Water Master is responsible for managing the kitchen, the tea room, and the water cisterns in all the halls. He must ensure that they are always kept full and clean. Whatever is required for use must not be allowed to run short;
nor should he be stingy or refuse to provide it, nor should he become angry. As soon as the water buckets have been filled, they should be turned over.
During the summer months, a water filter (parisrāvaṇa) should be placed nearby for the purpose of straining the water. He should follow the assembly through the hall during meal times.

When honored guests arrive or depart, and their luggage is transported, these matters must be handled with clear and personal accountability. Payments for services shall follow the established precedents of the monastery;
those who privately solicit or demand excessive compensation shall be penalized.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* says: "The person you see standing in the water was, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, a renunciant who managed the water for the Saṃgha.
Seeing the monks using water, he would give them only as much as he deemed sufficient for their needs;
he would supplement the water where it pleased him and withhold the remainder from others. By reason of this karma, he has entered hell and stands alone in the water."
He cried out, "Water! Water! and has been enduring great suffering until now, without ceasing.

On the millstone there is both dry [flour] and water. The dry portion is for grinding rice, wheat, and so forth (to be used according to the needs of the storehouse); the water is for making tofu and other such things.
All milling work must be kept clean and orderly; one must not leave it in a mess or trample upon it, nor may one give it away privately to others.

Punishment. ○ Regarding miscellaneous duties, these include serving as the head of the water-tub station: cleaning the *zhaitang* (vegetarian hall) tubs, collecting the tubs for offering rice, cleaning utensils, cleaning the pots, and managing the communal oil and sauces;

preparing side dishes and seasonings for guests; listening to the instructions of the *dianzuo* (superintendent of the kitchen) regarding the menu; entering the storehouse to receive issued goods; and serving meals to the kitchen staff.

Miscellaneous duties also include the *xingtang* (hall attendant) and the *caitou* (vegetable steward) serving the vegetables. In all matters that ought to be performed in the kitchen, one must not [neglect]...
Delegate responsibilities. Diligently change the water in the vessels. ○ Sweep the kitchen, both inside and out, and light the incense and lamps. Serve tea.

Urge the residents of this hall to perform their recitations and ascend to the hall for services. Except for matters of public business, if anyone fails to attend during periods of silence, report it to the Chief Cook (Dianzuo).

On the first and fifteenth days of the month, go to the storehouse to collect offerings for the Kitchen Deity—fruit, incense, and candles—as well as tea leaves for kitchen use. ○ Kitchen Regulations Ten.
[Appointments] must be filled by those who are robust and healthy, and who possess public loyalty and the Way-mind.
Attached are the Kitchen Regulations (in ten articles):
One grain of firewood and one grain of rice—know the hardships from which they come. A drop of water and a scrap of leek-pickles—one must reflect upon the labor required to produce them.
Since it is not easy to avoid wasting the products of Heaven, one should further consider harmonizing the various tastes:
ensuring that the sour and salty are balanced, the fragrant and soft are appropriate, and that cooking is performed with care and gravity, never with negligence.

With the intention of making offerings rather than merely seeking to fill the belly, even while performing communal tasks, one should always maintain the mind of the Way. During the three periods for rice gruel and meals, one must not neglect them for even a single day.
Mistake! During the two sessions of dawn and dusk, what prevents you from practicing pure cultivation for several moments? The inscription says:

“The rice steward of Xuefeng and the kitchen director of Guishan—the fragrant wind of these ancient worthies has not fallen away to this day. Restrain your wild mind; be careful of your verbal transgressions.

When carrying water or hauling firewood, do not forget this very thing. As for sitting in meditation inside the hall or sitting in meditation outside the hall—who knows that the transmission of the robe does not depart from here?”
The water-mill and the millstone: thus, this gate of practice is what the Buddhas and devas delight in. To seek merit one gains it; to create karma one loses it.
Diligence, prudence, integrity, and moral rectitude are the foundations of seeking merit. When the multitude is generally indolent, these are the bases for creating karma.

Adhere strictly to these rules and inscriptions; they shall serve as your good teachers. Regarding those who dwell together in the kitchen: the rice porridge, the main meal, and the light snacks are all kept below in the kitchen; share them equally with the assembly.
It is strictly forbidden to eat privately elsewhere or to keep fresh, delicious food for one's own consumption; those who do so shall be punished.
Those who fail to attend the morning service in the hall shall be punished. Those who steal the monastery’s oil, rice, or other provisions shall be fined double and expelled from the community.
The Vegetable Head (Caìtóu): Washes and cuts vegetables for the assembly; listens to the instructions of the Kitchen Steward (Diànzàozǔ) regarding the preparation of meals and other matters;
assists everyone collectively. Those who fail to do so shall be penalized. The Rice Head (Fàntóu) boils rice and congee for the assembly and washes the pots.

Two rice servers assist in carrying the rice vessels (commonly called "rice trays" [fànbiǎn]). These rice vessels are also washed by the Rice Head. When there is a meal requiring the large cauldron to be opened, three Rice Heads shall attend accordingly.

Appointments shall be assigned accordingly. Those who shirk their duties and cause failures shall be punished. Duties include: attending to the guest dishes; the junior head cook tending the fire; miscellaneous tasks such as washing the pots;

and those who keep private portions shall be severely punished. They must also attend to the sounding of the wooden clapper and the striking of the board, as well as lighting incense before the altar;
those who err in these matters shall be punished. Miscellaneous tasks also include going to the storehouse to fetch guest dishes and [ensuring that] no private portions are stolen.
Those who remain shall be punished severely and expelled from the monastery. Those on duty are exempted. Those who do not follow the communal labor schedule shall be punished.

Those who shout loudly in the kitchen shall be punished. Those who drink alcohol or gamble shall be punished severely and expelled from the monastery. (New addition) Those who smoke shall be punished.
On the day of the vegetarian feast, the remaining tofu and vegetables from the morning hall shall be provided again as evening gruel for the assembly. Failure to do so shall be punished.
It may be discarded; those who violate this shall be punished. One must not pour boiling water onto the ground, as it injures the lives of insects and ants;
those who violate this shall be punished. Incense and lamps shall be used to look after the belongings of the assembly; if anything is lost, the responsible party shall pay restitution.
○ [Date] ○ Recorded again by Abbot [Name] ○ (The above concludes the Sixth Quarters).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Buddhas and Patriarchs of the three periods have all emerged from the gate of practice.
For example, Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun initially served as the rice steward under Deshan; later, he presided over Xuefeng and became a spiritual teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*) for fifteen hundred people.
Likewise, Chan Master Lingyou of Mt. Guiyang in Tanzhou initially served under Baizhang.
The Kitchen Steward (Dianzuo) later resided at Mount Gui (Miaoshan), where he also led a community of fifteen hundred people;

thus, the present regulations cite these two individuals as examples to encourage the practice of solitary wandering. Furthermore, observing the sequences established by the ancients, there was originally no distinction between seniority and juniority, or between internal and external roles.
Yunqi’s *Fahui* states: "Recently, among the young, not even a single finger has been soiled by water, nor have they ever..."
Matters do not concern his heart. When sitting in incense meditation, he says his legs ache; when walking, he says his back hurts.
If he practices diligently day and night, he says, "My body is weak and prone to illness. If questioned further, he replies again: "The fool exerts physical effort;
the wise person exerts the mind. The fool cultivates merit; the wise person cultivates wisdom. Alas! If this is truly what he says, one will see that Kāśyapa...
"Head-of-the-Dhūta is ignorant. The Sixth Patriarch [was appointed] Head-of-Rice for Xuefeng and Huishan; [and] the Head-of-Meals was appointed Head-of-Seats.
Even the Buddha did not abandon the merit of threading a needle; would it not follow that even the Buddha is ignorant? Furthermore, the *Chongxing Lu* (Record of Revered Conduct) says:

Song Dynasty: Yunju Jian. When he first visited Xuedou Chanyue Ying, Ying spoke with him for three days and marveled greatly at his insight. He then instructed him to be diligent in serving the community.
Thereupon, Jian took charge of the well, saying, "While attending to the firewood and cooking, I shall oversee all temple affairs without hindering my reflections on antiquity and the present.
Alas! Such was the lofty spirit of the ancient sages. Hearing this, one is moved to inspiration. However, this is not...
The Head of the Kitchen alone shall provide ten exhortations. All those performing single duties must understand this principle.

When it is time for the annual agricultural tasks such as plowing, sowing, and collecting rents, one must attend the guest hall twice daily to discuss business. Furthermore, one shall oversee the bamboo and timber of the monastery;

if large-scale materials are required for the repair of buildings, [the assembly] must... [if the assembly... *Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of monastic regulations (Biqiujie or similar), likely from a manual on administrative duties within a Chan or Vinaya monastery. The final phrase "若眾" (if the assembly) suggests a conditional clause regarding the mobilization of the community.*

The council shall reach a consensus. Once this is reported to the Abbot and the mandate is received, only then may trees be felled. If one privately cuts down even a single tree, they shall be fined, required to compensate for the loss, and expelled from the monastery.
If one sells wood privately or gives it away to others out of personal favor, they shall be doubled in penalty and expelled.

Regarding all monastic duties, such as cultivation, planting, and the collection of rents, those who are negligent, seek only ease, or fail to manage their affairs with sincerity shall be fined and expelled.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: According to another version, it is supplemented by saying that one must prepare a month’s worth of firewood for the summer rains and several weeks’ worth of fuel for the winter snows;
this is of the utmost importance. When cutting firewood, one must select the site and leave behind tree sprouts so they may grow.
This applies to all activities such as mountain woodcutting and the communal labor of the assembly.
When arriving at a place of practice, one must not steal items such as axes, hatchets, ropes, or shoulder-poles; one should inspect oneself at all times.
Those accustomed to dwelling in deep mountains may keep these tools.

The *Zhishan* (the mountain official; the field manager known as the *Zongguan*; the one who knows the produce) must recognize the permanent assets of the monastery. Boundaries must be clearly defined;
one must not encroach upon or confuse them with those of others, thereby causing disputes. Every spring, the two orders of officials shall assemble to clear and demarcate the boundaries once.
Fields must be plowed and planted in due season; those who are negligent shall be punished. If there is private corruption, the penalty shall be doubled.

The offender shall be punished with expulsion from the monastery. Once the flowers have ceased and the transaction is finalized, the person shall go in person to the storehouse to take formal possession of the items.

All new holders of these offices, as well as those who have held them previously, must inspect the boundaries and become thoroughly familiar with them. They must consume the two daily meals of gruel and rice to prevent theft.
Should a thief be apprehended, they shall be sent to the guest hall for processing; private flogging or punishment is strictly prohibited. Otherwise, [the consequences will be severe].
To initiate trouble. ○ The Mountain Patrol shall follow the duties of the Mountain Administrator. Bamboo, timber, tea, bamboo shoots, and so forth, shall all be supervised by him.

Should anyone be caught stealing bamboo or timber, they must not be released privately; once discovered, they shall be severely punished. As for meals, two sessions of rice gruel and rice shall be provided.
○ The firewood-gatherers (i.e., junior laborers) shall have a fixed daily quota for felling wood; if they exceed this, a bonus shall be added.

Regarding money: if it is insufficient, the account shall be cleared; if there is none at all for the entire day, the cost of the meal shall be deducted. If one clears the mountain to chop firewood, one must consult the person in charge of the mountain for the year’s value;
one may not arbitrarily assume authority over the matter. Firewood and fuel may not be sold privately; if such an act is discovered, the offender shall be penalized and required to compensate.

The tools, such as knives and ropes, must each be provided by oneself. Upon encountering the death of a monk, the coffin shall be carried in rotation; funds for labor and the necessary firewood must also be prepared. These duties are mostly performed by laypeople.
In the mountain quarters (*shānlíáo*), the incense and lamp attendants prepare tea, water, congee, and rice, and tend the charcoal brazier.
On the third day after the full moon, they go to the storehouse to fetch straw sandals. On the first and fifteenth days of the month, they take incense, candles, and tea leaves to perform offerings.
Enter the kitchen and storehouse to take provisions. Sweep and clean one's own quarters. Inspect one's luggage;
should anything be lost or damaged, it must be compensated.
*Regulations for the Mountain Quarters (Seven Articles)* Now, mountain ridges constitute the dragon’s neck of a temple; forests and trees provide the temple’s shade. Trees, bamboo, and flowers...
Fruits are the provisions for the monastic quarters; the earthen ridges and rocky peaks are what the wind and water depend upon.
If nothing is damaged, then the entire temple will flourish, the assembly of monks will find contentment, and they shall dwell in peace.
Therefore, no bamboo or wood may be haphazardly cut down, and no earth or stone may be taken at will. This is the general principle for this mountain retreat. Its...
Other regulations are listed below. Regarding mountain patrols: regardless of wind or rain, one must remain in the mountains at all times, inspecting the surrounding areas above and below.
One must not be negligent, which could lead to incidents such as theft. Those who are lazy or seek only personal comfort shall be severely punished upon discovery.
No bamboo, wood, flowers, fruits, firewood, or grass within the mountains may be sold privately. As for...
Regarding offenders: they shall be severely punished and expelled from the quarters. Junior workers must obey the instructions of the Mountain Overseer.
When felling firewood and branches, one must not arbitrarily cut off the tops of trees, nor clear them entirely so as to leave no seeds behind. Violators shall be punished.
Laborers: If there is business for the monastery, you shall be permitted to be summoned; those who disobey shall be penalized.

Regarding gambling with money in the mountain quarters (*shānláo*), whether monk or layperson, any who violate this rule shall be expelled from the quarters. Regarding fighting or abusing one another in the mountain quarters, whether monk or layperson, any who violate this rule shall be expelled from the quarters.
Those who manage the mountain and oversee the various persons in the mountain quarters must administer rewards and punishments accordingly.
It must be equitable. Those who act with partiality or favoritism shall be punished. ○ [Date] ○ Recorded again by Abbot [Name] (actually posted in the Mountain Hermitage).

The Commentary on the Meaning states: All bamboo and trees in the vicinity of the monastic community that contribute to the scenic beauty of the mountain gate should be nurtured and maintained in full vigor.

By protecting them so they provide dragon-scale shade and conceal the geomantic energies (*fengshui*), the monastic community will flourish daily and the mountain’s vital energy will grow increasingly numinous.
Not only is this a gathering of eminent men, but it is also a magnificent sight.
The *zhishi* (administrator) of the bathhouse is responsible for bathing according to the correct principles, as well as overseeing matters such as medicine for the sick;

alternatively, he may simply manage the utensils within the bathhouse and the firewood and grass required for its use, ensuring these are prepared in advance and kept dry (this belongs to the duties of the *xuzhi*).
An Inscription on the Rules for the Bathhouse (in thirteen articles):
To cleanse thoroughly is not yet the original face; to bathe and purify oneself is still not the person of no station.

Failing to realize that form is emptiness, one merely perceives dust coming from outside the body; it is only when one fully understands cold and warmth that one clearly realizes the original spirituality of one’s own nature.
If there is truly a Chan practitioner who is "unencumbered by even a single thread," they should precisely seek [the truth] right here.

The inscription says: The mountain is lofty and the road is far; thus one brings firewood. Boiling water and lighting the fire, one exerts diligent labor. Those who are ignorant do not understand the matter of bathing.

Do not tighten [the belt] too tightly. Do not laugh or joke while young. Do not pour boiling water over one another. Regarding all such violent and indecent acts, you must forever admonish yourself. Wash your heart and cleanse your thoughts;
renew yourself daily. How shall you repay this kindness? Suddenly realize the cause of water. If this is not yet the case, then for now follow these rules and inscriptions.
On every day of bathing, the bath attendant shall adjust the depth of the water to five inches and manage the preparations accordingly.
Fire. Water heated. Having prepared the master’s station for the bath, burn incense and silently pray that the Holy Sangha will descend to bathe.
After a short while, first invite the Abbot, then invite the honored guests. (3) Strike the wooden gong three times; this is for the Head Officers and the two orders of officials.

(4) Ring the "Head-Notification" gong; this is for the Chan Hall and other hall masters. (5) Ring the second notification gong; this is for the various administrative officers. (6) Ring the third notification gong; this is for the visiting guests and former residents.

For the general bathing (puyu), those who enter before the sounding of the wooden clapper shall be punished. When honored guests arrive, or when bathing is held for the sake of sutra recitations or repentance rites (chan), the order of priority is as follows:

first the honored guests, then the repentance masters (chan-shi), followed by the incense-lighters (xiang-deng) and the ritual assistants; next are those with heavy duties or manual labor, and finally the general bathing.
From the Grain Rain Festival (Guyu) until the Summer Solstice (Xiazhi), a bath is held once every five days. From the Summer Solstice until...
At the commencement of Chu-shu (the beginning of autumn), one bathes once per day. From Chu-shu until Chiu-fen (the autumnal equinox), one bathes once every five days.
From Chiu-fen until Ku-yu (the beginning of spring), one bathes once every half-month. Inside the bathhouse, a small wooden board is hung; when the water becomes cold, strike the board twice.

When the water is hot, strike the wooden board three times; when it requires more water, strike the board once. One must not raise one's voice or shout loudly; those who violate this shall be penalized.

All who bathe must follow the sequence of the sounding of the gong and must not be out of order. Those (holding the list) who are junior in age shall bathe last; those who violate this shall be penalized.
One must not look left and right, nor engage in idle chatter, clamor, or spit.
Regarding punishments, changing clothes, and dressing, each should act with mutual consideration; one must not act with unrestrained license. Those who violate this shall be punished.
When bathing, each should exercise self-restraint; one must not linger in the hall for long, thereby obstructing those who come later. Those who violate this shall be punished.
Those who use soap pods shall be penalized. Those with sores or scabies must each wait their turn and bathe afterward;

they may not bathe first. Violators shall be penalized. The *Sengzhi* (Monastic Steward) shall supervise the bathing and attend to the inspection of all matters. Those who commit violations shall be penalized according to the established regulations.
Those who fail to exercise due oversight shall also be penalized. [Date] Recorded again by the Abbot [Name], [who has personally posted this notice on the wall outside the bathhouse].
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Buddha established the bathhouse so that one might cleanse the physical body (*rūpakāya*) and thereby become capable of bearing the Way.

The Buddha mandated the *poṣadha* (confessional retreat) so that one might purify the body of precepts (*śīlakāya*), whereby concentration and wisdom arise. If one is heedless when approaching the bath, then while the impurities of the body remain uncleansed, the impurities of the mind will first arise;
such a person is one devoid of shame and remorse. Furthermore, those who have entered the Sangha must avoid urinating and bathing in places where others may see them.
"Divine Light. When washing undergarments, do not hang them out in the middle of the road. According to the *Fozu Tongji*:
"The monk Ruyao was at Juehua Temple in Xiachuan. He heard that ancient worthies had dedicated the merit of bathing monks toward rebirth in the Pure Land."
He subsequently established a bathhouse for the assembly of monks until he reached the age of eighty-one. He invited the assembly to drink tea, spoke his final parting words, and passed away.

Based on this, it can be seen that the single matter of bathing yields great merit. Whether through personal devotion or from the monastery’s permanent endowment, one should provide for it as appropriate; it must not be omitted.

Regarding the duties of the *Jingtou* (Cleanliness Head): during the three periods of the day when passing through the hall for meals, he shall lock the rear gate. At the fourth watch, he shall light the path lanterns.

When the assembly recites scriptures or ascends to the main hall for worship, he shall carry the cleaning buckets (*jingtong*) to their respective locations (in the north, where cleaning buckets are often not used, one simply uses the latrines, which must be swept clean). He shall diligently change the hand-washing water and wash and sun-dry the hand towels.

After the evening service concludes, he shall deliver the cleaning buckets back to their respective locations. On days of communal bathing, if there is no designated bath attendant, he shall perform the task himself.
[The duty of] acting as an agent. One may burn the bath cauldron according to the rules of the bathhouse; alternatively, the head gardener (yuántóu) may also take charge of this task.
Regarding the meaning of the term "head cleaner" (jìngtóu): the latrine is the most defiled place, yet one who holds this title possesses both practical and doctrinal significance.
Practically, according to the Vinaya, those who perform this duty are mostly bhikṣus who have broken precepts and are performing penance for their offenses, because they constantly sweep away filth.
Abiding in purity, one can cause the assembly of monks to rejoice; by removing the defilements of broken precepts, one regains pure discipline.
Regarding this principle, the *Mahāyāna-śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "In all instances of excrement and urine, there is also śamatha and vipaśyanā.
As for what is called 'vipaśyanā,' when in a place of impurity, one should form this thought: 'All these impurities are entirely the mind.'"
That which exists is not truly existent. I should now transform this impurity and cause it to become pure.
One should then visualize this foul place as a jeweled pond and jeweled channels, filled with pure scented water or overflowing with ghee and curd.
One visualizes one's own body as a body made of the seven precious jewels; thus, the discarded excrement and urine become fragrant milk, ghee, honey, and so forth. Furthermore, one should know this.

This pure appearance is merely a construction of the mind; its empty form lacks reality. This is called the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). As for what is called the gate of cessation (*śamatha*):

one knows that these impure places and the impure things discarded by the body appear as visible impure signs solely because past evil karma has perfumed the mind. However, this mental perception—[as soon as it arises]...
It is not existent; it is simply this one mind, equal and without thought. This is what is called the gate of *śamatha*. Question:
All the pure and impure phenomena mentioned above, though produced by the mind, all arise from the perfuming of past karma.
How can they be transformed through present-world conceptualization, such that they revolve according to the mind? Answer: The essence of the mind is fully endowed with all phenomena.
Although their nature is such, they do not arise without conditions. Therefore, the filth within a latrine appears due to the manifestation of past karma;
likewise, the jewel-pools of ghee and curd do not manifest without the presence of contributing conditions.

If one can apply a mind of pure perception, it is because the karma of the jewel-pools and ghee has perfumed the mind, and thus the appearance of purity arises. This includes the mind of revulsion and the mind of emptiness-contemplation.
This is the condition for eliminating impurity. Because the mind is perfumed by purity, defiled appearances are extinguished accordingly.
This is likely because past karma has certainly perfumed the mind to give rise to such appearances; likewise, the merit of the present life can also perfume the mind to manifest sublime function.
Thus, in places such as those for excrement and urine, one should employ mental visualization to perfume the mind and transform them; as for the rest, it is the same.

Regarding all pure and impure objects, one must cultivate such mental imagery to transform their habitual perceptions; thus, one can eliminate hatred and attachment in the present moment, and so forth.
Ouyi said: "If one forms the perception of purity regarding excrement and urine, one can eliminate hatred;

if one forms the perception of impurity regarding clean food, one can eliminate attachment. When both hatred and attachment are entirely eliminated, one achieves the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)."
When mental cultivation through visualization reaches maturity, the recollection of dharmas (*dharmānusmṛti*) proceeds accordingly; what worldly expedient could surpass this?
If one can awaken to the source of purity and impurity, then one may awaken to the fact that the great trichiliocosm does not exist outside the mind.

From this point on, defilements are exhausted and the mind is purified, such that one no longer perceives the self as being distinct from the *dharmadhātu*, nor the *dharmadhātu* as being distinct from the self. I...
The body and the dharma-realm are neither one nor two; thus, the three poisons naturally depart and the laws of transgression naturally cease.
This contemplation is not to be practiced only by those who have shaved their heads; all people may practice this contemplation.
Regarding the knowledge of buildings and utensils: one must frequently inspect all structures, including the main halls, monastic quarters, kitchens, and stables.

If any roofs are leaking, they should be repaired promptly; whether it be a renovation or a new construction, one must inform the Superintendent (Jianyuan) in advance so that the necessary arrangements can be made in a timely manner.

Furthermore, regarding the Patriarch’s Stupa and its precincts, branch temples, and even the collapse of roads or the decay of utensils, these matters shall be deliberated upon with the Superintendent.
The Monastery Guest Hall: Repair it promptly. Whenever construction or repairs are undertaken, all matters concerning orientation must be treated with great care;
one should not make alterations lightly. If it is truly unavoidable, one must first consult a highly skilled geomancer (fengshui master) and proceed only after their inspection.
In general, ponds and wells must not be filled haphazardly; pavilions and galleries must not be built indiscriminately; bamboo and timber must not be cut recklessly; and the earth...

If one digs in a disorderly manner, or intentionally pulls, twists, fills, digs, or chops, thereby damaging the wind and water systems, and if the person in charge of the building knows of it, they shall be punished together with the administrator and expelled from the monastery.
If the abbot acts as a stubborn autocrat, the two orders of officials, along with the inner and outer Dharma relatives, shall hold a public deliberation;
if he remains obstinate and headstrong, the abbot shall be replaced. The Construction Supervisor is the deputy official for the person in charge of the building.

If there is no *jiwù* (house supervisor), then the *jiānzhèng* (supervisor of construction) shall oversee the planning, repair, and building, supervising the craftsmen and managing matters such as funds, materials, and timber.
This official must be practiced in manual labor and filled by one who is mature and experienced. (Both of these positions are administrative officials.
[Note: The proof for this meaning is found in the previous section on the *zhùchí* (abbot), under the article concerning the construction of monastic quarters.]

The types of fundraising masters (*huazhu*) vary greatly. In monasteries where resources are meager and there are no endowments, one should invite a master to solicit rice and wheat during years of famine when grain is insufficient.
Alternatively, for the large-scale construction of halls and buildings, one should invite a master to solicit funds for repairs and construction.
Beyond these, there are further masters who solicit for vegetables, salt, straw sandals, incense, candles, and so forth. These are all types of fundraising masters.

In soliciting and collecting funds for offerings, each person shall be assigned a specific area so that there is no overlap; one must only contribute with a spirit of joyful generosity and not through compulsion.
If one acts in accordance with the hearts of others below, one will naturally accord with the Buddha-mind above. In speech and response, one must be particularly dignified and magnanimous.

Should there be even the slightest trace of insincerity or parsimony, the offender shall be doubled in punishment and expelled from the community. In short, such solicitation is undertaken only when it is absolutely unavoidable.

Regarding solicitation for alms: if it can be ceased, then there is no need to establish this regulation. For instance, if there are those who are privately outside the monastery, falsely assuming names to solicit alms, they shall be immediately expelled from the monastery (the above concludes the seventh section).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: Lately, many monasteries have appointed "masters of transformation" (huazhu) and issued extensive fundraising petitions.

The abbot praises them and keeps them under his wing, while the administrators reward their labor with veneration. Consequently, these masters begin to boast of their achievements and deceive the assembly, seizing control of the monastery's affairs;

some even amass private wealth, thereby gravely distorting the law of cause and effect and alienating the faithful donors. During the Buddha’s lifetime, there were various disciples who came from afar...

Upon his return from his travels, the villages he passed through closed their doors upon seeing him from afar. When asked the reason for this, they said it was out of fear of the monks’ solicitation for alms.
Alas! This serves as a warning. They do not understand that what is called "conversion" (hua) refers to transforming others through virtue.

This does not merely refer to soliciting people for their wealth and goods; therefore, one should reflect upon the meaning according to the name. The *Pure Conduct Chapter* of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"Upon seeing one who does not relinquish [others], one should wish that all sentient beings never abandon the dharmas of supreme merit.
