Upon seeing one who is able to relinquish [attachments], one should wish that all sentient beings forever attain liberation from the sufferings of the three evil realms. Based on these two verses, regarding...
If one does not abandon others, one still gives rise to a mind of compassion; how much less would one, having already renounced wealth, harbor a self-interested intent?
Let those who act as masters of transformation know this.
This practice of transforming food differs from that of the former masters of transformation; here, there is merely the transformation of food, yet there remains the act of begging for alms.
This is the late master’s intention. Huayun shall compose a record to ensure the offerings are properly received. This officeholder frequently socializes with others;

therefore, he must not engage in idle wandering or idle talk on this account, nor manage secular affairs, nor converse in private with women in others’ homes, nor engage in the sending and receiving of goods. Those who violate these rules shall be punished.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: A "transformed meal" (huàfàn) is also called a "transformed host" (huàzhǔ). Those who hold this view are mostly close to worldly people;
therefore, it is cautioned that one must not converse with women in private places. This is to avoid public censure externally and to protect one's own mind internally. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
If there is a cause or condition that necessitates entering alone, one should simply maintain single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha.
When preaching the Dharma to women, one should not smile with bared teeth nor expose one's chest. Even for the sake of the Dharma, one should not become intimate;

how much more so for other matters. This is a pressing admonition from the Golden Mouth. Furthermore, the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Upon seeing a person adorned with ornaments, one should make this vow:"

Regarding sentient beings adorned with the thirty-two marks: upon seeing those without adornment, one should wish that all sentient beings abandon all finery and ornaments and fully practice the dhūta austerities.
... and so on, until it says: upon seeing a person of handsome appearance, one should wish that all sentient beings always give rise to pure faith in the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
upon seeing a person of ugly appearance, one should wish that all sentient beings [abandon] unwholesome deeds.
One should not give rise to attachment or delight. Now, women possess many characteristics of physical adornment and beauty;

therefore, these four verses should be kept in mind with great urgency by those who act as preceptors for ordination. Not only the preceptors, but indeed the entire monastic community should also keep them in mind with great urgency.

"Collecting offerings" (shōkū) refers to collecting the alms-food that has already been prepared for distribution. Laypeople offer this food to the *saṃgha*, and the *saṃgha* then offers it to the Buddha;
hence it is called "collecting offerings. This duty is mostly filled by those who have resolved their minds on ascetic practice.

There are also those who engage in this practice for the sake of both [self-interest and the benefit of others]. Generally, within the monastic communities today, it is common to calculate the weight of this rice and provide a certain amount of money for it.
For instance, if one can carry thirty or forty catties of the offerings daily, one may receive a certain sum of money.
Since the money is obtained through physical labor, there is no great fault in it; moreover, because one thereby makes offerings to the Great Assembly, there is merit to be gained.
One should simply act with sincerity and practice with vigor; further details are explained in the regulations below.

Upon collecting the leftover rice, the guest hall shall request the assembly masters to help carry it away (or have laborers carry it). On New Year’s Day, each person shall receive a certain number of administrative office vouchers (*jianyuan dan-tie*).

On the morning of the second day, [the abbot] ate at the upper quarters; the dishes consisted of six varieties, and the silver was six fen. Upon leaving the gate, he delivered a card to congratulate the patron on their birthday.
Regarding the measurement of rice for the permanent residents (changzhu), the rate is two and a half fen of silver per jin. At the beginning of each season, [the accounts are settled].

During the first ten days, the inner and outer [monks] shall request the Sangha to attend; the guest master (kètáng) shall oversee the distribution of robes and bowls, while the storekeeper (kùfáng) and guest master shall record the accounts.
Each month, straw sandals and tofu money shall be distributed: sixty *wén* per person, with half on the second and first days of the month, and the other half on the sixteenth.
When there is a meal, all shall go to the refectory to join the assembly.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Since the task of collecting offerings has been undertaken to replace the labor of the monastic community in begging for alms, one should, through this very act of collecting offerings, investigate the meaning of cultivating one’s own nature.
Now, the noble regulations of the Buddha’s era held that begging for alms alone constitutes right livelihood;
thus, the Sanskrit term *bhikṣu* is translated here as "mendicant" (*qishi*). As for what is meant by "begging," it refers to begging within.
The Dharma is for nourishing one's nature; externally, one begs for food to sustain the body. Regarding begging for food to sustain the body, see the section on "Lower-Grade Almsround" (*bun'e*).

As for "begging you to nourish your nature," the term "begging" (*goku*) here refers generally to that [former] begging. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Śīla-viśuddhi-parivarta*), states:
Entering a village to beg for food, one should wish that all beings enter the profound Dharma-realm with minds free from obstruction.
Upon reaching a doorway, one should wish that all beings enter the gateways of all Buddha-dharmas.

Having entered their homes, one should wish that all beings attain entry into the Buddha-vehicle, which is equal throughout the three periods of time. Based on these three verses, the practice is manifest while the meaning is profound.
This is precisely what one must investigate. What is called "entering the profound Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu) means that within the conventional, the ultimate is revealed;
within phenomena, principle is clarified. The Dharma-realm is the fundamental essence of the bodies and minds of sentient beings.

From the very beginning, it has been luminous, pervasive, vast, empty, and still—a realm of sole reality alone. It possesses no form or appearance, yet it encompasses the myriad phenomena of the universe.
It is a thousandfold and boundless, yet it encompasses and harmonizes all phenomena. It is vividly manifest within the space between the heart and the eyes, yet its form cannot be seen.
It shines brilliantly amidst the realm of sensory objects, yet its principle cannot be divided.
Were it not for the eye of wisdom that penetrates all dharmas and the clear intelligence free from discursive thought, one could not perceive the self-mind as being so utterly unobstructed.
This is called entering the gateway to all Buddha-dharmas; this is called attaining entry into the Buddha-vehicle. It is equal throughout the three periods of time.
Thus one begs for the Dharma to nourish one's nature, receiving offerings all day long yet seeing no offerings received.
Throughout the day one undergoes toil and hardship, yet no trace of such toil or hardship is perceived. Regarding the merit and wisdom [thus gained], how could they be conceived?
This is what is meant by the principle of "receiving offerings."

Appendix: Regulations for the Receipt of Offerings (Total of Eighteen Articles) The Buddhas of the three periods all emerged from the gate of practice. This being the case, the duty of receiving offerings involves carrying water and dragging mud, braving cold and enduring heat;
truly, those who do not offer their hearts sincerely to the assembly, or who do not constantly maintain the aspiration for the Way, cannot bear this duty. As the ancients said: [text continues]

It is said: To gather the offerings of the donors from the ten directions, to increase their merit and wisdom, and to bring the assembly of monks from the ten directions to fulfillment in their spiritual practice—this cannot be achieved without one who has made the Great Vow.

Having already made the vow and undertaken this practice, one must raise the banner of diligence, don the armor of patience, mount the wheel of long endurance, and harbor a heart of altruistic relief; then, the future rewards of merit will come naturally.

You have surpassed others; yet I fear that as days pass, decline may arise. If thoughts of negligence should emerge, what was intended to become the cause for attaining Buddhahood may instead become the warrant for hell—by then it will be too late for regret.

Therefore, strict regulations are required to preserve your resolve. We now specially dispatch two heads of the quarters to oversee matters morning and evening, acting with impartiality and vigilance.
Any transgression must be reported: minor matters shall be reported to the Guest Hall, while major matters shall be reported to the Abbot.

Venerable Sir. If the head of the quarters knowingly conceals [a transgression] and it is subsequently discovered by others through investigation, he shall be punished equally. The regulations are as follows; each should observe them accordingly.
Those who slander the permanent property of the monastery while outside shall be severely punished and expelled from the hall.

Upon returning from collecting offerings, wash your feet and return to the quarters to sit in meditation. You must not engage in idle chatter or intrude upon the quarters. Violators shall be punished equally.
Conduct. Those who quarrel with one another shall be severely punished. The rice tubs are repaired once every year at the beginning of the New Year.
Those who recklessly damage them and repeatedly demand repairs shall be punished. Those who incite strife or disturb the community and the assembly shall be expelled from the monastery.
For all matters, one must first inform the Head Monk (Tou Dan), who then transmits the report to the Abbot (Shang Fangzhang). Violators shall be punished.
Privately soliciting wealth or exchanging rice for money shall result in expulsion from the community.
If one neglects the communal meal due to attending to private affairs, they shall be penalized. If one loses their meal-bearer’s load due to wind, rain, cold, or heat, they shall be penalized.

Those who engage in quarrels or cause disturbances outside the monastery shall be punished. Those who give away the monastery’s bamboo, wood, flowers, fruits, or other property to others shall be punished.

Those who do not eat their meals in accordance with the community, those who waste resources, those who privately transport firewood or water from the monastery’s supplies, and those who privately prepare food or drink within their quarters shall be punished.
Furthermore, those who fail to collect the daily offerings without a valid reason shall be punished.

For such [offenses], the penalty shall be equal to the number of meals [involved]. If one is ill, one may request another person to act as a substitute; however, if the illness does not improve within half a month, the responsibility for the meal must be borne by both parties.

Those who violate this shall be penalized. Those who privately allow monastics or laypeople to stay overnight in their quarters to eat and sleep, or who go out privately to stay overnight elsewhere, or who give food to others, shall be penalized.
Those who speak or laugh loudly outside the quarters, or who go about bare-chested and wearing only trousers during the summer months, shall be penalized.
Any who violate the rules of the quarters shall be punished equally if the head monk fails to report them.

Those who strike the gong for rice or gruel without waiting for it to be sounded, or who consume the leftovers of the three meals or the vegetable rice without immediately returning to the kitchen, or who return at an improper time, shall be punished.
Dated [Year, Month, Day], recorded again by the Abbot [Name] (to be actually posted in the center of the Kitchen for Receiving Offerings).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: During the Buddha’s lifetime, wandering for alms was the established rule. However, in this eastern land today, offerings are extremely meager;
the food provided by several households is insufficient to sustain even a single monk. Furthermore, the monastic community is large and diverse, lacking any semblance of dignified decorum.

If they were to wander together for alms as prescribed, it would inevitably alarm the public and hinder their spiritual practice. Therefore, this regulation was established to represent the community.
This refers to begging for alms. However, since receiving offerings relieves the labor of the community, how could the monastics enjoy them with a sense of ease?

Therefore, the Vinaya prescribes that when receiving food, one must maintain the five reflections (*pañca-vipaśyanā*). The five reflections are: (1) Calculating the amount of labor expended and reflecting upon the source from which it came; (2) ... [text continues] ...

(3) Reflect upon one’s own virtuous conduct to determine whether it is complete or deficient regarding the worthiness of receiving offerings. (4) Guard the mind to remain free from faults, taking the abandonment of greed and other afflictions as the primary principle.
(5) This food is truly a wholesome medicine for healing the withered body. One should accept this food in order to accomplish the work of the Path.

Through these five reflections, one’s practice will correspondingly advance and the work of the Path can be accomplished. As it is said: "The body depends on food to abide; the Path is cultivated by means of the body."
In this way, one may hope not to squander the offerings of the faithful; otherwise, it will be difficult to avoid having to repay them. The *Secret Essentials of the Chan School* states:
Formerly, after Venerable Deva had attained the Dharma, he arrived at the kingdom of Kapilavastu. There was an elder named Brahmā Viśuddha.
One day, mushrooms grew from the trees in his garden, as large as fungi, and their flavor was exceedingly sweet and delicious. Only the elder [and...]
The second son, Rāhula, took the food; once he had taken it, his body grew accordingly, such that his other relatives were unable to eat it.
Deva, knowing the karmic cause from a previous life, went to the house. When the elder asked him the reason for this, Deva said: "Did you ever provide alms to a bhikṣu?
However, this bhikṣu’s insight into the Path was not yet clear; he falsely consumed the offerings of the faithful. As for the retribution...
"It is for mushrooms. Only you and your son have made such diligent and thorough offerings that you are permitted to enjoy them.
He asked the elder his age, and he replied, "Seventy-nine. Ti said, "If one studies the Way without penetrating its principles, one will return to the state of a lay donor upon rebirth;
you shall be eighty-one, and this tree will not grow. Later, it was exactly as he had predicted. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: "It would be better..."
"With this mouth, one shall constantly swallow hot iron balls and great torrents of fierce fire for hundreds of thousands of kalpas;
one shall never, with this mouth of broken precepts, consume the food of a hundred flavors offered by faithful donors.
Such are the sincere words of all Buddhas. Those who receive offerings from the Sangha should reflect upon them themselves.

The *zhuangzhu* (estate master) is also called the *jingzhu* (quiet-room master), for he is the master of the quiet room. In common parlance, he is known as the head of the lower monastery (*xiayuan*).
He is solely responsible for all matters concerning the estate and fields; the boundaries of the fields, the monastic buildings, and the farming implements are all under his inspection and repair.

Minor matters are to be delegated by him as circumstances require, but those involving major principles must be reported to the permanent community (*changzhu*) for a formal decision. [He shall] collect...

Regulations for Rent Collection: First, ensure fairness so that neither the landlord nor the tenant suffers loss. If a tenant is to be replaced, one must first investigate the character and circumstances of the prospective tenant;
only after reaching an agreement with the permanent residents (the monastic community) may they be permitted to take possession of the land. Do not covet small profits at the expense of others.
Yet, by distributing [the goods] according to private whims, one brings about future calamities. Regarding the supervision of collection:

whenever rent, interest, grain, rice, or other items are received or disbursed, they must be handed over and received in detail; errors must not be permitted. One must not report more as less, nor report less as more.

In all matters of collecting rent, both the steward (*shōzu*) and the supervisor of collection (*kanjū*) hold this responsibility. These two offices are prone to many abuses; therefore, those appointed must be upright, incorruptible, and experienced.

Those who have long since resolved to serve as assistants to the abbot shall fill these positions (under the old regulations, the *zhuangzhu* and *jianshou* were all classified as "listed officials," but they have now been changed to "sequential officials").
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* says: "As for the person you see in the first stage, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was an ordained monastic.

He planted crops for his own private use within the fields belonging to the Saṃgha without compensating the Saṃgha for their value. At that time, a monk who upheld the Vinaya reprimanded him according to the precepts, saying:
'Why do you now fail to compensate the Saṃgha for its value? This man, at that time, relied upon and took refuge with the king..."
He was stubborn and refused instruction. He replied to the bhikṣus, "I am your slave; if you have the strength, why do you not plant for yourselves?
Because of these causes and conditions, he has been undergoing the sufferings of the Fire Hell until now, without ceasing.
As for the person you see in the second hell, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a layman who planted in the saṅgha-field but did not pay the saṅgha the value of his labor. Because of this—
For these reasons, one falls into hell and becomes a great mound of flesh, undergoing various sufferings and afflictions that do not cease even to this day.
One who manages a garden must cultivate the grounds throughout the four seasons so they do not fall into ruin. All produce must be irrigated at the proper times;

do not allow things to exist in name only without substance, failing to provide for the great assembly. Regarding all seasonal fruits, melons, vegetables, and the like, [they must be cultivated with care...]

(Private Conduct): First, regarding eating [forbidden food]. Or, privately selling or sending garden vegetables. If these are discovered, there shall be severe punishment. The *Zhengyi* (Exegesis on the Meaning) states:

The "Chapter on Pure Conduct" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Upon seeing someone tending a garden, one should wish that all sentient beings, within the garden of the five desires, weed out the grasses of craving.
Based on this single verse, the principle is revealed through the phenomenon. Therefore, for one who serves as a head gardener, it is not [permissible].
One must simply exert all effort in weeding and planting; likewise, one may give rise to the Great Mind and thereby attain realization of the Great Way.
According to Zen records, there was once a garden overseer under the assembly of Master Liangshan Guan. Although he had attained realization, many among the monastics did not believe him.
One day, a monk went to provoke him, seeking to elicit some sign of his realization, and asked:
"Head Gardener, why do you not go out and ask the Abbot for one or two sayings to form a karmic connection? The Head Gardener said, "I will certainly not go out to ask.
If I were to go, I would have to force that old fellow off his meditation seat and make him stand on the ground.
By the time Yangshan was about to ascend the hall, the Head Gardener indeed went out and asked, "How is it when 'the house-thief is difficult to guard against'? Yangshan said, "Recognize him."
"Attaining [this] does not constitute being an enemy. Tou asked, "After one has recognized it, what then? Shan said, "Exile him to the realm of non-arising.
Tou asked, "Is this not the place where he establishes his dwelling and sustains his life?
Shan said, "Dead water does not harbor dragons. Tou asked, "What is a dragon of living water? Shan said, "It stirs up waves but does not create billows. Tou asked, "Suddenly..."
"But when the torrents pour down and the peaks collapse—how is it then?
Liangshan indeed stepped down from his Dharma seat, seized him, and said, "Dharma brother, do not let it soak the corner of this old monk’s cassock. Dahui Zonggao said:
"One must know that when one who has attained awakening meets another who has attained awakening, the natural interplay of granting and seizing can be observed. Alas! That too is a garden."
This is the Preface. His speech was such that people found it agreeable; why has it not been so lately?
Attached hereto are the Rules for the Garden Quarters (in nine articles):

Toiling with self-sacrifice, cultivate according to the Dharma. In the garden there shall be vegetables available throughout the four seasons; there shall be no plot of ground even three feet wide left uncultivated.
Upon this unplowed land, one diligently irrigates day after day and laboriously weeds and hoes morning after morning. Above, offerings are made to the Triple Gem, accumulating immeasurable merit;
below, they satisfy the mouths of the multitude, establishing universal causes and conditions. One should reflect upon letting go of all attachments.
Do not be indolent or negligent. All monastic regulations must be faithfully observed. Those who privately sell vegetables and other items shall be censured and expelled.

Those who privately give things to others or consume them privately shall be fined and required to make restitution. Those who lose tools, implements, seeds, or other such items shall compensate for their value.
If the head of the work detail leads the group in cultivation and there is any shirking or theft, [the penalty shall be applied].
Peace. Should anyone wander outside or fail to obey instructions, they shall be reprimanded and expelled from the quarters, and their status as head of the unit shall be revoked.

On each person’s turn of duty, if they shirk from serving rice porridge, meals, tea, or water, they shall be penalized. If irrigation is neglected at the appointed time, or if duties are performed in name only without substance, they shall be penalized.
Regarding the private taking of vegetables, gourds, or other items from various quarters, the head of the unit [shall be held accountable].
Regarding the showing of favoritism: those who privately grant permission without informing the permanent residents (changzhu) shall be punished equally.

Those who invite monks or laypeople to their quarters and provide them with private meals of gruel and rice shall be punished. Those who engage in such matters as consuming meat or alcohol, or gambling, shall be reprimanded and expelled.
As stipulated in the preceding article, if there is an offense, the Head of the Hall (Tou-dan) shall raise it. Those who know of it and fail to do so shall be punished equally.
[Date] Recorded again by the Abbot [Name] (actually posted in the Garden Quarters).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: According to the Vinaya, personally cultivating fields and gardens is a grave violation of the Buddha’s regulations.

Nevertheless, at the end of the Dharma, when the means of livelihood are difficult to secure, there are circumstances that render such actions unavoidable. Once one has accepted this responsibility, one must consider that the physical bodies of the Great Assembly depend upon it;

indeed, it is intimately connected to their spiritual life (*prajñā-jīvita*). One should therefore manage it with sincere intent and labor upon it with diligent effort, so that—perhaps—[the community may flourish].

One will be without shame and will likewise receive abundant merit and reward. If one can take this analogy of the field and apply it to one’s own mental field—the ground of the mind—then both merit and wisdom may be attained together.
As stated in the seventy-seventh fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the verses of Maitreya praising Sudhana:
"Sudhana beholds that the mental fields of sentient beings are extremely overgrown and defiled; to remove the thorns of the three poisons, the Honored One seeks their benefit."
Jñānaprasthāna. Now I shall again explain this in verse: My mind is like a field, wherein no seed is not received.
Whether green, yellow, white, or black, each grows according to what is sown. Bodhi is likened to a fine grain; once planted, there will be a harvest.
Upholding the precepts serves as the sturdy embankment; do not forget the aid of patience. Use generosity as the manure and irrigation; use diligence as the weeding hoe.
Wisdom is like rain and dew; when it arrives in season, it provides nourishment and moisture. Cultivating the mind is like tending a field:
if it falls into neglect, the sprouts will wither. If one does not violate this analogy, one is said to know the field.

Appendix: Agreement for the Attendants of the Lower Monastery (i.e., the Abbot’s Steward and the Garden Master; called the "Lower Monastery" because their residence is somewhat distant; in all nine articles).
Now, although the Lower Monastery is a place of labor, one should not forget spiritual cultivation while there, lest one fail the heart of renunciation.
Do not say that there is nothing to be accomplished beyond the duties of service; you must know that carrying water and hauling firewood are [the very practice of the Way].

This is not a Buddhist practice. While pounding rice to make meals, you should precisely seek the Way through inquiry. Throughout antiquity, there were many eminent practitioners among those who lived alone;
even those of dull and simple nature were each able to recite the Buddha’s name. You must all exert yourselves and do not fail your original resolve.
Since you have become members of this family of Dharma, you should strictly observe the ancestral instructions. I trust you will understand this and not bring shame upon our lineage.
When the donor arrives, the head of the lower monastery shall carefully manage all items and temporarily suspend them one by one according to their inventory.
He shall then send word to the workers while simultaneously attending to the donor with proper ritual hospitality.
The communal living regulations are the same as those for permanent residents; they must be observed uniformly. Those who violate them shall be penalized.

The administrative staff consists of six positions: the Master of the Estate (*zhāngzhǔ*), the Head of the Ledger (*tiē'àn*), the Garden Steward (*yuántóu*), the Fire Steward (*huǒtóu*), the Water Steward (*shuǐtóu*), and the General Affairs Officer (*záwù*).

Each position receives a fixed amount of salt and rice monthly and a specific sum of silver per quarter, according to the established standards of each household. During vegetarian feasts, double offerings (*shuāngqīn*) are provided.

Master of the Monastery: All matters, great and small, of the lower quarters are under your exclusive jurisdiction; your responsibility is therefore extremely grave. Aside from official business, you are not permitted to leave the premises.
Morning and evening, you must lead the assembly in recitation and prayer without negligence. You are forbidden from privately hosting guests for meals or lodging.
Should any of the attendants commit an offense, minor infractions shall be met with instruction, while serious ones shall be reported to the permanent establishment for deliberation.
The Punisher (Fashi) oversees the preparation of meals for the assembly in the lower hall, supervises the sounding of the wooden clappers and gongs, and cleans the kitchen area;

he shall recite the liturgical texts together with the assembly along with the Water-Head and Fire-Head. The Garden-Head (Yuantau) manages the garden grounds, planting crops according to the seasons, ensuring they are not neglected or left fallow;
he also serves as the Cleanliness-Head (Jingtou) and assists the Fire-Head in tending the bath cauldrons. The Fire-Head (Huatau)...
Extinguish the coals and handle fire and candles with extreme care; even in the cold, taking fire is strictly forbidden. Those who violate this shall report the offense to the Abbot and be penalized.
The Water Master shall also assist with splitting wood. The Assistant Manager of Miscellaneous Duties shall oversee the refectory, as well as general cleaning and sweeping, and manage the gates.

They may go to the monastery’s permanent property (changzhu) to take items, provided they are authorized by the monastery officials—specifically the Prior, the Assistant Steward, the Guest Prefect, and the Storekeeper.
[etc. There are circumstances in which it is permitted to eat and rest in the lower quarters; otherwise, all disturbances are strictly forbidden.

Should anyone violate this, the head of the estate shall report the matter to the permanent community (chángzhù), and the offender shall be penalized. ○ [Date] ○ Recorded again by the Abbot (Name) (to be pasted in the lower quarters).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The lower hall is separated by a somewhat greater distance, and thus shares in the same hardships.

Although it does not extensively accommodate many worthy individuals, it is in truth one body with the upper hall in both its great and small aspects. Someone asks: "Since those in the lower hall are occupied with manual labor, their minds cannot be divided;

yet the Pure Rules (Qinggui) command them to practice cultivation—what does this mean? The answer is: If one considers silent sitting and contemplation to be the primary practice, [then this is what is meant].
Those whose conduct and actions are deemed improper will inevitably encounter obstacles wherever they go. The *Record of Yunqi’s Revered Conduct* states:
During the Song dynasty, Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben studied under Yong’an Sheng. Sheng held him in high esteem, and disciples flocked to him like clouds.
Ben wore tattered clothes and had a soiled face; he performed the duties of a cook to provide for them, and at night he would enter the master’s room.
In the *Sanchao* (Notes on the Path), Sheng asked: "The *dhūta* who bears the burden of the assembly undergoes great hardship; are you also weary? Ben replied:

"If one were to abandon even a single dharma, it could not be called the fulfillment of bodhi. Since I must personally realize it in this very life, how could I dare speak of weariness? Master Lianchi said:
"He manages the affairs of the community without hindering his deliberations on the ancients and moderns; he oversees the kitchen hearth without obstructing his entry [into meditative practice]."
In the chamber of the practice hall (sammado), the śramaṇas now receive offerings with their hands folded [in idleness], saying:

"We are those who cultivate the Way; they are those who perform worldly tasks. How is this different from the ancients? Therefore, the Way declines day by day. (The above concludes the Eighth Chamber).

The Head of the Quarters (formerly, the various administrative officers of each hall were appended to the end of their respective sections; however, as this present section does not pertain to those halls, it is listed separately here).

In ancient times, he was in charge of the scriptures, ritual implements, tea, soup, firewood, and charcoal for all the quarters, as well as requesting and distributing supplies, sweeping, washing, shaving hair, providing racks for robes, and towels.
Nowadays, his primary responsibility is the *Danguo Hall* (also known as the *Yunshui Hall*). For all guests...

When the guest master arrives, they receive him with formal courtesy. One person escorts him to the east and another to the west to show him his quarters, while instructing him on the regulations for visiting masters, the monastic tradition of the monastery, and the character of the resident monks—all of which rest upon the charge of the *liàoyuán* (cell master). One must select a senior practitioner of long-standing cultivation to serve in this role.
Appendix: Rules for the Guest Quarters (i.e., the Yun-shui Hall; total of thirteen articles).
If you can let go here, there is no hindrance to knowing your home right where you are. Tomorrow you will carry it away again; as before, the path of Stonehead is slippery.

Staying for but one night, the roles of guest and host are clearly defined. Joining the assembly for the three meals, you must provide for both the refined and the coarse. The mountain streams and peaks...
These are each distinct; ultimately, they are not the final causes and conditions. Though the clouds and moon may be the same, this is not yet the news of having arrived home.

If you do not understand this point, I shall briefly offer this small incense as an offering to my fellow practitioners. Cultivate pure deeds together; you must both reach the goal during the two daily recitations.

If you can stay, stay—be careful not to waste time in delay. If you wish to go, go at once—do not trouble yourself with deliberation. You must know that one carries the books upon a satchel and a staff upon the back.
To clarify your own practice: do not find comfort in physical ease, nor be lax when your strength is exhausted.
The Cloud Hall and the Meditation Hall must both be established according to the same standard. As for one’s own mind and nature, what hindrance is there to invoking them at any time?
All regulations are carefully listed below. Regarding the assignment of quarters in this hall, one shall be assigned to the east and one to the west. For all recitations and seated meditation:

The incense periods for cessation and tranquility, as well as all other matters, shall follow the regulations of the meditation hall. During the two periods of morning and noon, the board and incense are struck;

in the evening, after four sticks of incense have burned following the opening of the Great Cessation (dàjìng), the session is dismissed. Those who violate these rules shall be penalized. Furthermore, those who are found idling outside the premises on a daily basis shall be penalized.

Those who talk or laugh while others are sleeping shall be punished. Arriving near noon, one partakes of the midday meal with the assembly. Arriving near evening, one partakes of the evening congee with the assembly.

If one arrives after these times have passed, they shall eat as a supplement. If one arrives late in the evening, they stay for one night; on the following day at the midday meal, they depart. If it rains, one waits until the rain ceases.
If one is ill, one waits until the illness has healed. For those who arrive in a sedan chair due to illness, their background and circumstances shall be investigated and distinguished.

At the appointed time, the *fangna* (attendant) shall immediately record the names on the register and maintain a separate ledger. If there are those among the assembly who do not observe the pure rules (*qinggui*), the head of the quarters (*liaoyuan*) shall offer kind exhortation;

if they do not listen, he shall report this to the assembly for investigation and require them to kneel before the incense burner (*guixiang*). Those who refuse to comply shall be reported to the guest hall (*keting*) to have their quarters transferred.
If anyone bypasses the assembly and directly engages in disorderly shouting or abusive cursing, they shall be punished; those who engage in physical assault shall receive severe punishment.
The incense and lamp master of the main hall shall attend to the tea and water for visiting masters. In the absence of a *liàoyuán* (head of the quarters), he shall assume overall supervision.

Those who leave the monastery grounds without permission and fail to return to the hall within a reasonable time shall be penalized. Those who hear the general gong and do not join the assembly in going out to labor shall be penalized.
Those whose deportment is not orderly and solemn shall be penalized. Those who smoke shall be penalized. (New addition: those who eat...)
Those who drink alcohol shall be expelled from the monastery. Those who discuss the merits, faults, strengths, or weaknesses of various masters and scholars shall be penalized.

Those who indulge in displaying their intellectual sharpness (*jīfēng*) shall be penalized. When passing through the hall or ascending to the Dharma Hall, those who do not wear their robes shall be penalized (except for those who have not yet received the precepts).

When departing, observe whether there are among the assembly any elderly or infirm individuals traveling alone who may be in need; report this to the Guest Hall so that they may be provided with convenient escort.
If anyone is encountered whose tracks are suspicious or whose speech is evasive, one must immediately conduct a detailed interrogation;
for there may be a rogue posing as a guest who could incite disaster. Those who fail to investigate with thoroughness shall be punished.
Recorded anew on [Day] [Month] [Year] by the Abbot, [Name].
The Commentary on the Meaning states: Among the monastics of the ten directions, there are two types: those who remain in residence and those who travel as itinerant monks (*xingjiao*).

Those in residence dwell in the meditation hall; those traveling as itinerants are settled like drifting clouds and flowing water. Among them, some have thoroughly realized the Great Matter and travel according to conditions;

some have not yet clarified their own matter and seek out teachers and friends; and some find that their karmic conditions do not coincide with their current circumstances and thus seek out other masters.

Regarding those with knowledge [of the Way]: there are those who come to the mountain to offer incense and partake in the merit of shared affinity; there are those who delight in wandering by nature and do not do so solely for the sake of the Path.
Once they have arrived at this place, all must be received. Those appointed as the Head of the Quarters (Liaoyuan) should attend to them with their whole heart.
As it is said, "Those with affinity dwell together"; in principle, one ought to be harmonious, magnanimous, and generous, for only then can one guide and transform others.
"Three. If there are those who truly seek to resolve the matter of birth and death and have resolved their minds to cultivate the Way, they shall be led to the Guest Hall (kètáng) to request a bed.

The Guest Hall will then inform the Abbot (zhùzhí), who will send them into the Meditation Hall (cántáng) or another quarters. For a monastic community (cónglín) to flourish or decline depends solely on whether it has the right people;
thus, the six harmonies (liùhé) prevail in their shared residence, and no discordant words are heard from without. As for the name of the hall being 'Dānguò' (Passing the Night):"
The meaning is that he arrives late and stays for two nights; on the following day at the midday meal, he departs.
As for his being renamed "Cloud and Water" (Yunshui), it takes up the image of having no fixed destination for either coming or staying.

The *xiánzhù* (literally "idle-dweller"; refers to a senior monk who resides in the empty quarters and has no administrative duties; "senior" means elderly, while "former" means one who formerly served in administration and has rendered service to the monastery).

He must remain entirely secluded (*quánpō*; being elderly, he is exempted from labor). For all recitations, he follows the assembly. If entering the hall for sitting meditation (*zuoxiāng*), he acts according to the hall regulations.

When receiving food in the refectory, as well as during recitations and circumambulations of the Buddha, once he has finished his duties in the Zen hall, he must not intrude or wander about at will when there is no business. This is because:
In the monasteries of antiquity, there were no single quarters or solitary beds.

Therefore, these private rooms are permitted only for those who are elderly and have nowhere else to go, or for those who have served as administrators for a long time and request to retire due to physical exhaustion.
Even so, they must be those who have read the Tripitaka, practice mindfulness of the Buddha, and perform prostrations; otherwise, they are not permitted.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* says: "As for the first mound of flesh you see, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was the senior monk (*sthavira*) of the Saṃgha.
He was unable to practice meditation or recite the scriptures, nor did he maintain the precepts. He ate his fill and slept soundly, engaging only in useless talk.
When fine delicacies were offered as alms, he consumed them before the others. Due to these causes and conditions, he has entered the earth."
In prison, one is made into a great mound of flesh, suffering under the burning fire without ceasing even to this day.

Regarding the Rules for the Hall of Venerable Elders (Note: "Venerable Elder" [qijiu] differs from "Senior Monk" [qisu]. "Old" [jiu] refers to those who are aged and have long resided there; "Senior" [su] refers to those who are elders of virtuous character):
The Hall of Venerable Elders in the monastic groves was the ancient "East Hall" (commonly called the "Hall of the Aged"). Anyone entering this hall must give rise to a sense of shame.

One should feel shame. One should contemplate this body: the eyes grow dim and the ears deaf; the hair turns white and the face wrinkles; the back becomes hunched and the waist bent; the bones ache and the tendons contract;
one’s gait becomes faltering and the spirit grows clouded and obstructed. Thus, one knows that this body will not last long and must inevitably enter the gate of death.
The path ahead is vast and desolate; where, in the end, shall one go? If one has already accomplished one's own task, there is no need for much further talk. But if it is not yet so...

However, those who have maintained the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) and reached seventy years of age, provided they have lived with careful cultivation and remained free of transgressions while at the monastery, may be admitted.
Those aged eighty shall be admitted after due consideration; for those aged ninety, no such consideration is required.
Regarding the medicine, food, and drink required by these elders, the storekeeper, the head cook, and the steward shall be punished if they are stingy and refuse to provide them.
In truth, it is not appropriate to withhold [food]. One must clarify matters before the assembly; if there is partiality based on private bias, the offender shall be punished.
For elderly persons who have lost their teeth, if they are unable to eat hard food along with the rest of the community, soft and well-cooked food should be provided separately.

Elderly persons in decline need not attend the morning service, but they must attend the evening service with the community; those who do not attend shall be punished. This applies to those aged eighty.
Regarding the measurement of the hall: the ninety [cubits] are the standard diameter. Within the hall, there is frequent clamor and dispute;
furthermore, those who go out on excursions to cause trouble must leave the hall. Serving as an attendant in the Hall of the Elder (Lao-tang) is more arduous than at other locations.

Beyond lighting lamps, drawing water, sweeping, and washing clothes, one must additionally attend to tasks such as assisting the elderly and preparing medicinal decoctions. Therefore, one must be vigorous, robust, and strong to undertake this.
Those who are senior in years shall fill these positions. Once filled, those who are negligent or seek only personal ease shall be punished.
○ [Date] ○ Abbot [Name] records this anew. (The above concludes the Ninth Quarters.)

The Commentary on the Meaning states: "Venerable Elder" (*sthavira*) is a title for one of high virtue and seniority in years. In this context, one may simply be called a "venerable elder" based solely on seniority in years.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* says: from zero summer retreats up to nine summer retreats, one is called a junior monk (*navaka*);

from ten summer retreats up to nineteen summer retreats, one is called a middle-ranking monk (*madhyama*); and from twenty summer retreats up to forty summer retreats, one is designated a senior monk (*sthavira*). Five...

Those with ten years or more of summer retreats (*varṣa*) who are revered by the monastic community are collectively termed "venerable elders" (*sthavira*). This is based on the calculation of the sequence of ordination years;

since one receives full ordination at twenty, reaching seventy years of age constitutes the rank of a venerable elder. However, the establishment of monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*) was originally intended for the aged and the infirm.
In the *Cánlín Bǎoxùn* (Precious Instructions from the Zen Forest), Gāo'ān said: "I, this poor monk, have often perused the Tripitaka teachings."
Upon careful examination of the Buddha’s intent, he did not permit bhikṣus to sit and receive food without exertion, as this gives rise to a lazy mind and the view of a self.
Every morning, they should carry their alms bowls to beg for food, making no distinction between the noble and the lowly; all such acts can plant the seeds of merit.

Later, what was called "permanent property" (sangha-āstha) was originally established for those who were elderly or ill and unable to go begging; it was not intended for the young and strong to consume.
Since the passing of the Buddha, these [monasteries] have reached our Middle Kingdom; those deemed capable were appointed to them, and thus they received offerings.

The gains and sustenance obtained were pooled together as *caityas* (public monasteries) to provide for a vast assembly. Now, I hear that the abbots of several monasteries do not recognize cause and effect;
they fail to care for the elderly and the infirm, acting contrary to the Buddha’s intent and weakening the Dharma-gate. If they do not reside in their monasteries, when they grow old...

Peaceful Return. Formerly, when the World-Honored One was in the world, he would sometimes not attend invitations, but instead would traverse the monastic quarters to visit the elderly and the infirm, inquiring after each one personally.
He further exhorted the bhikṣus to show mutual respect, and so forth. This is indeed a model for consoling the elderly and the infirm.

The Abbot shall offer pure water at the fourth watch of the morning. He shall burn incense and wait for the completion of the great bell. Upon lighting the candles and striking the wooden clapper, he shall offer gruel.

After three strikes of the chime, the gruel service concludes; he shall then wipe away dust, arrange the tables and altars with solemn purity, and sweep the Buddha Hall as well as the corridors and the vermilion courtyard.
Any surplus incense or candles from the lay devotees must be retained for use during communal recitations and shall not be sold privately.

Send [the items] out. At noon, strike the wooden clapper for the midday meal offering. In the evening, light the glass lamps. On the first and fifteenth days of the month, as well as on festival days, prepare the morning service by placing the gongs, cymbals, and small drums in the hall in advance.

Whenever making offerings or returning them after an offering, if there is a scripture recitation or ritual assembly (*jingchan*), go to the Vestments and Alms-bowl Office (*yiboliao*) to receive the ornamental ritual implements.
Inspect each one individually to ensure they are accounted for, and arrange them neatly. Carefully attend to the lamps and candles. When the scripture recitation and ritual assembly are concluded:
Each point is clearly illuminated and returned to its original place. Upon emerging halfway down the slope, the Buddha and sacred images are wiped once every half-month and bathed once a year;
the rules for bathing the Buddha are as seen previously. If one carries a bell, refer to the ninth section on ritual implements below.

○ Regarding the method for cleaning the Dharma Hall and tending the incense and lamps: The interior and exterior of the hall must be kept clean and pure. The Abbot shall perform his rites and spread out the rush mats at morning and evening.

Incense is burned and lamps are lit; at night, the lanterns along the corridors are lit. The "Great Silence" (dàjìng) is opened and extinguished accordingly. At dawn, the fourth board is struck and the lights are lit; they are extinguished when day breaks.

When the assembly enters the hall for formal teaching, the attendant strikes the great drum. The *pósì* (hall supervisor) oversees half of the duties, while the others follow the assembly through the hall during the meal services.

Recite [the scriptures]. At the main hall (Zanglou), burn incense and light lamps at both morning and evening services; prepare tea and water; sweep and clean; inspect the luggage of the masters reciting the Tripitaka; partake of the two meals;
and when attending the morning assembly, strike the great bell. For all offerings, take the offerings and return them as offerings;

any remainder is treated the same as for the incense and lamps in the Dharma Hall. The inner stupa master is solely responsible for the incense and lamps of the Buddha stupa, as well as sweeping and cleaning.

Duties: Follow the assembly to ascend the hall and pass through the dining hall (*guàngtáng*). There are those who attend to the incense-burning at the pagodas; all matters are managed by them. Where there is no Buddha-pagoda, this office does not exist.
The Outer Pagoda Attendant sweeps all ancestral pagodas and weeds them in a timely manner. Morning and evening, he diligently attends to the incense and lamps.

For all offerings made during Qingming and other occasions, the procedure is the same as that for the aforementioned lamp-attendants. Whenever a deceased monk is interred in a pagoda, [the attendant performs the necessary rites].
Preparation of meals shall follow the prescribed rules. If guests from outside regions enter the *tā* (stūpa), they must notify the Guest Hall (*kètáng*) before proceeding.

Those who enter surreptitiously after receiving private offerings shall be punished. In the Patriarchs’ Hall (i.e., the Hall of the Worthy)—the same applies to the incense and lamp duties regarding the fixed incense and the closing of the hall at night as in the Meditation Hall;

all other matters are the same as those for the Library’s incense and lamps. (Regarding incense and lamp duties in other locations, although the specific tasks differ, the lighting of lamps, burning of incense, and acts of veneration are identical morning and evening.)
Burn incense. Rinse the mouth and wash the hands. Next, after reciting the "Praise of Incense" (*Gandha-stotra*) upon the initial burning of the burner, continue by reciting the mantra:
Oṃ śavali-damana aparājita suparṇi vikāśi huṃ hūṃ. (Recite three times. Next, recite the mantra for offering incense: Oṃ sarva-tathāgata dhūpa-pūjā-karma samudra spharaṇa samaye hūṃ.

(Recite three times. Offer incense and recite the mantra. Visualize that these clouds of incense pervade the Buddha-fields of the ten directions. All the sages and worthies arise and provide protective mindfulness. That is to say: As the incense in the burner is first lit, the Dharma-realm is suffused with its fragrance; the ocean-like assemblies of all Buddhas hear it from afar.

Auspicious clouds form in every place, and as the sincere intention is met, the Buddhas manifest their entire bodies. If one has previously lit lamps or burned candles, one should recite the Offering Lamp Mantra, saying: Oṃ. Sarvatathāgata.

*Nyūba*, *Bujamieya*, *Samudra*, *Sulurana Samaye*. (Recite these three times to pay respect to the oil lamp, or the lamp and candle; likewise recite the mantra while visualizing clouds of lamps reaching before each of the holy sages.

As it is said: "The jade lamp suddenly shines, its light universally illuminating the Dharma-realm. By reciting these three mantras, lighting incense and burning candles, one can extinguish sins, eliminate calamities, and increase immeasurable merit.

If one does not recite the mantras and perform visualization, nor possesses a sincere heart, then even if incense and candles are burned, I fear that the Three Jewels and the celestial deities will not accept them.)

The Commentary on the Meaning states: The *dianzhu* (temple master) is the chief of those who provide incense and lamps for the assembly; he serves the Buddha on behalf of the monks with diligent devotion.

The meaning of the term "incense and lamp" (*xiangdeng*) in other contexts is likewise the same. Among the six types of offerings—incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, fruit, and music—that which is designated by the name "incense and lamp" refers to a time when the world is defiled by the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), its stench is unbearable to smell, and it is shrouded in the darkness of night.

At that time, it was dark and invisible. Desiring to seek the Three Jewels and the celestial deities who always dwell here to protect and mind us, we constantly burn exquisite incense to dispel its impurities.

When encountering darkness, we light lamps to illuminate the objects, so as to eliminate the obstacles of foul odors and obscurity, thereby establishing a subtle fragrance and a pavilion of radiance. This is the significance of this incense and these lamps.
Thus, this practice depends entirely upon sincerity of heart to constitute a respectful offering. As it is said: "Incense arises from the mind;
the mind reaches [the Buddha] through incense. Abiding in neither the past, present, nor future, it may pervade the ten directions.

When the lamp illuminates the Buddha’s wisdom and the illumination of the mind clarifies the ultimate principle, one must further rely upon the recitation of mantras and mental visualization to complete the respectful offering; only then is the incense and lamp fully perfected.
This is the essential principle. It is not only the case for incense and lamps; all people should act in this manner. It is not only the Three Jewels who are thus;
those who revere any deity should likewise act in this manner. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings," states:
"This wondrous fragrance reaches our various celestial palaces in a single moment of thought. Its...

The incense immediately transformed into incense canopies. Their fragrance was subtle and exquisite, and their golden hue shone brilliantly, illuminating our palaces, the palaces of Śakra, the palaces of Brahmā, and even the worlds of all Buddhas.
Above those Buddhas, within the void of space, incense canopies likewise formed, and their golden light shining everywhere was exactly the same.
As the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: Furthermore...

They emit light adorned with fragrances; various exquisite perfumes gather to form canopies, which are scattered everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions as an offering to all the Greatly Virtuous Honored Ones. Furthermore, they emit light adorned with powdered incense;

various kinds of powdered incense gather to form canopies, which are scattered everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions as an offering to all the Greatly Virtuous Honored Ones. Based on this:
It relies entirely upon sincere visualization as an offering: thus, a single incense pellet fills the ten directions;
it becomes a radiant *ūrṇā-kośa* (crown-tuft), playing celestial music, burning celestial precious incense, presenting celestial delicacies, and arraying celestial precious robes.

Expounding the great Dharma teachings, each and every one pervades the others without obstruction. Accomplished solely through the visualization of a sincere mind, one should thus advance with incense morning and evening;
thus recite the liturgy morning and evening; thus perform chanting and prostrations; and thus repent and make aspirations.
Then the Three Jewels and the celestial deities will respond like an echo. Therefore, every day, constantly...
One should serve with incense, flowers, lamps, and water morning and evening, maintaining the utmost sincerity and reverence; the merit and reward thus obtained will be inconceivable.
Furthermore, regarding how a sincere mind that lights a lamp invokes a superior retribution, the *Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru Receiving the Prediction* states:
After the King had invited the Buddha for a meal, he asked, "What else would be appropriate? Jīvaka replied, "Only the lighting of lamps is appropriate."
The King issued a decree to prepare a hundred *hu* of sesame oil for lamps, which were lit from the palace as far as the Jetavana Monastery.
At that time, a destitute mother was moved by emotion and begged for two coins to buy oil. The shopkeeper said, "Mother, you are extremely poor; why not buy food instead?

The mother replied, "I see the King performing such great meritorious deeds; though I am truly impoverished, I wish to light a single lamp to establish a foundation for my future lives. The shopkeeper praised her.
He added another three *he* (measures), totaling five *he*. Calculating this, it was not even half a night. He made a vow:

"If, in a future life, I attain the Way as the Buddha has, may this oil last through the entire night without its light fading. The next morning, Maudgalyāyana extinguished the lamps one by one in order.

The mother’s single lamp was extinguished three times but never went out completely. Then, by means of his supernatural power, he drew forth a *vilana* wind to blow upon the lamp, and the lamp burned even more intensely.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: "This is the radiance of a future Buddha; it cannot be extinguished by your supernatural power.
In her past lives, this mother devoted herself solely to the teachings of the sūtras and lacked the leisure to practice giving (*dāna*). Therefore, she is poor now. Thirty..."
Kalpa. He shall attain Buddhahood and be named Sumeruprabhāsa Tathāgata. Furthermore, the *Dīpadāna-puṇya-sūtra* states:
"If a person offers a lamp at a Buddha’s stupa or temple, they shall obtain three kinds of illumination at the time of death.
First, at the moment of death, all previously performed merits will manifest before them; remembering them without loss, the mind will give rise to exultation. Second...
Because of this, one is able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and perform acts of giving, attaining a heart of joy and being free from the suffering of death.
Third, because of this, one attains a mind that contemplates the Dharma. Furthermore, at the time of death, one further obtains four kinds of light:
first, seeing the rising sun; second, seeing the rising moon; third, seeing various devas; and fourth, seeing the Buddha seated at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
He saw the trees and his own body, joined his palms in reverence toward the Buddha, and having seen these four things, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The "Bhadramukha" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Furthermore, it emits a light named 'Illumination,' which outshines all the lights of the devas;
there is no darkness or obstruction that it does not dispel, universally bringing benefit to all sentient beings. This light awakens them."
"Let all the assembly hold lamps to make offerings to the Buddha. Because one makes offerings to the Buddhas with lamps, one shall attain the status of the unsurpassed lamp within the world.
Based on this, by holding even a single incense lamp, one can swiftly accomplish immeasurable merit."

The rounds of inspection are distinguished by day and night. The daytime rounds are the duty of the *xu-zhi* (order supervisor); he is primarily responsible for the miscellaneous affairs of the monastery and assists the *seng-zhi* (monastic steward).
He must constantly and diligently urge all locations to sweep and keep them clean, and shall not permit the monastics to play outside the mountain gate.
Whenever an official arrives, he must notify the guest hall in advance and partake of the two meal periods. The nighttime rounds are the duty of the *lie-zhi* (senior attendants).
At dusk, the fixed incense is lit. Waiting for the incense to reach the mark, three strikes of the board are sounded. The lamp of the tea room is brought out; the water is prepared well.

Four strikes of the board are sounded. The kitchen lamp is lit. When one *cun* of incense remains, five strikes of the board are sounded. The fixed incense must be measured with precision; if it is late or early, the timing will be lost.

When passing through the hall for the early morning congee, one is penalized by kneeling in the *zhāitáng* (meditation hall). For the daily services: upon hearing the great bell strike three times, the *cuībǎn* (urging gong) is struck;
the same applies to the universal Buddha-recitation service. For the evening service: upon hearing the *chándiàng* (meditation hall) signal bell strike three times, the *cuībǎn* is struck.

One joins the assembly to ascend the hall for recitation. After the evening *dàjìng* (great silence) has been opened, the *cuībǎn* is struck once. During spare time, one shall continue to assist the hall master with his duties. If...
Carrying the drum-head. See the ninth chapter below, "On Ritual Implements," for details. Regarding sweeping:

every day one must sweep the upper and lower, eastern and western, inner and outer paths, as well as the corridors in front and behind and the vermilion courtyard; all must be cleared of weeds and kept pristine.
This also includes attending to the incense and lamps in the Hall of the Heavenly Kings (the tenth section, "The Abbot’s Quarters," concludes here).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* says that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada would go every morning to the Jeta Grove to sweep the ground and pay homage to the Buddha.
On another day, as the householder was preoccupied with other affairs and unable to enter the monastery, the World-Honored One saw that the ground was not clean and personally swept it.
He specifically instructed Śāriputra and the others to do the same, and they all swept the ground until it was thoroughly cleared.
They entered the hall and sat together. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In sweeping the ground, there are five benefits.
First, by sweeping the ground, one's own mind becomes pure. Second, others see that the ground is free of dust and filth, which purifies their minds.
Third, the devas rejoice; as the ground is clean and free of dust, the dust of pride is removed. Fourth, one plants the karma for physical beauty. Fifth, one achieves self-mastery."
Because of this intention, there are five reasons why sweeping the temple grounds causes merit to increase and ensures that after one’s life ends, one will be reborn in the heavens.

The *Cānlín Bǎoxùn* (Precious Admonitions of the Meditation Forest) states: "When the paths to the temple are cleared and the corridors and eaves are kept in good repair, by this one knows him to be a virtuous elder."
Requesting the Officers of the Two Orders (Note: For the listing of officers, this ritual is not required).

Whenever requesting the officers of the two orders, the Guest Hall and the Rector (Weina) shall, on the day prior, open the register of the monks and determine those who are appropriate for each specific office.

Present this for the Abbot’s perusal. If the Abbot grants permission, the Rector (Vina) and the Guest Master (Zhike) shall remain in their posts, while another attendant is dispatched to invite the Chant Leader (Yuezong) along with the masters who have accepted the offices.

They proceed to the Abbot’s quarters; after the formal salutations are performed, they are commanded to sit. The Abbot converses with them and, having assessed their talents, assigns them to offices as appropriate.
The following day, after the morning gruel and the communal meal, the offerings are recited within the refectory, the office-holders are invited, and they are escorted to their respective positions.

(4. The Head of the Fourth Class, the Abbot’s Assistant, the Chief Administrator, the Deputy Steward, and the Abbot escort the official to his position; the rest, led by the Guest Master, escort them to their positions. A notice board shall be posted in advance. (The board reads:
"By order of the Venerable Abbot, we respectfully invite Master [Name] to serve as the official for [Position]... and so forth. After the second board-strike, the sequence board is sounded.

The newly appointed officials of the sequence wear their robes and carry their implements; the former officials do not wear their robes. They all arrive together at the Guest Hall, where the Guest Master immediately announces their names in order.

[The new attendant] takes up the single staff. (And so forth. When the announcement is finished, he addresses the assembly, saying: "Congratulations to all the masters; please offer a universal prostration.

The former attendants first proceed to the Abbot’s quarters and stand in formation on both sides. Next, the guest master leads the new attendants to the Abbot’s quarters. [The new attendants] speak as follows:

The newly appointed administrators spread out the ritual implements and prostrate to the *upādhyāya*. After the three prostrations are completed, the new administrators withdraw to the corridor, while the former administrators leave their positions and line up facing the seat.
The head of the former administrators says, "We prostrate to the *upādhyāya*. Once the prostrations are finished, the Abbot says:
The assembly enters the hall. The former officers arrive first and take their positions standing on both sides of the hall. The guest master strikes the announcement board three times and says:

"The newly appointed officers shall enter the hall to perform the rites. (And so forth) until the rites are completed. Once the four class leaders have escorted the abbot to his seat, [the ceremony concludes].
(The Abbot immediately withdraws. The remaining attendants take up the ritual implements and escort the [newly appointed] officers to their respective positions in order.

Once each has been escorted, the Rector says, "Congratulations to all you masters," and they perform one prostration. Having finished bowing, each returns to his original seat and arranges his bedding, sitting down in sequence.
That evening’s evening service involves escorting the meditation cushions to their positions in the Great Hall and then to the quarters. When the service is concluded, the Rector says, "The new..."

Please invite the newly appointed office-holders to emerge from their positions to perform the rites. When the rites are concluded, the head of the assembly takes up the whisk as described below (*etcetera*). The *Vina* (Chamberlain) says:
"The newly appointed office-holders shall ascend to the Patriarchal Hall to pay respects to the ancestors" (without striking the bell). Next, they proceed to the Abbot’s quarters.

When the rites there are concluded, the *Kichaku* (Guest Master) leads the new office-holders on a tour of the various administrative offices, ringing the *ing-king* (small hand-chime) as they go, saying: "The newly appointed assembly of office-holders are touring the offices to exchange formal greetings."
[The name of] such-and-such master, and so on, until the circuit is completed. Once everyone has returned to their respective places, the Guest Hall (Kettang) strikes the *xu-ban* (sequence board).

The assembly gathers to inspect the seating charts (*kan-dan*), then returns to the hall. The Abbot invites tea. When the tea ceremony concludes, they return to the hall and sit according to their assigned positions for the incense period (*xiang*). As the time approaches the end of the sitting, the *weina* (recluse director) distributes the incense. Once the sitting is finished, the *weina* says:
"The newly appointed officers shall leave their seats and perform the ten-direction prostrations (*shifang li*). If they are heads of a section (*ban-shou*)," [they shall do so].
Then, when performing the ritual, the various officers of the two orders (*liuxu*) should descend from their platforms and stand at their respective positions;

only the pure assembly (*qingzhong*) does not follow the officers back to perform the salutation, as this ritual was established specifically for the sake of the officers. When the ritual is concluded, the *weina* (ritual master) speaks again:

"The masters of the two orders shall represent all the other masters in inspecting the seating charts" (having finished the announcement), the *weina* then inspects the charts of the main hall together with the various officers.
Each person performs one prostration toward the east and one toward the west. When the ritual is concluded, each returns to their assigned seat and observes *zhijing* (stilled silence).

Regarding the appointed attendants (*zhishi*), those whose names are posted on the list within the hall enter the hall to perform the rites. However, those in the *shiliao* (attendant quarters) merely record their attendance at the hall;

although the attendants of the *yingtang* (portrait hall) have their names posted, they do not enter the hall. Furthermore, figures such as the *dujian*, the *jianyuan*, and the *zhike* likewise do not enter the hall.

Regarding the general protocol for appointing and installing the administrative officers: the Chief Administrator (Jianyuan), the Rector (Weina), the Guest Master (Zhike), and the Attendant (Shizhe)—these four shall jointly escort the new appointee to his quarters.
Once the assignment has been completed, the Guest Hall shall invite the new officer for tea and a meal.

Furthermore, the heads of the four classes of laborers are called "Holy Officers" (Shengzhi), as figures such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra during the Buddha’s lifetime all served as his assistants. The Chief Administrator, Guest Master, and Rector are called "Worthy Officers" (Xianzhi).
In the Buddha’s world, all worthy and holy ones serve as scribes, attendants, and stewards;
these are called "those who can uphold," for they are capable of accomplishing all matters pertaining to both the mundane and supramundane Buddhas.
Such individuals must exhaust their strength for the sake of others, offering their hearts to protect the community, benefiting one another, and not failing in the duties they have undertaken.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: When monastic communities are filled with officials, the Buddha-Dharma cannot be propagated;

if one’s wisdom-life is difficult to harmonize, the worldly ways will not be understood, and it will be difficult to manage the permanent abode. Therefore, one must be appropriately matched before being considered excellent.

Generally speaking, when selecting an official, if one is a newly arrived visiting master and cannot yet know that person deeply, they may be appointed to an intermediate position within the two orders (*liuxu*). After a long time, their true character will naturally become apparent.

Once you have understood this to the very bottom and without doubt, only then may you entrust me with the responsibility. As for those who receive and uphold [this teaching], they should simply strive to exhaust their own efforts;
they must not fear difficulties or seek to evade them. If one can truly devote heart and strength to the ground of the Triple Gem, there is no need to worry about not finding a favorable outcome.
*Zhigu* says: When Chan Master Yunfeng Yue first arrived at Dayu, he entered the inner chamber and requested instruction.

Kaishi instructed him, saying, "Foolish man, you must act as the head of the alms-round. After he had finished his rounds, Kaishi ordered him to beg for charcoal for the community because of the snowy cold;
the Master also complied with this command. When the task was completed, Kaishi said that the Hall Office was lacking personnel and now assigned it to him;

the Master accepted it with diligent effort. While he was sitting on the back rack, the hoops of a wooden bucket suddenly gave way, and it fell from the rack. At that moment, he attained sudden enlightenment.
Suddenly, he saw the wondrous function of Yankuan’s teaching. He threw on his robes and entered the room; Yankuan smiled and said, "Venerable Vinaya Master, you may rejoice.

The Master bowed twice but did not utter a single word as he departed. Alas! It was easy to change the three attachments, yet the bottom of the bucket remained stuck. Was it that the attachment itself was betraying him?
The Head of the Assembly Holds the Whisk (Divided into Two): First, Regarding the New Appointment of the Head Seat (*shouzuo*).
This position is the banner of the monastic grove (*conglin*), the eyes of the Buddhas and patriarchs, one who leads the assembly in seated meditation and proclaims the spirit of the school.

Such a person is difficult to find. Whenever the Head Seat is to be appointed, the Abbot shall, on the day prior, announce it to the assembly in the refectory, saying: "Now there is [Name], a Great..."

[The Master] (or Venerable So-and-so) is endowed with both talent and virtue; he is universally esteemed and respected by the assembly. His insight is lofty and clear, and upon him rests the life of the Dharma.

We await his presence so that the rain of the Dharma may fall everywhere. After a short while, the assembly respectfully invites the Master [saying]: "We humbly pray that you will compassionately grant us your consent.

Afternoon: When the second board sounds in the quarters, the assembly gathers. The Guest Hall respectfully invites [the Master] (the ritual for the invitation is as seen previously). Once the invitation is concluded, the Master proceeds to the Abbot’s Quarters. Upon completion of the rites there, he enters the hall for the formal assembly.

The Abbot escorts [the guest] to their position. Once the assembly has finished their prostrations, he escorts him to the quarters. That evening, during the recitation period, the attendant transmits the "Bǐfú" (Whisk-Bearing) plaque.
A red slip is affixed to the upper right of the plaque, on which it is written: "We respectfully invite Venerable Head Seat [or Master]" (other officers' titles are adjusted accordingly).

The Abbot orders the attendant of the quarters to transmit the incense burner, the red robe, and the staff to the Head Seat’s quarters. When the recitation is finished, the Head Seat dons his outer robe; the attendant...
The staff-bearer follows behind. The Rector says, "Welcoming the Head Seat Master. The lead chime is struck to lead the procession.
They are welcomed to the front of the seat. The Head Seat performs the prostrations. Once the prostrations are complete, he ascends the seat. Attendants stand in attendance on both sides.

When the Rector has finished chanting the praises for the Head Seat’s offering of incense, the Rector says, "Prostrate to the Head Seat Master. The Master says, "No need," and immediately stops. After the preaching of the Dharma is finished... the Rector... [stops].

The Cloud (the name of the abbot’s attendant) prostrates to the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera). Having completed the prostrations, he descends from the seat. The assembly escorts him back to his quarters; once he has taken his leave, the escorting ceases.
The Head Seat then proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to pay respects to the Resident Master (Abbot). After presenting the draft manuscript, he performs one prostration to thank the Attendant.

The Abbot serves tea. The Record Keeper writes the Dharma words on a plaque for hanging. On the following day, the Head Seat provides his own funds to request the Kitchen Office to prepare tea and refreshments.

Providing for the Assembly. (If the Head Seat is of modest means, the monastery shall provide for his support. Whenever the new and full moon or seasonal festivals occur, one first pays homage to the Abbot, and next pays homage to the Head Seat.

If a newly appointed class leader receives the office or presides over the whisk, the ritual procedure is the same as this. Upon the completion of the recitation, the difference lies in setting up a level seat and an incense altar in the Great Hall.

Regarding the observance of the eight seasonal festivals (bājié) as prescribed for the four seasons: the abbot shall issue an order to the head of the assembly (*banshou*) who is to hold the *fú* (the formal discourse).

On the day prior, the abbot shall direct the *dūjian*, the *zhikè*, and the *shizhě* to go to the quarters of that specific head of the assembly and invite him, stating: "Tomorrow morning, you are requested to hold the *fú* for the assembly. On the actual day, this takes place before the early morning congee.

After the second board has been struck, the Chief Administrator (Duguan) and others, bearing the plaque and whisk, return once more to the abbot’s quarters. After the Chief Administrator has respectfully offered incense and performed prostrations with the assembly, the attendant says:

"By the compassionate command of the Abbot, Venerable Master, we have been ordered to respectfully present this plaque and whisk specifically to invite you to preside over the whisk for the assembly at noon.
Thereupon, the Head of the Assembly (Ban-shou), together with the attendant, proceeds to the abbot’s quarters to pay respects at the seat.

Having received the command, he again performed the ritual of prostration to the assembly and immediately returned to his quarters. He instructed the attendant of his own quarters to hang the plaque and set up a *pingzuo* (level seat) in the center of the Dharma Hall.
Furthermore, another seat was set up on the left for the head monk to serve as the abbot’s position (*fangzhangwei*).

When the time arrived, the bell was struck three times; the Chief Supervisor held incense and, together with the two orders of monks, went to the quarters to perform a single prostration with touching heads (*yichu li*) and welcome him to the Dharma Hall.
