In the hall, the head of the assembly performs the ritual of inquiry (wèn-xùn) facing the ten directions. He then proceeds to the position before the abbot’s quarters (fāng-zhàng) and performs a single prostration with the forehead touching the ground (yī-chù lǐ).

Turning, he ascends the seat. The Chief Supervisor (dū-jian) offers incense, and the assembly performs a single prostration; the head of the assembly does not return the salutation. The attendant who burns incense (shāo-xiāng shì-zhě) then offers incense.

If a person of renowned virtue from one of the ten directions serves as the head of the assembly, the abbot goes before the seat where the whisk is held (bǐng-fú zuò) to perform an inquiry. The whisk is then held.
The attendant brushes the person up and stands to one side. [The master] returns to his seat and says, "Attendant, please invite the Abbot to sit in the lotus posture.

Having finished speaking, he takes his seat. The Director of the Assembly strikes the *yin-ghaṅ* (leading chime) three times. This continues until the preaching of the Dharma is concluded and he descends from the seat.

He then proceeds to the position of the Abbot’s quarters and performs a single prostration with touching the ground (*chu-li*). (This includes prostrating to the two orders of officials and the attendant; the two orders escort the Head of the Class back to his quarters. Once the formal farewell and escorting have ceased, the Head of the Class goes to the Abbot’s quarters.
The *bǐfú* (ceremonial whisk-bearer) returns to his quarters. The *dùjiān* (General Supervisor) orders the storehouse to send a table of tea and refreshments to that quarter.
On this day, the Guest Hall invites the head of the *bǐfú* class to partake of a day’s meal in the Guest Hall. That evening at the second board, the Abbot waits to serve tea for the *bǐfú*.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Chief Seat (shouzuo) was anciently called the Head Official (toushou) and was also titled the Seat-Head (zuoyuan).

When inviting a person of renowned virtue, one must address them as "Upādhyāya" (Heshang); if they are a Dharma heir, one should call them "Great Master" (Dashi). The *Shan'an Zalü* (Miscellaneous Records of Mountain Hermitages) says:
At Yongfu Temple in Rāozhou, Hāolíngjiāng served as the Chief Seat and presided over the whisk (bǐngfú). A monk asked: "What is it like when taking a step forward? He replied: "To collide."
"Wall-bumping, wall-hitting. [The student] asked, "What is it like when one takes a step back? [The Master] replied, "Falling into a pit, falling into a ditch.

[The student] asked, "What is it like when one neither advances nor retreats? [The Master] replied, "A man dead standing on the spot. Someone said, "The Head Seat’s three responses to the questions all accorded perfectly with the student's intent;
they were excellent. Abbot Gulin said, "In what way were they excellent? Have you not heard it said: 'One phrase must accord with...'"
A Headword: "The Ten Thousand Kalpas' Donkey Stake. Although this is so, you must by no means act in such a manner.
Furthermore, at Mount Xiangfeng, when Zhan Tianyuan served as the head seat and held the whisk, he said: "Before Mount Xiangfeng, walk and watch the white clouds as they unfurl and curl;
atop the Youquan Pavilion, sit and listen to the flowing stream as it ebbs and flows. Let the place of the eye become the place of the ear."
The Buddha-work: the ear-faculty performs the Buddha-work of the eye-faculty, and one immediately sees that it is not only Avalokiteśvara who does so;
I too have realized it from within this. Zhuzhi Yiyuan said: "When the words 'one immediately sees' are present, it is speaking to others;
when these two words are absent, it is speaking for oneself. Tianyuan said: "A single grain of elixir can transform iron into gold."
"Jin" (Gold) refers to the words of the Abbot. Observe these two instances of holding the whisk (*bǐfú*):

the abbot and the one holding the whisk examine and praise one another, mutually extolling each other’s virtues without the slightest hint of flattery or arrogance. This is the noble tradition of holding the whisk.

Regarding the invitation for a vegetarian meal (or tea): When the Abbot invites the community for a vegetarian meal (or tea), the head of the hall shall first notify the hall with the following announcement:

"Today, the Abbot, the Venerable Master, has invited the assembly for a vegetarian meal (or tea). (All monks shall assume their respective dignified postures. Subsequently, the administrative officers from the various quarters shall assemble at the Guest Hall.
The attendant shall request [the assembly] to gather. The Hall Master shall direct the attendants to maintain the proper order as they line up together before the Abbot’s quarters.

When the Abbot takes his seat, the Rector says: "Great Assembly, prostrate to the Preceptor. Once the prostrations are completed, the assembly shall take their seats according to rank, each maintaining dignified decorum and remaining silent.
No noise shall be made with cups, plates, bowls, or chopsticks. When the meal is finished (or the tea ceremony), if the Abbot...
Upon hearing this, those holding the position rise together, leave their seats, and stand in a row facing the front. The *Weina* says: "The assembly bows in thanks to the *Heshang*.

Once the prostrations are finished, each returns to their respective place. Furthermore, the two orders of officials serve as the internal and external pillars of the community and the leaders of the assembly;

they must respect one another so that the fundamental principles may be revitalized. This applies to all occasions of entering retreat (*jie zhi*), concluding retreat (*jie jie*), the winter solstice (*dong zhi*), and New Year’s Eve (*chu xi*).

On major festivals such as New Year’s Day, the Abbot shall invite the Head of the Monastery (the *fangzhang*) for a meal, and provide tea and soup as rewards for both the senior and junior ranks (*liǎngxù*), including the distribution of five-colored fruits.
Those who have retired from their administrative duties for one full cycle are not included; this serves both to manifest the etiquette of the monastery and to express gratitude for their services.
Regarding other minor rewards, those who have performed meritorious service must certainly be compensated, provided it is done according to one's discretion and what is appropriate.

Furthermore, those who occupy separate quarters outside [the main hall] and receive their provisions from the guest hall, or those who follow their own original quarters— if they are truly austere and possess a genuine aspiration for the Way—
even if they are among the common assembly in separate quarters, they must be provided with special consideration regarding their provisions and clothing.
This is to cause them to practice with single-mindedness, so that they do not give rise to deluded thoughts.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: "The Abbot’s invitations for meals or tea are not of a single kind;

this [text] refers only to the regulations for the general communal labor (*pǔqǐng*) according to the seasonal sequence and the duties of the office-holders. Whether it be new arrivals at the quarters, new appointees to an office, or those with other specific matters, [the same applies]."
There is the provision of meals and tea. Generally, when the abbot attends to the assembly, he should choose [his associates] with care and extend [the invitation] with sincerity.
Each member should assist the leader with integrity and deliberate with harmony.
Even if there are differing opinions, they should all ultimately follow the one whose reasoning is superior; their sole hope is that it may bring benefit to the permanent monastery.
The Two Orders Resigning from Office:
Whenever members of the two orders resign from their offices, they first go to the Abbot’s quarters after the afternoon meal to pay respects and resign.

In the evening, they attend the hall session and remain in their positions until the end of the period. Upon completion of their term, they must retire to the Guest Hall to resign; they do not go to the Abbot’s quarters, nor do they attend the hall session.

When members of the pure assembly (qingzhong) request leave from within the hall, they must first take leave before the Rector (weina). Once the Rector grants permission, they proceed in the afternoon to the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) and the Guest Hall (kètáng) to pay their respects and bid farewell.
They then attend the evening formal assembly (wanzantang); nowadays, this is often changed to taking leave after the completion of the evening recitation (wankè).

On the following day, they pack their bedding and depart. The pure assembly provides one meal, followed by tea and food at the Guest Hall. The administrative officers provide tea and food, and finally, tea and food are provided by the Abbot. Upon the conclusion of these meals, [the departure is finalized].
He shall see him off. When the period of leave expires, he shall request leave to return home, offering his incense-contribution (dang-sin) to the monastery as travel expenses.
The Commentary on Proof states: "When an official retires, one must examine the person; if they are someone who may or may not be of use," [one should act accordingly].
It is not improper to allow him to withdraw from his request. However, if the person is someone who can be relied upon, one should not readily grant his leave.
For talent is difficult to find and is vital to the monastic community; often, the prosperity or decline of the community follows the departure or stay of a single individual.
Therefore, it is perfectly appropriate to employ tactful means to entreat him to remain, prioritizing the interests of the community above all else.
One must wait until that person truly possesses the circumstances where they cannot help but decline before granting permission.

The seventh chapter, "The Multitude," states:
Water returning to the void and the trees of Mount Denglin are so called because they gather together; this is what constitutes a multitude.
Now, when thousands or hundreds of people dwell within a great granary, cooking from overturned storehouses and burning fires that redden the mountains, this too is a form of gathering.
Yet those who come from the four quarters do so as if returning home, as if it were something they already possessed; what indeed is the reason for this?
It is because the Buddha, seeing people transmigrating through the three realms and appearing and disappearing within birth and death, sought to uproot their suffering and grant them happiness;
thus he transmitted it to his disciples to perpetuate his teaching. Although the common folk cannot fully [comprehend it]...
They followed his teachings, and their hearts were drawn to the Way as something sufficient to rely upon for their support.
Furthermore, they honored his disciples by virtue of that Way; thus, they constructed dwellings to establish their residence and provided grain and provisions to satisfy their needs.
Even though people arrived in such numbers that they brushed shoulders and followed one another’s heels, they feared only that their offerings might not be sufficient.
It was not because of his great numbers that he did not fall into slight negligence.
Otherwise, there would have been many who, for the sake of a foot of land or a peck of grain, would have fought one another.

How could he alone be so foolish as to willingly surrender his wealth to expand my dwelling, and cease his own meals to feed my followers? What indeed is the purpose for which my followers eat here and dwell here?

First, the Master must select one of virtuous character and seniority (one who is fully endowed with the five virtues, whose conduct is reliable, and whose ten years of seniority are complete; for if one’s own weaning has not yet ceased, how can one expect others to cease theirs?).

The sacred regulations are solemn and rigorous; how could it be easy to be a teacher of men? According to the second division of the Vinaya Piṭaka, within the *Upasampadā-khandhaka*, at that time there were bhikṣus who, having not yet completed ten years of seniority, would suddenly ordain others without knowing how to instruct them.

Others, though having completed ten years of seniority, were nevertheless foolish, so that their disciples received no instruction and were unacquainted with the proper deportment. When the bhikṣus reported these matters in detail to the Buddha, the Buddha said: "I allow the Saṃgha to grant formal authorization (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to those who ordain others and bestow full ordination. Those who wish to ordain others should go before the Saṃgha."

Baring the right shoulder, removing leather sandals, and prostrating at the feet of the monks, one should kneel with palms joined and make three sincere requests. If [the candidate] is not fit for instruction, lacks the Dharma, or cannot be sustained by the community through food, clothing, and shelter, the Sangha should say: "Venerable One, please desist; be careful not to ordain others.

If, however, they possess wisdom and can be sustained by these two matters, the Sangha should assemble in harmony and grant the procedure for ordaining others through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation). Thus, one knows that a teacher of men must revere the Buddha’s regulations; the granting of the Dharma depends entirely upon the consent of the Sangha. How much more so in the Vinaya!...

The conferring of the full ordination upon others involves such careful selection; the same applies to the selection of a *upādhyāya*. This is primarily to ensure that the sons of other families are not led into pitfalls, but rather that they may grow into the Dharma-body and be polished as vessels for the Way.

It is for this reason that the boundless kindness of a teacher and the difficulty of repaying the milk of the Dharma are spoken of. Regarding the formal procedure for requesting the *śrāmaṇera* ordination, it is detailed in the Vinaya-piṭaka.

2. Discerning the Capacity for Faith and Resolve (The Vocation of Renunciation). The undertaking of renunciation is not like ordinary affairs; it requires profound and steadfast faith to aspire toward the Path. Even in matters of secular virtue and literary talent, one does not fall short of the scholars within the academies, let alone in the study of the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom—how could there not be world-transcending great men among them?

However, I fear those who leave home out of superficial faith, failing to constantly contemplate the Way. Their outward form is that of a Śākyaputra, yet their minds are fixed on worldly attachments. They waste their time until their hair turns white in vain, content to sit idly and await old age and death.

For such a class of people, even if thousands or tens of thousands were ordained, what benefit would they bring to the Dharma-gate? Therefore, those who seek renunciation must first examine the causal ground. If their faith and resolve are determined and their vows are unchanging, and if their life history is further scrutinized and found to be clear, only then may they be admitted.

One should aim for their deliverance. If, however, their faculties are inferior and their thoughts falter, they may be temporarily lodged in the practice quarters while their conduct is closely observed—whether for one year or three years—until their faith becomes firm and their earnest request is sincere; it is not too late for them to shave their heads. Therefore, a teacher values possessing the discerning eye.

If even a single disciple excels, what need is there for many? As the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa said: "The teacher and the disciple must mutually examine each other’s capacity. If one does not first observe this, both shall incur the offense of transgressing the Dharma."

3. Regarding the announcement to the Saṃgha for tonsure: (The conditions for the relationship between teacher and disciple, the timing for taking refuge and prostrating, and the application of the teachings according to individual capacity, each have distinct applications. If one dwells alone without a companion, the Dharma rests with the teacher. However, if one lives together with the community, there are explicit regulations.

According to the Vinaya, at one time various bhikṣus privately ordained people without authorization. The resident bhikṣus were all unaware of it. When the parents went to search for them, they could find no trace; later, they saw their sons with shaven heads, having become monks, entering the village to beg for alms. Consequently, they gave rise to criticism and disdain. The Buddha, knowing this, established the rule:

"If one wishes to have one's hair shaved within a saṃghārāma, one must first announce it to the entire Saṃgha. If the Saṃgha cannot assemble, one may go from room to room to inform them. Only after that may the shaving take place."

Regarding the hair: if the Saṃgha can assemble in harmony, one performs the *jñapti* (single-announcement) procedure first, and only thereafter does one shave the hair. Since the monastic communities today are in disorder and the ordination of people deviates from the standard, I pray that you will revere the Vinaya regulations; this would truly be a way to sustain the True Dharma in this degenerate age.
As for what is called the *jñapti-karman*, it is a procedure performed in the absence of the person concerned (this shall be made clear in the ritual below).

4. Regarding the Avoidance of Worldly Censure: When the monastic community is solemn and tranquil, when internal discipline is flawless, when the Supreme Way flourishes, and when those outside look to the virtuous for refuge, one must employ worldly conventions to establish the Buddha-dharma.

This necessarily requires renunciation, yet one must also compassionately protect those remaining in the household life. If one knows only how to guide others toward leaving secular life, yet fails to encourage them to formally bid farewell to their sovereign and parents, one will incur worldly ridicule and bring disgrace upon one's fellow monks. How can the Way flourish in this way? What benefit does it bring to the Sangha?

Therefore, whenever one encounters persons of noble rank or the sons of renowned clans who pay respects to a master seeking ordination and joyfully wish to become śramaṇas, one should first inquire tactfully into their circumstances and examine the certainty of their motivation. If it is indeed the case that their sovereign and parents have granted them leave to wander and they have been freed from worldly entanglements, they may then ascend the four stages of the [ordination] platform.

The tower. He was received by the assembly of the six harmonies (ṣaḍ-ārya-vamśa), and at that moment, he performed his farewells from afar into the void. First, he did not forget the profound and heavy grace of his sovereign and parents; second, he fulfilled the final rites of a minister and a son.

This neither transgresses the Buddha-dharma nor fails to manifest worldly dharma (*laukika-dharma*). If it is asked whether secular ties have not yet ended, it is appropriate to offer consolation and encourage him to return home. Although he may not yet accept the three clusters of precepts (*tri-vidha-saṃvara*) for renunciation, he will certainly generate faith and wisdom through practice. Alternatively, he may receive the five prohibitions of the layperson (*gṛhastha-pañca-śīla*), cutting off evil, accumulating good, and planting merit.

This neither departs from worldly dharma nor fails to establish the Buddha-dharma. Such skillful means (*upāya*) in protecting the world can be called the brilliant manifestation of the Dharma-gate. According to the Vinaya, there was once King Prasenajit and a valiant minister who, without having informed [the Buddha],...

The King entered a monastery in person and sought ordination as a monk among the Saṃgha. The bhikṣus immediately conferred ordination upon him. Later, when the King learned of this, he established strict national prohibitions. Furthermore, many bhikṣus were ordaining the young sons of their Śākya kinsmen and loved ones. King Śuddhodana then addressed the World-Honored One regarding this matter.

Parents provide great benefit to their children, nourishing and caring for them until they reach maturity, serving them throughout their lives, and ensuring that their lineage does not fail. May the Buddha’s great compassion command the bhikṣus that no one shall be ordained unless their parents give permission.

For this reason, the Buddha established the rule that royal officials may not be ordained. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are four types of royal officials: some have titles but no emoluments; some have emoluments but no titles; some have both titles and emoluments; and some...

There are those who have neither name nor stipend; there are those who have a name but no stipend; and there are those who have both a name and a stipend. Regarding those who have both a name and a stipend, this country does not permit their going forth, and other countries likewise do not permit their ordination. Regarding those who have a stipend but no name, this place does not permit it, but other places may permit it.

Regarding those who have neither name nor stipend, this place permits their ordination, and other places likewise permit it. There are three kinds of sons: first, the biological son, born of one’s own parents; second, the foster son, raised from childhood; and third, the self-arrived son, who has come to depend on one as a child. Among these, the biological son... [this country does not permit his going forth].

If one's home country does not permit ordination, other countries likewise will not permit their admission. Regarding adopted children or biological children, these are not permitted here, yet they may receive ordination elsewhere. If we apply this principle by analogy, even among biological children, four categories may be opened for the purpose of providing skillful means for their rescue and deliverance.

The Sages will surely bestow their compassion. There may be cases where parents reside at home and there are many sons; or where the father is alive but the mother has passed away and there is an only son; or where the mother is alive but the father has passed away and there are many sons; or where both parents have passed away and there is an only son.

Among these, if there are one or two sons whose parents reside at home, or whose mother is alive but the father has passed away, who travel afar to another region to leave the household life out of faith, seek a teacher to shave their heads, and upon their initial departure have not yet received permission from their kin, but later return to present their circumstances and request approval—if their parents joyfully grant them leave, and the teacher ordains them, there is no fault.

The same principle applies to those with an only son whose father is alive but the mother has passed away. As for those with an only son whose parents have both passed away, since there are no two parents to inform, they may cultivate practice to repay their profound kindness; this is permitted by both parties, and they may leave as they wish.

Regarding the family: according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, if one's ruler or parents have not granted permission, ordination is not permitted. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one must carefully examine whether they are a subject or a child; while these texts internally allow for renunciation, any master who understands the Vinaya must skillfully explain this intent. By no means should one take advantage of these allowances to evade prohibitions or follow personal whims to insult the regulations.

5. Regarding the assessment of the old and the young: [The monastic] shaves his hair differently from the laity, renounces profit and fame, and does not pride himself on his nobility, valuing only virtue. Thus, he serves his teacher and performs manual labor, sharing in the toil of the community;

he receives the scriptures, inquires into their meaning, practices seated meditation, and cultivates contemplation. If one is too young, they lack proficiency; if too old, they find it difficult to endure. Through diligence, the myriad practices are all perfected; through indolence, all matters fail. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "If one is under seven years of age, or exactly seven, yet understands good and evil;

or if one is over seventy, or exactly seventy, and is able to cultivate wholesome deeds—in all such cases, the Sangha is permitted to ordain them. If one is under seven years of age, or exactly seven, and does not know good and evil; or if one is over seventy, or exactly seventy..."

Tenth: Those who require assistance for rising and reclining shall not, in either case, be permitted to receive ordination. This is because rotten wood cannot be carved, while fine jade may be polished. Alas! In these times, which mark the autumn of the Dharma, the holy instructions are no longer heard. Consequently, the gateway of the True and Pure Dharma has fallen into corruption and abuse. Some, driven by the need for laborers, shave the heads of the elderly and the young without distinction. Others sell ordination for bribes, so that the poor are made monks not for the sake of cultivation, but merely to support themselves in old age. They rely on the teachings to secure their own comfort, improperly donning the black robes and vying with the pure assembly for prestige. Such as these— [The text continues: ...are those who, having been ordained, do not cultivate the Way; they are like the "five kinds of dead trees" mentioned in the scriptures. Furthermore, there are those who, though they have received the precepts, fail to observe them; they are like the "five kinds of blind people. There are also those who, though they have cultivated the Way, do not seek liberation; they are like the "five kinds of deaf people. And finally, there are those who, though they have sought liberation, do not attain it; they are like the "five kinds of crippled people. These four categories of practitioners are all considered failures in their respective capacities. Therefore, one must be extremely careful in the selection of candidates. If one fails to examine them thoroughly, the Sangha will suffer decline. If one examines them too strictly, the number of ordinands will diminish. Thus, one must exercise moderation and discernment. To summarize: those who are physically infirm, mentally dull, or lacking in the capacity for practice should not be admitted. Only those who possess the potential for cultivation and the aspiration for liberation should be allowed to enter the Order. This is the fundamental principle for ensuring the longevity of the Dharma. May all future masters of the precepts take this to heart and act accordingly. If they do not, after the four months have passed, they shall be expelled from the Saṃgha. This is to be carried out through a formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. If, during the period of co-residence, they grow weary of the non-Buddhist path or of being a layperson... [they may remain]. If they do not, after the four months have passed, they shall be expelled from the Saṃgha. This is to be carried out through a formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. If, during the period of co-residence, they grow weary of the non-Buddhist path or of being a layperson

Regarding the Dharma: if one hears others speak of the faults of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and censures those who are unwholesome, yet that person likewise censures what is unwholesome; and if one hears others speak of the virtues of the Triple Gem (*triratna*) and rejoices with praise, yet that person likewise rejoices and praises it well—such a person may be granted full ordination (*upasampadā*) to become a member of the Saṅgha.

However, if they still practice the ways of non-Buddhists or laypeople, and upon hearing it said that the activities of non-Buddhists are unwholesome while the activities of the Triple Gem are wholesome, they instead become angry and feel no joy—such a person is not permitted to receive full ordination as a monk.

Nevertheless, although in this region there are currently no followers of the Six Heretical Teachers (*ṣaṭśāstṛ*), nor biased and heterodox treatises that manifest differences to lead and convert others, nor those who harbor hatred toward and obstruct the gates of the Dharma, it is not that teachings such as the Five Sects, the Six Volumes, and the White Lotus do not exist. They gather in secret to proclaim their doctrines, deluding the minds of ignorant people. Because of this...

Lately, perverse winds have spread far and wide, infecting both cities and the countryside. You must revere the sacred regulations and skillfully protect yourselves. If the Dharma is maintained with dignity and solemnity, it will serve as a beneficial supplement to the King’s civilizing transformation.

7. Regarding those who deliver others without partiality: whether one has left the household life and severed all attachments, or remains in the secular world yet maintains pure intent, the goal is liberation through the Ultimate Way. One does not establish the distinction between self and other; this is the Dharma-gate of non-contention, wherein the distinctions between the distant and the intimate are obliterated.

Thus, Rāhula took Śāriputra as his teacher, and Ānanda (the Joyful One) paid homage to Kausthila (the Pea-Eater) as his model. Even among the sons and disciples of the Dharma-Prince, such was the established precedent. How much more so for the śramaṇas of later generations, who instead fail to follow these examples!

This is truly because the time since the Sage departed is remote, and people are full of worldly affection. Some, driven by the five kinds of perverse greed, accumulate wealth, fearing that their possessions will become too vast and lack heirs to inherit them. Others, dwelling alone like solitary shadows, worry that they will grow old with no one to look after them. Consequently, they repeatedly ordain others and constantly recruit disciples. In this way, the Buddha-Dharma is neither propagated nor expanded, and the life of wisdom is said to... [come to an end].

What is the continuity? When investigating its origin, one finds that all faults are attributed to oneself; having brought harm upon others through one's own delusion, it is deeply lamentable. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu must not harbor the intention of ordaining others for his own sake. He should instead reflect:

'By virtue of my ordaining this person, may they cultivate various wholesome deeds and attain the fruits of the Path. Only then is such ordination permitted. If one cannot subdue oneself yet wishes to subdue others, if one cannot discipline oneself yet wishes to cause others to be disciplined, or if one cannot liberate oneself yet wishes to cause others to be liberated—such a thing is impossible."

Eight: The Fundamental Basis of the Path’s Practice. Those who remain at home are submerged in worldly affairs; they are mired in confusion and vexation, remaining unaware [of the truth]. Those who leave the home life dwell in emptiness and stillness; for them, there is a basis for awakening and illumination. This basis is none other than the precepts (*śīla*). Concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) arise in dependence upon them.

When concentration is perfected, confusion and vexation are clarified; when wisdom is developed, the obstacles of delusion are severed. For this reason, when the Great Sage established his teachings, he placed primary importance on the *vinaya*. Furthermore, the precepts encompass the seven classes of followers. Although one ascends through four stages, and though the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) differ, their fundamental basis is non-dual.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one does not receive the five precepts, one cannot receive the ten precepts, nor can one receive the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). If one does not receive these three kinds of precepts, one cannot receive the bodhisattva precepts. In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the Buddha commanded Śāriputra to ordain Rāhula.

First, one should confer the five precepts of an upāsaka, followed by the shaving of the head and the conferral of the ten śrāmaṇera precepts. One should understand that these constitute four successive stages, demonstrating that the sequential arrangement (pravibhāga) is not disordered. Furthermore, the conferral of the precepts occurs at two distinct times, revealing the distinction between the conventional (saṃvṛti) and the ultimate (paramārtha).

As for the shaving of the head, if one has not yet received the categories of precepts, although one is said to have "left the home," one is merely called a śrāmaṇera in form. Only when one shaves the hair and receives the precepts from a teacher does one truly leave the home; this is called being a śrāmaṇera in dharma. If the pure precepts are not fully possessed, one's essence remains that of a layperson (avadāta).

Such clothing is not fit for a field of merit; it is difficult to receive the four requisites. Even if one can diligently practice, it will be hard to escape the three realms. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not strictly uphold the prohibitive precepts, they will inevitably fall into the paths of demons and heterodoxy."

Therefore, know that the precepts constitute the fundamental basis. How could those who study the Buddha’s teachings ever lightly discard them and fail to believe and accept them? 9. Admonishing Ascetics:

To indulge the body and mind, to be addicted to and defiled by the five desires, to be cowardly and afraid of toil and hardship, and to cherish and pamper the four limbs—these are the habitual tendencies of many kalpas and the common sentiments of worldly fools.

Thus, one knows that the pleasures of the household life all belong to the causes of suffering, while the ascetic practices of leaving home will surely lead to the fruits of happiness. The Vinaya states: "If one first wishes to leave home, one should first explain for them the hardships of the homeless life: eating once a day, dwelling alone, sleeping alone, and engaging extensively in study. If...

The answer is: "If they are capable, the Sangha may grant them the precepts for ordination; otherwise, it shall not be granted. The reason one acts as a teacher to ordain others is that, first of all, one must instruct them according to the Vinaya, observing their capacities and encouraging their progress. It is better to be difficult at the outset than easy at the beginning. This is like one who wishes to gather treasures from the sea—they certainly do not shrink from the perils of wind and waves;

how much more so when seeking the Buddha-way—how could one fear the hardships of ascetic practice? If one does not earnestly and thoroughly awaken those who are still dim-witted, the blame falls upon the teacher. Once they have heard detailed instruction and guidance, they should exert themselves with diligence, so that they do not fail their own spiritual roots and do not violate the compassionate command."

Tenth, regarding the ritual for the arrangement [of the site] (within which there are two parts: first, manifesting the Dharma through the actual objects; second, setting out the seats and establishing the positions). In any place where one seeks ordination, one should select an open space with four openings toward the cardinal directions.

Each [participant] steps back seven paces and sprinkles scented water to cleanse away dust and defilement. At the four corners, banners are planted, and streamers are hung all around. Regarding the various arrangements established for the altar, those which signify the manifestation of the Dharma through concrete actions are as follows:

incense symbolizes faith; water symbolizes purity. For unless there is pure faith, one cannot eliminate the various afflictions (*kleśa*). One must select an open space to represent the transcendence of the three realms (*tridhātu*). As for planting banners and hanging streamers at the four corners and all around, this represents the stages of abiding, practice, orientation, and the ground (*bhūmi*), signifying the gradual progression through them until they are perfected. (4)

The seven steps taken in each direction symbolize the renunciation and practice that pass through the forty stages of the noble ones (*ārya-pudgala*), thereby becoming fully endowed with both merit and wisdom. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "When the Buddha was first born, he immediately walked seven steps in every direction and proclaimed these words:

'Among gods, humans, and asuras, I am the most honored and supreme. He walked seven steps to the south to manifest his desire to serve as the supreme field of merit for sentient beings. He walked seven steps to the west to manifest that his births were exhausted, that he had forever severed old age and death, and that this was his final body. [He walked seven steps] to the north...

He took seven steps, manifesting that he had already transcended all realms of existence (*bhava*) and brought an end to birth and death. He walked eastward for seven steps, manifesting his desire to act as a leader and guide for all sentient beings. Second, regarding the arrangement of seats and positions: in the center of the altar, one offers to the Master Śākyamuni Buddha.

To the immediate east, one spreads the seat for the Holy Sangha; to the immediate west, the seat for the Upādhyāya; to the immediate north, the position for the King; and to the immediate south, the position for the parents. For each, offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, and candles are arranged.

Should it rain or other circumstances prevent the arrangement of these offerings outdoors, they may instead be placed in the Dharma Hall or the Abbot’s quarters. These five sets of seats must be arranged with solemnity and precision; they are indispensable. Furthermore, those who seek ordination and shave their heads are said to be renouncing the secular household.

One is born into the family of the Tathāgata; only when all aspects of the monastic body are orderly and dignified will it be truly honored. If even a single matter is negligent or casual, one’s renunciation becomes commonplace. Therefore, the excellence and firmness of the initial resolve depend entirely upon supportive conditions.

Second, honoring the orthodox and refuting the erroneous. Regarding what is called "honoring the orthodox and refuting the erroneous": shaving the head and receiving ordination is the primary duty of those in the monastic order (*saṃgha*). The Buddha established explicit regulations, and the patriarchs established formal rules. Yet, later generations have largely followed errors and customs, failing to investigate the truth.

In the *Vinaya*, there was a non-Buddhist who sought ordination; a bhikṣu immediately ordained him and conferred the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) upon him. Subsequently, he grew weary of and loathed the life, no longer wishing to be a monk. The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "If one wishes to ordain a person and shave their hair, one should..."

On the crown of the head, one lock of hair (cūḍā) is left. Question: If one is able to renounce the world, only then is it shaved away. In Sanskrit, *cūḍā* is translated here as "small knot" (*xiǎojié*) or "topknot" (*dǐngjì*). This refers to leaving a small amount of hair at the center of the crown and tying it into a small knot.

The *Zang* (Collection) contains the *Qinggui* (Rules of Purity), compiled by Chan Master Baizhang Hai of the Tang dynasty. It was intended as an instruction for the monastic community (*conglin*) and a fundamental manual for pure cultivation. When the Master first established it, the matters and principles must have been complete and perfect.

However, due to successive dynasties, further additions and revisions were made, resulting in many matters and principles that deviate from the Buddha’s regulations. To provide proof for future generations, I shall briefly describe some errors within the section on "The Ordination of Śrāmaṇeras. It states: "Once the date has been fixed, the head is shaved the night before, leaving a topknot at the crown. The next day, the assembly is gathered to request [the preceptor]. [Note: This passage highlights discrepancies between the traditional Chinese monastic rules and the original Vinaya prescriptions.]

The Master instructs the barber to prostrate and kneel. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) intones the *brahmā-svara*, and the assembly joins in the chant: "The seers possessing the five supernatural powers Established this incantation and ritual. For the sake of those who possess shame, To restrain those who lack shame, The Tathāgata established the prohibitive precepts.

Expounded every half-month; Having spoken of the merit of the precepts, I bow my head in homage to all Buddhas. When this chanting and response have concluded, the hair is shaved. The *kāṣāya* robe is then placed upon the candidate's head, and the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera* are conferred.

To receive the five precepts of a lay follower all at once is a profound violation of the Vinaya regulations; it certainly does not accord with the original rules and rituals of our patriarchs. Furthermore, the practice of shaving the head the night before, leaving a topknot on the crown, and then requesting a master the following day to shave off that topknot is likewise erroneous.

One must know that matters pertain to the present moment and that principle admits no delay until the next day. On the very day of the tonsure, beginning from the time the Master is invited to ascend the seat and continuing until the instruction is concluded, once one has prostrated to take leave of one’s sovereign and parents, one should have water poured over the hair; the Master has not yet raised the razor.

First, the hair is tied into a topknot. Next, starting from below, one shaves around until reaching the edge of the topknot; at this point, the preceptor halts the blade and inquires three times with earnest instruction. The candidate likewise answers three times that they are able to renounce the world. Then, the topknot is severed, and for the first time, their appearance becomes identical to that of a śrāmaṇera.

Furthermore, the verse recited by the *karmadāna* originates from the first fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka*, consisting of one hundred and eighty-six lines of verse. The final eight lines were excised and adopted as the verse for shaving the hair.

This verse was composed by the Venerable Upāli, together with five hundred arhat-monks, at the time of the compilation of the Vinaya-piṭaka. It begins with prostrations to the Triple Gem and a prayer for their empowerment, followed by verses describing the benefits of the precepts; it was placed at the head of the volume to signify that while the Buddha was in the world, he gathered the Saṃgha through the precepts of the True Dharma.

Maintaining oneself with a sense of shame and remorse, one fulfills the holy life (*brahmacarya*). This is not like the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who devise incantations and spells to delude the ignorant and increase their craving. For this reason, the Tathāgata established the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony), commanding that all bhikṣus gather in one place every half-month to recite the precepts as prescribed.

"Reciting the precepts" (*śīla-vinaya*) refers precisely to the chanting of the *Prātimokṣa*. It is a double error to take those verses for the *poṣadha* recitation and use them as the formal proclamation when ordaining a śrāmaṇera.

Furthermore, regarding the simultaneous bestowal of the five precepts and ten precepts upon completion of the tonsure: this stems from a failure to examine the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, which states that the Buddha ordered the five precepts for lay upāsakas to be conferred before the hair was shaved, lest they later regret it and fail to plant roots of goodness. If...

His faith and resolve did not waver, and his aspiration for the Way grew ever firmer. Only then was he to have his hair shaved; subsequently, he was conferred the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera. For this reason, the five lay precepts were not conferred simultaneously with the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera. Furthermore, once his hair had been shaved, his appearance became identical to that of a śrāmaṇera.

This is not because he is a lay *upāsaka* living in the secular world. Regarding the discussion of the matter (*vastu*) above, the specific task to be accomplished differs; regarding the discussion of the person (*pudgala*), the appropriate individual is distinct; and regarding the discussion of the dharma (*dharma*), this is the rite of tonsure and ordination, not the *poṣadha* rite.

Thus, in this single instance, all three—person, dharma, and matter—slightly contravene the sacred regulations, and the transgressions are not few. Now, if there is one who has newly resolved to seek the Way and requests a teacher to shave his hair, he should follow the regulations of the *Pañcavargīya-vinaya*. Furthermore, one must not chant or recite the verses of the *Prātimokṣa* on such an occasion. If it is...

For those who have already received the five precepts and come seeking ordination, one should follow the *Dharmaguptaka*, *Mahāsāṃghika*, *Sarvāstivāda*, or *Mūlasarvāstivāda* Vinayas to confer the ten śrāmaṇera precepts; it is unnecessary to confer the five precepts again. Although they later receive the ten precepts, some erroneously practice according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
One should know that the authentic regulations are difficult to disrupt, and erroneous rules must be scrutinized.
The Fundamental Basis of the Thirty-Five Precepts (divided into ten sections). First, the Preliminary Guidance (a detailed study of the *Vinaya*):

regarding all actions, if they accord with one's disposition, they are permitted; however, for the most part, one must request permission through formal speech. Now, concerning the tonsure and ordination of a *śrāmaṇera*, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the Buddha stated: "First bestow the five precepts of an *upāsaka*, then perform the tonsure, and subsequently bestow the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera*.

Based on this principle, we have added ritual procedures to facilitate practical application. The precepts are the tracks; they are truly the vessel for the Three Jewels. Meditative concentration and wisdom take the precepts as their foundation;
Bodhi and Nirvana take the precepts as their root. When setting out on the path, the precepts are the sovereign lord; the precepts are the vanguard that repels evil.

This is the dwelling place of virtue. Now, there are many grades of precepts; that you now seek to receive the five prohibitions is the very beginning of the path toward goodness and the essential ford for escaping suffering.
