These words of repentance should properly be spoken by you yourself; fearing that you might be unable to do so, I shall now instruct you. [Having stated your own name:

Recite all the following words according to my request for repentance. (Recite the two lines provided by the Preceptor; the Ritual Master leads the instruction, having him recite the next two lines. For every two lines, perform one prostration, ensuring your voice is clear and distinct.)
I, [Name], one of Your disciples, from beginningless time until this present life, have (knocking) destroyed the Three Jewels;
I have become an icchantika, slandered the Mahāyāna sūtras, severed my study of Prajñāpāramitā, murdered my parents, shed the blood of a Buddha,
defiled monasteries, violated the pure conduct of others, and burned down stūpas and temples.
Misappropriating the property of the Sangha; giving rise to various false views; denying cause and effect; associating with evil friends and turning away from virtuous teachers;
committing such acts oneself and instructing others to do so; and rejoicing upon seeing or hearing of them—such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless.
Therefore, on this day, I give rise to great shame and remorse, and with sincere devotion, I disclose them all.
Seeking mercy through repentance, I pray that the Triple Gem will compassionately accept me.

May they emit pure radiance to touch my body, so that all evils may be extinguished, the three obstructions may be cleared away, and I may return to the source of the original mind, ultimately becoming pure. (Thus, perform this repentance three times.)
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra-rāja (Recite three times and prostrate three times).
(This verse provides a detailed exposition of repentance; if time is short, one may instead use the four lines from the Great Sūtra, as seen below in the *Zhengfan*.)
If one is sincere and reverent, the four impediments will be eliminated; if one lacks sincerity, they will be vast and difficult to repent.
Question Seven: Regarding Obstacles (the Preceptor strikes the ruler and says):
Now that you have completed the repentance for your past transgressions, I shall follow the *Sujāta-sūtra* and first inquire about the seven kinds of obstructing impediments;
only then will I confer the precepts upon you. Answer truthfully whether they exist or not; do not conceal or hide anything.

First: Have you ever stolen property belonging to the Saṃgha present before you? (If not, you should answer "no"; if so, you should answer "yes. Hereafter, all questions shall be answered accordingly.)
Second: Have you ever committed sexual misconduct with the sons or daughters of your six types of relatives?
Third: Have you ever defiled or violated the celibate conduct (*brahmacarya*) of monks or nuns?
Fourth: When your father was ill, have you ever abandoned him and failed to look after him?
Fifth: When your mother was ill, did you ever abandon her and disregard her?
Sixth: When your teachers and elders were ill, did you ever abandon them and disregard them?
Seventh: Have you ever killed a sentient being who has generated the bodhicitta?
Eighth: The bestowing of the precepts of refuge (the Preceptor strikes the *shaku* and says):
"O son of noble family, since you are free from the seven kinds of obstacles in this present life, your body and mind are pure and bright. The Way..."
The vessel is perfect. I may now act for you: first, I shall bestow the Three Refuges to generate the essence [of the precepts]; next, I shall proclaim the Five Precepts for you to uphold.
Regarding the Three Refuges, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "One takes the Triple Gem as the object of refuge because one desires protection and does not wish to be oppressed.
As for taking refuge in the Buddha, one takes refuge in the Dharma-body, which is omniscience and the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Merit is that which is accomplished through five factors. Taking refuge in the Dharma means taking refuge in the pure state of both oneself and others—namely, the Truth of Cessation, which is the extinction of desire and the departure from desire.

Taking refuge in the Sangha means taking refuge in the Sangha of the ultimate meaning (paramārtha)—namely, the field of merit consisting of the virtues of the Śrāvakas who are in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa). These Three Jewels possess true, pure qualities and functions capable of purifying.
It purifies the three types of action; it can block the three miserable realms; it can destroy the three obstacles; it can prevent one from leaking into the three realms of existence;

it can enable one to transcend the three worlds; and it can lead to the realization of the three vehicles. Therefore, the Buddha-dharma takes these Three Refuges as its foundation, for they universally give rise to all categories of precepts and bring all merits to fulfillment.
You should, with a heart of profound reverence and compassionate protection, pervasively...

Taking as objects of focus the realms of phenomena, sentient beings, and non-sentient things, one vows to sever all unwholesome conduct, vows to cultivate all that is wholesome, and vows to deliver all sentient beings.
If you can indeed give rise to such a vast and superior state of mind, that which you receive is the superior Three Refuges and Five Precepts.
Now is the very moment for you to receive the Three Refuges and be moved to generate the precepts.
At this time, you should sincerely direct your thoughts, take the object as your focus, and give rise to the resolve. Receive [the precepts] following my words.

First, state your own name (having stated it, wait for the Preceptor to finish speaking one phrase; the Ritual Master shall instruct the newly ordained to repeat that phrase immediately, ensuring there is no discrepancy or delay).
I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha for as long as life lasts; I take refuge in the Dharma for as long as life lasts; I take refuge in the Sangha for as long as life lasts.
(Thus, having performed the threefold refuge and completed the three prostrations,) the Preceptor strikes the wooden sounding-block and says:
The three refuges mentioned above constitute the actual reception of the essence. To this, three further recitations are added, which are called the *karmavācanā*.

You should maintain a sincere mind and follow my words. (For the following ritual recitation: wait for the Preceptor to speak one phrase, then the newly ordained person repeats that phrase. According to the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, when the recitation is finished, bow once to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; repeat this three times for each.)
I (so-and-so) have completed my taking of refuge in the Buddha. Even at the cost of my body and life, I shall never take refuge in the Lord Māra or other celestial demons.
I take refuge in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; he is my World-Honored One. Out of his compassion, may he grant me grace.
I, [Name], have completed my refuge in the Dharma. Rather than sacrifice my body and life, I shall never take refuge in the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths.
I take refuge in all the sutras of the Three Piṭakas and Twelve Divisions taught by the Tathāgata; these are what I revere (out of compassion). I, [Name], have completed my refuge in the Saṃgha.
Rather than sacrifice my body and life, I shall never take refuge in the heterodox assemblies of non-Buddhists. I take refuge in...
"I rely upon the Sangha of the pure field of merit; they are my honored ones, out of their compassion.
(Next, formally proclaiming the characteristics of the precepts, the Upādhyāya strikes the wooden sounding-block.)
I have already completed the formal declaration of the Three Refuges for you. You have now received the essence of the Five Precepts;
I shall now further proclaim the characteristics of the Five Precepts so that you may recognize them, maintain them, and guard their essence, calling upon your own name (having called it).
First, abstaining from killing;
second, abstaining from stealing;
third, abstaining from sexual misconduct.
The fourth is abstaining from false speech;

the fifth is abstaining from intoxicants. These are the precepts of an upāsikā. Are you able to observe them for as long as you live? [Answer: I am able to observe them. (Thus the characteristics of the precepts are proclaimed three times. After three prostrations, there is once again a summary conclusion consisting of one question and answer.)
"Good son, these five precepts are the root of all precepts; they are the stairway for entering the Path, the gateway to liberation, and the means to realize the fruit of Bodhi.
Beginning from the first, non-killing, up to the fifth, abstaining from intoxicants—can you maintain them in their entirety?
[He replied: "I can maintain them in their entirety."
The Ninth Vow (the Preceptor strikes the ruler):
The *Āgama* Sūtras state that after one has received the five precepts, they should be taught to make vows. This is because practice and vows support one another;
only when both merit and wisdom are present can they be perfected. It is like a precious chariot: without its wheels, it can never carry a load. Therefore, I now instruct you.
Follow my instructions and visualize the Triple Gem. Facing the Buddha with reverence, resolve your heart upon making this vow and call out your own name.
(Having called it, say: I, [Name], resolve my heart upon making this vow: By the merit of these five precepts, may I not fall into the three miserable realms or the eight difficult conditions.
Taking this merit, I bestow it as a gift upon all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm.

All shall resolve to attain Bodhicitta. Together they shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). Upon the blossoming of their lotuses, they shall behold the Buddha and hear the Buddha Vehicle (*Buddhayāna*).
Having received the Buddha’s prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), they shall return to the Sahā world to transform and guide sentient beings.

All together they shall be born in the Pure Land, forever free from all suffering. (This is the Superior Grade, Superior Birth. [Wait for the Preceptor to speak one phrase; the newly ordained monk follows with one phrase. Repeat this three times, bowing three times at the end.]
The Tenth Admonition on Dedication (The Preceptor strikes the ruler and says):
"Good son, because you have planted roots of virtue in past lives, you now encounter this auspicious condition;

having been born into a family of right faith in this world of five turbidities, you have taken refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts. You must cherish and protect them with vigilance; you must not violate them."
Regarding transgressions: they are like a black dragon guarding its pearl, or a yak cherishing its tail;

they are like protecting a dam so that no water leaks through, or defending a city's moat so that it remains unimpaired. If one commits any of these five, especially the first four grave offenses, one is like a corpse.
The great ocean does not accept those who have broken their precepts; likewise, the ocean of the precepts does not tolerate such persons.

Furthermore, they may no longer receive the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera*, the full precepts of a *bhikṣu*, or the Bodhisattva Great Precepts, because their fundamental basis has been destroyed and wholesome dharmas are difficult to generate therein.

Are you now able to uphold each of these precepts? [The candidate] replies: "I am able to uphold them according to the Dharma. [The Upādhyāya says: "Since you are able to uphold them according to the Dharma..."

The Preceptor shall come to the assembly of monks at dawn to shave your hair, drawing you out from the burning house to the cool and refreshing state, and leading you from the path of delusion back to the True Way.
(The Preceptor strikes the wooden sounding-block, rises from his seat, joins his palms, and makes the dedication:)

With this merit from bestowing the precepts, may it be spread throughout the sands of the world-system. Let the great assembly, with one voice, recite the Buddha’s name and dedicate the merit (reciting the Buddha’s name several hundred times).

(The Ritual Attendant calls for the candidates for ordination; they perform three prostrations in gratitude and stand to one side. (The Rector Master recites the Dedication of Merit. (The assembly joins in unison.)

The supreme practice of the merit of bestowing the precepts—may all boundless and excellent blessings be dedicated so that all sentient beings drowning in saṃsāra may swiftly proceed to the buddha-field of Amitābha.
To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas: Mahāprajñāpāramitā.

(The Abbot descends from his seat and finishes prostrating to the Buddha. Once the verse of dedication is completed, the two ritual masters lead the way, followed by the ordinands, escorting the Abbot back to the abbot’s quarters. The ceremonial protocol is as usual. They then return to the front of the seat; after the ordinands have bowed in thanks to the ritual masters, they depart.)

Gradually, each returns to their respective place. △ The *zhikeshi* (guest prefect) leads the newly ordained monks to the presence of the Patriarch to perform prostrations, as well as to all venerable elders and *bhikṣus*; they should all perform the rites of salutation until completion. Furthermore, according to the Vinaya, regarding the ordination of women:

Please request the *niṣīdana* (preceptor) to recite the five precepts and ten precepts. The *karmadāna* shall lead the ritual. All [participants], including the *niṣīdana*, [should address the candidate as]: "Virtuous man" (for a male) or "virtuous woman" (for a female; for a *śrāmaṇera*, add the character "nun" [*bhikṣuṇī*] below).

IV. The Ten-Branch Model for the Correct Ritual (divided into ten parts). First: The General Announcement and the Spreading of Seats. (The above concerns the bestowal of the Five Precepts of an Upāsaka;

from here below is the shaving of the head and the bestowal of the Ten Precepts of a Śrāmaṇera. As there are prior and subsequent stages, the ritual is performed in two sessions. Therefore, these items are established separately for the convenience of arranging seats and assembling the assembly.

If other circumstances arise, or if time is short such that it can only be completed in a single day, one must still distinguish between the two sessions of the morning and midday. △ The person seeking to have their hair shaved shall, on the following morning, first go to the office of the Karmadāna and the ceremony master, prostrate three times, and then stand up.
(With palms joined, he says:
"I, [Name], having yesterday received the guidance of the various masters, have attained the rank and title of an upāsaka. The five precepts have already been ascended."

Desiring to escape the worldly conventions of the household life, yet having not yet advanced to the ten precepts, I now again earnestly entreat you to once more bestow your skillful means, so that [I, so-and-so] may have my hair and beard shaved off and the appearance of a monk quickly perfected.
My gratitude for your virtue shall be boundless, and I shall bear it in mind for the rest of my life.
(The Karmadāna said): "O son of noble family, the discipline has already been established; the Dharma must proceed in its proper sequence.

I shall now select a place for you and arrange the seats, strike the gong to assemble the Sangha, and respectfully invite the Upādhyāya to preside over the assembly and bear witness as I shave your hair and confer the precepts upon you. You have heard the *gaṇḍī*...
At the sound of the mallet, one waits for the preparations to be completed.

[The official] bows once more and withdraws. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) then accompanies the ritual master (*yinke*) to select a location and arrange the seats, whether on open ground or elsewhere.

Whether in the Dharma Hall or in the Abbot’s quarters, he shall command a *karmadāna* to sprinkle and sweep the area until it is clean and pure; as for the seats to be spread out, they shall be arranged according to the protocol explained previously.
Second, the Assembly Assembles and Invites the Preceptor:

When the candidate for ordination hears the sound of the *ghanṭā*, he takes his five robes, seven robes, two robes, and his alms bowl, and follows the barber upon whom he relies to join the assembly. The *karmadāna* then takes the robes and bowl brought by the candidate and places them to the right of the seat of the Noble Sangha;
the razor and the purification flask are placed on the seat of the *upādhyāya*. Each of the hair-washing basins and vessels is prepared.
(The Karmadāna said): "O son of good family, the Dharma seat has been spread and the great assembly has gathered. You should proceed to the center and face upward;
with reverence and care, perform contemplation and prostrate yourself with single-minded devotion."
Three prostrations to the Triple Gem of the ten directions to seek their compassionate acceptance. (After he has finished bowing, it is said again:
Three prostrations before the seat of the Holy Sangha facing east to seek their witness and seal. (After he has finished bowing, it is said again:)
Facing the assembled great assembly gathered before him from all sides, each person performs three prostrations. (Once they have finished bowing, he says again:
"Stand fixedly to one side. The one serving as the barber then steps out from the assembly, takes incense, and proceeds to the abbot’s quarters.

The invitation of the Abbot. (Second, the two ushers ring the hand-chime and proceed forward; those holding incense follow in succession. They enter the room; the ritual procedures are as usual. The Abbot accepts the invitation and exits the room. He proceeds to the front of his seat. The two ushers approach the Buddha’s seat and stand in a line to the left and right. Those holding incense stand to the side in front.

The Abbot spreads his ritual mat, performs three prostrations to the Buddha, and then rises from his mat. He proceeds to the seat of the Holy Sangha, spreads his mat, and performs three prostrations. The attendant rises from his mat. The Abbot ascends the seat and offers incense. The Rector (Vina) intones the liturgy.)
[The assembly chants] "All in harmony.
[They recite] "Namo to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Cloud-Arrival-Assembly" three times. (The Ritual Master says: The incense-bearer approaches before the Buddha’s seat.
Having arrived, they kneel long on their knees and offer incense. (Having inserted the incense, they return to their position. Standing in the center, they hear the sounding of the chime.
[Proclaiming] "The Sound," perform three prostrations with utmost sincerity. Rising and arranging the sitting cloth, proceed to the east before the seat of the Holy Sangha.

Upon arrival, unfold the sitting cloth. Hearing the sound of the chime, perform three prostrations. (Having finished the prostrations), rise and arrange the sitting cloth, proceeding to the west before the seat of the Upādhyāya. Upon arrival, unfold the sitting cloth.

Upon hearing the sound of the *qing* gong, perform three prostrations with full obeisance (*sanbai*). (Having completed the prostrations,) rise and adjust your attire, then return to your original position (retreating to stand in the left rank).
Third, the dismissal of those seeking ordination (the *vinaya-dhara* says):
"Good sons, now the Preceptor has ascended the seat and the assembly of monks has gathered like clouds.

As we are about to perform the *karmavācanā* and the Saṃgha shall carry out the ritual procedure, you must first depart and stand where you can see but cannot hear. Only when summoned may you enter the assembly."
(The person being removed proceeds to the center, bows once, and rises; the ritual leader leads them to a place where they can be seen but not heard, where they stand still.

The ritual leader then returns to the assembly to hear the *saṃgha-karman*. This follows the Vinaya regulations and is called the *aprakṣya-karman* [the formal act performed in the absence of the subject]).
The Fourth: The *Saṃgha-karman* for Harmony (the Upādhyāya strikes the *śalākā* and says):

"Has the Saṃgha assembled? (The Karmadāna replies): "The Saṃgha has assembled. "Is there harmony? (Reply): "There is harmony. "Have those who have not received the full ordination departed? (Reply): "They have departed.

"Have any Bhikṣus who did not come conveyed their consent (*chanda*)? (If there is no one to convey consent, reply): "None. (If there is someone, that Bhikṣu conveying the consent immediately replies): "There is [consent]. [He then] departs from the assembly.

One prostrates once toward the higher direction, kneels for a long time, joins the palms, and says: (Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, the bhikṣu [Name], have received the consent of that person. That person is acting in accordance with the Dharma.)

[Regarding monastic affairs: the *yuyu-kaṇma* (conferring of consent). The presiding *upādhyāya* replies: "Excellent. The other should say: "So be it," bow once, rise, and return to their original seat.

As for what is called *chanda* (consent): *Chanda* refers to an urgent matter; because one cannot follow the assembly, one entrusts another to speak on one's behalf, saying: "I, [Name], have a matter to attend to."
"The Saṃgha is now in harmony. What shall we perform? [The answer was: "We shall perform the *karmavācanā* for shaving the hair. "Who among this assembly is able to perform the *karmavācanā*?"

The *karmavācanā* master, with palms joined in the midst of the assembly, replies: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], am capable. Once the Elder has declared his capability, he steps out from the assembly and makes the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

Regarding the regulations for the *karmavācanā*: if sitting, all must sit together; if standing, all must stand together. If the one performing the *karmavācanā* stands while the listeners sit, or if the listeners stand while the one performing the *karmavācanā* sits, it is in every case an illegality (*adharma*), and the *karmavācanā* is not accomplished. The same applies to walking or lying down.

Therefore, when the Preceptor asks whether there is anyone present who knows the *karmavācanā*, those present should stand up and listen. The one performing the *karmavācanā* shall step out from the assembly toward the center, perform three prostrations, stand up, join their palms, and make the following announcement:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. That [person A] wishes to have his hair shaved by the bhikṣu [person B]. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let it be permitted to shave the hair of [person A].
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Is the motion completed? [The present Saṃgha, with palms joined, replies in unison: "It is completed."

When the *karmavācanā* master has finished this announcement, he performs one prostration toward the upper direction within the assembly and rises. He then returns to his original position. The barber, having heard that the Sangha has granted its consent and authorized the tonsure, shall immediately leave the assembly, face the Buddha’s seat in the center, arrange his robes, and perform three prostrations.
He then performs three prostrations each toward the seats on the east and west sides. Having risen from his prostrations, he withdraws and stands at his original position.
Fifth, summoning the candidate for ordination to enter (the ritual for communal harmony having concluded, the *karmadāna* steps outside and, facing the candidate, beckons with his hand, saying):
"Virtuous son, come here. (He follows the summons and arrives, standing fixedly to one side. "Just now, the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) was carried out; the Sangha has all granted their assent."
You may have your hair shaved within the monastery. You should go inside and proceed toward the upper [section]. (Having arrived inside) approach the Buddha’s seat.
Kneel upright with utmost sincerity and offer three incense sticks, earnestly entreating the Triple Gem of the ten directions for their compassionate protection and blessing.

(He approaches, kneels, and offers incense. The Rector recites the incense hymn; the assembly joins their palms and chants in unison. The Master of Ceremonies calls for him to rise, move down to the center, and, upon hearing the sound of the chime, perform three prostrations with utmost sincerity.)

The Buddha was born in the Western Regions, and his teachings flowed to the East. Their profound purport and deep discourse reveal the emptiness of self and other; through faith, one emerges from the cage of worldly existence, where loyalty to sovereign and parent is truly one and the same.
Such an opportunity is indeed difficult to encounter.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gandhameghavyūha. (Recite three times; after three prostrations, the incense praise is concluded. Call out: Kneel long with palms joined.
(Next, the formal invitation of the Master) (The Rector says):
"Now, the ordinary mind is the very substance of the realization of the Sage; it is known only through awakening. This illusory body is the vessel for carrying the Way;

it cannot fulfill its purpose without cultivation. Since you have now left the household life with faith and delight in practicing the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), you ought by right to request an enlightened teacher."
The Preceptor, relying upon the compassionate model of [his own] teacher, now accepts your respectful invitation for [Master] So-and-so of the Hall.

This Upādhyāya shall serve as your witness and your primary preceptor for the tonsure and the reception of the precepts. Furthermore, this master is one who strictly observes the Vinaya and is skilled in instructing later students.

You should maintain a focused and upright mind and follow me as I extend this request. As for the words of the request to the Preceptor, you ought to state them yourself; however, fearing that you may not yet...
"I can. I shall now instruct you: recite your own name. (Having so recited,) all subsequent words shall follow my lead.
Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind: I, [Name], disciple, now request the Venerable Sir to act as my witness and preceptor for the tonsure and the reception of the precepts.
May the Venerable Sir act as my witness and preceptor for the tonsure and the reception of the precepts. I rely upon the Venerable Sir..."

Because of his virtue, he has been permitted to shave his head and receive the precepts. Out of compassion (three times he requests; three times he prostrates; at the end, he says "out of great compassion" for each round).
This is the sixth section on guidance (the text is from the *Gutan yi*; the Preceptor strikes the wooden ruler and says):
"Good son, since you have now earnestly requested me three times, I shall serve as your witness, your preceptor for tonsure, and your root teacher for receiving the precepts.
Listen attentively to all my words. To begin with, the source of the mind is profoundly still and tranquil; the ocean of Dharma is deep and vast."

Those who are deluded shall sink and wallow for eternal kalpas; those who awaken are liberated in this very place. If one wishes to transmit the wondrous Way, there is none superior to leaving the household life.
Vast and expansive like empty space, pure and serene like the bright moon, when the conditions for cultivation are complete, the fruit of the Way is not far off.
Beginning with the merit of moment-to-moment mindfulness, one ultimately realizes the stage of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). This is why the Great Awakened World-Honored One—

He renounced the precious throne of the Golden Wheel and, at the hour of midnight, leaped over the city walls. He cast off his rare and imperial dragon robes and severed his hair upon the green mountains.

He allowed a magpie’s nest to rest upon his crown and hung a net of pearls between his brows. By cultivating quiescence, he realized the True and Eternal; by severing worldly toil, he attained Perfect Enlightenment.
Among the Buddhas of the three periods of time, none have said that one achieves the Way while remaining a householder. Thus it was with the Patriarchs of successive generations.
Who is it that practices the path of defilement to deliver others? This is why Buddha after Buddha hands over the transmission, and patriarch after patriarch transmits the mind.

Only by remaining unstained by worldly conditions does one become a vessel for the Dharma; thus, the heavenly Māras are prostrated and subdued, and the non-Buddhists submit. In this way, one repays the fourfold debt of gratitude.
He descends to relieve the suffering of the multitudes of living beings. As it is said: "Wandering through the three realms, one cannot sever the bonds of affection;

to cast aside such affection and enter the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is truly to repay that kindness. After leaving the household life, his conduct transcends ordinary sentiment; he does not prostrate before kings.
"You do not prostrate before your parents. You should now leave my seat; recollecting the kindness and virtue of your lord and kin, you must pay your respects with single-minded devotion.
This one prostration is called the 'final prostration.'"
Seventh: Taking Leave of Ruler and Parents (The Ritual Master says):
"Good son, rise after one prostration and follow me to the positions facing south and north. First, perform the rites of the secular world."
Having offered words of apology to their lords and parents, they next follow the rites for transcending the world and take refuge in the Buddha-dharma.
(First, the ritual leader guides the seeker of deliverance to stand before the northern position and calls out:)
"Good son, you should straighten your body and face north. Contemplate the profound kindness of the king’s land and waters.
With utmost sincerity and a bowed posture, perform four prostrations. (When the four prostrations are completed, lead him again to stand before the southern position and call out.)"
"Good son, you may straighten your body and face south. Focus your mind on the profound virtue of your parents who gave birth and raised you.
With utmost sincerity and a bowed head, perform four prostrations. (After he has finished the four prostrations, he is led back to the center and made to stand. The guide calls out:)
"Good son, you have already taken leave of the sovereign, bid farewell to your parents, and sought refuge in the Triple Gem as a disciple of the Buddha.

You should now straighten your body, join your palms, and contemplate with utmost sincerity. Upon hearing the sound of the chime, prostrate nine times before the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions.
(When those nine prostrations are completed, return to stand before the seat of the Upādhyāya. The ritual master leads you back to your original position.)"
"Stop. Call out: 'O son of good family!
Before the seat of your Upādhyāya, upon hearing the sound of the *ghaṇṭā*, prostrate yourself with utmost sincerity three times, then kneel for a long time with palms joined.'"
The Eighth: Shaving the Hair (The Preceptor strikes the ruler and says):
"O son of good family, at this moment all conditions are complete and the assembly of monks shares in this joy. I shall now rise from my seat;

first, I shall pour the nectar of immortality upon the crown of your head, so that the ground of your mind may be cooled and afflictions may not invade it. Next, with the razor of the precepts, I shall sever..."
"By this hair of yours, may the defilements of your mind be forever extinguished and your holy life (brahmacarya) flourish.
This is the result of virtuous causes accumulated over many kalpas and numerous lifetimes, not a mere stroke of luck on this single morning. You should deepen your faith and give rise to great joy."

(The Master takes the *śikya* water flask in his hand, rises from his seat, and approaches the candidate for ordination. Using the water from the aforementioned flask, he drips three drops upon the candidate’s crown with his finger. Excellent, O Great Man, Able to comprehend that the world is impermanent, You have abandoned the secular life to seek Nirvāṇa;

It would not be too late to release you and return home. Therefore, I now ask you before this great assembly: can you truly resolve this?"
"Are you determined to leave the household life, and will you have no regrets or turn back later? (He replied: "I am determined to leave the household life; I shall have no regrets or turn back.
"If you are indeed able to resolve to leave the household life and have no regrets or turn back later," (thus he asked three times, and he likewise answered three times).

"Since you are able to resolve to leave the household life without regret or turning back, I shall shave the top-knot beneath the blade so that the bonds of attachment are forever severed, and you may cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*) among the ranks of the Saṅgha. [This is] merit and wisdom..."
[The disciple] gradually increases [the hair]. (When the master has finished shaving the hair, he again goes before the Preceptor’s seat, holding the razor in his hands and says:

(The Preceptor replies: “Excellent. (Having made this announcement, he places the razor on the seat, performs a prostration by touching it once, rises, and withdraws to his original position.)

The Ninth: Bestowing the Śrāmaṇera Precepts (The Upādhyāya strikes the ruler and says):
"Good son, since you have had your hair removed and your appearance differs from that of the laity, you are called a śrāmaṇera in both name and form.
If you receive the ten branches of pure precepts, you shall dwell in a monastery, study under a teacher, eat together with the great monks, and wear the robes while subsisting on alms."

Only then may one be called a *śrāmaṇera* who conforms to the Dharma. For this reason, I shall now first show you the *śrāmaṇera’s* robes and bowl, and subsequently confer upon you the ten *śrāmaṇera* precepts, so that you may practice them without violating the Vinaya discipline. (The Preceptor, holding the five-strip robe, says:

"This is the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭhina*) to be worn by you as a *śrāmaṇera*. 'Strip' (*kaṭhina*) means it is not made by cutting and piecing together; rather, it consists of strips of uniform length."
[The Master] says: "This robe is for you to wear at all times while performing labor, entering and exiting, coming and going within the temple, and serving alongside the assembly;

Therefore, it is called "the robe for entering the assembly. [He sets down the seven robes and holds up the alms bowl, saying: "This is the alms bowl held by you, the śrāmaṇera.

You should drape [the robe] over your right shoulder, with the inner garment tucked into the armpit. (Setting down the bowl, he says: "Good son, your robes and bowl are in accordance with the Dharma; you may receive the precepts.
From beginningless time until this present life, you have been shrouded by the source of the mind with delusive thoughts.

Your consciousness and emotions have craved and attached to sensory objects, failing to realize that all phenomena are fundamentally devoid of self-nature. Within this state, you have engaged in various acts of grasping and rejecting, extensively creating evil karma."
Since body and mind are already defiled, one must receive the pure precepts with composure.

Therefore, you now respectfully stand before the Triple Gem of the ten directions, seeking compassionate rescue. May all the roots of goodness not yet cultivated since beginningless time be diligently practiced from this moment forth.
Regarding the evil deeds committed in the past, do not commit them again. May the Three Jewels bestow their compassion so that you may receive the precepts.

Follow my words, give rise to great shame and remorse, cleanse your heart, and repent. Call out your own name (having called it, recite the verse above and then follow with the confession; bow once for each phrase).
All evil karma created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed,
hatred, and delusion— I now, before the Buddha, seek to repent for all such sinful obstructions.
Arising from body, speech, and mind—[I] repent of all roots of transgression. (Thus, threefold repentance; twelve prostrations.)
The confession is now complete. I shall first administer the Three Refuges for you; this is precisely the time for you to receive the essence of the precepts.
You should give rise to the highest grade of mind and receive the highest grade of precepts.

As for what is called the "highest grade of mind," it is the resolve to sever evil, cultivate goodness, and benefit others, made now before the Triple Gem, directed universally toward the entire Dharma-realm, including all sentient and non-sentient beings.
Regarding the object: upon the object of focus, one vows to sever all evil, such that there is no evil not severed;
one vows to cultivate all good, such that there is no good not cultivated; one vows to deliver all sentient beings, such that there is no being not delivered. One is able to give rise to such a mind.
The śrāmaṇera precepts you shall receive are based upon this superior state of mind; they constitute the superior level of ethical discipline.

You should internally generate such a mind, focus upon such an object, and externally follow my words. Contemplate and receive them with clear attention, without allowing other thoughts or reflections to arise.
Recite one's own name (Having recited it, wait for the Preceptor to speak one phrase; the candidate for ordination should repeat that phrase immediately, without any confusion).
I (so-and-so), for as long as life shall last, take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Saṃgha. I now follow the Buddha into the homeless life;
so-and-so shall be my preceptor (the "preceptor" being the upādhyāya on the seat, who speaks his own name).
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One. Out of compassion... (Recite thus three times. Prostrate three times. At the final repetition, add: "Out of great compassion.")
The three refuges mentioned above constitute the formal reception of the essence into one's mind. To further ensure the perfection of the rite, three additional recitations are performed;
this is known as the threefold *karmavācanā*. [Having recited] your own name, follow my instructions.
I (so-and-so) have completed my refuge in the Buddha; I have completed my refuge in the Dharma; I have completed my refuge in the Saṅgha.
I have now followed the Buddha into homelessness. So-and-so is my preceptor.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One. Out of compassion [for me]... (Thus three times, with three prostrations).
"Good son, the three refuges and the three knots are now complete; you have already attained the essence of the pure precepts.

I shall now proclaim for you the characteristics of the ten precepts, so that you may recognize them, maintain them, and thereby protect their substance. [Recite your own name] (having finished reciting it)..."
(The Abbot said): "The ordination having been completed, you now possess the essential nature of a śrāmaṇera.

You should don the five, seven, or two robes and carry an alms bowl to manifest the external marks of a śrāmaṇera. The Preceptor for Ceremonies may now assist him in donning the robes and reciting the verses."

Instructing on the practice of wearing and maintaining [the robes]: (The ritual master takes the upper robe and bowl from the seat and gives them to him. He first hangs the bowl over his shoulder, then puts on the five-layered *saṃkakṣikā* robe. Instruct him to recite the verse as follows).
Excellent is the robe of liberation, the unsurpassed seven-layered *kaṣāya*. I now receive it upon my head; may I never be parted from it in life after life. Oṃ siddhye svāhā.
(Furthermore, for the donning of the seven-layered *kaṣāya*, instruct them to recite this verse:
Excellent is the robe of liberation, the unsurpassed seven-layered *kaṣāya*. I now receive it upon my head; may I always wear it throughout all lifetimes.
Oṃ. Dupa dupa svāhā. (Furthermore, instruct them to spread their mats toward their seats and recite this verse:
"The bedding and the *niṣīdana* mat nourish the seed-nature of the mind; by spreading them out, one ascends to the ground of the noble ones, upholding the command of the Tathāgata."
Oṃ. Damba damba svāhā. (Have them perform three prostrations. The *vina* master raises [the chant], and the assembly responds in unison:
Namo Ratnotpala Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. (Recite three times and perform three prostrations.)
The Tenth: Exhortation and Dedication (The Preceptor strikes the ruler and says):

"You, *śrāmaṇera*, have now had your hair and beard fall to the ground and donned the *kāṣāya* upon your body. You have entered the assembly of wholesome dharmas and emerged from the realm of worldly clamor.
Daily renew your spiritual practice and forever abandon all clinging to external conditions. I shall now show you the five virtues and ten [precepts]."

Numerous [monks], their youthful vigor delighted in the aspiration for the Way, relied upon and practiced it accordingly. Regarding what are called the "five virtues," the *Futian jing* (Sutra on the Field of Merit) states:

First, they have resolved to leave the household life, cherishing and wearing the Way within their hearts; second, they have altered their physical appearance to accord with the dharma-robes; third...
First, to sever affection forever, because there is neither partiality nor aversion; second, to cast aside body and life, because one reveres and honors the Way;
third, to seek the Mahāyāna with resolve, for the sake of delivering sentient beings. Regarding what are called the "ten items," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

First, all sentient beings depend upon food and drink (as for the present practice of the five contemplations while eating, it is to restrain greed, hatred, and delusion); second, [to know] name-and-form (which is provisional, leading to the realization of non-self).

Third, because dharmas are empty of both [self and phenomena], there is consciousness, sensation, and perception (which are the false mind’s discriminations that sever the afflictive hindrances and the cognitive hindrances). Fourth, there is the illumination of the Four Noble Truths.

(1) Knowing suffering; (2) abandoning the origin; (3) aspiring for cessation; (4) practicing the path; (5) clearly seeing that the five aggregates are all empty; (6) knowing that the body is false and illusory, like an empty village inhabited by the bandits of the fetters and the six sense bases;
(7) skillfully employing the seven factors of enlightenment; (8) constantly practicing the eightfold noble path; and (9).

(Realizing that) the sentient beings dwelling in the nine realms (all fail to escape suffering, because they are empty, impermanent, and non-self), tenth: (one contemplates) the ten universal bases (as fundamentally unborn).
Because their nature is without combination, this is the rule for a *śrāmaṇera*. Having heard and understood this, you must always bear it in mind and never forget it.

If you can study diligently and practice with your own body, the ten branches of the *śrāmaṇera* precepts will be purified; the twenty-four sections of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) and the five virtues will gradually be established;

and the ten numerical categories of cultivation will be thoroughly practiced. In the future, when you ascend the platform before the ten masters and receive full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, you will become a *bhikṣu* and enter the Saṃgha.
Regarding the enumeration of the Three Jewels: they perpetuate the lineage of the Sages, and their merit is inconceivable.

From this point forward, may you redouble your pure faith; do not be indolent or allow your body and mind to run wild. Can you thus follow the teachings and practice accordingly? (Answer: I shall follow the teachings and practice accordingly.

(The Abbot says: "Since you are able to practice in accordance with the teachings, by virtue of this merit of shaving the head and receiving the precepts, may you repay the four debts of gratitude above and succor the three realms of existence below.

Let the assembly join in unison to recite the Buddha’s name and perform the dedication of merit. (The Abbot strikes the *chizi* once, rises from his seat, and joins his palms while reciting the Buddha’s name.

The Ritual Master calls for the novice to prostrate in thanks to the Abbot; he performs three prostrations and stands to one side. The *Vinaya-master* recites the verse of dedication (the assembly joins in chorus).

The supreme practice of the merit of bestowing the precepts—may all these boundless and excellent blessings be dedicated so that all sentient beings drowning in suffering may swiftly proceed to the Buddha-field of Amitābha.
To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and to all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas:
Mahāprajñāpāramitā. (The Upādhyāya descends from his seat and, having finished prostrating to the Buddha, proceeds according to the usual ritual.)

Escort the Preceptor back to his quarters. The assembled multitude gathers with joy to pay three prostrations before the Buddha. That novice then proceeds to the front of the seat to offer thanks to the surrounding assembly and the presiding ritual master (weina).

Once the procession has concluded and the assembly has departed, the tonsure master leads the novice back to the Patriarchs’ Hall to pay respects to the patriarchs. The Commentary on the Meaning states: At the time of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he upheld the Vinaya while expounding upon the eternal. He exhorted the bhikṣus to take the precepts as their teacher.
This so-called "continuation of the life-vein of the Saṃgha" and the long-term abiding of the True Dharma depend entirely upon the observance of the precepts.
Now, at the inception of the codification of the Vinaya, the Five Precepts were first established; at the beginning of renunciation, the Ten Branches (Śīla) were first taught. —Compiled by Baizhang.

This has been recorded within the *Qinggui* (Rules of Purity) as the authentic model for tonsure; it is truly essential. Lately, many copies in the repositories have been erroneous, leading them to remain long on high bookshelves.
A good edition for circulation is rarely seen in the world, and thus the rites of tonsure and the administration of precepts have fallen into silence and are unheard of.
How can one not lament the decline of the Buddha-dharma? Now, fortunately, I have obtained this true rule and am able to behold it.
Model. Compiled by Jinling. Revised by Vinaya Master Jianyue of Baohua Mountain.
May it be widely circulated to rectify the evils of the times, so that newly ordained śrāmaṇeras may hear this authentic model, and even veteran bhikṣus must study and reflect upon it.
Let all follow the Buddha’s injunctions and ensure they are not forgotten. It is hoped that those who see, hear, receive, and uphold this shall together [cross] the sea of suffering.

As a bridge and raft, may you transmit the Buddha’s correct practice and forever serve as a pillar and cornerstone for the Dharma-gate. Internally, by honoring the holy teachings, may you ensure that the True Dharma flourishes eternally;
externally, by supporting the King’s transformation of the people, may you preserve the mountains and rivers so they remain forever secure. I hope you will not treat these rites with disregard.

We have already performed the ritual reenactment of the narrative elsewhere. This present section merely concerns the practical method of transmission; therefore, we do not record the explanatory commentaries on the scriptural proofs here at length.

What is most valued is that one internalizes the Buddha’s intent so that name and reality correspond. Only then will you not fail the profound kindness of your sovereign, your parents, and those who have granted you ordination.

(Appendix) Regulations for Ordination (Eight Articles in Total) The establishment of monastic communities (*seng-lin*) is fundamentally intended for monks from all directions (*shifang na-zi*) to prepare for the Way and cultivate their practice. We do not maintain a following of "crow-chasing" disciples, fearing that this would lead to corrupt practices.
Therefore, those who undergo tonsure at a young age mostly reside in hermitages or quiet chambers; however, they must still request ordination from a monastic community.
The Abbot serves merely as the Preceptor for the Recitation of the *Śīla-sūtra*.

If, however, one in the prime of life is resolved upon the Way and desires to become a monastic seeker, seeking tonsure within the monastic community (*saṃgha*), this ordination of a *śrāmaṇera* is the very first matter for the Great Assembly.

Since that which is at stake is of such great importance, one cannot but exercise careful discernment in order to establish the foundation for the worthy and the sage. All relevant regulations are set forth in full below.

Left. If one's parents do not permit it, one shall not remain [in the monastic order]. (If one truly intends to renounce the world, one must first instruct them to petition their parents for permission, and then [return after receiving it]).
Those who have committed crimes and fled justice shall not be retained.

Those whose bodies are held in custody by others shall not be retained (if they hold official posts or belong to the class of servants and the like, provided their resolve for the Way is firm, one may either seek the master’s favor for their release or petition their master on their behalf; if one practices compassion to fulfillment, it must be granted by the master before they can be ordained).

Those who have returned to heterodox teachings or who have infiltrated the Buddhist gate to corrupt the True Dharma shall not be retained (heterodox teachings include those such as the Wuwei, Bailian, Changsheng, and Tianzhu [Heavenly Master] sects).

In such cases, if the individual truly regrets their past transgressions, they may remain at the monastery for over a year. Only after verifying their sincerity shall permission for tonsure be granted. If they belong to the Daoist tradition and seek to convert to the Buddhist teachings, they may have their hair shaved provided it is confirmed that they harbor no ulterior motives.
If there is no kinsman to escort them and their background is unknown, and they have no sponsors, one must observe their disposition before making a decision.
If they have not traveled from thousands of *li* away but seek to leave the household life with sincere intent, bestow upon them the Three Refuges and extend the period for several months;

then bestow the Five Precepts and extend it for one year, or even up to three years, before permitting their ordination. Once they have been granted permission to remain, they must recite the liturgical texts with proficiency and apply themselves diligently.
There is no greater fault than parsimony. When you are about to have your hair shaved, those who are examined and found to be unsuitable shall not be permitted.

Since you have come to seek ordination, you must observe every detail of the rites and pure regulations. If you indulge in self-indulgence and negligence, or associate with those of improper character, [you shall be expelled].

Those who do not reform despite repeated admonitions shall not be retained. In the monastic groves (*saṃghārāma*), one must follow ancient prohibitions and regulations by relying solely upon the Abbot (*sthavira*);
the monks and assembly alike may not each receive [instructions] independently. Should anyone violate this, both teacher and disciple shall be expelled from the monastery.

We humbly submit that when the World-Honored One shaved his hair, he regarded the royal throne as a discarded cap; when the Holy Sangha left the household life, they were like soaring birds breaking free from their snares.
May you lead others from the mundane to the sacred, and vow to deliver yourself while benefiting all living beings, thereby loftily upholding the ancestral tradition of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

May he forever serve as the eye for humans and devas. The newly ordained śrāmaṇera (So-and-so) has long remained mired in the mundane world, failing to understand the path for transcending the dust. Having recently studied the Great Teaching, he gradually comes to know the gateway for entering the Way.
He laments how his karma binds him within the cage of the ordinary and feels shame that his person is fettered by the net of the secular.

He has resolved to cast off his white robes and set his mind upon donning the black. Fortunate to have encountered these superior conditions, he has thus fulfilled this profound vow; for this reason, he respectfully presents this pure fast.

I pray that Your compassionate light may shine universally and the Dharma rain nourish all beings, so that this newly ordained śrāmaṇera may don the robes and hold the alms bowl to become a pillar of the Buddha-Dharma;
may he listen to the teachings and practice Chan to overturn the old nests of birth and death; and may his physical body remain healthy and free from the encroachment of demonic obstacles. Truly...

This is the ritual text for the tonsure and reception of the precepts, respectfully requesting the Three Jewels to bear witness. The practitioner has truly trodden the path and arrived at the wondrous gate of the inconceivable.
Entering the world as a human being, they have shaken forth the fundamental purport of the supreme vehicle. Thus, this expressed vow has been fulfilled according to its intended purpose.
On this day, the [Year, Month, and Day], the tonsured bhikṣu [Name], leading the newly ordained śrāmaṇera [Name], respectfully submits this document.
Commentary. The *Zhengyi* states: "The ancients said that leaving the household life is the business of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can perform.
Master Yunqi Lianchi said: "Generals settle calamity and disorder through martial prowess; ministers promote the Way through literature."
In times of great peace, all affairs of the world are managed by generals and ministers; yet it is said that leaving the household life (renunciation) is not within their capability.
If this were so, then renouncing the household life would surely not be a trivial matter. According to the words of Yunqi, he draws the bowstring but does not release the arrow;

this is because he intends for one to transcend the flow of birth and death and ascend to the shore of Bodhi. After being bound by fetters through vast eons, one attains liberation in a single moment. From [self-...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated at the end.*
Benefiting oneself and benefiting others, the work of delivering sentient beings is inexhaustible; yet it all begins with the single act of leaving the household life.
This is why it is no small matter. The eminent figures of antiquity perceived this truth, and thus regarded renunciation as a most significant karmic condition and a source of profound fortune.
Like a fish released into a valley stream or a bird soaring through the sky, once they have cultivated such a resolve, they naturally let themselves go.

Regarding all aspects of practice—from the ten precepts and the two hundred and fifty precepts to the ten major and forty-eight minor rules—they were observed and maintained without weariness or fatigue. Now, however, it is not so;
some abandon their parents for the sake of poverty and suffering and enter the empty gate of the Dharma, while others, driven by the exigencies of worldly affairs, seek ordination with great effort.
Originally, they have never once given rise to a mind of truth; therefore, later on, they do not take pleasure in true practice either.

It depends entirely upon the teacher to first receive them into the discipline of the precepts and then to provide frequent instruction, so that their habitual tendencies may gradually be eliminated and their aspiration for the Way may gradually become firm. This is how those of middling capacity enter through teaching.
This is the prevailing view. It is hoped that through the influence of habit upon nature, they may achieve progress and advance toward higher states.
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the Buddha commanded Śāriputra to ordain Rāhula; first, he conferred upon him the five precepts of an upāsaka.
Subsequently, he shaved [the candidate's] hair and conferred the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera; this was the original model for shaving the head and conferring the precepts.

Alas, how many of those who leave home today are not people who have truly resolved their minds [to seek enlightenment], and yet the masters, in turn, do not provide for the fundamental concerns of their disciples. Thus, what the master teaches and what the disciple learns remains—
This is what is called the mind of seeking fame and profit, responding merely to worldly affairs. Those who seek the reality of saving themselves and others from birth and death are rare.
Even among those who do so, there are none whose foundations are established at the outset, for they ultimately end in abandonment.
To speak of the single matter of receiving the precepts, they use the excuse that one must wait for the collective conferral at the three altars; thus, [the practice] does not exist.
In this discourse, there are not a few who, lacking the necessary provisions for robes and bowls, or being delayed by various affairs, fail to receive the precepts year after year.
Even those who fortunately ascend the ordination platform often remain habituated to what is contrary to the Dharma;
they treat sacred rites as mere routine, entering and departing like travelers, merely managing to endure until the conclusion of the ceremony. Alas! Regarding the reception of the precepts—
"Thousands and hundreds [of people]—how many among them actually receive the precepts? The decline of the Dharma-Door arises from this very cause.

I venture to say that herein both teacher and disciple share in the fault, yet the teacher’s fault appears to be the more significant. As the *Cane Forest Jewel Instructions* (Cánlín Bǎoxùn) records, Huanglong said:

Objects. Re-entering the shift. Fangyuanli: Whenever there is a period of stillness (*zhijing*), perform three prostrations. For each prostration, strike once; for the inquiry (*wenxun*), strike once.
