Whenever the sutras or vinaya are being expounded, or during the formal assembly (*shangtang*), the informal discourse (*xiaocan*), and so forth, after the incense praise (*xiangzan*) is finished, the bell is struck three times in alternating fashion facing the opposite direction; it must be done with a broad and slow tempo. Three.

When the recitation is finished, only then does one open the mouth. In all instances of inviting the saints, making offerings to the Buddha, or offering vegetarian feasts to the devas, the handbell is struck once for each word.

When ascending to the hall, passing through the dining hall, or traveling on the path, the leading chime (yin qing) is not sounded. In all cases of performing Buddhist rites, whether exiting the hall or entering the hall, [the same protocol applies].

The geese-walk (雁行). Except when receiving invitations on the road, do not use the leading chime (引磬). Whenever calling the assembly in the Dharma Hall, the voice must be self-possessed, high, and clear;
call out by alternating between the left and right. If one side remains silent for a long time, continue calling from that same side first.

Generally, when following the ritual implements, do not call out "adjusting the robes" (撩衣). Generally, when assembling in the Dharma Hall, the Great Hall, the refectory, or the abbot’s quarters, [do not... in all cases.
Inquiry after health (*praśna*). If it is the occasion for such an inquiry, the ritual attendant shall still call out [the title].

Regarding all acts of repentance (*kṣamāpana*), as well as the formal recitations of the First and Third Platforms, when the ritual attendant leads the assembly, they first pay homage to the Buddha. Whenever newly ordained monks gather in the Dharma Hall, they do not pay homage to the Buddha;

this is because the ritual attendant opens the hall. This is a provisional practice for the duration of the retreat. All liturgical rites and Buddhist services during the precept period must be performed with meticulous care.

**Mastery.** Regarding the three masters at the upper level: they must master the timing of the rituals. At the middle level: they must collectively rehearse and perform the liturgies with their colleagues. At the lower level:

they must instruct the newly ordained monks on how to attend the hall according to the Dharma. As for the Ritual Master (Yinli): he leads the assembly to ascend to the Hall, to pass through the refectory, and to sleep and rise.

For all Buddhist services performed during the ordination period, he presides as the host of the opening ceremony. Should anything be improper, he shall consult with others in harmonious discourse. If the assembly is discordant, he shall skillfully mediate and admonish them.
Exhortation: The Great Ritual Master and the Ceremonial Director shall lead all the heads of the assembly in calling the ranks in their proper order.

For the first altar, there are the formal announcements for requesting the precepts and the formal announcement for the recitation of the precepts; for the second altar, within the section on requesting the precepts, the verbal responses follow as above.

The three sets of formal announcements for the submission of petitions: the announcement for the recitation of the precepts (*śīla-uddeśa*), the petition for ordination, and the verses for praise and prostration; the verse for harmonizing the Sangha;

the call to the assembly; the call to attendants; the invitation to the deities; and the dismissal back to the hall—down to the very end, including first leading the assembly in kneeling to see them off—and so forth.

For the formal announcements of the three platforms for requesting the precepts, the announcement for the recitation of the precepts, the petition, the invitation to the deities, the words for begging the precepts, and the verse for the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), all are required.

One must thoroughly memorize the two methods for the ritual leader who leads the standing assembly. This is the same as the ritual leader who leads the standing assembly, with the sole addition of calling out the ranks;

it is to be performed in conjunction with the Great Ritual (Dà Zuòfǎ). The sequence of its stages must be thoroughly memorized. The ritual leader who leads the standing assembly is also called the "Leader of Praise" (Yǐn Zàn).

One must also thoroughly memorize the incense praise for the Three Altars, the liturgy for paying homage to the Patriarchs, the praises, the three rounds of the text for repentance, and the invitation [to the deities].

The Sacred Correct Words (Śabdavidyā), the White Words of the Treatise School, the Staff Verses and Mantras, the Chime for the Three Masters, the Chime for Invitation, all musical modulations, the Chime for New Ordination, and the Rituals for Individual Invitations and General Invitation—all of these must be thoroughly practiced and committed to memory.

These are clearly detailed in the *Supplement to the Three Altars* (*Santan Bu-yi*) and the *Extensive Ritual for the Master of Ceremonies* (*Yinli Guangyi*). This is the protocol for the Master of Ceremonies.
The "Master" (śāstr) refers to the five kinds of ācāryas; the fourth is the ācārya who transmits the scriptures (*śāstrācārya*). (Regarding the five kinds of ācāryas:

first, the *pravrajyā-ācārya*, which is the original preceptor for tonsure as well as the one who explains the precepts of tonsure. Second, the *karmācārya*, who performs the *karma-vācanā* on the ordination platform. Third, the *anuyoga-ācārya*, who instructs on matters such as dignified deportment during the reception of the precepts.

Fourth, the *śāstrācārya*, who teaches the recitation of the sūtras and vinaya and elucidates their meanings and principles; this includes those who serve as ritual masters. Fifth, the *niśraya-ācārya*, who is the presiding abbot of various monasteries; I once sat at his feet and received from him...)

The benefit of the Dharma, or the benefit of receiving food, even for one who stays for a single night. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle seventy, it is said that a preceptor must possess five virtues: First, the virtue of having no lapses in ethical conduct (*śīla*). This means that even at the cost of one’s body or life, one never violates the pure precepts, being able to constantly maintain them without fail.

Second, the virtue of skillfully establishing the Dharma. This means being well-versed in collecting the Vinaya-piṭaka as taught by the Buddha, skillfully discerning what to adopt and what to discard according to the needs of the occasion, and instituting sublime teachings that are easy for others to learn and free from contradiction.

3. The quality of skillfully establishing the trainings: because one is able to properly formulate and establish the dharmas to be studied within the sūtras and vinaya, providing clear commentaries so that no errors or deviations occur. 4. The quality of skillfully severing doubt: regarding the sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras...

Fifth, the virtue of being able to expound the established teachings: he is well able to explain and lecture upon the Dharma according to what people have studied and what they inquire about, thereby enabling them to sever their doubts, as this accords with the Tathāgata’s correct regulations. Fifth, the virtue of teaching the way of transcendence:

by means of the Buddha’s sūtras and vinaya, he instructs others so that they may receive and uphold the Dharma according to the law, thereby accomplishing the Noble Path and transcending birth and death. A bhikṣu who possesses these five virtues is permitted by the Tathāgata to act as an *ācārya* for others—that is, a teacher of virtue. Furthermore, in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, fascicle thirty-four:

Fascicle. There are five conditions under which one must not confer the precepts upon others: First, a lack of faith. Without faith, the precepts will certainly not be firm. If the root of all myriad virtues is absent, how can the foundation for manifold merits be established? Second, a lack of shame. One who lacks a sense of shame will inevitably indulge their passions and break the precepts; if even the heart of modesty and remorse is absent, [how can they be maintained?]

How can there be right view in one who possesses these three [faults]? First, lack of shame: such a person will inevitably commit acts openly and, having violated the precepts, will feel no remorse. Since shame is absent, how can they reform their errors? Second, laziness: such a person will certainly not engage in cultivation; they do not understand the Sūtras or Vinaya, being confused even about what is heterodox and what is orthodox—how then could they comprehend the rules of observance and transgression?

Third, excessive forgetfulness: such a person will certainly lack strong memory; they will forget all the dharmas of the precepts. If even their recitation is deficient, how can there be any understanding of their meaning? If a bhikṣu violates these five dharmas, the Buddha does not permit him to serve as a teacher of others.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The *Zhengfan* (Correct Model) for the transmission of the precepts across the three platforms originally belongs to the Vinaya Piṭaka.
As the texts of the Vinaya Piṭaka are voluminous, the ancients extracted their essential passages and core meanings to compose this *Zhengfan*. Unfortunately, over time errors crept in.

When Master [Hu]jian of Mount Hua examined the ancient manuscript of the *Zhengfan*, he collated and corrected it before carving it into printing blocks for circulation. This new edition from Hangzhou bears the title above.

The inclusion of the two characters "Jianzu" (見祖) is an error resulting from a lack of investigation. According to Jianzu’s own account in his *Random Remarks on a Dream* (*Yimeng manyan*), he states:
"In the tenth year of the Chongzhen era, I was at Haichao An in Dantu, where I received the precepts under the guidance of Master Sanmei."
Having no money to hire a preceptor to recite the Vinaya, he sat in silence on his single mat all day long, listening as the assembly of fellow practitioners recited the Vinaya.
He did not violate the hall regulations. The Ritual Master (Yinli) reprimanded him, saying, "Moon-seeing! This place is not for sitting. You do not speak of Chan;

why do you not request the Vinaya so that you may recite it thoroughly? When the time came for the final ordination examination, nine men holding slips approached the Preceptor (Jiaoshou), and he prostrated before him.
"End. Recite the remainder with a clear, resonant voice, concluding as prescribed.

Based on this, one can see that Master Jian himself stated that when he received the precepts, he also followed this very ritual manual for the ceremony. As for that which lies outside the ritual manual:

The *Sandaan Fubi* (Aids for the Three Altars), the *Buyi Guangyi* (Supplement to the Extensive Rites), and other such works are likewise conventional frameworks. They are intended to serve as a basis for adapting to the circumstances of specific occasions.
Why is this so? For instance, at great ritual sites such as Mount Hua, where the assembly is vast, one may elaborate according to the formal rules.
However, in places where the assembly is small, how could one rigidly adhere to fixed regulations? One must simply master the training of the rites and ensure that newcomers... [are properly guided].
The precepts spur the aspiration for the Way; attaining the superior grade of precepts is the golden cord of the path to enlightenment.
If both teacher and disciple are indolent, seeking comfort at the expense of one another, and possess only the name without the reality, this constitutes the black cord of perverse karma.

However, regarding that which must not be altered, one must by no means take liberties or make arbitrary changes. Furthermore, in recent times, regarding the requesting of precepts, the recitation of precepts, and attending...

Regarding matters such as the *zhāi* (fasting) ceremony, there are differences between the Chan and Vinaya traditions. In the Vinaya school, when the assistant (*fǔbì*) reaches the front of the Dharma seat, he waits for the *heshang* (preceptor) to emerge from his room or until the preceptor has already ascended the seat.
Once the assistant has unfolded his ritual implements and performed three prostrations, he takes his formal seat while the assistant stands.

In the Chan school, the assistant merely touches the implements and performs one prostration; alternatively, if the three masters stand in a line, they perform the prostration together, and the assistant sits to the side.
In these matters, each has its own appropriate practice; one must not be dogmatic.

If the person occupying the central seat is a senior teacher and those assisting are juniors, it is permissible for them to perform three prostrations and stand at the side of the seat to demonstrate the principle of junior students reverently serving their seniors.

However, if the person on the central seat is of equal standing to the assistants—whether they are fellow practitioners or if the central seat is held by a junior while the assistants are more senior—then [the former practice would not apply].
The Elder [should] simply hold the ritual implements and perform one prostration, or stand with three people in the shape of the Chinese character "品" (piǎn) and bow together.

When ascending the seat, sitting to the side, or sitting upright, this is precisely to manifest the gravity of assisting in the propagation of the Dharma. Furthermore, as when presiding over a meal, the person on the central seat is the senior, while the nine teachers are all juniors;
when meeting them or announcing one's departure, the person on the central seat may accept the prostrations. The newly ordained monk bows to the nine teachers.
The Nine Teachers should decline and wait; because a senior is present before them, they do not dare to accept the prostration.

If among the Nine Teachers there are those whose rank is equal to that of the presiding seat (zhèngzuò), or who are seniors, or guests, and who announce their departure upon meeting, the presiding seat should respond with a bow.
When a newly ordained monk bows to the Nine Teachers, the Nine Teachers should accept the prostration, for the Way of teacher and disciple is honored.

Next, regarding the determination of the period for receiving the precepts according to the Vinaya: there is no provision for a simultaneous reception of the three stages [of ordination], nor is there a fixed date.

Rather, the transmission occurs according to the conditions and affinity between teacher and disciple. Furthermore, in the Vinaya, when the Buddha taught the Bhikṣu precepts, he permitted only three persons in a single ordination platform;
if there were four, one would not receive the precepts. This matter is of no small importance; one should therefore abide by the Buddha’s regulations. I...

In the Eastern lands, there are many who receive the full precepts all at once upon three altars; thus, the establishment of fixed periods is a provisional measure, divided into spring and winter sessions. Regarding the spring session: on the eighth day of the second lunar month, the hall is opened.

First, the attendant in charge of the altar (zhítán) is ordered to light the incense, sweep, and arrange the furnishings. Then, the guest prefect (zhīkè) leads the candidate to the Abbot’s quarters, where the Abbot personally escorts him into the hall—(in the Chan school, when opening the hall, the Abbot accompanies the candidate through the hall)—and subsequently leads him to seek the precepts and enter the hall. (Note: *Dànshòu* means "receiving all at once"; *qí* refers to the fixed period; *zuòquán* means "provisional expedient"; *chūndōng* refers to the spring and winter periods; *kāitáng* means "opening the hall" for the ceremony;

*zhí tán* refers to the monk responsible for the altar; *xiǎosǎo* means "to sweep and clean"; *pùshè* means "to arrange or set out"; *zhīkè* is the guest prefect; *lǐnyǐn* means "to lead and guide"; *shàng fāngwǎng* means "to go to the Abbot's quarters"; *suísòng* means "to escort along"; *jìn táng* means "to enter the hall"; *shàn mén kāi táng péi táng* refers to the practice in the Chan school where the Abbot accompanies the candidate through the hall during the opening ceremony; *hé shàng sòng wèi* means "the Abbot escorts [the candidate] to their seat"). (Note: *qiú jiè* means "to seek the precepts"; *jìntáng* means "to enter the hall").
The Abbot questioned him in detail regarding his background and verified his place of origin. On the fourteenth day of the third month, the two masters registered at their quarters.

After the evening service, he conducted a tour of the quarters; at the second board, he made a public confession in the Main Hall. On the fifteenth day, the Senior Master made a confession, and the Abbot presented his own transgressions.
From the sixteenth day, the repentance began; incense, candles, and other necessary items were prepared, and the first altar for the *chanmo* (repentance) ceremony was hung.

On the twentieth day, the invitation for the precepts is issued; the attendant of the right chamber leads the procession and recites the formal petition. On the twenty-first day, the repentance is completed;

the official records are submitted, the silver is presented, and the ritual implements are taken. On the twenty-second day, the instructions are returned; the begging bowl is taught, and the private rehearsal for the invitation to receive the precepts is conducted.

On the twenty-third day, the invitation to receive the precepts takes place; the robes and bowls are inspected, and the teaching on the relinquishment of stored goods is given. That evening, the rehearsal is performed.
The Ritual for Receiving the Precepts: On the twenty-fourth day: shave the head and bathe. That evening, perform repentance (*sāṃmārjana*) and prostrate throughout the night.

On the twenty-fifth day: return and arrange the precept platform with its adornments. Recite the precepts (*śīla*), make vows, tour the quarters, and provide instruction on the hall regulations (the regulations for the Precept Hall are found below).
On the twenty-sixth day: submit the draft of the *karmavācanā* record, distribute the text concerning impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*), recite the Vinaya rules that were studied, and make vows.

Circumambulation of the quarters. On the twenty-seventh day: the *śrāmaṇera* precepts are administered; the plaques for the two altars are hung; the vow is made; and there is circumambulation of the quarters. On the twenty-eighth day: the altar lots are distributed;

the presentation of invitations is practiced; and the request for the vegetarian feast is practiced. On the twenty-seventh day [of the following month]: the notice for full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) is posted;

the notice for the seven masters is posted; the lots are distributed; and the grand rehearsal of the ritual is performed. On the thirtieth day: the precepts are requested; the names and characteristics of the robes and bowl are demonstrated; invitations are presented; and they are sent out.
Send out invitations. Bathe. Shave the head. Perform repentance (*sāṃmā*). Conduct the all-night prostrations. Tour the quarters (if it is a short month, perform these on the day before).

On the first day of the fourth lunar month: offer incense and food; invite the assembly for a vegetarian meal; arrange the altar of the Precepts Platform with solemnity. That night, recite the precepts, make vows, and tour the quarters.

On the first and second days, gather the ritual ornaments and recite four-fifths of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. On these days, hang the name-plates for the three altars. On the third and fourth days, perform the grand ritual procedures.
On the fifth day, invite the preceptors and prepare the incense bearers; post the accounts for entries and exits, perform the *kṣamāpanā* (confession), and observe the all-night prostrations.

On the sixth day, return to the hall, shave the head, and bathe. On the seventh day, provide instruction on the practice of asceticism while burning incense, and arrange the *śīla-maṇḍala* (precept altar).

The eighth day of the first month: the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), making vows, and touring the quarters (*luó*). Passing through the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (the ordination platform). The ninth day:
issuing certificates, sending in records, opening the storage, returning to the monastery, reporting for leave, and touring the quarters. Thus, the duties of this period are concluded.

Winter Session. On the eighteenth day of the tenth month, the hall is opened (the specific procedures are as previously explained). By the tenth day of the eleventh month, the two masters register their names.
After the evening service is completed, they conduct a tour of the quarters. At the second board of the evening, the master of the main hall performs a public confession.

On the eleventh day, the senior master performs a public confession, and the abbot presents his own transgressions. On the twelfth day, the repentance ceremony begins; incense, candles, and other necessary items are prepared, and the plaque for the first altar is hung.

The fourteenth day: The Right Master’s faction submits their written statement. The seventeenth day: The confession (prāyaścitta) is completed; the private rehearsal of the ritual is performed. The eighteenth day: A return audience is granted; the requisites for solemnity are taken up;

instruction on the alms bowl is given; the rehearsal of the ritual is performed; and the removal of stored items is explained. The nineteenth day: The invitation to receive the precepts takes place; the robes and bowls are inspected; the head is shaved; bathing and repentance are performed; and the all-night liturgy is observed.
On the twentieth day: The return audience is held; the requisites for solemnity are laid out; and the recitation of the precepts (Poṣadha) is delivered.
On the twentieth day: making vows; inspecting the quarters; and announcing the regulations for the hall. On the twenty-first day: reciting the Vinaya; sending the official records and silver;
and hanging the plaques for the two altars. On the twenty-second day: sending the draft records and the text for the dispersal of obstacles. On the twenty-third day: sending the altar lots.
The twenty-fourth day: the invitation cards are received. The twenty-fifth day: supplementary items are prepared; the throwing of the cards is practiced. The twenty-sixth day:
the offering money for the vegetarian feast is delivered; the ritual is privately practiced. The twenty-seventh day: the offering of the vegetarian feast is practiced. The twenty-ninth day:

the proclamation for the full ordination is posted; the lots are distributed; the grand rehearsal of the ritual is held. The thirtieth day: the request for the precepts is made; the proclamation for the seven witnesses is posted; the names of the robes and bowls are announced.

Exchange invitations and deliver them (if the month is short, do both on the day before). On the first day of the twelfth month: present offerings, invite [the assembly] for a vegetarian meal and repentance, and perform the all-night ritual.
On the second day: return to shaving the head, bathe, and arrange the sacred ornaments. That night, the precepts are recited.

Make the vow; conduct the inspection of the quarters; collect the ritual ornaments. On the third day of the first month, hang the plaques for the three altars and distribute the *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Vinaya).

On the fifth day, prepare the incense heads. On the sixth day, invite the preceptors for the ordination, perform the *sāmāyika* (confession), and observe the all-night vigil. Post the accounts for entries and exits.
On the first seven days: recovery; shaving the head; bathing; instruction on ascetic practices; burning incense. On the eighth day: arranging the precept platform with its adornments;
reciting the precepts, making vows, and inspecting the quarters; passing the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* examination; removing the adornments. On the ninth day: issuing the certificates.
The record of the opening of the storage was sent; a reply was received; leave was requested to inspect the quarters. One period [of training] was completed (ten days less during the winter season).
The *Zhengyi* states: Regarding the Bhikṣu precepts, the Buddha ordained that three persons should be on one platform until the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is concluded.
Regarding the four *pārājika* offenses, the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*), and so forth, these are still recited collectively by the entire assembly; only the *bhikṣuṇīs* recite them separately.
These two periods of spring and winter were also established by the ancients, according to what is stated in the *Yi-meng-man-yen*. It is seen that the Patriarch was at Dantu.
At Haichaowan (Sea Tide Hermitage), he sought the precepts under the guidance of Master Samadhi.

This also began on the eighth day of the second lunar month and concluded with the full ordination on the eighth day of the fourth lunar month. However, according to the Buddha’s regulations, one may receive the precepts at any time.
For example, in the tenth year of the Chongzhen era, Master Samadhi was invited to the Vinaya Hermitage in Taixing County to open the ordination session; this was on the eighth [day].
The retreat began on the fifteenth day of the month and was completed on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month.
Next, he accepted an invitation from Chengtian Temple in Gaoyou; the retreat began on the first day of the twelfth month and was completed on the fifteenth day of the first month of spring.
Furthermore, on the twentieth day of the first month, he began the retreat at Shanqing Hermitage. It continued until...
The three-month period is thus fulfilled. Based on this, it can be seen that while some ancients fixed the periods for spring and winter, others did not set specific times;
however, it is sufficient to act according to what is appropriate and in accordance with conditions.
Next, after the Right Master (youshī) has led the newly ordained monks (xīnjiè) in performing their repentance, the Right Master shall pre-inscribe the title of the formal petition (*bái cí*).

The Hall Master (*kāi táng shī*) shall prepare refreshments consisting of four types of food on two tables for the large assembly. He shall instruct the newly ordained monks to serve tea at the Right Quarters (*yòu liáo*). There, the assembly is gathered, and the Ritual Master (*yǐn lǐ*) leads the proceedings:

the tea is consumed, the formal petition is distributed, and the monks' origins and lineages are inquired after so that they may be recorded in the registers. The formal petition follows the [standard] Great... [text truncated].
The ritual procedures (*vidhi*) are initiated; they conclude with the final invocation of the preceptor.
In all instances of reciting the *Poṣadha* and the minor announcements (*śukla-vācanā*), the calling of the assembly is collectively performed according to the ritual rules.

Whenever it is time for a kneeling announcement, whichever monk has reached his turn shall kneel in the center, perform the prostrations, and then return to his original seat. Whenever it is an announcement made while standing, one remains standing at one’s own seat.
[The candidate] says: "I announce. [He] merely joins his palms and does not perform a formal greeting. After the introductory remarks have been recited, he requests the precepts at the initial altar.

He announces this to the Preceptor on the left; (he likewise) announces it to the Preceptor on the right. He inspects the robes and bowl and announces this to the Preceptor on the right. He performs the *kṣāmaṇā* (confession/asking for forgiveness) and announces this to the Preceptor on the left. For the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, he announces it to the Upādhyāya.

Second, for the special request for the precepts, he announces it to the Upādhyāya; (he likewise) announces it to the Preceptors on the left and right. He demonstrates the names and characteristics of the robes and bowl and announces this.
The Right Master offers a note to the Abbot; (likewise) offers it to the two Senior Masters; (likewise) offers it to the seven [other] masters, apologizing; and offers it to the Left Master.

The *Poṣadha* (Recitation of Precepts): announce to the *Upādhyāya*. The *Trisāṃghika-śīla-prārthanā* (Request for Precepts from the Three Assemblies): announce to the two masters (*Ācārya* and *Upādhyāya*). (Also) announce to the *Upādhyāya*. The *Kṣamāpanā* (Confession/Expiation):

announce to the left master (*Upādhyāya*). The demonstration of ascetic practices (*duṣkaracaryā*): announce to the *Upādhyāya*. The *Poṣadha*: announce to the *Upādhyāya*. There are nineteen such formal announcements (*jñapti*) in total. Recite them thoroughly according to their sequence.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: This also refers to the various stages described in the *Yili* (Book of Rites). If the number of people is small, it is permissible to adapt and change according to circumstances.
Inviting the ten masters for a meal should be fixed before the formal recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*; the beginning of the midday hour is the proper time.

It has become common in recent times for some to first recite the precepts and only afterwards invite the masters for a meal; this is incorrect. The invitation for the meal should take place after the recitation.
This is a great error. As the Right Master, you ought to exert yourself to rectify this.
Regarding the regulations for the Hall of Receiving Precepts (totaling fourteen articles):

All Buddhas of the three periods of time have declared that one achieves the Way through leaving the household life; among the Bodhisattvas of the six perfections, there are none who do not cherish and respect the *śīla* (precepts).
Truly, it is only by strictly purifying the *vinaya* that one can establish a grand model for the three realms. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "To restrain the mind is the precept;

from the precept arises concentration; from concentration issues forth wisdom. These are called the Threefold Learning of Non-outflow (*anāsrava-śikṣā*). This is the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood and the root of the ten thousand practices.
Therefore, those who seek the precepts should do so like a person gathering treasures—cherishing them with every thought and longing for them in every moment.
One should diligently maintain the recitation and restrain both body and mind at all times. Should there be a deliberate transgression, punishment shall be meted out without leniency.

To guide the gathering of the mind, the following regulations are set forth. Regarding the method for receiving the precepts: one should bring the sutras and vinaya, as well as the three robes and alms bowl, and enter the hall.
If items are old, torn, or borrowed, they shall generally not be accepted for use. As for other clothing and articles, even if old, they may be used provided they are clean.
At the fifth watch, upon hearing the first strike of the fourth board, the person on duty shall lift the curtain and everyone shall rise together to don their robes and descend from their seats.
If anyone is ill, they must inform the community so that all are aware. During the day, if there is no business, one must not lower the curtain.

Curtains and canopies must be maintained; those who violate this rule shall be punished by kneeling before the incense burner. During the four periods of stillness, all shall assemble and stand in formation with dignified decorum.

One must not engage in jesting or idle chatter. Only after the ritual observances are completed may one return to one’s seat. Those who violate this rule shall likewise kneel before the incense burner.
During practice sessions, focus your mind and memorize thoroughly. When at leisure, read the Vinaya; do not engage in idle chatter or miscellaneous talk.

Whenever it is your turn to serve on duty, pay close attention to the tickets and do not shirk your responsibilities. Those who violate this rule shall kneel upon incense. When the various masters enter or exit, [pay due respect].
Stand up. Join your palms. When the Master sits, you may then sit. On the table, there shall be only the Sūtras and Vinaya; clothing and miscellaneous items must not be placed there.
When eating tea or meals, you must cover the Sūtras and Vinaya. You must not speak while eating, nor cough or spit loudly.
Those who violate these rules shall kneel before the incense burner. Each monk’s quarters has its designated east and west; for walking and sitting, each has its proper place.
At one's own assigned seat, one must not wander aimlessly from east to west, nor pass straight through the hall, nor speak in a loud voice.
When ascending the bedding, one should remove one’s shoes and arrange them close by. One must not occupy another’s seat extensively. One must not sleep with inner garments removed.
One must not converse with those on neighboring beds, nor make noise with utensils that disturbs the assembly. When lying down, one must lie on the right side and must not snore or shout loudly.

When entering or exiting the quarters, one must walk with light steps. Those who violate this rule shall kneel before the incense burner. One must not shake the bedding to make noise; bedding and robes should be folded neatly.
When ascending or descending from the platform, one must not be coarse or reckless. Those who violate this rule shall kneel before the incense burner.

When ascending the hall, passing through the corridors, or performing any Buddhist rites, one must proceed according to the established order. One must not jostle to get ahead or fall behind; one must keep the eyes fixed on the nose.
Maintain an upright and solemn posture. Those who violate this must kneel before the incense burner.

When leaving the hall for private business, if one encounters the Abbot, or two masters, various teachers, or even those with senior precepts, one must perform prostrations, join the palms, and stand to the side to yield the path.

Even when walking together with fellow practitioners of the same precepts, one must likewise maintain dignified deportment and silence. Those who violate this must kneel before the incense burner. When washing the face, one must not splash water onto others.
When paying respects to the Buddha, one must not occupy the seat for too long. One must be careful while observing the hall;

those bound by the same precepts must look after one another and must not quarrel or cause a disturbance—those who violate this shall be punished. When a superior enters the hall, one must stand up and bow immediately; when told to sit, only then may one sit.
When entering or leaving for one's own business, one must inform the supervisor and report back upon returning. While outside, one must not remain idle.
Entering the Hall improperly or losing one’s dignified demeanor: those who violate these rules shall kneel before the incense burner.
The above regulations must be strictly observed. Should any violations occur, this hall shall impose punishment. [Date] Recorded again by Abbot [Name] (to be actually posted in the Precept Hall).

The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Sūtra says, "If śīla is not pure, samādhi will not manifest.
It further says, "Unimpeded, pure wisdom arises entirely dependent upon dhyāna-samādhi. Therefore, we know that ethical discipline (*śīla*) serves as the vanguard for concentration and wisdom.

If the practice of ethical discipline is impure, there is no way for concentration and wisdom to arise. This is why the Buddha prescribed that until five summer retreats have passed, one must focus exclusively on [the precepts].

Regarding the precepts, for one who is single-mindedly diligent, it is by no means merely a matter of outward decorum. The foremost essential within the Vinaya is to constantly restrain the mind so that mindfulness is never confused;

this is what is meant by practicing the path of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). The wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness is the universal gateway to the Buddha-dharma.
As the *Lingfeng Zonglun* states: "Without the wisdom of the foundations of mindfulness, wearing the kāṣāya is like a wooden banner."
Prostrating like a pestle moving up and down—such that the six perfections and myriad practices are all identical to the asceticism of non-Buddhists—is not true cultivation.

Why? Because it does not involve the gathering of the mind, it is not the precepts. If one practices the path according to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), then the merit of observing the precepts will enable one to realize the four fruits of the śramaṇa in the present life, and even to perfectly attain the ten stages (*bhūmi*) without difficulty. Why is this so?

It is because one gathers the mind that it is easily attained. This is the second essential task: to thoroughly understand the principles of the two hundred and fifty precepts regarding what is permitted, what is prohibited, and the nature of upholding or violating them.
Otherwise, throughout the six periods of the day and night, one will merely have the name of "upholding the precepts" while actually committing many offenses through error.
Someone may say: "That which was established for the Hīnayāna is entirely opened [permitted] in the Mahāyāna; this is what the bhikṣu adheres to."
"Bodhisattvas fully integrate [all things]. From what source is this said? The answer is: The *Lingfeng Zonglun* (Treatise on the Essential Teachings of Lingfeng) states:
"To 'open' means to open up the small-vehicle mind of seeking self-deliverance and to give rise to the vow-mind of the Great Vehicle.
To 'integrate' means to dissolve untransformed attachments to dharmas and to return to the principle of immeasurable truth. Therefore, for a renunciant bodhisattva, there are no separate precepts."

The Dharma is such that all equally uphold the *bhikṣu* discipline; yet, those who resolve their minds solely for their own liberation are called followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*), while those who resolve their minds to liberate others are called Bodhisattvas. Lately, erroneous interpretations have frequently contravened the intent of the Vinaya.

Formerly, at the time of the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the *bhikṣus*, saying: "Take the precepts as your teacher. He further said: "If my Dharma should decline, it will begin with..."
Nyi: Truly, you were prescient. Alas, how could it be that you misunderstood Kai and Rong, leading to the same slander of the Dharma?

This is a revised edition by Duti (Dutai). The original work consisted of two volumes: the first volume contained the *Gangmu* (Outline) in twenty-seven pages; the second volume contained the *Zhengfan* (Model Texts) in forty-four pages.
Now, from within the *Gangmu*, I have again extracted the major outlines and recorded the essentials of its ten sections.

First, the General Discussion of the Two Vehicles (*liangsheng*)—(1) the Mahāyāna and (2) the Hīnayāna. Regarding the seven classes of followers in the Hīnayāna: the first is the *Zhendi* (True Meaning), namely the Bhikṣu, Bhikṣuṇī, Śikṣamāṇā, Śrāmaṇera, and Śrāmaṇerī.

There are five assemblies. The second is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which refers to the two assemblies of *upāsaka* (laymen) and *upāsikā* (laywomen). As for the seven assemblies of the Mahāyāna, these are precisely the aforementioned two truths of the ultimate and the conventional, having generated the great bodhicitta and received the bodhisattva precepts.

2. Regarding the Veneration of the Correct and the Rectification of Errors: The Buddha ordained that every month, the fifteenth day constitutes the *poṣadha* of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*), and the thirtieth day constitutes the *poṣadha* of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*).

If the month is short, the twenty-ninth day constitutes the *poṣadha* of the dark fortnight. Yet, from time immemorial until now, those who perform the *poṣadha* on both the first and the fifteenth days of each month recite the precepts twice during the bright fortnight, while performing no *poṣadha* at all during the dark fortnight.

Investigating the origins of this practice, it remains uncertain when the error first occurred, leading to a situation where the former precedes the latter and has become an established custom. According to the *Śīlaskandhaka* (Section on Precept-Recitation) in the Vinaya, it is stated: "One who has committed an offense may not recite the precepts; one who has committed an offense may also not hear the precepts."

One must not seek confession from an offender, nor may an offender accept the repentance of another; rather, one should confess and engage in recitation and listening before those who are pure. This clarifies that prior to the *poṣadha*, one should perform the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) for the disclosure of transgressions.

Therefore, following the Vinaya to correct errors, I have established this as a constant rule: during the bright fortnight, one first repents on the fourteenth day and performs the formal *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day. During the dark fortnight, one first repents on the twenty-ninth day and performs the formal *poṣadha* on the thirtieth day.
If the month is short, one first repents on the twenty-eighth day and performs the formal *poṣadha* on the twenty-ninth day. This is the fixed rule.

Third: Following the teachings and honoring the ancients—if a bhikṣu dwells in a residence that violates established regulations, then the uposatha ceremony, the recitation of the precepts, and all other administrative affairs will fail to achieve their purpose;

instead, they will incur the offense of transgressing the Dharma. This is because since the basis is invalid, that which depends upon it is also invalid. Thus, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "If one performs a *karmavācanā*, one must first establish the boundary (*sīmābandha*).

Although the five schools—the *Mahāsāṃghika*, *Mahīśāsaka*, *Sarvāstivāda*, *Mūlasarvāstivāda*, and others—each uphold their own traditions, regarding the single method of *karmavācanā*, none do not rely on the establishment of the boundary as their primary task. Furthermore, there are two types of boundaries: first, the formal boundary (*dharmasīmā*), which is established by assembling the community, setting up markers, proclaiming the characteristics, seeking consensus, performing the formal motion, and obtaining approval. First...

First, one establishes the boundary for receiving the precepts (*śīla-sīmā*). Next, one establishes the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). Finally, following the markers of the great boundary, one establishes the "boundary where robes need not be kept" (*acīvara-sīmā*). Second, there are four types of natural boundaries (*prakṛti-sīmā*): first, the village; second, the forest hermitage (*araṇya*); third, the path; and fourth, the water.

Each of these four has its own natural extent as its limit and is established without the use of physical markers or formal proclamations. The boundaries upon which the community of bhikṣuṇīs relies are also determined according to the above principles. Furthermore, when bodhisattva-bhikṣus and others establish boundaries, it is likewise [according to these rules].

As stated above, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* says: "If bodhisattva bhikṣus do not demarcate a boundary (*sīmā*), they show contempt for the Buddha’s word. If they do not observe the monastic regulations, then whatever they undertake will not be accomplished. Why? Because they have not established a field of precepts (*śīla-kṣetra*)."

In that case, for the ten preceptors, there is the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations). Because there is no designated place for receiving the precepts, the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is not demarcated. Because they cannot perform the *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts in harmony with the Saṃgha or communicate their consent (*chanda*), the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) is not demarcated. Consequently, individuals would lack support, like a bird without its wings.

For this reason, it is known that wherever Bodhisattvas, Bhikṣus, or the Saṃgha assemble, they follow the rules of the Bhikṣu Saṃgha by means of two types of *jñapti-karman* to demarcate the boundary. As for the three groups of smaller assemblies, they are subsumed within the boundaries of the two larger Saṃghas.

4. Regarding the selection of a person of virtue and capacity: For the *śukla-kṛṣṇa-poṣadha* (the white and black confession ceremony), which serves to clarify the fixed schedule for the ritual procedure, the Saṃgha assembles to recite the precepts (*śīla*).

One must select a capable model who possesses both virtue and seniority (*vassa*), whose learning is complete, who has observed the five-year mark, whose memory is clear, and who can resolve the doubts of the assembly. It is permitted to appoint such a person through a formal motion and second (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) within the Saṃgha. Therefore, anyone presiding over the precept laws of the two vehicles must thoroughly study the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*.

Since the selection and appointment for these two vehicles differ—both in their familiarity with such procedures and in the specific applications of their general and particular rules—they are not the same. As for the restricted application, when the seven classes of followers of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) happen to assemble together to recite the precepts they have received, if this occurs within the boundary (*sīmā*) of a Bhikṣu-saṃgha, one should then appoint and invite [an officiant].

First, a bhikṣu who is able to recite it shall recite it. As for the bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, they have no part in either reciting or listening. If one is within the boundary (sīmā) of the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha, then one bhikṣuṇī who is able to recite shall be appointed to recite it;

as for the bhikṣus, upāsakas, and so forth, they likewise have no part in reciting or listening. Therefore, this is called "restricted. If, however, it is "general"—that is, when members of the seven assemblies of the Mahāyāna gather together by chance to recite the Brahmajāla Sūtra—then regardless of which boundary they are in, one person from among the assembly of Bodhisattva bhikṣus must be requested to recite it.

If there are no bhikṣus, then next, one from among the six assemblies [the bhikṣuṇīs and so on] must be requested; that is, one from among the assembly of Bodhisattva bhikṣuṇīs. Even if there are none of the aforementioned six assemblies, and there are only Bodhisattva upāsikās, [one from among them shall be requested].

[Regarding this,] one should immediately request one person from among them to recite it. Because the seven assemblies of the Mahāyāna are all permitted to recite and listen to it, it is said to be "universal" (*tong*).

Fifth, regarding the purification of the hall and the assembly: according to the Vinaya, on the day of the *poṣadha*, one should order the sweeping and sprinkling [of the hall], the arrangement of seats, and the preparation of lamps, water vessels, and *śalākā* (voting sticks). The Elder (*upādhyāya*) should instruct the junior bhikṣus [in these matters].

As for the juniors, they should perform the preparations according to the instructions and in accordance with the Dharma. If those above do not instruct and those below do not prepare, all commit the offense of *vyatikrama-vinaya*. There are two kinds of seats to be spread out: one is a high seat for the reciter to ascend, and the other is a low seat.

This is established for the sake of the listeners. The high seat should be adorned with incense and flowers; the dharma assembly must be provided with lamps to prevent the darkness of night. There are two types of water vessels: first, for washing the feet; second, for cleansing the hands. *Śalākā* (Sanskrit: *śalākā*; Chinese: *chou*) refers to counting sticks, which serve as a method for recording numbers—by knowing the number of monks, one may receive the offerings of food.

Sixth: Regarding those who respect the Dharma and are humble toward others—when residing together with others of either greater or lesser status and reciting the Bodhisattva precepts, one follows the sequence of the Mahāyāna precepts; however, when reciting the Bhikṣu precepts, one still ranks according to the seniority of the monastic age (*saṃgha-ratna*). The *Shiqian* states:

"When a Bodhisattva is among a community of Hīnayāna practitioners, they sit according to the sequence of the Hīnayāna precepts; when among a community of Mahāyāna practitioners, they sit according to the sequence of the Mahāyāna precepts.

Furthermore, for one who first received the Bhikṣu precepts and later received the Bodhisattva precepts, the monastic age of the Bhikṣu precepts is used. If one first received the Bodhisattva precepts and later received the Bhikṣu precepts, within the Mahāyāna context, one follows the sequence of the prior Bodhisattva precepts, while within the Hīnayāna context, one follows the sequence of the subsequent Bhikṣu precepts. As for that Bhikṣu...

The bhikṣuṇīs are likewise. Regarding the three minor assemblies, there are two methods: for the Śrāvaka vehicle, it is based on seniority by birth; for the Mahāyāna, it is based on the sequence of ordination. The two lay assemblies are also like this.

If the seven classes of bodhisattvas assemble within a single boundary, the order is as follows: first the bodhisattva bhikṣus, then the bhikṣuṇīs, then the śikṣamāṇās, then the śrāmaṇeras, then the śrāmaṇerīs, then the upāsakas, and finally the upāsikās. Such is the ritual of honoring the preface to the precepts (*śīla-sūtra*). However, regarding the regulations for entering and exiting the hall:
As has been explained in detail previously). Seven.

Regarding the collection of similarities and the discernment of differences (there are approximately five types: first, worldly laypeople who have mistakenly entered a monastery; if they encounter a *poṣadha* ceremony, they should be respectfully sent away. Second, pure-faith laymen and women.)

First, when the sūtras are expounded and their meanings established within the boundary (sīmā), one should encourage them to listen, reflect, and practice. Second, when the *saṃgha* recites the Prātimokṣa or performs *karmavācanā*, one must instruct them to distance themselves to avoid [the proceedings]. Third, as for the small number of those who have left home, although they have shaved their heads and donned the dyed robes, they have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*);

therefore, whenever *karmavācanā* is performed, they should be sent to a place where they can see but not hear, and they must not eavesdrop. Fourth, a bhikṣu who has violated the precepts is not permitted to listen to the recitation; one must wait until he has repented and become pure before he may be admitted.

Fifth, while nuns are considered subordinate to the *saṃgha*, the hall for their *poṣadha* is distinct from that of the bhikṣu *saṃgha*. Thus, on the fortnightly occasion for requesting instruction, the bhikṣus first go to invite the teaching; once the morning *poṣadha* of the bhikṣu *saṃgha* is concluded, they then inquire whether it is permissible to proceed, at which point it is the day for the nun’s assembly to recite the Prātimokṣa.
The Vinaya states: "Bhikṣus perform the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day; bhikṣuṇīs perform the *poṣadha* on the sixteenth day. (This refers to the aforementioned). Eighth:

Regarding those who respectfully receive the Dharma and request instruction. (According to the Vinaya, during the fourteen years following the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment, his maternal aunt and five hundred Śākya women sought ordination; the Buddha commanded Ānanda to transmit and proclaim the Eight Respectful Rules.)

Once the nuns have been ordained, they must all go to the assembly of bhikṣus on the fortnightly *poṣadha* day to request instruction and admonition. They should further inquire whether it is permissible; then, at the time of reciting the precepts, the assembly of bhikṣus should ask who has sent the nun to request instruction and admonition.

If there is such a person, one should appoint her according to the Dharma—as will be seen in detail later. If they can follow these instructions and practice them, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for another thousand years.

9. Regarding the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) established according to the *dharmas* of the *dhātu*: the *dhātu* serves as the locus upon which the formal acts of the Dharma rely, while the Saṃgha consists of those who are capable of performing these formal acts.

In the Hīnayāna tradition, the Dharmaguptaka school possesses approximately one hundred and eighty-four types of *karmavācanā*, which encompass all matters pertaining to both timely and untimely occasions. As for Mahāyāna bhikṣu-saṃghas, their ritual for the fortnightly *poṣadha* is likewise the same as that of the Hīnayāna;

however, the difference is that in the Mahāyāna, the seven classes of followers, including bhikṣuṇīs, may all together hear the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. Those who, finding such details tedious and cumbersome, abandon the study of the Hīnayāna teachings are ultimately not sons of the Buddha; they are truly deluded persons. The *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha Sūtra* states: "Delusion and arrogance are called 'great'."

Those who ride upon [the vehicle] but lack the power of wisdom are still deluded regarding the teachings of the Two Vehicles; how much less could they understand the Mahāyāna? Thus, among the Bodhisattva Saṃgha, there is none who does not follow the laws of the Bhikṣu Saṃgha. Regarding the formal recitation of the precepts (*śīla*), there are four distinct types:

first, those who practice only the Mahāyāna while concurrently observing the Hīnayāna; second, those who practice only the Hīnayāna while concurrently observing the Mahāyāna; third, those who practice only the Hīnayāna without the Mahāyāna; and fourth, those who practice only the Mahāyāna without the Hīnayāna. For the present occasion, considering the specific capacity of the audience, let us set aside the first three. As for the fourth—those who practice only the Mahāyāna without the Hīnayāna—if within a single boundary (*sīmā*) all are Bodhisattva Bhikṣus...

When the Saṃgha dwells together and encounters the day of the Poṣadha, they first assemble in the Poṣadha hall to recite the Bhikṣu precepts; next, within the Buddha Hall, they recite the Bodhisattva precepts. If they encounter difficult circumstances such that it is still far from the boundary, they shall first recite the Bhikṣu precepts briefly and then recite them extensively.

Recite the Bodhisattva Precepts. If danger is imminent, both vehicles may be recited in brief. If danger is pressing and even a brief recitation cannot be performed, one should say: "Venerable sirs, today is the fifteenth day of the Uposatha; each of you should rectify body, speech, and mind, and do not be negligent."

Having spoken thus, they each departed as they pleased. Even under such difficult circumstances, it was still so; yet I have never heard of anyone who received the precepts but did not recite them, and yet could be called a Bodhisattva Bhikṣu. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states:

"If one receives the Bodhisattva precepts but does not recite these precepts, one is not a Bodhisattva, nor is one a seed of the Buddha. Indeed, if the Sangha Jewel is maintained, yet there is no Bhikṣu Vinaya, then one cannot perpetuate the lineage of the Buddha. Without this, one will fail to attain the Bodhisattva’s *muci* (the wooden staff).

Regarding the Great Rituals and Minor Precedents: Those who wish to uphold the pure precepts must refine the ten branches [of the śrāmaṇera precepts] so that they are free from defilement; it is from these that the three aggregates [of the bhikṣu precepts] first become complete. Thus, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If one has violated the five precepts after receiving them, one may not receive the five precepts or the ten precepts again. If one violates the ten precepts, one may not receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) again. Therefore, although a śrāmaṇera may encounter the occasion of the *poṣadha*, there is in fact no method for him to recite the precepts.

As for the examination of one's observance and violation, and the exhortation to practice, gathering once every half-month is truly appropriate. Accordingly, when performing repentance prior to a *poṣadha*, one should first summon the śrāmaṇeras to enter and examine their transgressions one by one; likewise, at the time the assembled monks recite the precepts..."

Summon the śrāmaṇeras into the hall to pay homage to the saṃgha; once they have been dismissed, the assembly shall then rise to perform the *pravāraṇā* recitation. This ensures that even this minor group follows the example of the great monks by assembling every half-month to exhort one another in their practice and to cause them to remember the precepts they uphold.
