Having completed the direct answers, the presiding master evaluates the person and the Dharma. If there is one who has committed any of the first four *pārājika* offenses, he shall be expelled according to the Vinaya by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), performed in absentia (*aprakṣa*).

He is no longer a son of the Śākya, nor is he a *śrāmaṇera*. He may not share communal duties with pure *śrāmaṇeras*, nor may he rely upon the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) to dwell. If the procedure is performed but not successfully accomplished, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession; in such a case, the *pratyekamukha-karman* (the formal act performed before a single person) should be carried out.

The Dharma provides for the expiation of offenses. If one encounters circumstances involving life-threatening danger, there are clear instructions in the Vinaya. If one commits any of the latter six *pārājika* (defeats), it constitutes a deliberate slighting of the Buddha’s words;

one should perform the *pratideśanīya* (confession) for a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) and carry out the *praty-ādeśa-karman* (formal act before another) for expiation. If the offense was committed unintentionally through error, it constitutes a failure in maintaining the precepts; one should perform the *citta-smaraṇa-karman* (mental recollection rite) for expiation of a *duṣkṛta*.

If one commits any of the two hundred and fifty *śaikṣa-dharmas* (rules of conduct), one must carefully examine the conditions of the offense and distinguish between intentional and accidental transgressions before performing the appropriate confession. If there is no offense, one should remain silent. Once each of these rites has been completed, the *karmadāna* (precentor) calls out: "All *śrāmaṇeras*, prostrate three times together and leave the hall in order. Listen.

At the sound of the *gandī* bell, the assembly ascends to the hall together to pay homage to the Buddha. However, this ritual protocol is set forth here for reference; it is employed when there are *śrāmaṇeras*. If there are none—whether they be those with the five precepts or the ten precepts—the assembly shall consist solely of *bhikṣus* for the rite of repentance.
Striking the sounding-block upon the seat, he asks:

"Is the assembly gathered? (The *vinaya-dhara* replies: "Gathered. "Are you in harmony? (He replies: "In harmony. "Have those who have not yet received full ordination departed? (He replies: "They have departed.")

"The Sangha is now in harmony; what shall we perform? (Answer): "The *karmavācanā* for confession. (This inquiry is made as in the usual procedure; the ritual action (*vidhi*) is no different, except that there is no inquiry regarding the declaration of consent (*chanda*).

According to the Vinaya regulations, one must confess by one's own words. If one does not speak for oneself, one should not be subject to disciplinary measures. Therefore, this differs from other instances in that there is no inquiry regarding the declaration of consent.)
Venerable sirs, now, before the *poṣadha* of this fortnight—whether it be the bright or dark half—we have gathered together in one place.
Each person shall lay a hand upon their heart and reflect with threefold consideration:

from the time the precepts were recited during the previous fortnight until today’s fourteenth day (if it is a short dark month, say "until the thirteenth day"), if there has been any transgression of the Buddha's regulations that has defiled the body of your precepts, you should...
Give rise to shame and remorse, and swiftly seek purification. Confess directly to me with frankness; by no means conceal or hide it. Thus, the *Adbhutadharma-sūtra* says:
"An evil mind committed previously is like clouds covering the sun; a virtuous mind arising afterwards is like a torch dispelling darkness.
This shows that purity and defilement depend on the mind, and that repentance relies upon the Vinaya. If one cannot give rise to a mind of deep faith and possess great dread [of wrongdoing]...

Such thoughts, even if the Buddha were still in the world, would be difficult to repent and eliminate. You, venerable ones, vow to purify the five categories of offenses and achieve the fivefold Dharma-body;
you hope to adorn the three groups of pure precepts so as not to be bound by the birth and death of the triple world. If you have committed an offense, speak out among the assembly;
if you have committed no offense, remain silent and pure. (Strike the ruler once. Then ask: Now I ask the venerable ones: Is there anyone present here...?

Regarding those who have committed an offense (the names and categories of the precepts can be found in works such as the *Jièxiàng míngmù* and the *Sāntán chuánjiè zhèngfàn*; whenever there is an offender, they shall step out of the assembly in order, perform three prostrations toward the high seat, kneel for a long time with palms joined, and declare the matter of their offense;
the master on the seat shall then thoroughly investigate the underlying intention and the circumstances of the offense, while the scribe records each detail clearly).

(The Venerable Karmadāna says: "The assembly shall prostrate three times together. [He] recites the "Excellence of the Merit of Repentance," and so forth. When the assembly has chanted in unison and completed the prostrations and the dedication of merit, the Master, together with the Karmadāna and the Scribe, leads the offender to the Abbot’s quarters.

The Karma Master first prostrates once to the Abbot; the Karmadāna and the Scribe likewise prostrate once. They present the names of the offenders and the details of their transgressions. The Abbot examines them clearly. The Karmadāna calls for the one who must confess, who then prostrates three times.)

Kneeling with the right knee on the ground and joining the palms, the Abbot, having questioned the Karma Master once more, shall adjudicate according to the gravity of the offense as prescribed by the Vinaya.

Once the instruction for repentance has been given, he further directs the offender to perform recitations and invocations (*adhitiṣṭhati*) according to their own intention, relying upon the power of the Buddha’s compassion and the power of the *karmavācanā* repentance, so that their karmic obstructions may melt away like ice and wholesome dharmas may flourish daily. Having thus instructed them, they pay their respects and withdraw. Those who have committed no offense hear the *gaṇḍī* bell and proceed together to the Buddha Hall to pay homage to the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.

If there are those who apply themselves with redoubled vigor, it is well to perform recitations and prostrations throughout the night according to their respective means; one should not weary of such detail, for the more thorough one is, the better.

If this [place] were established as a Dharma-realm center where Bodhisattva Bhikṣu-saṃghas reside, then regarding the confession prior to the half-monthly *poṣadha*, the analysis according to principle is twofold: First, although the Bodhisattva Saṃgha assembles constantly every half-month for confession, they still follow the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) of the Bhikṣu-saṃgha.

How could it be that while their physical precepts are impure, they claim their mental precepts are pure? This does not mean abandoning the Great [Vehicle] for the Small; rather, it is because Bodhisattvas skillfully protect the monastic regulations.

Second, even if one possesses the pure precepts of a great-capacity practitioner, if a sudden outburst of habitual tendencies occurs and proves difficult to restrain in familiar circumstances, then should a transgression occur, one must follow the two Mahāyāna sūtras—the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*—to perform Mahāyāna repentance. This is as described in the *Mahāyāna Twelve Gates Treatise*.
This has been clarified in the *Vibhaṅga* (and will not be cited here at length).
First, the third section: the formal procedure (*kamma*) for the Saṃgha’s recitation of the precepts (*pātimokkha*).

If the boundary (*sīmā*) has been established, on the full moon, new moon, or the proper *uposatha* day, when a community of four or more monks—even up to a hundred thousand—reside together, fearing that they might be difficult to assemble at the last moment, the Vinaya prescribes that one should first announce the gathering and then proceed.
[The assembly] meets. One senior monk (*sthavira*) announces at the time of the great meal or the small meal:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Today is the fifteenth day of the [black or white] fortnight (if it is the black fortnight, the fourteenth day of a short month), the day of the Poṣadha.

I inform the community that we shall assemble at such-and-such a place to recite the Prātimokṣa. [Having spoken this once, he stops. Then the senior monk should appoint two or three junior bhikṣus to go to the Poṣadha hall to sweep and sprinkle water, arrange the seats, prepare offerings of incense and lamps, and make the necessary preparations.]

The *śalākā* (voting sticks) and water vessels are prepared. When the time arrives, the *gandī* is struck to assemble the community. All who hear the sound must come quickly; those who do not come must grant their consent (*chanda*). This is called the "single boundary" (*ekasīmā*) for both Dharma and food, as all share equally in the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*), and separate assemblies are not permitted.

Regarding the procedure for granting consent: if one truly belongs to the Three Jewels but is unable to personally attend the assembly due to being bound by circumstances such as illness, one should go to a pure and capable monk who is authorized to receive consent.
After prostrating three times, kneeling with palms joined, one should speak as follows:

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], regarding this legal matter of the Saṃgha, grant my consent and offer my purity. (Having spoken thus once, one stops; one bows, rises, and departs.

If the one granting the consent is the senior monk (*upādhyāya*) and the one receiving it is the junior monk, the junior monk shall bow, rise, and stand, making the following formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made the announcement, he bows once and departs. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One should not hastily give one's consent to another.

One should give it only to someone capable of carrying the consent to the assembly and announcing it there. The *Xing-shi-chao* states: "In performing any monastic rite, it must be that both body and mind are fully assembled for it to constitute a harmonious union (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*). Even if there is a valid reason for absence, it is not permitted [to proceed otherwise]."

If the minds [of the assembly] are not unified, then the spiritual capacity and the teaching will not meet; how then can they be rescued? Therefore, it is necessary to transmit the intent through speech to respond to the affairs before the Saṃgha, so that both sides may fully accomplish their tasks. For this reason, the granting of *chanda* (consent) is permitted.

However, for the formal acts of establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) and the resolution of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), the granting of *chanda* is not allowed. For all other formal acts (*karmas*), the granting of *chanda* is permitted. When the time approaches for the recitation of the precepts, the wooden mallet is struck three times.

The great assembly adjusts their deportment and gathers together in the Poṣadha Hall, each sitting in order according to the sequence of seniority by precept. The leader holds incense and requests a pure, virtuous, and senior elder (*sthavira*) to recite the precepts. Once he has entered the hall and ascended the seat, the one who invited him performs three prostrations and then returns to his own place. As the Vinaya states: "Once the Saṃgha has assembled, those sitting nearby..."

Monks, you shall examine one another to ascertain who has arrived and who has not. If there are *śrāmaṇeras*, the *karmadāna* shall call out: "All you *śrāmaṇeras*, enter the hall in order and line up facing upward. Upon hearing the sound of the *ghaṇṭā*, prostrate three times before the senior monks, then kneel with your right knees on the ground and join your palms.
Then, the ruler of the seat shall strike the *shaku* and instruct them as follows:

"Listen attentively, all you śrāmaṇeras. A human body is difficult to obtain; the Dharma of the precepts is difficult to encounter; time passes easily; and the path of practice is difficult to accomplish.
Each of you must purify your body, speech, and mind, diligently study the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras, and be careful not to be negligent. (The śrāmaṇeras replied:)

"Practice according to the instructions. (The Rector calls out: "All śrāmaṇeras, prostrate once and then rise; exit the hall in order. Once the śrāmaṇeras have exited, the assembly each opens the *Caturvarga Vinaya Sūtra*.)
The *karmadāna* proclaims it; the assembly joins in harmony, saying:
"Namo to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha" (recited three times). Then, he recites the verse from the *Vinayavibhāṣā*:
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra is difficult to hear even after the passage of immeasurable koṭis of kalpas; likewise, its recitation, retention, and upholding are rare.
Yet, one who practices according to what is taught is even more difficult to encounter. (At this point, the ruler strikes the sounding-block and asks:)
"Is the Saṃgha assembled? (Answer: "It is assembled. "Are you in harmony? (Answer: "We are in harmony. "Have those who have not received full ordination departed?

(Answer: "They have departed. "Do the monks who did not come declare their *chanda* and purity? (If there is no answer, say: "There are none. If there are those who declare their *chanda* and purity, the monk receiving the *chanda* should say: "There are.")

Immediately leaving his original position, he approaches the seat, performs one prostration toward the upper direction, kneels long with palms joined, and speaks as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name]..."

"I receive from him the *chanda* (consent) and the *pārisuddhi* (purification). This is the formal act (*kamma*) of the Saṃgha according to the Dharma; [he] gives the *chanda* and the *pārisuddhi*. (Recite once. Those on the seat should say: "Excellent.

(The monk who conveys the *chanda*, having prostrated once and risen, returns to his original place and sits to listen to the recitation of the precepts. If one can remember the clan, name, and physical characteristics [of those whose consent is being conveyed], one may, as one wishes, receive the *chanda* of however many people. If one cannot remember them, simply say: [End of segment]

When many bhikṣus have given their consent and purity (*chanda-śauca*), if the bhikṣu holding that consent has personal business arise and cannot reach the assembly of monks, he may entrust his consent to another bhikṣu. He should approach a pure bhikṣu, assume the proper demeanor, and say:

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have received the consent and purity from many bhikṣus. For them and for myself, regarding the legal matters of the Saṃgha, I entrust my consent and purity.
(This should be said once. The one who receives this entrusted consent should then go before the Saṃgha and speak as above.
Who has sent a bhikṣuṇī to request instruction? (If there is none, reply: "There is no bhikṣuṇī here to request instruction.

If there is one, the bhikṣu who has received the commission shall rise from his original seat, go before the [presiding] seat, perform a single prostration toward the upper direction, kneel with palms joined, and make the request on behalf of the bhikṣuṇī community, saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. The bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha of such-and-such a place is in harmony.

They have dispatched the bhikṣuṇī [Name], who for half a month pays homage at the feet of the bhikṣu-saṃgha and requests a person to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. Having spoken thus three times and performed a single prostration, he rises and goes before the first *upādhyāya* (senior elder) and requests: "Venerable One, in your compassionate aid, would you be able to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?"

"No. If this senior elder is able to instruct, he answers 'I am able'; if he is not able to instruct, he answers 'I am not able. From those with twenty or more years of seniority, each is questioned one by one. If none among them are able, they return to the presence of the first senior elder."

One prostration. Kneeling, he says: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], have inquired throughout the Saṃgha, but there is no one capable of instructing the bhikṣuṇīs. Thereupon, the Elder should immediately explain the brief method of instruction and inform the bhikṣu who has received the commission, saying:

"Venerable Sir, since this assembly lacks anyone capable of instructing the bhikṣuṇīs, when the bhikṣuṇīs come tomorrow to request your presence, you should reply to them: 'Last night, we inquired throughout the community of bhikṣuṇīs, but there was no one capable of instructing them.'"

Nevertheless, the Elder addressed the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, saying: "Exert yourselves in the practice of the Path; be diligent and do not be negligent. The bhikṣu who had received the commission replied, "So be it," prostrated once, and returned to his place. This was because the Vinaya regulations stipulate that only one endowed with specific virtues is permitted to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.

Here, we have merely recorded the inquiry and request made from the seat to clarify the ritual procedures of that time. As for the methods regarding the dispatch of messengers by the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, such as the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation) used to go and invite [the preceptor], these are detailed extensively in the second section of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka*;
they are not recorded here in full.

The Saṃgha is now in harmony. What is to be done? (He replied: "The recitation of the precepts and the *karmavācanā*. As for the recitation of the precepts, one first makes a formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Saṃgha, making the following announcement:)”
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today is the fifteenth day of the [dark] month of the Saṃgha (the fourteenth day of the dark month). We shall perform the *poṣadha* and recite the precepts.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha consents, let us recite the precepts in harmony. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). (Strike the wooden gavel once. Venerable sirs, it is the spring equinox.

Three months constitute one season. When half a month has passed—(that is, when the Uposatha is recited on the fifteenth day of the first month, it is because half a month has passed; when it is recited at the end of the first month, it is because one full month has passed;

when it is recited on the fifteenth day of the second month, it is because one and a half months have passed; when it is recited at the end of the second month, it is because two months have passed; when it is recited on the fifteenth day of the third month, it is because two and a half months have passed;

when it is recited at the end of the third month, it is because three months have passed)—the remaining three seasons of summer, autumn, and winter are to be adjusted accordingly. If one night is lacking, there remains one night.

Regarding "the middle of the second month is short by one night": this refers to when one encounters a small month (a month with twenty-nine days) and recites the *Prātimokṣa* on the twenty-ninth day, as there are not thirty days; in such a case, one may say it is "short by one night.

However, if one encounters a large month (a month with thirty days) and recites it on the thirtieth day, this phrase need not be mentioned. Regarding "there remains one night": if one recites the *Prātimokṣa* during the daytime, the night of that very day has not yet passed, and thus one may say "there remains one night. This applies if there is a specific cause or condition.

One does not recite during the day; one recites during the first watch of the night. It should be changed [in the formula] to say: "Half a night remains. If one does not recite during the first watch but recites during the middle watch at the hour of Hai (亥), this phrase need not be spoken, because the watches of the day and night for the original *poṣadha* have already been exhausted;

thus, the Vinaya prohibits holding the *poṣadha* during the final watch. Regarding the phrase "with two and a half months remaining": this refers to the recitation of the precepts on the fifteenth day of the first month. Since the spring equinox has passed and half a month has elapsed, only two and a half months remain.

If the recitation is held at the end of the first month, it should be said: "Two months remain. If the recitation is held on the fifteenth day of the second month, it should be said: "One month remains. If the recitation is held at the end of the second month, it should be said: "One month remains. If the recitation is held on the fifteenth day of the third month... [the formula follows accordingly].
Half a month remains; by the end of the third month, this phrase shall no longer be recited at all (the same applies to the summer, autumn, and winter).
O Venerable Ones, old age and death are drawing near and the Buddha-dharma is about to perish. For the sake of attaining the Way, you must with single-minded diligence seek progress.
Why is this? Because it was by seeking progress with single-minded diligence that the Buddhas attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If one cannot attain even *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how much less other wholesome dharmas? While each of you is still strong and healthy, exert yourselves and diligently cultivate the good;
why do you not seek the Path? How can you wait until old age? What joy is there in that? This day has already passed, and life likewise diminishes accordingly;
like a fish in shallow water, what joy can there be in such a prospect?

(While seated, recite clearly from the introduction of the *Śīla-sūtra*—from the four *pārājika* offenses through to the end of the scroll—so that the assembly may understand each point. Then, turn toward the audience and descend from the seat. The *Vina* recites a verse, and the assembly joins in harmony:)

The Supreme Merit and Practice of Reciting the Precepts, etc. (Regarding those who previously invited [the preceptor]: they rise from their seats, perform three prostrations, and escort the teacher back to his quarters.

Once the assembly has each departed the hall with composure, those originally appointed to arrange the seats and prepare the requisites must collect everything one by one so that nothing is lost. If there are monks requested to provide instruction and admonition, and there are those capable of teaching, then once the recitation of the precepts is finished and before the assembly has risen from their seats, a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) shall be made to appoint a messenger.

Following the usual procedure for asking for consensus and declaring one’s intent, the master of the *karman* makes the following motion: "May the venerable Saṃgha listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha appoint the monk so-and-so to instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs."... [and so forth].)

The Bhikṣuṇī makes this announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. Those elders who consent to the appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, remain silent.

Whoever does not consent, please speak. The Saṃgha has consented; the appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs is concluded. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
Furthermore, the fourth section on the abbreviated recitation of the precepts according to the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*).

(The Buddha said in the Vinaya: "If there are obstacles such as kings, thieves, water, fire, illness, humans, non-humans, or other circumstances; or if the seats are small; or if it is exposed and damp; or during rain; or if the night of the *poṣadha* is nearly spent;

or if disputes or preaching the Dharma have lasted long—one is permitted to recite the precepts in an abbreviated manner. The one who recites must well understand the appropriate timing and weigh the nature of the obstacles. Now, according to the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*: once the introduction to the precepts has been recited and the inquiry into purity has been completed, one should address the assembly, saying:)
Venerable sirs, these are the four *pārājika* and thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* [offenses].
Two undetermined rules,
thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules,
and ninety *pāyattika* rules.
The four *pāṭidesanīya* rules, the one hundred *śaikṣa* rules (i.e.,
those which should be practiced), and the seven methods for settling disputes.

The Dharma and the Saṃgha have constantly heard this from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* recited every half-month. Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter? (Three times asked. Since the Venerable Ones are silent, they are pure in this matter. Thus it shall be held.

(Above, based on the text, the brief procedure for announcing the *pārisuddhi* has been explained. However, if difficult circumstances arise unexpectedly such that one is unable to recite it briefly down to the seven methods for settling disputes (*sattavidha adhikaraṇasamatha*), one should announce according to the point reached, saying:)
"Venerable sirs, we have recited up to [such-and-such] point. The remainder is as the Sangha has regularly heard it (each may now depart as they please).

If one encounters difficult circumstances that prevent compliance, or if the time for reciting the precepts is imminent and even the *Prātimokṣa* introduction cannot be recited, one should follow the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya, which says:"
Venerable sirs, today is the fifteenth day of the [black/white] fortnight for the uposatha. Each of you should rectify your body, speech, and mind; do not be negligent.

(Stop after one recitation; each may then depart as they please. Nevertheless, this abbreviated recitation is the essential core of the *poṣadha* and a marvelous method for accomplishing virtue. If, upon first receiving full ordination, one has not yet mastered the *Sifen lü jieben* (Four-Part Vinaya Code), then even if one were to recite it in its entirety, comprehension would still be difficult—how much more so when only the main outlines are presented?

Therefore, one must study after receiving the precepts, and having studied, one must practice them. If one performs the ritual assembly merely as a matter of duty, there will ultimately be no benefit for oneself or others.

Now, these three abbreviated forms have been clearly established by the Buddha’s skillful means according to the needs of the times. As for those who are monastics, who can say that they lack the leisure due to busy affairs and thus neglect the *poṣadha*?)
Next, the fifth section: the *karmavācanā* ritual for reciting the precepts through face-to-face confession (*pratimukha*).

According to the Vinaya regulations, when a single bhikṣu resides at a dwelling, on the day of the *poṣadha*, he should cleanse the hall, arrange the seats, and prepare the necessary implements. If visiting bhikṣus arrive—whether there be four or more than four—they shall perform the *saṃgha-karmavācanā* and recite the precepts according to the aforementioned procedure for the Saṃgha.

If there are only three, they may not receive formal consent (*chanda*). First, one bhikṣu shall assume the proper posture and perform three prostrations toward the other two bhikṣus; then, kneeling with palms joined, he says:
"Venerable sirs, please bear witness. Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha recites the Prātimokṣa. I, [Name], am pure. (Recite this three times. (The same applies to the other two bhikṣus;

they should each recite it three times in turn, face-to-face. If two bhikṣus dwell together, they should follow this same method. If anyone among them has committed an offense, they must first confess and repent before those who are pure;
only then should the words "pure" be added to the text. If there is an offense that has not been confessed, the phrase "pure" should not be added.)
The Sixth [Section]: The Ritual of Mindful Recitation of the Precepts (The Vinaya states:
If a single bhikṣu, on the day of the poṣadha, has swept and prepared as before and awaits [others], and if no one comes, he should personally assume the dignified demeanor and speak as follows).

Now, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha recites the Prātimokṣa. I, [Name], am pure (recite three times as before; the addition of the ritual formula may be understood accordingly). The *Bhikṣu-vinaya* clarifies what is correct and what is incorrect. Seventh:

The *Vinaya* clarifies the conduct of bhikṣus, consisting of one hundred and eighty-four *karmavācanās*. Within each of these legal procedures (*dharmas*), there are seven types of "incorrectness. Because such incorrectness violates the regulations, it is termed "ruination of the conditions" (*pratyaya-bhaṅga*). Thus, the ritual act is not accomplished. This, then, is according to the rule.

This is called "accomplishment through conditions. There is efficacy in performing the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*). This refers to weighing the person, the Dharma, and the matter; one must act as is appropriate, as ought to be done, and as is permissible. Now, within the single procedure of the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony), I shall briefly clarify how to distinguish the correct from the incorrect, so that good may arise and evil be obstructed.

If within a single boundary (*sīmā*), those of the Great and Small Vehicles dwell together, the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Saṃgha shall first assemble with the Bhikṣu Saṃgha in the Poṣadha Hall. The assembly of Bhikṣus proceeds to the Poṣadha hall and recites the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya). Although it is permissible by way of expedient means to recite the Bhikṣu precepts in the Buddha Hall, this is not intended as the regular practice. The Bodhisattva Vinaya clarifies that this is not the ninth [offense] (regarding the seven non-offenses of the Mahāyāna, one must further exercise discretion; only if there is no transgression does it constitute compliance with the Dharma). Regarding those who have already received the Bodhisattva precepts, such as śrāmaṇeras and others: whether they assemble or do not assemble, whether they grant their consent (*chanda*) or do not, and whether the order of the precepts is distinguished by seniority or not—these matters are like the ranks of soldiers or slaves; allowing laypeople to enter the assembly and permitting novices to sit among the equals is called "the impairment of conditions" (*pratyaya-bheda*). If the *poṣadha* is thus conducted, it is difficult to achieve its fulfillment.
Conversely, if one acts otherwise, it is in accordance with the Vinaya, and the recitation of the precepts will be meritorious. The second case is "the non-dharma" (*adharmatā*):

(This refers to) not inquiring about the assembly of the Saṃgha, nor requesting instruction and admonition according to the Bodhisattva ritual. Whether it be Bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, they perform a *jñapti-karman* (single-motion formal act) to harmonize the Saṃgha. Alternatively, they fail to understand the text while reciting or listening, or the phrasing is inverted. Or, three people ascend the seat to chant together in harmony.

Regarding the "Beautiful Sound" (Sudatta): for one period, there is no formal connection (*pratyaya*). One may recite briefly as desired, or everyone may kneel together to read the sūtra text. Abandoning the established rules for seated recitation, performing it face-to-face with another, or reciting mentally (*manasikāra*), or alternating between three and one person, or inverting the order—these are all considered cases where the conditions have failed (*pratyaya-bhagna*).

Under such circumstances, the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) is difficult to accomplish. If one acts contrary to these [faults], it is in accordance with the Dharma, and the *poṣadha* is thereby perfected. This is the third matter concerning what is not [in accordance with the Dharma] (i.e., the failure of conditions): namely, when the ground has not yet been formally consecrated (*karmavācanā*), the boundary (*sīmā*) lacks a basis, or when there are difficulties or obstacles regarding the training (*śikṣā*) that must be guarded against.

Although one may establish a minor boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), set up markers, and proclaim the boundaries, if one binds it but does not subsequently release it and so forth, this is called "destruction by conditions" (*pratyayavipanna*); the *poṣadha* is then impure. If one acts contrary to this, it constitutes protection through restraint (*saṃvara*). [The phrase] "reciting the precepts well" refers to the fourth case: "the person and the dharma are non-existent" (*pudgaladharmābhāva*).

This means that while the matter and the boundary are well-protected, both the person and the dharma are in violation; understand its accomplishment based on the above, like a broken scale. clarify this by analogy with the preceding case; by performing the task, one obtains benefit. The sixth is "the matter and the person are non-existent" (*vastupudgalābhāva*). This means that while the dharma accords with the holy teachings, the matter and the person treat it with contempt; regarding the gain or loss of what was previously obtained, one understands its accomplishment for oneself.

The seventh case concerns the invalidity of the ritual for the *dharma* (the *poṣadha*). That is to say, one instance is inconsistent with the Vinaya, and all three possess faults. Conversely, as prescribed, if the *poṣadha* is performed according to the rules, it may be established. This example from the *Bhikṣu-vinaya* definitively distinguishes between what constitutes a valid establishment and what constitutes a failure.

As for the other forms—such as those performed before another person (*pratyekapuruṣa*) or by mental recitation (*manasikāra*)—these do not exist in the Mahāyāna; therefore, I shall not cite them at length here, lest I fall into the error of mere conjecture, which would be a fault in the examination of the Vinaya.

(Regarding the two groups of lay followers of the Mahāyāna, the characteristics of the precepts they receive differ. The six grave precepts and twenty-eight minor precepts apply exclusively to laypeople and do not include those who have left the household life. If one has received the ten grave precepts along with the minor ones, during the fortnightly *poṣadha*, one should go to a boundary where there is a community of Bodhisattvas to hear and recite them.

However, if no such monastic boundary exists nearby, it is permitted to recite them by oneself in the Buddha hall of one’s own home. If one has received only the six grave precepts and twenty-eight minor ones, one should simply kneel before an image in one’s own house to recite them; even if a monastic boundary is nearby, one must not go to hear or recite them, because the characteristics of the precepts differ.

For this reason, the ten grave and minor precepts are listed first, followed by the sequence of the six grave and minor precepts, so that one may clearly understand the specific articles for the convenience of the *poṣadha*. [End of] Two Sutras.
