It is evil and unwholesome. Furthermore, there is the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) occurring independently, which is divided into nine grades of lightness and heaviness, as explained in the "Chapter on Repentance" of the *Samayakarmavastu*.
It is divided according to the Vinaya into the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, which is translated here as "abandonment and forfeiture.
These thirty rules mostly involve falling away due to craving and attachment; if one abandons this craving and attachment, then [one does not fall].
Because one falls [into an offense], it is called *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The Sūtra states that one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

As for the lifespan in Tuṣita Heaven being four thousand years, one falls into the Raurava Hell; since four hundred human years correspond to one day and night for those gods, the number of years spent in hell can be calculated accordingly.
The third section: *pāyattika*, which is translated as [an offense requiring expiation].

"Downfall. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One falls into the hells of burning, boiling, and concealment. The eight hot hells collectively constitute 'burning' and 'boiling,' while the eight cold and dark hells collectively constitute 'concealment.
When the preceding thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses are combined with these ninety *pāyattika* offenses, they total one hundred and twenty.
The Sūtra says: 'The offense of a *pāyattika* is like the lifespan of the Yāma Heaven.'"

For two thousand years, one falls into the Saṃghāta Hell. Since two hundred human years constitute one day and night for that heaven, the number of years in that hell may be calculated accordingly; this is the fourth group.
The fourth section concerns the *pātideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession). This is translated as "confessing to another. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "This offense..."
One should confess. To "confess" means to speak of one's remorse before each individual bhikṣu. The Sūtra states:
"The offense of *pāyattika* (pāratideśanīya) results in a lifespan of one thousand years in the Black Rope Hell, equivalent to the lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
According to this calculation, one hundred years in the human realm constitutes a single day and night for that heaven; by such reckoning, one falls into hell for that many years."
The year can thus be known. This is the fifth aggregate. The Fifth Chapter: The Rules of Training (*Śaikṣa-dharma*).
These are also called *duṣkṛta*, which here means "misdeed" (*èzuò*) or translated as "guarding the precepts. This refers to these one hundred minor precepts;

because they are subtle and extremely difficult to maintain, one must train in and observe them accordingly. Hence, they are called "rules for training" (*śikṣitavya*). As the Sūtra says: "One incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
As for the lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings, which is five hundred years, they fall into the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell.
Since fifty human years constitute one day and night for those gods, the number of years spent in hell can be calculated accordingly.
This constitutes the sixth group. Alternatively, it may be divided into seven groups by splitting this sixth group into two.

Regarding bodily actions, they are termed "misconduct" (*duṣkṛta*) and are included within the sixth category. Regarding verbal actions, they are termed "evil speech" (*durbhāṣita*) and are included within the seventh category.
Furthermore, the two indeterminate rules (*aniyata-dharma*) are subsumed within the first three sections and the aforementioned four categories.

Finally, the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) are subsumed within the ninety *pāyattika* (offenses requiring expiation). Moreover, the third category herein, [the offense of] theft...

Regarding the *Rāṣṭrapāla-dharma*: it emerges from the four parts [of the Vinaya]. Beyond the two hundred and fifty precepts, these characteristics of the five categories of offenses are further divided into three types of transgressions:

if one commits the first two categories, it is called a "transgression of the precepts" (*śīlavipatti*); if one commits the latter three categories, it is called a "transgression of dignified conduct" (*ācāravipatti*);
and if one commits the sixty-eighth offense among the ninety [minor rules], namely the arising of slander through false views, it is also categorized as such.

"Precepts" (śīla) refers to the breaking of [wrong] views. For a detailed explanation, one should consult the *Vinaya-jñapti-caryā* (作持), the *Vinaya-pratiṣedha-caryā* (止持), the *Poṣadha-gāthā*, the *Zhengfan* (正範), and other such works.
Furthermore, Master Ouyi’s *Chongzhi vinishi yiji jiyao* (重治毗尼事義集要) is currently in circulation.
Additionally, there are other texts such as the *Sifen jieben zhiniao rushi* (四分戒本津要如釋) and the *Zhiyao* (摭要) that are in circulation.

Furthermore, there are works such as the *Direct Explanation of the Brahma Net Sūtra*, the *Combined Commentary*, and the *Unfolding of the Hidden Meaning*. Although these have not yet been included in the canon, they all should be consulted.
[Regarding] guarding the precepts...

The Sanskrit term *poṣadha* is translated here as "confession before another" (*wò duì shuō*), meaning to confess one's transgressions face-to-face; it is translated thus in reference to the fortnightly ritual of repentance (*chánmó*).

It is also translated as "pure abiding" (*jìng zhù*) or "abiding in goodness" (*shàn sù*), meaning that by relinquishing turbid evil, one realizes pure goodness and attains purity of body and mind, abiding in accordance with the precepts.
It is further translated as "reciting the precepts" (*shuō jiè*), meaning the assembly gathers every half-month to recite the precepts, which can increase [virtue].
Wholesome dharmas are so called because they sustain one’s own mind; therefore, know that the *poṣadha* (confession and restoration) is truly the essential rule for guarding the precepts.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "I now recite the Buddha-dharma precepts every half-month.

You all Bodhisattvas who have resolved to attain enlightenment should also recite them, including the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten adamantine stages, and the ten bhūmis."
Recite: For this reason, the light of the precepts issues from the mouth. This light exists because there are conditions; it does not arise without a cause.
This light is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black. It is neither form nor mind; it is neither existence nor non-existence. It is not a phenomenon of cause and effect.

It is the primordial source of all Buddhas and the foundation for practicing the Bodhisattva path. It is the foundation for the sons of the Buddha within this great assembly. Therefore, O great assembly...
O Sons of the Buddha, you should uphold, read, recite, and study well that which is called the protection of the precepts (*śīla*).

The protection of the precepts has both its essence and its specific characteristics. From the fortnightly *poṣadha* ceremony down to the ritual implements, these constitute the protection of its characteristics.

Receiving the precepts occurs but once; upholding them lasts for a lifetime. Regarding the various articles of the new precepts—such as the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera*—[the second... (Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at the end.)
Regarding the fourteen modes of deportment, the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu, and the ten grave and forty-eight light offenses of the Brahma Net Sūtra,
those who have already thoroughly studied the permissions, prohibitions, observances, and transgressions within the Precept Hall and have also heard them expounded—

how could those who have slightly awakened their resolve not observe them? What is feared is that after leaving the hall, they gradually draw near to unwholesome people and gradually hear heterodox doctrines, thereby violating [the precepts].
They turn their backs on the *poṣadha* and, failing to uphold the precepts, they lose their true mind; thus they bring about demonic affairs.
First they eat at improper times, then they drink alcohol, and even go so far as to eat meat; further still, they engage in sexual misconduct and gambling, doing everything that should not be done.

How tragic! Beneath the *kāṣāya*, they have ultimately forfeited their human form. Reflecting back upon leaving home and receiving the precepts, what was the purpose of it all? Therefore, the Buddha...
He said: "You bhikṣus, you should rub your own heads. To 'rub one's head' means to reflect to oneself: 'I am a son of the Buddha;
I must rely on the Buddha’s words, take the precepts as my teacher, and abide in the four foundations of mindfulness. It would be better to die with the Dharma than to live without the Dharma.'"
When *śīla* (precepts) are pure, wholesome dharmas arise spontaneously. Thus, a sutra says: "One who exerts diligence in upholding the pure precepts is like one protecting a bright pearl.

This refers to guarding the precepts by relying on their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Next, regarding guarding the precepts by relying on their essence (*svabhāva*), from the initial five precepts up to the three clusters of pure conduct (*trisaṃvara*), all characteristics of the precepts are identical in their single essence. Therefore, before reciting the precepts, the Vinaya regulations state:
It is said: "Now, for your sake, I shall perform the *karmavācanā* of the Three Refuges (*tri-śaraṇa*), causing you to evoke the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*).

... [and so on] ... until the conclusion states: "The aforementioned Three Refuges are precisely the reception of the essence within the mind; therefore, one knows that the Three Refuges constitute the essence of all precepts.

Regarding what is called this "essence," the *Zhengfan* (Correct Model) says: "By means of the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa-prajñā*), one awakens to and realizes that all phenomena are neither empty nor non-empty."

It is neither existent nor non-existent; it is the simultaneous forgetting and simultaneous illumination of both emptiness and existence. The perfect awakening of the three wisdoms is the self-nature Buddha Jewel.
The principle of the dharma-nature that is awakened to, wherein the three truths are fully present, is the self-nature Dharma Jewel.
This awakening-wisdom in union with principle and phenomena is the self-nature Sangha Jewel. These three refuges are called the essence of the precepts. Furthermore, one requests the bhikṣu precepts.
Jeongbam said: "This refers to the very moment when, tomorrow morning, you are properly performing the *karmavācanā* before the seats of the ten masters.

At that time, through the power and function of the mental karma of your superior resolve, you should visualize the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), universally taking all sensory objects as your object of focus.
Thus, the objects appear from the mind; yet these manifested objects have no substantial form—they are the entirety of the sensory objects within the dharma-realm."

The substance [of the object] is also the cause for obtaining the precepts. Prior to the point when one has mentally conceived and formally accepted it, this substance of the sensory object has no connection to you;
it is merely a single instance of generating the thought to conceive and accept it. Once this has occurred, the substance of this dharma-realm sensory object constantly relies upon your own minds.
You must keep it in mind without forgetting and protect it at all times; therefore, the precept is that which is supported, while the mind is the support.

The basis is the union of the mind and mental factors, which is termed the "precept-substance" (*śīla-tattva*). This substance is that which is referred to in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* as being neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black;
neither form nor mind; neither existent nor non-existent; and not a phenomenon of cause and effect. Fundamentally, there is nothing to be protected.

Because [the mind] unites with sensory objects through awakening, it loses its original truth and becomes attached to false views—namely, the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the clinging to precepts and the clinging to views: from these five views arise the sixty-two views. Because of these various views, birth and death do not cease;
therefore, one maintains the precepts to guard against them and keep them at a distance. This is what it means to protect the precepts by relying on their essence.

Within this, the ten entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), the ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and even the eighty-four thousand afflictions and deluded thoughts must all be guarded against, so that they may be brought to stillness.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings, because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind and instead employ various deluded thoughts—since these thoughts are not true—undergo the cycle of transmigration. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"I now see universally that all sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, due to deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize it. If...

Free from deluded thoughts, all-encompassing wisdom and teacherless wisdom will spontaneously manifest before you. This is what is meant by: "To establish knowledge within seeing and knowing is the very root of ignorance;
to see and know without seeing is itself Nirvana. To observe and awaken in this manner is to protect the precepts.
Should one be unable yet to reach the ultimate perfection, it will suffice for now to rely on the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness. This, too, will bring one close to the goal.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: There are seven assemblies of precept-holders; here, by citing the single assembly of *bhikṣus*, one may take this as an analogy for all the other assemblies.

Within this context, taking the precepts as one's teacher and abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), it is better to die with the Dharma than to live without the Dharma.
These four phrases already encompass all rules of training (*śikṣāpada*). Now, I shall briefly cite several further articles to clarify the protection of the precepts. First: [text follows].

Regarding these matters, one must apply diligent care and maintain them with precision across all scales—from the great to the minute, and from the heavy to the light—and must never treat them with negligence.

As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* records, the Buddha told Ānanda: "You practice samādhi for the purpose of emerging from worldly toil; yet if the mind of lust is not eliminated, you cannot emerge from the dust.
Even if you possess vast wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall into the realm of Māra."
"Regarding the Way: those of the highest grade become Mara-kings; those of the middle grade become Mara-subjects; and those of the lowest grade become Mara-demons.

Each of these various Maras claims for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way, and so forth. Furthermore, it says: 'If you practice samādhi, its purpose is fundamentally to emerge from worldly toil.
If the murderous intent is not eliminated, you cannot emerge from the dust. Even if you possess great wisdom and dhyāna-samādhi manifests before you, if you do not sever killing...'"
They will certainly fall into the path of spirits. Those of the highest grade shall become powerful ghosts;
those of the middle grade shall become flying yakṣas, various ghost generals, and the like; those of the lowest grade shall become earth-walking rākṣasas.

These ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way, and so forth. Furthermore, it says: "The original purpose of your cultivation of samādhi..."
If one has emerged from worldly toil yet does not eliminate the thieving mind, one cannot escape the dust of defilement.

Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever this thievery, they will inevitably fall onto deviant paths—becoming high-grade spirits, middle-grade demons, or low-grade deviants possessed by various malevolent entities.
These various deviant beings also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained Buddhahood.
The *Shangdao* (Supreme Path) says, and so forth. It further states: "If the three practices are already perfected, yet one utters a great falsehood, then one's samādhi will not attain purity;

one becomes a demon of craving and views, losing the seed of the Tathāgata. This is what is meant by 'claiming to have attained what has not been attained' and 'claiming to have realized what has not been realized.
Such a person is an icchantika who extinguishes the Buddha-seed, just as a person uses a sword to cut down a tāla tree. The Buddha...
It is said of such a person: "Their roots of goodness are forever destroyed," and so forth. This is the greatest and most serious violation of the precepts.

The *Secret Essentials of the Chan School* states: Formerly, when the Chan Master Fuheng of Wuyun was sitting in meditation, a divine being suddenly appeared before him, kneeling with his knees on the ground.
The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am a guardian deity of the precepts. The Master...
He said, "I have a grievance regarding past transgressions that have not yet been extinguished; do you know of it? He replied, "What offense does the Master have?
It is but a minor oversight. The Master asked, "What is it? He said, "Generally, even the water from a rinsed bowl is the property of a donor.
Yet the Master pours it away; this is not appropriate. Having spoken, he vanished. From then on, the Master drank all the water used for washing his bowl. Furthermore—
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is told that there was a bhikṣu who was walking in meditation along the edge of a lotus pond in a forest.

He smelled the fragrance of the lotuses, and as his nose perceived it, his mind became attached. The deity of the pond manifested her form and said, "Why have you abandoned dhyāna to steal this fragrance?

Because of your attachment to this scent, all the latent defilements (*anuśaya*) that were lying dormant have now awakened. At that time, another person arrived and began plucking the flowers and digging up their roots.
He departed. The deity had nothing to say. The bhikṣu said, "This man broke the pond to take its flowers, yet you said nothing at all;
I merely smelled the fragrance and immediately rebuked him. The pond deity replied, "Worldly evil people are always immersed head-deep in the filth of sin and defilement;
I do not speak with them. You, however, are a good person who practices dhyāna, yet you are attached to..."
This fragrance ruins your good reputation; therefore, I rebuke you. It is like a piece of white cotton cloth, fresh and pure, which everyone pities when it is stained by a black mark.
As for that evil person, they are like a black garment already smeared with ink—who would pity them?
This is the most minute and subtle aspect of guarding the precepts. Alas! Only by being thus can one truly be called [a practitioner].
This is the observance of precepts that accords with the original aspiration when first seeking the precepts without any sense of debt.

As for guarding them in accordance with their essence, one should extensively study the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Brahmacarya-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and even the scriptural texts of the Tiantai school;
all these should be practiced. This is what is meant by: "From the precepts, concentration arises; from concentration, wisdom is developed. Should it be otherwise...
For those who have not yet attained [the goal], one should first contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness: first, contemplating the body as impure; second, contemplating feelings as suffering;

third, contemplating the mind as impermanent; and fourth, contemplating phenomena as selfless. These contemplations of the four foundations of mindfulness are the very root of spiritual practice and the weapon for guarding the precepts; therefore, this exhortation is offered.
Requisites, requisites: these are the material supports for Bodhisattvas, Bhikṣus, and the Saṃgha; they are the implements for following the Path and increasing virtue.

According to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, there are eighteen kinds, which differ slightly from those in the Vinaya. I shall now describe them by combining both sources. First: the *antarvāsaka* (i.e., the five robes).

2. The *Uttarāsaṅga* (i.e., the seven-piece robe). 3. The *Saṃghāṭī* (i.e., the great robe; it has three grades: the superior grade consists of twenty-five strips, twenty-three strips, or twenty-one strips; the middle grade consists of nineteen strips, seventeen strips, or fifteen strips;

the inferior grade consists of thirteen strips, eleven strips, or nine strips). Regarding the origin of the field-robe (*kṣetravastra*): the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that while the Buddha was staying before the Indra Cave, he saw the ridges and furrows of a rice field clearly demarcated.

He said to Ānanda: "The robes of the Buddhas of the past were of such appearance; from now on, let this be the standard for their form. The *Zenghui ji* states: "Just as a field of ridges holds water to grow fine seedlings that nourish the physical life, so too the field of the Dharma-robe is moistened by the waters of the four benefits to increase the seedlings of the three virtues, thereby nourishing the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body;
thus it is called the 'Field of Merit Robe' (puṇya-kṣetra-cīvara). 4. *Niśīdana* (the sitting mat, also called the *anujñāta-cīvara*;

the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states it is kept to protect the body, protect the robes, and protect the monastic beds and bedding). 5. *Saṃkakṣikā* (the side-covering garment, also called the *bāhu-praticchādaka-cīvara*, and further termed the *kaksāparyanta-cīvara*). 6. *Nivāsana* (the lower robe).

7. *Baxiluo* (i.e., the meditation skirt; colloquially called the "Vajra trousers"; extremely useful for practitioners of seated meditation). 8. *Zhizhui* (colloquially called the "robe"; also named *haiqing*; the three items above...)

8. *Pātra* (translated here as "measured vessel"). This refers to the alms bowl used by monks in the Western Regions, who all subsist on food obtained through begging. This bowl corresponds to one's own capacity; its size is determined by the principle that a single bowlful of food is sufficient for satiety.

Hence, it is called a "measured vessel. 9. *Khaṭvāṅga* (i.e., the mendicant’s staff). According to the sūtras, there are two types: one with four prongs and twelve rings, which is the type currently in use;

and another with two prongs and six rings, which is slender in form and weighs about one *jin*. This was the type used by bhikṣus during the Buddha’s lifetime. 10. Walking Staff (*yaṣṭi*). The *Vinaya* states that the Buddha permitted the keeping of a walking staff for those who are aged, emaciated, or lacking strength, or for those whose bodies are afflicted by illness and suffering.

11. The Whisk (Camarī). [The Vinaya states: "Because bhikṣus suffered from grass insects, the making of whisks was permitted. [The Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states: "The Buddha permitted the making of whisks with threads or whisks made of *tāla* palm leaves. However, those adorned with horsehair, gold, silver, or precious materials for their handles were not permitted."

12. Rosary (commonly called a "Buddha-remembrance bead" in the secular world). It is mostly made of *kṣaumaka* seeds (*huánzǐ*), with one hundred and eight beads constituting one string, which is carried on the person. (The above three items are from the *Bhikṣu-vinaya*). 13. *Kuñcika* (i.e., *junzhì*).

This is a vessel for constantly storing water to be carried on the person for the purpose of purifying the hands. The *Nanhai Jiguai Neifa Zhuan* states that there are two types of *kuñcika*: those made of ceramic or earthenware are for pure use, while those made of copper or iron are for contact use.
14. Soap powder (i.e., *sòjiǎo*, or soapberry, used for washing and purification). 15. Hand towel. 16. Fire-starter (i.e., the fire-knife, the fire-stone, or the fire-lens).

17. Paper and so forth; 18. A water filter (the *Zenghui ji* states: "Though the vessel is small, its function is great. To protect living beings, it is made of fine, dense silk so that aquatic insects may be filtered out");

19. A ritual knife (a type of razor); 20. According to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, a tooth-stick is added (used for cleaning the teeth); 21. A corded bed (in the Eastern Land [China], this refers to a round mat of *zōng* or *pú* grass used as a substitute for a corded bed);

22. Tongs; 23. An incense burner and casket; 24. Sūtras; 25. Vinaya texts; 26. Images of Buddhas; 27. Images of Bodhisattvas. (The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* emphasizes traveling on pilgrimage, hence these items are used...)

Regarding the sūtras, vinaya, and images of the Buddha: the Vinaya-piṭaka places primary emphasis on wandering for alms (*piṇḍapāta*). Therefore, items such as the staff, the whisk (*śikya*), and the rosary (*akṣamālā*) are to be used together [with other requisites]. In total, there are twenty-six objects.
For any wandering monk (*cārikā-bhikṣu*), these twenty-six objects are like the two wings of a bird; they must always accompany his person. Thus, they are called "requisites" (*pātrabhoga*).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The *Lüxue Gangwei* (Outline of Vinaya Studies) says: Regarding the eighteen types of requisites for protecting the precepts that are always carried with one:

to purify the mouth, there is the *yāñci* (willow branch); to cleanse the body, there is the *zǎodòu* (soap beans). To transcend worldly defilement, there are the three robes (*trīcīvara*) to cover the form; to sever improper food, there is the single alms bowl (*pātra*) to sustain life.

To fully open the ground of the sages, there is the water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*) which pours forth the spring of Dharma; to uphold the ranks of the worthy and holy, there is the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*).
The incense burner signifies the essence of purity; the water filter rescues sentient beings; the cloth napkin sweeps away dust; the knife is used to subdue demons;
the fire-stirring rod provides the means to dispel darkness; the tweezers pull out and eliminate afflictions (*kleśa*); and the meditation bench allows for the casting off of arrogance.

The sutras and commentaries unify the mind, while the monastic rules govern the three karmas. The Buddha image represents the fruit [of enlightenment], and the Bodhisattvas clarify the cause. Furthermore, according to Ouyi...

The *Jièyī biànwéng* (Discerning Errors Regarding the Precept Robe) states: "For those who have left the household life, there are precept robes (*śīla-cīvara*), just as those holding office have official robes (*gōngfú*).
Since the precepts differ for the seven classes of practitioners, how could their robes be uniform without distinction? The Buddha ordained three robes:

first, the *saṃghāṭī*, originally consisting of nine strips or thirteen strips. For those who were impoverished and had no means, and for whom circumstances left no other choice, twenty-five [strips] were then used."
1. The *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe), consisting of seven strips; it is not of the "superior-to-the-superior" grade. 2. The *uttarāsaṅga*, using only seven strips. 3.

The *antarvāsaka* (inner robe), using only five strips. These three are all called *kāṣāya*. They are so named because they are dyed with a "ruined color" (*kṣānta-varṇa*) rather than being multicolored.
They are also called the "field of merit robe" (*puṇyakṣetra-cīvara*), because their shape resembles a rice paddy field. Furthermore, the Saṃgha serves as a field of merit for the human world.

It is also a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). For a bhikṣuṇī, she must possess the five robes and the three robes as described above, with the addition of the *kacchaka* (arm-pit covering) and the *saṃkakṣikā* (shoulder-covering).
For a śrāmaṇera, two robes are prescribed: first, the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), which is a seamless *kaṣāya* also called the *mañca-vastra*.
Its color is the same as that of a bhikṣu, but its construction differs from that of a bhikṣu; it is simply sewn straight.

Cutting the leaves [of the robe] is not permitted. The Vinaya states that for those who are *śrāmaṇeras*, the *mantao* (unsewn robe) is the proper garment; to suddenly don a *jiejie* (cut-and-sewn) robe is a grave offense of overstepping the bounds.
This is because although a *śrāmaṇera* has already left the household life, they have not yet been counted among the ranks of the Sangha Jewel;

therefore, even the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*) is not cut-and-sewn, let alone the seven-strip or nine-strip robes. Second, the inner garment (*antarvāsaka*), which is the *nikai yan* (additional covering).
The *yèfùjiān* (arm-pit-shoulder-covering) robe is for those who serve as bodhisattva lay practitioners (*upāsaka*).

It requires that one possess the five seamless robes (*wu-se wǔ-yī*), with regulations identical to those for śrāmaṇeras. However, it is permitted to wear them only when entering the ritual platform (*tán*) to perform practices;
they must not be worn during ordinary daily life. This is how it differs from the śrāmaṇera’s attire. Today, monastic robes violate these regulations; there are nine such errors.
Upon receiving the śrāmaṇera precepts, they were immediately required to possess the three robes; this is the first error.

Śrāmaṇeras arbitrarily wore the seven-strip robe with cut-and-sewn edges, ultimately making no distinction from the bhikṣus; this is the second error. Those who came before, being ignorant, acted recklessly by allowing lay devotees (upāsakas) to wear the three robes;
those who followed, in their attempt to correct this, went too far and prohibited lay devotees from even possessing the plain (uncut) robe.
Regarding the "five robes," the [specification of] three [cubits] for the vertical is an error. All regulations for robes take three cubits vertically and five cubits horizontally as the standard;

while the vertical dimension may be slightly increased or decreased, it must always conform to the body and the hand. Now, to have three vertically and six horizontally, falsely claiming that this is done to achieve a square shape when folding, is the fourth error.
As for the *tiānyī* (field robe), one simply takes its form to resemble the ridges of a field; now, to falsely claim that it must be uniform throughout is an error.

"Waterway" is the fifth error. As for the "five strips," "seven strips," and so forth, these were formed according to the size of the old cloth available, resulting in a greater or lesser number of strips.
To now erroneously claim that a certain piece represents Mount Sumeru, another represents the sun, another the moon, and another the Four Heavenly Kings, etc., is the sixth error.
*Saṃghāṭī* originally translates as "Great Robe" (*Dàyī*), or it is also named...
The *saṃghāṭī* (heavy robe) may also be translated as the "variegated robe" (*cīvara-kaṇṭhaka*). It is made according to whatever cloth is obtained;

yet nowadays it is erroneously made of silk gauze (*liángzhòu*), or even embroidered with flowers upon it, being called the "Thousand-Flower Robe. This is the seventh error. The regulation for the three robes is the same for the thousand Buddhas;
therefore, they are called the "Robes of the Thousand Buddhas. Yunqi has already corrected these errors. Nowadays, there are those who embroider Buddha images [upon them].
Regarding robes: the eighth error is that all clothing and bedding used by those who have left the household life should be dyed with austerely colored cloth (*kasāya*);

yet now, on the contrary, five-colored silk is used instead. This is the ninth error. Furthermore, according to the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), in the Western Regions it is used only for the distinction between sitting and reclining;
in the Eastern Land, it is used exclusively for prostrations. It is unknown from whence this practice originated.

Regarding this, according to the fifteenth section on the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture) in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: whenever one makes a new sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), it is required that a piece of old material be used to patch over it to conceal the newness.
Nowadays, however, there is a widespread error in which bright-colored new cloth is used to patch the four corners, calling them the "Four Heavenly Kings.
This mistake is profound indeed. As for the *pātra*, it is translated as "measured vessel," for it is to be used in accordance with the portion of food allotted to a monk.
The Buddha permitted the use of bowls made of iron or ceramic; nowadays, however, they have erroneously used copper, tin, porcelain, or wood—all of which violate the Buddha’s regulations.
Furthermore, the Vinaya records that if a bowl is fumigated with medicinal herbs, its contents will not spoil and it will not become stained by oily substances.
Consequently, people today merely know that one must not defile the bowl while eating soup, yet they remain unaware of the rule regarding pre-treatment with medicinal fumigation. Thus...

If a curved spoon turns from beneath the bowl and enters the mouth, it is yet another breach of decorum. Furthermore, the precepts strictly prohibit the possession of gold, silver, and precious objects;
thus, in the *Mañjuśrī-parīkṣā-akṣa-sūtra* of the Mahāyāna, lotus seeds, *bhūrja* seeds, and bodhi seeds are considered the most excellent.
Nowadays, rosaries often employ gold, silver, and precious materials for their beads.
Inlaid and ornamented with various pieces, they grow long through greed and attachment, yet are easily stolen or lost;
all such matters are errors that must be corrected. As for the remaining ritual implements, they have been abandoned and left unused;
within, there is no heart to protect the precepts, and without, there is no outward observance of the precepts. How can the monastic rules avoid falling into ruin? I pray that I...
O sons of the Śākya, together support the True Dharma to turn back its declining corruptions and guide the monastic community so that all shall abide by the Buddha’s regulations.
Strive for self-benefit and the benefit of others; do not say, "This is attachment to forms," and hide yourself in the pit of formlessness.
Nor should you say, "I belong to the Chan school; what use have I for these dhūta requisites? If you examine the matter thus, [you will see that] Mahākāśyapa...
He was the first patriarch of the Chan school. Why is it that his practice of the dhūta ascetic observances is considered foremost?

This is appended to the discussion on the *śikṣamāṇā* to correct the many errors currently prevalent in the transmission of the precepts; regarding the category of the *śikṣamāṇā*, the errors are particularly numerous.

This is an extreme matter that must be clarified. According to the records of the Buddha’s era, various nuns would frequently ordain others for renunciation and confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon them;

because they did not understand the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*), they committed unrighteous acts. The Buddha stated: "One should grant them the *karmavācanā* for two years of training in the precepts."

Having first practiced and studied these, one should subsequently receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). One must study all the precepts for *mahābhikṣuṇīs*, with the exception of taking food with one's own hands and giving food to others.

Therefore, in various sūtras, vinayas, and the Liang Emperor’s Repentance Ritual (*Liang Huang Chan*), the sequence of the five groups of renunciants places the *śikṣamāṇā* above the *śrāmaṇera*, because she fully studies the precepts of a *mahābhikṣuṇī*. That is to say:

These are the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs. When the assembly gathers, because of the inconvenience of the formal protocol, even the great bhikṣuṇīs are seated after the śrāmaṇeras, and the śikṣamāṇās are seated after the great bhikṣuṇīs;
thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that they sit below the bhikṣuṇīs and above the śrāmaṇerīs. This is established by its own [tradition].
During the middle period of the Ming dynasty, the ordination platforms were closed off, and the rules of the *śīla* (precepts) became almost unheard of.

Not only was the method of training in the precepts long abandoned, but even the name and meaning of *śikṣamāṇā* were no longer known. It came to the point that unmarried women who had not yet shaved their heads and sought to receive the five precepts were called *śikṣamāṇās*;
this error was passed down through generations and remains unchanged to this day. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*...

*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. During the time when the Buddha was in the world, there was the wife of an elder who became pregnant without her knowledge. She left the household life and received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Subsequently, as her body grew large and became apparent, the other elders criticized and disparaged the bhikṣuṇīs.

Because of this, it was established that there must be two years of training in the precepts and the reception of the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*) before one may receive full ordination. (Text) Based on this, it follows that a woman may also serve as a *śikṣamāṇā*.
The term *śikṣamāṇā* does not refer exclusively to unmarried girls. Furthermore, the treatise states: "There are two kinds of *śikṣamāṇās*:
first, those who are eighteen years old and receive the six rules; second, those who are ten years old and have entered the household of their husband, and may receive the six rules."

(Text) This refers to a young girl. Regarding the phrase "ten years at her husband's house," commentators say that perhaps due to the mother’s death or because the maternal family was poor and unable to provide protection and nourishment, the young girl was brought to her husband's house. Having been raised there for ten years, her emotional faculties gradually opened;
furthermore, while living in her husband's house, it is difficult to be free from sexual desire. Moreover, as for an eighteen-year-old girl, even though she has not yet married...
As one has already reached an advanced age, it is necessary to take precautions. However, it need not be questioned whether she is a maiden or a married woman;
if she has already left the household life, there is no doubt regarding this. As for her rank, she stands above that of a *śrāmaṇera* and below that of a *bhikṣuṇī*.
This is because, having left the household life with the resolve to seek full ordination (*upasaṃpad*), she merely delays it for two years due to considerations of social censure and suspicion.
It is considered a ground for training in the precepts, unlike the śrāmaṇerī and others who have not yet attained the resolve for full ordination.

Furthermore, this reception of the six dharmas differs from that of the upāsikā, who possesses only the five precepts. Now, I shall record in full the method for the śikṣamāṇā’s training in the precepts so as to preserve its original form.

(According to Master Daoxuan’s *Jìfēnlǜ suíjí jiémó*, Chapter Three, Section on the Method for Receiving Various Precepts, within the "Method for Bestowing Precepts upon the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha," this is also recorded.)

Having received the śrāmaṇerī precepts, one next receives the *śikṣamāṇā* dharma. One again receives the fundamental dharma (*mūladharma*) before ten bhikṣuṇī masters, then proceeds to the assembly of bhikṣus to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

However, according to the *Jīkènmó* (Karmavācanā), the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts are conferred first; this is considered the proper sequence. As for the term "fundamental dharma," it refers to the bhikṣuṇī who originally upholds the precepts. A *śikṣamāṇā* is the preliminary stage for becoming a bhikṣuṇī; therefore, she is designated as a "fundamental dharma bhikṣuṇī" (*mūladharma-bhikṣuṇī*). Furthermore, this represents the advancement to the single rank of *śikṣamāṇā*.

In the ninth fascicle of the *Jīkènmó* compiled by the Cao Wei śramaṇa Tandi, found in the "Fù" case of the Fangce edition, following the section on the śrāmaṇerī receiving the precepts, it says: "It is permitted for a maiden of ten [years]..."

8. Regarding those who receive the śrāmaṇerī precepts: they shall study the full precepts for two years. Once they have reached twenty years of age, they receive the full ordination (mahā-śīla) within the Saṃgha, and so forth. Furthermore, the *Śikṣamāṇā-ṣaḍ-dharma-vinaya* states:
"A śrāmaṇerī should go before the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs. Exposing her right shoulder and removing her leather sandals, she should prostrate at the feet of the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha.
Then, placing her right knee on the ground and joining her palms, she should speak as follows:"
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen. I, the śrāmaṇerikā [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts.
My precept-mother is [Name]. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me deliverance and bestow upon me the two-year training in the precepts.

(The second and third [proclamations] are also spoken in this manner. Having led the śrāmaṇerikā to a place out of earshot but within sight, a person appointed from among the assembly who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should address them as follows):"
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen. This śrāmaṇerikā [Name], now requests from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts, with [Name] as her precept-nurse (upādhyāyinī).
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing, may the Saṃgha grant this śrāmaṇerikā [Name] the two-year training in the precepts, with [Name] as her precept-nurse.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). (This is the single announcement. [The following consists of three such announcements.]
Sisters of the Sangha, listen. This śrāmaṇerikā [Name], now requests from the Sangha the two-year training in the precepts, with [Name] as her preceptor-ni (upādhyāyī).
May the Sangha now grant this śrāmaṇerikā [Name] the two-year training in the precepts, with [Name] as her preceptor-ni.
"Whichever sisters approve that the Sangha grant two years of training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerikā [Name], with [Name] as her precept-mother, let them remain silent.
Whoever does not approve, let them speak. This is the first (second, third) motion. (Thus it is said three times.)
The Saṃgha has consented. The two-year training in the precepts for the śrāmaṇerikā [Name] with the bhikṣuṇī preceptor [Name] is hereby completed.
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. (The six dharmas should be conferred in this manner.)
Listen attentively, [Name]. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has taught six rules.
One must not commit impurity by engaging in sexual intercourse. If a śikṣamāṇā engages in sexual intercourse, she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā;
she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan. If she has physical contact with a man of defiled mind, her precepts are deficient and she must receive the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit [any offense]. Are you able to uphold [this]? (Answer:

Yes. You must not steal, even so much as a blade of grass or a leaf. If a śikṣamāṇā takes five coins or more than five coins belonging to another—whether she takes it herself, instructs another to take it, cuts it herself, instructs another to cut it, or breaks it herself, instructs another to break it—if...
If she burns [the robes], buries them, or alters their color, she is no longer a *śikṣamāṇā* and no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
If she takes less than five *māṣaka* coins, her precepts are deficient; she must receive the precepts again. Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not commit an offense.
Can you maintain this? (Answer: Yes. One must not take the life of any living being, even down to an ant. If a *śikṣamāṇā* intentionally cuts off [life] with her own hand...
If one takes human life; hands a knife to another and instructs them to die, encourages them to die, or praises death;

if one administers non-medicinal substances, causes an abortion, or performs incantations and spells—whether doing so oneself or instructing others to do so—one is no longer a *śikṣamāṇā* and no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
If one takes the life of an animal that cannot undergo transformation, the precepts are deficient and must be received anew. In this matter, [the rule] lasts for as long as one lives.
"Venerable One, can you undertake not to commit [these offenses] and maintain them? (She answers:

"I can. "One must not speak falsely, even in jest. If a śikṣamāṇā, being untrue and not possessing it herself, claims to have attained the state of a superior person, saying she has attained dhyāna, attained liberation, attained samādhi and right reception, or attained srotāpanna..."

The fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, and the fruit of non-returning. To say that devas come, nāgas come, or spirits and deities come to make offerings to me—this is not to be a *śikṣamāṇā*, nor is it to be a woman of the Śākya clan.
If one intentionally utters a falsehood within the assembly, the precepts are deficient;
the precepts must be conferred again. Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit an offense. Can you maintain this? (Answer: I can.
"One must not eat at improper times. If a śikṣamāṇā eats at an improper time, she violates the precepts and should be given the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not commit this offense. Can you uphold it? [She] replies, "I can."
"One must not drink alcohol. If a śikṣamāṇā drinks alcohol, she commits a transgression of the precepts and should be given the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, can you refrain from violating [this] and maintain it? (She answers: "I can. Regarding all the bhikṣuṇī precepts, the śikṣamāṇā...

One should train in these matters. With the exception of eating after the prescribed time for a bhikṣuṇī and eating food that one has received for oneself, if one commits any of the first four [offenses] herein, it is called a "grave offense" (pārājika);

such a person should be expelled. If one commits sexual contact with a man with a defiled mind, stealing less than five coins, taking the life of an animal, speaking a minor falsehood, eating at an improper time, or drinking alcohol, this is called a "deficient precept. Because of the aforementioned...
All practices and dharmas are subject to decay; therefore, one should perform repentance and then request a *karmavācanā* for another two years to practice them once more.
If one has violated any of the precepts studied by a *bhikṣuṇī*, one must repent in accordance with the Dharma in all such cases.
Only after training in the precepts for two years and becoming pure may one receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the assembly of the two divisions of the Saṃgha.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: "If one has committed the six dharmas, one must in every case repent according to the Dharma.

Regarding this, in the *Zhengfan* (Correct Model) for the Three Altar Transmission of Precepts, during the third stage of examining the precepts (*shen jie*), while examining the second type of person, it says:
"If she is a *śikṣamāṇā*—which is translated as 'a woman training in the precepts'—the Buddha established that she must train in three dharmas. If [one] examines...
When performing the confession, one should inquire about each point individually: 1. Training in the fundamentals refers to the four grave precepts (*catur-guru-dharma*).

2. Training in the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharmāḥ*) refers to: touching with a defiled mind; stealing less than five *kārsāpaṇas*; taking the life of an animal; speaking minor falsehoods; eating at improper times; and intentionally drinking alcohol. 3.
Training in the rules of conduct refers to the various precepts for full nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), namely the intermediate rules of decorum (*vinaya-śaikṣā-dharmāḥ*). If it is...

For śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, one should examine only the ten chapters of the fundamental precepts. Regarding the seven grave offenses that constitute obstacles (*antarāyika-dharma*), all three assemblies are questioned.
If, among these three assemblies, anyone has committed a violation of the seven fundamental obstacles, each shall be expelled according to the Vinaya.
Exclusion. If a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā) is impure regarding the six rules, she shall undergo the *karmavācanā* again for two years.
Since she has already received the śikṣamāṇā precepts, she is no longer included within the community of female novices (śrāmaṇerī);

yet, because she is deficient in her training as a śikṣamāṇā, she is not a truly pure female trainee. Thus, she belongs to neither category and lacks a foundation in the three aggregates (*triskandha*).
Therefore, they are unable to proceed to receive the Bodhisattva precepts. Regarding the three minor groups [of the śrāvaka discipline], these rules for *śikṣamāṇās* alone are established;
they are twice as strict as those for *śrāmaṇeras* and *śrāmaṇerīs*, precisely because their stage is close to that of the full *bhikṣuṇī* precepts.

Generally, according to the Vinaya regulations, before receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, one must examine the categories of precepts, which are divided into four types. The first is the *pravrajita-bhikṣu*...
First, bhikṣuṇīs; second, female śrāmaṇerīs who have left the household life;

third, male and female lay practitioners who delight in cultivating the ten wholesome paths of action, or who receive the five precepts, advancing through these stages—this is called "gradual reception";
fourth, suddenly giving rise to the great mind and receiving the bodhisattva precepts—this is called "sudden reception. According to the regulations of the Vinaya, the śrāmaṇerī...
This refers to the precepts for ordained nuns, not the precepts for lay daughters.

According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when Sudhana visited the great city of King Anala’s capital wishing to pay his respects to the female lay practitioner (upāsikā) Acalā, he could not find her location.
A vast multitude of people all told him: "The female lay practitioner Acalā is a maiden by body; she is within her own home."
"Parents shall protect [her]," and so forth. Based on this, it is evident that a maiden may also be called an *upāsikā*.

Regarding the Eight Rules of Respect for Nuns (*bhikṣuṇī-aṣṭa-guru-dharma*), according to the *Shisao* (Commentary on the Vinaya), the "Nun Section," it quotes the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, stating: "At first, the Buddha did not permit women to leave the household life and become ordained."
To reduce the duration of the True Dharma by five hundred years, [the Buddha] later preached the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) and permitted women to leave the household life.

Because they practiced according to these teachings, the duration was restored to one thousand years; however, as it is not practiced now, the Dharma perishes wherever it goes. The *Huìzhèngjì* states:

"In the fourteenth year after the Buddha attained enlightenment, his maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred Śākya women, came to seek permission to leave the household life. The Buddha did not..."

[The Buddha] granted permission for her ordination. Ānanda made the request three times on her behalf. The Buddha instructed Ānanda to convey the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) as previously explained, saying, "If she can practice these, I permit her to go forth.
She replied, "I shall receive and uphold them with the highest reverence. Thereupon, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) was completed.
Having explained the eight rules for expulsion (*pārājika*), he then explained the eight rules of respect (*gurudharma*). As for the eight rules of respect:

first, when a *bhikṣuṇī* who has been ordained for a hundred years sees a *bhikṣu* who has newly received the precepts, she must rise to greet him, prostrate, inquire after his well-being, and invite him to sit.
Second, a *bhikṣuṇī* must not revile or slander a *bhikṣu*. Third, she must not accuse a *bhikṣu* [of an offense].
1. To speak of their faults. A bhikṣu may speak of the faults of a bhikṣuṇī. 2.
A śikṣamāṇā who has already trained in the precepts should seek to receive the full ordination from the Saṃgha. 3.

A bhikṣuṇī who commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense should undergo the mānatva penance for half a month within the two assemblies of the Saṃgha. 4. Within every half-month, a bhikṣuṇī must [report her offenses] before the Saṃgha.
One should seek out a person to provide instruction. Seventh, one should not observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) where there is no bhikṣu.

Eighth, at the conclusion of the retreat, one should go before the community of bhikṣus and request the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*) regarding three matters: namely, what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
These eight dharmas should be respected, honored, and praised; they must not be transgressed for as long as one lives.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: This was the very first established precedent for the ordination of the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha.

Even those who receive and transmit the teachings today do not know this rule, let alone practice it. Furthermore, regarding the seventh point of respect—that one should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) where there is no bhikṣu—this refers to the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary).
For according to the Vinaya, the establishment of a *mahā-sīmā* is required before [the retreat may be entered].
Within ten *li*, or even within forty *li*, if there is no great monastic community (*mahāvihāra*) of *bhikṣus*, one may not observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

Therefore, regarding the eighth precept of respect: once the retreat has concluded, one should go before the assembly of *bhikṣus* and request the three matters for the invitation to critique (*pravāraṇā*), namely those based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
According to what is stated in this eighth precept of respect, the *bhikṣuṇīs* and the great assembly of monks [are not to be considered as separate entities].

The fact that they resided together in one temple can be known from the following account. The Vinaya Master Shuyu of Zhaoqing Temple, in describing the origins of the ritual for conferring the full precepts upon the two assemblies of monks, stated:
"In the spring of the Dingwei year, the Bhikṣuṇī Abbot Mizhao of Kunshan, together with Lady Xu, went up Mount Hua to make offerings.
A group of female students of the precepts followed them there to request full ordination. They practiced the observances for half a month. (Abridged)

Familiar with the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*), she first appointed the nun Mìzhào as the *upādhyāyī*, the nun Cháochén of Yangzhou as the *karmakārī*, and the nun Yuánzhèng of Zhēnzhōu as the *śikṣamāṇā-ācāryā*.
She carefully selected nuns of high virtue and seniority to serve as the seven witnesses for the assembly of over forty nuns receiving the precepts.
They then crossed the boundary to Yè’ān on the southern side of the mountain, where they gathered their respective groups.
For a bhikṣuṇī, first the fundamental precepts (*mūla-dharma*) are conferred. On the following day, the *upādhyāyī* strikes the gong to assemble the community.

After the formal announcement of the Tathāgata’s injunctions has been made, she leads the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, together with the nine masters on the altar, up the mountain to request the reception of the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
The Elder then assembles the two assemblies of monks and nuns to perform the ritual for her full ordination. This was how the Elder previously followed the Buddha’s [teaching].

The regulation concerning the two divisions of the Saṃgha refers to the ritual for bestowing the precepts upon bhikṣuṇīs; in this case, the attendants and those presiding at the altar are all from the bhikṣuṇī assembly.

According to this, one should go outside the boundary to the Yeyuan (One-Leaf) Hermitage to the south of the mountain to assemble the bhikṣuṇīs there; this can be seen in the seventh point of respect.
It states that one should not observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) where there are no bhikṣus, which refers specifically to within the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), and not elsewhere.
This refers to bhikṣus observing the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) together in one location. Furthermore, in the lower fascicle of the *Yi-meng-man-yán* (Random Words from a Dream), it says:
"In the second month of the tenth year of the Shunzhi era, at Hanyang Prefecture in Hubei, the nun Xinwen, aged fifty, was determined to uphold the precepts.
Together with eight fellow disciples, she did not shrink from the dangers and distances; this group of ten ascended the mountain to seek a place for the three-month retreat and provided offerings."
[She offered] sixty *shí* of rice and twenty *liǎng* of silver. Observing that her intention was sincere and her words earnest, [the Master] took pity on her and granted her permission.
On the day the vegetarian feast (*zhāi*) was prepared, she refused to enter the hall to prostrate. Once the feast was concluded, he gathered the assembly and called her forward, saying:
"You have resolved to come from afar to study the precepts; why do you not enter the refectory to pay respects to the monks? According to the Vinaya regulations for *bhikṣuṇīs*—"
"Even if one is a hundred years old, one should pay homage to a *śrāmaṇera* who has completed his first summer retreat (*pravāraṇā*). Nowadays, there are arrogant monks who do not study the precepts.

They say, 'I was in the region of Chu; if there were virtuous friends, we would go together to provide a vegetarian feast,' and the abbots treat them with guest-hospitality, yet they themselves do not perform prostrations. I said: 'They covet gain and offerings, thereby ruining the Dharma-gate.'"
Whenever one encounters a nun with whom they have a karmic connection, they treat her with the respect due to a biological mother, hoping thereby to receive even greater offerings;

such a person is a "lion-insect" (a parasite) and not a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Although my practice at Mount Hua is now meager, I would rather go without grain or food than ever dare to violate the regulations for the sake of profit.
The vegetarian feast prepared today shall be used for the permanent endowment of the monastery; as for the silver—

"Return it to you. The rice is in the lower hall; you may take it and depart. He interpreted this as a sign of ignorance and, gathering his disciples, he immediately went down the back mountain to dwell in the Seon chamber at Chwisu-dong. There was a disciple named Gu-tan who entered the room and said:
"That nun has come from afar and dwells constantly in emptiness; you, Preceptor, should receive her with skillful means. First, this will prevent her mind from regressing;

second, it will provide the assembly with offerings for half a month. Yuru corrected him, saying, "If she is willing to practice authentically, the assembly will naturally not have to hang out their bowls.
Establishing a Dharma gate is precisely a matter of maintaining one's conduct amidst simplicity and austerity."
"A Vinaya master practices the Vinaya; how could he see a personal gain and violate the sacred regulations? Ancient Tan bowed his head in shame, performed a prostration, and withdrew.
Three days later, Xinwen again led his disciples up the mountain and knelt together outside the gate of the Abbot’s quarters.
Weeping, he said, "To suffer such confusion and distress as this, I am truly not an arrogant or conceited monk. I beseech the Venerable Master for his compassion."

He was permitted to perform repentance. He followed and relied entirely upon all the verbal instructions [of the Buddha]. The various leaders interceded on his behalf, whereby he was stationed at Lushe Mountain (Lùshān Zhāng).
A boundary (*sīmā*) was established for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), and *ācāryas* were dispatched to go there every half-month to provide instruction.
For them, he expounded the *Vinaya* of their own school. It was on this basis that he initiated the compilation of the "Model for the Instruction of Bhikṣuṇīs."
One scroll in circulation. The standards and traditions of the ancient worthies were so resolute and meticulous; hearing of them inspires one to exert oneself.
