Verified by Miaoyong, Abbot of Jiezhu Temple in Yuecheng. Chapter Seven, Part Two:
The Section on Hanging Up the Bedding for the Assembly.
"Guā-dān" (Hanging Up One’s Mat) is the ancient term for "guà-dá" (Hanging Up One’s Lodging). This is because when monks travel on pilgrimage, they carry nothing but their robes and alms bowl;

thus, it is called "hanging up one's lodging," meaning one hangs up the robes one is staying with. Nowadays, as students of the Dharma also carry luggage, the term has been changed to "guā-dān" (Hanging Up One’s Mat).
Whenever a monk arrives to hang up his mat, the Guest Hall receives him with due ceremony, inquires clearly into his background, and issues a mat accordingly. As follows:
The heads of the various quarters and the two orders shall escort honored guests to the Guest Quarters (*zūnkè liáo*), where the Guest Hall (*kètáng*) will provide hospitality.
For visiting monks who have come to study Chan, they shall be escorted to the Upper Guest Hall (*shàngkè táng*); they shall join the assembly for meals and ascend the hall for services.

However, those without robes, alms bowls, ordination certificates, or travel gear, as well as anyone whose appearance is suspicious, shall not be granted a private room under any circumstances. This is clearly detailed in the regulations of the Guest Hall and the specific instructions for the Head of the Quarters (*liáoyuán*).

The Commentary on the Meaning states: According to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, within the precept against traveling while disregarding hardships, there are two periods for the itinerant practice (*xingjiao*) of a patch-robed monk (*nàzǐ*).
First, from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month; second, from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month.
During these two periods, one originally travels for the purpose of studying the Way, journeying no less than a thousand li to consult [a master].
When a master seeks the Way, he leaves one monastery to enter another, traveling everywhere until his journey is complete, never resting.

It is for this reason that the matter of hanging up one's bedding (guāndān) has arisen. As the guest prefect (zhīkè), you must provide bedding as appropriate and never treat the visitor with disrespect.
As the abbot (zhùchí), maintain a heart of compassion and do not lightly dismiss or restrict the hanging of bedding. This is the proper monastic tradition (dàofēng).
"The long endurance of the Buddha-Dharma depends entirely upon this," said Master Yunqi Juelian.

"When I was traveling alone as a wandering monk, I endured hunger and thirst, braved cold and heat, and experienced every kind of hardship. Now, fortunately, I have found a place to shelter myself under a roof.
Although I do not understand formal cultivation, I recognize a sense of shame and remorse. When guests arrive from afar, I serve them with diligence; as for my own personal use—"
I dare not be excessive. As the saying goes, "One who was once a wanderer feels particular compassion for travelers. Regarding the lodging:
for monks returning to the hall after a long stay (*dà guàdā*), there is one night’s stay and three meals; they depart after one or two days. This is called [the *āgantuka*].

Regarding "hanging up one's mat" (guàdā): if a guest remains on the guest list for several weeks, it is called "major hanging up" (dà guàdā). Because they have hung up their mat for a long time, their conduct and practice are known;

if they are deemed suitable to live with, they are then sent back to the hall, which is called "settling in a mat" (ānshàn). When encountering such seekers of residence, the Guest Hall (kètáng) shall inquire into their background thoroughly;
if they may be retained, they are retained and sent to the guest quarters. The Guest Hall shall invite them for a meal and instruct them to follow [the established procedures].
He ascends the hall with joy. After one, two, or three days, he requests permission from the *ho-shang*, who grants it.

The night before, he notifies the *wei-na*. Only then does he post his name on the register (*hao-pu*), recording: "The person named so-and-so, aged so many years, a resident of such a province, prefecture, and county; the son of the family of such-and-such; what was his occupation in lay life;

on such a month and day at such a place, he left the household life and took such-and-such as his teacher; on such a month and day at such a temple, under such-and-such a *ho-shang*, he received full ordination; and now, on such a month and day, he has arrived at this temple," and so forth.
The following morning, after the second serving of congee, he prepares the incense and ritual implements and leads them to stand outside the Abbot’s quarters.

The Attendant announces this to the Abbot. When the Abbot takes his seat, the Guest Master joins his palms and says: "There is a certain Master who has come specifically to attend upon the Venerable Abbot.

Next, the new guest enters, spreads his ritual implements, and performs three prostrations. Upon completion of the bows, the Abbot may question him, and he should answer truthfully. The Abbot then asks: [Question].

Having finished answering, he leads them to the entrance of the meditation hall (*zhandang*). He strikes the *baoban* three times; the duty-holder (*jianzhi*) rolls up the curtain, and the assembly stands in their places.

The guest prefect (*zhike*) first performs the ten-direction prostrations (*shifangli*), then addresses the newly admitted practitioners: "Fellow practitioners, enter the hall and perform the prostrations. Once the prostrations are completed, the guest prefect withdraws.
The rector (*weina*) receives their ritual implements and escorts them to their seats, assigning them to the east or west side of the hall according to their order of entry. They then follow.

The assembly sits in meditation. Awaiting the opening of the small *jing* (period of silence), the *vinaya-dhara* (recluse leader) calls the roll numbers and records them in the register. He orders the new arrivals to unpack their luggage and enter the hall to settle into their quarters.

During the evening service, the newly ordained monks, accompanied by the ritual implements, ascend the hall; when the service is finished, the *vinaya-dhara* says, "Newly entered hall masters" (and they exit the assembly to perform prostrations).

Having completed the prostrations, they return to the hall. The *yuèzhòng* (attendant for the assembly) leads them to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*). After the prostrations there are finished, they return to the hall. The *vinaya-dhara* then leads them to...
In the resident quarters, they converse. At the second board in the evening, the Abbot invites the new entrant for tea, accompanied by the *yuèzhòng* (Director of Affairs).

The following day, the name plaque for the assigned seat (*ānshàn*) is posted. After the incense has been offered and before the third board signals the end of the period of silence, the incense is distributed.

Once the assembly has finished sitting, the *wéinà* (Rector) calls out: "Newly entered monks, please leave your seats and perform the rites. They perform three prostrations before the Buddha as a rite for the new entrant, then three prostrations toward the Abbot’s seat.
Prostrate. Perform the ritual circle. Offer one prostration toward each of the two sides; all members respond accordingly. Without leaving their seats, the ritual is concluded.

The *weina* leads the head of the assembly, the *yuezhong*, the *xiangdeng*, and the *si-shui* to perform their prostrations. Once these are finished, they immediately prostrate to the *weina*, return to their positions, and observe silence.
If the Abbot invites them for a meal, the *yuezhong* accompanies them; or, if they are invited separately by the Abbot, the *yuezhong* may accompany them as well.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: To dwell in solitude is fundamentally for the purpose of seeking the Way. As guest and host, both must avoid mutual failure.
The abbot must possess genuine virtue and conduct, and must be diligent in examination. The student must possess genuine inquiry and pursuit.
Enduring hardship with a patient mind. *Zhigu yun* says: Formerly, at Guangjiao Monastery in Ye County, Ruzhou, Chan Master Guisheng served as abbot. He was stern and austere;
the monks revered him with awe. When Fushan Yuan and Tianyi Huai heard of his lofty reputation, they went specifically to visit and consult him.
It happened to be a time of snowy cold, yet Guisheng scolded and drove them away, even using water [to douse them].
He splashed [water] on the ground, soaking all their clothes. The other monks departed in anger, leaving only Xuanxue and Huaihuai. They sat down again for a short while.
The Master scolded them once more, saying, "If you do not leave, I shall beat you.

Xuanxue said, "We two, Xuanxue and Huaihuai, have come from thousands of miles away specifically to study the Chan of the Master; how could we leave just because of a ladle of water? The Master smiled and said:

"You two have come specifically to practice *chán*. Have the guest prefect send you a registration form. Yuan was appointed as the steward (*diànzù*). The community suffered from a lack of sustenance and austerity.
Xing went out of the monastery to procure oil and flour to make a five-flavor congee. Just as it was about to be cooked, Xing returned. After the meal, he summoned the steward;
Yuan arrived. Xing said, "You procured oil and flour; this constitutes the theft of communal property. Yuan replied, "It is true."
He confiscated Huayan’s oil and flour, vowing to impose a fine. He ordered that Huayan’s robes and bowl be appraised and used to compensate for their value;
furthermore, thirty days’ worth of rent was demanded. One day, while Huayan was out, Huisheng saw him in the corridor of the monastery and said, “This is the corridor of the temple gate.
You have been here for a long time; have you ever paid your house rent? He then pursued the arrears. Huayan showed no sign of distress.
He begged for some coins from the market and returned them [to the master]. Still not dismissed, he said to the assembly, "Yuan truly intends to study Chan," and thus ordered him to return home.

Upon ascending the hall, he bestowed the robe upon him before the assembly, saying... Alas! The ancients served their teachers and chose their friends with such diligence that they did not dare to be idle day or night;
even when tending the hearth or carrying out the pounding of grain, they never shied away from labor. People today—
If one finds the tea and rice to be bland, one immediately thinks of moving elsewhere; if the labor and toil of the mountain slope are exhausting, one seeks other means for ease and comfort.
How, then, could such a person ever study the Way? As for the abbots of today, they entangle themselves solely in mundane affairs and ultimately fail to examine or encourage their students.
Such lofty styles as those mentioned above can no longer be seen; truly, both guest and host are at fault.
It is lost! How deeply lamentable it is! Regarding the general assembly (pǔqǐng) and the work period (chūpō):
the Guest Hall first hangs a notice board. (The board reads: "Venerable Assembly, upon hearing the sound of the wooden mallet, proceed to [insert location] at such-and-such time."

For the sake of [Name]’s work on the mountain slopes, a general labor call (*pǔqǐng*) is issued for going out to work. ○ The storehouse office (*kūsī*) shall first ensure that all necessary implements and utensils are prepared.

Upon hearing the three rounds of the wooden sounding-block (*bāngshēng*), if it coincides with the second board, the standing board, or the time for evacuation (*chōujiě*) in the Zen hall (*cāntáng*), the laborers shall immediately cease according to the regulations.
If it is early, the rector (*wéinà*) shall strike the incense board and go out to work; the assembly shall then leave the hall in successive order. Do not...

When you have leisure for idle talk, laughter, and indulgence, each person must maintain their own assigned *hwadu*. At the conclusion of the work period, return to the hall. The Master of Ceremonies (*Jungui*) says:
"The method of communal labor (*pulgyeong*) is that those high and low share the effort equally. In mountain monasteries, manual tasks are particularly numerous.
When the appointed time arrives, the wooden clapper is struck and everyone proceeds together; even the abbot may not seek ease or shirk toil. If one is ill,"

Thus, one does not exert oneself; it is only upon reaching old age that one may finally rest. This principle regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited applies equally to those living together in the community.
According to the records of Tang-dynasty Tongzhou, Zhichao was a native of Fengyi who left the household life under Chan Master Zhan of Kaihua Monastery in Bingzhou.
He subsequently became the abbot of Moku-ji Temple. He purified his body and mind and diligently attended to the affairs of the community.
He provided for several hundred monks, ensuring that food and clothing were always available. Whenever there was arduous labor, he invariably led by example.

Such was the nature of most abbots in antiquity; consequently, the monastic centers flourished. By contrast, contemporary abbots maintain a position of honor and live in luxury, leaving the labor to others while seeking ease for themselves.
To wish for the monastic community to be restored to order is indeed difficult!

Regarding the "Daily Usages and Standards" (*Riyong Guifan*), the preceding six fascicles have already clarified the specific duties of each individual; this present chapter on the "Great Assembly" (*Dazhong Zhang*)...
This is shown for all people to practice. Regardless of who one is or what attachments one holds, one must not transgress any of these points.
Whether one is a resident monk or a visiting monk, everyone must individually observe them. First: To esteem and uphold the virtue of the precepts is the very root of Bodhi.
1. To lay the foundation for nirvana. 2. To find sweetness in simplicity and detachment, remaining content in poverty while delighting in the Way, thereby protecting the mind of the Path.

3. To be tranquil, pure, and single-minded; to reduce external conditions and attend to the fundamental, without dividing the mind. 4. To eliminate selfishness and reject the heterodox, honoring the public good and maintaining rectitude.

5. To be harmonious and patient, being cautious in one's affairs and respectful toward others. 6. To follow the assembly and obey its commands, with dignified and solemn deportment. 7. [To maintain these practices.]
8. Diligently cultivate your practice; be neither indolent nor negligent. 9. Observe the rules when dwelling among the assembly; be upright and not sycophantic. 10.
Rest content with your lot and maintain a cautious mind; do not act recklessly. 11. Accord with established regulations and together contribute to the Dharma-gate.

The above ten points constitute a brief summary of the general framework of wholesome dharmas. I am not weary of explaining them in detail; furthermore, there are specific prohibitions and examples listed below, which I have carefully set forth as follows.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: An ancient saying goes, "A foot of practice is better than ten feet of talk;
an inch of practice is better than a foot of talk. Niaoke said to Bai Juyi, "Commit no evil; perform all good deeds.
Bai Juyi replied, "Even a three-year-old child can say that. The Master said, "A three-year-old child..."
Although one may attain the Way, an eighty-year-old elder cannot practice it.
How profound these words are! One must not violate the fundamental great precepts; one must not fail to join the assembly without cause during the recitation of the precepts;
one must not be unfilial toward one’s parents; one must not deceive or treat superiors with contempt; and one must not willfully disobey the imperial court.
Prohibitions of the Official Monastery: One must not associate closely with women; one must not remain ignorant of the characteristics of the precepts after having received them;
one must not draw near to false teachers; and one must not drink alcohol or gamble. These nine matters, when not transgressed, are termed "revering and upholding the virtue of the precepts.
If they are transgressed, those that are minor incur a penalty, while those that are grave result in expulsion from the monastery.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Tathāgata’s final teaching took the support of the Vinaya and the discourse on the eternal as its core principle.

If one were to discard phenomena to discourse only on principle, that principle would become a mere nothingness. Among the various schools of Chan and the Exoteric Teachings, there are none whose monastic conduct is not as pure as ice and frost;

only then can they serve as a model for a thousand ages. How could one allow a vessel of poison to hold *amṛta* (clarified butter)? Therefore, those who wish to support the Buddha-dharma so that it does not decline must uphold...

Vigilance regarding the precepts is urgent. As it is said: "A journey of a thousand li begins with a single step. If that one step is not sufficient, one cannot be said to have reached the destination.
It may be said that the entire thousand li is contained within that one step; yet from this present body to the Buddha-body, it is precisely this one step.
However, one must by no means remain stationary and fail to advance. For if one advances, then this one step will be preserved in every thought-moment.
Cease. Then this single step will immediately subside; it is not that one step is itself a thousand miles.

As for the method of advancing, it lies in abandoning the habitual steps of beginningless time. These habitual steps are precisely greed, delusion, and hatred, each of which possesses its own partiality and stagnation;
you must awaken to them yourself and tame them yourself.
One must not prepare sumptuous delicacies; one must not wear gaudy or elegant clothing; one must not engage extensively in worldly affairs; one must not compete for offerings of money;
one must not engage in farming, sericulture, or animal husbandry; one must not gather men and women together to hold secular feasts and assemblies.
Not violating these six matters is called "abiding in poverty while delighting in the Way. If one violates them—
Those who are light offenders shall be punished; those who are heavy offenders shall leave the monastery.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding these six articles, when the head of the quarters attends to the monks residing in the quiet chambers, the monks will possess a sense of shame and remorse.

If even those [in ordinary circumstances] dare not transgress, how much less so for one dwelling in a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*)? For instance: by eating fine food, one is constrained and attached to the dust of flavor;
by wearing elegant garments, one is bound by the dust of form. One seizes upon scriptures and competes for alms, drowning in the poison of greed.

By farming, sericulture, and animal husbandry, one utterly destroys the precept against killing. When assemblies are convened, a hundred evils arise together. Furthermore, regarding the aforementioned four matters, the *saṃgha*...
It is easy to commit [the first] offense, while the latter two matters concern only the duties of the preceptor. All of these are the roots of resentment and the foundation of suffering.
The *Lianghuang Chanwen* (The Repentance Text of Emperor Wu of Liang) asks: "What are the roots of resentment and suffering? The eyes crave forms; the ears crave sounds;
the nose craves fragrances; the tongue craves flavors; and the body craves smooth textures. One is constantly bound by these five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), and thus for kalpas on end..."
At night, because one has not yet attained liberation, one must remain content in poverty and delight in the Way.

One must not wander idly outside for no reason, nor frequently visit the dwellings of the laity. One must not practice the composition of literary verses for official occasions, nor learn miscellaneous arts such as instrumental performance or singing.
One must not study astronomy, geography, or external practices such as ritual talismans, water-mantras, or alchemy.
Regarding the matters: one must not practice breath-holding, seated meditation, or heterodox paths such as "Non-action" (Wuwei) or the White Lotus Society;

nor shall one take pleasure in engaging in useless labor or similar activities. These five points—refraining from such transgressions—are termed "restraining conditions and attending to the fundamental.
If a minor offense is committed, there is a penalty; for a major offense, one is expelled from the monastery.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: An ancient said, "An inch of time is an inch of gold.
This was intended to admonish those who study the Way, so that they may know time passes easily and must not be wasted. If one commits these five matters, it is not merely a vain squandering of time;
it is truly a self-sabotage of one's own mind and character. How can one fail to exercise restraint? The *Lianghuang Chanchan* says: "Each person should..."

Everyone should give rise to the intent for awakening and contemplate that the world is impermanent and the physical form does not endure long. Youth must inevitably decline; do not rely upon your appearance.
Do not dwell in defiled conduct. All things are impermanent and must all return to death. Unless one diligently practices superior deeds, there is no way to escape [suffering];
therefore, one must examine conditions and take the fundamental as the priority.
One must not solicit alms through improper means; one must not embezzle offerings of faith; one must not appropriate the property of the monastery (caitya) for personal use;
one must not damage utensils or implements without making restitution; one must not eat apart from the assembly;
and one must not move the property of the masterless monks without informing the assembly. Not violating these six matters is called serving the public interest and maintaining integrity.
If one commits a minor offense, there shall be punishment; if a grave offense, expulsion from the monastery.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: "Public" means not private; speaking in terms of wealth and profit, "correct" means not deviant; speaking in terms of love and desire.
However, among these six articles, those spoken primarily in terms of material goods are as stated in the Sūtras and Vinaya. If it concerns objects...
They belong to others; they are guarded by others. Among the possessions of others, one does not take even a single blade of grass or a single leaf if it is not given, let alone commit theft.
This is because sentient beings perceive only immediate benefit, and thus they seize property through various unrighteous means.
This causes one to suffer much misfortune and entanglement in the future. Therefore, one must always maintain a mind of impartiality and integrity, observing these six principles.
An ancient verse says: "My mind is like a scale-beam; this is called impartiality. My mind is like a standing wall; this is called integrity.
Impartiality and integrity cause others to submit; impartiality and integrity are the foundation of the Way. Serve the public and uphold [these principles].
The upright person is pure; who can stain them?
One must not break out into verbal abuse or exchange blows with fists. One must not accept humiliation nor show it in one’s words or countenance.
One must not use power to oppress others. One must not treat elders with contempt. These are the four matters.
This is not an offense; it is called gentle forbearance (*mṛdu-kṣānti*). If one commits a minor offense, there is a penalty;

if a grave offense, expulsion from the community. The commentary on the meaning states: "In obstructing the path of cultivation, nothing is equal to anger and pride. As it is said: 'When a single thought of anger arises, a million doors of obstruction open.
Pride is like a high mountain where the waters of the Dharma do not rest. Furthermore, irrational anger is coarse and easy [to recognize]."

Eliminate it. Clinging to principles makes anger subtle and difficult to sever. Whether in worldly or supramundane affairs, nothing succeeds through loving-kindness and patience, while everything fails through anger and resentment.
Therefore, the gentleman cultivates virtue through loving-kindness and nourishes the mind through patience. When the small cannot endure, great schemes fall into chaos.
The turbidity of the *kalpa* of weapons is summoned by the accumulation of anger; this all stems from self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*), which is why anger accumulates.
Yet, how could there ever have been a real self? Once one realizes that the grasping at a self is fundamentally empty, hatred and pride will naturally be severed.
In both the present and the future, one will surely realize the essence of non-self. *Zhigu* says: During the Xiaosheng era, there was the Venerable Cheng Sanmu of Yunmen.
A monk attended at his seat for nearly ten years, receiving exceptional treatment and being highly praised by him.

He shared his seat with him, never once making distinctions based on left or right. Yet, as soon as the Master shifted the focus of his regard even slightly, the monk Xin spread slander and sent a letter of insolence, filled with the most vile and contemptuous insults.
The Master burned it before the assembly, saying, "Whether this is right or wrong, whether it is good or bad—only the spirits know.
He ultimately paid no heed to it. Alas! Formerly he bestowed kindness upon him, yet now he repays it with resentment; I praise his virtue.
When others reviled me and exposed my faults, I was able to endure it without retorting; this may be called the ultimate degree of patience and gentleness.

The *Lianghuang Chanwen* states: "Toward all sentient beings, one should regard them as equal and without distinction, entering into the contemplation of equality and harboring no thoughts of enmity or affection.
One should always look upon all sentient beings with eyes of love. Even if sentient beings harbor resentment toward a Bodhisattva or give rise to thoughts of malice and rebellion..."
Such a person is a Bodhisattva who acts as a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Having well-subdued their own mind, they preach the profound Dharma.
Just as the great ocean cannot be destroyed by any poison, so too is the Bodhisattva;
even if sentient beings who are foolish, ignorant, ungrateful, and commit immeasurable evils should arise, they cannot disturb or agitate the Bodhisattva’s resolve for enlightenment. This is...
This is called patience and gentleness.
One must not engage in excessive joking; one must not converse in a loud voice; one must not affect artificiality;
and one must not sit or stand leaning. Not violating these four matters is called having a dignified and orderly demeanor. If one violates them—
Those who are light in offense shall be punished; those who are grave shall be expelled from the monastery.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: "Majesty is manifested through virtue; it is not the majesty of power and force. Dignity is the outward expression of the mind;

it is not a dignity feigned through pretense. Furthermore, as for "majesty," it arises from the strict observance of the precepts and practices, whereby all virtues become majestic and awe-inspiring. As for "dignity," it is...

Because their movements and stillness accord with the proper form, their advancing and retreating are serene and composed. This is what is meant by pure conduct being perfected as the ritual of the Path, and the white purity being fulfilled within the categories of the precepts.
Thus, the bhikṣu proceeds upon the Path with dignified grace, inspiring the common people to find faith and joy and to leave the household life.

The Buddha’s disciples beg for food with composure and dignity, gathering in those of external paths so that they may turn from error and return to the right. Thus it is called "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*);

it is a teaching beyond words. Furthermore, dignified deportment is termed "taming and guiding. This means taming the body so it does not move recklessly, the mouth so it does not speak recklessly, and the mind so it does not harbor reckless thoughts.
When these three karmas are thus tamed and made virtuous, the six sense faculties are naturally restrained.
*Zhagu* says: Chan Master Fanyun was in his daily conduct and movements such that he gazed straight ahead without blinking.

For thirty years presiding over the assembly, he never once allowed himself a light smile. In all places where he resided, upon seeing a sacred image in a standing or walking posture, he would not sit down.

If food is named after fish or meat, one must not eat it. Thus, one’s physical deportment should be orderly and solemn, so as not to bring shame upon the appearance of one who has left the household life.
To serve as a model for the monastic community within and to benefit those who have taken refuge and faith without, how can the two characters for "deportment" (wei-yi) ever be neglected?
One must not fail to perform prostrations and recitations without cause; one must not be negligent in performing duties; one must not resent admonitions from others;
and one must not do that which is unbeneficial or harmful to what is beneficial. These four matters, when not transgressed, are called the diligent practice of one's vocation.
If they are transgressed, those who violate them lightly shall be penalized, while those who violate them severely shall be expelled from the monastery.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding "diligently practicing the path," diligence means not being indolent; cultivation means refining one's merits and remedying faults so that time is not wasted in vain—this is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
There is a distinction between mundane and supramundane paths of practice, yet the supramundane path is taken as the foundation and the essential.
As the Sūtra says: "Do not disparage even small virtues, thinking they bring no merit; though a drop of water..."
A tiny drop gradually fills a great vessel; if small virtues are not accumulated, one cannot achieve sainthood. Do not underestimate a minor evil, thinking it is without fault;
through the accumulation of minor evils, one’s very self may be destroyed. This is what all Buddhas have taught—dare anyone disbelieve it?
Therefore, one must diligently cultivate supramundane virtuous deeds and practices.
One must not incite strife; one must not form factions; one must not be deceitful or dishonest; one must not slander those of renown and virtue;
one must not falsely defame the pure assembly; one must not yield to private interests or show partiality.
Not violating these six matters is called "conforming to the rules when dwelling among the community. For minor violations, there shall be punishment; for serious ones, expulsion from the monastery.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The *Lianghuang Chan* says, "The remaining verbal transgressions are likewise gateways to all manner of enmity and calamity.
Therefore, the Buddhas have admonished that one must not engage in double-tongued speech, harsh words, false speech, or frivolous talk.

One should know that sycophantic crookedness and flowery rhetoric, which incite discord and stir up right and wrong, cause no small harm; the retribution they attract is truly grave. When a person dwells in the world, their mind harbors..."
Poisonous thoughts, poisonous words spoken with the mouth, and poisonous deeds performed with the body—by means of these three matters, one inflicts harm upon sentient beings.
When sentient beings are poisoned, they immediately form resentment and harbor a vow in their hearts to retaliate, either fulfilling this wish in the present life or carrying it out after death.
Such cycles of enmity are all sustained by the three karmas; among these three karmas, the karma of speech is truly the most grave. Thus...
When the retribution is received, one will endure all manner of agonizing torments. Therefore, when dwelling among the assembly, one should follow the ancient verse which says:
"First, harmony is precious; only then can the multitude be at peace. Do not open the mouth for double-tongued speech; one must refrain from useless words.

For those who hold administrative office, one must by no means indulge in personal favoritism. When requests and entreaties arrive in profusion, a hundred evils will arise within the monastic community. In all matters...
As one who manages affairs: do not purchase a single person based on their reputation; do not employ a single person based on their reputation.

In all matters, everything is subject to inversion. One must not recklessly initiate new undertakings; one must not misinterpret the sutras and treatises; one must not arbitrarily cite the karmic conditions of ancient worthies;
one must not compose works out of ignorance to mislead others; and one must not admit those who are unworthy. Do not...
One may establish one's own assembly of followers; however, one must not arbitrarily retain young novices or śrāmaṇeras.
One must not be ignorant of one's own affairs while delighting in acting as a teacher to others. One must not entice or seduce the disciples of others. One must not abandon one's original teacher.
One must not enter the gates of official authority without a grave reason. One must not recklessly judge the merits and faults, or the right and wrong, of contemporary governance.
One must not, with a disrespectful mind, slander or disparage the ancient sages and worthies; one must not give away communal property or assets to others;
one must not encroach upon or seize the property of others; and one must not establish a separate kitchen for cooking.

These fifteen matters, if not transgressed, are termed "maintaining one's station with a cautious mind. If they are violated, those that are minor incur a penalty, while those that are grave result in expulsion from the monastery.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: There are twenty further phrases concerning maintaining one’s station with a humble mind: that for a monastic community, non-involvement in worldly affairs constitutes prosperity;

that for spiritual practice, acting in accordance with one’s capacity is what is stable and appropriate; that diligence takes the observance of the precepts as primary; and [the treatment of] illness.
Take reducing one’s food as the medicinal decoction for afflictions; take patience as the sublime resolution for right and wrong;
take non-contention as liberation in dealing with others; and take sincerity as true feeling in attending to affairs; take wholehearted devotion as meritorious achievement in performing duties.
In speech, brevity is straightforwardness; in conduct toward superiors and subordinates, benevolence and harmony are the advancement of virtue;
in study, diligent practice is the gateway; in cause and effect, clarity is the absence of error; in aging and illness, impermanence is the admonition;
in Buddhist services, spiritual sincerity is the essential; in honoring guests, the increase of humility is the offering. Gate.
In one's courtyard, take simplicity as one’s adornment. In all affairs, take preparation in advance as the means to avoid toil.

In dealing with the multitude, take circumspect speech as the constant rule of etiquette. When encountering danger, take remaining undisturbed as the guiding principle. In aiding sentient beings, take compassion as the foundation.
With such a cautious mind, one will commit few errors. An ancient verse says: "Of us who have left the household life, for the most part..."
A Son of the Farming Family: You must remember the times of poverty and hardship; you must carefully maintain your humble station.

Even those of wealth and nobility, once they have entered the Empty Gate (the monastic order), should recognize the meaning of that "Empty Gate"—it is fundamentally intended for you to let the worldly mind die. Yet people fear that their minds will not die.
It is better to be poor with a dead heart; it is better to maintain one's lot and remain poor. Thus, one will be free from affliction for the rest of one’s life.
One must not allow [the mind] to fail to act, nor can it be stopped by prohibitions. There shall be no transgressions.

If one does not submit to punishment, they shall not reside in the temple, their name shall not enter the ranks of the monastics, they shall not study the Dharma, and they shall not be permitted to hold office.

Matters: One must not act as an administrator. Furthermore, one must not alter established regulations. One must not fail to inform one's teachers and friends. One must not act arbitrarily or recklessly.
One must not intentionally grant expulsion to those who have committed offenses. The above seven matters, when not violated, are termed "conforming to regulations.
If they are violated, minor offenses incur a fine; serious offenses result in expulsion from the monastery.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Including the preceding ten categories, there are sixty-seven matters in total. To maintain all of these without transgression is called "conforming to the regulations.

Furthermore, to speak in detail: from the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, the Śrāmaṇera Precepts, the Bhikṣu Precepts, and the Bodhisattva Precepts, up to the Baizhang Qinggui, and even the three hundred rules of etiquette and the three thousand points of dignified conduct, as well as the six pāramitās and the myriad practices—[one must maintain them all].
Practice. In the worldly codes of conduct, all that is free from transgression is collectively termed "conforming to regulations.
These are not limited to these seven matters alone. Appendix: Ten Matters for Cultivating the Person by Master Lianchi (from *Yunqi Fahui*).
One must not deceive oneself. One must not covet wealth. One must not employ villainy. One must not resort to scheming. One must not provoke...
Calamity. One must not be extravagant or wasteful; one must not be intimate with women; one must not pursue external distractions; one must not shirk diligence;

one must not lose the proper timing. (Original note states: That which is called "deceiving the heart" includes all instances of stealing property belonging to the Sangha, defrauding donors, or misappropriating funds intended for making Buddha images, printing sutras, feeding monks, convening assemblies, building temples, casting bells, repairing bridges, or paving roads—using such wealth for private expenses, or even deceiving people and officials, and deceiving Heaven and the gods through obscure and clandestine acts;
all these are termed "deceiving the heart. Even if one does not steal or defraud as previously described, yet merely delights in accumulating wealth and being stingy...)

Not practicing generosity; instead, amassing property to collect interest, lending money at usury, and seeking profit—all these are termed "coveting wealth. When it is time to speak [the truth], one remains silent out of forbearance; when there is a transgression that requires admonition, one sits by idly and fails to counsel; outwardly feigning dull-wittedness while inwardly harboring derision and disparagement—all these are termed "instigating wickedness.

Not accepting the mandate of Heaven but relying solely on human scheming—whether plotting for a residence, plotting for a following, plotting for sutra recitations and repentance rituals, plotting for almsgiving, plotting to serve as a Dharma master, or plotting to serve as a preceptor;

even down to associating with evil friends, frequenting government offices, judging the depth of personal relationships, harboring private likes and dislikes, devising schemes, and engaging in activities that contravene principle—all such matters are termed "employing stratagems. Disparaging others, ridiculing others, scolding others, slandering others, envying others' abilities, and exposing others'...

To harbor malice; to seize others' lost property; to occupy others' estates; to delight in instigating litigation; and to refuse to yield to others—all these are termed "provoking calamity. To construct extensive dwellings; to provide sumptuous food and drink; to wear elegant clothing; to acquire many properties; to craft exquisite utensils; to treat the five grains with contempt; to indulge in idle wandering; to maintain servants;

and to bribe and cultivate wild companions—if one does not know shame for any of these acts, they are all termed "extravagant waste. For young nuns and monks to form spiritual bonds as "dharma-friends"; for human women to be taken as "godmothers";

to frequently visit relatives and kin, disregarding public censure and suspicion—all these are termed "approaching women. To frequent wealthy households; to solicit audiences at noble gates; to beg for poems or prose; to seek plaques or inscriptions; or to feign authority—[all such acts are likewise condemned].

Regarding these matters: to seek wealth and property, to be in constant motion all day long, or to fail to contemplate remaining in stillness—all these are termed "running outward. To perform morning and evening liturgies and recitations with frequent transgressions, or to be negligent and fail to follow the assembly during communal activities despite diligent labor—all these are termed "avoiding laziness.

Life exists but for a breath; time does not wait for anyone. Since the Great Matter remains unclarified, even a moment of time is precious; to let it pass by in vain and indifference is termed "missing the opportune time. These nine preceding points are things one must strictly guard against. As for the final word: exert yourself and strive with diligence.
Appendix: Inauspicious Matters for Those Who Have Left the Household Life (Thirty-two Articles.
From the *Yunqi Fahui Yigao*) To sit before the Buddha and receive the prostrations of others is inauspicious. To revile others before the Buddha is inauspicious.

To scold or rebuke people on the Dharma-seat, or to speak lightly of and disparage the errors of former sages, is inauspicious. To receive offerings while wearing informal or sacrilegious clothing is inauspicious.
It is inauspicious for people to prostrate [before one]. It is inauspicious to eat while reviling others.

It is inauspicious to harbor feelings of hatred and aversion while discriminating between the good and the bad at the dining table. It is inauspicious to use silk gauze, damask, brocade, and fine silks as everyday clothing for members of the Sangha.
It is inauspicious to use heavy mattresses, thick mats, silk quilts, and gauze curtains for one’s bed. It is pure.
To scold others at dawn is inauspicious. To harbor resentment toward those who offer alms, whether they be meager or small, is inauspicious.
To purchase servants for one's service like a wealthy or noble family is inauspicious. To think, "Others labor while I alone am at ease," is inauspicious.
To think, "Others are destitute while I alone am wealthy and abundant," is inauspicious. For a youth to act as a Dharma-preacher, a master of food-offerings, or [a ritual officiant] is inauspicious.
It is inauspicious for an abbot to act thus. It is inauspicious for a youth to rely on his own petty cleverness and treat elder monks with contempt.
It is inauspicious for one who relies on his seniority to treat those junior to him with contempt. It is inauspicious to receive a significant gift without cause.
It is inauspicious when others treat me with sincerity, yet I respond to them with craftiness and deception. It is inauspicious to delight in speaking ill of others.
It is an ill omen to conceal faults and secret matters. It is an ill omen to use public property for the benefit of lay families.
It is an ill omen to lavishly provide fine robes and delicious food to one's own śrāmaṇeras and disciples.

It is an ill omen to speak with such habitual coarseness and severity that others find it difficult to endure. [Furthermore,] to have many protectors of the Dharma and much offered alms—this is... [an ill omen].
To become arrogantly self-important is inauspicious. To cause a healthy person to empty the chamber pot is inauspicious.
To become angry with one's attendants while ill is inauspicious. To urinate while wearing a short tunic is inauspicious.
To harbor resentment toward Heaven and Earth during droughts or floods is inauspicious. To hear of the death of someone to whom one owes a debt and feel joy in one’s heart is inauspicious.
To be cheerful [at inappropriate times] is inauspicious. To smile before speaking is inauspicious. To sigh in sorrow when there is no cause is inauspicious.
To have a superficial grasp of the teachings and principles, yet recklessly criticize the ancients and look down upon one's contemporaries, is inauspicious.

To possess only limited knowledge and insight, yet presume to act as a patriarchal master, is inauspicious. These things diminish one’s merit and shorten one’s lifespan, frequently inviting calamity and retribution.
Therefore, it is called inauspicious; we should mutually admonish one another regarding this.

The *Zhengyi* (Verification of Meaning) states: The *Canzong biyao* (Secret Essentials of the Chan School) records that Chan Master Chenghao of Yuquan visited Beita [Chan Master] to investigate the essentials of the mind.
Having attained the samādhi of great mastery (*mahāsvatantra-samādhi*), he fashioned a loincloth—commonly known as a "ox-head trousers"—and inscribed upon it the successive generations...
The Master’s name was Wen-shu Pu-hsien (Mañjuśrī-Bhadrakapāla). He remarked, "Only Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra could compare with him for a moment," and thus he wrote these characters upon his sash.

Consequently, the monastic community came to call him "Hao Bu-k'un" (White Linen Pants). During the Yuanfeng era, while the Master was leading the assembly at Guyin in Xiangyang, a local monk also imitated this practice.
Upon seeing him, the Master rebuked him, saying, "What kind of principle do you possess that you dare to treat this as a joke?"
It was a matter of fact. He vomited blood, and it was too late to help him. Shortly thereafter, at Lumen (Deer Gate), he passed away just as he had said.
Alas! This is indeed a model of inauspiciousness. Dharma Master Yujü of the Qi dynasty resided at Upper Zhushan in the sixth year of the Xuandao era.
A certain monk violated the rules, and the Master rebuked him, saying: "You are ignorant; you are nothing more than a beast. Later, he regretted this, saying: "Although he was..."
Xiao reviled [the Buddha] as a beast, thereby defiling the Triple Gem. For three years thereafter, he repented before the Buddha;
in this way, one might perhaps transform misfortune into fortune. Yet, how does this compare to being cautious with one's speech from the very beginning?
Let scholars take this as a mirror.
Regarding the regulations for communal living (to be posted in the meditation hall):

To settle the mind and withdraw from worldly shadows, one must rely upon a renowned monastery; to cultivate the Way according to the rules, one must necessarily associate with those of like-minded resolve who have long served as venerable seniors.

Because their travels were profound, a hundred threads of thought sprang forth from them; yet later generations, following the current of the times, possessed shallow knowledge and views, causing their original resolve to gradually decline.
This led to the loss of the core principles of the school and a proliferation of deviations from the model, which became accepted as the norm until they accumulated into a pervasive corruption.
I, [Name], preside over this mountain. I am ashamed of my own meager virtue; though I harbor the Buddha’s precepts in my heart, I have failed to repay the Dharma-gate.

Desiring to restore the declining customs of the past, I can only hope that the worthy assembly of the future will together observe the Buddha’s spoken precepts and the regulations established by our patriarchs.
To regulate the three karmas and subdue transgressions, one dwells in this forest grove for the purpose of practicing accordingly. Should it not be so, there is no need for communal residence.
Those who violate the fundamental major precepts are expelled from the monastery. Zen values genuine inquiry and true awakening;
those who dabble in mere verbal Zen are expelled. Those who gather in groups of three or five and play outside the mountain gate shall likewise be expelled.

Miscellaneous Discourse: Those who sit idly shall be penalized. Those who refuse to comply shall be expelled from the monastery. Those who consume meat or alcohol, or attend theatrical performances, shall be penalized and expelled.
However, in the event of a serious illness where it cannot be cured without alcohol, one may consume it only after informing the assembly. (New Addition) Those who smoke shall be penalized.
Those who intentionally associate with persons of transgression, harbor thoughts of harming the monastic community, or disturb virtuous practitioners shall be expelled.

In the monastery, if there is strife over right and wrong, with parties cursing one another until their mouths are bloody and striking one another with their fists, they shall be expelled regardless of who is in the right or wrong.

If one party is correct in principle and remains patient, while the other commits an offense and becomes angry, the one correct in principle shall not be punished, whereas the offender shall be reprimanded and expelled.
As for rice, wheat, and other such items, if one sells them privately or uses them without informing the abbot, they shall be fined and required to make restitution.

Discharge from the monastery. Those who damage or deplete the property of the monastic community (*saṃgha*), or who cut bamboo, wood, flowers, or fruit to give to others, must pay restitution before being discharged.
Regarding patrons (*dānapati*) entering the temple, if the administrative staff solicits private alms on their behalf, they shall be punished according to the gravity of the offense.

Those who refuse to comply shall be discharged. As for those who leave for private reasons without official business—whether to visit patrons or return to their secular homes—their punishment shall be determined.
Those who have not practiced in seclusion shall be expelled from the monastery. Those who know of such persons but fail to report them shall be punished equally.
Furthermore, those whose own vision is clouded, who recklessly judge the insights of others, and who speak without realizing their errors, shall likewise be expelled.

Those who do not join the assembly during recitation, sitting meditation, or going out to work shall be penalized, except for those attending to public duties or those who are ill. Those who refuse to comply shall be expelled from the monastery.

Those who speak in the Zen hall shall be penalized; if the hall officers do not report such individuals and instead wait for them to be reported by those outside the hall, the hall officers shall be penalized along with the offender.
Except for public duties, those who leave their own quarters and enter other quarters to indulge in negligence shall be penalized.

Those who do so shall be punished. Those who gamble or play games of chance with money shall be severely punished and expelled from the monastery. Those in charge who fail to report such matters shall be punished in the same manner.
When there are no duties to perform, one must not eat in two halls simultaneously. During meals, one must not engage in conversation or laughter. One must not dispute over seating positions.

One must not sit in a seat that does not correspond to one’s assigned rank. One must not rise before the meal has concluded. One must not personally rinse one’s bowl and enter the kitchen to fetch [water].

Regarding meals: those who violate this rule shall be penalized. Upon encountering a general tea service, one must observe the regulations. Those who do not join the assembly except for official business shall be penalized.
One must not entrust others to fetch tea or fruit to take back to the quarters; both the giver and the taker shall be penalized equally.

The permanent property of the monastery, including scriptures and ornamental vessels, may not be borrowed out under any circumstances; violators shall be penalized. If it is absolutely unavoidable, one must inform the assembly before borrowing.
Those who treat elders with contempt, who loathe hearing direct admonition, or who give rise to groundless slanders shall be expelled from the monastery.
Those who do not obey the instructions and regulations of the administrative officers, or who request leave before their term has expired, shall be punished.

Unless suffering from a serious illness, those who consume food and drink apart from the assembly shall be punished. Those who privately allow friends or relatives to stay overnight shall be punished. [These matters] shall be reported by each quarter.
Failure to strike the signal bell shall be punished. Those who rely on their own merits and refuse to comply with discipline shall receive severe punishment.
Anyone who accepts offerings from the laity without informing the administrative officers shall be punished with double the fine, except in the case of relatives or neighbors.
When growing out one's beard and hair, one must not leave them unkempt. In the summer, one must not go bare-chested nor leave the trouser legs untucked. In the winter...
Those who roast food over an open fire or wear small hats shall be penalized. All income and expenditure of the monastery’s funds must be recorded;
those who fail to record them or are evasive in their accounts shall be penalized. Those who cause trouble by leaving the hall to go outside shall be strictly expelled;
they may take up temporary quarters on leave but shall never be allowed to re-enter. Only those with grave offenses shall be retained [for disciplinary purposes].

Furthermore, those who are young or who privately recruit disciples shall be expelled from the monastery. If there is no *sengzhi* (monastic steward) in the monastic community, then both internal and external affairs will be improper;
how can faults be eliminated, and how can the Dharma be established? As the *sengzhi*, you should exert your utmost effort in investigation and oversight.

One must not yield to personal sentiment. Should anyone violate this, they shall be punished according to the specific offense. If the punishment is omitted, the *sengzhi* (monastic administrator) shall receive the penalty.
The above regulations are the rules for those who truly cultivate the Way. All members of the community residing together should hold them in high esteem.
Dated [Year, Month, Day]. Recorded again by the Abbot, [Name].

The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Buddhas and Patriarchs established the teachings and founded the monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*) to guide their disciples and gather the assembly for pure cultivation and ascetic practice.
To repay the four debts of gratitude and purify the three karmas, the abbots did not spare their own bodies or lives, wading through mud and carrying water.
Therefore, in nurturing and cultivating talent, and in forging both the holy and the ordinary, the gateway of instruction cannot but be lofty;
ritual and law cannot but be strict; and rules and measures cannot but be established. When rules and measures are established, those above and below find peace;

when ritual and law are strict, the treacherous and the wicked withdraw; and when the gateway is lofty, the Way of the Teacher is honored. Now, one who receives others with humble radiance is like a mountain...

To possess a capacity for vast inclusion is the lofty character of an abbot; yet, when it comes to making practical arrangements according to the occasion, one cannot help but be stern-faced and dispassionate.

By preventing faults at their inception and blocking them before they develop, one may ensure that both internal and external affairs remain peaceful, free from the upheavals that follow in their wake.
However, if one wishes to protect others, one must first protect oneself; only when one has successfully protected oneself can one protect others.
Only after one has subdued a portion of one’s own habitual tendencies can one subdue a portion of the habitual tendencies of others.
To regard others as oneself and to abandon oneself for the sake of others—this is the ancestral rule that must first be put into practice. *Zhigu* says:

Chan Master Nandang Kong was naturally vigorous and his insight was exceptionally high. He maintained rigorous discipline over himself and did not attend external invitations. There was one who wished to...

The master was invited to his residence to receive the midday meal offering, and the patron provided funds to construct a mountain gate. The master said, "I am grateful that you have generously donated your wealth; however, to eat while turning one's back on the assembly—how can I break the precepts for my own sake? He ultimately did not go. Yūan’s verse says: The patron’s heart was vast and deep; He sought the Way with sincere devotion. The Master of the Mountain Gate declined the invitation; His conduct was truly worthy of praise. The Dharma is not something to be grasped by the mind; If it were grasped, it would become a hindrance. How could the Buddha-Dharma ever be found? It is only through non-seeking that it is attained. The Master of the Mountain Gate declined the invitation; His conduct was truly worthy of praise. The patron’s heart was vast and deep; He sought the Way with sincere devotion. These two matters were accomplished together, providing a twofold merit. That which you desired as merit is what I have followed through with my observance of the precepts. Though the mountain gate may be completed and then decay, the Vajra-precepts suffer no defeat.
Even if a single offering is most minute—like a tiny speck of mustard seed damaging a life-preserving skin (uraga-saṃnāha)—from this moment on, there shall be not even a single leak.
The Golden Embankment: The entire body of the Jewel-Awakened One was sold by you. Have you not seen the Master of Qingliang, who was Mañjuśrī incarnate?
