Regulations for the Pure Practice Hall (fifteen articles):
Now, the sea of birth and death is deep; how can one cross it without the practice of *nien-fo*? The path to Bodhi is far; if not for the Pure Land, who could reach it?
This may be relied upon as a standard. Therefore, the great assembly today follows the same path: we shall exclusively uphold the six-character Great Name;

with unified resolve and gathered in one hall, we shall exert all our efforts toward "single-mindedness without distraction. Yet, I fear that as time passes and practice endures, indolence will easily arise, resulting in the loss of substance while only the name remains, and our diligent toil will be in vain.
Unless we apply the whip of self-exhortation, there will be no means to restrain body and mind; thus, there must be established rules.

Only by aligning ourselves with this chapter can we bring both self and others into harmony. May you mutually examine and exhort one another, refraining from contending for oneself while contending against others.
Thus, may pure karma be swiftly accomplished and the lotus pedestal attained early; may Amitābha be beheld in this very life and samādhi realized in this very body.
If this is truly so, then my aspirations shall not be in vain. I hereby set forth the regulations as follows: The Daily Course: Recite the Buddha’s name for ten periods.

Dedicate nine periods to *guan* (contemplation)—the character for "reciting" (*nian*) is derived from the heart-radical, signifying that it is not merely oral; since one recites with the mind, it necessarily involves contemplative visualization. Dedicate one period to ritual repentance (*li-chan*). This must not be neglected even during the severest cold or the most intense heat.
During both the waxing and waning phases of the moon, carefully study the Four-Part Vinaya Code (*Sifen lü*). After a short interval, chant the *Fan* (Sanskrit) scriptures.

When the netting is complete, one kneels long and recites the text of the aspiration, dedicating the merit toward the Western Pure Land to meet Amitābha Buddha, as well as on the anniversaries of the births of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
(According to Master Siqui, the birth of Śākyamuni Buddha, his day of attaining enlightenment, his day of parinirvāṇa, and the day of the monks' *pravāraṇā* are also added.
Every year, during the two months of the first and twelfth lunar months, a seven-day period of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nianfo*) is commenced. On the first day of the New Year...
The renewal of things is the image [of the New Year]. The *lajie* (winter solstice) day symbolizes the impermanence of human life.

Every evening at dusk, one should prepare *shengfan* (birth-food) and recite the *Bianshi zhenyan* (Mantra for Transforming Food) forty-nine times, followed by a thousand recitations of the Buddha’s name, to provide relief for ghosts and spirits.
Each day, when reciting the Buddha’s name and receiving the fast, one should don the ritual robes and refrain from wandering about.
One must not leave the monastery to look about, nor wander idly through the streets. Exceptions may be made for the purpose of visiting a parent, a teacher, or an elder who is ill;
in such cases, a temporary leave of absence may be granted. For all other matters, such leave is strictly prohibited. When requesting leave, one must fix a specific date for its expiration.

Should one fail to return by that time, a penalty of prostrating before the incense burner shall be imposed. It is appropriate to decline visitors coming to see one off or greeting one upon arrival; when receiving honored guests, one should merely exchange brief pleasantries.
Speak a few words of the Way, with the duration of a single incense stick as the limit. If there is an occasion for questioning regarding the Dharma, this rule does not apply.
○ First: One should set aside all miscellaneous affairs. All scriptures, books, pens, ink, poems, gāthās, and writings should be placed on a high shelf and not handled again (other editions add:
"All constant temple duties are likewise exempted, nor shall their attendants be assigned"). One should not respond to external matters.
Regarding the intermediate periods of sutra recitation and repentance: even if they come to the temple, one should not permit them to participate at will.

Should it be unavoidable, they should merely recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*, perform the *Pure Land Repentance*, and engage in mindfulness of the Buddha. Within the hall, apart from the recitation of the Buddha’s name, all miscellaneous conversation is improper.
Even when necessary matters require questions and answers, these should be conducted in a low voice. When mindfulness of the Buddha becomes drowsy, one should use...
One small banner for the incense procession. We shall mutually exhort and admonish one another. When the processional banner arrives, those who do not rise shall be penalized with incense.

Those who commit a transgression and do not repent, or who persist in refusing to desist despite repeated admonitions, shall be penalized with incense. Those who lose their temper, speak crudely, or engage in mutual strife shall be penalized together.
If one person remains patient while the other is angry, the angry one shall be penalized with incense. Whenever there is a transgression, it is appropriate...
One another shall offer counsel and admonition, causing [the offender] to repent immediately; one must not allow a lapse of days, nights, or hours.

Those who enter the quarters without cause or engage in idle chatter shall be penalized with incense sticks (*xiang*). Those who do not return to the hall during periods of silence unless for essential business shall be penalized with incense sticks.

Regarding the above regulations, if any are violated, the *yuèzhòng* (Director of Affairs) shall raise the matter. Should the offender refuse to comply after being raised, they shall be expelled from the hall.

To know [the transgression] and yet fail to report it, one shall be punished equally by kneeling before a branch of incense for one period. On this day, month, and year, recorded again by the Abbot (Name).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: As for the establishment of the school of Pure Practice (*śuddhakarma*), it first began in our Eastern Land with Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu.
That Master exhorted people to abandon the *sāṃsārika* world and seek the Pure Land. His teaching held that gold and silver constitute the defilement of a stained mind.
Regarding material things: they take rank and emolument as fetters that torment the body; they take female beauty as the axe that fells their lives;
and they take fine clothing, exquisite food, fields, gardens, and houses as the pits and traps for falling into the three realms.
They pray only to escape the human world to be conceived within the nine lotuses, rejoicing in purity and loathing filth; thus, they compiled [the works of] Liu, Lei, and others—ten in total.

There were eight noble worthies who carved a lotus water-clock and performed their devotions at the six periods of the day with such intense spiritual fervor that each attained their aspirations upon death.
Since then, those who have followed their teachings and cultivated the practice of purity to be reborn in the Land of Bliss have been numerous from generation to generation.

Yet among them, there have been many who possessed the name but lacked the reality, and not a few who merely exhausted themselves in outward formalities. This remains the case down to the present day.
Since human faculties have become diluted and falsehoods arise daily, many people gather together under the pretext of the Lotus Society (*Lianshe*).
Those who falsely seek clothing and food, or where men and women mingle, often give rise to trouble; such cases occur frequently.
Therefore, those within the Lotus Society should be few rather than many. As for men and women living together in the same society, this was never seen in antiquity.

There is. It is fitting for women to practice mindfulness of the Buddha while remaining at home; they should not mingle with groups of men, thereby avoiding worldly censure and protecting the Buddha’s True Dharma—this must not be neglected.
According to the "Inscription on the Hall of Pure Practice" by Master Ansiji: "The hall is named 'Pure Practice. What is its meaning? It is simply this:
to be refined and singular, focusing one's thoughts exclusively on Amitābha. If the mind is not single-minded, then practice will [not be pure]."
Impurity consists solely of dullness and distraction; as soon as these afflictions arise, take heed, O assembly! As you pass through this gateway, you should examine yourselves at all times:
whether you are diligent or indolent. If you are indolent, you must rouse yourself with vigor; if you are diligent, you must press forward.
If you do so for the remainder of this life, you will certainly behold Amitābha. Furthermore, at Zifu Temple on Hongluoshan in Beijing, Chan Master Chewu said: "The mind..."
The mind is able to transform karma; karma is created by the mind and follows the movement of the mind.
When the mind cannot transform karma, it is bound by that karma, and the karma no longer follows the mind but instead binds the mind. Why is the mind able to transform karma?

Because when the mind is in harmony with the Path and in harmony with the Buddha, it is able to transform karma. Why is karma able to bind the mind? [Because the mind is not in harmony with the Path and the Buddha.]
The mind relies on the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and, functioning spontaneously, undergoes experience; this constitutes bondage by karma.
All present objects and all future retributions are solely induced by karma and are solely manifestations of the mind. Because they are solely induced by karma, [they are such].
When external objects and retributions arise, they all possess a fixed certainty, because karma is able to bind the mind and because [all things] are manifestations of the mind alone.
However, when external objects and retributions arise, they do not necessarily possess fixed certainty, because the mind is able to transform karma.

If, at the very moment when karma is binding the mind and external objects and retributions are appearing with fixed certainty, a person suddenly gives rise to a vast and great mind and cultivates the truth...

Practice. When the mind merges with the Buddha and the mind merges with the Way, the mind can transform karma. Thus, when the retribution of the external environment arrives, it is fixed yet not fixed.

Furthermore, when the mind can transform karma such that the arrival of environmental retribution is uncertain, if the Great Mind suddenly regresses and true practice suffers a deficiency, then karma will bind the mind; consequently, the arrival of environmental retribution is no longer uncertain.
However, karma has already been created in the past; this is beyond remedy. Fortunately, the arousal of the aspiration (*cittotpāda*) depends upon oneself;

the creation and transformation of karma do not rely on others. For example, if we now arouse the aspiration to recite the Buddha’s name, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, or contemplate the environment and its inhabitants, or uphold the Name, maintaining these thoughts in continuous succession—this is the power of our own resolve.
When mindfulness reaches its ultimate limit, the mind merges with the Buddha. Merging again and again, until that merging reaches its ultimate limit, the mind is able to transform karma.
Thus, the prior realm of Saṃsāra is transformed into Sukhāvatī, and the retribution of the womb and prison is transformed into the lotus calyx;
one then becomes a person of sovereign mastery in the Land of Bliss. If, at such a time, the mind should happen to...
However, if one loses this illumination, or suddenly gives rise to regret and retreat, failing to accord with the Buddha, then karma will be able to bind the mind;
the external objects before one will remain as they were, and the retribution received will still be that of the Saha world—suffering sentient beings.
Therefore, those among us who are resolved to transcend [saṃsāra] and seek birth in the Pure Land should be stirred by alarm and exert themselves with vigor.
Also: The Seven-Day Buddha Recitation Regulations (actually posted in the Main Hall; totaling twenty-two articles).

Now, as for the "Seven Days of the Buddha" (*butsushichi*), it was originally intended to settle the matter of birth and death. With seven days set as the period, one practices without interruption throughout the six periods of the day and night.
Beginning with the first seven days, the second, and so on up to the third and fourth weeks, the monastics and laypeople from all four directions gathered together.

At this grand assembly, fearing that indolence might easily arise and diligent effort be difficult to achieve, [I consider]: if there were no restraints, how could one urge forth one’s own body and mind?
Without a formal framework, how could one inspire the respect and faith of others? Having carefully deliberated upon these matters, I briefly set forth [these regulations].
As follows: During these seven days, you must cast aside all worldly concerns so that your efforts shall not be in vain.
It is essential that you remain single-minded and undistracted. If you can truly do this, the present moment is itself the assembly at the Lotus Pond.

At the fifth watch, upon hearing the sound of the bell, everyone shall descend from their seats together. After washing their faces, they shall enter the hall in unison to recite the Buddha’s name; do not remain lying down.

Do not rise; avoid indolence and seek only temporary ease. Once the dawn light has appeared, partake of gruel. After the meal, once you have finished chewing on the willow branch (*yángzhī*), enter the hall to recite the Buddha’s name.
Wait until one *cùn* of incense has passed, then rise and perform walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). Strike the large wooden fish drum.

When there is one remaining *cùn* of incense, return to your place and sit in recitation. When the incense is exhausted, recite with urgency for over a hundred times, striking the bell and the fish drum three times with urgency.

At the end of the session, everyone stops chanting at once. After a short while, when the tea has been finished, two strikes on the small fish-bell signal them to rise and attend to their bodily needs.
When the incense period has passed by one *cun*, the two leaders from the east and west sections stand up;

they exchange a greeting facing each other and another greeting toward the upper [altar], then slowly walk forward to take up the banner, holding it firmly with both hands, and stand facing one another.
They proceeded. After a short while, the fish led the two men along, illuminating one another as they walked so that they could not deviate or become disordered.

When it saw anyone who was drowsy, the person holding the walking banner would call out the Buddha’s name at a loud voice to awaken them and hand the banner to them; that person would then begin walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). The one who had handed over the banner would take his seat in that position.
The one who received the banner would walk while reciting the Buddha’s name to dispel sleep. In this manner, they took turns exhorting one another until—
When one cun of incense remains, the fish-shaped burner leads the way back to its original position, and the banner likewise returns to its place.

From the two sides facing each other, once the banner has been inserted into the rack, they perform a greeting and return to their positions. When the incense is finished, it is as before. One must observe the movement of the banner closely;

even if the eyes are closed, the practitioner should sit upright with the head straight, reciting along with the assembly. This may be during a period of clarity or of dullness. Or perhaps it is precisely [the moment].
When one has attained the proper state of mind, one must not give the banner; those who give it when they ought not to do so shall be punished.

If someone’s head is bowed and they are drowsy, the banner should be given to them. If a drowsy person, seeing the banner being passed to them, refuses to receive it out of anger, they shall be punished by kneeling and reciting the incense verse once.
If one receives the banner in hand and wanders about restlessly according to their own whims, they shall be punished.
Those who hold the banner and see people becoming drowsy or distracted shall be punished. When distributing incense, one must proceed in proper order;

no disordering of the sequence is permitted. Those who push forward, jostle those behind, or turn their heads and bodies about shall be punished. This applies if they are shirking their duties or seeking personal ease.
Those who hide away in the monks' quarters to engage in idle chatter shall be subject to double punishment.

Internal and external attendants, except when performing official duties, must recite the Buddha’s name as soon as they have a moment of leisure; those who gather together for idle conversation shall be punished.

Those who use various pretexts to leave the premises for aimless wandering shall be severely punished upon discovery. However, if one is unable to attend due to official business, they must inform the leaders.
One may only depart after requesting leave; violators shall be punished. When each stick of incense is finished, the person on duty shall pour tea for both sides, who shall drink it in succession.
One must not spill the dregs of the tea on the floor; violators shall be punished. Those who break cups must provide compensation.
Only after finishing the tea may one stand up; those who rise first shall be punished. For the "great evacuation" (defecation), the time is limited to one inch of incense.
The limit for the small incense stick is half an inch. When fellow practitioners enter or exit, they must not engage in idle laughter, conversing face-to-face, or whispering.

Those who violate this rule shall be penalized with an incense stick. If the sitting period exceeds two inches, the *yuèzhòng* (joyful assembly) on both sides shall conduct inspections; those who fail to attend will be held accountable.
Move that meditation cushion (pūtāna) to the front of the Buddha image. When the time arrives, have him join his palms, kneel, and recite. Once the incense is finished, the session concludes;
he shall rise to bow to the Buddha, turn to pay respects to the Abbot, and personally carry the meditation cushion back to its original place.
Beginners who are unable to sit cross-legged may instead rest their knees on a support, provided they maintain an upright and dignified posture while reciting the Buddha’s name with a clear voice.
It must be clear and distinct. It should not be too loud; if it is too loud, it will not last long. It should not be too low; if it is too low, one will fall into dullness and drowsiness.
Rather, let each syllable emerge from the lips and tongue, with the mind reciting as the mouth speaks and the ears listening.

Even while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is nothing that is not this single phrase, "Amitābha Buddha. Only in this way can you truly believe that every sound gathers and sustains the mindfulness.
The practice of gathering the mind with every thought will, after a long time, naturally become a single unified whole.
If an illness should arise within the hall, you must have faith that Amitābha Buddha is the unsurpassed King of Physicians.

If you can exert yourself without slackening, the demonic afflictions of disease will immediately recede. If you truly cannot sustain yourself and must rest, request leave from the presiding masters and others.
Next, he shall announce his leave to the entire assembly. Only after setting aside his meditation mat may he exit the hall.
He must not feign illness as an excuse to waste his pure practice. Should anyone leave the hall privately without announcing their leave, they shall be severely punished.

If there are those within the assembly whose conduct is improper or who engage in verbal disputes, thereby disturbing the community and confusing the multitude, they shall be removed from their seats and expelled from the hall.

If there is a transgression among the assembly, it shall be raised by one who gladdens the assembly. If one raises it but does not repent, they shall be penalized; those who know of it but do not raise it shall be penalized equally.
If there are those who are elderly or infirm within the assembly, they should naturally act with skillful means and compliance, and need not be bound by formal regulations.
Those who come for a brief time out of sympathetic joy while recollecting the Buddha are also not subject to these rules. After the gruel, three sticks of incense [are burned].
Use four sticks of incense for the morning snack. Use four sticks of incense for the midday meal. After the meal, use four sticks of incense for lighting.

Use six sticks of incense for the evening meal. At night, use four sticks of incense for lighting. When half of five sticks of incense have burned, one should immediately kneel upright toward the [image] and recite for about one hour.
Then, recite the names of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the oceanic assembly of bodhisattvas one hundred times each. Recite the Short Text on the Pure Land and pay homage to Amitābha.

Perform twelve prostrations to Amitābha Buddha; perform three prostrations for each of the three Bodhisattvas. Having completed the ritual of the Three Refuges and the veneration of the Patriarchs, drink tea.

After a short while, (with palms joined, walk back and forth) while reciting the visualization of the Buddha (recite the visualization with the voice, which is called "visualizing the Buddha") one thousand times. (With every sound, as if facing the Buddha before you, exert yourself with even greater diligence.

When the recitation is finished,) kneel in the *brahmāsana* posture and recite the verse of dedication. Each person then returns to their quarters to rest. Recite silently while sleeping. On subsequent days, follow this same procedure, fixing a specific time.

Wait. Do not allow for errors. On the night of the seventh, perform the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*). Recite the text for the Western Paradise. Kneel and recite the names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, burning one incense stick for each.
Perform forty-eight prostrations before the Buddha, and three prostrations for each of the three Bodhisattvas. Having completed the Three Refuges, pay respects to the Patriarchs.
Proceed to the Abbot’s quarters and prostrate three times before the *zhuchi* (abbot). Wait for the instructions to conclude, then perform prostrations of gratitude.

Having finished, each person shall return to their respective place; at the conclusion of every seven-day period, incense shall be burned for half a day. Whether sitting or reclining, all must silently recite the Buddha’s name.
One must strictly avoid idle chatter and miscellaneous talk. The second and third seven-day periods shall follow this same rule.

All mentions of "penalties" in the regulations refer to kneeling before the burning incense while reciting the Buddha’s name. This is what is meant by "falling on the ground where one stands, and rising from that very ground. However...
One should rise immediately after prostrating; one must not rise and fall repeatedly. One’s own error would be no small matter.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Although the *Jingye Tang Gui* (Regulations for the Hall of Pure Practice) and the *Foqi Guiyue* (Rules for the Seven-Day Buddha Recitation Retreat) are divided into two sections as exhortations, in their general essence they are not different;
the Buddha Recitation Retreat is simply the preparatory practice (*prayoga*). Master Siqui said: "Buddha Recitation is not a difficult matter.
What is difficult is one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*). One-pointedness is also not difficult; what is difficult is severing the root of craving. One should contemplate thus:"
This physical body is foul and impure beyond full description; within, without, and in between, there is not a single pure thing.
Since one’s own body is thus, so too is that of others. One should develop a deep sense of revulsion and ensure that a mind of attachment never arises;
instead, one should contemplate the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where all is born from lotuses without reliance on a parental womb, and where lifespan is originally without limit.
Regarding the measure: at the moment of reciting the Buddha’s name in a single thought-moment, one is immediately born through transformation within a lotus flower.
If one can practice without interruption, one will certainly be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Furthermore, it is said: "Namo Amitābha. Who would not know how to recite this?

Yet, though they recite, if their practice is not in accord with the Way, mother and child may find it difficult to see one another. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one should at all times gather this mind inward; in every thought-moment, maintain self-reflection.
Continuing: As mindfulness develops into a single expanse, by thus recollecting Amitābha, Amitābha will naturally appear.
You will certainly be reborn in the Western Land, never regressing for the rest of your life.
Preface to the Dedication of Merit for the Seven-Day Buddha Recitation Retreat I humbly submit this:

With deep blue eyes, clear and serene, the dust of the lands beholds the auspicious sign of the blue lotus; with the curling white tuft of hair between his brows, he casts the radiance of the full moon upon devas and humans.
He has extensively opened the gates of the sixty-eight vows, reaching out to every single capacity without exception, gathering and transforming beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In this category, one attains rebirth through ten recitations of the name; its wondrous response is boundless, and its compassionate conditions universally encompass all.

Thus, there is the "Announcement of the Completion of the Seven-Day Buddha-Recitation Retreat" (Foji gowen wenshu), which is proclaimed before the Buddha. We look up to your compassion and pray that you will deign to grant us your witness and discernment.

Now, according to the Great Qing Dynasty, in the [Name] Province, [Name] Prefecture, [Name] County, at [Name] Temple, we uphold the bequeathed teachings of Śākyamuni Tathāgata and carry out the practice as the presiding master of this retreat.

Pure Karma Ritual: The śramaṇa [Name], residing in [Village] Ward of [District] County under this Prefecture, has reverently prepared a vegetarian feast to make offerings to the Holy Ones and inaugurated a seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat (*buddha-śaptāha*). The presiding bhikṣu is [Name]; the participating bhikṣus are [Names];
and the upāsakas, lay believers, are [Names]. (If held at a nunnery, change "bhikṣu" to "bhikṣuṇī" and "upāsaka" to "upāsikā.")

The woman (so-and-so), together with those present at this assembly, on this day bow their heads and offer incense, single-mindedly taking refuge in the Holy Lords of the Two Lands—Amitābha and Śākyamuni—and in Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and all the great sages and worthies beneath the golden lotus seats.

We respectfully communicate our sincere intentions: for while the physical lives of the multitude differ, their mental aspirations are one; we all reflect upon being reborn during the Dharma-Ending Age.

Swept away by the surging waves of desire, they have forgotten their way home; as the time since the Sage departed grows ever more remote, they encounter his compassionate light yet remain unable to behold him.

Therefore, relying upon the monastic groves, we shall inaugurate a seven-day Buddha-recitation retreat (*buddha-śaptāha*). We aspire to achieve the essential merit of these seven days, vowing that our single mind shall remain undisturbed.

Accordingly, we select [the period from] the [blank] day of the [blank] month until the [blank] day for its conclusion. We extend invitations to the fourfold assembly, who gather like clouds at this temple to maintain the recitation.

For seven days and nights, we have recited the vast and majestic name of Amitābha Buddha, endowed with ten thousand virtues. We humbly pray that wherever the sound of the sutra reaches, the sense-bases and their objects may be purified;
and whenever the Buddha’s name is proclaimed, may merit and wisdom increase instantaneously. Whether monastic or lay, may all form the causes for the nine grades of rebirth;

whether female or male, may all aspire together to the fruits of the three ranks. Regarding such prayers and aspirations, we humbly entreat you to accept them. This petition is respectfully submitted.

I request the Three Jewels to bear witness. This is the Memorial for the Dedication of Merit of the Buddha’s Seven-Day Retreat. On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], the Abbot [Name] respectfully submits this memorial.
Regarding the meaning of the testimony, according to the *Revised Public Document for the Western Paradise*:

on the first day of the fifth month in the fifty-third year of the Qianlong era, Lu Jintang of Suzhou descended from the altar and said to his sons: "There is one matter most urgent to my own person."
No one can escape it; everyone forgets it. You should know this clearly. Before you, your four elements are light and at ease, and your spirit is strong and healthy.

Yet you never consider that one day you may lie ill upon your bed, your soul and breath scattered, unable to distinguish east from west or south from north, facing a vast and uncertain path with no firm hold—driven along by...

One revolves through the cycle of karma, suffering endlessly. Only those who have diligently cultivated pure karma throughout their lives will, at that time, see the Tathāgata personally come to welcome and guide them, so that they are born within a lotus flower, experience all manner of bliss, and enjoy an immeasurable lifespan.
For those of you, my children, who aspire to this path, you should focus on the three essentials: faith, practice, and aspiration. As for faith, it is faith in the Western [Pure Land]...
There is a Pure Land, just as this city has Chang-xu. Saha is to the east, just as this city has Lou-feng.
Since Saha is truly and substantially existent, how could the Pure Land not be truly and substantially existent?

Both reside within the perfectly luminous ocean of enlightenment; to reach them by a single thought is just like being within the same city, where one can travel from one place to another with a mere gesture.

It is possible to reach it. Once you have gained the conviction that the Pure Land can certainly be reached, you must further maintain the practice of the Buddha-remembrance method as naturally as one puts on clothes or eats food.
Wearing clothes prevents cold; eating food prevents hunger; and reciting the Buddha’s name prevents birth and death.
To believe today and not believe tomorrow does not constitute true faith. One must believe throughout one's entire life. [If] for even a single thought-moment...
However, if one does not believe, it cannot be considered true faith. From this day forward until the end of life, one must maintain faith to the very end without even a hair’s breadth of doubt;

only then is it true faith. Once one has believed that the Western Pure Land exists and that there is the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation, what benefit will mere empty words of praise bring to the cycle of birth and death? Therefore, for all who give rise to the mind of faith:
One should immediately practice in accordance with these instructions. Believe today and act today; believe tomorrow and act tomorrow.

Even the single word "aspiration" (*praṇidhāna*) is of paramount importance. Although there are certainly not a few people in the world who believe in the Buddha and recite His name, some may seek wealth and status in this life, while others may seek blessings, longevity, or rebirth as a noble person in future lives.
To remain in this body without falling away from it is to act contrary to the Buddha’s intent. The Buddha teaches you to transcend birth and death, yet you insist on entering birth and death.
The Buddha teaches you to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, yet you insist on remaining in the Sahā world.
To let one's lifelong faith drift away like water down a stream is like a farmer who sows weeds and yet expects to harvest grain.
Is there not such a principle? Therefore, those who have given rise to true faith should practice true conduct; those who practice true conduct should give rise to true vows.
Throughout this single lifetime, they must resolve never again to be born among gods or humans, but must resolutely seek birth in the Western Pure Land.
Only such mindfulness of the Buddha is in accordance with the Buddha’s words; otherwise, one will merely waste one's time in vain.
"O sons, exert yourselves!

Regarding alms-gathering (piṇḍapāta), it was practiced during the Buddha’s lifetime. The community of monks daily gathered alms by begging for food; however, this system has not yet been followed in the Eastern Lands. Therefore, [monasteries] remain as clusters..."

The monastery may have fields and gardens as its resources, or it may rely on offerings for its sustenance. Whenever winter, summer, or years of famine arrive, the abbot leads the assembly on a single alms-round (*piṇḍapāta*).
When the time arrives, the guest master (*karmadāna*), the disciplinarian (*vinayadhara*), and the administrative head (*karmika*) consult together with the abbot to determine the date.
Whether early or late in the day, after the second board has been struck, the abbot instructs his attendant to invite the providers of the offerings.
The Guest Master (Kekkatsu) prepares tea and discusses the details for the alms-round (kechien). On the day prior to the event, the Guest Hall (Kyokudō) shall post a notice (which reads as follows):

"Starting from the [day] of this month, the entire assembly of masters shall hear the bell and don their robes, proceeding together to the Great Hall to await the departure of the monks from the temple for the alms-round at [location] on [date]. Bowl-Protectors: [Name] and [Name] Notice Issued by the Guest Master: [Name]"
[The name of] the attendant carrying [the incense] (and so forth). ○ After the second board has sounded for the morning meal each day, the great bell is struck three times.
The assembly gathers in the Great Hall to burn incense and pass the incense burner. The Guest Master invites the Abbot to offer incense; the Rector recites the incense hymn.
Once the Abbot has prostrated to the Buddhas and to Vemacitra, the Attendant for Joy sounds the leading chime, and the entire assembly prostrates together to the Buddhas.
After the three prostrations are completed, the head of the assembly (ban-shou) takes the staff and walks ahead, while the rest of the group follows in order.
The attendant holds the alms bowl before the Abbot; the Abbot stands at the rear, with the staff-bearer following behind him.

The offerings are collected by the guest master (chi-ke), and the monks on both sides of the path beg for alms, walking slowly and steadily. Their deportment is dignified and orderly: when standing, they stand in unison; when walking, they walk in step.
Walk in unison; do not be out of step. If you must relieve yourself, you should first gather your robes and entrust them to a fellow practitioner.
Having relieved yourself in a secluded and private place, wash your body and rinse your hands, then immediately return to join the assembly with your robes properly arranged.

If you encounter a donor providing tea and refreshments, or if they provide the midday meal, you must maintain dignified deportment and proper order when sitting down to receive the food, so as to allow them to observe.
Those present shall give rise to a mind of reverence and cultivate the vow of joyful equanimity. Upon returning to the temple, they proceed to the main hall and stand in their usual positions.
The Rector strikes the chime, and the assembly chants the incense hymn (*xiangzan*) in unison. The Abbot offers incense and pays homage to the Buddha;

the assembly then pays three prostrations to the Buddha and to the Great Assembly of Vemacitra. Returning to the hall, the assembly partakes of fermented rice that evening, continuing until the day of completion.

This can be understood from the following example. When carrying rice back from transport, the Superintendent (Jianyuan) and the Rice Officer (Mitou) shall count the stones as they are weighed and record the number.
Once the rice has entered the granary, they shall present the tally to the Abbot and hang a notice board to inform the assembly. This is the very life-force of the monastic community;
therefore, the officials on duty must exercise careful oversight to ensure no corruption occurs that would lead to karmic error. If the monastery’s provisions are sufficient, the process shall cease.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding "begging for alms" (*piṇḍapāta*), in the Western Regions (India), there are often many monks in a single monastery; it is not possible for them all to eat together at one household.
Therefore, they must go out to beg for food according to the amount offered by various donors. Thus, it is called "dividing the alms" (*fenwei*). This refers to begging for food.
The meaning of this is seen in the "Chapter on the Two Orders" (*Liǎngxù zhāng*). Regarding the textual evidence for the provision of offerings, the commentary states:
"When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, he admonished his disciples not to accumulate surplus goods, preemptively blocking the mind of greed lest it hinder their spiritual practice.

They were to possess nothing but a single alms bowl carried at their side and three robes worn upon their bodies. Whenever it was time to eat, they would lead all their disciples to beg for food among the people, making no distinctions."
Whether pure or defiled, noble or humble, they practice and transform others with equanimity; this is the lingering tradition of the alms-round (pindapāta) established by former Buddhas.
Jiaoshan Xinghai said: "The precepts of a bhikṣu take the four parājikas and the four reliances as their foundation. Among these, the four parājikas are what must be strictly observed."
There are four reliances that should be observed. These so-called four reliances are: first, always practicing alms-gathering;
second, wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*); third, sitting under trees in forest hermitages (*araṇya*); and fourth, treating illness with medicines of putrid decay.
Anything other than alms-gathering constitutes living by wrong livelihood. Subsequently, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, for those consisting of four or more monks...
Regarding their dwelling: by opening the acceptance of impure objects, one may rely on pure food within the Sangha instead of begging for alms;

by residing together in a monastery, one may rely on shelter under a tree instead of living in the open air; by accepting robes offered by donors, one may rely on rag-robes instead of wearing discarded rags;
and by receiving medicine provided as a long-term gift, one may rely on medicinal herbs instead of decaying substances. Thus, Yunqi Zhuhong opened the way for all four reliances.
Master Chi said: "In the time of the Buddha, wandering for alms was the very custom of the noble families. In the monasteries of this eastern land, it can no longer be practiced;
it is not that we dare to let it fall into ruin, but rather that it is driven by the exigencies of the times. Now, cities are filled with clamor and dust, where men and women live together in crowds;
mountain forests are solitary and still, where monks practice pure cultivation. To divide these two is to attain their respective purposes; to conjoin them is to create confusion. Furthermore,"
Within the assembly, dragons and snakes are intermingled; as such, it is easy for incidents to arise that would, in turn, tarnish one’s pure reputation.

Therefore, from ancient times, venerable masters have dwelt amidst cold crags and remote ravines, tilling the soil and weeding the fields, sustaining themselves on a single meal per day, free from other deluded thoughts.

In both cities and mountain monasteries, there are likewise those specifically assigned to solicit alms, so that the assembly does not have to travel on foot every day, thereby neglecting their spiritual practice.
Although this is not prescribed by the Buddha’s regulations, it accords with the Buddha’s spirit. As for the annual practice of going on alms-round once, this merely preserves the traditional model.
As for wandering monks who travel from place to place, they are certainly not hindered by doing so alone.
Regarding the ritual for begging alms, Yi-run said: "The abbots of the monastic forests strictly adhere to the Buddha’s regulations.

I shall now cite one instance of those who constantly practice the carrying of the alms bowl, using it as an illustration for the rest. During the Kangxi era, Chan Master Nan-yuan Xìn resided at Xīfāng Temple in Wéiyáng. For thirty years he led the assembly;
he did not visit officials, nor did he attend weddings or funerals, nor did he engage in worldly affairs. He did nothing but..."

The Master’s way was one of total ease. Throughout both winter and summer, he wore but a single robe; through cold and heat, he carried but a single bowl. He practiced begging for alms with equanimity, making this his constant routine.

Even after reaching an age beyond eighty years, he never once slackened for even a single day. Aside from his recorded sayings (*yulu*), there exists another work circulating in the world titled *Verses on Alms-Begging* (*Tuo-bo-ji*) in one fascicle.
Herein I record ten of these verses, so that students of future generations may understand the conduct of our predecessors.

"The Buddha’s ritual protocols still remain," they say. △ The Golden Immortal [the Buddha] established that one should only hold the alms bowl; I emulate him to guide my followers through this non-dual mechanism.

The Way is fundamentally without transmission—who can understand how to succeed it? The moon pierces the bottom of the pond as the ripples swell. Trimming the weeds and donning the black robes, I do not shrink from toil.
Emulating the "imitation of the beauty" (p'ing), I beg for alms and admire solitary loftiness. Now, old age and illness have caused me to decline.
Aspiration: The nine tripods and single strands of silk await you; naturally begging for food, how could this be mere poverty? Trailing through water and mud, one remains unstained by dust.
The lotus in the alms bowl is no ordinary herb; as for the pupils in one’s eyes—who are they?
Do not feel shame for meager merit and little talent; with a single bowl for the rest of one’s life, one does not stray from the mundane world. This decaying form follows conditions as it may.

Maintain your station. There is no "eternal spring" beyond the kalpas; on the long street, the single bowl treats all alike, whether kin or stranger. Whether moving or still, proceed slowly to inquire into existence and non-existence.
Rich or poor, follow conditions as they arise to plant the seeds of merit. When the function is perfected and the fruit is full, it takes but a moment.
Do not say that holding the bowl frequently throughout the year is a burden; a single grain of rice can extinguish the madness of many kalpas. In the bustling marketplace, there is no entanglement.

Dust settles of its own accord; amidst leisure, one feels carefree while observing others' busyness. Begging for food among the people, how could one dread the toil? Arrogance and pride are gradually eliminated with each passing moment.
Though affairs are many, the principle remains still as one holds only the alms bowl. A hundredfold is the family tradition; the power of one's vow is abundant.
In the bustling market, the ground is freshly cleared and slick as oil. With single-minded focus on seeking alms, all sorrow has vanished. May the Buddha’s teachings circulate far and wide.
Restraining oneself without remainder, one destroys evil and subdues Māra through the freedom of faith; begging for food, one propagates the Great Teaching and achieves great wisdom.
This matter of the gate and courtyard relies upon a steadfast mind; it is not transmitted through the power of mere practice throughout the three realms.

Who would believe that the ancestral Way and its guiding principles are so profound? Wisdom has never come from any other place; the single bowl passed down in the family is free from doubt and suspicion. That which is known—
All afflictions have been completely extinguished; this is my fellow practitioner, certainly not at odds with me.
Question: Does begging for alms not hinder the practice of Zen? Answer: It is precisely because of Zen practice that the ritual of begging for alms is manifested;
how could there be any hindrance? Long ago, one day the World-Honored One commanded Ānanda: "The time for the meal is approaching; you should enter the city and carry the bowl. Ānanda responded.
"Yes, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "Since you are carrying this bowl, you should follow the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past.
Ānanda then asked, "What is the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past? The Buddha called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes. The World-Honored One said, "Carry the bowl and go.
Based on this, it is clear that the Buddha used the essence of Chan as the ritual for begging for alms. Now...
For those who are resolute in their pursuit of the Way, if they can truly observe and practice these rules when receiving alms, such that their conduct is identical to that of the Buddha’s time,
what obstacle could there be to their Zen cultivation? *Shiyi* (Supplement).
Whenever the monastic community finds lost property, they shall immediately inform the Administrative Head (Jiānyuàn) to have it deposited in the storehouse for safekeeping.

A signboard marked with the two characters "Found Property" (Shíyí) shall be hung so that the owner may recognize it. Should anyone find lost property and fail to deliver it to the storehouse, they shall be severely punished and expelled from the monastery.
All owners of lost items shall affix a ticket, upon which they write: "I, [Name], on [Date], lost [Item]."

It is like seeing a "Lost and Found" sign; one goes to the storehouse, verifies the item clearly, and returns it. If anyone falsely claims ownership, they shall be severely punished and expelled from the monastery.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding "lost and found," when someone happens to pick up discarded items, they are returned to the storehouse and a sign is hung.

This is merely a temporary measure and not intended for long-term suspension. Lately, however, in monastic communities, [signs] have been permanently hung on the rear pillars on both sides of the dining hall.
To affix the characters "Recovered Lost Items" (Shiyi) is highly inappropriate. It should be corrected by affixing the characters "Remaining Inventory" (Yuxu).

This is because the Buddha’s precept against stealing dictates that not even a single blade of grass or a single object shall be taken if it has not been given; if one were to take recovered lost items for private possession, this would constitute taking what has not been given.
This also constitutes a violation of the precept against stealing, as it fosters the poison of greed and contravenes the Buddha’s regulations.
Even the gentlemen of Confucianism and Daoism would not accept wealth acquired through unrighteous means; how much more so for a monastic who picks up lost items, thereby increasing their own greed?

For this reason, one should return such items to the treasury and hang a sign there, so that others may know of them. The *Yunqi Chongxing Lu* states: During the Sui dynasty, the monk Fushang once relied upon [the community] in Yizhou.
He stayed overnight at Jingde Temple. It was said that he would sit by the roadside to recite the scriptures, and people passed on his reputation as "Jietuo" (Vimukti).
At that time, Zhao Zhongshu, the Regional Inspector of Lingzhou, heard of this and went there specifically to test him. Riding his horse past the monk, he feigned dropping some cash coins.

The monk continued reciting the scripture as usual, appearing as if he had not even noticed them. After they had gone a considerable distance, Zhongshu sent someone to retrieve the money; the monk likewise [remained unmoved].
He paid no heed. After a short while, he turned back and asked the monk, "There were strings of coins on the ground; when you saw someone taking them away, why did you not stop him?
The monk replied, "They were not my property; why would I falsely claim them? Xu dismounted, prostrated himself, and departed full of admiration.

(Appendix) Regulations for the Hall of Reducing Practice (also known as the Nirvana Hall; in the Western Regions it is called the Court of Impermanence; colloquially referred to as the Infirmary). There are fifteen articles in total. This hall was established to accommodate the sick. Because sentient beings are attached to worldly things, they remain unaware until death; thus, Buddhism provides a means to shift their focus. 1. This hall is established to provide lodging for those who are ill. Due to the greed and attachment of sentient beings, they fail to realize [the nature of life] until death approaches. Buddhism therefore provides this place for them to be moved there. 2. When a patient arrives at the gate, the attendant shall immediately notify the *shangzuo* (abbot) and the *weina* (precentor). The *shangzuo* shall assign a monk to assist with the patient’s care. The *weina* shall oversee the distribution of food and medicine. 3. The patient’s bedding and clothing must be kept clean and orderly. The attendant shall ensure that the patient’s personal effects are not lost or damaged. 4. The patient’s meals shall be provided according to the monastery’s standard rations. If the patient requires special dietary adjustments, the *weina* shall arrange for them accordingly. 5. If the patient’s condition worsens and they require assistance with bathing or changing clothes, the attendant shall promptly summon the monks to provide help. 6. The patient’s room shall be kept quiet and free from noise. No one shall enter or leave without permission. 7. If the patient passes away, the attendant shall inform the *shangzuo* and the *weina*. The body shall be washed and dressed in clean robes. The *weina* shall organize the funeral rites in accordance with the monastic rules. 8.

All offerings and gifts received on behalf of the deceased shall be recorded and managed by the *weina*. 9. The attendant shall ensure that the patient’s final wishes are fulfilled. If the patient has specific instructions regarding burial or cremation, these shall be carried out as requested. 10. The attendant shall maintain a record of the patient’s medical expenses and other expenditures. 11. If the patient dies and leaves behind property or valuables, these shall be inventoried and reported to the *shangzuo*. The proceeds shall be used for the funeral expenses or distributed according to the deceased’s will. 12. The attendant shall ensure that the patient’s room is cleaned and tidied after their passing. 13. Monks who have been assigned to care for the sick shall serve for a fixed period. Upon completion, they shall report back to the *shangzuo*. 14. If the patient’s condition improves and they wish to return to their original quarters, the *shangzuo* shall arrange for their transfer. 15. These regulations are intended to ensure that the sick receive proper care and that the deceased are treated with dignity. All members of the community shall observe these rules with diligence.
This causes one to realize that impermanence is approaching, prompting the arousal of mindfulness and a vigorous awareness of one's transgressions, so that one may diligently practice.
Those who dwell in this hall should reflect that human life is impermanent and as brief as a breath; if even the healthy are thus, how much more so the sick?

Furthermore, one should contemplate this body: the four elements are no longer in harmony, the hundred bones are about to disintegrate, food and drink gradually diminish, and medicine loses its efficacy.
One relies on bedding for excrement and urine, groaning upon the pillow and mat. This is like a fish swimming within a cauldron, suddenly being scorched and consumed;
or like a lamp before the wind, extinguished in an instant. Thus, know that this body will not last long and must inevitably enter the gate of death; the path ahead is vast and obscure.
Vast and boundless—where, in the end, does one go? If you have already accomplished your own task, there is no need for haste. If this is not yet the case, seek the Pure Land early;
resolve to be reborn there, relinquish all worldly attachments, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. There are specific regulations for this, which are set forth below:
In the hall, those with minor illnesses shall occupy long beds, while those with serious illnesses shall occupy single beds. Should these arrangements be violated:

Punishment. When a patient lowers the curtain, it is to avoid the wind and conceal their infirmity; one who violates this is a shameless person, and furthermore, they will suffer from cold that is difficult to treat.
Those attending the patient must stand outside the lowered curtain. For those with terminal illnesses who enter the hall, incense and candles must be prepared before the Buddha.
The Prior, the Secretary, the Rear Hall Official, and the Rector shall escort them in. Once the patient’s final instructions have been read aloud, [the proceedings continue].

One shall immediately record the accounts on wooden tablets. If one records them without following the prescribed format or arbitrarily increases or decreases entries, one shall be penalized. If a patient does not wish to have their account recorded, they shall not be assigned a bed.
If the illness is minor, no wooden tablet account need be kept; instead, incense and candles shall simply be offered before the Buddha, which the Superintendent of the Monastery shall deliver.

The Hall Attendant for the Sick must be a person who is robust, sincere, and compassionate. He shall maintain a register, recording that on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month, [Name] entered the hall;
subsequently, he records that on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month, [Name] recovered and left the hall, or passed away. If these records are lost, a penalty shall be imposed.
The hall should be swept and cleaned at all times, and the clothing of the patients should be washed as needed.
Regarding the administration of medicine, one must pay careful attention to its preparation through decoction; it must not be treated with negligence or indolence.

If there are only one or two patients in the infirmary, the incense-lighter shall personally attend to them. If there are more, the Guest Hall shall issue a general summons for those who have developed the resolve to care for the sick.

Should no one respond after three such requests, the administrative officers shall assign the duty by rotation through the various quarters, with shifts changing every three days, unless the patient makes a specific request otherwise.
Those who provide funds to hire others are permitted to do so. Among the monastic community, those who possess clear understanding of medical principles shall be appointed as attendants.

Those who lack such understanding yet prescribe medicine recklessly shall be penalized; those who cause harm to others shall be expelled from the monastery; and those who are greedy for profit shall be expelled.

Regarding the medicinal decoctions, food, and drink required by the sick, if the storekeeper, the head cook, or the director of the kitchen, being stingy, refuses to provide them, they shall be punished.

Penalties shall be imposed for those who fail to grant what is rightfully due or for those who, out of private bias, treat others with partiality or unfairness; such individuals shall be censured before the assembly.
When a person with a terminal illness enters the hall, they should immediately entrust their final affairs and relinquish all worldly attachments, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, in attending to the seriously ill, two or three people must take turns, remaining by their side day and night without departing, even when going out to work on the slopes or elsewhere.

They shall also be exempted. If one is approaching the end of life, one should immediately notify the Guest Hall (*kètáng*). The guest master shall then dispatch several people to recite the Buddha’s name to see the deceased off.

Furthermore, following the *Anityatā-sūtra* (The Sutra on Impermanence) from the Tripiṭaka, the final rites for the end of life are prepared. In accordance with the Buddha's regulations, the deceased monk changes into pure robes.
At the time of entering the coffin, at the time of cremation (*tápí*), and at the time of entering the stupa, *vimala-mantra* sand is scattered inside in all cases. It shall not be otherwise.
One may forget this; however, one should beforehand request eminent monks to recite the mantra. It is best to do so many times;
at the very least, one thousand and eighty recitations. The mantra is: Oṃ vīmukhe vilocane mahā-maudgalyāyani.
*Bhāṭṭama / Avavara / Parayata ya hūṃ.* According to the scriptural text, by sprinkling sand empowered with this mantra upon the corpse, the deceased shall obtain inconceivable benefit.
Those who are mildly ill should remain in seclusion, recollecting the Buddha;

if they do not know how to preserve their health and instead wander about outside engaging in many affairs, they must leave the hall. [The same applies to] the sick and the hall master... and so forth.
As a caregiver, do not loathe or despise impurities. Do not act contrary to the patient’s wishes, thereby causing their illness to worsen.
Do not leave the bedside for long, leaving those who seek assistance unheeded. Do not harbor a greedy or deceitful mind, nor create difficulties by attempting to defraud them of their property.
Even if the patient becomes vexatious or troublesome, do not give rise to anger or aversion; instead, single-mindedly perform meritorious deeds and do not crave the patient's condition.
When people offer their thanks, one must know that among the eight fields of merit, nursing the sick is foremost. One must serve with joyful diligence.

Whenever a patient’s illness is severe, there will inevitably be foul odors; therefore, one should use mugwort leaves, *cang-zhu* (Atractylodes), pine needles, cypress leaves, and the like, applying them over a gentle, low-temperature fire (*wen-huo*) to produce a slight smoke, so as not to cause harm to others.
This applies to traveling monks (*yun-shui seng*) and those from other locations.

When someone arrives bringing the sick monk’s belongings, the Guest Hall (Kektang) shall verify their provenance; only when it is clear shall they be admitted. Immediately, a board-register (banjang) shall be written and a separate ledger shall be kept.

Regarding the funeral rites for a deceased monk, beginning from the board-register of his terminal illness and ending with his placement on the ancestral altar (jeodang), all procedures are found in the chapter on the Former Abbot;
these should be applied with appropriate adjustments as needed. [Date] [Note: The original text contains a placeholder for the date.]
Recorded again by the Abbot [Name]. The Commentary on the Meaning states:
Formerly, the Layman Chao Ran (Zhao Lingjun) composed the "Record of the Hall for Contemplating Practice" at Fahua Temple on Mount Nanyue, saying:
"Among all sufferings, the suffering of illness is the most profound; among the cultivation of merit, nursing the sick..."
This is the foremost [virtue]. Therefore, the ancients regarded illness as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and taught people that nursing the sick constitutes a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra).
Nowadays in the monasteries, whenever anyone falls ill, they are sent to the Hall for Reflection and Reform;

this is not only intended so that they may cultivate introspection and reform their conduct to recover from the illness, but also so that, amidst the stillness of night and the solitary lamp, they may investigate the Great Matter (mahā-vastu). How could it be otherwise?

How futile this is! On one hand, the hall master is appointed to oversee medicines and prescriptions; on the other, the monastery's permanent assets are dedicated to ensure that all necessities are provided.
This was the regulation established by the Buddhas of the past, yet in recent times it has not been so. The sick do not reflect upon their own faults and instead harbor further afflictions;

consequently, the hall master exists in name only while his duties are neglected, or he becomes resentful and disdainful. Meanwhile, the monastery’s permanent assets are squandered for immediate daily expenses.
If they do not provide care and comfort at all, minor illnesses will thereby turn grave, and grave illnesses will lead to death—is this not tragic?

Therefore, the permanent administrative officers and others should understand that nursing the sick is a field of merit; through compassion and skillful means, they should pull others from suffering and restore them to life.

As for the patient, they should clarify the law of cause and effect, examine themselves, and reflect upon their transgressions; the very moment the mind of repentance arises is [the beginning of liberation].
The vital energy of life. Once the mind is clear and serene, the illness will naturally subside.

Furthermore, at times when the head aches and the brow feels feverish, or when one cries out in grievance and suffering, investigate closely and silently: who is it that suffers this illness? Since no person is to be seen, from where does the illness come?
When both person and illness are forgotten, what is it, then? Even if you can perceive this clearly, it is precisely at such a moment that you should act.
He shall rest. Furthermore, within the regulations, regarding the scattering of *vīraja* (holy dust) over a deceased monk, the Sūtra states:
"By means of this mantra, one empowers the earth and sand and scatters it upon the body [of the deceased] as well as the foundation of the stūpa.
If that deceased person is in an evil realm, they shall immediately obtain light and a body, whereby all karmic retributions for their sins are eliminated, and their suffering body [is transformed]."
"Born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss," and so forth.

[This is] appended to the *Caturvargika-vinaya* regarding the care of the sick. The Buddha said: "From this day forward, one should attend to the sick; one should act as a caregiver for the sick. If one wishes..."

Those who wish to make offerings to me should first offer them to the sick. Even when encountering members of the fivefold assembly of renunciants on the road who are ill, the Buddha ordained that all seven groups of followers must go to visit them.
If one neglects them and does not visit, one incurs an offense. This is truly because the four elements are difficult to harmonize and past karma is difficult to exhaust;
having abandoned the secular life to leave home, one wanders alone and sleeps solitary, where poverty and illness converge. There is no...
If one does not provide mutual care for those who serve as attendants, where can their lives be entrusted? Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If one encounters a sick person among the five groups of renunciants on the road, one should immediately seek a vehicle to carry them and provide them with offerings according to the Dharma, even until the time of their death."
They should likewise be cremated or buried; they must not be abandoned. All those who attend to the sick should always speak with them kindly and never transmit malicious words.
This is because at the time of death, many signs of evil karma appear, and the dying person is unable to resolve their mind to cast them aside.
Therefore, those attending the sick must employ skillful means and use tactful, persuasive speech to lead them to recite the Buddha’s name. If they are unable to do so...
Make sounds; however, simply bring them to mind, ensuring that these thoughts continue in succession without a single moment’s pause.

Relying on the power of this merit, create the cause for rebirth in the Pure Land. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "If one performs wholesome deeds from birth but harbors evil thoughts at the time of death..."

If one has already been reborn in the evil realms and committed evil deeds, yet at the moment of death gives rise to a wholesome thought and is reborn in the heavens, one should further take a scripture and an image—(the scripture being the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and the image being an image of Amitābha)—to the bedside of the patient.
One should write the titles of the scripture and the image and speak to them, instructing them to open their eyes and behold them, so as to cause them to awaken.
To care for the sick in this manner brings forth vast merit.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: According to the *Jātaka-nidāna-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Origin of Births), the twenty-sixth discourse in the section on Illnesses, it is said:
"In the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden, there was a sick bhikṣu who was all alone, lacking food, clothing, and medicine.
Unable to rise or move about, filth and excrement flowed from him as he lay upon them. He looked in the four directions, but there was no one to come and rescue him."
At that time, Ānanda saw him and went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha immediately went in person to the sick bhikṣu’s location and asked him:
“Now that you have fallen ill, do you have anyone to attend to you, or medicine, or bedding? The sick bhikṣu replied to the Buddha: “I am alone and without anyone;
I have no food, clothing, or medicine. My home is very far away. The Buddha said: “While you were strong and healthy...”
At that time, [the Buddha] looked at him with concern and asked whether he was ill. He replied, "No.
The Buddha said, "When you were strong and healthy, you did not look after others nor inquire after their illnesses; who then shall look after you? Good and evil have their counterparts;
sin and merit have their retributions. Kindness is reciprocated, while righteousness is severed by neglect. The Buddha supported him up, wishing to...
[The Buddha] washed [him] with water. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wished to bathe him. The Buddha said, "You dwell in the fragrance and purity of the heavens;
how can you rescue and wash this defiled and turbid sick man? Śakra replied, "The Buddha is the savior of all beings throughout the ten directions.
Since he possesses such perfected merit, he still attends to the sick; how much more so should I, whose karma of sin and merit is not yet severed, not cultivate merit?"
Yes. At that time, the Buddha washed his hands, and the Heavenly Emperor poured water over him. He was laid back down again and administered medicine; immediately he was cured.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the Way at once. The World-Honored One spoke in verse:
