He sighed with deep sympathy as if the illness were his own, inquiring after him morning and evening, even going so far as to personally prepare his food and medicine;
he would not give him food until he had tasted it himself. Whenever the weather grew slightly cold, he would pat the man’s back and ask, "Are you not wearing too few clothes? Or when the season...

During the summer, he observed their appearance and said, "Is it not too hot? If they were unfortunate enough to die, he would not inquire whether the monastery had sufficient funds, but would instead perform the funeral rites with full ceremony.

If an administrator made excuses for lack of resources, Gao'an scolded him, saying, "In the past, Baizhang established the *changzhu* (monastic estate) for the sake of the elderly and the infirm; do you not grow old or die? Master Yunqi Lian said: "The Sūtra..."

The eight kinds of fields of merit are enumerated, yet nursing the sick is foremost. Is it not because monastics have no home, wandering solitary upon lakes and seas, and being alone in their suffering from illness that they are truly objects of compassion?
As the master of this monastery, if you do not attend to me when I am ill, how can you claim to be compassionate?
"To die and not have one’s funeral rites performed by me—how could this be the Way of compassion? All who serve as abbots should strive for themselves so as to encourage others.
*The Mirror for the Assembly* (Composed by Master Jiaochao Ze).
In compiling these pure regulations, the assembly is taken as the foundation; the remaining eight sections all arise from this. Therefore, at the end of this volume, their significance is summarized.

Now, when the two cassias cast their shade and a single flower manifests its auspiciousness, from that moment on, the establishment of the monastic groves (seng-lin) was fundamentally intended for the sake of the Saṃgha.
Thus, it is to instruct the Saṃgha that the elders (zhǎng-lǎo) were appointed, and to serve as models for the Saṃgha that they were established.

There is the *shouzuo* (head seat), who bears the responsibilities for the community of monks; therefore, there is the *jianyuan* (superintendent), who harmonizes the community of monks; therefore, there is the *weina* (rector), who provides offerings for the community of monks;

therefore, there is the *dianzuo* (steward), who performs labor for the community of monks; therefore, there is the *zhisui* (year-steward), who manages the income and expenditure for the community of monks;

therefore, there is the *kutou* (storekeeper), who oversees the treasury for the community of monks; therefore, there is the *shuji* (secretary), who handles calligraphy and correspondence for the community of monks; and there is the one who guards for the community of monks.
Because of the holy teachings, there is the Librarian (*zangzhu*). Because of welcoming and attending to donors for the sake of the assembly of monks, there is the Guest Master (*zhike*).

Because of inviting and summoning [guests] for the sake of the assembly of monks, there is the Attendant (*shizhe*). Because of guarding the robes and bowls for the sake of the assembly of monks, there is the Dormitory Master (*liaozhu*).

Because of providing and serving medicinal decoctions for the sake of the assembly of monks, there is the Hall Master (*tangzhu*). Because of washing and laundering for the sake of the assembly of monks, there is the Bath Master (*yuzhu*) and the Water Head (*shuitou*). For...

To protect the community of monks from the cold, there are those who manage the charcoal stoves and hearth-stoves. To solicit provisions for the community of monks, there are the fundraisers (*huazhu*).

To perform manual labor for the community of monks, there are the estate managers (*zhuangzhu*), the gardeners (*yuantou*), and the millers (*motou*). To cleanse and maintain the quarters for the community of monks, there are the sanitation officers (*jingtou*).
To provide service and attend to the needs of the community of monks, there are all the lay-attendants (*zhengren*). Thus, the conditions for practicing the Way are fully provided in every respect.
The requisites for sustaining the body are spontaneously provided in a hundred forms; all affairs are free from anxiety, and one directs the single mind toward the Way.

Most noble among those in the world and most leisurely beyond mundane things, pure and non-active, the Sangha is supreme. Reflecting upon the efforts of many people, how could one not recognize this kindness and repay it?
By attending at dawn and requesting instruction at dusk, never wasting a moment of time, one repays the elders. Thus is the distinction between the honorable and the humble.

To maintain order and conduct oneself with composure is how one repays the Chief Seat (Śayanāsana). To comply with external regulations and laws while internally adhering to the rules and discipline is how one repays the Administrative Head (Karmadāna).
To dwell together in the six harmonies, blending like water and milk, is how one repays the Rector (Karmadāna).

One should accept this food in order to accomplish the work of the Path; thus is one repaying the *diànzuò* (the kitchen steward). One should dwell peacefully in the monastic quarters and cherish the communal utensils;
thus is one repaying the *zhìsuì* (the storekeeper). One must not violate even a hair’s breadth of the property held in common; thus is one repaying the *kùtóu* (the storekeeper).
One should not take up a pen with one’s hand, but focus the mind solely on the work of the Path; thus is one repaying the *shūjì* (the secretary). With bright windows and a clean desk...

Illuminating the mind with the ancient teachings is how one repays the Librarian. Concealing one's brilliance and hiding one's traces, refraining from socializing and accompanying others, is how one repays the Guest Master.
Having a constant place of residence and arriving first when requested for duties is how one repays the Attendant.

Carrying only a single flask and a single bowl, dwelling among the community like a mountain, is how one repays the Dormitory Master. It is better to suffer the affliction of illness than to neglect the provision of gruel and medicine as appropriate.
To repay the Hall Master: one should move with lightness and composure, remaining silent and still, never neglecting the cause of water. To repay the Bath Master and the Water Head:
one should maintain silence and keep one’s hands clasped in reverence, withdrawing oneself and yielding to others. To repay the Charcoal Head and the Stove Head:

one should reflect upon one’s own virtuous conduct and feel self-reproach for being worthy of offerings. To repay the Fundraiser: one should calculate the amount of labor expended and measure the distance from which the provisions have come.
Thus, one repays the garden master, the miller, and the head cook by drawing water and managing the logistics; this is how one repays the *jingtou* (purifier).
One repays the *jingren* (attendants) by personally cherishing their labor, being broad-minded and easy to follow, and being simple and easy in one's tasks.
Consequently, within the monastic groves, the path of practice is ever renewed; those of the highest capacity achieve completion in a single lifetime, while those of middling ability—
To nurture the holy embryo: even when one has not yet realized the source of the mind, one does not waste time in vain;
such a person is a true jewel among monks, a field of merit for the world, and a bridge and raft for the final age, destined to ultimately realize the supreme fruit of the two-fold adornment.

If, however, the monastic groves are not well-ordered and the Wheel of Dharma does not turn, this is not what an elder should do for the sake of the assembly. If the three karmas are not harmonized and the four modes of deportment...

If one is not solemn, it is not the way for the Head Seat (shouzuo) to lead the assembly. If the capacity to accommodate others is not broad and the heart that loves the assembly is not profound, it is not the way for the Chief Administrator (jianyuan) to protect the assembly.
Thus, those who practice the Way will find no peace, and those who ruin the community will not be expelled.

If the *karmadāna* does not harmonize the assembly, he fails in his duty as a *karmadāna*. If the six flavors are not refined and the three virtues are not pure, he fails in his duty as a *sthavira* (abbot) to serve the assembly.
If the quarters are not maintained and the utensils are not provided, he fails in his duty as the *varṣopeta* (steward) to settle the assembly.

If he hoards the permanent property of the monastery and embezzles from the monks, he fails in his duty as the *koṭṭhāgārika* (treasurer) to provide for the assembly. If his calligraphy is not skillful...

If characters are torn or illegible, it does not serve the purpose of a record for adorning the assembly. If the desks and tables are not kept in order and clamor and distraction do not cease, it does not serve the purpose of a library keeper to assist the assembly.
If one hates the poor and loves the wealthy, or values the laity while slighting the monastics, it does not serve the purpose of a guest master to support the assembly.
If etiquette is not respectful and the order between the honorable and the humble is lost, it does not serve the purpose of an attendant to facilitate the assembly.
If one is not diligent in maintaining order and not careful in providing protection, one does not fulfill the role of a *liáozhǔ* (cell master) who dwells among the assembly.

If one is unskilled in serving others and causes distress to the sick, one does not fulfill the role of a *tángzhǔ* (hall master) who should show compassion to the community. If hot water and broth are insufficient, or if the temperature is improperly regulated, [the hall master fails in his duty].
If the bath master does not provide the water supply, he cannot purify the assembly. If the preparations are incomplete, the multitude will harbor restless thoughts.
If the incense burner master or charcoal master does not provide warmth for the assembly; if one is unjust in handling wealth or fails to exert full effort in service;
if the grounds master, garden master, or miller master leaves resources untapped or fails to fulfill their duties—then they do not serve the assembly as intended.
To represent the assembly, one must eliminate negligence and ensure all conditions are met; this is how a *śikṣādattaka* (purifier) serves the community.
If prohibitions are not heeded and commands are not carried out, this is not how a *śramaṇera* (novice/purifier) obeys the community.

If the monks themselves treat their teachers with contempt and the Dharma with arrogance, acting according to their own whims and following external conditions, this is not how they repay their elders. If their sitting and reclining are irregular, and their coming and going...
To act with discord is not the way to repay the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera). To hold the royal law in contempt and disregard the monastic community is not the way to repay the Steward (Karmadāna).
For superiors and subordinates to be at odds and for strife to become entrenched is not the way to repay the Rector (Karmadāna).

To covet fine delicacies and disparage coarse food is not the way to repay the Cook (Mahānasa). To be heedless regarding one’s dwelling and daily requisites—[is not the way to repay the Administrator].

To fail to honor the anniversary of the founder’s passing is not the way to repay the founder. To be greedily attached to gain and offerings while showing no concern for the monastery’s permanent assets is not the way to repay the steward.
To delight in fiddling with brush and ink and to run wild with literary compositions is not the way to repay the secretary.
To treat the sutras and vinaya with contempt and to study secular texts is not the way to repay the librarian. To accompany worldly scholars and form intimate ties with them...
To treat a noble guest with such neglect is not the way to repay a host. To forget an invitation and trouble the messenger repeatedly is not the way to repay an attendant.
To damage communal utensils and store them carelessly, thereby inviting theft, is not the way to repay the head of the quarters.
To be prone to anger and lacking in joy, thus failing to accord with the conditions of illness, is not the way to repay the hall master. To let buckets and ladles make noise while using water...

To lack discipline is not the way to repay the bath master (*yùzhǔ*). To crave warmth for oneself and hinder others is not the way to repay the charcoal master (*tànzhǒu*), who serves as the head of the furnace.
To neglect spiritual cultivation while complacently receiving offerings is not the way to repay the patron (*huàzhǔ*).
To eat one's fill all day long without applying the mind to practice is not the way to repay the steward (*zhuāngzhǔ*) or the garden master (*yuánzhǒu*).
To spit and vomit upon the walls and leave the latrine in such a state of disarray is not how one repays the *jingtou* (sanitation head).

To employ harsh tones and violent gestures, issuing commands without moderation, is not how one repays the *jingren* (sanitation attendant). The above points set forth the essential texts, yet they do not fully encompass the regulations for both the ordinary and the sage.
I only wish that you would discard the shortcoming and follow the excellence, together accomplishing the affairs of those who have left the household life. It is my hope that the Lion...
Within the caves, all have become lions; beneath the sandalwood groves, there is nothing but sandalwood. May this latter five-hundred-year period once again behold the assembly on Vulture Peak.
You should know that the rise and decline of the Dharma depends upon the monastic community. The Sangha is the field of merit.

One must accord them with the respect they deserve. If the Sangha is honored, the Dharma is honored; if the Sangha is slighted, the Dharma is slighted. Once internal protection is strict, external protection will naturally be diligent.
Even if the master who provides the meals flourishes for a single term, or the administrative officers of the monastery happen to hold power for a brief period—

One should always treat one’s fellow practitioners with respect and must not arrogantly exalt oneself. If one is conceited and self-important, treating private matters as public affairs, all things are impermanent;
how could such a state endure? Once one returns to the assembly, what face will there be to show? Cause and effect do not err; it is difficult to evade them.
Now, as monks are the sons of the Buddha, our right to offerings is no different from that of others; whether in heaven or among men, all...
This is what is revered. For two thousand years, the World-Honored One’s legacy has provided shade and cover for us, his descendants.
Even a single portion of the merit within the light of his white tuft of hair is inexhaustible in its enjoyment; one should know only to serve the assembly and need not worry about poverty.

Since there is no distinction between ordinary and sage within the Sangha, and they universally assemble from the ten directions, once it is called a "temple of all quarters" (caitya), everyone has a share. How can one falsely give rise to discrimination and treat visiting monks with contempt?

In the *danguo liao* (i.e., the *yunshui tang*), one stays temporarily for three mornings and receives offerings with full ceremony. When seeking a meal in the Sangha Hall, one is provided for with an impartial mind.
If even lay guests are welcomed with such hospitality, how could the monastic community fail to provide care?

If one possesses a boundless heart, there will naturally be inexhaustible blessings. When the gates of the Sangha are harmonious and those above and below are of one mind, though there may be mutual strengths and weaknesses, all shall be resolved.

They cover one another over, ensuring that the family’s disgrace and corruption do not reach the ears of outsiders. Although this does no harm to worldly affairs, it ultimately diminishes the respect and veneration of others.
It is like the worms within a lion’s body that eat the flesh of the lion itself; this is something neither celestial Māras nor external paths can destroy.
If you wish for the wind of the Way not to fall and for the Sun of the Buddha to shine forever bright, [you must act with vigor].
The radiance of the Patriarchal realm; it supplements the sagely transformation of the Imperial Dynasty. I pray that this writing may serve as a mirror for reflection.
The *Zhengyi* (Verification of Meaning) states: In the "Chapter on Honoring the Sangha" by Chan Master Mingjiao Song, it says: "The Teaching must honor the Sangha. What does this mean?"
As for the monk (*saṃgha*), he takes the Buddha as his nature, the Tathāgata as his family, the Dharma as his body, wisdom as his life, and the joy of meditation (*dhyāna-prīti*) as his food.
Therefore, he does not rely on secular surnames, he does not cultivate a worldly lineage, and he does not maintain his physical form.

They do not crave life, nor do they fear death, nor are they addicted to the five flavors. In guarding the body, they possess precepts; in restraining the mind, they possess meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
in discerning with clarity, they possess wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding their precepts: they purify the three delusions, remaining untainted for the rest of their lives. Regarding their concentration:
they quiet their thoughts and rectify their spiritual intelligence, remaining undisturbed all day long. Regarding their wisdom: they revere...
Virtue distinguishes the deluded; yet one must necessarily cultivate by means of this, which is called the cause. To achieve perfection by means of this is called the fruit.
Regarding all things, there is kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), the great vow, and the great benefit. As for kindness, it is the constant desire to bring peace to all beings.
As for compassion, it is the constant desire to exhaust the manifold sufferings of the multitude. As for the vow, it is the vow that the whole world shall perceive the Truth.
He is truly wise. As for this wisdom, he bestows the True Dharma upon all living beings, manifesting it through spiritual penetration such that even Heaven and Earth cannot conceal it;
he practices it with such subtlety that even ghosts and spirits cannot fathom it. In expounding the Dharma, his eloquence is unhindered;
in protecting the Dharma, he exerts himself without regard for his own person. He can endure what others cannot endure and perform what others cannot perform.
In his conduct, he maintains right livelihood; he begs for food and eats it, yet feels no shame.
In his fewness of desires, he wears patched robes and carries a mendicant’s bowl, yet does not consider himself poor. In his lack of contention, he may be humiliated but cannot be slighted.
In his freedom from resentment, he may be moved [by circumstances] but cannot be harmed. He treats all things with sincerity and cultivates himself with supreme compassion. Therefore, regarding...
The world universally reveres him; his words are without falsehood, and thus his sincerity reaches its ultimate point. His dharma is without self, and thus his yielding is truly sincere.
Possessing a majesty that can serve as a warning and a decorum that can serve as a model, gods and humans regard him with solemn awe.
He is able to bestow blessings upon the world and guide the common folk. As for his forgetting of form, he would cast away even birds and beasts without regret. As for his reading...
He recited [the scriptures], never ceasing even amidst cold and heat, for he had emerged through the Dharma.
Wandering among the people, he traveled through all the villages, regarding fame as an echo in a valley, regarding profit as drifting dust, and regarding material forms as a mirage.

He mingled with commoners and servants on equal terms without considering himself base, for he dwelt according to the Way. Even in deep mountains and remote valleys, wearing grass garments and living by the trees...
He ate his meals with serene contentment; he could not be enticed by profit nor compelled by power. He declined the honors of the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords without considering himself aloof.
In his solitude, he overcame himself through the Way, so that even when his physical form was accompanied only by its shadow, he felt no loneliness.
In his company, he bound others together through the Dharma, so that even when meeting people from all quarters of the world, he did not become confused with the crowd.
As for what he studied: although there were the Three Baskets and Twelve Divisions of the Canon, as well as the books of a hundred schools and heterodox paths, there was nothing he did not know.

The languages of other regions and different customs were all those through which he was proficient. In his ancestral transmission of the Dharma, he possessed both literary elegance and formal structure;
in his practice of the Middle Way, he adhered to neither emptiness nor existence. As for his ultimate learning, it was free from conceptual thought and pure.
Pure. Of the singular essence of True Suchness (tathatā), they no longer engage in further conceptual discrimination.
As for the Saṃgha: their person is ultimate; their mind is universal; their virtue is complete; their Way is great. Their worthiness is not that which the world calls worthy;
their sagehood is not that which the world calls sage. They are the extraordinary and preeminent sages and saints who have transcended the world.
The Sangha is likewise so; how can they not be revered? Alas! The Great Dharma has declined, and our distance from the Sage grows ever greater.
Though those who don the black robes are numerous, those who seek the Way are rare. They vie for fame and profit as their own achievements, regarding the Buddha-dharma as a mere child’s play.
Consequently, the gates of the Dharma seldom open and the pillars of the teachings are on the verge of collapsing. We truly rely upon future generations to be able to shoulder this Way.
You all have sincerely requested the Dharma and purified yourselves to rely upon a teacher. Your immediate aim is to establish yourselves and bring renown to your names;

your ultimate aspiration is to transform the mundane into the sacred and to cause the Semblance Dharma to flourish once more. Since there is no one else to whom the Sangha can be entrusted, you must cultivate your conduct and practice what you preach.

Be as cautious at the end as you were at the beginning. Diligently apply yourself to learning and inquiry. Be circumspect in both your conduct and your private life. Shun evil and associate with the virtuous. Serve your teacher with the utmost propriety.
If you possess goodness, do not boast of it yourself. If you commit a transgression, strive to correct it immediately. Uphold benevolence and righteousness so firmly that you remain unshakable.
Abiding in poverty and low station, one finds joy that forgets sorrow; seeing the virtuous, one thinks of equaling them; when it comes to practicing benevolence, one does not yield.
Fame and profit cannot stir the heart; life and death cannot trouble the mind. Wisdom is sufficient to illuminate delusion; compassion is sufficient to gather others.
In times of adversity, one perfects oneself alone; in times of success, one benefits the whole world. Thus, the true wind of the Way flourishes.
He revived the tradition once more; when the torch of wisdom had been extinguished, he made it shine again. He may truly be called a great man, and may truly be called an emissary of the Tathāgata.

How could one whose person dwells among the treasures of the Sangha yet whose traces are mixed with those of ordinary folk, who at first admires superior sages but in the end sinks to the level of the lowest fools—how tragic such a person is! Reading this as a mirror for the self, one should deeply reflect upon it.

Reflect upon this: the flourishing or decline of the Buddha-Dharma depends upon the conduct of the Sangha. As it is said, "When the Sangha is honored, the Dharma is honored; when the Sangha is slighted, the Dharma is slighted.
Those who wish to transcend the world and repay the Buddha’s kindness should exert themselves in this endeavor.

"Transmitting the Dharma, transmitting the Dharma. Originally, this was called "transmitting the robe. From the successive patriarchs above, it was transmitted from one to another, using the robe as a token of faith. Upon reaching the Sixth Patriarch in the Eastern Land, this became a cause for contention;
he ceased the practice and no longer transmitted it. Recently, those who transmit the Dharma have also claimed they are transmitting the robe—this is what they maintain.
It merely retains its name; for the Dharma is the mind itself, and since the mind cannot be seen, how could there be any ritual protocols to manifest it?

If master and disciple are in accord through the Way, with mind meeting mind, then the transmission of the Dharma is already complete. As for the handing over of the letter or sharing of the seat, these are but secondary matters and are therefore not recorded here.
I shall only briefly recount the source and lineage of the Chan school, so that future generations may know the origin of the Dharma.

This has its basis. It is also presented here to express the intent of encouragement. According to the lineage of the Chan school, it originated when the Buddha Śākyamuni, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, held up a flower. Mahākāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said:
"I now entrust to you all that I possess—the unsurpassed True Dharma, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the true mark which is formless, this subtle and wonderful Dharma-gate."
"To you, you must well protect and maintain [this Dharma] so that it is not severed. A verse says: "The Dharma is originally without Dharma;
the absence of Dharma is also Dharma. Now, when the absence of Dharma is transmitted, how could any dharma have ever been a dharma? He thus became the First Patriarch of the Chan school.
The patriarchs have transmitted [the Dharma] from one to another; I shall now describe them in full detail. The First Patriarch, Mahākāśyapa, transmitted it to Ānanda;
Ānanda transmitted it to Śāṇakavāsin; Śāṇakavāsin transmitted it to Upagupta; Upagupta transmitted it to Dhītika; and Dhītika transmitted it to Miśraka.
Cajjapa transmitted it to Vasumitra; Vasumitra transmitted it to Buddhanandi; Nandi transmitted it to Buddhamitra; Mitra transmitted it to Pārśva;
Pārśva transmitted it to Pūrṇayaśas; Yaśas transmitted it to Aśvaghoṣa; Aśvaghoṣa transmitted it to Mātṛceṭa;
Ceṭa transmitted it to Nāgārjuna; Nāga transmitted it to Kāṇadeva; Deva transmitted it to Rāhulabhadra; Bhadra transmitted it to Saṃghanandi.
Dì. Dì transmitted it to Jñānayaśas; Yaśas transmitted it to Kumārajīva; Jīva transmitted it to Śayananda;

Siṃha transmitted it to Vajrasena; Sena transmitted it to Ratnamitra; Mitra transmitted it to Prajñātāra.
Luo. The twenty-eighth patriarch in the lineage of Luo was Bodhidharma. Upon his initial arrival in the eastern lands, he became the First Patriarch.
The Patriarch transmitted the Dharma to Huikē (Shenguang). Guang transmitted it to Sēngcàn (Jiànzhi).

Dahui Huairang had one branch: Xingsi (of Qingyuan in Qingzhou).

"The ancestral path takes precepts and meditative concentration as its foundation; the Fangguang [Vaipulya] school realizes perfect penetration. Practice transcends the manifest reality-limit; thorough understanding awakens to true emptiness.
This refers to Chan Master Jin of Bifeng’s lineage, Chan Master Zu Ding, who entered Min Province and resided at Xuefeng Temple.

The forty-seventh generation from Bifeng [Hui] begins with the character "Zu" (祖). This established a separate branch comprising twenty characters, which were not derived from the original transmission of the Linji school.
Reaching the time of Huanyou [Zhixu], who followed the lineage of Zu, there emerged two branches: those of Tiantong Wu and Qingshan Xiu.
It was only then that the characters beginning with "Yuan" (圓) were employed, extending the lineage down to the present day. At present, the character "Kong" (空) is used.
As the lineage was nearing completion, the minds of the assembly were not in accord. Some followed the ancestral line of Longshan; others established a separate branch;
some began again from the ancestral character of the original verse; others appended continuations beneath the character "Kong" (空). However, none of these were ultimately correct.

Inscription. Ming transmitted it to Li, whose source was as vast as a great flood. Li transmitted it to Su, who transmitted it to Lian, who transmitted it to Xingzhu. Zhu transmitted it to Huijue, who transmitted it to Quancheng.

Cheng transmitted it to Honghai, who transmitted it to Xingfu (from Nāgārjuna onwards, this constitutes the thirty-seventh generation). ○ (This is a brief account of the origins and lineage of the True Lineage of Tiantai Teachings; as for the other branches, they are too numerous to be recorded in detail one by one).

The Commentary states: In the *Tàizōng Yuánliú* (The Source and Lineage of the Tiantai School) and the *Zhǐyuánjí* (Collection on Pointing to the Source), there are brief biographies for all the patriarchs;
however, regarding the twenty-eighth patriarch, he is identified as Chan Master Míngwēng in the *Yuánliú*, while he is identified as Yuetíng Dégōng in the *Zhǐyuánjí*.
According to the records, Dōngchán Míngwēng passed away at the beginning of the Wànlì era, whereas Bǎisōng was born during the Jiāqīng era.
In the year Jìngdīngyǒu (1297), at the age of twenty-two, I went to Dōngchán to listen to the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Although we were together at the same time, the lecturer at Dōngchán was Master Yuetting, not Myeongung;
therefore, the *Jiyuanji* states that although Baeksong emerged from the lineage of Master Deokgong Yuetting, his direct transmission from Myeongung alone constitutes the twentieth generation.

Regarding the nine generations, one must still leave room for doubt. Upon re-examining the *Jiayù Lòuzé Sì* (The Leuze Temple of Kindness and Benefit), it produced a work titled *Tài zōng shìxì* (Lineage of the Tiantai School), which directly identifies Miaofeng and Baisong as the eighteenth patriarchs, tracing their lineage back to Siming.

Thus, the succession of the Tiantai school is regarded as having been re-established through a remote connection. In short, because the generations were so distant, descendants failed to maintain proper records.
As for the lineage of the *Cizhi* school, there is no means by which it can be examined. This is not the case only for the Tiantai school;
today, the dharma lineages of the Tiantai school are all widely transmitted. Furthermore, there are works such as the *Zhishuyuanji*, *Shixi*, and *Yuanliu* that may be consulted.
As those who inherit the Dharma, one should at all times and in all places take care to record these matters, so that they may continue on without end.
As for the dharma-lineage verses of the Hundred Pines (Bǎisōng), they are used to determine one's name; the verses expressing conduct (biǎoxíng) are used to establish one’s title.
Therefore, the true transmission of the dharma-lineage and the great teachings expressing conduct are two aspects that exist simultaneously, with no sequence between them.
Regarding the Xianshou school of Teaching and Contemplation:

the Xianshou school flourished in its propagation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. From the time Mañjuśrī compiled it, down to Nāgārjuna, who personally traveled to the Dragon Palace and read the *Avataṃsaka* in its entirety, our own land’s five patriarchs of the Xianshou lineage received the transmission from afar in succession; thus, it should be understood as being like the Tiantai school.

The school traces its lineage back to Nāgārjuna as its first patriarch. Du Shun, whose mind accorded with the Emperor’s, composed the *Huayan fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Huayan Dharmadhātu) as the second patriarch.

Du Shun transmitted it to Yunhua, Zhiyan, and Zhixiang; the latter composed the *Huayan souxuan yi chao* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Huayan) as the third patriarch. Zhixiang transmitted it to Fazang, Xianshou, and Guoyi;

the latter composed the *Jinyi huayan tantuan ji* (Record of Exploring the Profundities of the Chinese Translation of the Huayan) and the *Yicheng jiaoyi fen* (Classification of the Teachings and Meanings of the One Vehicle).
Zhi Zhang and others authored over one hundred fascicles, greatly propagating his teachings and contemplations; he was named the Xianshou School and served as the Fourth Patriarch.

According to the *Zangzhuan*, Chengguan, the Great Master Qingliang, inherited the lineage. He followed the Tang dynasty translations of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and composed commentaries and sub-commentaries, serving as the Fifth Patriarch.
Qingliang transmitted it to Guifeng Zongmi, who authored the *Commentary on the "Practice and Vows" Chapter* of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, serving as the Sixth Patriarch. Zongmi transmitted it further.
Xuanguī (Xuanhui) was the Seventh Patriarch for his profound penetration of the subtle. Haiyin Yuelang was the Eighth Patriarch for his brilliant and radiant clarity.
Ranshou Dengde was the Ninth Patriarch for the manifestation of his virtue. Changshui Zixuan inherited the lineage from afar as the Tenth Patriarch.
Jingyuan Jihai and Qiansou were the Eleventh Patriarchs. Xichong Shenjian and Chengzhao were the Twelfth Patriarchs. Miaoguan...
Daoming Zhanren was the thirteenth patriarch. Master Huihui Guiyuan Yufeng was the fourteenth patriarch.
Liaoxin Shen Daohuizhu was the fifteenth patriarch. Daowu Benjue Guanhui was the sixteenth patriarch.
Qingjie Yiru Jie’an was the seventeenth patriarch. Huiqiong Liangbi Zhenlin was the eighteenth patriarch. Miaocui...
Chaolun Zhen Cui was the nineteenth patriarch; Jiyu Chonggu was the twentieth patriarch;
Dadian Yunchun (also known as Puji and Bifeng) was the twenty-first patriarch; and Mingshan Xianxian Gufeng was the twenty-second patriarch.
Qiyuan Huijing (行成) succeeded him as the twenty-third patriarch; Guangtong Dajian (達菴) was the twenty-fourth patriarch;
Lu’an Putai (普泰) and Yean’an were the twenty-fifth patriarchs; Zhenyuan Dafang Bianrong (大方遍融) was the twenty-sixth patriarch;
Yunqi Lianchi Shuhong Fohui (殊宏佛慧) was the twenty-seventh patriarch; and Tuoqiao Shao... [continued].
Jogwang Seungmyeong-ri was the twenty-eighth patriarch; Nyeunui Daerin of Yeonju was the twenty-ninth patriarch;

and Boryun Deoksu Myeongwon was the thirtieth patriarch. (This is a brief account of the origins and transmission of the orthodox lineage of the Honorable Teaching; as for its other branches, they are too numerous to be recorded in full detail.)
The Commentary on the Meaning states: Among the most prominent schools that have flourished in this land, there are three: namely, Tiantai, Xianshou (Huayan), and Cien (Faxiang).
At present, of these three, only the Cien school remains in its propagation of the Dharma of *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only), though the personages who uphold it are no longer present.
As for the other two, the Tiantai and Xianshou schools, their lineages have proliferated and continue without end; yet, among them, it is the Tiantai school of the South that [remains preeminent].

It was particularly flourishing; however, those who attained prominent names and high positions mostly emerged from the Northern School of the Xianzong lineage. Was this not also brought about by the workings of destiny?
This is appended to the Nanshan Vinaya School.
The Nanshan Vinaya School vigorously propagated the *vinaya*. *Vinaya* is translated here as "extinction" (*mie*), for it can extinguish the evils of body and speech;
it is also the "disciplinary law. While the *vinaya* was exclusively established by the Buddha, the compilation and arrangement of its sections were not performed by a single individual.
Initially, five hundred noble disciples, including Mahākāśyapa and others, convened within the Vipaśyanā Cave and charged Upāli with the compilation; this is known as the "Superior [Collection]."
The Sthaviras. Subsequently, Vāsika and others—consisting of one thousand ordinary and noble ones—held a council outside the cave;
this was called the Mahāsāṃghika school. These two schools are collectively known as the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya.

From Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Madhyāntika, Śāṇakavāsin, and Upagupta, through these five generations, they exercised spiritual authority and maintained the Way; therefore, they did not divide the teachings. After Upagupta...
There were five disciples, each adhering to a different view, and consequently the Vinaya Piṭaka was divided into five schools:
(1) the Dharmaguptaka school, namely the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya); (2) the Sarvāstivāda school, namely the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya);

(3) the Kāśyapīya school, namely the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Liberation Vinaya); (4) the Mahīśāsaka school, namely the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya); and (5) the Vātsīputrīya school, the *Vinayamātṛkā*.
In the future, this land shall divide the *Vinaya-piṭaka* of the Wondrous Joy [Sūtra] into five sections, just as a golden staff may be split without losing its utility as gold.
According to the ten great disciples of the Tathāgata, Upāli was foremost in upholding the Vinaya;
therefore, the single school of Vinaya-holding in my eastern land should take the Venerable Upāli as its first patriarch, with the lineage being transmitted from one to another in succession.
Dharmakāla (translated as Fashí; a śramaṇa from Western India) arrived in the eastern lands in the second year of the Jiaping era of the Wei dynasty and translated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
He was the first patriarch for the transmission of the Vinaya in the eastern lands. Fǎcóng of Beitai (a contemporary of Emperor Wencheng of the Northern Wei who studied the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*;

because he investigated the reception of the precepts, he was the second patriarch who first transmitted the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*). Fǎcóng transmitted it to Dàofú of Yúnzhōng. Dàofú was the first to compose the *Shù* (commentary) in six fascicles, explaining the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*; he was the third [patriarch].
The Patriarch [Daoxuan] further transmitted it to Da’jue Huiguang (who was versed in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and composed a ten-fascicle commentary; he served as the Fourth Patriarch);

Huiguang transmitted it to Gaozhai Daoyun, Huiyuan, and Yuanyuan (who composed a nine-fascicle sub-commentary and provided detailed exegesis on the extensive text; he served as the Fifth Patriarch); Yuanyuan transmitted it to Dao Hong of Hebei (who also authored a commentary; he served as the Sixth Patriarch); Dao Hong transmitted it to Zhishou of Hongfu Monastery (who composed a twenty-fascicle commentary;
he served as the Seventh Patriarch); and Zhishou transmitted it to Daoxuan of Shiming Monastery in the Western Mountains of Zhongnan, whose true mark was clarity.

Zhao. (The Vinaya school flourished greatly from this point onward; thus, people of the time all referred to the Vinaya tradition as the Nanshan School and designated Zhao as the Eighth Patriarch. Thereafter, it was transmitted in succession, establishing the patriarchal lineage. Zhao transmitted [the dharma to] Chongsheng Wen’gang of the capital, who became the Ninth Patriarch.

Wengang transmitted [it to] Chimu Yanyi of Chongfu Temple, who became the Tenth Patriarch. Yanyi transmitted [it to] Daliang Daosheng of the Chang’an Guanyin Temple, who became the Eleventh Patriarch.
Daosheng transmitted [it to] Tan’i of the Kaiyuan Temple in Shaoxing, who became the Twelfth Patriarch. Tan’i transmitted [it to] [the master of] Suzhou...
Fenxiu of Kaiyuan was the twelfth patriarch. Xi transmitted it to Zhang Xinda and Chen Deng, who were the fourteenth patriarchs.
Deng transmitted it to Chengchu of Dongjing Xiangguo, who was the fifteenth patriarch. Chu transmitted it to Yunkan Zhenwu of Hangzhou Zhaokai, who was the sixteenth patriarch.
Wu transmitted it to Yuanzhao Zhanran of West Lake Lingzhi, who was the seventeenth patriarch. Ran transmitted it to Shixiang Yuanming of Dapuqing Temple in the Capital.

Guangjiao became the eighteenth patriarch. His transmission passed to Daofu (Beijing, Xishan, Jietaisi, Wanshousi). Ruohan became the nineteenth patriarch. His transmission passed to Ruxing (Jinling Tianlongsi).
Guxin Huiyun became the twentieth patriarch—at this time, the Vinaya teachings were revived and flourished with brilliant clarity;
it is traditionally said that he was an emanation of Upāli. Huiyun’s transmission passed to Jiguang Samādhi (Jinling Baohuashan Longchangsi), who became the twenty-first patriarch.
The Patriarch. (At this point, the Vinaya School flourished even more greatly. A verse from the *Fapai* [Lineage of the Dharma] says: As for tranquility, it reads: virtue is true and eternal;

the nature of merit is perfect and bright, while concentration and wisdom flourish. The Sea-Seal emits light, merging with the moon of precepts; the *Udumbara* flower manifests as an auspicious omen, continuing the celestial fragrance.

Branching into ten thousand streams, the source of the Vinaya is distant; fruiting in a thousand blossoms, the root of the school is long. The Dharma succeeds the Nanshan lineage, expanding the orthodox pulse; the lamp transmits the mind-ground.
Yonglian Fang transmitted it to Tuijian Yue, who was the twenty-second patriarch. Yue transmitted it to Deji Ding’an, who was the twenty-third patriarch.
An transmitted it to Zhenyi Songyin, who was the twenty-fourth patriarch. Yin transmitted it to Changsong Minyuan, who was the twenty-fifth patriarch.
Yuan transmitted it to Shiwang Zhenhui, who was the twenty-sixth patriarch. Hui transmitted it...
Fujū Bunkai was the twenty-seventh patriarch. Hōun transmitted the teachings of the nature of words and principles to Jinkyō (this is a brief preface to the authentic lineage of the Vinaya school;
as for its other branches, they are too numerous to be recorded in full detail).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: Tonsure is the initial matter for the Great Assembly; the transmission of the Dharma is the final matter for the Great Assembly.

Without tonsure, there is no way to enter the ranks of the Sangha. Once one has become a monk, if one merely follows the routine of two-meal rice gruel and formal recitations, wasting one’s time without addressing the great matter of birth and death, it is truly in vain.
If one aims for that supreme point above, may it be possible to receive the prediction of enlightenment and transmit the mind?

Therefore, this preface specifically treats the matter of the transmission of the Dharma as its primary focus, providing a chronological account of the successors of the Chan school to demonstrate the ancient models. This serves to awaken those of the present;
how thorough and complete it is! Furthermore, the Teachings serve as an aid for clarifying the mind, while the Vinaya serves as the foundation for concentration and wisdom. It is also...
Appended herewith. Combined, these complete the religious teachings, the monastic discipline, and the regulations for the assembly;
thus, the matters pertaining to the Great Community are fully provided. *Bai Zhang Conglin Qinggui Zhengyi Ji*, Fascicle Seven, Part Two;
*Bai Zhang Conglin Qinggui Zhengyi Ji*, Fascicle Eight.

Chapter Eight: On the Observance of the Retreat (Varṣā).
The commentary states: Monks do not rank themselves by age, but by their seniority in the religious life (*yasa*) to distinguish themselves from the laity.

In the Western Regions, there are three seasons, and one season is designated for the *an-gu* (the rainy retreat), lasting from the fifteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month. During this period, there are prohibitions on entering or leaving [the monastery]. As for all meditation...
Regarding the practice of recitation, walking meditation, and sitting, one follows the sequence of receiving the precepts to establish a ninety-day period for advancing along the Path.

During three ten-day periods, one prepares the requisites for sustaining the body (a total of four months), ensuring that both the internal and external are equally nourished so that body and mind are both at peace.
One should strive toward cultivation within this fixed timeframe, not wasting even a moment, while protecting life and practicing both compassion and forbearance.

How profound are the holy instructions! They shall be followed eternally for ten thousand generations. Yet, as the lands of the Five Indias are vast, with climates ranging from heat and cold to torrential rains, the seasonal conditions are not uniform;
thus, the commencement of the retreat (jie) may occur in the fourth, fifth, or twelfth month. Nevertheless, all begin on the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth day.
Adapting to the local terrain and the timing of the seasons, they simply seek what is most comfortable. Some call this "sitting through the summer" (zuoxia).
Some say this was the origin of the *zuo-la* (sitting for the *la*). The meaning of the *jie-la* (precept-ages) begins here.

Nowadays, in the monastic communities (*conglin*), the summer retreat (*jie-xia*) begins on the full moon of the fourth month and concludes on the full moon of the seventh month; these three months constitute the *an-ju* (rainy-season retreat).

Furthermore, the winter retreat (*jie-dong*) begins on the full moon of the tenth month and concludes on the full moon of the first month; during these three months, one devotes oneself exclusively to *chan-na* (dhyāna). This is the established rule.

We have stood for a long time. Transformation occurs according to what is appropriate. For over a thousand years, we have followed the prescribed rules and regulations, gazing in awe at the assembly of dragons and elephants.
As host and guest exchange their songs and toasts, we repeatedly hear the roars of lions. How magnificent and glorious this is!
Regarding the *Varṣā* (also known as the Summer Retreat, or *Jiezhì*): first, counting sticks (*chóu*) are distributed; second, the ritual for entering the retreat (*Ān-jū*) is performed.

According to the regulations of the Vinaya, the matters concerning the retreat are detailed; however, following current practice for convenience, the summer retreat begins on the sixteenth day of the fourth month.
On the preceding day, the Guest Hall (*Kètáng*) hangs a notice board. (The board reads: "Summer Retreat. On the fifteenth day, the Guest Master (*Zhīkè*) notifies the Rector (*Wéinà*) and all others.

In the Hall, the names and ordination years (jie-la) of each individual shall be fully recorded for inclusion in the register. Furthermore, lay attendants (yue-zhong) shall be assigned to collect the counting sticks (chou), distribute them, and escort the participants;
each person must identify themselves so that no confusion occurs at the time of the ceremony.

As for the external monks, novices, and lay servants, once their numbers have been announced, the guest master (zhi-ke) shall instruct the incense lamp master (xiang-deng-shi) of the Dharma Hall to prepare the meditation mats (pu-tuan). (If there is no Dharma Hall...)
Once the mats have been laid out in the refectory according to the number of people present, a square table is placed at the center for the head monk.

Upon it, a small image of Śākyamuni Buddha is enshrined; if there is no image, a name tablet (paili) is used instead, inscribed with: "The Teacher of the Central Heaven, Our Original Master Śākyamuni Buddha, for the Summer Retreat Assembly.
Furthermore, to the right, along the side of the front corridor, a formal desk is set up to enshrine Vajrapāṇi. The abbot’s seat is located [there].
To the left of the Buddha table, and again in the center of the hall, place one small table upon which a counting tray and an empty plate may be set.
Outside, prepare three large counting sticks for the positions of the Buddha, Vajrapāṇi, and the Abbot. Having thus made all preparations according to the Dharma:

After the light meal and the period of quiet seclusion have concluded, the guest prefect strikes the large bell three times. The assembly each dons their seven-piece robes and takes up their ritual implements, gathering in the Dharma Hall.
Two attendants invite the Abbot to come before the Buddha, where he offers incense and performs three prostrations.

Turning, he proceeds to the altar of Wei Tian, offers incense, and after performing three inquiries of respect, returns to his place. Once the head of the assembly has finished offering incense, the lead chime is struck, and the entire congregation performs their prostrations.

The Abbot performs three prostrations. Turning toward the Veda-deva (Weitian), he makes three inquiries. He then returns to pay homage to the presiding abbot with three prostrations. (The Shang says: "One prostration.

Having finished the prostrations,) each person sits according to their assigned seat. The presiding abbot delivers an exhortation, concluding with: "Now, Master Yuezhong [Name] shall distribute the tally-sticks, and Master Yuezhong [Name] shall collect them.
I have now assembled the Sangha; hereafter, we shall proceed with the ritual procedures in sequence. (According to the Vinaya regulations, at this point there is one...)

After the *jñapti-karman* (the formal motion consisting of a single announcement) has been made, the assembly rises with joy. They prostrate three times before the Buddha, inquire after his well-being, and each takes up a counting-slip (*śalākā*) tray.

They proceed to stand facing one another to the left and right of the Buddha. The *karmadāna* (precentor) takes the counting-slip tray, places it upon an empty tray, prostrates three times before the Buddha, inquires after his well-being, and kneels for a long time.
Taking one large counting-slip, he holds it crosswise with both hands and announces aloud: "The Great Qing [Year], the [X]th year..."
During the three months of summer, at the assembly for the *varṣā* retreat, the Teacher from Central India, our original master Śākyamuni Buddha, received the first tally.
Having spoken, he placed it upon the incense burner and rose to perform a single prostration.

The collector, using an empty tray, placed it upon the tray for the tallies, performed three prostrations before the Buddha, and inquired after his well-being while kneeling long. With both hands, he collected the tallies and placed them upon the empty tray, performing another salutation.
The Buddha performs one prostration. Thereafter, they carry the trays and proceed in separate lines, divided left and right, beginning with the abbot and the senior monks in order of rank.
Those receiving the tally should squat down to take it and place it into the empty tray. Having proceeded in this manner according to the sequence, [the ceremony concludes].
Returning once more to the presence of the deity Weituo, they stand facing him in stillness. The *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) again takes the counting sticks (*shou*) and places them upon the tray.
After performing three prostrations with inquiry (*wenshen*), he holds up a large counting stick with both hands and speaks aloud:

"The Great Qing [Name], in the [Number] year, during the summer retreat of the third month, at this assembly for the *an-guo* (rainy season retreat), the Dharma-protecting deity Vaisravana accepts this final counting stick. Having finished speaking, he places it down.
On the table. After another salutation, the person collecting the counting sticks (chou) places them on the tray for circulating the counting sticks.

Having performed three salutations toward Weitian, they take the counting sticks with both hands and place them in the tray. After another salutation, the people collecting the counting sticks all go before Weitian together to calculate the total number of persons.
They also report the count of those who wish to join the assembly and those who do not, and having verified this as well, [the procedure concludes].

The leader walks in front at the end [of the procession]. Upon reaching the presence of the Buddha, the two ranks—upper and lower—take their positions. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) speaks aloud, saying:

"In the Great Qing year [year name], during the third month of summer, at this assembly for the *varṣā* retreat, there are [number] hundreds and [number] tens of *bhikṣus* in the seats, along with [number] *śrāmaṇeras*.
Having reported this, he places his bowl on the table. The *vinaya-dhara* speaks again: "For the sake of the Saṃgha, I shall perform the ritual."

The distribution of *śalākā* is finished. (The Abbot replies: "Excellent. (The Rector says: "Understood. (They all bow in unison and return to their places. The Abbot says: "Venerable members of this community, you are already aware of this matter. This summer, there are [a certain number] of people in retreat. During the upcoming period for reciting the precepts, there is no need to distribute counting sticks (*śalākā*). Each person must restrain body and mind, striving diligently for the Way throughout these ninety days. The distribution of counting sticks is now complete. When the Dharma flowed eastward to this land, it likewise proceeded first with the Sūtras and Vinaya, followed by the Chan School. From this, one can see the relationship between the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Chan School.
Both must be valued equally. As models for dwelling in the world, winter retreat and summer study are mutually necessary and not contradictory.

That the present Chan school remains indifferent toward both the Sūtras and the Vinaya is an error. Furthermore, when listening to the Sūtras and studying the Vinaya, one must clarify five essentials.
The first essential is to believe that the realm of all Buddhas is inherently possessed by each and every person. It is originally non-existent [as a separate entity].
First, do not give rise to discouragement or timidity. Second, you must realize that all things return to oneself; one must not merely count others' jewels while eating one's own food.

Third, you must maintain a humble mind and delight in the good; whenever there is even a slight degree of excellence, regard it as a teacher or friend—this is what is meant by "selecting the good and following it," and "having no friend who is not one's equal. Those who can be alerted by this intention should not spare their bitter words. Fifth, one must forgive others and blame oneself.
When others do not act according to the Dharma, give rise to a heart of compassion and do not look for their faults; if you yourself become negligent and harbor arrogance, [you will fail].

Therefore, it is utterly unacceptable to abandon [this practice]. Whenever I observe people of this world who wish to study the Sūtras and Vinaya and enter the lecture halls, they encounter all manner of obstacles and difficulties.
That you have now encountered such a favorable opportunity, yet instead aspire toward the superficial and shallow—how can you not find this regrettable?

Furthermore, one who lectures on the Sūtras must grasp the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; do not merely rely on the literal text to explain the meaning, for that will conversely obstruct the realization of the students.
One should know that these individuals proclaim the teachings on behalf of the Buddha; they are the focus of the gaze of humans and devas, and must not be disregarded.

According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, when people in the human realm lecture on the sūtras, receive precepts, cultivate the path, realize the fruits [of practice], or perform Buddhist rites, they report this from the earth deities to the sky deities.
In this manner, it is successively reported upward to all the devas of the three realms, and even to the Buddhas.

The *Chanzong biyao* (Secret Essentials of the Chan School) states: While the Dharma Master Suiyu was lecturing on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, there was a clerk named Li who, after his death, would occasionally manifest as a ghost and engage in conversation with people. The Master asked him, "Now that this sūtra is being lectured, what kind of beings have been moved to listen?
He replied, "From human heads upward, they are all ghosts and spirits; above them are the various heavens. Furthermore...

whenever there is a Dharma service, they do not fail to descend. Based on this, when performing any Dharma service, one ought truly to be sincere and reverent."
Regulations for the Lecture Hall (Total of Twelve Articles) Now, Chan and the Teachings are not two distinct things.
The Teachings serve as the explanation of Chan; Chan serves as the essence of the Teachings. To cling to the literal meaning while adhering to the explanation is for Chan to become the Teachings.
To transcend the literal meaning and realize the mind is for the Teachings to be called Chan. This refers to the ritual conduct.

Thus, True Suchness is manifested; by relying on these models, the wondrous Way is perfected. Sudhana traveled throughout the Dharma-realm in search of the truth, and the World-Honored One Śākyamuni displayed the process from the stage of a learner to the attainment of enlightenment.
These serve as banners for those who study and practice, providing a model for future generations.

Therefore, we know that one proceeds from faith and understanding toward practice and realization, and through instruction and revelation, one attains awakening and entry. These scriptures are of supreme importance; without systematic rules and regulations, there would be no means to uphold them.
Regulations: These are respectfully set forth below. May they be strictly observed.

During the period of the sutra lecture, should anyone violate a root precept, drink alcohol or indulge in negligence, engage in disputes over personal enmity or right and wrong, or slander the teaching of the Dharma, as well as the Dharma Master or fellow students—should any one of these offenses be committed, that person shall be expelled from the monastery immediately and barred from remaining within the precincts on any pretext.
Those who go out for leisurely excursions, as well as those who attend sutra recitations or repentance rites, shall leave the monastery;
those who do not follow the assembly shall be penalized. Those whose robes and headgear are improperly adjusted upon entering or leaving shall be penalized.

After the small meal, the Master shall be invited to lecture on the sutras. All must attend the lectures in unison. When the *Dazhuan jing* (Great Seat Sutra) is being lectured, those who fail to attend three times shall leave the hall.

On the day prior [to the lecture], one should carefully read through the scriptural text to be delivered from the high seat. In this way, when listening to the discourse, it will be easier to comprehend.

Should there be points that remain unclear, one may inquire about them after the session has concluded. If one is indolent and fails to review the text, and instead succumbs to dullness and negligence while listening, one must leave the hall.
Listening to the sutras requires understanding their meaning so that awakening may be expected; it is not merely a matter of consuming the words without reflection.
Regarding the interpretation of the meaning: if one lacks the resolve for awakening, even the text itself will not be digested.
Those who merely follow the crowd, superficially responding to established customs, may leave the hall. For a small-scale lecture (*xiǎzuò*), first strike the bell three times;

when those inside and outside have all assembled, if there are points of error or ambiguity during the lecture, one must not laugh, mock, or show disrespect. Those who are arrogant and refuse to listen shall be penalized.

Regarding the person who delivers the minor lecture (*xiǎozuò*): the Abbot shall announce the commencement of the lecture from the Abbot’s quarters, continuing until the announcement is made before the entire assembly.

The members of the assembly shall likewise stand in their ranks, and one person on duty shall also offer incense. The person delivering the minor lecture must perform a return bow; this continues until the lecture is concluded.

The procedure for the small seat (*kṣudra-āsana*) remains as previously announced. Each day, following the rotation, one shall draw lots from among those designated for the small seat to deliver a lecture, thereby verifying daily progress.
This excludes only those who are truly dull-witted. The above regulations are to be observed by all.
