Regarding the meaning of "comprehensively" (*xi*): it is truly because the single matter of expounding the sutras is the time for proclaiming the Buddha’s teachings on his behalf and the place where devas and humans listen with joined palms.

It is therefore appropriate to be reverent and cautious. In the past, when Ānanda compiled the Dharma-treasury, he ascended the seat and took up his pen, and it was moved that his physical marks and excellence became like those of the Buddha.
Compiling the sutras and expounding the sutras share the same principle. To distance oneself from all faults—how could this be easily achieved?
This is indeed a matter of utmost importance. Therefore, nine articles of protocol have been established to solemnize one’s deportment and manifest sincerity and reverence.
One must possess great compassion, instructing others without weariness; preach the Dharma with equanimity, making no distinction between high and low;

and show no partiality toward enemies or kin, nor take account of offerings. One should don pure robes, ensuring that both the interior and exterior are clean, and must never wear vulgar or untidy clothing.
Ascending the seat, even though it be the height of summer, one must don the formal robes. With gentleness and patience, one must not remove the robe because of sitting for a long time.
Purifying the mind in tranquil illumination, one contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena. The sound of the Brahma-voice is heard afar as humans and devas gather together.

One realizes that the very substance is provisional; illuminating emptiness, it is not empty; illuminating the provisional, it is not provisional. The very substance is the Middle Way. Gathering phenomena back into principle, at that very moment—

One should be capable of entering into the subtle principles. When seated, one should be upright and dignified; one must not lean the body or sit in a squatting posture. One’s speech and laughter must not be coarse or vulgar.
One must not set aside the correct meaning and fail to expound it, nor speak excessively of peripheral details. If one is to elucidate the profound essence, [one must do so with gravity].
The analogy is indeed apt. Although it is conventional discourse, it is not contradictory.

While expounding the sutras, one must certainly extract the essential points and probe the fundamental principles to clarify their meaning; nevertheless, the literal exegesis of the text is the foundational practice.

One must not elaborate on the meaning while neglecting the text, causing those of shallow understanding to be bewildered and unable to comprehend, thereby failing to attain a true realization of what is seen.

In such instances, one must not engage in forced interpretations or arbitrary allegorical attachments, nor should one twist the scriptures to conform to one's own views, thereby misleading future generations.

When encountering these points, one should frankly admit ignorance rather than pretending to know. One must not use illustrative anecdotes as a pretext to discuss matters of lust, depravity, or other base inclinations, treating the Dharma as a mere game.
Furthermore, if there are nuns or women present in the assembly, one should exercise even greater caution. Do not.

One might, out of fear of being troublesome, seek only ease and settle matters perfunctorily. Regarding the points above, they are intended to prevent errors and faults on the part of Dharma masters who claim to clearly understand the meaning of the scriptures.
If one’s own mastery of the scriptural meaning is not yet thorough, how easy would it be to ascend this seat?
With humans and devas arrayed before us, the laws of cause and effect are manifest; each person should exercise the utmost care.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: That devas listen to the sutras has already been explained previously.

Furthermore, within any grove or forest, even when people are merely chatting or conversing casually, spirits and deities invariably come to listen and observe. As the *Zhigu* says: "Master An of the Song dynasty’s Guangxiao Temple resided at Qingtai Temple;
he took no pleasure in worldly affairs and spent his days solely in quiet sitting, remaining solemnly in meditative concentration. Once, while in this state of concentration..."
He saw two monks leaning against the railing and conversing. Initially, a celestial deity had been present, guarding them as they listened; after a long while, they dispersed.
Shortly thereafter, malevolent spirits spat curses and even swept away their footprints. Dao’an then emerged from his meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to inquire about the cause.

At first, the monks discussed the Buddha-dharma; next, they spoke of worldly truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*); finally, they talked of livelihood and sustenance. Master Dao’an took the conduct of these two monks as a standard for self-discipline until the end of his life.
Throughout his life, he never spoke of worldly affairs. After his passing, when his body was cremated, his tongue remained unburnt, as supple as the petals of a red lotus flower.

This account is also recorded in the *Yunqi Chongxing Lu*. Alas! If even while leaning on a railing and conversing, there is still a divine ear that listens, how much more so when ascending the dais to preach the sutras—should one not be cautious?
Summary of the *Lanpen* Ritual (the full text is found in the *Lanpenhui Zuan*).
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the *Lanpen* offering is established. On the preceding day, one should affix a plaque at the mountain gate reading:

"The Auspicious Assembly of the *Lanpen*. Immediately thereafter, sweep the main hall, as well as the inner and outer courtyards, and prepare the offering vessels and various ritual implements for adornment.

All items and such are fully prepared in equal measure. ○ Regarding the morning service on the following day, matters such as prayers and supplications shall follow the precedent of the "Lantern Festival" and "Winter Release" rituals;
these are detailed below and need not be elaborated upon here. In the early morning, the assembly is invited to establish the *pūrnāṃsa* altar.
On the vermilion courtyard, tables are arranged in five rows: each row consists of one square table and four long rectangular tables. In the center of the very first row at the top is a square...
A large tin alms bowl filled with rice was placed on the central table. On the four long tables to the left and right, fruit offerings were arranged in rows of more than ten plates each.
In the center of the second row, a single *urṇapātra* (alms bowl) was set out; it was so named according to the sutras to signify its extraordinary spiritual significance.
Within the basin, stack sweet, ripe vegetables in twenty-four colors; they must not be sparse or pale.
On both sides, arrange long tables according to the aforementioned style, offering various fruit delicacies and other items.

In the center of the third row, on a square table, place one large bowl of pure water with several fresh flowers immersed within it. The long tables remain as described above, offering fruit delicacies and other items.
Objects: At the center of the fourth row is a square table, upon which a large jar of lotus flowers is offered.
The long tables remain as described above, with offerings of fruit and other items. At the center of the fifth row is a square table, where an incense altar is set up.

The articles for the *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence) monks are placed upon the long tables, which remain as described above, with other remaining items arranged thereon. Wooden railings are used around the four sides.

The enclosure is surrounded by a railing. Laypeople who consume pungent foods or alcohol must not enter and mingle with the assembly. Small gates are opened on both the north and south sides for the monks and donors to pass through;

two people shall be stationed at each gate to guard them and strictly prohibit unauthorized entry. (Many prohibitory notices are posted around the four sides of the altar; the text of these notices reads as follows).
This is the pure offering altar, the place where the Triple Gem and the celestial deities are respectfully invited to descend.

All should maintain sincere reverence. Those who have consumed alcohol or meat must not enter. (This is the ritual for establishing the altar. △ After two strikes of the board following the morning congee, the Guest Master strikes the great bell three times.
The Zen Hall immediately stops its three-board silence and opens the minor silence. The assembly dons their robes and takes up their ritual implements.

Once they have entered the altar area together, two practitioners hold the leading banners (*yindao fan*), two *yuèzhòng* strike the leading chimes (*yin qing*), and eight senior officials (*shouling zhishi*) hold small banners.
Upon arriving at the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), they divide into ranks and stand facing one another. The leading chimes are struck four times.

The Abbot exits the room without bowing; he is the first to proceed at the very end. The two guiding banners are positioned in front of the small banner, and the leading chime is in front of the Abbot.
One attendant holds an incense burner, and another attendant carries a censer tray, following behind the Abbot.
The guiding banners enter the altar area and station themselves at both corners. The small banner parts ways. When the Abbot arrives before the incense table:
Incense is offered. The Rector recites the eulogy; the assembly joins in.
Purifying the altar and circumambulating the sutra (that is, circumambulating while reciting the *Ullambana Sūtra*):

Maudgalyāyana initiates the teaching, and the World-Honored One proclaims it. With the food from the *pātra*, benefit is brought to both the living and the deceased; they are liberated from suffering and proceed to heaven.
Sublime bliss is boundless; filial conduct shall forever spread its fragrance. *Namo* to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gandhavyūha. (Recite three times.

After the presiding monk has finished bowing to the Buddha, he takes up the incense burner and makes inquiries. He then raises his voice: *Namo* to the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. (Recite three times. The Rector holds the pure water cup.)
Recite the Verse for Purifying the Altar: The nectar-water from the Bodhisattva’s willow branch Can cause a single drop to pervade the ten directions;

All taints of raw meat, pungent odors, and filth are utterly removed, And the consecrated altar site is rendered entirely pure. As the teachings contain these secret mantras, I shall now reverently recite them.

(Then, recite the Great Compassion Mantra while circumambulating the altar. The *yuèzhòng* strikes the "large fish-egg" gong. The assembly recites together. The *weina* purifies the wine. At each of the four corners, set out a small table, upon which place one scroll of the *Lanpen Jing*.)

The four *yuèzhòng* (assembly leaders) stand at four tables. With palms joined, they chant aloud in unison. Guiding the banners to the foot of the Great Hall steps, they stand facing one another. The small banners proceed first; the *heshang* (abbot) follows them. One attendant carries a censer and follows, with the *bānshǒu* (senior monk) following behind.

The assembly each holds their respective implements and proceeds in order, circumambulating the altar by its right side. They ascend the hall, circumambulate the Buddha by his right side, and descend. Without stopping, they perform one circuit while reciting mantras and sprinkling water for purification, then immediately chant the *Buddhabhāṣita-urundabhadra-sūtra*, etc.

Recite the scripture three times. Upon completing the circumambulation, the assembly takes their places according to the seating order for recitation. The Abbot proceeds to the incense altar. When the recitation is finished, the attendant takes over the hand-incense burner;

the assembly kneels and joins their palms. The Abbot joins his palms and makes this aspiration: "With one mind in filial devotion, we cultivate the causes of the Pure Land. Through repentance, we eliminate the sins of the three obstacles, repaying the kindness of our two parents.

May those who remain obtain blessings and longevity; may those who have passed attain transcendence. Together we shall be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, delivering all enemies and kin. (When the aspiration is finished...)
All stand up together and join their palms. (The Rector leads: Homage to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha. (Twelve prostrations) Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
(Three prostrations) Homage to Maitreya Bodhisattva. (Three prostrations) Homage to all Buddhas of the ten directions. (Three prostrations) Homage to all Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
(Three prostrations) Homage to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who initiated the teaching of the *Ullambana* Sūtra. (Three prostrations. Three Refuges)
The conclusion of the ritual: Having performed three prostrations, they withdraw and each returns to their own place to put away their robes, relieve themselves, and drink tea (with snacks).

Next is the *Ullambana* offering (after drinking tea and eating snacks; after a short while, the bell is struck three times. The assembly all enters the altar and performs three prostrations to the Buddha. The Abbot presents incense; the Rector recites the hymn for the offering. The assembly sings in unison):
The Ullambana Assembly begins; the Gate of Universal Deliverance is opened. We reverently welcome the Three Jewels to descend and take their seats, each upon a flower pedestal.
We pray only that, out of compassion, you will accept this offering of sublime incense. *Namo* to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who receive these offerings.

(Recite three times. [The Venerable Vinaya Master, having approached the center to offer incense, performs three prostrations with full prostration gear, then kneels long with palms joined and speaks as follows:]
I reverently hear that the Dharmakāya is eternally quiescent, fundamentally without departure and without arrival; its wondrous wisdom is perfectly interfused, truly neither empty nor material;
its numinous clarity is beyond dependence, and the ocean of awakening is unfathomable. It looks down to moisten the deluded and obscured, manifesting its influence from time to time.

Now, coinciding with the Tathāgata’s occasion of joy and the Sangha’s *pravāraṇā* ceremony, we shall provide the hundred-flavored *pātra-puṣpa* offering for the sake of our parents of seven generations.
In ritual, follow the example of Changguo; in filial piety, emulate Maudgalyāyana. May the fragrance of the sacrificial millet and grain reach the Awakened King.
We pray that you will descend with your compassionate light and accept our offerings. (Having finished the announcement, perform one prostration, stand up, and recite:)

To the Tathāgatas of the Three Bodies (Chorus): We respectfully offer this *bowl* (Lanpen). Having made this supreme offering to the Triple Gem, [the officiant] holds the incense burner and recites the words of invitation as follows:
The Great Hero appeared in the world; together we attended the feast within the city of Śrāvastī. The True Dharma spread abroad;
together we received offerings within the palace of King Bimbisāra. Having manifested signs according to the capacities of beings, he has likewise universally rescued all living creatures.
On this day, we, the assembly, have reverently prepared the *urṇā-paṃtra* (lotus bowl) offering; with sincere hearts we prostrate and single-mindedly present these offerings.
Upon the thousand-petaled lotus pedestal, amidst the radiance of a hundred jewels, is the Sage of the Thirty-two Marks, the Great Awakened One of the Eighty Minor Characteristics.

To all the Buddha-treasures throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma realm—past, present, and future, immeasurable in number—I pray that you do not forsake your compassion and accept this offering.

(Recite the three "Whites" and perform three prostrations. Next, recite the Verse for Offering to the Buddhas while sounding the bells, drums, gongs, and cymbals; chant it three times in unison, or once.)
Homage to the Teacher of Gods and Humans seated upon the lotus throne, whose majestic virtue and dignified appearance are peerless.
May the Buddha Jewel, in his great compassion, accept this offering of the *Ullambana* bowl. Homage to the Fragrant Water Ocean and the Flower Treasury World.

[The assembly chants: "We offer this *urabon* [Lanpen] to the Buddha of True Suchness. (When the chanting has concluded, the *vinaya-dhara* takes up the incense burner and loudly requests the Dharma, saying: "On this day, we, the assembly..."
With deep reverence, we prepare this *urnapātra* (lotus vessel).

With a sincere heart, we prostrate ourselves and offer it specifically for the sake of the *sūtras* of definitive meaning, the supreme vehicle brought from the land of India on white horses, and the twelve divisions of the wondrous scriptures of ultimate emptiness.
We pray that you will never abandon the immeasurable Dharma-treasures of the ten directions and the entire *dharmadhātu*, throughout the past, present, and future.

Compassion. Accept this offering. (Recite the three "white" verses and perform three prostrations. Next, chant the verse for raising the offering, while sounding drums, cymbals, and so forth, three times or once.)
Homage to the most supreme Dharma that accords with reality, which brings about the fruits of Bodhi and Nirvana.
We pray only that the Great Compassion of the Jewel of the Dharma will accept this offering of the Ullambana vessel. Homage to the Sea of Fragrant Water, the Flower Treasury World.
Lanpen Offering: To the Dharma of the Ocean Treasury. (The assembly finishes chanting. The Rector, holding the incense burner, calls out loudly to the monks: "This day, all of you..."
I reverently prepare this *āraṇyaka-pātra* (lotus vessel) and prostrate with a sincere heart,

solely to make this offering to the countless treasures of the Saṅgha throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm— past, present, and future— who possess the three knowledges and eight liberations, the five fruits and six supernormal powers,
and who manifest their bodies here and in other realms, providing sustenance among humans and devas. I pray only that you will not forsake us.

Compassion. Accept this offering. (Recite three times "White" and perform three prostrations. Next, recite the verse for offering to the Sangha while sounding the drum and cymbals—either three times or once.
Homage to the Honored One among the Sovereign Assembly, who dwells with a tranquil mind within the sandalwood forest.
I pray that the Great Compassionate Sangha Jewel will accept this Ullambana offering. Homage to the Fragrant Water Ocean, the Flower Treasury World, and the Ullambana...

[Offering the basin to the Field of Merit Sangha] (After the chanting is finished, the Rector returns to his place. The Abbot offers incense. The Director of the Assembly strikes the leading chime. The entire assembly recites slowly in unison, saying:)
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, who abide eternally. Homage to the Dharma of the ten directions, which abides eternally. Homage to the Sangha of the ten directions, who abide eternally.
Homage to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha. Homage to Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhāsa Buddha.
Homage to the past Buddha Jñānakusuma-samādhi-vaśavarti-rāja. Homage to Viśuddhapadmanetra Buddha. Homage to Bahudharmakauśalya... [and so forth].
Homage to the Tathāgata Ratna. Homage to the Tathāgata Ratnavijaya. Homage to the Tathāgata Suvarṇavarṇa. Homage to the Tathāgata Vipulaśarīra. Homage to the Tathāgata Bhayaviśodhana.
Homage to the Tathāgata Amṛtarāja. Homage to the Tathāgata Amitābha. Homage to the Tathāgata Lokavipulavikrāntagāmbhīryatejorāja. Homage to...
The Buddha-spoken *Ullambana Sūtra*. Homage to the Greatly Compassionate Kṣitigarbha Rāja Bodhisattva.
Homage to the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Homage to all the Dharma-protecting Deva Bodhisattvas.
Homage to the Bodhisattvas of the Sacred Assembly of the Monastery. Homage to the Bodhisattvas of the Patriarchs of Successive Generations. Homage to the Ullambana Assembly.
[Offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Homage to the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas of the past who were free from attachment.

Homage to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Great Filial One. Homage to the holy and mundane, the hidden and manifest, and all venerable deities of the three realms. (After these three invocations, recite the *Bhaktābhivardhana-dhāraṇī* twenty-one times and the *Amṛta-dhāraṇī* seven times.

The text for the superior offering is as usual. Furthermore, after reciting the *Sarva-saṃpūjya-dhāraṇī* seven times, the Rector proceeds to the center, offers incense three times, performs three prostrations with robes spread out, bows in inquiry, and kneels long. With palms joined, the bell and drum are sounded, and they chant in unison:)

Homage to the Three Jewels, eternally abiding throughout the ten directions. (After reciting this three times, when the Rector proclaims the memorial text, the Abbot and the assembly shall all kneel with palms joined.)
I humbly reflect that when reciting the chapter on "The Taro and Mugwort" from the secular classics, it is difficult to fully express one's feelings toward boundless gratitude.

When contemplating the principles of the *Ullambana* (Lan-pen) in the sacred teachings, I dare to exhaust my devotion in cultivation and practice. I pray for the ferry of compassion to carry me across, and hereby extend my sincere sincerity. [Name of Village/Temple/Abbot, etc.

We, the assembly, earnestly reflect that we have long severed worldly ties and bid eternal farewell to our kin and loved ones; whether our venerable parents passed away prematurely, leaving us suddenly bereft...
At the ancestral sacrifices, some may already have star-like hair while still in the hall of their parents, forever deprived of the simple offerings of beans and water.

Lacking both the practice of benefiting oneself and others, they yet vainly receive the charity of men, harboring feelings of shame when looking upward and remorse when looking downward. I dare to set my heart upon the ultimate source:

since this physical life is entrusted to the kindness of one's parents, and instruction cannot exceed the virtue of one's teachers, these origins are infinite and shall not be cast aside for the sake of accumulated kalpas.
The ancestral lineage of this [tradition] seeks to universally deliver all beings through the perfect mind, leading all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm to transcendence.
Thus, I lay bare my sincere heart, drawing water and gathering flowers to present as offerings, and reverently take refuge in the precious volumes that spread their grace across heaven and earth.

May all suffering be utterly uprooted from the wheel of existence, and may all beings ascend the path to enlightenment. For this reason, beginning on the [day] of the [month] and concluding on the [day], the assembly of monks gathers in great numbers to ascend the precious hall.

They shall recite the [specific] sutra and perform the [specific] repentance ritual (or, if the great assembly has resolved to do so, each shall maintain their own recitation as they all ascend together).
We humbly pray that the compassionate light will shine forth, so that throughout the Sahā world, there is nowhere that is not illuminated; may the ocean of Dharma be vast and boundless.

May all sentient beings throughout the great earth be moistened with grace. May our many parents from past lives, our kinsmen across kalpas, our teachers and elders, and all our relatives—both those still living, may their merit and wisdom increase; and those who have passed away, may they attain high realization within the lotus womb.

May the excellent conditions for every single virtue flourish universally, and may the realms of suffering as numerous as the sands of the Ganges be equally benefited. Furthermore, we pray that the mountain monasteries remain peaceful and that the assembly of monks be at ease.
May all that is undertaken be fulfilled according to one’s wishes. This is the formal petition. Respectfully requesting the Three Jewels to bear witness, and so forth.
(If there are laymen or laywomen present in the assembly, one should further proclaim the petition for the prayers of the laity.)

I humbly submit that the teaching of the *Ullambana* was expounded as a fragrant legacy in Śrāvastī that has not yet faded; its merit transcends heaven and earth, and the filial conduct of Maudgalyāyana is ever praised.
If one wishes to provide for seven generations within the womb of the lotus, one should pay homage to the Three Bodies upon the flowered seat. [Insert place of origin, temple name].

May the assembly of noble men and women present here all bear this in mind. Let us chant the perfect sound of the single flavor, following the various lands and the various sentient beings, so that all may enter this auspicious assembly of equality.

We shall expound the filial principles for a thousand autumns. Whether they be virtuous men or faithful women, let them all follow the legacy of Śrāvastī and look up to the grand strategy of compassionate salvation, rescuing those in the utmost agony of being "hanging upside down. Therefore, in this month...
On a certain day, we respectfully encountered the grand assembly for the *Ullambana* festival being held at [Name] Temple.

To universally deliver all sentient beings who have received our kindness, we, [Names], deeply grieve for our boundless debt of gratitude and seek to offer a small measure of recompense for past roots of goodness. We personally attend this Dharma assembly to look up to you for compassionate salvation.

Therefore, each has prepared incense and ritual implements, presenting these meager offerings like wild herbs. Relying upon the majestic virtue of the *bhikṣus* and the radiant grace of the Triple Gem, may they be delivered across.
May the departed spirits be sustained by these merits for the benefit of those currently living. (All respective recitations should be recorded here one by one.

We humbly pray that their true compassion may respond to our invocation and that the sages may act according to our capacities, so that a single rain may nourish all universally and the great trichiliocosm may receive its moisture.

May my many parents throughout successive lives and all kinsmen and associates alike partake of these hidden blessings, together be liberated from the sufferings of the three evil realms, and upon passing away, realize the joy of rebirth in the heavens.
In the ancestral hall, we celebrate the spring of longevity; the five blessings renew daily, while the three calamities roll away like lightning.
Whatever prayers are offered, may they all be fulfilled. [The foregoing memorial, etc. (Upon the conclusion of the recitation, everyone stands up together. The assembly chants the hymn of praise:)
The five fruits and hundred flavors, fragrant and fresh in color, are offered to the Able One (Śākyamuni) at the Great Festival of Self-Indulgence (Pravāraṇā).

May you personally deliver us from the depths of samsara and universally save those in the dark realms. May the warmth of spring spread throughout the sands of the universe. Namo to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Offering.

(Chant three times. If this assembly lasts for seven days, five days, or three days, these two scrolls shall be transformed [into light] upon the conclusion of the dedication of merit. If one merely provides vegetarian offerings and does not perform recitations or hold an assembly, these scrolls shall be transformed immediately.

The assembly recites the Buddha’s name to escort the scrolls; the Abbot offers three libations of tea and performs prostrations. The Rector then leads the dedication of merit, saying: By the roots of goodness from this offering of the *Lanpen* (Bowl of Repose), I repay the labor and kindness of my parents.
May those still living enjoy boundless blessings, happiness, and longevity; May those who have passed away leave suffering behind and attain transcendence.

Sentient beings of the four modes of birth and nine states of existence, And suffering beings of the three evil paths and eight difficulties— May each repent their transgressions and wash away their blemishes, All receiving compassionate salvation to emerge from the depths of samsara. (When reciting this verse, the abbot performs three prostrations before the Buddha. Upon the conclusion of the inquiry verse, the guide-fan proceeds at the front.)

Small banners follow behind. Two *yuèzhòng* (choristers) ring the leading *qìng* (chime). Two attendants hold incense burners and carry incense trays. They escort the abbot back to his quarters (*fāngzhàng*). The assembly each returns to their respective places.

Once the assembly of monks has finished receiving the food offerings, the *yuèzhòng* (the one who delights the assembly) shall take the items for the *zìzī* (invitation to admonish) intended for the Sangha—namely, items bestowed by donors such as hand towels, hemp thread, shoes, socks, and the like—and place them in one location.
On this day, many stools, tables, bowls, and chopsticks are laid out outside the refectory (*zhāitáng*) to facilitate the guest masters receiving their meals. Its...
Serve the various fruits and vegetables equally to all, regardless of whether they are guests or long-term residents.

Once all matters in the refectory have been fully prepared, strike the *bang* for noon and ring the great bell three times. The Abbot puts on his robe and takes up his bowl, entering the refectory first to take his seat.
The assembly then puts on their robes and takes up their bowls to enter the hall. When everyone is seated, the attendants first serve the fruits; the Abbot then says: (Great...)
After the assembly of masters has first finished consuming the offered fruits and food, the cloud-board (yunban) is struck.
The attendants take the vegetables from the *urņa-patra* (lanpen) and the offered rice, and distribute them evenly among the vegetables of the great assembly.

Once the hall servers have served the vegetables and rice, the assembly raises their bowls and recites the mantra of offering, changing the phrase "May all beings... to: "May our parents of the past and seven generations transcend [to higher realms]; may those in the present..."

[May] both parents be forever free from illness and affliction; may they benefit themselves and others, receiving grace both in life and death, and may they forever leave the evil realms behind to attain ultimate, eternal bliss.
(Having finished this recitation, do not chant the Five Contemplations. The Abbot says: "The assembly shall first cultivate the mind of meditative concentration, and thereafter receive the food.

(The assembly enters contemplation, observing their own minds—within, without, and in between—and finds them all ungraspable. After sitting in silence for a short while, the Abbot says: "The assembly shall now receive the food. (When the assembly has finished eating, the Rector rises from his seat and takes...)

Regarding the items for the *pravāraṇā* (i.e., hand towels, socks, soles of shoes, thread, belts, and the like): first, offer one portion before the seat of the *upādhyāya*, and perform one prostration.

Furthermore, the assembly rejoices together. Taking the articles for the *pravāraṇā*, they divide them into two trays and distribute them, proceeding from top to bottom, moving eastward and westward respectively, according to the order of guests and residents, until the portions are evenly apportioned.
Once the distribution is complete, they return to their seats. After the meal has concluded, the *Sengzhi* (Monastery Manager) says:

"The fruits offered to the assembly for consumption and the articles for the *pravāraṇā* shall each be placed within one's bowl (or tucked inside the sleeve). The assembly rises in unison, holds up their bowls, and each returns.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding the Great Ullambana Fast, the Buddha’s decree for the lifting of the summer retreat means that even if one has not attained the four fruits [of the path] through ninety days of intensive practice during the single summer *anāgārika* retreat, one still gains meritorious achievement by making offerings on this day; its virtue is immense.
As for performing this practice year after year: it is because the love between parents and child is such that it never departs from the mind moment by moment;

thus, a filial son seeking to repay their kindness must provide offerings without ceasing year after year. Furthermore, the intent of the sutra is to take the uprooting of suffering as the primary means of repaying kindness, which differs from worldly custom.
Worldly filial piety consists in complying with their emotions, whereas this [practice] additionally accords with their true nature. Worldly...
Filial piety [of the worldly kind] relies solely upon the physical form; this [Buddhist practice], however, relies upon both the form and the spirit.

That people of the world do not understand or believe this, and instead claim that the Śākya school lacks loyalty to sovereign and kinship, is likewise the result of failing to examine the matter deeply. Indeed, the Way of following one's nature and relying on the spirit—
This is indeed difficult to clarify. Yet, in the relationship between physical form and inner sentiment, how could it be far removed from humanity?
Consider, for instance, when the Buddha Śākyamuni visited his mother in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, or escorted his father’s coffin upon his back—what kind of filial piety was this?
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* establishes filial piety as a precept, stating: "Filial obedience is the dharma of the ultimate Way. The *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* says: "Ordinary people..."
Serving Heaven, Earth, and the spirits is not equal to being filial toward one's two parents; the two parents are the supreme deities.

According to the Vinaya, if one’s parents do not grant permission, one is not allowed to leave the household life. The *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* begins by extolling the filial support of one’s parents.

They constitute the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood. The *Sūtra on the Great Requital of Kindness* and the *Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground* extensively explain the gravity of parental kindness and the methods of filial piety.
The *Sūtra of Śyāma’s Son* fully manifests acts of filial devotion. Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva made his vow to deliver sentient beings because of his filial piety toward his mother.
Furthermore, when our Buddha instructed his disciples, he stated that parents are equal to a Bodhisattva in the stage of succession to Buddhahood (*abhiṣeka*).
And so forth. It is permitted for a disciple to reduce the resources for their robes and alms bowl in order to support their parents.

If the parents possess right faith, one may give to them as much as they wish; if they lack right faith, one may give only a small amount. If one has no property of one's own, it is permitted to transform one’s assets to provide for them.
Within the *Kanjur*, exhortations to filial piety appear repeatedly and in abundance; how could this not be because filial piety is regarded as the foremost duty?

There is nothing that can restrain it; its dharma-benefits are extraordinary. How could they be limited merely to the abundance of the five tripods or the diligent practice of the three ways of filial piety?
Thus we know that regarding the principle of teaching filial piety, only Buddhism is uniquely profound.

During the period of repentance (*chánqī*), when entering the latrine or bathing, one must not allow clean robes (*jìngyī*) to come into contact with soiled robes (*chù yī*).
First, remove the clean robes and clean shoes and place them in a clean location. Then, put on the soiled robes and shoes to enter the latrine.

After washing and rinsing, and having finished washing the hands, remove the soiled robes and shoes to enter the bath. Finally, put on the clean robes and shoes to return to the hall and wash the hands.
Wash your face and rinse your mouth before entering the altar. During the period of this retreat, do not engage with outsiders, nor speak privately with anyone.
Furthermore, do not read other scriptural texts. For the superior offerings, use flavorful cooked food;

once the offering is completed, collect it immediately and wipe the offering table clean, leaving only incense, flowers, and pure water. These provisions for the fast are established by the Buddha’s command.

During the incense periods, all must diligently cultivate meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*) and must not indulge in negligence or mental torpor (*styāna-middha*).

If one is unable to enter meditation during the sitting period, it is permissible either to silently recite sūtras and dhāraṇīs or to chant the names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. One is strictly forbidden from being dissolute, engaging in idle chatter, laughing, or sleeping.
Upon hearing the bell strike, one shall immediately attend to the calls of nature and perform ablutions; as soon as the long bell is heard, one shall proceed according to the sequence.

Thus, on this day, one offers the *lǎnpén* (lotus bowl) and reverently honors the Triple Gem; at night, one bestows *hùshí* (offering of food) to universally succor ghosts and spirits.

The Summer Retreat Self-Examination (After the assembly has chanted together, the Rector joins his palms and announces in a loud voice).

The summer retreat and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony are truly the essential path of the Buddha-dharma; the confession of faults and the repentance of transgressions are indeed the excellent strategy for monastic practice.
To cultivate wholesome causes and realize the perfect fruit of bliss—without relying on the vessel of precepts and meditative concentration, how could one reach the shore of *nirvāṇa*?

On this day, the sixteenth of the seventh month, coinciding with the occasion when our Buddha concluded his summer retreat (*varṣā*) and ended his formal confinement, the assembled monks gathered at the precious hall to recite the secret scriptures and release themselves from the disciplinary restrictions. From this day forward, those who violate the four grave offenses—
Treading upon the ten evil deeds, acting with unrestrained self-indulgence, giving rise to the three poisons, and committing the seven grave transgressions;
following what others say, whether seen, heard, or suspected—one must repent for each and every instance. Whether through body, speech, or mind, one must repeatedly perform confession.

Bound by the faculties and their objects, entangled by sounds and forms, one accumulates a multitude of karmic offenses that block the source of the mind. If these are not proclaimed, by what means can they be cleansed?
Purification. A special door of *sāmāyika* (confession and repentance) is opened to extensively cleanse the transgressions of oneself and others.

"Confessing" refers to repenting for what has already been done; "regretting" refers to vowing not to commit it again in the future. Therefore it is said: "I pray that my past transgressions may be extinguished; as for transgressions yet to be committed, I dare not do them again.

Thus, upon the conclusion of the retreat, we perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) and repentance. (After the announcement, one prostrates. The *vinaya-dhara* returns to his place. The *yuèzhòng* strikes the introductory *qiǎng*. The assembly sings in unison:)
"Venerable Sirs, attend with one-pointed mind. Today is the day of the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha. I, the bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *pravāraṇā*.
If you see, hear, or suspect any transgression in me, Venerable Elders, out of compassion, please speak to me. If I see, hear, or suspect a transgression, I shall confess it according to the Dharma.

(When the three recitations are finished—or when each has been spoken—the assembly recites the Great Compassion Mantra three times and circumambulates the hall. Having finished, each returns to their original position. The *karmadāna* intones the verse of confession, and the assembly chants:)

All evil karma created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion, Produced by body, speech, and mind— I confess all roots of transgression. Oṃ. Trātāgata svāhā. (Recite three times.
Having finished kneeling and reciting the Great Confession Text, raise the voice for the dedication and praise: The summer retreat has concluded; the Buddha-fruit is perfectly realized. All...
Karmic obstructions are suddenly purified like ice melting; the nature of the ocean of awakening is perfectly clear and still.

May the light of wisdom universally bestow its grace upon the entire dharma realm. *Namo* to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Seeking Repentance (recite three times). Next, recite the Verse of Dedication: "The meritorious practice of the extraordinary resolution at the end of the summer retreat... (and so forth).

While this verse is being chanted, the abbot prostrates three times before the Buddha and performs the ritual of inquiry (*wèn-xùn*). Upon the completion of the verse, he immediately returns to the Abbot’s Quarters (*fāngzhǎng*). The assembly strikes the *yǐn-qìng* (leading stone gong), and they prostrate three times before the Buddha, then proceed to the Abbot’s Quarters to pay homage at his feet.

Pay respects to the Abbot; if excused, return directly to the hall. That evening, after the evening recitation is finished, the retreat concludes. The Rector (Vina) strikes the lead chime (yin-ghing), proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters, and conducts the rounds of the quarters (xun-liao).

Matters such as requesting leave follow the same protocol as the conclusion of the winter retreat (unless it is based on the Ullambana Festival, in which case the retreat concludes and leave is requested on the fifteenth day).

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding the "Liberation at the End of Summer" (Pravāraṇā), when bhikṣus first enter the summer retreat at the beginning of the season, they observe the *kaṭhina* and remain in seclusion without begging for food;

this is called "resting during the summer. Now, as the period has reached its full term and the retreat is concluded, those who know they have committed transgressions are permitted to confess them freely, while those who do not recognize their own faults allow the Saṃgha to point out their errors as it sees fit; hence it is called "Self-Liberation" (Pravāraṇā). Someone asked Master Lianchi:
[The questioner] asked: "To permit the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) for the Saṃgha—what does this mean? The Master replied: "One who has faults is like a sick person;

one who points out those faults is like a king of physicians. To conceal one's illness and loathe the physician is called great folly. Thus, we know that it is right to acknowledge one's faults and have them pointed out. Another said:
"It may be acceptable for one to point out one's own faults, but when others point them out, one should not fear that it will give rise to contention."

Question: Is this correct? Answer: The Vinaya records that when a monk commits a transgression, a fellow monk informs the Buddha. The Buddha summons the offending monk and reprimands him in various ways, subsequently establishing the rules of the Vinaya.
In monastic communities today, direct admonition is practiced daily; this is based on that precedent. This follows the Buddha’s regulations.

This does not arise from personal bias; how could there be grounds for contention? Furthermore, according to worldly conventions, it is said that a ruler has ministers who remonstrate with him, a father has sons who remonstrate with him, and a scholar has friends who remonstrate with him.
Thus it is said: "A founding monarch rewards ministers who offer direct counsel," and "The sagely sovereign established the 'trees of slander' (feibang zhi mu).
How much more so for one who has become a monk and cultivates the supramundane Dharma—should he not rely on friends to perfect his virtue?

If one does not speak straightforwardly regarding evil, then those who are slanderous, sycophantic, and flatterers will arrive. To reject counsel and gloss over one's faults harms virtue and ruins one’s enterprise;
this is no small failing. Therefore, he again composed a verse: "In the past, we were at ease together, like golden and camphor flowers entwined.

Now, we are at ease apart, like thorns growing on a bush. With mouths speaking of others' transgressions, anger gives rise to strife; Facing the Vinaya with our own eyes, we are blind and do not see. How [can this be]?
How strange that the True Dharma is declining and the armies of Māra are flourishing! The Master of Yunqi lets out a long sigh;
on one hand it grieves my heart, and on the other it consoles my resolve. Do you not see? Because he cherished the ritual, Confucius once told Dan-er Ci that the sheep should be preserved.
The *Secret Essentials of the Chan School* says: Formerly, the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and spread forth [the teaching].
The Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao). Bianxing said: "I have just now rebuked you before the assembly; are you not troubled in your heart?
He replied: "I recall that seven kalpas ago, I was born in the Land of Constant Peace and Bliss, where my teacher was the Wise One Moon-Purity."
"Record this for me: before long, you shall realize the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin. At that time, a Bodhisattva named Mahāprabha appeared in the world.
Because I was old, I leaned on a staff as I went to pay my respects to him. The Master rebuked me, saying, "You honor your son and slight your father; how can you be so base?
At that moment, I considered myself without fault and requested the Master to show me where I had erred. The Master said, "When you prostrated to the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha..."
Śāriputra, because I leaned my staff against the wall and drew upon it the face of the Buddha, I lost two fruits of the path due to this arrogance.

Since I have taken personal responsibility for my faults and repented, even when hearing various evil words, they have been like the wind or an echo; how much more so now that I have obtained the drinking of the unsurpassed nectar of immortality?
Yet, on the contrary, one gives rise to feverish distress. Alas! This may truly be called a mirror for those who indulge themselves in self-indulgence.
The practice of *zazen* is divided into five parts.

The *jiānzhí* (duty supervisor) collects the cushions from the central area and opens the door. The attendant performs the prostrations to the ten directions.

Return to your positions. The supervisor on duty shall close the gate. Upon hearing the sound of the wooden clapper, the officer on duty shall strike the "fish" once to signal the beginning of *xiaojing* (minor silence) [or it may be omitted].

The incense-burner attendant sweeps and cleans before the Buddha and at the abbot’s seat. When the gruel meal is finished, he returns to the hall, distributes the incense, and requests the incense-brushes.

When the duty-holder sees that half of the incense stick has burned away, he strikes two wooden boards and one bell. The assembly stands still, waiting for the incense to burn down by one *cùn*. The duty-holder then proceeds to the northeast.

[The bell] strikes the corner. The *cuibǎn* (small wooden clapper) is struck twice. When one inch remains on the incense stick, the *weina* calls for the assembly to rise; he raises the incense board and urges them to walk.
The head official supervising the incense follows closely, harmonizing with him. When six-sevenths of the incense remain, the *weina* swings the incense board downward.

When the time comes for the "striking the fish" (the signal to begin), everyone stands still. The supervisor pulls back the door curtain and, together with the incense-distributor, proceeds to the entrance.
They stand one on each side for a brief moment, then perform a counter-clockwise circumambulation once.
The *vinaya* master returns to his original position and strikes the incense board. The supervisor enters and arranges the meditation cushions; the incense-distributor strikes the incense-rattle.
Three rounds. When everyone has finished their brief rest, they return to their positions. The attendant on duty closes both side doors. Again, he strikes the incense-dispensing mallet once more.
The attendant lowers the door curtains. The incense-dispensing master returns to the hall, proceeding in order, and hands over the incense-dispensing plaque.

Strike the desk once to inquire after the assembly. Proceed to the center of the hall to inquire after them. Insert the incense sticks into the burner. Return to the center to inquire once more, then go back to your respective positions.

The attendant on duty puts on his robe and takes up his implements. Strike three wooden blocks followed by one bell to signal the cessation of silence, and perform the prostrations to the ten directions.

Perform three prostrations before the Buddha. The Director of the Assembly strikes the lead chime four times. After the inquiry, exit the hall. Turn over the "Silence" signboard. Exit from the east side and enter from the west side. Perform an inquiry.
Proceed to the seat of the Vimalakīrti and perform one prostration before the Preceptor. Return to your position. The Duty Monitor collects the meditation cushions and locks the door.
The person responsible for the saddle-cloth spreads it, while the Duty Officer pushes the incense tray. The Incense Distributor leaves his position and proceeds to the center.
The *yāng* (attendant) asks after his health. He takes the incense board (*xiāngbǎn*) from the eastern side and descends on the western side with one bow.

He performs one circuit in a counter-clockwise direction until he reaches the *zhāngzhí kànxiāng* (the official in charge of the incense). He leads [the official] to the incense stand. The *yuèzhòng* (director of communal harmony) strikes the *yǐnqìng* (leading chime) once, and the small silence (*xiǎojìng*) is opened.

(This section should have been moved to after the handing over of the incense board. The *wéinà* (chant leader) strikes the incense board three times and releases his legs. The *xúnxīng shī* (incense-circulating master) hands over the incense-circulating tablet (*xúnxīng pái*), goes to the center to perform a greeting, and hands it over.
Incense Board. The incense distributor steps out of his position, bows in greeting at the center, and proceeds from the west side upward to request the incense tongs.

He returns to the east side downward to bow in greeting, circumambulates half a circuit clockwise, and strikes the incense board once. The attendant strikes the *jingxing* (walking) signal two times for the fish-shaped pattern.
The walking incense lasts for half an incense stick; then he strikes the standing board once. For the standing incense, he counts the number of inches and strikes the urging board twice.

[The bell] strikes once. When the incense for walking meditation is finished, the fish-shaped gong is struck once; this is the signal for the "withdrawal and release" (choujie). The duty supervisor rolls up the door curtains and waits for the incense for the distribution of seats to be offered.
The incumbent strikes the fish-shaped gong three times to signal the cessation of silence. The duty supervisor closes the doors. The incense board is requested as described above.
In the afternoon, at the third watch, the wooden fish gong is struck. The attendant strikes it once. A minor silence is observed. The *vinaya-dhara* strikes the incense board three times.
They put on their shoes and finish dressing. The *yuèzhòng* strikes the lead chime once. Each person returns to their respective position and stands. The attendant then steps forward.
[The abbot] takes his seat. He performs prostrations facing the ten directions. The name-tablet is turned over. The assembly leader strikes the *yin-磬* (guiding gong) with joy.

The duty monitor (*jianzhi*) strikes the wooden board (*ban*) three times; the bell is struck three times (the *qin* is also struck three times). The assembly performs one prostration to the Buddha and settles into their seats. Upon hearing the call for the board to be struck, they strike the *yin-磬* as they proceed to the hall.

When the meal is finished and it is time to conclude the midday fast (*jiezhai*), the duty monitor, the incense-lamp attendant, and the water server return to the hall first to open the doors and wait for the rest of the assembly to return and complete the gathering.

Ceremony: Request the distribution of incense as before. The person on duty strikes one board and one bell; the "Incense Fish" signal is struck twice. A single stick of incense is lit for the formal offering of fragrance.

The assembly rinses their mouths and finishes chewing the willow twigs (*yāshācī*). After walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), the supervisor collects the willow twigs and the cups, washing them with hot water.
When the person on duty observes that half a stick of incense remains, they strike two boards and one bell. The assembly stands in formation. The supervisor...
When it is time for the tea service, wait for the *weina* (ritual director) to return to his position and strike the incense board. The assembly sits down as they please.

The incense distributor leans the incense-distributing bamboo fan against the front of the Buddha altar, and then distributes the cups. The supervising official serves tea three or four rounds. When the tea service is finished:

The incense distributor and the attendant collect the cups. Once the door is closed, the attendant washes the cups in the attendant’s quarters and returns to the hall for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*).

When the incense offering is finished, the duty-holder strikes the *chūjie* (release) signal once, like a fish leaping. The assembly stands as before; the *vinaya-dhara* returns to his position and strikes the incense board.
The attendant opens the door, pulls back the curtain, spreads the meditation mats, and the incense distributor performs three rounds of distribution. This is the minor relief (*svalpa-vihāra*).
Seeing that the purification room is empty, he again incenses it once more. He returns to the hall and, as before, distributes the incense.

The duty monitor collects the door curtains and returns to his position. The duty officer strikes three wooden blocks and one bell. When performing the ritual prostrations, the attendant for the assembly rings the lead chime four times to signal the cessation of silence.
The duty monitor collects the meditation cushions and closes the doors. The duty officer pushes back the incense tray, and the incense distributor acts as before.
Circulating the Incense. When the incense reaches its destination, the person on duty strikes the lead chime once to signal the opening of the small period of silence.

The incense-circulator hands over his duties as before. The supervisor opens the door and strikes two pots of tea. The incense-circulator distributes the cups, beginning from the position of the Assistant Abbot (Wei-na).

If the Abbot is present in the hall, five cups are distributed; the Great Joyous Assembly (Da Yuezhong) serves tea to the Abbot, and then the cups are distributed again to the positions of the Joyous Assembly according to the number of persons.

The cups are distributed, beginning with the head of the assembly. They are set out one pair at a time. When the attendant for tea arrives, he stirs the tea several times with a stirring stick and distributes it four or five rounds.
Once everyone has finished their tea, the incense-circulator and the attendant collect the cups. The incense-distributor proceeds according to the previous protocol.
The duty-holder strikes the fish-shaped gong twice; the incense for walking meditation burns for half an incense-stick, and then the station-board is struck once.

Pause briefly for a moment of incense. Strike the *cuibǎn* (rushing board) twice. When the *jingxingxiang* (incense for walking meditation) is finished, strike the *yú* (fish-shaped bell) once for the *choujie* (relaxation).

Wait for the incense tablet for the distribution of incense to be passed; the incumbent then strikes the *yú* three times to signal the cessation of silence. The incense is distributed and the doors are closed. Once the incense period is complete, open the small hall for tea.
For the walking meditation and other activities, follow the same procedure as when sitting in formal meditation.

During the fourth evening service, upon hearing the sounding of the evening wooden gong, the incumbent strikes the "fish" bell once and the minor silence is opened. The director of the assembly strikes the introductory chime;

the assembly stands, and the head of the class steps forward from his position with hands clasped. Thereafter, the director of the assembly strikes the introductory chime together for twelve strokes, while the supervising official strikes the wooden board.

Three strikes on the bell (three strikes on the chime). The attendant on duty shall turn over the signboard and perform the ritual. Upon hearing the sounding of the wooden board (*yunban*), the assembly shall pass through the hall.

The attendant on duty and the supervising official shall sweep the floor within the hall. The attendant on duty shall arrange the meditation cushions (spreading the straw mats). After the morning gruel is finished, they shall return to the hall. While the community is chewing *yangzhi* (willow twigs), the attendant on duty and the supervising official shall eat their second meal.
When this is completed, each shall don their outer robe (*sāṃghāṭī*) and perform three prostrations before the Buddha. Each shall then return to his own seat. The attendant on duty...

Strike the *baogong* bell three times. The attendant on duty collects the meditation cushions (*pútuán*, i.e., *zōngqiān*). Wait for one strike of the *yǐnqìng*. The assembly leaves their seats and stands in formation.

The attendant on duty strikes the *baogong* bell three times; the assembly enters the hall. When the recitation is nearly finished, after the Three Refuges, the attendant on duty, the incense lamp keeper, and the water server first return to open the doors.
The attendant on duty lowers two single-layered curtains. The assembly returns to the hall and performs the full prostrations. At this point, the ritual is concluded.

When the first board and bell strike, the *yú* (fish-shaped gong) is struck once for the "break" (*chūjiè*). The assembly gathers their robes and performs the break. The attendant on duty stands outside the gate, waiting for the door curtain to be lowered;
once it is raised, the assembly returns to the hall and all take their places on the mats. The attendant on duty strikes the *yú* three times to signal the end of the period of silence.
Returning to his own station, he sits and lights one stick of incense. The attendant on duty closes the front and rear gates and leans against his mat.
Circumambulate once in the direction of the ritual sequence. Then, at the window, go to the upper platform to rest and recuperate. One who is on duty shall not rest.

At the fifth watch of the night incense, if one on duty does not see the bright light outside the window, strike the fish-shaped drum once. Open the small meditation hall. Go to the lower platform beneath the incense and lamps to light them.
At each location, the lamps are lit. The attendant on duty rolls up both side curtains and opens the central door.

The *vinaya-dhara* strikes the incense board three times, and the assembly descends from their seats. The attendant on duty prepares one stick of sitting incense; the incense-bell is struck twice for the rising incense.

The incense distributor follows the previous procedure to request the bamboo fan for distributing incense. When the attendant on duty observes that the incense is half-burnt, he strikes the second board, and the assembly stands.
The Abbot enters *samādhi*. The attendant strikes the tea gong, and the Rector returns to his position. The incense board is struck, and everyone sits down as they please.
The incense distributor leans the bamboo whisk against the front of the Buddha altar and distributes the cups to each person’s hand. The attendant serves the tea for one or two rounds.
Then, the incense distributor and the attendant each collect their respective sides. The incense distributor takes the incense and holds the whisk in hand, proceeding clockwise for half a circuit.
Circumambulate once more. Strike the desk once again. The attendant strikes the *cuī* board twice. Walk in meditation (*jīngxíng*). The supervisor closes the door.
When the incense reaches [the altar], the attendant strikes the *chōujiě* fish-pattern once. The assembly stands still. Proceed according to the previous ritual. The supervisor opens the door.

Draw the curtain. Enter and arrange the meditation cushions. Distribute incense as before and close the door. The duty officer calls for silence. Perform the prostrations. The attendant strikes the *yinjing* four times.
The supervising officer closes the door. The incense patrol requests the incense board. When the incense is finished, strike the *yinjing* once.
Open the "minor silence. Hand over the incense board to the patrol. Release the incense for the evening meal. Upon finishing the meal, the duty officer strikes the fish-shaped bell twice.

When half a stick of incense has been burned during walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), the station board (*zhàn bǎn*) is struck once; the incense is then paused for one *cùn*. The urging board (*cuī bǎn*) is struck twice, and walking meditation resumes.

When the incense is finished, the fish-shaped gong (*yú*) is struck once, followed by a period of release (*chōujiè*). The duty monitor (*jiānzhí*) pulls back the door curtain and awaits the handover of the dispersal incense board.

The monitor then strikes the fish-gong three times to signal the end of the session (*zhìjìng*). The dispersal incense board is used to close the doors. Once the incense is finished, the duty monitor strikes the fish-gong once.

[The bell] strikes low. Open the small silence (*kṣaṇa*). Patrol the incense and strike the wooden board (*phala*). Open the door. The *yuèzhòng* (joyful assembly) rings the introductory chime (*yǐnqìng*) to open the great silence (*dàjìng*).

The incumbent performs the rites. The supervisor strikes the board three times; this concludes. Then, as before, distribute the incense and raise it, saying "... and so forth, up until the sixth branch of incense.

Strike the *chōujiě* (relaxation) signal and the fish-shaped gong. The supervisor spreads the straw mat (*zōngwàn*) and rings the bell to strike for the three prostrations of worship to the Buddha. The supervisor...

Upon arriving, two single-layer curtains are opened. The assembly removes their upper bedding. The incense and lamp master lights the glass lamps and extinguishes the lamps in the *jianzhiliáo* (the office of the duty officer).
The duty officer closes the front and rear gates, then performs one circuit in order, closes the lattice doors, extinguishes the lamp before the Buddha, and finally ascends to his bedding.
Thus the day’s affairs are concluded; this is the constant rule for every day. Those who have newly entered or are junior students must [follow this].
You must memorize this thoroughly so that you may practice it in rotation. However, if these five sections were recorded in full detail, the text would be half as long again;
since this is an abbreviated version, it is easy to master with precision, while the remainder can be understood through visual inspection and mental reflection.

Regulations for the Meditation Hall (Total of Thirty-two Articles) Ancient rules have fallen into neglect, and indolence has become the prevailing custom. The current malaise is manifold; therefore, upholding them requires secrecy.

Although these are established public cases (*kōan*), they must be known by the entire assembly. When practice and understanding correspond, one will have no cause for shame before the ancestral school. This is the Way and its Virtue.

Providing for both [the clergy and the laity], this will be of benefit to those of us who have recently entered the study. It is incumbent upon all of us to be of one mind and together observe these rules.

Those who cause discord regarding the striking of the bell and board during the morning assembly must go on rounds through the quarters and kneel before the incense burner to perform their prostrations.

Those who refuse to comply must leave the hall. Those who instigate disputes or provoke quarrels must exchange fist-blows; those who break out into verbal abuse must leave the hall. Except in cases of old age, illness, or official business, those who abscond from their private quarters shall be punished.
The sign shall be hung; no one is permitted to remain. Those who engage in idle chatter or miscellaneous conversation inside or outside the meditation hall shall be penalized.

Those who make noise or cause a disturbance during periods of stillness that alarms the assembly shall be penalized. Those who refuse to comply shall be expelled from the hall. Regarding the striking of the fish-shaped gong and the small wooden blocks, those who are irregular or unclear in their timing shall be penalized.
Those who disregard their fundamental duty by whispering to one another shall receive a heavy penalty. Above.

For the morning hall *chansong* (small *chan*) and other services, each participant shall don their ceremonial robes and carry their ritual implements, assembling in the Dharma Hall and standing in orderly succession.

If there is an inquiry, one must step forward; no one shall be out of place. Those who violate this shall be penalized. Until the term is completed, leaving the hall is not permitted, except for those serving as public officers.
Those who take private leave shall be penalized; those who fail to comply shall receive severe punishment. Those who secretly peruse the monastic regulations shall be penalized.

Those who sleep privately at improper times shall be punished. Those who enter or exit without informing the administrative officers shall be punished. Those who fail to attend the periods of silence shall be punished.

Those who fail to attend the periods of incense-offering or seated meditation shall be punished. Those who cause errors or neglect their duties as incense-distributors or incense-inspectors shall be punished.
Those who fail to clarify the handover of duties on their watch day shall be punished. Those who damage utensils shall be punished and required to pay restitution.

Those who disregard their own practice and recklessly display intellectual "sparks" (ji-feng) shall be punished. Those who arbitrarily compose *nian-song* verses or offer critical commentaries on public cases (*gong-an*) shall be punished.
When entering or exiting the hall, one must proceed in proper order; those who violate this shall be penalized.

Should anyone skip their station, disrupt the seating order, pass straight through the hall, or enter the quarters without business, they shall receive severe punishment. Those who privately borrow items from within the hall to take outside shall be penalized.
Those who cause disturbances, fail in decorum, or refuse to heed the admonitions of the administrators shall be penalized. Those who remain insubordinate shall be expelled from the hall.
Those who do not follow the assembly during walking meditation, sitting, recitation, receiving food, or going on work detail shall be penalized.

Those who scrutinize the faults of others or disturb and disorder the community shall receive heavy punishment. Those who fail to strike the "arousing board" (sengban) to admonish those who are drowsy or distracted shall be penalized.
Those who intentionally succumb to drowsiness shall be penalized. Those who quarrel over the arousing board shall be penalized. Those who are disobedient shall be penalized.
Those who leave the hall after the admonition, or whose drowsiness remains as before, shall stand for *can*. If their drowsiness persists despite repeated admonitions, they shall kneel for *can*.
Those who refuse to comply shall leave the hall. If one walks back and forth, talks, laughs, sneezes, or spits, or makes noise with their shoes or belongings, they shall be punished.
Those who refuse to comply shall leave the hall. Upon leaving the hall, one must not fail to wear the *chik* (straight robe).

Those who wear patched robes (commonly called *haiching*, also known as *pianshan* or *paozi*) shall be punished. Those who go abroad on business and fail to return within the prescribed period shall be punished.
When honored guests enter the hall, each must occupy their assigned seat; failure to maintain proper decorum shall be punished.

Entering the guest hall without permission or engaging in idle chatter with others shall be punished severely. After the period of Great Stillness has begun, those who speak or laugh shall be punished;
those on duty in the administrative quarters shall be punished, as shall those who wander idly into the outer quarters. Those who privately prepare food or drink shall be punished.

(Addendum) Those who smoke shall be severely punished. Those who disturb the silence shall be punished. Incense patrol officers who show favoritism, or who use public office for private gain, or who strike others out of malice, shall be punished;
those who violate these rules shall be severely punished. For minor ailments, leave of three days shall be granted.
Those who are gravely ill shall leave the hall for convalescence; they must not remain intentionally to hinder the assembly.
Those who violate this shall be penalized. The above regulations concern one's fundamental practice. Should you fail to comply, you will lose the benefits of the good Dharma yourself.
May all members of the community take heed and exert themselves. Dated [Year, Month, Day]. Recorded again by the Abbot, [Name].
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The meditation hall is the place where sages and worthies are forged; it is the field for realizing life and transcending death.
If one wishes to penetrate the ultimate barrier above, there is no way to enter it except through this. This refers to the saying: "The ten directions gather together;
each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas; with an empty mind, one returns as a top graduate. Since one studies non-action...
Therefore, you should immediately withdraw from all conditions and quiet the mind, applying yourself with single-minded diligence to investigation and study.

If you remain lax and continue to follow your own whims, not only will you be unable to learn non-action (*wuwei*), but I fear it will instead increase your heterodox views; this is what is meant by "lacking rules and regulations."
One cannot restrain one's depravity; there is no diligent effort; one cannot fulfill one’s resolve—this is precisely it. As the Sūtra says: "From precepts arises concentration;

from concentration issues forth wisdom. These two phrases encompass everything. The *Secret Essentials of the Chan School* states: "In the past, there was a son of noble family who left home to study the Way.
Upagupta expounded the essentials of the Dharma for him, and he immediately perceived the Truth, attaining the stage of a Stream-enterer."
The Srotāpanna thought to himself, "I have severed the three fetters; what more need I seek or strive for? I may wander with ease and mastery for up to seven more births.
The Venerable One told him, "The nature of birth and death is utterly loathsome and vile, just like excrement and filth."
Everything was foul-smelling. He then took them to a village of caṇḍālas, where he saw a young boy whose body was covered with malignant sores from which worms and blood issued together;
he was in great agony. [The Buddha] asked, "Bhikṣu, do you see this child? This young boy was a srotāpanna.
Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world, there was an arhat who suffered slightly from an itch and scratched it.
When he made this sound, the *karmadāna* (monastic official) said angrily, "Do you have maggots and sores on your body now?
You ought to go out toward the village of *caṇḍālas*! The Arhat spoke, saying, "Now you have committed an offense; do not utter such words.
At that time, the *karmadāna* immediately repented and practiced with diligence, attaining the stage of *srotāpanna*. Later, however, he became indolent and ceased seeking further progress.
He proceeded upward and was thus born into this family, undergoing such suffering and affliction.
Moving forward a short distance further, he saw a man being burned by fire, his body scorched and mangled, his agony unbearable. As he advanced even further, he again saw another person.
Having violated the king’s laws, he was impaled upon a great wooden stake, crying out in lamentation and experiencing extreme suffering.
At that time, the Venerable One asked the bhikṣu, "Do you see these two people? The bhikṣu replied, "Yes, I have seen them.
The Venerable One said, "The person before [you] here is a Sakṛdāgāmin; the one seen behind him is an..."
They were all *anāgāmins*, yet they were all indolent and made no effort to advance further; therefore, they were born among humans and subjected to such bitter suffering.
For this reason, you should now apply yourself with diligence and seek liberation early.

Having heard this, the bhikṣu practiced and studied day and night, and before long he attained the path of an *arhat*. Alas! According to these several individuals, all possess the fruits of the Path.
Because they consider a little attainment to be sufficient, they become indolent and lazy, and thus fall into the retribution of suffering.

As for the Chan practitioners of today, as soon as they have spent a few winters [in training], they immediately claim, "I am a veteran practitioner. Why do you then exert yourself so urgently in this?
You do not know whether this "veteran practitioner" has ever realized any fruit of the path. If you do not cultivate with diligence, there will be great retribution of suffering awaiting you.

In the first ten days of the tenth lunar month, during the early part of the "Almond Winter," the *vina* (chant leader) orders the *yuezhong* (attendants) to take their turns as *dangzhi* (on-duty), *jianzhi* (supervising on-duty), *xiangdeng* (incense lamp keeper), and *si shui* (water steward).

They shall sweep the quarters, post the bed tickets, plaster the doors and windows, provide straw for each bed, and attend to matters such as gathering up the incense boards, name tablets, and divination sticks.
The Guest Hall Attendant and the Rector shall pre-arrange the names of all those in the temple, opening up their pure precepts and the duration of their seniority.

After presenting these for the Abbot’s review and finalizing the appointments to the administrative offices, they shall command the Record Keeper to draft the appointment slips. The Secretary shall write them out in formal, upright characters;
the two sets, for the East and West halls, shall be arranged in strict order without any confusion of sequence. These shall be placed upon a cloth mat and secured with a ruler. Upon reaching...
The fourteenth day. At early morning congee, the Guest Hall hangs a notice (the notice reads: "Affixing the List"). The Attendant places two trays of list-slips upon the Dharma-seat.
At the second board-strike, the great bell is struck three times; the assembly first gathers and sits in meditation.
The Rector orders the current and supervising duty-holders to spread mats on either side of the Buddha’s seat. All the hall masters then settle their belongings upon the mats.

[The Abbot] ascends. A seat for the Guest Master (the Abbot) is prepared before the Buddha. The Rector (Vina) announces: "Today we invite the Venerable Master to serve as the teacher for the great assembly;

please sign the register. Having finished this announcement, the two classes of officials stand in formation. The Attendant (Yuezhong) strikes the introductory chime and leads two pure monks to the Abbot’s quarters.

The assembly says, "The Abbot has taken his seat. The Attendant says, "Please unfold your sitting cloths and prostrate to the Venerable Master. After the prostrations are completed, he says, "At the end, first..."
[Action: Two attendants precede [the abbot], holding the seating chart and ticket; the whisk and staff follow behind. Upon entering the hall, the abbot bows to the Buddha and ascends the seat.

When the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) recites the eulogy, [the abbot] approaches the seat, offers three incense sticks, performs three prostrations with the full ritual implements (*dagu*), and rises from the prostrations to return to his position.
This continues until the third invocation of "The Clouds Gather" (*yun lai ji pusa*) is completed. The *vinaya-dhara* then says: "I prostrate to the Honored One..."

After the assembly has performed the three prostrations with their ritual implements fully displayed, the two *yuèzhòng* (chant leaders) strike the *yǐnqìng* (leading chime) three times in succession.

The Abbot delivers a sermon. When the sermon is finished, the assembly stands together. The head of the assembly stands alone with his *dāntiáo* (single-layered robe), while the Abbot stands beside him. Once they have stood together, the *wéinà* (ritual director) says:
"The Great Assembly bows in thanks to the *héshàng* (Venerable Master). The Abbot exits the hall. The *wéinà* speaks again: "The Great Assembly escorts the *héshàng*. If...

The *mian* (exemption) is then terminated. For the remaining matters, the *weina* (rector) posts notices for the two orders (*liangxu*). The sequence of seating is determined by the rank of their administrative duties;

among those with equal duties, it is determined by the seniority of their precepts. Within the hall, each person arranges their luggage according to the order of their own name and rank on the roster.

After the evening service is concluded, they go to the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to express thanks for the posted roster. Following the light meal (*xiaoshi*), the incense is announced (*gaoxiang*), as detailed in the preceding section on the Abbot.

[The text continues with] "Middle. The Commentary on the Meaning states: According to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the rules regarding the violation of the order of seniority, as well as the regulations on bedding and requisites in the Vinaya Piṭaka, both clarify the sequence of ranks.
Thus, the debates between the two orders are essentially the same in their adherence to the precepts; this is the Buddha’s authentic regulation.
