Nowadays, in monastic communities, when assigning bedding, people disregard both precepts and seniority; within a single group, those who arrived first are placed in front and those who arrived later are placed behind.
This appears to be correct but is actually erroneous, as it violates the Buddha’s injunction that those who received the precepts earlier sit in front and those who received them later sit behind.
The Winter Retreat begins on the fifteenth day of the tenth month. This is the ninety-day period for monastics to cultivate the Way. Both internally and externally, all must be solemn and strict:

nothing is allowed to go out from within, and nothing is allowed to enter from without. Having set aside all distractions, they focus their energy exclusively on cultivating the Way during the morning services.
First, incense is burned and the censers are passed. The assembly gathers like clouds, and the Rector (Vina) recites the hymns.

The Abbot (Zhu-zhi) offers incense, prays for the Emperor, and so forth, until he reaches the Head Quarters (Shang-fang). The Abbot’s preaching of the Dharma and other rites are all conducted according to the format of the New Year.

The specific differences are as follows: at the conclusion of the evening service on this day, [the Abbot] proceeds to the Patriarchs’ Hall and then to the Head Quarters. The Rector strikes the leading chime (yin-磬) and conducts the inspection of the quarters (xun-liao).

[The Abbot] says: (At the conclusion of the retreat, while making rounds through the quarters, he addresses Master So-and-so, etc.). Having finished the rounds, he returns to the hall, spreads his sitting cloth facing [the Abbot], and performs three prostrations.
Upon completion, he returns to his seat. After a short while, when the serving of general tea in the refectory is nearly finished, the Rector (Vina) proclaims the rules for communal living.
At the second board [of the evening bell], the Head of the Hall (Bentang) proclaims the hall regulations. That evening, the seven-day Chan retreat begins.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The commencement of the retreat in the first month of winter is precisely for the sake of life and death.
If you do not sweep the ground of the mind until it is clear and bright, but merely fixate on the tip of the nose and put on a show, what use is there?
People may see you as if you were practicing Chan, yet when they open their bellies, it is pitch black inside. How pitiful! They do not know what Chan actually is.
Simply focus on twisting and wringing him out. If you are willing to suddenly cast away your thieving mind, there will be some degree of resonance.

An ancient said: "When one's practice lacks power, the fault lies in having too much knowledge and understanding, in over-analyzing public cases, and in being stuck by habitual tendencies that cannot be shaken off; for this reason, one fails to attain penetrating clarity."
Regarding Buddha-nature: if one is a person who is truly intent upon birth and death, they must not allow their mind to be distracted.
With a single *huatou*, they should be like one biting an iron ball, determined to chew it to pieces. If it cannot be chewed, they must bite with all their might;
even if body and mind should fall into hell, they will never let go of the *huatou*. Possessing such power of faith and such a state of doubt, day by day—
After many years have passed, the True Eye bursts open; its radiance shines everywhere, and in every object and at every point, there is no longer any distinction.
Someone asked: "The patriarchs of old mostly used skillful means (*upāya*) to guide people; why now do you give people a 'dead' koan and a 'dead' method of practice?
He replied: "Alas! What kind of talk is this? As for the method of investigating a koan, it has come down from..."
Huangbo initiated the tradition, which successive masters have followed and upheld; yet it was Dahui who most emphatically championed it.
Since Dahui revitalized the Way of Jibei, could it be that his capacity for skillful means was lacking?

Rather, in instructing future students, he employed a single "critical phrase" (huatou) to block their throats and exhaust their intellectual artifice, thereby manifesting great capacity and great function to spur them toward spiritual refinement.

Those who advanced and attained realization numbered more than forty. Indeed, the pedagogical methods of the master and the diligent practice of the student must both be mutually appropriate for success to be achieved.
If one does not exert oneself in their practice, yet relies solely on the master’s pedagogical methods to guide others, [success will not follow].

Thus, among those of superior faculties and sharp capacities, how many are there who can immediately know where to return? As for those of middling and inferior capacities, they will forever lose the benefit of the Dharma;
yet those who plunder emptiness will ride the wind and catch the echoes, until the single school of Bodhidharma is swept clean from the earth. Alas!
When Bodhidharma came from the West, he sat facing a wall for nine years; this may be called "standing like a wall ten thousand fathoms high.
Yet even his reception of Shen Guang was an application of skillful means. He said: "You must simply cease all external conditions and let the internal mind be free of agitation.
When the mind is like a wall, only then can you enter the Way. This is precisely what is meant by the teaching of "dead effort"; for if the effort were not dead, it would not be true cultivation.
Sentient consciousness arises recklessly; it does not pursue fame or profit, yet it clings to intellectual understanding. Although there may be functional utility, how can it be applied?
Therefore, those who now request to enter the retreat for the fixed period of meditation (anzen kessei) must take the investigation of a "dead koan" as their primary task.
I hope you will not intermingle this with the functional utility of koans or allow the mind to be distracted by them. Now, what is meant by "investigating a dead koan" is precisely...
To apply one's effort toward the *huatou* (critical phrase) is called "examining the dead *huatou*"; it is not merely sitting blankly while contemplating stillness.
The *Zen School’s Secret Essentials* states: "The Dharma Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions traveled to Mount Wutai and arrived at Dingxiang County."
He saw a monk sitting in a thatched hut and asked him, "Why are you sitting here all alone? The monk replied, "I am practicing *zhiguan* (calm observation).
The Master said, "Whose school do you follow? He replied, "The Great Master Shenxiu. The Master said, "I am a follower of a different path from the West;
even those of the lowest capacity there would not fall into such a view. What benefit is there for the Way in sitting thus in a daze?"
Regarding the commencement of the Seven-Day Zen Retreat (it may be commenced at any time; it is not restricted solely to the full moon of the tenth month):

On the day prior to the commencement of the Seven-Day Zen Retreat, the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina), the *yuezhong* (Yuezhong), and others shall go together to the storehouse to deliberate upon all necessary items and materials, as well as to invite those to serve as "Protectors of the Retreat.

Once these matters have been arranged and assigned, they shall leave the management to the *yuezhong*. This includes the duties of the "Incense Watcher" (*kanxiang*) and the "Supervisor of Incense" (*jianxiang*).

Wait for the Abbot to display the notice board. The seven-day period begins. After the midday meal, the minor retreat (small jìng) commences. The Rector (Vina) announces: "Tonight the seven-day period begins; please ascend to your seats to rest.

At the evening service, the practitioners take their ritual implements and enter the hall. When the service is concluded, the bell is struck, they pay homage to the Patriarchs, and then proceed to the Abbot’s quarters.

The Abbot finishes his sermon and provides instruction. The Rector says, "I thank the Venerable Master" (lit: *li-xie heshang*). After the prostrations are completed, the lead chime is struck, and it is announced:
"The seven-day retreat has commenced; go to the various quarters to pay respects to [Name] Master, etc. Once the rounds are finished, they return to the hall and rest.

Before the second board at evening, the Rector strikes the incense board three times to instruct the incense-lighter to guard the retreat site while each person attends to their respective duties. Next, at...
Three strikes of the incense board are sounded before the Zhai Hall, ordering all the various halls and quarters to assemble together in the Chan Hall.
When the assembly is seated in unison, the incense is inspected and the second board is struck for tea. Once the tea service is finished, the Rector (Weina) recites the hall regulations as follows.

Having finished the recitation, the Rector orders the attendant (Yuezong) to carry the incense board; once the Rector has escorted the supervisor (Jianxiang) out with the board, he strikes the incense board three times, and the assembly [proceeds].
Rising, the *hushiqi* (guardian-of-seven) collects the sitting mats from the floor. The *weina* (chant master) says:
"All fellow practitioners, pay homage to the Head Seat Master, the Xitang Master, the Houtang Master, the Hall Master, the Incense Lamp Master, the *hushiqi*, and the Water Officer."
Three prostrations. The Head Seat follows by saying, "[Prostrate to] the Rector (Weina). When the rites are concluded, he orders the Incense Overseer to perform his prostrations.

Next, he calls for the "Seven-Day Guest" (the deceased) to pay homage to the Buddha and prostrate to the two orders of officers. (Generally, those who are Dharma-relatives of this mountain monastery, as well as those from distant or nearby hermitages who have come to serve as the Seven-Day Guest, shall enter the hall and join the rear ranks.

If a layperson serves as the Seven-Day Guest, they remain in their quarters outside. All those serving as the Seven-Day Guest follow these two precedents; only upon the completion of the period may they leave the hall. Nuns and women are not permitted to enter the hall. However, honored guests or donors who participate out of sympathetic joy in sitting the incense periods are not subject to these rules. Nevertheless, one must not...)
After the "Fangyi" (Releasing the Restraint) prostrations are completed, the *yuezong* (joyful assembly) strikes the lead *qing* (chime). A pair of lanterns is used to welcome the *ho-shang* (abbot).

If the *zhuchi* (abbot) has issued a notice (*pai*), then the *ban-shou* (senior officers) are invited according to that notice. The *weina* (chant master) says: "The two orders of practitioners together pay homage to Master [Name].

After the prostrations are finished, the Dharma talk begins and the seven-day retreat is inaugurated. Two sticks of incense are offered for the light refreshment; four sticks of incense are offered at the meal hall.
Use the *pufang* (universal offering) [rice, noodles, or as available]. The kitchen staff shall prepare the cooking, while the seven *hu* (protectors) attend to it.
Six branches of incense for pure tea; eight branches of incense, with one cup of fried glutinous rice per person; ten branches of incense for resting.

During the branch of incense for resting, strike four rounds of the wooden sounding block (*suan*). Wash the face, and each return to their seat. Drink sugar soup; each person receives a portion of sugar.

One steamed bun. Upon hearing the board struck in the kitchen, one immediately practices walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). Two or three *yuezong* (attendants) take turns ascending the hall to respond to the chanting and recitation.
After completing the circumambulation of the Buddha in the Great Hall and the *choujie* (release from meditation) recitation, the lamps are extinguished.

Upon hearing the morning gruel gong, the retreat is opened (*kaijing*)—[the small retreat is opened two incense sticks after the small gruel]. Four pieces of rice cake for lunch; the retreat is closed (*zhijing*) at the midday meal. Green fruit and tea; four incense sticks. For snacks, six incense sticks. Upon hearing [the signal], [the retreat is reopened].

When the evening bell has sounded and the evening service is concluded (upon the opening of the hall, one returns to the hall to burn incense, etc.), one ascends the platform to rest. At the second board of the evening rising incense, one is given a block of fermented soybean cake (this is done every night and every day).
The same applies for the following six days. (If during this period a donor provides small snacks for the assembly, they are distributed as they arise.

Upon reaching the time of completion, the Head of the Assembly leads two pure monks to the Abbot’s quarters to request the abbot to perform the "examination of merit" and the "release from the seven-day vow," or to request the head of the class to do so.

Explanations for the Examination of Practice: In all seven-day meditation retreats (*zen-ji*), when the master examines the practitioners' progress, he focuses solely on their fundamental inquiry (*honzan*).

When students request instruction, he asks only about the *hwadu* (critical phrase), not permitting them to bring up miscellaneous public cases (*kongan*) indiscriminately. Regarding the practice of standing during incense periods (*tansō*): when the incense stick is nearly half-burnt, one must stand with both feet together and aligned.

One must not stand with feet spread apart or unevenly. Both hands should hang down naturally; crossing the arms is not permitted. Furthermore, one must avoid tucking the sleeves into the armpits while walking.

[Regarding] the hands: during seated meditation, one must refrain from dangling the feet. In all seven-day *zen* retreats, a fixed period is set to attain realization and to settle the matter of birth and death.

One’s sole task is to engage in intensive investigation (*k'an-hua*). The head of the assembly must not speak excessively, as this would hinder the primary practice. [This applies to] the periods of meal service and the rising of the incense burner.

Releasing the incense. Standing by the incense. The *weina* strikes the incense board three times. Regarding the types of incense boards: the "Circulating Incense Board" (*xunxiangban*), two feet long, is used solely for striking those who are drowsy.

The "Supervising Incense Board" (*jianxiangban*), one foot eight inches long, addresses both drowsiness and restlessness (*auddhatya*). The "Incense Board for Exhorting the Head of the Assembly" (*banshou cexiang*) is used specifically to observe their meditative practice.
The Abbot’s inspection of the incense consists solely of directly realizing it. Therefore, as for the circulating of the incense, it must be...

Hold [the incense] with both hands; it is not permitted to let one hand hang down. When the incense supervisor holds it, he may hold it in one hand while letting the other hang down, but he must not drag the incense board downward.
One should maintain the thought of making an offering. As for the head of the assembly (*ban-shou*), there are no restrictions regarding whether they are above or below;
whether they are drowsy or agitated, they may all be struck. Furthermore, observe the incense board (two chi and two cun long). The incense-dispensing bamboo rake (three chi and six cun long).
[The measurement is] one *cun*.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: "In the monastic groves (*sōrin*), practitioners sit in incense meditation (*zōkō*) for many years; why, then, is there also the 'Seven-Day Zen Retreat' (*zen-shichi*)?
It is because one desires to achieve realization within a fixed period. At this time, the student should exert their utmost vigor and brilliance, surpassing their usual state."
Daily, you must apply yourself with redoubled effort to investigate. To "investigate" means to investigate this one *huatou*.
Investigating the *huatou* does not lie outside the arousal of the state of doubt. As it is said: "A small doubt leads to a small awakening; a great doubt leads to a great awakening;
without doubt, there is no awakening. Doubt is itself the investigation. Now, while the thought of doubting is indeed an obstacle to the essence of awakening, it is...
If one skillfully utilizes its momentum, it can conversely be employed as a technique for breaking through obstacles.
This is because the mechanisms of doubt and awakening are mutually dependent, and their momentum is causally linked; therefore, those who seek awakening must value doubt.
Indeed, if the mechanism of the human mind does not coalesce into a state of tension, it cannot achieve clarity and openness—just as in the depths of winter, when [the earth] is frozen shut...
To block [the leaks] is truly to nurture the Great Origin (*taiyuan*). If the vital energy (*qi*) escapes and is not complete, then its manifestation will necessarily lack power.

Therefore, doubting is valued; for when one doubts, there is concentration and integration. If the source of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is not deeply investigated, one will certainly be unable to reach far.
Thus, all who doubt must investigate deeply. It is known, therefore, that doubt is the cause of awakening, and awakening is the cessation of doubt.
The fruition is such that it is as if there must be light where there is darkness, and inhalation must be followed by exhalation. Can one not be free from doubt?
Can one not be free from doubt? As for attaining awakening through doubt, once awakening no longer exists, how could doubt remain?
Thus, the work of refinement and polishing is accomplished.

After the seven-day, or perhaps two or three seven-day periods of meditation have been completed, the Abbot transmits the plaque to the Rector (Vina). The Rector addresses the assembly, saying [the appropriate words].

Having finished his address, he strikes the *yin-ghing* (leading chime). Announcing that he has received the Master’s command, he requests Master [Name] to provide the formal conclusion for the assembly.

After the three prostrations are completed, the Dharma talk for the resolution of the seven-day period is finished. The Rector (Weina) announces: "The two orders of practitioners have undergone much hardship over these many days;
they offer their thanks to the Head Seat Master [and so forth, down to] the Master who protects the seven-day period and the Water Master. They then perform three prostrations.
Having washed one's feet and rested, and the evening service being completed, the bell is struck to pay respects to the Patriarchs. One proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters;

once the prostrations are finished, one tours the various administrative offices (the seventh tour of the offices), performing the ritual inquiry (*wensun*) with each master, saying, "Venerable [Name]," and so forth. Upon completing the tour, one returns to the hall. The remaining protocols are as usual.
Sent back to its original location seven times.
Zhengyi said: "As for what is called 'understanding the sevens,' it merely refers to understanding the duration of several weeks; it is not the understanding of Chan meditation.
Someone asked: "I have already heard your instructions regarding the meaning of Chan meditation, yet I do not yet know how the practice of Chan meditation begins."
When? The answer is: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states, "One should, within this state, investigate the wondrous clarity with precision.

It further says, "Investigate internally and externally," "investigate profoundly and far-reaching," and "investigate with precision and vigor. This is not merely about "participating" [in the practice].

Among these, the seven locations where the mind is sought, the eightfold analysis of seeing, the flying light, the raising of the fist, the hanging down of the hand, and the shouting—all of these are [methods of investigation].

This indicates the arising of doubt. From this point forward, whenever one is instructed to contemplate a *gong'an* (public case) to give rise to the "doubting mind" (*yiqing*), it all originates from this.
Furthermore, as for other texts such as the "Brahmacarya Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, and the *Awakening of Faith*, they all contain Chan.
As for the most detailed and clear explanations, none surpass those of Master Dayi of Gaohu, who said: "If a person, in stillness..."
"Sitting requires no effort. "In what year did you attain the degree and awaken to the emptiness of mind? It is also said: "One must directly raise the sharp blade;
one must dissect the primary meaning of the Westward Transmission. And it is also said: "Pop open your eyes and raise your eyebrows;
look back and forth—'who' is this person? Such words as these should be inscribed upon the girdles of those who practice Zen. Nevertheless, if...

If one engages in speculative interpretation within the words and phrases, or employs intellectual calculation and estimation based on conscious consciousness (*vijñāna*), one will again misunderstand the meaning of what is called "applying effort," "analyzing," and "repeatedly examining.
In that case, although the practice differs from that of one who sits in silent meditation, the underlying affliction is the same; this must be distinguished. To state it briefly: Zen...
In the School of the Patriarchs, there is no Zen for intellectual comprehension; there is no Zen for piecemeal deliberation;

nor is there any Zen acquired through gradual cultivation. For this reason, I require you to practice with total simplicity, forbidding all confused thinking and the arbitrary generation of intellectual interpretations.
If you can have full confidence, then investigate in this manner; there is no need to ask about this or that.
Questioning the West: Since the Great Matter has not yet been clarified, among these seventeen hundred cases, which one is not subject to doubt?
It simply requires that you exert yourself with all your might upon a single case. If you can pass through one case, you will pass through a hundred thousand without exception.
Exert yourself.

On the fifteenth day of the first month of the winter retreat, before the Buddha and the sages, burn incense and light candles. That evening, perform the incense-offering at the stupa and the morning recitation to offer prayers.

The prayer service continues until the ascent to the seat, which is identical to the New Year’s Day ceremony. Upon the conclusion of the Dharma talk, the *vinaya-dhara* strikes the *yin-qing* (leading chime) and makes rounds through the quarters, announcing:
"This is the round of the quarters for the lifting of the retreat (*jie-zhi*); I inquire after the health of Master [Name]," and so forth.

Having completed the rounds, he returns to the hall to perform the formal rites, including the offering of incense and other services, according to the standard procedure for the new and full moon days. If one is requesting leave, they must wait until the evening recitation is finished, then don their robes and carry their requisites to first announce their departure.

After the *vinaya-dhara* has finished, the *yuèzhòng* leads [the assembly] to the guest hall to request leave. Next, they lead them to the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*). They form ranks and wait for the abbot to take his seat.
Each spreads their sitting mat (*ju*) and prostrates three times to the *ho-shang*. Rising from the mat, they perform a formal inquiry (*wèn-xùn*) and, with palms joined, speak as follows:

(The applicant requests leave). The Abbot grants the leave. [The applicant] returns to the hall. After the second board at evening, the Abbot orders an attendant to go to the Zen Hall and inform the Rector (Vina), saying:

"Please invite the masters on leave to have tea. The attendant shall then join them for the tea service. Upon returning to the hall, they must observe the period of silence and perform the prostrations.
Once the prostrations are completed, they shall sit according to their assigned positions and must not engage in idle chatter or miscellaneous conversation. Next...
At dawn, take a light meal. The Abbot invites you for a midday meal. Return the offerings (*xiangxin*). Return to the hall. Break camp (*qidan*).

If you have not yet reached your term of service and depart, the Abbot does not wait for the midday meal, nor are the offerings returned; your belongings (*xingli*) do not leave the hall. Upon reaching the end of your term, take your belongings.
If anyone absconds privately, a notice shall be posted in the guest hall stating: "At such-and-such time today, such-and-such official, so-and-so, has privately absconded."

The Commentary on the Meaning states: The Buddha ordained that from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month is the period for concluding winter travel, and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month is the period for concluding summer travel.
Nowadays, many Zen practitioners travel for the entire year, which greatly violates the Buddha’s regulations; this refers to the formalization of the *an-guo* (rainy-season retreat).
As for the regulations, they are mostly empty formalities performed merely to follow precedent; there is little actual substance in their practice. Yunqi’s *Verses on the End of Winter* says:
"The sound of the firecrackers in the courtyard has just ceased; It is once again the festival of the Lantern Festival. A snap of the fingers: the flowing light of time departs without stopping.
When will the matter beneath the patched robe be resolved? Reflect deeply; it is truly heart-wrenching. Each and every one of you—[should reflect thus].
One must be fierce and resolute. Seize up the old koan of yore and, straightaway, cause the mass of doubt to be shattered through and through.
(The monthly instructions—those detailed in the preceding eight fascicles—have all been deleted and are not recorded here.)
On the first day of the first month (New Year’s Day), a notice board shall be hung on the preceding day. (The notice reads: "Tomorrow we respectfully encounter the New Year festival.

May the assembly of venerable monks from all the halls, upon hearing the sound of the bell, proceed together to the Great Hall for liturgical chanting and recitation. We offer prayers for auspiciousness for three days.

We humbly pray that the imperial domain may remain eternally firm, the Emperor’s Way may flourish far and wide, the Buddha-sun may increase in brilliance, and the Wheel of Dharma may constantly turn."

On New Year’s Day, one incense stick is struck earlier than usual; the three wooden blocks are sounded. The kitchen staff sweeps and sprinkles the area before the Sacred One Who Oversees the Pure Vegetarian Kitchen (Jianzhai Sheng), cleaning it thoroughly and setting out an incense altar.
The Kusi office prepares the offerings. Ten people from the Guest Hall and the Venerable Leader (Weina) arrive, burning incense and passing the incense burner, and the incense eulogy is chanted.
The Abbot offers incense, and after the prostrations are completed, the Chief Administrator (Jianyuan) offers incense, sets forth the offerings, and makes his presentation.
Tea. Burning paper. Wait for the hall to open and the assembly to gather for the ascent to the dais. Incense is burned and the incense burner is passed around.

The Rector (Vina) raises the precious censer and burns famous incense, offering prayers for the Emperor; this is identical to the procedure for the "Prayers for the State" (Chuli) section in the first scroll.

Upon reaching the recitation of the *Śūraṅgama-mantra*, the Head of the Assembly (Yuezong), leading the Chief Administrator (Janyuan) and about ten others, exits the hall and proceeds before the Four Holy Ones.
The prayers proceed in sequence. First, they arrive at the Hall of Wei-t'o (Vaiśravaṇa). Standing to the left and right, the two *yuèzhòng* strike the leading chime.
First, the *sàntiānnǚ zhòu* (Dhṛtarāṣṭrī Dhāraṇī) is recited three times. The *jiānyuàn* (Superintendent) bows in greeting and offers incense, then steps out beyond the railing and kneels prostrate.

The *dàyuèzhòng* (Senior Leader) also bows in greeting and offers incense, then performs three prostrations with the ritual implements spread out and remains kneeling prostrate. Following this, they chant: *Namo Hufǎ Wéituó* (Homage to the Dharma-protecting Vaiśravaṇa).

After the Venerable Celestial Bodhisattva has been invoked three times, the sounding of the *ding*, *chao*, *ling*, and *gu* drums follows (the same applies to all subsequent sections, with only the sacred name being changed).

The Great Joy Assembly (*Dayuezhong*) says: "The divine efficacy is unfathomable," and so forth. Next is the Temple Guardian (*Galan*), next the Patriarchs (*Zushi*), and next the Supervisor of the Hall (*Jianzhai*).

The ritual procedures are identical; however, the prayers and recitations are modified accordingly. These are all recorded in the *Chanmen Risu* (Daily Recitation of the Chan School) and are not transcribed here. [This concludes] the invocation of the Four Sages.
This concludes [the ritual]. Return to the main hall and circumambulate the Buddha with the assembly, proceeding until you reach your assigned positions.

Once the assembly has raised their ritual implements toward the upper direction, strike the *qing* to signal the cessation of the chanting of the Buddha’s name. The *vinaya-dhara* (ritual leader) strikes the *qing* to lead the melody for twelve prostrations to the Buddha, saying:
"Namo to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha; Namo to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; Namo to Maitreya Bodhisattva; Namo to the Ten..."
Having prostrated three times each to the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, one does not recite the text for dedication; thus, the Three Refuges are completed.
The Rector (Vina) calls out in a loud voice: "There is no need to rise from one's seat. He strikes the chime and says: "I pay homage to those of India and China."
Three prostrations to the ancestral masters of successive generations; three prostrations to the great virtuous teachers who have propagated the teachings of the universal school;

three prostrations to the founding patriarch of this monastery. (Thereafter, continue with prostrations to the successive ancestral masters of one’s own specific lineage. Prostrations to one’s respective Preceptor for Ordination (*upasampadā-ācārya*).
Then, perform three prostrations to the masters upon the altar; three prostrations to one's own tonsure master; three prostrations for one's parents on one's behalf;
and three prostrations to the Abbot (Changzhang Heshang). Having completed these prostrations, unfold the sitting mat (*juzu*) facing [the Abbot].
The Rector (*Weina*), striking the *qing* gong, announces: "In the [number] year, [number] month, and on this auspicious day of [name], of the Imperial Qing Dynasty..."
The great assembly gathers like clouds. They perform three prostrations in unison. Upon the third prostration, they say: "No need to rise from one's seat.
They then remain prostrate and recite the verse: "[Name] Master, three prostrations," and so forth. The internal and external attendants all follow the order according to the attendance list.

Once the prostrations are concluded, they say: "Prostrate again to the Abbot, Venerable Master, three times; then rise from one's seat and inquire after his well-being. The assembly gathers before the Patriarch.

The assembly performs the ritual of paying respects to the Patriarchs in the Hall. Upon completion, they proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (*upādhyāya-śālā*). Arriving in order, they stand facing one another.

The *karmadāna* (Venerable Leader) and the attendant invite the Abbot to emerge and take his seat. The assembly lines up facing the direction of the Abbot. The *karmadāna* says: “[Unfurling the ritual implements, prostrate to the Venerable Master]” (*ujjvalayitvā pūjayata upādhyāyam*).

When the prostrations are finished, he calls for them to rise from their implements and perform a formal greeting (*praṇāma*). They divide into ranks and stand facing each other. The eulogy is recited, and so on, until the preaching of the Dharma is concluded. The *karmadāna* then calls out.

(Performing the ritual prostrations. Prostrate to the Abbot. (The above applies every month on the first and fifteenth days, as well as on various festival days; however, for the New Year’s Day: The Abbot says:

(The assembly, together with the teachers, shall proceed before the Great Hall to perform universal prostrations). When the assembly has gathered, they perform the ritual prostrations. The Abbot says:

(I, [Name], together with the assembly and the teachers, offer greetings for the new season and perform three universal prostrations). The head of the assembly follows by saying: (Prostrate to the Abbot). When the prostrations are finished, they return.

In the Hall, two rows of seats face one another for prostrations. No private salutations are permitted among any members, whether internal or external, except for those directed toward one's own teachers (during the winter retreat and its conclusion).

[The same procedure applies for] the commencement of the summer retreat (*kṣetra-bandha*), the conclusion of the summer retreat (*kṣetra-mokṣa*), and the beginning of spring. At dawn on New Year’s Day, the Guest Master (*vidyā-karmika*) goes to the storehouse and takes the paper talisman of the Auspicious Deity (*xi-shen*).

The Guest Master commands the bell-ringer to strike the bell three times. Holding a handful of incense in his hand, the Guest Master stands before Maitreya and distributes it to the assembly of masters;
each person takes a stick of incense and proceeds out through the mountain gate in order to reach the direction of the Auspicious Deity. [Then] they chant: (To be continued...)

Having lifted the incense, insert it into the ground. Ring the *yin-ghaṅ* three times and perform three prostrations of inquiry (*wèn-xùn*). The paper for the transformation ritual (*huà-zhǐ-yuán*) is then transformed at the place where the incense was inserted;
each item returns to its original position in due order. In the morning, there are steamed buns and fermented bean curd soup in the refectory (alternatively, rice cakes or glutinous rice balls).
[Whether it be flour or other offerings, both are acceptable. After the three-board period of silence, one immediately requests the Abbot to ascend the hall (as seen in the section on the Abbot).

Upon the conclusion of the ascent to the hall, the Hall Master prepares offering positions for the parents and elders of those residing together, as well as for the donors and Dharma protectors from the ten directions, near the hall (it may also be prepared beforehand on New Year’s Eve).
Once the fruits, vegetables, incense, and candles have all been arranged, [the meal is served] following the second board of light refreshments and tea.

Immediately cease all activities and remain in stillness. Ring the bell three times. The assembly shall divide into classes to perform the Universal Offering (*pǔgòng*). Upon completion of the offering, return to the hall (it is advisable to pre-assign the number of classes and their respective locations;

one may recite the "Praise for the Universal Offering" in advance, which is appended at the end). After a short while, having finished drinking tea and relieving oneself, ring the bell three times again.

The assembly gathers in the Great Hall to recite mantras and chant the Buddha’s name. This is performed six times daily (or four times). On the third day of the third month, morning snacks are discontinued.

After *jing* (meditation), the assembly hears the bell and performs the general offering (*pusong*) according to their original seating order. After the midday meal, they perform the dedication of merit through reciting the Buddha’s name and transform the memorial tablets (*paiwei*).
On New Year’s Day and New Year’s Eve, there are no holidays; the meditation hall does not serve tea. At noon, the food consists of oil-soaked tofu and white rice;

in the morning and evening, it is plain tofu and regular rice. Upon completion of the evening service, after paying respects to the patriarchs and the abbot’s quarters, the Hall Master (*xingtang shi*)...

Upon arriving at the meditation hall, go to the Hall of Duty (Jianzhiliao) and ask the officer on duty for the tea gong and the teapot. At the second board of the evening, upon hearing the sound of the drum, the assembly shall proceed together to the refectory.
The two *yuezong* (monks who manage the assembly) shall strike the *yinjing* (leading stone chime) to invite the *ho-shang* (abbot).

The hall attendant shall bring the tea and pour it in succession until all have been served. The two monks serving tea and fruit shall set them out on a single table; once everything is arranged (or alternatively, one bowl per person may suffice), the *yuezong*...
The assembly rings the *yin-ghaṅ* twice. The Superintendent of the Monastery (Jiànyuàn) then says: "The Abbot invites you to tea; the Great Assembly Master invites you to tea.
After a short while, the Superintendent speaks again: "The Abbot invites you to partake of fruit offerings; the Great Assembly Master invites you to partake of fruit offerings.

When the general tea ceremony is concluded, the recitation of the monastic regulations (*yīguī*) is waived. The Director of the Assembly (Yuèzhòng) rings the *yin-ghaṅ* twice; everyone rises together and returns to their quarters. The third board is struck to signal the end of the period of silence.

After reciting the *Pǔfó* (Universal Buddha) liturgy at the Dharma Hall and returning to the hall, incense is offered in the Meditation Hall until the third day of the third lunar month; thereafter, the practice of sitting and walking meditation resumes as usual.

(The rites for visiting and sweeping the stupas are detailed in Volume Three. The Abbot, the Chief Administrator, and the Guest Master shall each go to their respective familiar locations to offer New Year’s greetings.
Within the first ten days, if messengers are sent by various mountain temples or dispatched by Shihu to offer congratulations, they shall be treated with six-colored tea and vegetables;
after the first ten days, four types of vegetables and rice shall be served, and tea and fruit are not used.
On all occasions such as New Year’s Day, the Little New Year, the Eve of the Lunar Year, and the entry into the monastery, the Guest Hall shall hang a notice during the morning congee service.
(The notice shall read: "Venerable Assembly: Upon hearing the bell, attend to the assigned locations and offer universal offerings.
The Guest Master and the Rector shall divide the assembly into several groups, determining the number of people assigned to each location for the offerings, and shall draw up a roster.

The notice for the *zhaitang* (meditation hall) shall be posted accordingly. Whether it be for the morning meal or the light meal (*xiaoshi*), when the second board is struck, the bell is then tolled three times.

When the third board is struck, silence is maintained; the minor period of stillness (*xiaojing*) begins. Monks put on their robes and take up their ritual implements, assembling in the Great Hall for the offerings.

Once the offerings have been made, they divide into groups according to their assigned ranks and proceed to make offerings at their respective locations. One group has the Abbot (*zhuchi*) offer incense; another group has the Chief Administrator (*jianyuan*) offer incense; as for the remainder...

Whether it be the General Supervisor (*dutuan*), the Vice Abbot (*fusi*), or the various heads of the administrative classes (*zhoubanshou*), any of them may act as the representative to offer incense. Once the offerings have been completed, each person shall return to their respective quarters. Regarding the vegetables offered:
they must be cooked until tender and flavorful, but not so much that they lose their essential juices. For fruits, use three parts dry fruit to two parts fresh; both must be kept pure and clean.

Upon completion of the offering, everything should be cleared away immediately, with the exception of the flowers and pure water. This is because the Buddhas and Sages do not eat after midday and always maintain a state of purity.
Offerings should not be accepted; such elaborate adornments are for laypeople and are unsuitable for the Sangha, being a grave violation of the Buddha’s regulations.
On the ninth day, it is the birthday of the Honored Deity Śakra (i.e., the Jade Emperor).
The Commentary on the Meaning states: "Universally making offerings to all the sages and ordinary beings of the world" refers to:

first, the world of the perfectly awakened ones, namely the four types of noble beings such as Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; second, the world of sentient beings, namely the six classes of ordinary beings such as devas, humans, and asuras;
and third, the receptacle world, which includes the various classes of deities presiding over earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth within the environmental support of the three realms. Now...
Among the Four Noble Beings, one makes offerings to those such as Amitābha, Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Cundā, Kṣitigarbha, and Bodhidharma;
as well as Baizhang, Tiantai, Xianshou, Nanshan, and Huiyuan, even extending to the hall for the vegetarian feast.
Regarding fields, gardens, land, and so forth, these have all already appeared in the preceding eight fascicles and are not recorded here again.

For the four types of offerings for the Noble Ones (ārya), paper-money (zhīyuán) must not be used; to use it would be disrespectful. For the six types of offerings for ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), paper-money must be used.
Furthermore, for the gate deities, toilet deities, field and garden deities, and others, one must use paper offerings (*zhiyuan*).
Among these, for the toilet deity alone in the latrine, one provides only food and paper offerings without performing recitations.

As for offerings made to parents, teachers, elders, and spirits, one must perform recitations and use spirit-money lamps (*mingding*). One should take care not to confuse or conflate these three cases.
Appendix: Verses for Concluding the Rituals in Each Hall (In addition to the aforementioned Universal Offering, these may also be used as appropriate).
(Zen Hall) The definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna is that the essence itself is entirely empty. Seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are themselves within emptiness.
By manifesting traces and revealing the golden countenance, through diligent application of effort, one casts off the hand and breaks free from the cage. *Namo Vairocana Buddha.*

(Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva), the Master of Perfect Penetration, eternally abiding on Mount Potalaka. Responding to conditions and manifesting according to needs, he never errs; he rescues the deluded from the burning house.
With willow branches sprinkling dew, a single drop reaches the ends of the earth. *Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*.
(Canonical Scripture Library) The oceanic assemblies of all Buddhas respond perfectly throughout the great trichiliocosm. With compassion and pity, they deliver humans and devas.

The meaning of the holy teachings is profound and primordial; the Tripitaka proclaims it extensively. Through understanding, practice, and realization, one attains the state of the Golden Immortal. The Treasury of Dhyāna-Bliss.
(Avatamsaka Hall) The Ocean Assembly of the Avatamsaka. Śākyamuni Tathāgata sits upon a flower pedestal within the Lotus Treasury Ocean. All Buddhas exclaim, "How marvelous!
Ten thousand phenomena shine forth; darkness is instantly dispelled. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Ocean Assembly of the Avatamsaka.
Upon the thousand-petaled lotus pedestal, the World-Honored One Vairocana returns each to their original realm to deliver those submerged in the depths of saṃsāra.
With the precepts of the mind-ground as the cause, the bodies of a thousand billion Buddhas harmonize in a single melody like a springtime song. *Namo Vairocana Buddha*.

(Bhaiṣajyaguru Hall) Medicine Master Buddha, King of Extended Life, you graciously descend upon this water-moon altar. With a compassionate heart, you rescue those in suffering and bestow auspicious blessings.
You deliver us from calamities and dissolve all obstacles and hindrances. Through this repentance, may the transgressions of the donors throughout the three periods of time be purified.

We pray for the blessing of long life; may the auspicious stars shine brightly as we bathe in your radiant grace. May all be as wished, forever peaceful and secure. Medicine Master Buddha who Eliminates Calamities and Extends Life.
(Pharmacalpa Stūpa Lamp) Praise and Homage to the East. In the world of Pūrṇacandra, the wondrous realm of vaidūrya is most extraordinary;

the brilliance of the flaming net was manifested through vows made within the causal stage. Bhaiṣajyaguru Buddha, you unfurl a vast auspicious radiance to extinguish the calamities and obstacles of sentient beings.
May you bestow blessings and peace. The present assembly sings your praises; may their merit and longevity be boundless. The present assembly extols you; may their merit and longevity be boundless.
Boundless! Namo to the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Tathāgata.

(The Pavilion of Great Compassion) With compassionate majesty, they provide equal salvation; their great compassion is of one essence with all beings. With hands and eyes manifesting throughout their entire bodies, they proclaim the dhāraṇīs, which all Buddhas praise as marvelous.
Their meritorious virtues are wondrous and inconceivable. O Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara!

(Arhat) The nine heavens are cleansed of outflows; the fruit of non-arising is realized. Receiving offerings from devas and humans who respond with sincerity, he bestows blessings and descends with auspicious portents.
Tigers submit and dragons welcome him; his fame stands towering for ten thousand ages. Arhat Venerable (East).

(Arhat) Fully endowed with the holy life (*brahmacarya*), he realized the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Sporting in right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), he manifested supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). He was able to revitalize the tradition of the Buddha’s house;
those who heard of him turned to him in reverence. His benefit and salvation were eternal and without end. Arhat Venerable (Xi).

(An Epitaph for Master Zizong of the Hall of Repentance) A bird’s nest marked his manifested traces; a revered master of the Liang dynasty. He once displayed his majestic demeanor at Baohua Temple, and the mountain is named after the foundation of Master Bao.
His Dharma transformation is inconceivable; for ten thousand ages, repentance relies upon him—the Teacher who delivers all beings.

(Grand Master Puan) Puan’s spiritual efficacy was vast; his great virtue and fame were renowned. The eight classes of devas followed him forever; the lands and regions were entirely peaceful. His wondrous Dharma was reverently heard;
he planted the seeds of good fruit for eternal stability. He was a teacher who delivered all beings.

(Before the Birth Platform) The Great Golden-Winged Bird and the Goddess Haritī cease their malevolence and come to prostrate before the World-Honored One. Having received the precepts, they protect the source of the mind;
their vows are vast and firm. They shall depart for the wilderness and be reborn in the celestial realms.

(Grain Chamber Deity, Treasury Chamber Wealth God) Material provisions advance the Way; of the five types of pure food, the first comes first. The donor gives without stinginess, breaking through their parsimony;
With faith and reverence, they plant the field of merit. As their offerings flow like a gentle stream, They invoke the response of the dragons and heavens To protect the Dharma-treasury.
(Imperial Temple of Guandi) Loyal in heart, repaying the state; a valiant and heroic man. Protecting the Buddha-Dharma, he expels external demons; May the monastic community dwell forever in peace.
Advancing on the Path without peril, For ten thousand ages, he acts as a golden embankment to protect the Dharma-treasury.
(The Hall of the Three Offices) The Great Emperor of the Three Offices possesses inconceivable merit. Upon Mount Yuntai, he radiates rays of light, bestowing blessings and descending auspiciousness;
he pardons transgressions, eliminates calamities, resolves misfortunes, and secures peace and well-being, protecting the treasury of the Dharma.
(Daowang Hall) Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa: may they support the state to ensure peace and stability.
May the Dharma Garden be like a golden city, protecting the ranks of the Saṅgha so that the transformation of the Way may endure forever and safeguarding the treasury of the Dharma.

(Deities of the Mountain Gate) To the deities who dwell within the realm of the vessel-world, and to the Honored Deity who presides over the household records: We pray that you protect the monastic precincts and ensure peace and security.

Relying upon the great majestic power and spiritual authority of the Buddha, drive away malevolent spirits and expel impurities, so that calamities and obstacles may never again intrude. Protect the treasury of the Dharma.

(Before the positions of the parents and teachers of each fellow resident: In this jewel-like community of the forest monastery, we dwell together in the six harmonies; may we constantly remember and be mindful of the kindness of our parents and teachers.
Relying upon the compassion of the King of Awakening, strive diligently in practice. By impartially bestowing the food of the Dharma, one is reborn in the celestial realms.

(From the Release of Life Pavilion) Beings born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation have been mired in delusion for many kalpas. By taking refuge in the Triple Gem and generating the bodhicitta, they shall forever escape from cages and nets.
Leaping from the sea or soaring through the sky, may they exhaust their karmic retribution and be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. May they be reborn in the celestial realms.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: Regarding the universal offerings (*pūjā*), various families differ in their additions and subtractions. Nevertheless, sincerity and reverence must be taken as the foundation.
In the monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*) of today, although offerings are made according to established custom, they are for the most part performed in a perfunctory manner.

Some even use raw, cold, or inedible items, attending merely to the social formalities. They fail to reflect that the ritual of offering arises from the mind; thus, the ceremonial etiquette becomes lax and superficial.
Their intentions can be discerned. Since their hearts are not sincere, what is the point of making offerings? To offer in such a manner—who would they be deceiving?

This is nothing more than treating ritual propriety as a mere game. The resulting retribution will be severe indeed. I universally pray that all monastics and laypeople throughout the world [will refrain from this].
Together we shall turn back from these habits. In the first month, when the branch sign is Yin, it is called *Shètígé*, also called *Tàicú*, and also called *Mèngzōu*.

Furthermore, from the winter solstice in the eleventh month when the first Yang begins to arise, up until the fourth month known as the "Six Yangs," this current first month is named the "Three Yangs" month.
On the first day of the second month, the fire-hearth is sealed. If the mountain temple is cold, there is no such restriction.

The second month is the *mǎo* lunar mansion; it is called *Dānyé* (Single Goat), also known as *Jiázhuōng* (Clamping Bell). It is further termed "Middle Spring" (*zhòngchūn*) and also referred to as "Fragrant Spring" (*fāngchūn*).
The third month is the month when the *jia-chen* day is established; it is also called *Guxian*, *Mochun*, *Wanchun*, or *Miaochun*.
It is further referred to as the "Month of the Constellations."

In the fourth month, when the weather is warm, hang the warm curtains (nandian) inside the Sangha Hall and raise the cooling curtains (lianglian). Remove the bedding from the single mats and transport them out.
On the fifteenth day—the birthday of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva (other texts state the twenty-eighth day)—[perform the rites].

The fourth month is Jishi (Ji). It is called Dahuangluo; it is also called Zhonglü. It is further named Maiqiu (Autumn of Wheat); it is also termed Qinghe (Pure Harmony) and named Kuimue (Moon of Chrysanthemums).
It is also referred to as Mengxia (Early Summer) and Chuxia (Beginning of Summer), among other names.

The Fifth Month, the Dragon Boat Festival (Duanwu Jie). After the morning service is concluded, either the Abbot delivers a *xiaocan* (short discourse) or he appoints a head of the assembly (*ban-shou*) to hold the whisk.

The monks proceed upon receiving the signal from the Abbot’s quarters. At the morning gruel, *zong* (rice dumplings) are distributed, four pieces per person. At the midday gong, offerings are made in the Great Hall; at the refectory, fermented bean curd is served.
During this month, the drainage ditches are dredged and the "Green Sprouts Assembly" (*qingmiao hui*) is established, where the monks chant prayers for the protection of the young crops.
A canopy was hung within the hall.
Chengyi said: "In our school, there is not a single thing or a single detail that does not serve to awaken people through the teaching of the Dharma.
I now record one instance of a Dharma talk given on the Dragon Boat Festival to illustrate the rest."—Master Chan Master Zhanran Cheng.
Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth, he said: "The fifth day of the fifth month is the Festival of Midsummer. Red mouths and white tongues are all extinguished.
Peach talismans and tiger-shaped mugwort are stuck full upon the head; realgar and calamus are swallowed with wine. Drunk and reeling, one knows not that the years and months have passed.
A thousand sprites and a hundred monsters are driven away into darkness. Who cares whether demons come or Buddhas come? All at once, they are gone."
Lifting up the forehead for you all: why is it so? Have you not heard the Way said: "To protect life, one must kill;
only when killing is exhausted does one dwell in peace"? If you wish to understand the principle of this killing, seize this auspicious occasion to take mugwort leaves as your banner.

Taking calamus as a sword, with a fierce and sharp mind and the courage of a hero, regardless of right and wrong, gain and loss, sage and ordinary person, truth and falsehood—even greed, anger, delusion, and attachment—seize all these thieves of affliction with one stroke and cut them in two.
Thus, you shall directly attain a state that is pure and bare, stark and clear, perfectly round and vibrantly alive; become such a one.
"Great men of the world and beyond the world, brothers, is there such a person? Have you truly attained such a state?
If you have not attained such a state, I, this mountain monk, have a talisman for protecting the body that I shall send to you."
He held up his staff and said, "Look! Look! Supreme Lord Laojun, act with the utmost urgency according to the command! *Bì*!
The fifth month, established in the *wǔ* position, is called *Dúnzāng* and also *Ruíbīn*. It is sometimes named the *Tiānzhōng Jié* (Festival of Mid-Heaven) or the *Xiūyuè* (Cultivating the Moon).
It is also called the month of Gao, the month of Pu, the month of Ai, the month of Liu, and so forth. At the summer solstice, Yin begins to arise.
The sixth month is when the lunar station Wei is established; it is called Xiéqiá, also Línzhōng, and is further known as the month of Qiè and the month of Hé.
The twenty-fourth day of the seventh month is the birthday of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.

The seventh month is designated as *shen* in the sexagenary cycle, known as *tun-tan*, and also as *yizze*. It is further called the first month of autumn (*mengqiu*) and is also referred to as the month of *xiang*.
The eighth month, known as Qiǎoyuè (Skillful Month) and others; the twenty-second day of the eighth month is the birthday of the Ancient Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
The eighth month is the Jìyǒu (Jiǔ) year, also called Nányǔ, sometimes named Qīngqiū (Clear Autumn), and also referred to as Zhuàngyuè (Mature Month).
Regarding the "Cinnamon Moon" and so forth:
on the ninth day of the ninth month, the Double Ninth Festival, after the morning liturgy is completed, a *xiaocan* (small discourse) is given, identical to that of the Dragon Boat Festival.
The ninth month is established as *shu*, called *yanmao*, and also known as *wushê*; it is alternatively termed the final autumn, the late autumn, or the deep autumn.
The late autumn month is also called the first month of the year, the month of chrysanthemums (*kuk-gwol*), and so forth.

Furthermore, when the two harvests of summer and autumn reach the time for collecting rents, the head of the manor first inspects the rental ledgers of each estate and prepares the measures, bushels, and other necessary items.
Subsequently, he informs the Abbot and proceeds to the estate to collect the rent; he must act with fairness and integrity, never resorting to oppression of the tenants.

Furthermore, one must not harbor personal grudges or seek private favors at the expense of the monastery's permanent assets (*changzhuang*). Once the harvest rent has been collected, one shall return to the temple and present the accounts of the rental proceeds to the abbot for inspection and entry into the ledgers.
When these matters are concluded, one shall immediately offer new offerings to the Buddha, and the assembly shall partake of the new grain with the addition of fermented bean curd (*fǔ*).
This is the same as on the days of the new and full moon.
On the first day of the tenth month, the furnace is opened.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: "Opening the furnace" refers to opening the fire-hearth of each hall; it is now used metaphorically for the commencement of the *chanji* (seven-day meditation retreat).

It is the opening of the furnace. ○ The tenth month is the *jiǎ-hài* day; it is called *Dàyuánxiàn*. It is also termed *Yìngzhōng*, or named *Mèngdōng* (Early Winter), *Kāidōng* (Opening Winter), or *Xiǎochūn* (Little Spring).
It is further referred to as the *Yángyuè* (Yang Month) or the *Liángyuè* (Auspicious Month).
The Winter Solstice Festival on the first day of the eleventh month. On the designated day prior, the Guest Hall hangs a notice (the notice reads):

"On this auspicious occasion of the Winter Solstice, the assembly of venerable monks shall, upon the conclusion of the morning service, pay homage to the Patriarchs and proceed to the Abbot’s quarters. On the following day, during the morning service, the incense burner is passed around.

The Abbot offers incense, prays for blessings, and offers prayers for the Emperor. After circumambulating the Buddha and returning to their positions, they perform twelve prostrations before Śākyamuni Buddha and recite the service.

When the ritual for the ancestral name has concluded, the practitioners face one another and unfold their sitting cloths; the assembly gathers, the bell is struck, and they perform three prostrations in unison.

They proceed to the Ancestral Hall to pay respects to the ancestors, then go to the Abbot’s quarters. Once the Abbot has finished preaching the Dharma, the Rector says: "Prostrate to the Venerable Master. When the prostrations are completed, the ceremony ends.
The Abbot descends from his seat and says: "I, [Name], along with the Great Assembly, pay our respects to the Master. The Rector says: "The Great Assembly prostrates to the Preceptor.

When the ceremony is concluded, they return to the hall and unfold their sitting cloths facing one another. The Rector says: "Prostrate to Master [Name]," and so forth. The Head of the Monastic Class (Ban-shou) says:
"The two rows of seats prostrate to one another. They perform three universal prostrations. Upon completion, the Attendant of the Quarters returns to the Abbot’s quarters and performs a prostration.

Venerable Master: At the striking of the midday bell, offerings are made at seven locations (the Great Hall, the Four Saints, the Portrait Hall, and the portrait of the Senior Monk). One partakes of fermented bean curd in the refectory, or performs tomb-sweeping and ancestral rites, which are identical to those observed during the Qingming Festival.

The first month of winter, when the *zi* branch is established, is called *kundun*. It is also termed *huángzhōng*, sometimes named *zhòngdōng*, and further referred to as *gūyuè*, *zhìyuè*, and so forth.
On the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month, the Bodhisattva of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* was born.
Three days before the New Year’s Eve, the Guest Hall shall post a notice stating: "The end of the year draws near.

All halls housing Buddhas and saints, as well as the front and rear corridors, inner and outer courtyards, must be thoroughly swept and cleansed. On the day prior, the ritual for paying respects at the stupas is performed.

Details are as seen previously. ○ On the eve of the New Year’s Day, there is a light meal of white tofu; at noon, the meal consists of fried tofu and *zuancai* (stir-fried vegetables). At the morning congee, a notice is posted stating:

"All members of the assembly, upon hearing the sound of the drum, shall proceed from their respective locations to offer universal offerings" (as seen previously for the New Year’s Day). ○ In the afternoon, a notice is posted stating:

"This evening, at the second board-strike, upon hearing the sound of the bell, everyone shall go together to the Great Hall to recite the Universal Buddha Sutra. This is the third [practice] of the New Year.

The same applies to the midday meal. ○ At the evening service, each person shall wear their full monastic robes. When the service is concluded, they pay respects to the Patriarchs and proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*).

The Abbot ascends the seat and delivers a discourse on the Dharma; or, once the general discourse is finished, the Abbot says: (The two orders of the assembly shall together go before the Great Hall to perform a collective prostration of farewell for the year).
When the assembly arrives before the hall, they unfold their sitting cloths facing one another. The Abbot remains at the lower end and unfolds his sitting cloth facing upward, saying: (I, [Name]...)

The Abbot (Jiǎ) exchanges New Year’s greetings with the Great Assembly Master. The Head of the Assembly immediately says: “The Great Assembly Master prostrates to the Venerable One; may all join in. They perform three prostrations.

Once the prostrations are finished, the assembly proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to exchange New Year’s greetings. They prostrate to the Abbot. When the ceremony is concluded, they return to the hall, unfold their sitting cloths, and perform three prostrations.
The bell and wooden board are struck. Any senior masters or elders perform private salutations as appropriate, then return to the hall upon hearing the drum.

[The signal for] the meal. The assembly gathers together at the refectory for the universal tea service (*pucha*). The *yuèzhòng* (joyous leader) strikes the *yinqing* (leading stone chime) to invite the *heshang* (abbot).

When the universal tea service is concluded, they return to the hall, where the abbot’s quarters invites the administrative officers (*zhishi*) for tea. In the evening, after the second board [bell] has been struck, they recite the *Pufu* (Universal Buddha) liturgy; once the thousand recitations of the Buddha’s name have been completed.
Proceeding before the seats of each individual (parents, teachers, and elders), the abbot offers incense. The assembly recites the Heart Sūtra and the Rebirth Mantra.

The verse for dedication and the hymn of praise are chanted, followed by further recitation of the Buddha’s name. Each person returns to their original seat, withdraws the name-boards, spreads their sitting mats, and performs twelve prostrations before the Buddha.
Perform one prostration each to Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Return to the hall for the threefold refuge, then open the great silence, release the incense, and rest.
This same procedure applies for the first three days of the New Year. For other matters, refer to the previous section on the New Year’s Day.
During this month, at the end of the year, compile and present all various registers and documents.
The Commentary on the Meaning states: The ancients regarded the eve of the New Year as the day of one’s death; for the conclusion of a year is like the conclusion of a lifetime.
As the Chan Master Huangbo once said: "If you have not attained thorough penetration beforehand, then on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month..."
When it arrives, you will surely be thrown into a state of frantic turmoil. Thus, to attend to the affairs of New Year’s Eve on the first day of the first month is not too early;
to attend to the affairs of one's death from the very moment one first understands human relations is not too early.
Alas, as time slips away and drifts by, one does not realize that youth has passed into maturity, maturity into old age, and old age into death.
How much more so for those who have not yet reached middle age or old age; are they not all the more deeply pitiable?
Therefore, one must regard impermanence as the end of the year and remain constantly vigilant, making vows and commitments to oneself that one shall no longer continue to waste time as before.
This one matter of thorough penetration cannot be overlooked as something trivial. It is not attained by having mastered several volumes of sutras and treatises;
it is not attained by sitting for several incense sticks, remaining unmoving and unshakable;
nor is it attained by explaining several instances of the ancient masters' dialogues and karmic conditions, or by composing several verses on old cases (*songgu*) or critical comments (*niangu*).
"Thoroughly penetrated. This is not merely a matter of a few words of verbal facility or smooth eloquence; it must be truly "thoroughly penetrated. As the ancients said regarding this matter:
"It is as clear as when the bottom of a bucket suddenly falls out; it is as refreshing as waking from a great dream, with not a single hair’s breadth of doubt remaining.
Even if one has only a small measure of resonance with it—as in the case of a monk who was constantly at a shrine temple—[he would still be far from it].

He stayed overnight in a paper furnace. Another monk secretly entered the furnace, waiting for him to come and stay so that he might seize him by the chest and ask, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
He replied, "The wine table and dishes before the deity. Another monk was said to have attained enlightenment.
Yuansha intentionally traveled with him. Upon reaching the water's edge, [the other monk] suddenly pushed him into the water.
Shui asked urgently, "Before Niu-tou had seen the Fourth Patriarch, what was it like? The monk said, "The extended foot is within the contracted foot.
Such monks as these may be said to have already been struck through beforehand;

their chests are thus riddled with holes, everything is thoroughly settled, and they respond immediately to whatever is called upon. Even in moments of sudden urgency, they are able to act without hesitation.
At such times, his speech and utterances were so appropriate and so masterful.
When he was at leisure, he would deliberate with his mental consciousness and compose verses in response to circumstances; these were not without brilliance and worth observing.
Yet, when illness arrived and impermanence manifested—much like the arrival of New Year’s Eve—he became frantic with feet and hands in a state of total confusion. Is this not truly lamentable?
Ah! I pray that we may constantly use this to admonish ourselves until it reaches its ultimate limit. Even when the eight sufferings burn us simultaneously, there is no obstacle [to this practice].
If this is not yet the case, one cannot avoid self-deception. Formerly, the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai attained the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra.

While practicing meditation atop Mount Huading, suddenly during the latter part of the night, a great wind arose with thunderous peals, and thousands of *chimei* (goblins) appeared in forms most terrifying.
The Master settled his mind in empty stillness, and they naturally dispersed. They then manifested in the forms of his parents and preceptors, sobbing with grief and shedding tears.
The Master deeply contemplated their true nature (*lakṣaṇa*), and they soon vanished. When the time for his parinirvāṇa arrived, his disciples made their request.

One day, [Huishou] was asked, "I do not know in what stage of realization you have entered, Master. Having passed away here, where will you be reborn? The Master replied, "I do not lead a community of followers; I shall surely purify my six sense faculties.
For the sake of others, I have sacrificed myself, yet I am currently at no more than the level of the five ranks (*wupin*). Furthermore, I told the *vinaya* master Cheng:
'When a person's life is about to end, hearing the sound of bells and chimes increases their mindfulness. Let it be long and enduring, until the breath is exhausted. Do not wail or weep.'"

Regarding mourning attire: one should not perform [funerary rites] at all. Having finished speaking, he entered samādhi. Alas! Even the Great Master Zhi said that performing [rites] for others causes harm to oneself;
how much more so for people like us? How could we fail to admonish ourselves? The twelfth month is built in the *chou* branch; it is called *Chifunruo* (Zhengyu), and also *Dali*.

The commentary states: In the age of antiquity, there was transformation but no formal instruction. When transformation proved insufficient, ritual and music were established.
The song of those who beat the *rāng* clods was not equal to the performance of the nine-part *Jiǔchéng*; the drinking from hollow gourds was not as [refined] as the five [vessels].
The refinement of Qi has indeed been achieved; yet, as pattern arises from substance, one must contemplate its root.

Our Sage of India first manifested his transformation by teaching that every person possesses wondrous enlightenment, that fundamentally there is neither ordinary nor sage, and that every thing is entirely true.
How could there be purity or defilement? There is nothing to be attained through artificial cultivation or realization; it does not involve deliberate effort.
Yet those who are deluded are utterly bewildered and lose their way, as if they were deaf and blind. Therefore, teachings were established according to the capacities of beings:

the *ghanṭā* was struck to assemble the multitude, and these were expounded as the Tripiṭaka. They were cultivated as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This continued until the forty-nine years [of the Buddha's ministry], at which point his transformative ritual was complete.

It is finished. In Sanskrit, this is called *ghanṭā*. Generally, it refers to any object made of clay, wood, copper, or iron that produces sound—such as bells, chimes, gongs, drums, mallets, wooden boards, conch shells, or chanting. To this day, monastic communities follow this model in their practice.

By means of these sounds, one awakens those who are drowsy or indolent, solemnizes the religious commands, guides those who are spiritually obstructed, and brings harmony between the divine and the human. As for the Great Samādhi...
It is eternally responsive; its great function is eternally quiescent. Hearing is not hearing, and awareness is not awareness.
When examined and struck, the primal wind is further raised. Without thought and without action, the days of transformation naturally lengthen. How harmonious!
This is the realm of benevolence and longevity, the capital of purity and tranquility.

Among the various types of bells—small, large, and *bao*—the large bell is the primary means for issuing commands within the monastic community. Striking it at dawn shatters the long night and awakens those in slumber;
sounding it at dusk brings awareness to the dark path and dispels the obscurity of ignorance. When raising the mallet, one should do so slowly, allowing the sound to resonate fully.
For the *yùcháng* (desire-increase) [sequence], there are three cycles in total; with eighteen strikes each for both the tight and relaxed tempos, there are one hundred and eight blows in all.
At the beginning and end, there are three slightly tight strikes. This is to be coordinated with the great drum and the signal bell. Whenever the bell is struck, first silently recite the vow-gāthā:
"May this sound of the bell transcend the Dharma-realm, Reaching even the dark recesses of the Iron Ring Mountains; May those who hear it have their sensory dust purified."
To realize perfect penetration. After all sentient beings have completed the recitation of the verses for attaining true enlightenment, one then grasps the mallet.

Having grasped the mallet, one recites: "The great bell is struck for the first time; (for the second and third times, change 'two strikes' and 'three strikes' accordingly). The precious verses are chanted aloud, ascending to the heavens above and penetrating to the underworld below" (strike the first mallet).
Above, we pray for the present Emperor, who governs the universe with great authority. To the civil and military officials...
May the high monks attain their proper rank (two beats). ○ Within the three realms and four modes of birth, may each be exempt from saṃsāra;
amidst the nine states of existence and ten classes of beings, may all be freed from the ocean of suffering (three beats). ○ May there be five winds and ten rains, sparing us the years of famine;

may the southern fields and eastern outskirts alike bask in the sun of Yao and Shun (four beats). ○ May warhorses cease their expeditions; with the advantages of the land and the harmony of man, let the ranks be defeated [in battle].
The wounded and the deceased are all reborn in the Pure Land (Fifth Strike). Birds and beasts do not encounter nets;

wayward sons and orphaned grandsons return early to their ancestral registers (Sixth Strike). In boundless worlds, earth endures and heaven lasts forever; donors near and far increase in merit and longevity (Seventh Strike).
The śramaṇas flourish and the Buddha-dharma rises ever higher; the local spirits and dragon deities settle the monks and protect the Dharma.
(8th beat). ○ Parents, teachers, and elders—benefiting both the living and the deceased; ancestral patriarchs of successive generations—may all ascend to the other shore.
(9th beat). ○ Homage to the Pure Dharma-body Vairocana Buddha. (10th beat). ○ Homage to the Perfect Reward-body Rucika Buddha. (11th beat).
○ Homage to the Thousand, Hundred, and Ten-Thousand Transformation-bodies, our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha.
(Twelve strikes. ○ Homage to the Honored Buddha Maitreya, who will descend to be born in the future.

No Mount Jiuhua. Greatly Compassionate Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva (17 strikes). ○ Namo to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva of Great Compassion at Potalaka Mountain (18 strikes).
○ (Next, recite the eighteen verses of the *Gāndhārī*; one strike per syllable, totaling eighteen strikes. May our imperial domain be eternally firm; may the Emperor’s Way flourish far and wide;
may the Buddha-sun increase in brilliance; may the Wheel of Dharma turn forever. (Thus, the two sequences—*gāndhārī* and slow recitation—comprise a total of one hundred and eight strikes.)

(Alternatively, it may be struck before or after the *bào* bell, according to the established custom of each house. If striking the *yōumíng* bell for the sake of delivering the deceased, the sound must resonate continuously day and night—neither too hurried nor too slow.
One must also recite the Buddha’s name, or the names of Bodhisattvas, or chant sutras and dharanis, striking the bell in coordination with the recitation.

The benefit of this is immense; therefore, the *zhōngtóu* (bell-master) is considered an essential instrument for the wondrous task of delivering sentient beings. Whenever the assembly gathers, each house shall strike [the bell].

Regarding the Dharma procedures: according to their established rules, such as the ancestral memorial services, the Universal Buddha (Pufo) ceremonies, and the Buddhist rites during the precept-retreat period, all require three strikes of the lower gong;
