When accompanying the abbot to the upper hall, it is appropriate to use the large drum, and here too there is no fixed limit on the number of strikes; this is also presided over by the Hall Administrator. For all other Buddhist rites...
Regarding these matters, each house shall follow its own established ritual procedures; however, there must be strict adherence to the rules, and no deviation or disorder is permitted.

As for the *bào zhōng* (announcement bell), this is explained in the aforementioned "Constant Regulations of the Zen Hall. As for the *xiǎo zhōng* (small bell), it is used for occasions such as chanting praises and reciting the Buddha’s name; one must strictly designate the specific timing for its use.
One must not strike the bell irregularly or in a chaotic manner.
The *Zhengyi* (Exegesis on Meaning) states: Regarding the great bell being struck one hundred and eight times at dawn and dusk, this manifests the principle through the phenomenon.

By means of these one hundred and eight instances of ignorance, each stroke awakens the mind; by means of these one hundred and eight samādhis, each blow brings them to completion. The sound must be slow and sustained.
Formerly, Master Zhi borrowed the "Eye of the Way" from Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty to observe the suffering conditions within the hells.
When the Emperor asked how this suffering might be brought to an end, Zhi replied, "Only upon hearing the sound of a bell does that suffering momentarily cease.

The Emperor subsequently issued an edict to all monasteries throughout the realm, ordering that whenever the bell was struck, its sound must be drawn out slowly. Regarding those who recite during the ringing, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "If..."
When striking [the bell], one should pray: "May all the sufferings of the various evil realms be brought to a complete halt.
If one hears the sound of the bell while reciting the Buddha-mantras, one shall be freed from the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over five hundred billion kalpas.

Furthermore, the *Jinling Zhi* (Gazetteer of Jinling) records that there was a commoner who died a violent death and was seen by the authorities of the underworld bound with the five wooden stocks and manacles. They addressed him, saying: "I am the former sovereign of Southern Tang."
He was killed because he was misled by Song Qichu. It was due to these people that more than a thousand surrendered soldiers from Hezhou were executed.
Whenever he heard the bell, his suffering would briefly cease, and he would rely upon it to return and inform the successor to the throne, saying, "Have a bell made for me.

When the people returned, they reported this in detail to the Later Ruler (Emperor Yizong), who consequently had a great bell cast at Qingliang Temple, inscribed with the words: "Dedicated to the late Emperor Liezu Xiaogao Huangdi, to deliver him [from suffering]."

[This] emerged from obscurity to deliver [the author] from distress. Furthermore, the *Record of Venerable Conduct at Yunqi* states: During the Sui dynasty, the monk Zhixing resided at Dazhuangyan Temple and was in charge of the temple bell.

I struck the bell. At first, I made this vow: "May all the sages and worthies together enter the Dharma-hall. Then I struck it three times. Upon striking it long and sustained, I again vowed:

In the bitter cold of midwinter, when the skin cracks and the flesh is chapped, and blood congeals within the palms, one does not shrink from such toil. It is for this reason that [one is able to...]

As for the *ban* (board), there are distinctions between inner and outer, as well as between iron and wood. The *baozhong* (awakening bell) is struck at the base of the board. (The methods of striking vary according to the specific regulations of each monastery. [This applies to] Chan.

There are small wooden boards both inside and outside the hall. The one outside the hall is called the *bào-bǎn* (announcement board); it is struck when entering the hall. (When the *heshang* enters the hall, he strikes the board once.)

When the honored guests enter the hall, strike the board twice. When the Hall Master enters the hall, strike the board three times (the procedure for striking is modified accordingly). Within the hall, the board used when standing in incense order is called the *zhàn-bǎn* (standing board);
the board used during the incense offering is called the *cuī-bǎn* (urging board). The method of striking these is seen in the "Constant Regulations of the Zen Hall" and the "Hall Rules.

Chapter on the Two Orders. Regarding the duties of the Night Patrol: The kitchen possesses a large board made of cast iron, called the "calling board" (*kō-han*).

The wooden fish (*muyu*) and the round wooden fish (*yuanyumuyu*) are used for chanting and recitation. Tradition holds that fish remain awake day and night; thus, wood was carved in their likeness.
One strikes them during recitation to alert those who are drowsy or indolent, and to harmonize the voices of the assembly. The long fish is the *bang*; it is suspended in the refectory.

The Hall bell: it is struck in the kitchen for the two daily meals and the evening service; it is struck three times when summoning the community for work outside (the Guest Hall Master presides over this).

each may modify the striking according to their own convenience.

*Kaṇṭhī* (犍椎), *kaṇṭhī*: a term from the Sanskrit language. According to the treatises on phonology (*śabdavidyā*), it is translated as "gong" (*qing*) or sometimes as "bell" (*zhong*). The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"When Ānanda ascends to the lecture hall and strikes the *kaṇṭhī*, this is the drum of faith of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, all the Vinayas and Śāstras likewise [state this].
It is called a *gandi* (or *gandī*; the character for "hammer" is pronounced *di*). In the *Jie-mo shu* (Commentary on the Karma), it is simply referred to as *gandi*.
Thus, the *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya) states: "Whatever makes a sound—whether made of tile, wood, copper, or iron—is all termed *gandi*.
Judging from this, anything that produces a sound to assemble the community qualifies. As for striking the chime (*qing*) before ascending the hall to preach the Dharma, it is called...

The mallet is raised (the *baizhui* is announced). [The announcement says: "In this Dharma assembly, you, the dragons and elephants, should contemplate the primary truth. For all ritual services (*buddhakārya*), each house should follow its own established method of striking, maintaining a constant standard so that the measure is never lost.

The Commentary on the Meaning states: In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa dreamed one night of a golden drum, its form magnificent and vast.

Its radiance shines universally, surpassing the light of the sun. Within that light, one beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions beneath various jeweled trees, seated upon lapis lazuli thrones and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of attendants as they preach the Dharma.

Sāha. Having awakened from his dream, he went to where the Buddha was and spoke at length to the Tathāgata concerning the golden drum he had seen in his dream, as well as the verses of repentance.

...and so forth. It is evident that from the beginning, the Buddha’s work has always been carried out through sound.

The Commentary on the Meaning says: Why do the monastic communities of the "forests" refer to themselves as being from the "ten directions"?

It is because their household registers (*huànjì*) differ, and they rely upon [their respective locations] according to conditions. There are cases where names on the registers are identical but the locations are distinct;
for example, there are two places named Taiping Prefecture: one in Huizhou and one in Guangxi. Furthermore, there is a Taiping State in Guangxi, and a Suifu in Sichuan.
There is certainly a Taiping Prefecture (廳). Furthermore, there are Taiping Counties in Ningguo, Jiangnan, and Taitai, Zhejiang;
thus, there are six locations with the name "Taiping. Among these, Baoding, Ninghai, Xin'an, Lin'an, and others all share the same name yet exist in multiple places.

Since there are cases where the names differ but the locations are the same, there are also instances where the locations differ while the names are identical. These are recorded in the registers accordingly.
Errors in the *Guān* and discrepancies in biographical records stem from this; how can one not exercise meticulous care?
Accordingly, I have compiled a general index of geographical locations here, annotating their names in detail so that those who consult them may verify them for practical use.
This is merely one means of resolving doubts.
